IOANNES Abbas monasterii Sancti Martini episcopi in Spanhem, ordinis Divi Patris Benedicti; Moguntinae dioecesis, natione Teutonicus, patria Mosellanus, ex villa Tritenen Treverensis dioecesis oriundus. Quamvis non sim dignus, quod nomen meum cum scriptoribus ecclesiasticis poneretur propter ingenii paupertatem; tamen amicis urgentibus compulsa sum in fine huius Catalogi, mearum quoque lucubrationum titulos, et exordia ponere; exemplo divorum patrum Hieronymi, Gennadii, Honorii praesbyteri Augustudunensis, et Sigeberti monachi Gemblacensis; qui se quoque in fine suorum tractatum de his ipsis rebus aeditorum posuerunt. Life of Abbot Johannes Trithemius, written by himself in the Book of Ecclesiastical Writers.

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin the bishop at Sponheim, of the order of the divine Father Benedict, of the diocese of Mainz, a German by nation, a Mosellan by homeland, born in the village of Trittenheim in the diocese of Trier. Although I am not worthy for my name to be placed among ecclesiastical writers, because of the poverty of my talent, nevertheless, urged by friends, I was compelled to place at the end of this catalogue the titles and beginnings of my own writings as well, following the example of the divine fathers Jerome, Gennadius, Honorius the priest of Autun, and Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, who also placed themselves at the end of their treatises published on these same matters. Therefore, besides this work, I have also written the following. And first, by command of the presidents of the general chapter, I abridged:

The Statutes of the same Chapter, one book: “Since they wish.” On the Visitation of Monks, one book: “Your brothers.” On the Manner of Observing the Chapter, one book: “Since in heaven.” On the Rule of Saint Benedict, two books: “Come, children, listen.” An Exhortation to Monks, two books: “Of Christ’s warfare.” On Temptations, two books: “The human race.” On the Life of Priests, one book: “You ask of me.” On the Vice of Possessiveness, one book: “All who come to life.” On the Misery of This Life, one book: “Since there is nothing.” On the Ruin of Our Order, one book: “Since of the order.” On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, four books: “As I was considering.” Praises of the Order of the Carmelites, two books: “By prayers and entreaties.” On the Praise of Scribes, one book: “To the venerable father.” On the Lights of Germany, one book: “Since there are.” Letters to Various Persons, one book: “You ask that copies.” On Saint Anne, one book. Various Sermons, one book.

As for conferences, whether delivered in general chapters, in observantial chapters, or elsewhere, they are without fixed number; some are extant, and some have been taken away. These, then, apart from those which still lie unfinished in my hands, are the works I recall having written up to the present: in the thirty-fourth year of my age, the tenth of my assuming the office of abbot, and the twelfth of my conversion, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, and the Supreme Pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which I have now for the third time corrected, enlarged, and completed the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, having labored on it for nearly seven years: 1493, in the twelfth indiction.

Letter

Johannes Trithemius, called abbot of Sponheim, to the Reverend Father and his preceptor, Lord Johannes de Colenhausen, abbot of the Monastery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs, in Seligenstadt, formerly abbot of Sponheim, my predecessor: reverence and honor.

4
Nescio, praecessor mihi semper venerande, sub quo sydere infortunato monasterium istud Spanheimense constet extructum, quod Abbas in eo moritur rarus, sed omnes pene taedio affecti, iam ferme ab annis septuaginta, sicut ex annalibus reperi, spontanea voluntate cesseruunt. Tu etiam praecedentium exemplo, nos pauperes ante tempus quare deserueris, non penitus ignoramus, qui nostram, et inopiam accusamus merito, et rebellem quorundam temeritatem. Experior iam nunc, prob dolor, causam, quae trum impulit animum, ut Spanheimensem dimiteres Abbatiam, sterillem penilus, et infructuosam, in qua tredecim a reformatione praesedisti annis, non sine animi solicitudine continua, et laboribus infinitis. Transeo, quas pertuleris fratrum iniurias plurimorum, quae quidem super me quotidiom omnia duplicantur. Librum Exhortationum mearum ad fratres, quem nuper inter furentes mundialium rerum occupationes lucubravi, ut Paternitati tuae transmitterem, praecepisti: qui etsi tua sit lectione indignus, nolui tamem obsistere iussioni parentis. Unde precor mansuetudinem tuam, limam correctionis dignanter adhibeas: et, si quae desunt, adiicias: superflua rescindas: ineptaque, vel tradas ignibus, vel certe componas. Vale dulcissime Pater, memor nostri. Ex Spanhem, sexta die mensis Augusti, Anno Christianorum MCCCCLXXXVI. OVH. Pia 1605 n. 409 SERMONES ET EXHORTATIONES AD MONACHOS IOANNIS TRITEMII ABBATIS SPANHEIMENSIS, POSTEA HERBIPOLENSIS: QUORUM SERMONUM DUO SUNT LIBRI: PRIMUS VOCATUR HOMILIARUM, SECUNDUS SERMONUM. IN NOME DOMINI NOSTRI IESU CHRISTI, INCIPIT LIBER PRIMUS EXHORTATIONUM AD MONACHOS. De militia spirituali Monachorum. Homilia I. MILITIAE Christianae convenit frates, et praecipue Monachorum, variis mundi huius subiacere calamitatibus, et sicut aurum in forna, continuis exerciti, atque probari tribulationibus. Monachorum est enim militiae Christianorum communem normam altiore modo vivendi transcendere, et non solum praeciptis dominicis, sed etiam consiliis obedere. Monachorum est divitias, honores, et omnes praesentis mundi voluptates pro Dei amore penitus contemnere, et superatis carnalibus desideriis, soli Deo ingiter vacare. Monachus namque quasi solitarius ab unitate dicitur, qui etiam ipso nominis sui vocabulo ad contemptum seculi moneatur. Monachi proinde officium est secum in solitudine mundum, et purificatum a vitiis consistere, et Christum super omnia dulciter amare. Scopus enim Monachorum, ad quem regularis institutio dirigitur, Christus est, quem imitari quisquis recusat, nec Monachus quidem, nec christianus est. Unde fratres mei scire debemus, quoniam quisquis Dominum, et Salvatorem nostrum in vera patientia, et humilitate non sequitur, nihil ei prodest ad salutem, quod christianus, vel Monachus nuncupatur. Ipse namque est, qui in sacro Evangelio dicit: Non omnis, qui dicit mihi Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum coelorum, sed qui facit voluntatem Patris mei, qui in coelis est, ipse intrabit in regnum coelorum. Quae autem sit Dei voluntas, sanctus Apostolus aperuit, dicens: Haec est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra. Sed cum huius praeciptae nobis sanctificationis necessaria consummatio magnam requirat in omnibus tolerantiam malorum, et humilitatem, quoniam nemo sanctus viribus suis: oportet nos fratres mei continuam vocationis nostrae penes nosmetipsos habere considera 6 De militia spirituali Monachorum.

I do not know, my ever-venerable predecessor, under what unlucky star this monastery of Sponheim was built, since an abbot rarely dies in it, but almost all, overcome by weariness, for nearly seventy years now, as I find from the annals, have resigned of their own accord. Nor are we wholly ignorant why you too, following the example of those before you, abandoned us poor men before the time: we rightly blame both our poverty and the rebellious rashness of certain men. I now experience, alas, the reason that moved your mind to leave the abbacy of Sponheim, utterly barren and unfruitful, over which you presided for thirteen years after the reform, not without continual anxiety of spirit and endless labors. I pass over the wrongs you endured from very many of the brothers, all of which are indeed now doubled against me every day.

You instructed me to send to your Paternity the book of my Exhortations to the brothers, which I recently composed by night amid the raging occupations of worldly affairs. Although it is unworthy of your reading, I nevertheless did not wish to resist a father’s command. Therefore I beg your gentleness kindly to apply the file of correction: and, if anything is lacking, add it; cut away what is superfluous; and what is unsuitable either consign to the flames or at least put in order. Farewell, sweetest Father, remembering us. From Sponheim, on the sixth day of the month of August, in the year of the Christians 1486.

Sermons and Exhortations to Monks by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, afterward of Würzburg; of these sermons there are two books: the first is called the Book of Homilies, the second the Book of Sermons.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the first book of Exhortations to Monks.

On the Spiritual Warfare of Monks. Homily I.

It belongs to Christian warfare, brothers, and especially to that of monks, to be subject to the various calamities of this world, and, like gold in the furnace, to be exercised and tested by continual tribulations. For it belongs to monks, in the warfare of Christians, to surpass the common rule by a higher manner of living, and to obey not only the Lord’s commandments but also his counsels. It belongs to monks to despise utterly riches, honors, and all the pleasures of the present world for the love of God, and, having overcome carnal desires, to be continually free for God alone. For a monk is so called as one solitary, from oneness; and by the very word of his name he is admonished to contempt of the world. Accordingly the office of a monk is to remain with himself in solitude, clean and purified from vices, and sweetly to love Christ above all things.

For the goal of monks, toward which the regular institution is directed, is Christ; whoever refuses to imitate him is neither a monk nor even a Christian. Hence, my brothers, we must know that whoever does not follow our Lord and Savior in true patience and humility gains nothing for salvation from being called a Christian or a monk. For he himself says in the holy Gospel: Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he shall enter the kingdom of heaven. And what the will of God is, the holy Apostle disclosed, saying: This is the will of God, your sanctification. But since the necessary completion of this sanctification commanded to us requires great endurance of evils in all things, and humility, because no one is holy by his own strength, we must, my brothers, keep continual consideration of our calling within ourselves.

5
1. Pet. 5. tionem: ut nunquam ocio torpentes perniciosissimo, in agone militari ab hoste vincamur, qui tanquam leo rugiens circuit quaerens incautum, et languescentem animo, quem devoret pereuntem. Milites enim sumus Dei contra adversarium triplicem pugnantes, carnem videlicet, mundum, et diabolum. Anceps bellum, et nimis durum certamen, illum pati hostem, quem natura dedit familiarem. Armemus nos igitur fratres charissimi ornamentis virtutum: quoniam non facile ab adversario vincitur, quisquis bonorum operum splendore decoratur. In primis mu- niamus nos fide constantissima Sanctae, ac Individuae Trinitatis: cuius devota, et sincera mentis, et oris confessio, cunctas daemonum iniquas machinationes, et fraudes procul eliminat, et maximum hostem devin- cens prostrernit, ac penitus enervat. Arripiamus deinde nobis ferventis- simam Dei, et proximi charitatem, quae daemonibus super omnia est formidabilis, maxime si in vera humilitate christiana fuerit radicata. Non demus animae nostrae confidentiam, quoniam beatus dicitur, qui semper est pavidus: qui autem mentis est durae, corruet in malum. Ducem nostrum sequamur Christum, qui in Evangelio dixit: Ego sum via, veritas, et vita, quia nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Nunc ergo fratres attendite his, quae in sanctis scripturis de Salvatore nostro leguntur, quoniam qui dicit se in Christo, hoc est via veritatis manere, studeat sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambulare. Oportuit autem illum primum pati opprobrium crucis, et sic intrare in gloriam suam, quo moneremur, et nos milites eius quamvis indigni, quoniam oportet nos per multas tribulationes intrare in regnum Dei. Idcirco Dominus ipse Rex universorum nos admonuit in Evangelio, dicens: Qui vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam quotidie, et sequatur me. Ecce Christus via nobis ad vitam aeternam proponit, qui cum esset Dominus caelestium, et mundanorum, pro nobis exinanivit semetipsum formiam servi accipiens, in qua voluntarie, non coactus, infirma nostra portavit, factus Patri obediens usque ad mor- tem: mortem autem crucis. Itaque si Dominum totius universitatis primum oportuit pati, fieri certe non potest, quin et nos imitato- res eius iniquos, et vilissimos peccatores oporteat multa pati, qui totum, quod patimur, nostro merito iuste sustinemus. Nemo enim venit ad glo- riam supernae civitatis, nisi fuerit hic primus iustificatus a peccato, sed cum multae sint tribulationes iustorum, nequaquam iustus esse poterit, qui adversa sustinere pro iustitia in hoc mundo recusavit. Imitemur ergo fratres mei charissimi, in multa patientia, et humilitate Dominum, et Salvatorem nostrum Iesum Christum, qui homo factus pro nobis maxima voluntarie sustinuit, et in hoc mundo nunquam sine amaritudine per- secutionis fuit. Ab hora enim sacratissimae nativitatis suae usque ad exitum spiritus sui de corpore, semper in amaritudine praesentis vitae

lest, growing sluggish in most destructive idleness, we be conquered in military combat by the enemy, who, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking the unwary and faint-hearted man whom he may devour as he perishes.

For we are soldiers of God, fighting against a threefold adversary: namely, the flesh, the world, and the devil. It is a doubtful war and an exceedingly hard contest to suffer as an enemy one whom nature has given as a familiar companion. Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let us arm ourselves with the adornments of virtues, since whoever is adorned with the splendor of good works is not easily conquered by the adversary.

First, let us fortify ourselves with the most steadfast faith of the Holy and Undivided Trinity; the devout and sincere confession of it in mind and mouth drives far away all the wicked schemes and deceits of demons, and, overcoming the greatest enemy, casts him down and utterly weakens him. Then let us take up for ourselves the most fervent love of God and of neighbor, which is more fearful to demons than all else, especially if it has been rooted in true Christian humility.

Let us not give confidence to our soul, since blessed is said to be the man who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil. Let us follow Christ our leader, who said in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life, for no one comes to the Father except through me.”

Now therefore, brothers, attend to these things which are read in the holy Scriptures concerning our Savior, since he who says that he remains in Christ, that is, in the way of truth, should strive to walk just as he walked. But it was necessary for him first to suffer the reproach of the cross and so to enter into his glory, so that we too, his soldiers, however unworthy, might be warned that we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations. Therefore the Lord himself, King of all things, admonished us in the Gospel, saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”

Behold, Christ sets before us the way to eternal life: though he was Lord of heavenly and earthly things, for our sake he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; in that form, willingly and not under compulsion, he bore our weaknesses, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death, death on a cross. And so, if it was necessary for the Lord of the whole universe first to suffer, it certainly cannot be that we, his imitators, wicked and most vile sinners, should not have to suffer many things, we who justly endure, by our own desert, everything that we suffer.

For no one comes to the glory of the heavenly city unless he has first been justified here from sin; but since the tribulations of the just are many, a man will by no means be able to be just if he has refused to endure adversities for justice in this world. Therefore, my dearly beloved brothers, let us imitate in great patience and humility our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who, having become man for us, willingly endured the greatest things, and in this world was never without the bitterness of persecution. For from the hour of his most sacred birth until the departure of his spirit from his body, he was always in the bitterness of the present life.

6
Homilia I. 7 pro nobis patientissimus extitit, et futurae passionis amaritudo praecognita nunquam ab eius praescientia recessit. Cum enim Deus esset omnipotens, homo factus pro nobis, omnia novit, omnia scivit, omnia praevidit, nec eum quicquam eorum, quae passurus erat, latere potuit, qui, ut pateretur in mundo, passibilis factus, Deus quod erat, impassibilis permansit. Natus autem de Virgine Maria sine virili commercio, ut legem consummaret, octavo mox die circumciditur, et qui nullum habuit peccatum, pro nostris reatibus vulneratur. A facie persequentis noctu puer in Aegyptum ducitur, et qui dominus erat omnium, pauper, et egens in medio gentium incognitus septennio exulat. Denique cunctis vitae suae diebus in hoc mundo labores continuos patientissime sustinuit, et nulla unquam subire adversa pro gloria Patris recusavit. Omnia namque dura, et aspera voluntarie iustus, et innocens pro nobis in dignissimis passus est, morte nos amarissima crucis de interitu perpetuae damnationis redemit, et in proprio sanguine nos Patri misericorditer reconciliavit. Christo igitur passo pro nobis in carne, sicut Princeps Apostolorum praemonuit, eadem cogitatione fratres mei armemur: ut ea, quae pro nobis ille sustinuit, nos compatientes innocentis, ad memoriam sedulo revocemus. Nam si compatimur, et conregnabimus gloriose triumphantis. Ecce Christus nos vocat, quo praecessit ad gloriam, arma dat, quibus ipse prius mundi principem superavit, praescripsit formam, qua miles regem sequi debet ad coronam. Ad coeli palatium Christus milites suis vocat, quos comitantibus donis virtutum praessurae deducunt, praemique victores suscipiunt perpetuo regnatos. Unde militiam nostram fratres charissimi semper studiosissime prosequentes, bellum vitiiis, et concupiscentiis iugiter indicamus: ut quemadmodum caro militat adversus spiritum, ita nos pugnemus assidue vigilantes in oratione, et ieiunio contra incentorem vitiorum. Quamdiu enim vivimus in hoc mundo, peregrinamur a Domino, et quasi athletae certamus in stadio, necessarium vitae cursum in agone continuo peragentes. Pugnamus autem non viribus nostris, sed regis nostri miseratione suffulti, qui suis imitatoribus in sancto Evangelio dixit: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Et ne pugnam militiae nobis propositam, ut impossibilem refugeremus, alibi dixit: In mundo pressuram habebitis: sed confidete, ego vici mundum. Et ut sciremus Dominum Iesum servulis suis in hoc mundo semper esse praesentem, ita nobis in Apostolis pollicetur: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi. Hac securitatis accepta pollicitatione O milites Christi fratres mei charissimi, cur haesitamus? quare non fortiter stamus adversum omnes huius insolentias mundi? Regem, et protectorem nostrum pugnantibus nobis semper habemus praesentem, et dimicare contra infirmum hostem, qui nemo superat nisi volentem, miseri formidamus? Accingite, vos precor, ad. De militia spirituali Monachorum.

He proved most patient for us, and the bitterness of his future passion, foreknown by him, never departed from his foreknowledge. For although he was almighty God, having become man for us, he knew all things, understood all things, foresaw all things; nor could anything of what he was to suffer be hidden from him, who, in order to suffer in the world, was made capable of suffering, while remaining impassible as the God he was.

Born of the Virgin Mary without intercourse with a man, in order to fulfill the law, he was circumcised on the eighth day; and he who had no sin was wounded for our offenses. At night, before the face of his persecutor, the child was led into Egypt; and he who was Lord of all, poor and needy, lived unknown in exile among the nations for seven years. Finally, throughout all the days of his life in this world he endured continual labors with the greatest patience, and never refused to undergo any adversity for the glory of the Father. For the just and innocent one voluntarily suffered all hard and bitter things for us in the most unworthy ways; by the most bitter death of the cross he redeemed us from the ruin of eternal damnation, and in his own blood mercifully reconciled us to the Father.

Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, as the Prince of the Apostles forewarned, let us, my brothers, arm ourselves with the same thought: so that, sharing in compassion for the innocent one, we may diligently recall to memory the things he endured for us. For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him as he triumphs in glory.

Behold, Christ calls us to the glory to which he has gone before; he gives us the weapons with which he himself first overcame the prince of this world; he has prescribed the pattern by which a soldier must follow his king to the crown. Christ calls his soldiers to the palace of heaven, whom hardships lead onward with the gifts of virtues accompanying them, and rewards receive as victors to reign forever [unclear].

Therefore, dearest brothers, as we always pursue our warfare with the greatest zeal, let us continually declare war on vices and desires, so that, just as the flesh fights against the spirit, so we may fight in return, ever watchful in prayer and fasting against the inciter of vices. For as long as we live in this world, we are pilgrims away from the Lord, and like athletes we contend in the stadium, carrying out the necessary course of life in continual struggle.

But we fight not by our own strength, but upheld by the mercy of our King, who said to his imitators in the holy Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing.” And lest we flee the battle of the warfare set before us as impossible, he said elsewhere: “In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage: I have overcome the world.” And so that we might know that the Lord Jesus is always present with his little servants in this world, he promises us thus in the Apostles: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age.”

Having received this promise of security, O soldiers of Christ, my dearest brothers, why do we hesitate? Why do we not stand bravely against all the insolence of this world? We always have our King and protector present while we fight; and do we wretchedly fear to struggle against a weak enemy, who overcomes no one unless he is willing? Gird yourselves, I beg you, for [unclear].

On the spiritual warfare of monks.

7
runt nomina Imperatori Christo. insuperabilem militiam Christi, quam estis duplici conditione professi, altera quando in fonte sacri baptismatis abrenunciantes Satanae, in verba christianae institutionis iurastis: altera vero quando hoc indumentum monasticae religionis solemniter induistis. Magna vos proficendi necessitas constringit, si professionem vestram debita consideratione pensetis, quoniam ut mandata servare debeatis Evangelica, ratio nominis christiani praecipit: et, ut monasticae institutionis praecerta custodiatis, votum, quod emisistis voluntarie, requirit. Non vobis iam sufficit ad salutem, ea completere praecerta, quae christianis in communi proponuntur servanda, nisi etiam diligentissime custodiatis instituta, quae promisistis, monastica. Vovete, inquit scriptura, et reddite. Iterumque alia scriptura dicit: Si quid vovisti Deo, ne moreris reddere, disiplcit enim ei infidelis, et stulta promissio, multoque melius est non vovere, quam post vatum promissa non reddere. Et sanctus Augustinus, quam sit necessarium Deo reddere promissa, nos admonet dicens: Sunt quaedam, quae etiam non voventes Domino debemus, et sunt quaedam, quae nisi voverimus, non debemus. Sed postquam ea Domino promittimus, necessario reddere constringimur. At nunc fratres mei quid voveritis Domino Deo vestro, solerter quaeo perpendite, et sub qua necessitate redditionis promissorum sitis constituti, sedulo pensate. Vovistis enim Deo vestro, non homini, obedientiam, et conversionem morum vetrorum secundum regulam sanctissimi legislatoris nostri Benedicti, et perpetuam in hoc religionis ordine stabilitatem: Obedientiam vero, quam Deo promisistis, eius vicario homini debetis, quem vices Christi gerere in monasterio ex regula, quam profitemini didicistis. Conversio morum qualis debat esse secundum regulam, in capite quarto de instrumentis bonorum operum praenotato plane conspicit, in quo totius perfectionis monasticae summiam paucis comprehensam invenitis. Enimvero quod faciendum circa novitos divus pater noster praecipit, omnes audivistis, et in unoquoque vestrum factum in exordio professionis sua non ignoratis. Sic enim dicit: Suscipiendus autem in oratorio coram omnibus promittat de stabilitate sua, et conversione morum suorum, et obedientia, coram Deo, et sanctis eius, ut si aliquando altere fecerit, a Deo se damnandum sciat, quem irridet. Considerate nunc itaque fratres sub qua sitis necessitate constituti observantiae regularis: quoniam nisi opere compleveritis, quod in susceptione monastici habitus promisistis, non servi Dei, non amici, non monachi, sed irrisores coram omnipotenti Domino eritis iudicandi. Semper ergo memores estote eorum, quae vobis regula praecipit, secundum quam instituere mores vestros promisistis, et laborate, sicuti veri milites Iesu Christi, assidue in timore Domini vigilantes, quoniam sicut dicit scriptura, nisi vos constanter tenueritis in timore Domini, cito subvertetur domus vestra. Monachi foedifragi non Monachi, sed irrisores.

[unclear] their names to Christ the Emperor.

You have professed the unconquerable warfare of Christ under a twofold condition: the one when, at the font of holy baptism, renouncing Satan, you swore to the words of Christian instruction; the other when you solemnly put on this garment of monastic religion. A great necessity of making progress binds you, if you weigh your profession with due consideration, since the meaning of the Christian name commands that you must keep the Gospel precepts, and the vow that you voluntarily made requires that you preserve the appointed rules of monastic discipline.

It is no longer enough for your salvation to fulfill those appointed things which are set before Christians in common to be observed, unless you also most diligently keep the monastic institutions which you promised. “Vow,” says Scripture, “and pay.” And again another Scripture says: “If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him, and it is much better not to vow than, after vows have been promised, not to pay.” And Saint Augustine admonishes us how necessary it is to pay to God what has been promised, saying: “There are certain things which, even without vowing them, we owe to the Lord, and there are certain things which, unless we have vowed them, we do not owe. But after we promise them to the Lord, we are necessarily constrained to pay them.”

And now, my brothers, carefully consider what you have vowed to the Lord your God, and diligently weigh under what necessity of paying what you promised you have been placed. For you vowed to your God, not to man, obedience, and conversion of your way of life according to the Rule of our most holy lawgiver Benedict, and perpetual stability in this order of religion. But the obedience which you promised to God you owe to his vicar, a man, whom you have learned from the Rule you profess to hold the place of Christ in the monastery.

What the conversion of your way of life ought to be according to the Rule is plainly seen in the fourth chapter, marked “On the Instruments of Good Works,” in which you find the sum of all monastic perfection briefly comprehended. Indeed, what our blessed father commands to be done concerning novices you have all heard, and you know that it was done in the beginning of the profession of each one of you. For he says: “The one to be received shall promise in the oratory, before all, concerning his stability, the conversion of his way of life, and obedience, before God and his saints, so that if he should ever act otherwise, he may know that he will be condemned by God, whom he mocks.”

Consider now, therefore, brothers, under what necessity of regular observance you have been placed, since unless you complete in deed what you promised when you received the monastic habit, you will be judged before the almighty Lord not as servants of God, not as friends, not as monks, but as mockers. Therefore always remember those things which the Rule commands you, according to which you promised to shape your ways, and labor like true soldiers of Jesus Christ, always keeping watch in the fear of the Lord, since, as Scripture says, unless you hold yourselves steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown.

Monks who break their covenant are not monks, but mockers.

8
Homilia I. 9 Attendite vocationem vestram, quia non ad ocium, non ad huius mundi voluptates, neque ad carnis prosequendum desideria: sed potius ad la- borem continuum, ad omnium deliciarum abstinentiam, et iugem carnis macerationem sub imagine crucifixi, ut portetis in cordibus vestris eius stigmata, Dominus vos vocavit. Misistis iam certe manus vestras ad aratum sanctae agriculturae coelestis, in qua vobis praecipitur continuo desudare labore, et non solum retro nunquam respicere, sed proficiendo semper de virtute in virtutem ad supremae culmen perfectionis anhe- lare. Nihil enim aliud est monachum vivere, quam hominum declinare consortium, in solitudine soli Deo per amoris ferventissimi desiderium actualiter placere. Hinc scriptura dicit: Bonum est viro, cum portaverit iugum Domini ab adolescentia sua, sedebit solitarius, et tacebit, quia levabit se supra se. Unde si vultis esse perfecti vos, qui perfectionem ex regulari instituto tenemini amare, a conversatione, quam Christus docuit, incipite, et qui iam pro eius amore contemnitis omnia, etiam vosmetipsos vincere, superare, et contemnere humiliter non negligatis. Servus autem Christi nihil habet praeter Christum, nihil amat, nihil curat, nihil quaerit nisi Christum, ut possit esse perfectus, et ei pla- cere, cuius militiam voluntarie est professus. Monachus autem, qui ali- quid habet praeter Christum, non potest esse perfectus, quoniam verus amor non dividitur, nec diversis, atque contrariis mens veraciter unitur. Propterea Dominus dicit: Si vis perfectus esse, vade, et vende omnia, quae habes, et da pauperibus, et veniens, sequere me. Vos quidem amantissimi fratres iam, ut confido, reliquistis mundum, et quicquid habuistis in mundo, nec solum res mundi omnes, quas possedistis, et habere potuissetis: sed etiam desiderium omne depo- suistis habendi, venistisque ad hoc divi praesulis Martini coenobium, in quo rerum temporalium paupertas est magna, et hoc solum est nobis divitiarum loco donatum, avaritiae causas non invenire. Ver- rum sicut poena martyrem non facit, sed causa, sic inopia beatum non efficit pauperem, sed voluntaria pro Christi amore in ipsa pau- pertate patientia. Non enim quoslibet Dominus in Evangelio pauperes praedicavit beatos, atque regno donandos coelorum: sed pauperes spi- ritu praenuntiavit esse, ut noster, dumtaxat beatos. Contemptus nam- que divitiarum non sufficit ad salutem, nisi renunciator auri studeat etiam totis viribus per patientiam, et humilitatem constanter imitari salvatorem. Facilius est enim contemnere mundum, quam spernere, et abnegare semetipsum. Attamen quicumque vult imitari Filium Dei, et perfectionem consequi Evangelicam, oportet, non solum mundi, et rerum temporalium, sed sui quoque ipsius, fieri contemptorem. Dicit namque Salvator in sancto Evangelio: Nisi quis renunciaverit omnibus, quae possidet, non potest meus esse discipulus. Et ne putaremus hoc De profectu militiae spiritualis. sufficere ad perfectionem: iterum de proprio contemptu protestatur apertius dicens: Si quis vult me sequi, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam, et sequatur me. Qui enim voluerit animam suam salvam facere, perdet eam: qui autem perdiderit animam suam propter me, et Evangelium, salvam faciet eam. Christus factus est obedientis Patri usque ad mortem, quem, si ut promisistis, imitari volueritis, necessarium est fratres, ut vosmetipsos vobis abnegetis. Monachus enim esse non po- terit qui suae voluntati propriae non in toto prius renunciavit. Vos qui coram Deo, et sanctis eius omnibus promisistis secundum regulam monasticam vivere, propriam voluntatem non licet vobis deinceps usur- pare, quoniam quod semel est Deo consecratum, in humanos usus non est amplius revocandum. Non enim vobismetipsis, sed Christo regi militatis, unde neque velle, neque nolle in potestate vestra retinetis. Mortui nanque estis, ut sacer Christophilus inquit, et vita vestra ab- sccondita est cum Christo in Deo: cum autem Christus apparuerit vita vestra, tunc, et vos apparebitis cum ipso in gloria: cum quo si gaudere sine fine cupitis, oportet, ut nunc in tempore hoc pro eius amore stre- nue militetis. Nemo enim coronabitur cum Christo, nisi qui legitime certando perseveraverit usque in finem, cum non possit vincere, qui nescit perseverare. De profectu militiae spiritualis. Homilia II.

Homily I.

Consider your calling: the Lord has called you not to idleness, not to the pleasures of this world, nor to the pursuit of the desires of the flesh, but rather to continual labor, to abstinence from all delights, and to the constant mortification of the flesh under the image of the Crucified, so that you may bear his wounds in your hearts. Surely you have now put your hands to the plough of the holy heavenly husbandry, in which you are commanded to sweat continually in labor, and not only never to look back, but, by advancing always from virtue to virtue, to strive toward the summit of highest perfection.

For to live as a monk is nothing other than to withdraw from the company of men and, in solitude, actively to please God alone through the desire of most fervent love. Hence Scripture says: It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth; he shall sit alone and be silent, because he shall lift himself above himself. Therefore, if you wish to be perfect, you who by your regular institution are bound to love perfection, begin from the way of life that Christ taught; and since you already despise all things for love of him, do not neglect humbly to conquer, overcome, and despise even your very selves.

The servant of Christ has nothing except Christ, loves nothing, cares for nothing, seeks nothing except Christ, so that he may be perfect and please him whose service as a soldier he has voluntarily professed. But the monk who has anything besides Christ cannot be perfect, because true love is not divided, nor is the mind truly united to things diverse and contrary. Therefore the Lord says: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me.

You, my most beloved brothers, have already, as I trust, left the world and whatever you had in the world; and not only all the things of the world that you possessed and could have possessed, but you have also laid aside every desire of having. You have come to this monastery of the holy bishop Martin, in which the poverty of temporal goods is great, and this alone has been given to us in place of riches: not to find occasions for avarice.

Yet just as punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause does, so want does not make a blessed poor man, but voluntary patience in that very poverty for the love of Christ. For in the Gospel the Lord did not proclaim all poor people blessed and destined to receive the kingdom of heaven, but he foretold that the poor in spirit are blessed. For contempt of riches is not enough for salvation unless the one who renounces gold also strives with all his strength, through patience and humility, constantly to imitate the Savior.

For it is easier to despise the world than to scorn and deny oneself. Yet whoever wishes to imitate the Son of God and attain evangelical perfection must become a despiser not only of the world and temporal things, but also of his own self. For the Savior says in the holy Gospel: Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple. And lest we should think this sufficient for perfection, he again bears witness more openly concerning contempt of oneself, saying: If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake and for the Gospel will save it.

Christ became obedient to the Father even unto death. If, as you have promised, you wish to imitate him, brothers, it is necessary that you deny yourselves to yourselves. For no one will be able to be a monk who has not first renounced his own will entirely. You who before God and all his saints have promised to live according to the monastic rule may no longer claim your own will for yourselves, because what has once been consecrated to God must no longer be recalled to human uses.

For you serve as soldiers not for yourselves but for Christ the King; hence you do not retain in your own power either to will or not to will. For you are dead, as the holy Christophilus says, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. If you desire to rejoice with him without end, you must now, in this present time, fight bravely for love of him. For no one will be crowned with Christ unless he has persevered to the end, striving lawfully, since he cannot conquer who does not know how to persevere.

9
Q uotiescunque fratres charissimi ad memoriam illius recordatio mo- menti venerit, quando reclamantem, et renitentem me vobis indi- gnum constituitis abbatem, toties amaritudine cordis mei totus in meme- tipso concutior, et lachrymas etiam invitus, et nolens fundere compellor. Novi enim, quod meritis meis non sum vobis praelatus: si autem vestris id factum sit, nescio: concedat omnipotens Deus, ut demeritis non sit facta vel meis, vestrisve haec ipsa de me ordinatio. Cur ita voluistis fratres? juvenem me indoctum, et nequaquam idoneum ad militiam, quam profitemur, erexitis in ducem, ut mihi, docere simul, et discere omnino iam sit necessarium, quando nec vitae perfectio commendat doctrinam, nec aetatis consideratio necessariam pastori adhuc consequi- tur auctoritatem. In isto iam triennio satis experior, quantis sum miseriis involutus, dum omnium vestrum portare infirmitates solus ipse com- pellor, et a nemine infoelix ego supportor. Quis me liberaverit de mundi huius vanitatibus, in quas revocatus sum, qui, ut omnem prae- sentis vitae curam, et solicitudinem subterfugerem, monasterium intravi? Quoniau quidemvero necesse est onus portare humeris meis impositum, vos precor fratres, sedulo manus adiutrices mihi orationum vestrarum porrigite, quatenus in medio vestrum Domino largiente ita conversari Homilia II. merear, quo spiritualis militiae conditionem, quam regula nobis praecipit, non excedam. Eiusdem nanque militiae sumus professores, nec votum discernit officium, quo me pastorem cum ovibus professio solemnis in exordio huius vitae fecit obligatum. Unde cum vobis loquor de spirituali militia, quam sumus Deo miserante professi: intentio est mea, quantum Dominus Iesus donare dignabitur, et meipsum de plumis ignaviae, ac tepiditatis ad fervorem sanctae novitatis excutere, et vos omnes pro viribus ad custodiam militaris ordinis provocare. Sumus enim fragiles, et infirmi, nec diu stabiles in sancto proposito consistimus, nisi quotidianis exercitiis fervorem spiritus continue renovemus. Mei nanque ratione officii astringor vobis ea, quae ad salutem vestram vobis possunt conducere, in medium proponere: ad vos pertinet loquentem me, ut pastorem animarum vestrarum, patienter in omnibus audire. Quamvis enim ad docendum tantam multitudinem seniorum iuvenis non sim idoneus, quia tamen me vobis constituitis pastorem, compellor sub necessitate salutis gregem pascre, quem suscepi gubernandum. Ego quod meum est libenter pro viribus, et ago, et agam quandiu in hac sollicitudine curae pastoralis vixero: senes vos iuvenis docebo, et quemadmodum illi militare debatis in cuius arma iurastis, sine intermissione demonstrabo. Non enim me fugit horrenda legislatoris nostri comminatio dicentis: Sciat abbas culpae pastoris incumbere, quicquid in ovibus pater familias utilitatis minus potuerit invenire. Et vos fratres mei concernit quod sequitur, si me praedicante, et monente Dei verbum contemptus oriatur. Tantum, inquit, iterum erit liber, ut si inquieto, vel inobedienti gregi pastoris fuerit omnis diligentia attributa, et morbidis eorum actibus universa fuerit cura exhibita, pastor eorum in iudicio Domini absolutus, dicat cum propheta: Domine, iustitiam tuam non abscondi in corde meo, veritatem tuam, et salutare tuum dixi: ipsi autem contemnentes spreverunt me. Et tunc demum inobedientibus curae suae ovibus, poena sit eis praevalens ipsa mors. Nullum hic velamen excusationis relinquitur, subterfugiendi. locus non praestatur, sed periculum utrarumque partium publice describitur. Ego nanque locum tenens abbatis, si non vobis annunciaro iustitiam Dei, si peccantes vos non emendavero secundum regulam, officium meum negavi: et mihi totum imputabitur, quod minus in vobis sanctitatis invenitur. Meum est enim ratione pastoralis officii, quid vobis ad salutem animarum vestrarum expedit dicere: vestrum vero est ea, quae in nomine salvatoris pronunciavero, humiliter audire: et quantum unusquisque praevalet, corde magno fideliter adimplere. Audistis periculum meum si non clamavero: audivistis, et vestrum si me vobis contemptseritis verbum Dei praedicantem. Ut autem miseratione salvatoris omnes evadamus securi, id studiose prosequatur unusquisque nostrum, quod sibi in hac militia 12 De profectu militiae spiritualis.

Whenever, dearest brothers, the recollection of that moment comes to mind, when you made me, protesting and resisting, your unworthy abbot over you, just so often I am wholly shaken within myself by the bitterness of my heart, and I am compelled, even unwillingly and against my will, to shed tears. For I know that it was not because of my own merits that I was set over you; but whether it was because of yours, I do not know. May almighty God grant that this appointment of me was not made because of my demerits or yours.

Why did you wish it so, brothers? You raised me up, young, unlearned, and in no way fit for the warfare which we profess, to be your leader, so that now it is altogether necessary for me both to teach and to learn, since neither the perfection of my life commends my teaching, nor does regard for my age yet obtain for a shepherd the necessary authority. In these three years now I have experienced enough how great are the miseries in which I am entangled, since I alone am compelled to bear the weaknesses of you all, and I, unhappy man, am supported by no one.

Who will deliver me from the vanities of this world, into which I have been recalled, I who entered the monastery in order to flee every care and anxiety of this present life? But since indeed it is necessary to bear the burden laid upon my shoulders, I beg you, brothers: diligently stretch out to me the helping hands of your prayers, so that in your midst, by the Lord’s bounty, I may deserve to conduct myself in such a way that I do not transgress the condition of the spiritual warfare which the Rule prescribes for us.

For we are professed soldiers of the same warfare, and the vow does not distinguish the duty by which, at the beginning of this life, solemn profession made me, shepherd together with the sheep, bound. Therefore, when I speak to you about the spiritual warfare which, by God’s mercy, we have professed, my intention is, so far as the Lord Jesus will deign to grant, both to shake myself out of the feathers of sloth and lukewarmness into the fervor of holy newness, and to stir all of you, according to my strength, to the keeping of military order. For we are frail and weak, and we do not remain long steadfast in our holy purpose unless by daily exercises we continually renew the fervor of the spirit.

By reason of my office, I am bound to set before you in common those things which can serve your salvation. It belongs to you to listen patiently in all things to me as I speak, as the shepherd of your souls. For although, being young, I am not fit to teach so great a multitude of elders, nevertheless, because you appointed me your shepherd, I am compelled, under necessity of salvation, to feed the flock which I have undertaken to govern. What is mine to do, I both do and will gladly do according to my strength, as long as I live in this solicitude of pastoral care: young though I am, I will teach you elders, and without ceasing I will show you how you ought to serve as soldiers for him into whose army you have sworn.

For the dreadful warning of our lawgiver does not escape me, when he says: “Let the abbot know that whatever profit the father of the household has been unable to find in the sheep will be laid to the fault of the shepherd.” And what follows concerns you, my brothers, if, while I preach and admonish, contempt for the word of God should arise. “Only then,” he says again, “will he be free, if all diligence has been applied by the shepherd to a restless or disobedient flock, and every care has been shown for their diseased actions; then their shepherd, absolved in the judgment of the Lord, may say with the prophet: Lord, I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have spoken your truth and your salvation. But they, despising, have rejected me. And then at last, for the sheep disobedient to his care, let death itself, prevailing over them, be their punishment.”

Here no covering of excuse is left; no place for escape is granted, but the danger of both parties is openly described. For I, holding the place of abbot, if I do not announce to you the justice of God, if I do not correct you when you sin according to the Rule, have denied my office; and whatever holiness is found lacking in you will be wholly imputed to me. For by reason of the pastoral office it is mine to tell you what is expedient for the salvation of your souls; but it is yours humbly to hear the things which I shall proclaim in the name of the Savior, and, as far as each one is able, faithfully to fulfill them with a great heart.

You have heard my danger if I do not cry out; you have also heard yours, if you despise me when I preach the word of God to you. But so that, by the Savior’s mercy, we may all escape in safety, let each one of us diligently pursue what belongs to him in this warfare [unclear].

10
spirituali praecipitur: summopere caventes, ne veritatis surdi auditores facti, Domino mentiamur. Voti sedulo recordemur, quod emisimus: et ordinem sanctum, quem profitemur usque ad mortem inviolabilem conservemus. Audiamus Regem nostrum suis in Evangelio militibus dicentem: Si quis mihi ministrat, me sequatur: et ubi ego sum, illic, et minister meus erit. Ministri sumus regis aeterni sacerdotes atque levitae, omnes monachi claustrales: duplicique ratione ad magnam obligati sanctitatem: quippe qui ordinem simul susceperimus clericorum, et monasticae puritatis regulam profitemur. Sequamur ergo praecoptorem nostrum, cui militamus, per iter asperitatis omnium virtutum: et armemus nos per fidem rectam, spem firmam, Deique ac proximi ferventissimam charitatem: in qua totius sanctitatis perfectio comprehenditur. Quisquis enim charitatis munimine cingitur: nunquam ab adversario superatur. In charitate nanque veraciter Christi dulcescit militia: et eius fervor cum in corde militis ardere coeperit, nulla metuit adversa. Charitas enim, ut Divus Gregorius inquit, nunquam est ociosa, sed magna operatur, si vera est: quod si operari renuit, perfecta charitas non fuit. Milites ergo claustrales, qui vos aeterno regi perpetuo servituros spopondistis, abiicite iam nunc opera tenebrarum, et induite charitatem Dei, et proximi, quae est armatura salutis omnium fortissima: qua si quis indutus fuerit, nullos labores quantumlibet duros, nulla huius mundi contraria formidabit. Non timebit famem: non sitem: non persecutiones hominum: non opprobria: non irrisiones: non carceres: non vincula: non quaecunque dura, et adversa: sed omnis, qui charitatem Dei perfecte semel gustaverit, invictus contra quaecunque mundi furentia permanebit. Dei verus amator in tribulationibus gaudet: in adversis laetatur: in persecutionibus propter iustitiam exultat. Regem sequitur suum in Coelis residentem: ibi mente conversatur, et animi desiderio, ubi suum regnare non dubitat Salvatorem. Quicquid in mundo voluptatis, et deliciarum uspiam cernitur servo Christi in vera charitate fervescenti, quasi vilissimum stercus foetorem, et horrorem generat, quoniam nihil terrenum, nihil transitorium, nihil caducum, sed illum, cui se devovit, solum tota mentis intentione amat. Verus etenim Christi miles nihil de rebus mundi cogitat, non carnem, sed mentem curat, utpote qui scriptum non ignorat. Nemo militans Deo, implicat se negociis secularibus, ut illi placeat, cui se probavit. Enimvero quicunque terreno militant Imperatori, praecoptis eius in cunctis semper obedient, et statim quo iusserit ille, sine contradictione vadunt. Ducem sequuntur omnes unum, et quicquid ille regis nomine praeceperit, nemo ex omni militia contradicit. Vos quoque milites regis saeculorum, qui me vobis Ducem eius vice, ac praecoptorem constituitis, mandatum Imperatoris vestri Iesu Christi per os meum audite, et quod, ille praecipit nobis in sancto Homilia II. 13

It is enjoined in the spiritual life: let us take the greatest care that, having become deaf hearers of the truth, we do not lie to the Lord. Let us diligently remember the vow we made, and let us preserve inviolate until death the holy order which we profess. Let us hear our King saying in the Gospel to his soldiers: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my servant be.”

We are ministers of the eternal King: priests and Levites, all cloistered monks, bound for a twofold reason to great holiness, since we have both taken up the order of clerics and profess the rule of monastic purity. Therefore let us follow our instructor, for whom we serve as soldiers, along the harsh path of all the virtues; and let us arm ourselves with right faith, firm hope, and most fervent charity toward God and neighbor, in which the perfection of all holiness is comprised.

For whoever is girded with the defense of charity is never overcome by the adversary. Truly, in charity the warfare of Christ grows sweet, and when its fervor begins to burn in the soldier’s heart, he fears no adversity. For charity, as Saint Gregory says, is never idle, but does great things if it is true; but if it refuses to work, it was not perfect charity.

Therefore, cloistered soldiers, you who have pledged yourselves to serve the eternal King forever, cast away now the works of darkness and put on charity toward God and neighbor, which is the strongest of all armor of salvation. If anyone is clothed with it, he will fear no labors, however hard, no contrary things of this world. He will not fear hunger, nor thirst, nor persecutions by men, nor reproaches, nor mockeries, nor prisons, nor chains, nor anything hard and adverse; but everyone who has once perfectly tasted the charity of God will remain unconquered against whatever raging things of the world.

The true lover of God rejoices in tribulations, is glad in adversities, and exults in persecutions for the sake of justice. He follows his King, seated in the heavens; there he dwells in mind and in the desire of his soul, where he does not doubt that his Savior reigns. Whatever pleasure and delights are seen anywhere in the world produce stench and horror, like the vilest dung, for the servant of Christ burning with true charity, because he loves nothing earthly, nothing transitory, nothing perishable, but with the whole intention of his mind loves him alone to whom he has devoted himself.

For the true soldier of Christ thinks nothing of the things of the world; he cares not for the flesh but for the mind, since he is not ignorant of what is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has approved himself.” Indeed, all who serve an earthly emperor always obey his commands in everything, and at once go without contradiction wherever he has ordered. They all follow one commander, and whatever he commands in the king’s name, no one in the whole army contradicts.

You also, soldiers of the King of ages, who have appointed me as your commander in his place and as your instructor, hear through my mouth the command of your Emperor Jesus Christ, and what he commands us in the holy …

11
Evangelio, facite. Audite, quid iubeat, et, quemadmodum militare vos oporteat in observantia disciplinae regularis, considerate. Qui mihi ministrat, inquit, me sequatur. Audi Monache, claustralem portans militiam attende. Dicit ad te Christus, cui militas, te alloquitur Coelestis Imperator, cui ad altare ministras. Si meus vis esse minister, virtutem patientiae, et humilitatis, quam ex me didicisti, oportet, ut sequaris. Exemplum enim dedi vobis, O milites mei, ut quemadmodum ego feci, et vos simili[&]e faciatis. Charitas, O Monache, me compulit, ut ex virgine homo nascer in mundo, ipsa te mei amore purum, et humilem semper conservet in clau[&]stro. Pater quod mihi praecipit opus humanae salutis, tui causa studui semper indesinenti meditatione perficere: et tu si me diligis, sanctum Monasticae conversationis propositum, quod assumpsisti, pro peccatis tuis usque ad mortem cura inviolatum conservare. Ego Patri meo coelesti semper in cunctis voluntarie usque ad mortem crucis amarissimam subiectus, et obediens extiti: tu quoque, si venire ad me volueris, Abbati tuo loco mei constituto, in omnibus semper, iuxta regulam humiliter obedi. Ego mandatum, quod dedit mihi Pater meus, nunquam in aliquo sum transgressus, et tu, nisi tria principalia Monasticae institutionis vota usque ad mortem inviolata servaveris, inter ministros meos, et milites nequaquam es numerandus. Ego cum essem dives, propter salutem tuam factus sum pauper, et egenus: tu vero nisi amore mei contemperis, et dimiseris omnia, meus non poteris esse discipulus. Inopiam, famem, sitim, aestum, frigus, et continuos in mundo labores tui causa sustinui: in quibus, nisi me secundum regulam tuam pro viribus patienter, ac voluntarie secutus fueris, meus certe, nec minister, nec miles, nec Monachus eris. In patientia enim tua possidebis animam tuam. Ego in hoc mundo nihil concupivi, nihil habui, nihil terrenum amavi, sed pauper, humilis, et mansuetus incendis, me paternae voluntati perfectissime semper in omnibus susceptibilem iniuriarum, et verberum subieci. Tu autem O Monache claustralis, qui Monasticam regulam profiteris sub Abbate, vel Priore, si iam deinceps carnis tuae concupiscentias fueris secutus, si peculium, aut proprium in Monasterio possederis, si praeter me aliquid amaveris, si praecceptoris tui mandata contempseris, si mihi non perseveranter in humilitate militaveris, sciens scito, quoniam non militem te habebo, non Monachum, non Ministrum, non discipulum computabo, sed profugum, apostatam, perfidum, mendacem, irrisorem, et periurum infidelem te iudicans, cum traditore meo Iuda, et residentibus Angelis in aeternum (sicut meruisti) sine misericordia condemnabo. Quod mihi voverunt labia tua, non amplius est tuum, sed meum, si vero, quod meum est, tibi usurpaveris, non Monachus, et servus meus vis esse fidelis, sed fur, et latro perversus, impius, et iniustus, talem quoque te, cum 14 De profectu militiae spiritualis.

Do what the Gospel says. Hear what it commands, and consider how you ought to serve as soldiers in the observance of regular discipline.

“He who ministers to me,” he says, “let him follow me.” Listen, monk; attend, you who bear the cloistered warfare. Christ, whom you serve as a soldier, says this to you; the heavenly Emperor, whom you serve at the altar, addresses you. If you wish to be my minister, you must follow the virtue of patience and humility which you have learned from me. For I have given you an example, O my soldiers, that as I have done, so you also should do likewise.

Charity, O monk, compelled me to be born as man in the world from a virgin; may that same charity, for love of me, always preserve you pure and humble in the cloister. The work of human salvation which the Father entrusted to me, I strove always to accomplish for your sake with unceasing meditation; and you, if you love me, take care to preserve inviolate until death the holy purpose of monastic life which you have undertaken for your sins.

I was always voluntarily subject and obedient to my heavenly Father in all things, even to the most bitter death of the cross; you also, if you wish to come to me, must always obey humbly in all things, according to the Rule, your abbot, who has been set in my place. I never transgressed in anything the commandment which my Father gave me; and you, unless you keep inviolate until death the three principal vows of monastic institution, are in no way to be numbered among my ministers and soldiers.

Though I was rich, for your salvation I became poor and needy; but you, unless for love of me you despise and leave behind all things, cannot be my disciple. Poverty, hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and continual labors in the world I endured for your sake; and unless in these things, according to your Rule and to the best of your strength, you have followed me patiently and willingly, you certainly will be neither my minister, nor my soldier, nor my monk. For in your patience you will possess your soul.

In this world I desired nothing, possessed nothing, loved nothing earthly, but, going about poor, humble, and meek, I subjected myself most perfectly and always in all things to my Father’s will, ready to receive injuries and blows. But you, O cloistered monk, who profess the monastic Rule under an abbot or prior, if from now on you follow the desires of your flesh, if you possess private property or anything of your own in the monastery, if you love anything besides me, if you despise the commands of your superior, if you do not persevere in serving me as a soldier in humility, know for certain that I will not hold you as a soldier, nor count you as a monk, minister, or disciple, but, judging you to be a fugitive, an apostate, faithless, a liar, a mocker, and a perjured unbeliever, I will condemn you without mercy forever, as you have deserved, with my betrayer Judas and the [unclear] angels.

What your lips vowed to me is no longer yours, but mine. But if you usurp for yourself what is mine, you do not wish to be a monk and my faithful servant, but a thief and a robber, perverse, impious, and unjust; such also I will [unclear], with

12
venero, nihil dubites, iudicabo. Si autem in sancto proposito usque ad mortem fideliter perseveraveris, si voluntatem, quam mihi consecrasti solemuiter, sub potestate Vicarii mei, quem tibi constitui pastorem, inviolatam custodieris, si obedientiam, paupertatem, et castitatem cum humilitate pro amore nominis mei usque in finem observaveris, si mihi soli complacere in omnibus actionibus tuis semper studueris, si me per arduum iter virtutum sine intermissione sequi curaveris, scius indubitante certissime scito, quoniam, ut amicum ex servo te factum charissimum, te habebo militem mecum in regno meo coronandum, te amabo, te diligam, te in medio Sanctorum meorum in aeternum constituan gloriosum. Audi me nunc serve meus: qui propter nominis mei reverentiam, et honorem te militiae inscripsisti Monachorum, et corde magno, atque perfecto sequere vestigia pedum meorum, sicut praecceptor ille tuus quondam Benedictus amicus meus te docuit, et totis conatibus imitatus fuit. Non te decipient illecebrae carnis, O strenue miles: non seducant animum tuum mibi dicatum, vana, et perniciosa huius commercia mundi: numquam cedas immundi spiritus nimium dolosis suggestionibus, qui totus in tui perniciem debacchatur, sed memento tuum in hoc seculo brevissimum esse incolatum, et ante fores mortem astante, quam subterfugere nemo umquam potuit mortalium. Semper in memoria consistant tua illa, quae necessario subbis, novissima, et ex velocissimo transitu earum voluptatum carnis, quae praeterierunt: et futura- rum poenarum cogitatione, huius incolatus horrorem tibi necessarium assumito, et contemptum. Quemadmodum pro me labor brevis in mundo habitus cum patientia, et charitate, foelicitatem militibus meis aeternam praeparat, ita carnis desideria, et voluptates, quae subito transeunt, animam hominis peccatoris ad inferos demergunt sine fine cruciandam. Ad me igitur sint omnia desideria tua, Monache, qui mihi ministras, et, qui per arduum iter observantiae regularis me sequeris, praebi mihi cor tuum, si foelicitatem desideras: me solum quaerito, si vitam, et salutem propriam amas. Me cum amaveris, tranquillus, et sanctus eris, cum secutus fueris, beatus es, et sine fine gloriosus. Quid fratres mei faceretis, si vos contingeret haec verba, quae diximus nos, ex ore Salvatoris, et regis nostri audire loquentis? Quid, inquam, ageretis? Credo certe magnam in cordibus vestris compunctionem futuram, si Christum personaliter audiretis loquentem. Nos autem vicem Christi in Monasterio gerentes, loquimur sermones, quos ille donavit, et non attenditis? contestamur vobis necessariam salutis palaestram, et signa compunctionis nulla exhibetis? Quid causae fuerit, ut ista dicere, si nescitis, iam precor, intelligite. Video quosdam e vobis sacras abhorrire lectiones, vanitatibus deditos, et nihil minus curare, quam spiritualis militiae perfectionem, quorum Deus venter est, et gloria in confusione. Existimatis

When I come, have no doubt, I shall judge. But if you have persevered faithfully in your holy purpose even unto death; if you have kept inviolate, under the authority of my vicar whom I have appointed as your shepherd, the will which you solemnly consecrated to me; if, for love of my name, you have observed obedience, poverty, and chastity with humility to the end; if you have always striven to please me alone in all your actions; if you have taken care to follow me without ceasing along the arduous path of the virtues, know, know most certainly and without doubt, that, as one made from a servant into a most dear friend, I shall have you as my soldier, to be crowned with me in my kingdom; I shall love you, I shall cherish you, I shall set you in glory forever in the midst of my saints.

Hear me now, my servant: you who, out of reverence and honor for my name, have enrolled yourself in the knighthood of monks, follow the footprints of my feet with a great and perfect heart, just as Benedict, that former teacher of yours and my friend, taught you and strove with all his efforts to imitate. The enticements of the flesh will not deceive you, O brave soldier. Let not the vain and ruinous dealings of this world seduce your mind, which has been dedicated to me. Never yield to the exceedingly deceitful suggestions of the unclean spirit, who rages wholly for your destruction; but remember that your dwelling in this age is very brief, and that death stands before the doors, which no mortal has ever been able to escape.

Let those last things which you must necessarily undergo always remain in your memory; and from the very swift passing of those pleasures of the flesh which have gone by, and from the thought of punishments to come, take up for yourself a necessary horror and contempt of this sojourn. Just as a brief labor endured for me in the world with patience and charity prepares eternal happiness for my soldiers, so the desires and pleasures of the flesh, which suddenly pass away, plunge the soul of the sinful man down to hell, to be tormented without end.

Therefore let all your desires be directed to me, monk, you who serve me and follow me along the arduous path of regular observance. Offer me your heart, if you desire happiness; seek me alone, if you love your own life and salvation. When you have loved me, you will be tranquil and holy; when you have followed me, you are blessed and glorious without end.

What would you do, my brothers, if it befell you to hear these words which we have spoken from the mouth of our Savior and king as he spoke? What, I ask, would you do? I certainly believe there would be great compunction in your hearts if you heard Christ speaking in person. But we, bearing the place of Christ in the monastery, speak the words which he has given, and you do not heed them? We proclaim to you the necessary training-ground of salvation, and you show no signs of compunction?

If you do not know what cause there has been for saying these things, now, I beg you, understand. I see that some of you shrink from sacred readings, are given over to vanities, and care for nothing less than the perfection of spiritual warfare; their god is the belly, and their glory is in confusion. You think...

13
Homilia II. 15 ne vilissimi nebulones, qui nihil spirituale sapitis, quod Christus iterum de Coelo venturus sit, ut ea vobis loquatur, quae praedicatoribus suis dicenda commisit? An Paulum non audivistis dicentem, Christus resur- gens ex mortuis, iam non moritur, mors illi ultra non dominabitur. Quod enim mortuus est peccato, mortuus est semel, quod autem vivit, vivit Deo? Semel Christus in terra visus est: semel inter mortales visibilis apparuit: semel viam salutis aeternae praedicavit, secundo non adiciet. Constituit Pastores, et Vicarios super familiam suam, qui doceant igno- rantes, quorum volens manifestare auctoritatem in Evangelio dixit, Qui vos audit, me audit, et qui vos spertit, me spertit. Eos igitur audite, quos Christus vobis praefecit rectores, quibus tritici spiritualis dispen- sationem commisit, sicut in sancto Evangelio dixit, Quis putas est fidelis dispensator, et prudens, quem constituit Dominus super familiam suam, ut det illis in tempore tritici mensuram? Beatus ille servus, quem, cum venerit Dominus, invenerit ita facientem. Exhortamur vos itaque fra- tres in Domino Iesu, et qua possimus sedulitate, rogamus, ne dies vestros in vanitate consumatis, sed considerate huius vitae nimiam brevitatem, et facite condignos poenitentiae fructus, dum vobis oppor- tune conceditur, ne, si poenitere neglexeritis, tempus amputetur. Scitis enim, quid scriptura nobis dicat divina: Dies Domini, sicut fur in nocte, sic veniet. Cavete, praecor, differre bonum, quia nemo scit vestrum, quando sit moriturus: quin potius verum illud poetae lascivi Nasonis attendite, ita monentis. Sed propea, nec te venturas differ in horas, Qui non est hodie, cras minus aptus erit. Nemo vitam sibi fratres pro- mittat longaevam, sed unusquisque mortem cogitet potius instare vici- nam: ideoque sic vivat paratus, tamquam crastino die de corpore mi- graturus. Spes enim vitae longioris multos deceptit, et a fervore sancti propositi retardans subito ad inferos demersit. Militiam igitur vestram, quae non post multum necessario finietur, ita perficite, ut non timeatis coram rege vestro, cum venerit, apparere. Memores semper estote, quia non habetis hic manentem civitatem, neque in hac vita mortali diu potestis consistere, sed mors cito veniet, quae vos compellet emi- grare. Quicumque enim verus est monachus, et miles Christi desiderat esse fidelis, omnia huius mundi oblectamenta contemnit, praesentem sibi Dominum suum semper cogitat, et abiectis a se impedimentis, sar- cinulisque omnibus, quemadmodum illi valeat complacere, super omnia curat. In conquirendis vitae necessariis, non debet esse sollicitus, cum haec omnia subiectis disponat providentia pastoris. Omnis cura monachi sit mundum se custodire ab hoc seculo, ut liber, et absolutus ab omni- bus nihil quaerat, nisi Deum, nihil cogitet, nisi Iesum pro nobis cru- cifixim. O foelix Christi miles, cui regna promittuntur coelorum, si fidelis, prudens, ac vigilans in Dei amore usque ad finem permanserit. 16 De profectu militiae spiritualis.

Do not suppose, you vilest knaves, who taste nothing spiritual, that Christ will come again from heaven to speak to you the things which he entrusted to his preachers to say. Or have you not heard Paul saying, “Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God”? Once Christ was seen on earth; once he appeared visibly among mortals; once he preached the way of eternal salvation; he will not add a second time.

He appointed shepherds and vicars over his household to teach the ignorant, and, wishing to make their authority plain, said in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me.” Therefore hear those whom Christ has set over you as rulers, to whom he entrusted the dispensing of spiritual wheat, as he said in the holy Gospel: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season? Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he shall find so doing.”

Therefore we exhort you, brothers, in the Lord Jesus, and with all the earnestness we can, we beg you not to consume your days in vanity, but consider the excessive brevity of this life, and bring forth worthy fruits of repentance while the opportunity is granted you, lest, if you neglect to repent, the time be cut off. For you know what the divine Scripture says to us: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.” Beware, I pray you, of putting off the good, because none of you knows when he is going to die. Rather, attend to that true saying of the wanton poet Naso, who warns thus: “But hasten, and do not put yourself off to the coming hours; he who is not ready today will be less fit tomorrow.”

Let no one, brothers, promise himself a long life, but let each instead think that death is near at hand; and therefore let him live so prepared as if he were to depart from the body tomorrow. For the hope of a longer life has deceived many, and, holding them back from the fervor of a holy purpose, has suddenly plunged them down to the lower regions. Therefore fulfill your warfare, which of necessity will end before long, in such a way that you do not fear to appear before your king when he comes.

Always remember that you have here no lasting city, nor can you remain long in this mortal life; but death will come quickly and compel you to depart. For whoever is a true monk and desires to be a faithful soldier of Christ contemns all the delights of this world, always thinks of his Lord as present to him, and, having cast aside every hindrance and every little burden, cares above all how he may please him. He ought not to be anxious in seeking the necessities of life, since the providence of the shepherd provides all these things for those subject to him. Let the whole care of the monk be to keep himself unstained from this world, so that, free and released from all things, he may seek nothing but God and think of nothing but Jesus crucified for us. O happy soldier of Christ, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised, if he remains faithful, prudent, and watchful in the love of God to the end.

14
Nihil certe bono monacho foelicius: cui se Dei filius pollicetur in praemium, nihil etiam laboriosius: qui constitutus in agone certaminis quotidiané de sua periclitatur salute, et nihil monacho fortius, qui vincit mundum simul, atque diabolum, nihil quoque imbecillius eo, qui a carne propria superatur. Semper igitur tibi, O monache, contra occultum hostem salutis tuae vigilandum est: qui numquam facilius vincitur, quam si procul ab introitu mentis arceatur. Unde si contra eum victor cupis evadere, non patiaris tibi machinas dolis, ac fraudis illis propriis admoveri. Custodi sensus in primis tuos, ne mors per fenestras ingrediatur: et hostis tunc maxime caveto insidias, cum te ad tempus in tua devotione permiserit esse securum. Admonitionis nunquam obliviscaris viri sapientis, qui dicit: Si non in timore Domini tenueris te instanter: cito subvertitur domus tua, id est conscientia. Idecirco Salomon in Proverbis dixit: Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus: qui vero mentis est durae, corruet in malum. Mox enim, ut monachus de securitate praesumperit, iam sine dubio ad interitum tendit. Oportet ergo, militem Christi contra suos adversarios semper esse paratum, ut quamdiu vivit in hoc mortali corpore, non se confidat illos perfecte superasse. Semper enim caro concupiscit adversum spiritum, et nequando superetur animus, quamdiu contingit vivere, necessarium est pugnare. Quotiescumque hostem tuum invisibilem viceris, iterum semper insurgens cum maiore saevitia tibi congreditur, ut, qui fortitudine non potest obtinere victoriam, assiduitate saltem inducat desperationem. Tu autem Christi miles fortissime caveto ne in agone huius brevissimi certaminis deficias, cave, ne ante completum in fine praelium, arma necessarii munimini deponas. Dicit enim Salvator: Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, salvus erit. Non des requiem animae tuae quandiu tibi fuerit concessum in hac miserabili peregrinatione morari, sed semper aliquid boni facito, ne umquam diabolus inveniat te ociosum. Memento semper admonitionis scripturae dicentis: Quodcunque potest manus tua instanter operare: quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas. Nemo est enim, qui semper vivat: sed omnes morimur, et sic ut aquae in terram delabimur, quae amplius ad priorem statum non revertentur. Tunc non erit amplius tempus operandi honum ad meritum foelicitatis aeternae, sed quaecunque hic nunc in tempore seminaverit homo, tunc pro mercede recipiet. Idcirco iterum sancta dicit scriptura, Mane semina semen tuum, et vespero ne cesset manus tua. Et sanctus Paulus Timotheum admonens dicit: Labora sicut bonus miles Christi Iesu. Nemo autem militans Deo implicat se negotiis secularibus, ut ei placeat, cui se probavit. Nam et corum, qui certant in agone, nemo coronabitur nisi qui legitime certaverit. Omnis autem, qui in agone contendit, ab omnibus se abstinet. In alio quoque loco Homilia II. 17 idem Christophilus ait: Volo vos sine solicitudine esse. Tu ergo Christi miles, qui contendis in agone certaminis quotidiani, ut coram Deo tuo tandem in aeternum appareas gloriosus, gymnosophistam imitare corruptibilem, qui decertans in agone, pro corruptibili quidem corona, ne vincatur, ab omnibus se abstinet, ut nudus, et liber expeditius currat. Itaque si viam Dei ambulare in vera puritate desideras, si vincere hostem in agone certaminis optas, proiice abs te omnia vestimenta curarum terrestrium, capillosque depone omnes carnalium voluptatum. Quisquis enim capillis, et vestimentis a se proiectis nudus currere didicit, nihil praeter absolutum corpus, quo teneri queat ab adversario, circunducit. Nam qui nudus currat, omni se solicitudine spoliavit rerum circumstrepentium, et nihil aliud, quam victoriam cogitat, nec quid interim pae-nes uxorem geratur, aut filios curat. Non eum revocat a cursu, quicquam praesentium; non deterret agilitas sociorum, inter multos contendit quasi solus, ad praemium festinat anhelans quasi certus. Hunc imitare Christi miles in spirituali certamine, nudus in cruce pendentem Salvatorem nudum contemplare, quatenus tanto facilius adversarium queas proster- nere, quanto minus de mundi vanitatibus te videtur habere. Nudus ita-que, levis, et expeditus ex omni parte dimica, nudus, et absolutus ab omnibus in Caelum vola. Nudus in hunc mundum venisti, nudus in terram réversurus es. Haec fratres mei sedulo cogitantes sic currite, ut vitam comprehendatis aeternam cum omnibus sanctis. Amen.

Certainly nothing is happier than the good monk, to whom the Son of God promises himself as reward; yet nothing is more laborious, for, set in the arena of combat, he daily endangers his salvation. Nothing is stronger than a monk who conquers both the world and the devil together; yet nothing is weaker than one who is overcome by his own flesh.

Therefore, O monk, you must always keep watch against the hidden enemy of your salvation, who is never more easily conquered than when he is kept far from the entrance of the mind. So if you desire to come forth victorious against him, do not allow him to bring against you the devices of his own tricks and deceits. Guard your senses above all, lest death enter through the windows; and beware the enemy’s snares most of all when for a time he has allowed you to feel secure in your devotion.

Never forget the admonition of the wise man, who says: If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house, that is, your conscience, will soon be overthrown. Therefore Solomon said in Proverbs: Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil. For as soon as a monk presumes upon security, he is already, without doubt, tending toward destruction. Therefore the soldier of Christ must always be prepared against his adversaries, so that, as long as he lives in this mortal body, he should not trust that he has perfectly overcome them. For the flesh always lusts against the spirit, and lest the soul ever be overcome, it is necessary to fight as long as life lasts.

Whenever you have conquered your invisible enemy, he rises up again and attacks you with greater savagery, so that, since he cannot obtain victory by strength, he may at least bring on despair by persistence. But you, most valiant soldier of Christ, beware lest you fail in the arena of this very brief combat; beware lest, before the battle is completed at the end, you lay down the arms needed for defense. For the Savior says: He who perseveres to the end will be saved. Give no rest to your soul as long as it has been granted you to remain in this miserable pilgrimage, but always do something good, lest the devil ever find you idle.

Always remember the admonition of Scripture, which says: Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly, because neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge will exist in the lower world to which you are hastening. For there is no one who lives forever; rather, we all die, and like waters we flow down into the earth, and they will no more return to their former state. Then there will no longer be time to do good for the merit of eternal happiness, but whatever a man has sown here now in time, he will then receive as his reward. Therefore holy Scripture again says: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease.

And Saint Paul, admonishing Timothy, says: Labor like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has approved himself. For even among those who contend in the arena, no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully. Everyone who contends in the arena abstains from all things. In another place also the same lover of Christ says: I want you to be without anxiety.
