You therefore, soldier of Christ, who contend in the arena of daily combat so that at last you may appear glorious forever before your God, imitate the mortal contestant, who, competing in the arena for a perishable crown, abstains from all things lest he be defeated, so that, naked and free, he may run more swiftly. And so, if you desire to walk the way of God in true purity, if you long to conquer the enemy in the arena of combat, cast away from yourself all the garments of earthly cares, and put off all the hair of carnal pleasures. For whoever, with hair and garments cast away from himself, has learned to run naked, carries about nothing except the bare body by which he could be held by the adversary. For he who runs naked has stripped himself of all anxiety over the things clamoring around him, and thinks of nothing but victory, nor does he care what meanwhile is going on with his wife or his children. Nothing present calls him back from the race; the speed of his companions does not frighten him; among many he contends as if alone; he hastens breathlessly toward the prize as if certain of it.

Imitate him, soldier of Christ, in spiritual combat; contemplate the naked Savior hanging naked on the cross, so that you may be able to overthrow the adversary the more easily, the less he seems to have hold of you through worldly vanities. Therefore fight naked, light, and unencumbered on every side; naked and freed from all things, fly to heaven. Naked you came into this world; naked you will return to the earth. Diligently considering these things, my brothers, so run that you may obtain eternal life with all the saints. Amen.

15
Quae sit armatura militiae spiritualis. Homilia III. S̄anctum Apostolum, fratres charissimi, hodie audivimus ad Ephesios in epistola scribentem. Induite vos armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli, quoniam non est nobis collectatio adversus carnem, et sanguinem, sed adversus Principes, et potestates, adversus mundi rectores tenebrarum harum: contra spiritalia nequitiae in coele-stibus. Propterea accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo, et in omnibus perfecti stare. Quae autem sit armatura Dei, sub-iungit. State ergo succincti lumbos vestros in veritate, et induti loricam iustitiae, et calciati pedes in praeparationem Evangelii pacis; in omnibus sumentes scutum fidei, in quo possitis omnia tela nequissimi ignea ex-tinguere: et galeam salutis assumite, et gladium spiritus, quod est ver-bum Dei: per omnem orationem, et obsecrationem orantes omni tempore in spiritu, et in ipso vigilantes in omni instantia, et obsecratione pro omnibus sanctis. Ad Thessalonicenses quoque similiter ait: Nos autem, qui Dei sumus, sobrii simus, induti loricam fidei, et charitatis: et ga-leam spem salutis. Haec sunt arma, fratres, quibus induti milites Christi saevum debellant adversarium, haec sunt Monachorum insignia virtutum: 18 Quae sit armatura militiae spiritualis. sine quibus victoriam nemo consequitur vitiorum. Militiae humanae, quam plerique nimis studiose sectantur mortales, instrumenta sunt, galea, scutum, thorax, gladius, pugio, lorica, baltheus, lancea, et caetera id genus multa, quibus curiosissime armantur ad bellum processuri homi- nes: et nisi quam diligentissime in toto fuerint corpore muniti ad praeliandum certe minus indicantur idonei. Spirituales autem militiae nostrae arma sunt fides, spes, charitas, patientia, humilitas, obedientia, castitas, simul cum sanctis animae virtutibus per Divum praeceptorem nostrum Benedictum enumeratis in regula sub capite quarto, ubi de instrumentis bonorum operum pulchram facit mentionem. Et utinam, fratres mei, tam essemus curiosi, et diligentes pro his militiae nostrae armis spiritualibus, quam homines mundanos pro eorum corruptibili armatura videmus esse sollicitos. Nunc autem, quod nimis dolenter dico, quoniam arma salutis, quibus debellare omnes adversarios nostros debueramus, turpiter abiicimus, quid restat aliud, nisi ut hosti nostro in certamine succumbamus? Sed forsan dicetis, Si fides Christiana, sicut Apostolus testatur, ad armaturam spiritualis militiae pertinet, eam certe numquam abiecinus. Credimus enim firmer, quicquid nobis credendum Sancta Mater Ecclesia proposuit, et in ea fidei professione usque ad mortem constanter intendimus permanere. Sed esto, quid autem dicit Iacob. 2. Fides quae salvat. Sanctus Iacobus in epistola? Quid proderit, fratres mei, si fidem quis dicat se habere, opera autem non habeat? Numquid poterit fides salvare eum? Sicut enim corpus sine spiritu mortuum est: ita fides sine ope- ribus mortua est. Quoties igitur cumque de fide scriptura loquitur, non vulgaris, et mortua, sed bonis operibus formata, atque Divini amoris dulcedine illustrata semper oportet ut intelligatur. Nemo enim salvabitur per fidem tantum, sicut Iacobus dicit in epistola, sed oportet fidei con- iungere Christianae opera pietatis. Vos creditis in unum Deum Omni- potentem, Creatorem Coeli, et Terrae, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum Sanctum? Bene facitis. Et daemones credunt, et contremiscunt. Quid enim? Ubi sunt opera, per quae fides vestra declaretur in Christo for- mata? Ociosa, et mortua est fides, quae Sanctis, et necessariis non com- mendatur operibus. In Christum credimus, bene est, si Christi sequamur exempla. Nam si Christum pietatis operibus non sequimur, frustra nobis de sola fide blandimur. Vos inquam creditis, et daemones credunt. Cum dilectione fides est Christiani, sine dilectione fides diaboli. Recte cre- ditis, si Deum ex toto corde pro viribus amatis. Si autem vere Deum non diligitis, fidem ociosam, et mortuam habetis. Probatio autem di- lectionis, Sancto Gregorio testante, exhibitio est operis. Sic enim loquitur in Evangelio Dominus: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit. Haec ergo est fides vera, bonis, et sanctis operibus secundum Christi doctrinam ordinata. Si fide simul, et opere in Dominum Iesum creditis,

What the Armor of Spiritual Warfare Is. Homily III.

Dearly beloved brothers, today we have heard the holy Apostle writing in his epistle to the Ephesians: Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil, for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, that you may be able to resist on the evil day, and, being perfect in all things, to stand. And what the armor of God is, he adds: Stand therefore, having girded your loins in truth, and having put on the breastplate of justice, and having shod your feet with preparation for the Gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to quench all the fiery darts of the most wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God; praying at all times in the spirit, with every prayer and supplication, and in it keeping watch with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints. Likewise he says to the Thessalonians: But we, who are of the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and charity, and for a helmet the hope of salvation. These are the arms, brothers, with which the soldiers of Christ, when clothed in them, defeat the savage adversary; these are the monastic badges of virtue, without which no one attains victory over the vices.

The instruments of human warfare, which many mortals pursue with excessive zeal, are the helmet, shield, breastplate, sword, dagger, coat of mail, belt, lance, and many other things of this kind, with which men who are about to go forth to war arm themselves most carefully; and unless they have been most diligently protected over their whole body, they are certainly judged less fit for battle. But the arms of our spiritual warfare are faith, hope, charity, patience, humility, obedience, chastity, together with the holy virtues of the soul enumerated by our divine teacher Benedict in the Rule under the fourth chapter, where he makes a beautiful mention of the instruments of good works.

And would, my brothers, that we were as attentive and diligent about these spiritual arms of our warfare as we see worldly men to be concerned about their perishable armor. But now, as I say with too much sorrow, since we shamefully cast aside the arms of salvation with which we ought to have defeated all our adversaries, what remains except that we fall before our enemy in the struggle? But perhaps you will say: If the Christian faith, as the Apostle testifies, belongs to the armor of spiritual warfare, we certainly have never cast it aside. For we firmly believe whatever Holy Mother Church has set before us to be believed, and in that profession of faith we steadfastly intend to remain until death.

But be it so. What then does Saint James say in his epistle? What will it profit, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith, but does not have works? Will faith be able to save him? For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. Therefore, whenever Scripture speaks of faith, it must always be understood not as a common and dead faith, but as one formed by good works and illumined by the sweetness of divine love. For no one will be saved by faith alone, as James says in his epistle; rather, the works of Christian devotion must be joined to faith.

Do you believe in one almighty God, Creator of heaven and earth, Father and Son and Holy Spirit? You do well. The demons also believe, and tremble. What then? Where are the works through which your faith may be shown to be formed in Christ? Idle and dead is the faith that is not commended by holy and necessary works. We believe in Christ: that is good, if we follow Christ’s examples. For if we do not follow Christ in works of devotion, we flatter ourselves in vain about faith alone. You, I say, believe, and the demons believe. Faith with love is the faith of a Christian; without love, it is the faith of the devil. You believe rightly, if with all your heart, according to your strength, you love God. But if you do not truly love God, you have an idle and dead faith. The proof of love, as Saint Gregory bears witness, is the performance of the work. For thus the Lord speaks in the Gospel: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. This, therefore, is true faith, ordered by good and holy works according to the teaching of Christ. If by faith and work together you believe in the Lord Jesus,

16
Homilia III. 19 certe scutum salutis in manibus tenetis, in quo cunctos adversarios ipse largiente Domino facile superabitis. De hac armatura scriptum est: Sancti per fidem vicerunt regna, operati sunt iustitiam, adepti sunt repromissionem. Ioannes quoque ait: Omne, quod natum est ex Deo, vincit mundum: et haec est victoria, quae vincit mundum, fides nostra. Et Princeps Apostolorum Petrus, ita nos commonet, dicens: Fratres sobrii estote, et vigilate, quoniam adversarius vester diabolus, tamquam leo rugiens circum, quaerens quem devoret, cui resistite fortes in fide. Vera fides, et confidentia in Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum est armatura invincibilis, atque fortissima: cui nemo umquam adversariorum potuit resistere, sicut in libro Paralipomenon scribitur: Dixit Rex Iosaphat exercitui suo: Credite in Domino Deo vestro, et securi eritis. In Ecclesiastico etiam sic legimus: Qui timetis Dominum, credite illi, et non evacuabitur merces vestra. Et iterum. In opere tuo credite ex fide animae tuae, haec est enim conversatio mandatorum. Qui credit Deo, attendit mandatis: et qui confidit in illo, non minoratus erit. Curate nunc igitur fratres charissimi, et summo studio semper elaborate, ut scutum hoc fidei Sanctis operibus formatae, contra omnes hostium vestrorum in cursus, manibus portetis: quia nunquam ab adversario vincitur, qui hoc scuto inexpugnabili munitur. Hoc Divus confirmans Augustinus de verbis Domini ait: Nullae maiores divitiae, nulli thesauri, nulli honores, nulla huius mundi maior est substantia, quam est fides catholica, quae peccatores homines salvat, caecos illuminat, infirmos curat, catechumenos baptizat, fideles iustificat, poenitentes reparat, iustos augmentat, martyres coronat, virgines, et viduas, et coniugales casto pudore conservat, Clericos ordinait, Sacerdotes consecrat, credentes in haereditate aeterna cum Sanctis Angelis locat. Sicut in radice arboris nulla prorsus appareat pulchritudinis species, et tamen, quicquid est in arbores pulchritudinis, vel decoris, ex illa procedit: sic ex fidei humilitate, quicquid meriti, quicquid beatitudinis anima susceptura est, totum ex fidei fundamento procedit. Nam sicut Apostolus dicit: Quicquid sive omne, quod non est ex fide, peccatum est, quoniam sine fide impossibile est placere Deo. Credere enim oportet accedentem ad Deum, quia est, inquirentibus se remunerator sit. Quanto autem quisque plus diligit, tanto in fide amplius proficit. Nam fides sine charitate, est sicut proiectum inutile, ac sine retinaculo scutum. O, thesaurus omnibus opulentior, fides, quae formata in mente hominis mortalem immortalibus comparas, daemones vincis, et regna, cunctaque dura superas fortiter, et adversa. Fides est fundamentum omnium virtutum, sine qua nullum spirituale subsistit aedificium. Fides illuminatrix est mentium, et principale spiritualis militiae instrumentum. Nam sine fidei scuto diabolus non vincitur, nec lascivae carnis impetus superatur. 20 Quae sit armatura militiae spiritualis.

Homily III.

Certainly you hold in your hands the shield of salvation, by which, with the Lord himself granting it, you will easily overcome all adversaries. Of this armor it is written: The saints through faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, and obtained the promise. John also says: Everything that is born of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that overcomes the world, our faith. And Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, likewise admonishes us, saying: Brothers, be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith.

True faith and confidence in our Lord Jesus Christ is an invincible and most powerful armor, which none of the adversaries has ever been able to withstand, as it is written in the book of Chronicles: King Jehoshaphat said to his army: Believe in the Lord your God, and you will be secure. In Ecclesiasticus too we read as follows: You who fear the Lord, believe him, and your reward will not be made void. And again: In your work believe from the faith of your soul, for this is the keeping of the commandments. He who believes God attends to his commandments, and he who trusts in him will not be diminished.

Therefore now take care, dearly beloved brothers, and always labor with the greatest zeal, so that you may carry in your hands this shield of faith formed by holy works against all the attacks of your enemies; for he who is protected by this unconquerable shield is never overcome by the adversary. Confirming this, blessed Augustine says concerning the words of the Lord: There are no greater riches, no treasures, no honors, no substance of this world greater than the Catholic faith, which saves sinful men, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores the penitent, increases the righteous, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins and widows and married persons in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, and places believers with the holy angels in the eternal inheritance.

Just as in the root of a tree no appearance of beauty at all is seen, and yet whatever beauty or comeliness there is in the tree proceeds from it, so from the humility of faith, whatever merit, whatever blessedness the soul is to receive, proceeds wholly from the foundation of faith. For, as the Apostle says: Whatever, or everything, that is not from faith is sin, since without faith it is impossible to please God. For one who comes to God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.

Moreover, the more each person loves, the more he advances in faith. For faith without charity is like a useless discarded shield, a shield without a strap. O faith, a treasure richer than all, which, formed in the mind of man, makes the mortal comparable to the immortals, conquers demons and kingdoms, and bravely overcomes all hard and adverse things. Faith is the foundation of all virtues, without which no spiritual building stands. Faith is the enlightener of minds and the chief instrument of spiritual warfare. For without the shield of faith the devil is not conquered, nor is the assault of wanton flesh overcome.

What the armor of spiritual warfare is.

17
Cogitemus ergo, fratres, quam necessaria sit nobis fides per charitatem formata ad salutem, sine qua, in hac militia nobis certantibus, neque victoria conceditur, neque confidentia reservatur. Fides enim est scutum, in quo facillime hostem salutis nostrae vincimus, si ansam Divini amoris adiungamus. Dicit nanque beatus Papa Gregorius: Tunc enim veraciter fideles sumus, si, quod verbis promittimus, operibus adimplemus. In hac armatura fides, cum sit fundamentum omnium bonorum operum, cunctas operationes nostras iure debet praecedere, ut mens ad amorem valeat pervenire. Nisi enim fides prius teneatur, nullatenus ad spiritualem amorem pertingit. Non enim charitas fidem, sed fides praecedit charitatem, quia nemo potest diligere, vel sperare, quod bonum renuit credere. Quoniam vero iam, quod etiam iubet, fideliter creditis, fundamentum spiritualis aedificii super firmam petram collocastis: nunc oportet, ut etiam reliqua ad perfectionem restantia sine mora faciatis. Pacem igitur, et veritatem diligite, quatenus in fide Christi, ut veri milites possitis omni tempore stabiles, et firmissimi permanere. Nam sicuti scriptura testatur, veritas magna est, et fortior praec omnibus, nec est cum ea quicquam iniquum. Qui veritatem diligit, verus Christi discipulus est, ipsumque amat. Christum in evangelio dicentem: Ego sum via, veritas, et vita. Universae quoque viae Domini misericordia, et veritas: a quo Satanas per superbiam cecidit, quoniam in veritate semperiterna non permansit. Iubet ergo Sanctus Christophilus Paulus milites Domini in veritate se praecingere: in quo statum perfectionis, ad quem anhelare maxime debent claustraes, voluit demonstrare. Quidam aliud est veritatem diligere, quam esse hominem id, quod esse iubet: et ita vivere ad normam iustitiae, verum, et solidum, qualem naturae per gratiam sancta perfectio requirit? Hinc Firmianus Lactantius inquit: Qui veritati studet, abiicat inimicas illi, et anxias voluptates, quae animum sibi vincunt, et liberum esse non permittunt. Semper autem praefert vera falsis, aeterna brevibus, utilia iucundis. Nihil aspectui gratum sit, nisi quod iuste, quod pie, quod religiose fieri possit: nihil auditui suave, nisi quod animam reddit meliorem. Milites itaque lumbos in veritate habent praecinctos, quando carnis illecebris, et mundi vanitatibus pro Dei amore contemptis, ita student pro viribus conversari, et vivere, quatenus summae veritati, quae Deus est, valeant in omnibus complacere. Post haec miles Christi loricam iustitiae iubetur induere, sine qua nemo recte, ac fructuose poterit Domino militare. Iustitia vero est servare, et distribuere unicuique, quod sibi secundum legem, vel naturam debetur. Et haec est omnium virtutum praeclarissima, sine qua nulla potest esse pietas, nulla religio, nulla sanctitas, nullaque bonorum maiorumve discretio, ipsa enim est lux, et splendor magnus, ex qua totius boni consurgit inter mortales vis, atque dominatio. Iustitia mater

Let us consider, then, brothers, how necessary for salvation is faith formed by charity; without it, as we fight in this warfare, neither victory is granted nor confidence preserved. For faith is the shield with which we most easily overcome the enemy of our salvation, if we add to it the handle of divine love. For blessed Pope Gregory says: We are truly faithful when we fulfill in deeds what we promise in words.

In this armor, since faith is the foundation of all good works, it ought rightly to precede all our actions, so that the mind may be able to come to love. For unless faith is first held, one in no way reaches spiritual love. Charity does not precede faith; rather, faith precedes charity, because no one can love or hope for as good what he refuses to believe. Since, then, you now faithfully believe what it also commands, you have set the foundation of the spiritual building upon firm rock; now you must also do without delay the other things that remain for perfection.

Love peace, therefore, and truth, so that in the faith of Christ, as true soldiers, you may be able at all times to remain steadfast and most firm. For, as Scripture bears witness, truth is great and stronger than all things, and there is nothing unjust with it. He who loves truth is a true disciple of Christ and loves Christ himself, who says in the Gospel: I am the way, the truth, and the life. All the ways of the Lord also are mercy and truth; from this truth Satan fell through pride, because he did not remain in everlasting truth.

Therefore the holy apostle Paul commands the soldiers of the Lord to gird themselves with truth; in this he wished to show the state of perfection toward which cloistered men ought especially to strive. For what else is it to love truth than for a man to be what he is commanded to be, and so to live according to the rule of justice, true and solid, such as holy perfection requires of nature through grace?

Hence Firmianus Lactantius says: He who devotes himself to truth casts away pleasures hostile to it and full of anxiety, which bind the soul to themselves and do not allow it to be free. He always prefers true things to false, eternal things to brief, useful things to pleasant. Let nothing be pleasing to the sight except what can be done justly, piously, and religiously; nothing sweet to the hearing except what makes the soul better.

Thus soldiers have their loins girded in truth when, having despised the enticements of the flesh and the vanities of the world for the love of God, they strive with all their strength so to conduct themselves and live that they may be able in all things to please the highest truth, which is God. After this the soldier of Christ is commanded to put on the breastplate of justice, without which no one will be able to serve the Lord rightly and fruitfully. Justice, indeed, is to preserve and distribute to each person what is owed to him according to law or nature. And this is the most excellent of all virtues; without it there can be no piety, no religion, no holiness, and no discernment of good and greater things. For it is light and great splendor, from which the force and dominion of every good arise among mortals. Justice is the mother...

18
Homilia III. 21 innocentiae, concordiae nutrix, pares amicitiae, pietatis genitrix, et servatrix religionis. Iustitia, sicut testatur scriptura, perpetua est, et immortalis: inujustitia autem mortis est acquisitio. Quibus vero modis hanc iustitiae loricam Christianus miles debeat induere, ipse Salvator noster in Sancto Evangelio denunciat dicens: Omnia quaecunque vultis, ut faciant vobis homines, et vos facite illis similiter. Itaque fratres mei hunc vivendi modum in Monasterio servate, ut unusquisque commilitoni suo faciat in omnibus, quemadmodum sibi ab aliis fieri secundum rectum rationis iudicium omni tempore desiderat. Hoc est enim primum iustitiae munus, ne cui quis noceat, deinde, ut communibus utatur sine cuiusquam detrimento alterius: et, quod nostra ulterior requirit militia, id faciat fratri, quod ad salutem iusta ratione conducit, ut proprium. O quanta pace fruuerentur mortales, si hortamenta sectarentur Apostoli, qua onera portare alterius, alter praecipitur. Omnis inquit scriptura, qui facit iustitiam, ex Deo natus est. Haec est lorica iustitiae, fratres, mandata Dei custodire, proximum suum diligere, et Deum super omnia ferventissime amare. Hoc est indumentum militiae nostrae fortissimum, Deo cultum, et pietatem: nobis sanctimoniam: et proximo fraternam exhibere charitatem. Omnes sub iustitiae trophaeo Christo militamus. Si quis inujustus fuerit, non ad Christi militiam, sed potius ad daemonum se pertinere consortium ostendit. Iustitia namque virtus est maxima, quae uniuicuique, quod suum est, distribuit: quam nisi diligentissime custodieris, et Monachi, et militis vocabulum amittis. Redde igitur Deo cultum, et pietatem, superiori tuo, sive rectori obedientiam, simul, et reverentiam, quarum altera cordis, altera vero est operis. Neque enim sufficit exterius obtemperare maioribus, nisi ex intimo cordis affectu similiter de eis recte sentiamus. Haec namque vera iustitia Monachorum est, fratres, qua unusquisque iuxta praescriptam legis normam sine offensione conversatur, tribuens uniuicuique suam propriam dignitatem, maiori suo reverentiam, pari concordiam, minori disciplinam, Deo cultum, et obedientiam, sibi sanctimoniam, inimico patientiam, pauperi misericordiam, omnibus fraternam in Domino charitatem. Ergo sacer Christophilus inquit: Debitores sumus fratres, non carni, ut secundum carnem, vivamus. Si enim secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini: si autem spiritu facta carnis mortificaveritis, vivetis. Recte igitur militat Deo, qui distribuit uniuicuique, quod suum est. Calciatos dehinc pedes habere iubemur in praeparationem Evangelii pacis, quatenus bonum, quod ipsi Domino largiente cognovimus, etiam aliis hilariter communicemus. Lex enim nostra, fratres, secundum quam Domino militare iubemur, Evangelium est Iesu Christi, ad quod omnes claustralium regulae, et constitutiones ordinantur. Non enim propter constitutiones Monasticas Evangelium, sed propter Evangelium statuta sunt facta Mo- 22 Quae sit armatura militiae spiritualis.

Homily III.

the guardian of innocence, the nurse of concord, the parent of friendship, the begetter of piety, and the preserver of religion. Justice, as Scripture testifies, is everlasting and immortal; injustice, however, is the acquisition of death. But in what ways the Christian soldier ought to put on this breastplate of justice, our Savior himself declares in the Holy Gospel, saying: “All things whatsoever you wish that men should do to you, do you also likewise to them.”

Therefore, my brothers, keep this manner of living in the monastery: let each one do to his fellow-soldier in all things as, according to the right judgment of reason, he desires at all times that others should do to him. For this is the first duty of justice: that no one harm anyone; then, that he use common things without detriment to anyone else; and, as our further warfare requires, that he do for his brother, as for himself, what by just reason conduces to salvation.

O what great peace mortals would enjoy if they followed the exhortations of the Apostle, by which each is commanded to bear another’s burdens. “Everyone,” says Scripture, “who does justice is born of God.” This is the breastplate of justice, brothers: to keep God’s commandments, to love one’s neighbor, and to love God most fervently above all things. This is the strongest garment of our warfare: to show worship and devotion to God, holiness to ourselves, and brotherly charity to our neighbor.

We all serve Christ under the trophy of justice. If anyone is unjust, he shows that he belongs not to Christ’s army but rather to the fellowship of demons. For justice is the greatest virtue, which distributes to each what is his own; unless you guard it most diligently, you lose the name both of monk and of soldier. Therefore render worship and devotion to God; obedience, together with reverence, to your superior or ruler, the one belonging to action and the other to the heart. For it is not enough to obey superiors outwardly unless, from the inmost affection of the heart, we likewise think rightly of them.

This indeed, brothers, is the true justice of monks: by it each person lives without offense according to the prescribed rule of the law, giving to each his own proper dignity: reverence to his superior, concord to his equal, discipline to his inferior, worship and obedience to God, holiness to himself, patience to his enemy, mercy to the poor, and brotherly charity in the Lord to all.

Therefore holy Christophilus says: “We are debtors, brothers, not to the flesh, so as to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” Therefore he rightly serves God as a soldier who distributes to each what is his own.

Next we are commanded to have our feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace, so that the good which we ourselves, by the Lord’s bounty, have come to know, we may also gladly share with others. For our law, brothers, according to which we are commanded to serve the Lord, is the Gospel of Jesus Christ, to which all the rules and constitutions of cloistered persons are ordered. For the Gospel was not made for the sake of monastic constitutions, but monastic statutes were made for the sake of the Gospel.

19
nachorum. Christianus namque salvari potest, non Monachus, sed Monachus salvari non poterit, nisi fuerit Christianus. Pudeat quosdam nimis superstitionis, et fatuos claustrales, qui regulas, et statuta sua pluris faciunt, quam Evangelium Christi, qui traditiones hominum custodiant usque ad carceres, et vincula, Dei autem constitutiones, et Sanctae universalis Ecclesiae non advertunt. His verba Salvatoris nostri recte conveniunt, Iudaeis et Matthaeum dicentis, Quare et vos transgredimini mandatum Dei propter traditionem vestram? Evangelica namque doctrina, omnibus totius mundi constitutionibus longe est praferenda. Post Evangelium vero primum auctoritatis locum statuta obtinent Ecclesiae universalis: et nullae Monachorum constitutiones, aut regulae illis dignitate comparantur. Curemus ad Evangelicam vivere puritatem, et erimus in Monastica patrum conversatione perfecti. Sint pedes nostri calciati semper in praeparationem Evangelii pacis, ut mortificemus in nobis desideria carnis, et per amorem Dei, et proximi pacem habeamus cum omnibus. Nam sine pace, et concordia fraternitatis, nihil prodest maceratio carnis, Sancto dicente Hieronymo: Quisquis corpus affigit, sed concordiam deserit, Deum quidem laudat in tympano, sed non laudat in choro. Hinc Salomon pacificum laudans virum dicit in Proverbii: Melior est buccella sicca cum gaudio, quam domus plena victimis cum iurgio. Et iterum: Honor, inquit, est homini, qui separat se a contentiobibus, omnes autem stulti miscentur contumeliis. Sanctus etiam Christophilus amator pacis nos admonet dicens: Pacem sequimini cum omnibus, et sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo videbit Deum. Unde et Prophetae Zacharias: Pacem, et veritatem diligit, dicit Dominus omnipotens. Et Salvator noster dicit in Sancto Evangelio secundum Marcum. Habete in vobis sal, et pacem habeate inter vos. Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus. Is autem vere miles est Christi, qui pacem habet cum Deo, cum proximo, et in semetipso. Cum Deo pacem habere homo dicitur, qui bona voluntate motus, et conversus ad ipsum per continuum amoris desiderium, contemptis transitoriis, mentis aciem ad superna dirigit, et omnia, quae Dominus praecipit, diligentissime custodit. Nato enim in carne Dei Filio, Sancti Angeli Domino gloriam cecinerunt, qui super omnia residet in excelsis, et pacem annunciarunt hominibus bonae voluntatis. Impii autem, et iniusti homines hanc cum Deo pacem habere nequeunt, quoniam suas a Domino voluntates averterunt. Pacem vero habet cum proximo, qui nulli facit iniuriam, qui laesus non reddit vindictam, sed malum vincens in bono, fraternam numquam deserit charitatem. Si contra hunc tamem proximorum, quispiam iniuste murmurat, non ideo miles Christi deseruit pacem, quia forsan aliis instituit sine causa iusta iniustam murmurationem. Iustus homo, qui pacem cum Deo habet, nulli cupiens nocere proximorum, recte dicetur pacificus, etiam

of monks. For a Christian can be saved without being a monk, but a monk cannot be saved unless he is a Christian. Let certain overly superstitious and foolish cloisterers be ashamed, who value their rules and statutes more than the Gospel of Christ, who keep human traditions even to prisons and chains, but pay no heed to the ordinances of God and of the holy universal Church. To these the words of our Savior rightly apply, when he says to the Jews in Matthew: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?” For the teaching of the Gospel is to be preferred far above all the constitutions of the whole world. After the Gospel, the statutes of the universal Church hold the first place of authority, and no constitutions or rules of monks are comparable to them in dignity. Let us take care to live in evangelical purity, and we shall be perfect in the monastic way of life of the fathers. Let our feet always be shod for the preparation of the Gospel of peace, so that we may mortify in ourselves the desires of the flesh, and through love of God and neighbor may have peace with all. For without the peace and concord of brotherhood, the chastising of the flesh profits nothing, as Saint Jerome says: “Whoever afflicts the body but abandons concord does indeed praise God on the timbrel, but he does not praise him in the choir.” Hence Solomon, praising the peaceful man, says in Proverbs: “Better is a dry morsel with joy than a house full of victims with strife.” And again he says: “It is an honor for a man to separate himself from disputes, but all fools become entangled in insults.” Saint Christophilus, too, a lover of peace, admonishes us, saying: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God.” Hence also the prophet Zechariah says: “Love peace and truth,” says the Lord Almighty. And our Savior says in the holy Gospel according to Mark: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.” “There is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord. But he is truly a soldier of Christ who has peace with God, with his neighbor, and within himself. A man is said to have peace with God when, moved by good will and turned toward him through a continual desire of love, despising transitory things, he directs the sharp gaze of his mind to heavenly things, and most diligently keeps all that the Lord commands. For when the Son of God was born in the flesh, the holy angels sang glory to the Lord, who dwells above all in the highest, and announced peace to men of good will. But wicked and unjust men cannot have this peace with God, because they have turned their wills away from the Lord. He has peace with his neighbor who does injury to no one, who, when injured, does not return vengeance, but, overcoming evil with good, never abandons brotherly charity. If anyone among his neighbors murmurs unjustly against such a man, the soldier of Christ has not for that reason abandoned peace, because perhaps another, without just cause, has begun an unjust murmuring. A just man, who has peace with God and desires to harm none of his neighbors, will rightly be called peaceable, even [unclear].

20
Homilia III. 23 si contra illum consurgat iniuste quicunque perturbatus. Dicit enim vir justus: Cum his, qui oderunt pacem, eram pacificus: cum loquebar illis, impugnabant me gratis. Hinc Sanctus Augustinus loquitur: Apud veros Dei cultores etiam ipsa bella pacata sunt, quae non cupiditate, aut cru- delitate, sed pacis studio geruntur, ut mali coercentur, et boni suble- ventur. In semetipso pacem habet, qui puritate, ac sanctimonia illu- stratus, in conscientia sua vivit, sine errore securus, quem synderesis non remordet anxia, nec iniusta cogitatio perturbat, vel iniqua. Unde rursus Augustinus, Pax est serenitas mentis, tranquillitas animi, sim- plicitas cordis, vinculum amoris, consortium charitatis. Haec est, quae inimicitias, et simultates tollit, bella compescit, iras comprimit, superbos calcat, humiles amat, discordes sedat, inimicos concordat, cunctis est placida, nulli gravis, nulli molesta, nulli onerosa, nescit extolli, nescit inflari. Hanc, qui accipit, teneat, qui perdidit, repetat, qui amisit, ex- quirat: quoniam qui in eadem inventus non fuerit, a patre abdicatur, a filio exhaeredatur, et nihilominus a Spiritu Sancto alienus efficitur. Ad haereditatem Domini numquam potest accedere, qui testamentum pacis noluit observare. Locus enim Dei in pace est, diaboli autem mansio in ira, et perturbatione. Omnis itaque homo, qui hanc triplicem pacem in corde suo non habuerit, qui eam in ore non praestiterit, nec in operibus ostenderit, nec Monachus est dicendus, nec Christianus. Hinc dicit in Evangelio Dominus, Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur. Si Dei vocantur Filii, qui pacem faciunt, proculdubio Satanae sunt filii, qui pacem confundunt. Unde fratres mei charissimi habete inter vos pacem illam, quam mundus dare non potest, quae est pax Dei, et Do- mini nostri Iesu Christi, de qua dixit Esaias Prophetae: Et erit opus iu- stitiae pax, et cultus iustitiae silentium, et securitas usque in semp- ternum. Deus enim pacis, et dilectionis est Dominus: unde quicumque pacem, et fraternam dilectionem violat, quod verus Dei amator non sit, manifestat. Si pax Christi vera in cordibus vestris, et nulla huius mundi adversa formidabit. Inter vos etiam sit pax vera, non fucata, quoniam Christus pacem non ex ore, sed ex corde desiderat, et affectu potius, quam labiis vult proximum salutari. Unde si contristaverit quispiam ex vobis in aliquo fratre suum, satisfaciat illi quamprimum ante solis occasum, et cavete omnes, ne sol occidat super iracundiam vestram, quoniam ira inveterata generat odium, et spoliat animam omni ornatu virtutum. Ergo, Monache, si peccaveris in fratre tuum, mox age poe- nitiam coram eo, ac procidens ad genua veniam precare. Et gladium, inquit, spiritus, quod est verbum Dei, per omnem orationem, et obse- rationem in manibus Christi, milites, semper teneamus. Verbum Dei, quod in Sanctis continetur scripturis, victoriosum est contra omnes dae- monum incursiones munimen, sicut Salvatoris nostri monemur exemplo, Psal. 119. Pacis en- comion. Psal. 75. Matt. 5. Esa. 12. 1. Cor. 14. 2. Cor. 13. 1. Thes. 5. 2. Thes. 3. Eph. 4. Verbum Dei, gladius Spiritus. 24 De lectione, et studio divinarum scripturarum.

if anyone, being disturbed, rises up unjustly against him. For the righteous man says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.” Hence Saint Augustine says: “Among the true worshippers of God even wars themselves are peaceful, when they are waged not from greed or cruelty, but from zeal for peace, so that the wicked may be restrained and the good assisted.” He has peace within himself who, illumined by purity and holiness, lives in his own conscience secure, without error, whom anxious synderesis does not gnaw, nor any unjust or wicked thought disturb. Hence Augustine again says: “Peace is serenity of mind, tranquillity of soul, simplicity of heart, the bond of love, the fellowship of charity. It is this that removes enmities and rivalries, restrains wars, suppresses anger, treads down the proud, loves the humble, calms those at odds, reconciles enemies, is pleasing to all, burdensome to none, troublesome to none, oppressive to none; it does not know how to exalt itself, it does not know how to be puffed up. Let him who receives it hold it fast; let him who has lost it seek it again; let him who has let it slip search for it, because whoever is not found in it is cast off by the Father, disinherited by the Son, and likewise made a stranger to the Holy Spirit. He can never come to the inheritance of the Lord who has refused to observe the testament of peace.”

For the place of God is in peace, but the dwelling of the devil is in anger and disturbance. Therefore every man who does not have this threefold peace in his heart, who has not offered it in speech, nor shown it in works, is to be called neither a monk nor a Christian. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” If those who make peace are called sons of God, beyond doubt those who confound peace are sons of Satan. Therefore, my most beloved brothers, have among yourselves that peace which the world cannot give, which is the peace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, of which Isaiah the prophet said: “And the work of justice shall be peace, and the practice of justice silence and security forever.” For the Lord is the God of peace and love; hence whoever violates peace and brotherly love shows that he is not a true lover of God.

If the true peace of Christ is in your hearts, you will fear no adversities of this world. Among you also let there be true peace, not counterfeit, because Christ desires peace not from the mouth but from the heart, and wishes one’s neighbor to be greeted with affection rather than with the lips. Therefore, if anyone among you has in any way grieved his brother, let him make satisfaction to him as soon as possible before sunset, and all of you take care that the sun not go down upon your anger, because anger grown old begets hatred and strips the soul of every adornment of the virtues. Therefore, monk, if you have sinned against your brother, do penance before him at once, and falling at his knees beg pardon. “And the sword,” he says, “of the Spirit, which is the word of God,” through every prayer and supplication: as soldiers of Christ, let us always hold it in our hands. The word of God, which is contained in the holy Scriptures, is a victorious defense against all assaults of demons, as we are warned by the example of our Savior,

21
qui tentatus a diabolo, tranquilla mansuetudine in faciem eius scripturarum Divinarum testimonia iaculavit dicens, Scriptum est, non in solo pane vivit homo, sed in omni verbo, quod procedit ab ore Dei. Et tu monache, Christo militans, quotiescumque tentaris a diabolo, fronti mox imprimito signum sanctae crucis, et dico cum sancto Ioanne Chrysostomi in homilia quadam: Abrenuncio tibi, satana, cum omnibus iniqutatibus tuis, et coniungo me tibi, Iesu Christe fili Dei vivi, quia scriptum est: Anima, quae peccaverit, ipsa morietur. Hic est gladius spiritus ab utraque parte acutissimus, quem si manibus in hostem mox a principio tentationis semper vibraveris, cunctas eius machinationes, et insidias Deo protegente facile superabis. Dicit enim scriptura, Resistite diabolo, et fugiet a vobis. Itaque mane de strato consurgens eam mox facito, quam dixi contra salutis tuae adversarium contestationem: et neque diabolus, neque homo perversus tibi nocere poterit incantatione, aut maleficio, sive spaticum sit illud, sive aliud. Hoc ipsum dormiturus ad noctem facito: et quoties aliquam in cogitatione maligni spiritus perceperis insurgere tentationem. Sicque tutus eris in omnibus viis tuis, fugietque procul a te diabolus, nec tibi audebit accedere proprius, nisi tua te ignavia supplantaverit in primis, ut, vel abieceris gladium, vel mortale aliquid commiseris peccatum. Ait namque scriptura: Qui faciunt iniquitatem, et peccatum, hostes sunt animae suae. Salomon quoque dicit in Proverbiis: Iniquitates suae capiunt impium: et funibus peccatorum suorum constringitur. Ipse morietur, quia non habuit disciplinam: et in multitudine stultitiae suae decipietur. Idcirco, fratres charissimi, si habitare sub protectione omnipotentis Dei secure volueritis, peccatum fugite: quia peccatum nos a domini auxilio dividit: quemadmodum conscientiae puritas, et munditia Deo nos coniungit, dicente Esaia prophetae, Ecce non est abbreviata manus Domini, ut salvare nequeat, neque aggravata est auris eius, ut non exaudiat, sed iniquitates vestrae diviserunt inter vos, et Deum vestrum, et peccata vestra abscondentur faciem eius a vobis, ne exaudiaret. Hieremias quoque ait: Iniquitates nostrae declinaverunt haec, et peccata nostra prohibuerunt bonum a nobis. Omnis enim, qui mortaliter peccat, ianuam cordis sui diabolo aperit, Deo claudit, nec potest in adiutorium Altissimi confidere, quamdiu sine poenitentia in scelere permanserit iacere. De lectione, et studio divinarum scripturarum. Homilia IIII. Cum omnis scriptura divinitus inspirata, ut sacer Christophilus inquit, utilis sit ad docendum, vel ad arguendum, ad corripiendum, ad erudiendum in iustitia, ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum

who, when tempted by the devil, with calm meekness hurled in his face the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, saying: “It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” And you, monk, soldiering for Christ, whenever you are tempted by the devil, at once imprint on your forehead the sign of the holy cross, and say with Saint John Chrysostom in a certain homily: “I renounce you, Satan, with all your iniquities, and I join myself to you, Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, because it is written: The soul that has sinned, that soul shall die.” This is the sword of the spirit, sharpest on both sides; if you always brandish it in your hands against the enemy from the very beginning of temptation, with God protecting you, you will easily overcome all his schemes and snares. For Scripture says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Therefore, when you rise from your bed in the morning, at once make that protestation against the adversary of your salvation which I have described; and neither the devil nor a perverse man will be able to harm you by enchantment or sorcery, whether it be [unclear] or anything else. Do this same thing when you are about to sleep at night, and as often as you perceive any temptation of the evil spirit rising up in your thought. And thus you will be safe in all your ways, and the devil will flee far from you; nor will he dare to come nearer to you, unless your own sloth first trips you up, so that you either cast away the sword or commit some mortal sin. For Scripture says: “Those who commit iniquity and sin are enemies of their own soul.” Solomon also says in Proverbs: “His own iniquities ensnare the wicked man, and he is bound fast by the cords of his own sins. He shall die because he had no discipline, and in the multitude of his folly he shall be deceived.” Therefore, most beloved brothers, if you wish to dwell securely under the protection of almighty God, flee sin, because sin separates us from the Lord’s help, just as purity and cleanness of conscience join us to God, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened so that it cannot save, nor is his ear heavy so that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have made a division between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he would not hear.” Jeremiah also says: “Our iniquities have turned these things away, and our sins have withheld good from us.” For everyone who sins mortally opens the door of his heart to the devil and closes it to God, nor can he trust in the help of the Most High as long as he remains lying in wickedness without repentance.

On reading and the study of the divine Scriptures. Homily IV.

Since all Scripture, divinely inspired, as holy Christophilus says, is useful for teaching, or for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, for every good work

22
Homilia IIII. 25 instructus: libenter debemus lectioni divinarum scripturarum insistere, et omne studium literaturae secularis, in quo aliquando desudavimus, ad huius speculationis aciem ordinare. In scripturis namque divinis, quicquid salutaris requirit scientia, copiosissime reperitur expressum, ut, quod ibi non inveneris, minime ad salutem sit necessarium. Maiestas etenim divinarum scripturarum omnem totius mundi scientiam, atque doctrinam longe procul transcendit, quam spiritus sanctus hominibus Dei, ut scriberetur, infudit, et, ut intelligatur a studiosis lectoribus, illustrationis suae gratiam impendit. Hanc, fratres mei, scripturam sedulo cum puritate mentis, et fervore geminae charitatis revolvite, quoniam quisquis Deum veraciter diligit, omne tempus, quod invenife potest ad ocium, in sacris lectionibus consumit. Sint vobis incitamenta, precor, ad salubre studium scripturarum, furiosa, ut ita dixerim, gesta amatorum carnalium, qui literas, et eulogia suarum accipientes amatricum legere non cessant, saepiusque, et relegunt, et osculantur: et, quod maioris est indicium amoris, vel ad collum suspendunt, vel ad pectus, quatenus nunquam a mente recedat eius, quam cupiunt, dilectae memoria. Considerate, fratres, carnalium in amore dementiam, et vestram circa Dei amorem erubescite tepiditatem. Quis vestrum circa scripturas Dei sanctas tanto cordis amore afficitur, quanto caecus amator circa literas amato- rias spurcas, et vanissimas unius meretriculae insaniens praे dilectione inflammatur? Ille propter absentis, quam cupit, amore, literas, et mu- nuscula crebris osculis prosequitur, apices singulos praе nimio amore considerando, iteratis vicibus rimatur, in omnibus, quae agit, semper absentem cogitat, ad eius venire conspectum anxius festinat. O si nos, qui Monachi dicimur Christiani, qui Regi supremo, et immortali Christo Iesu militamus, qui Deum nostrum super omnia jubemur diligere, et nihil in hoc mundo praeter ipsum praecipimur amare, si inquam tanto Creatorem nostrum prosequeremur amore, quanto suas amicas corrupti- biles, et mortales observant, et diligunt homines carnaliter sapientes. Deum nobis scriptura sancta quotidie lecta insinuat, eius voluntatem nobis manifestat, quid facere debeamus, nos instruit, et, quid cavere pandit. Per ipsam Omnipotens nobiscum loquitur, et invisibili nos ma- gisterio informans consolatur, sancto dicente Apostolo: Quaecumque enim scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt; ut per patien- tiam, et consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Unde verus Christi miles, et praecipue claustralis, qui Deum in toto corde suo diligit, eique soli placere concupiscit, scripturas divinas, et maxime sanctum Evan- gelium affectuose amplectitur, et in eius lectione meditando assidue oc- cupatur. Quicunque autem divinarum scripturarum lectiones negligit, quod verus Dei amator non sit, manifeste ostendit. Sed quid ait ipsa scriptura? Qui avertit aurem suam, ne audiat legem, oratio eius erit 26 De lectione, et studio divinarum scripturarum.

Homily IV.

Having been instructed, we should gladly devote ourselves to the reading of divine Scripture, and direct all study of secular literature, in which we once labored, to the keen vision of this contemplation. For in the divine Scriptures whatever saving knowledge requires is found most abundantly expressed, so that what you do not find there is by no means necessary for salvation. For the majesty of the divine Scriptures far surpasses all the knowledge and teaching of the whole world; the Holy Spirit infused it into the men of God so that it might be written, and, so that it might be understood by studious readers, bestowed the grace of his illumination.

My brothers, diligently turn over this Scripture with purity of mind and the fervor of twofold charity, since whoever truly loves God spends all the time he can find for leisure in sacred readings. Let the frenzied actions, so to speak, of carnal lovers be an incentive to you, I pray, toward the wholesome study of the Scriptures: they receive letters and tokens from their beloved women and do not cease to read them, and often read them again and kiss them; and, what is a greater sign of love, they either hang them from their neck or place them on their breast, so that the cherished memory of the one they desire may never depart from their mind.

Consider, brothers, the madness of carnal men in love, and be ashamed of your own lukewarmness in the love of God. Which of you is moved toward the holy Scriptures of God with as great a love of heart as a blind lover, raving with desire for one little prostitute, is inflamed toward filthy and utterly vain love letters? Because of love for the absent woman whom he desires, he follows her letters and little gifts with frequent kisses; he examines each letter with excessive love and searches it again and again; in everything he does he is always thinking of the absent woman, and anxiously hastens to come into her sight.

O if we who are called Christian monks, who serve the supreme and immortal King Christ Jesus, who are commanded to love our God above all things and are instructed to love nothing in this world except him, if, I say, we were to pursue our Creator with as much love as carnally minded men attend to and love their corruptible and mortal women friends. Holy Scripture, read daily, makes God known to us, reveals his will to us, instructs us what we ought to do, and discloses what we ought to avoid. Through it the Almighty speaks with us, and, forming us by invisible instruction, comforts us, as the holy Apostle says: Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.

Therefore the true soldier of Christ, and especially the cloistered man, who loves God with his whole heart and desires to please him alone, embraces the divine Scriptures with affection, and especially the holy Gospel, and is continually occupied in meditating upon its reading. But whoever neglects the readings of the divine Scriptures plainly shows that he is not a true lover of God. But what does Scripture itself say? He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer shall be...

23
Psal. 118. execrabilis. Beati vero, qui scrutantur testimonia Domini, in toto corde exquirunt eum. Vos itaque, fratres mei, si Dominum Iesum in toto corde vestro veraciter diligitis, si complacere illi super omnia, ut veri milites desideratis, si denique ad perfectionem vitae Monasticae cupitis proficere, in lectione divinarum scripturarum debetis vos semper cum affectione fervida occupare. Quam sit utilis lectio scripturarum, Beatus Hieronymus insinuat dicens: Ama scientiam scripturarum, et carnis vitia non amabis. Nihil enim post Deum in hac vita suavius sumitur, nihil dulcius sentitur, nihil mentem ab amore huius mundi validius separat, nihil contra omnes adversariorum tentationes militem Christi adeo confortat, nihil Monachum ad omne opus bonum in tantum disponit, et confirmat, quemadmodum lectio frequens, et studium ardens scripturarum. Enimvero si Omnipotentis beneficia, quae humano impendit generi, per totam late scripturam legendo ad memoriam studiosa devotione reducimus, materiam, et occasionem praestabunt nobis maximam, qua in Dei amore per amplius ardentes proficiamus. Tota enim series divinarum scripturarum quid continet aliud, quam textum quendam bonorum ordinem, quae Deus hominibus, vel iam praestitit, vel etiam se daturum repromisit? Aut quid est, quod nos ad tolerantiam malorum adeo corroborare queat, et voluntarie reddere patientes, sicut si legamus in Evangelio passum innocenter pro nobis Dei Filium, et post eum martyrum victorias sanctorum? Sacra namque scriptura continet, quae nobis ad scientiam salutarem sunt necessaria, et monet nos, quid in hac peregrinatione militantes utiliter debeamus appetere, quid etiam declinare. Hinc divus iterum dicit Hieronymus: Nostrae divitiae sunt in lege Dei meditari die, ac nocte. Praeparemus igitur nobis fortitudinem, assumamus nobis perfectum robur, ut inter errorum tenebras, et confusionem noctis scientiae Christi lumen appareat, diesque, et noctes lucem habeant pro-tegentem, ut scriptura duce ad terram sanctam pervenire valeamus. Quidnam hac eruditione melius? quid suavius disciplina? Quid dulcius Domino nostro Iesu Christo, qui vera est salus, et dulcedo fidelium animarum? Sit autem nobis convivium Christus; sit lectio sacra cibus noster, et potus. Quid enim potest esse vita monachi sacerdotis sine scientia scripturarum? Christum non visu, non auditu, non tactu, sed lectione scripturarum cognoscimus; et quanto plus legendo ad veram scientiam proficimur, tanto in scripturis sanctis amplius delectamur. Quid enim dulcius, quam Dei scire voluntatem, et promissionum precia non ignorare? Nam sicut Hieronymus dicit: Pinguissimus est ager divini sermonis, qui omnes in se habet delicias, et quicquid volueris, ex illo nascitur, sicut tradunt Iudaei, quod manna in deserto quando co-medebatur, secundum voluntatem, et desiderium in ore sapiebat come-dentis. Divinas igitur scripturas fratres mei saepius legite, per quas

Blessed indeed are those who search the testimonies of the Lord; with their whole heart they seek him.

And so, my brothers, if you truly love the Lord Jesus with your whole heart, if as true soldiers you desire to please him above all things, if, finally, you long to advance toward the perfection of the monastic life, you ought always to occupy yourselves with fervent affection in the reading of the divine Scriptures. How useful the reading of the Scriptures is, blessed Jerome indicates when he says: Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.

For after God nothing in this life is taken up more pleasantly, nothing is felt more sweetly, nothing separates the mind more powerfully from love of this world, nothing so greatly strengthens the soldier of Christ against all the temptations of his adversaries, nothing disposes and confirms a monk so much for every good work, as frequent reading and ardent study of the Scriptures. Indeed, if by reading throughout the whole wide range of Scripture we recall with studious devotion the benefits of the Almighty which he has bestowed on the human race, they will provide us with the greatest matter and occasion by which we may advance, burning ever more in the love of God. For what else does the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures contain than a certain ordered text of the good things which God has either already bestowed on human beings or has promised that he will yet give?

Or what is there that can so strengthen us to endure evils and make us willingly patient as if we read in the Gospel that the Son of God suffered innocently for us, and after him the victories of the holy martyrs? For Sacred Scripture contains the things that are necessary for us for saving knowledge, and it warns us what, as soldiers in this pilgrimage, we ought usefully to seek, and what also to avoid.

Hence again the divine Jerome says: Our riches are to meditate on the law of God day and night. Therefore let us prepare strength for ourselves; let us take up perfect power, so that amid the darkness of errors and the confusion of night the light of the knowledge of Christ may appear, and days and nights may have a protecting light, so that, with Scripture as guide, we may be able to reach the holy land.

What is better than this learning? What is sweeter than this discipline? What is more delightful than our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true salvation and sweetness of faithful souls? Let Christ be our banquet; let sacred reading be our food and drink. For what can the life of a monk-priest be without knowledge of the Scriptures? We know Christ not by sight, not by hearing, not by touch, but by the reading of the Scriptures; and the more we advance by reading toward true knowledge, the more we delight in the holy Scriptures.

For what is sweeter than to know the will of God and not to be ignorant of the rewards of the promises? For as Jerome says: The field of the divine word is exceedingly rich; it has all delights within itself, and whatever you wish is born from it, just as the Jews relate that when the manna was eaten in the desert, it tasted in the mouth of the one eating according to his will and desire.

Therefore, my brothers, read the divine Scriptures more often, through which

24
Homilia IIII. 27 potestis voluntatem Dei plane cognoscere, et contra insidias diaboli fortissime vos armare. Nam si iuxta Apostolum Paulum Christus Dei virtus est, et Dei sapientia, qui nescit scripturas, nescit Dei virtutem, et sapientiam, et Christum quomodo sciet? Ignorantia enim scriptura- rum, ignorantia est Christi: et qui nescit Christum, ad eius non perti- nebit consortium, sancto dicente Christophilo, quoniam siquis ignorat certe, et ignorabitur. Quanto autem quis in studio divinarum scriptu- rarum magis assiduus fuerit, tanto ex earum lectione maiorem intelli- gentiam, et dulcitudinem capit. Vos autem maxime decet fratres divinas scripturas quotidie legendo, et discendo revolvere, quibus et tempus co- piosum ab occupationibus feriatum conceditur, et locus raritate occur- rentium satis conveniens affertur. Idecirco vos hortor, et moneo, si ve- stram salutem diligitis, ut divinas lectiones in manibus semper habeatis, quatenus omne tempus, quod vobis post orationis cultum sine labore permittitur, ad sacrae scripturae studium expendatur. Non praetereat dies ulla, fratres mei, in qua monachus Christo militans non aliquid legat ex sacris voluminibus, quod eum in sancto proposito faciat meliorem. Quin potius divi Hieronymi sequatur consilium dicentis: Sint scripturae semper in manibus divinae, et iugiter mente volvantur, nec tibi suffi- cere putes mandata Dei memoriae recondere, nisi studeas illa etiam operibus adimplere. Duo enim Deus a nobis, fratres mei, requirit. Primo enim vult nos scire sanctissimam voluntatem suam, secundo ut agnitus faciamus. Scire autem eius mandata non possimus, si divinarum scri- pturarum scientiam ignoraremus. Neque voluntatem Dei facit, qui eam ignorat, neque scit, qui non didicit. Discito igitur, quae sit Dei voluntas beneplacens, ut facias: facito cognitam, ut amplius intelligas. Nemo enim Dei voluntatem melius intelligit, quam ille, qui cognitam ex amore facit. Itaque si doctissimus divinarum scripturarum paraphrastes cupis evadere, non a verbis, sed a sanctis operibus scientiae studium discas inchoare. Tunc enim sacrae lectionis uberem comprehendes scientiam, si mundum custodieris cor tuum ab omni peccato, et fervens in Dei amore sanctam compunctus iugiter revolveris scripturam. Scientia enim divinarum scripturarum altus est mons, in quo cum domino Moyses loquitur, ad quem ascendere vitiorum sordibus pollutus homo prohi- betur. Sic nanque in Exodo legitur: Cavete, ne ascendatis in montem, Exod. 19. nec tangatis fines illius. Omnis, qui tetigerit montem, morte morietur. Sive iumentum fuerit, sive homo, non vivet. Homo si quidem montem tangit, et moritur, quoties quis literatura seculari turgidus in simpli- citate divinarum scripturarum scandalizatur. Bestia vero montem tangit, et lapidibus obruitur, quoties homo carnalium furore passionum im- mersus ad sacrae scripturae studium non purgatus animo progredivit. Si ergo lectiones divinarum scripturarum salubriter vultis evolvere, si 28 De lectione, et studio divinarum scripturarum.

you can plainly know God’s will, and arm yourselves most strongly against the snares of the devil. For if, according to the Apostle Paul, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, then he who does not know the Scriptures does not know God’s power and wisdom; and how will he know Christ? For ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ; and he who does not know Christ will not belong to his fellowship, as Saint Christophilus says: if anyone is ignorant, surely he too will be ignored.

Moreover, the more constant anyone has been in the study of the divine Scriptures, the greater understanding and sweetness he gains from reading them. But it especially befits you, brothers, to turn over the divine Scriptures daily by reading and learning them, since you are granted both abundant time, free from occupations, and a place sufficiently suitable because few people come there. Therefore I exhort and admonish you, if you love your salvation, always to have divine readings in your hands, so that all the time allowed you without labor after the service of prayer may be spent on the study of sacred Scripture. Let no day pass, my brothers, on which a monk fighting for Christ does not read something from the sacred books that may make him better in his holy purpose.

Rather, let him follow the counsel of the divine Jerome, who says: Let the divine Scriptures always be in your hands, and let them be continually turned over in your mind; and do not think it enough for you to store God’s commandments in memory, unless you also strive to fulfill them in deeds. For God requires two things of us, my brothers. First, he wants us to know his most holy will; second, that once it is known we should do it. But we cannot know his commandments if we are ignorant of the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Nor does he do God’s will who is ignorant of it, nor does he know it who has not learned it. Learn, then, what God’s pleasing will is, so that you may do it; do it once known, so that you may understand it more fully. For no one understands God’s will better than he who, once he has known it, does it out of love.

And so, if you desire to become a most learned interpreter of the divine Scriptures, learn to begin your pursuit of knowledge not from words but from holy works. For then you will grasp the rich knowledge of sacred reading, if you keep your heart clean from every sin and, fervent in the love of God, continually turn over holy Scripture with compunction. For the knowledge of the divine Scriptures is a high mountain, on which Moses speaks with the Lord; and a man polluted with the filth of vices is forbidden to climb it. Thus we read in Exodus: Take care not to go up the mountain, nor touch its borders. Everyone who touches the mountain shall surely die. Whether it is a beast or a man, it shall not live.

Indeed, a man touches the mountain and dies whenever someone, swollen with secular learning, takes offense at the simplicity of the divine Scriptures. But a beast touches the mountain and is overwhelmed with stones whenever a man, plunged in the fury of carnal passions, advances to the study of sacred Scripture without a purified mind. Therefore, if you wish to turn over the readings of the divine Scriptures in a healthful way, if

25
ad veram scientiam legendo cupitis pervenire, omnem curate in primis, et elationem superbiae, et temeritate perfidia deponere, ac deinde cubiculum cordis vestri ab omni immunditia carnalium voluptatum expurgare. Deus enim, ut ait scriptura canonica, superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Nemo superbus, elatus, arrogans, et temerarius, nemo carnalis animo, luxuriosus, vel inquietus ad studium sacrae scripturae habetur idoneus, sed humilis dumtaxat, mitis, mansuetus, pudicus, castus corpore, et mente tranquillus. Hinc Prosper in epigrammate dicit: Mandata Dei scrutari nisi quies mens non potest. Ut ergo religiosum exercetur studium, abiicienda sunt iurgia malignorum. Scrutari legem possunt utcumque quietae, si mundi a strepitu libera corda vacent. Ut mens ergo piis studiis intenta invenitur, praedia divinus carnea vincat amor. Nam templum Domini per sacra silentia crescit, et tacite struitur non ruitura domus. Mundatis igitur animis, et corde in Dei amore compuncto, atque in vera contritione humiliato ad studium scripturarum procedite, quia non illuminabit vos Dominus, nisi ab omni prius fecerit iniquitate purgatos. Nanque, ut scriptura ipsa dicit, perversae cogitationes separant a Deo, probata autem virtus corripit insipientes, quoniam in malevolam animam non introbit sapientia, nec habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis: quia spiritus sanctus disciplinae effugiet fictum, et auferet se a cogitationibus, quae sunt sine intellectu. Ideoque orandum nobis est cum sancto David crebrius ad Dominum: Cor mundum crea in me Deus, et spiritum rectum innova in visceribus meis. Nemo enim sacras Dei scripturas utiliter intelligit, qui se in toto corde suo ad Dominum per potentiam non convertit. Ideoque, si vultis divina eloquia et recte, et salubriter intelligere, summo in primis curate studio, mundos vos ab omni pollutione peccati pro viribus custodire. Non vos, precor, seducat quorundam monachorum vaesana stultitia, qui suam ignorantiam trito conantur excusare proverbio, dicentes: Ad quid nobis scientia scripturarum, qui praedicationis nullum habemus officium? Viri sapientis amplectimur consilium, qui dicit in libro Proverbiorum: Qui ambulat simpliciter, ambulat confidenter. Sufficit nobis simpliciter vivere: quoniam servus sciens voluntatem Domini sui, et non faciens vapulabit plagis multis: qui autem non cognovit, et commisit digna plagis, vapulabit paucis. O stulti, et perditissimi petrones, qui scientiam salutarem contemnitis, et ignorantiam divinarum scripturarum potius, quam intelligentiam amatis: Nunquid affectata ignorantia paucioribus vos plagis reddet obnoxios? Aut propterea delinquentes eritis coram Deo innoxii, quia mandatorum Dei voluntarie estis ignari? Duplici poena cruciandi eritis, altera quod scire viam mandatorum Dei contemnitis, altera quod sermones eius non custoditis. Non est, quam allegatis, simplicitas, sed duplex

If by reading you desire to attain true knowledge, take care first of all to lay aside every swelling of pride, all proud exaltation, and rash perfidy, and then to cleanse the chamber of your heart from every uncleanness of carnal pleasures. For God, as canonical Scripture says, resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

No proud, puffed-up, arrogant, or rash person, no one carnal in mind, lustful, or restless, is held fit for the study of sacred Scripture, but only one who is humble, gentle, meek, modest, chaste in body, and tranquil in mind. Hence Prosper says in an epigram: “A mind cannot search out the commandments of God unless it is at rest. Therefore, that religious study may be practiced, the quarrels of the malicious must be cast away. Hearts that are in some measure quiet can search the law, if, free from the noise of the world, they have leisure. Therefore, that the mind may be found intent on holy studies, let divine love conquer carnal battles. For the temple of the Lord grows through sacred silence, and the house that will not fall is built in quiet.”

Therefore, with your souls cleansed, and your heart pierced in the love of God and humbled in true contrition, proceed to the study of the Scriptures, because the Lord will not enlighten you unless he has first made you purified from every iniquity. For, as Scripture itself says, perverse thoughts separate from God, and tested virtue rebukes the foolish, because wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins; for the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding. And therefore we must pray very often to the Lord with holy David: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts.”

For no one profitably understands the sacred Scriptures of God who does not turn himself with his whole heart to the Lord through repentance. And therefore, if you wish to understand the divine utterances both rightly and healthfully, take care first, with the utmost zeal, to keep yourselves, as far as you can, clean from every pollution of sin.

I beg you, do not let the mad folly of certain monks seduce you, who try to excuse their ignorance with a worn-out proverb, saying: “What need have we of knowledge of the Scriptures, since we have no office of preaching? We embrace the counsel of the wise man, who says in the book of Proverbs: ‘He who walks simply walks confidently.’ It is enough for us to live simply, because the servant who knew the will of his lord and did not do it will be beaten with many stripes; but he who did not know and did things worthy of stripes will be beaten with few.”

O foolish and utterly ruined champions, who despise saving knowledge and love ignorance of the divine Scriptures more than understanding: will ignorance deliberately chosen make you liable to fewer stripes? Or will you, when you sin, be innocent before God because you are willingly ignorant of the commandments of God? You will have to be tormented with a double punishment: one because you despise knowing the way of God’s commandments, the other because you do not keep his words. It is not simplicity, as you allege, but a double

26
Homilia IIII. 29 potius impietas. Nam, si iuxta prophetar beati sunt, qui scrutinantur testimonia Domini, quis dubitet illos esse maledictos, qui nec Deum exquirunt, nec scripturas eius advertunt, sed indurato magis animo contemnunt? Audite, quid vobis Salomon dicat in Proverbiis: Ubi non est scientia animae, non est bonum, et stultitia hominis supplantat gressus eius. De vobis etiam, o stultissimi tenebriones, illud intelligitur sancti Hieronymi, quoniam ibi non est ignorantia iam excusabilis, ubi scitur, quod sit illud, quod ignoratur. Magis autem cavendum vobis, ne cum illis tandem computemini, qui dixerunt Deo, recede a nobis, viam scientiarum tuarum nolumus. Verbum Salomonis male intelligitis, qui de ignorantia dictum simpliciter putatis. Qui ambulat simpliciter sine aliqua deceptione proximi, ambulat confidenter in custodiendo mandata Dei: qui autem depravat vias suas, non potest laterre, sed manifestus erit. Hinc rursus ait, Labia iusti erudient plurimos: qui autem indocti sunt, in cordis egestate morientur. Quid miserabilius sacerdote indocto, qui etiam praedicationis non habeat officium, ratione tamem suscepti ordinis ad scientiam obligatur scripturarum? Vult enim Deus, ut omnis homo sanctam eius voluntatem impleat, quam nemo facere sufficit, qui ignorat. Primo itaque iubet Dominus, ut eius beneplacitum discas, secundo ut facias. Quomodo igitur legis ignorantiam putabitis excusabilem, per quam facti estis primae voluntatis Dei transgressores? Quare putatis omnipotens Deus volumina hominibus suarum tradiderit scripturarum? An ut legerentur ab eis, intelligerenturque, vel, ut non lectae, contemnerentur? Certe, ut legerent eas, mortalibus sunt datae scripturae mandatorum Dei, postea vero, ut opere complerentur. Vos autem, qui Dei scripturas animo deliberato vultis ignorare, quomodo voluntatem eius, quam insinuant illae, potestis facere. Aut quemadmodum legis factores esse poteritis, qui auditores ante non fuistis? Fieri nanque potest, ut sciens voluntatem Dei, aut observet eam, aut negligat, sed fieri non potest, ut eam ignorans impleat. Enimvero facilius aliquis non faciet bonum, quod novit, quam impleat opere, quod ignorat. Nemo autem facit bonum, quod nescit. Dicit de ignorantibus in quodam loco sanctus Augustinus: Non omnis ignorans immunis est a culpa. Ille enim ignorans potest excusari a poena, qui, quod disceret, non invenit. Illis autem ignosci non poterit, qui a quo discent habentes, disciplinae operam non dederunt. Hinc, et sanctus Leo Papa dicit: Si in laicis videtur intollerabilis inscitia, quanto magis in his, qui praesunt, nec excusatione est digna, nec venia? Unde, frateres, non facit vos ignorantia divinarum scripturarum excusatos coram Deo, sed dupliciter reos, qui, ne Dei voluntatem oporteat vos facere, eam penitus cupitis ignorare. Homo enim divinae voluntatis non debet esse ignarus, qui ad hoc in mundo ponitur, ut per illustrationem intellectus, et puritatem affectus, 30 De lectione, et studio divinarum scripturarum.

rather, impiety. For if, according to the prophet, “blessed are those who search the testimonies of the Lord,” who can doubt that those are accursed who neither seek God nor attend to his scriptures, but rather despise them with hardened heart?

Hear what Solomon says to you in Proverbs: “Where there is no knowledge of the soul, there is no good, and a man’s folly trips up his steps.” Of you also, O most foolish children of darkness, that saying of Saint Jerome is understood: that ignorance is no longer excusable where it is known what the thing is that is not known. But you must take still greater care lest in the end you be counted with those who said to God, “Depart from us; we do not want the way of your sciences.”

You misunderstand Solomon’s word, thinking it was spoken simply about ignorance. “He who walks simply,” without any deception of his neighbor, walks confidently in keeping the commandments of God; but he who corrupts his ways cannot remain hidden, but will be made manifest. Hence again he says, “The lips of the righteous will instruct many; but those who are untaught will die in poverty of heart.”

What is more pitiable than an untaught priest, who, even if he does not have the office of preaching, is nevertheless, by reason of the order he has received, bound to knowledge of the scriptures? For God wills that every man fulfill his holy will, which no one who is ignorant of it is able to do. Therefore the Lord first commands that you learn what is pleasing to him, and secondly that you do it. How then will you think ignorance of the law excusable, through which you have been made transgressors of the first will of God?

Why do you think almighty God handed over to men the books of his scriptures? Was it so that they should be read by them and understood, or so that, unread, they should be despised? Certainly the scriptures of God’s commandments were given to mortals so that they might read them, and afterward so that they might fulfill them in deed. But you who with deliberate mind wish to be ignorant of God’s scriptures, how can you do his will, which they make known? Or how will you be able to be doers of the law, when you have not first been hearers? For it can happen that one who knows the will of God either observes it or neglects it; but it cannot happen that one who is ignorant of it fulfills it. Indeed, someone will more easily fail to do the good that he knows than fulfill in deed what he does not know. No one does the good that he does not know.

Saint Augustine says in a certain place concerning the ignorant: “Not everyone who is ignorant is free from guilt. For that ignorant man can be excused from punishment who did not find what he might learn. But those cannot be pardoned who, having someone from whom they might learn, did not apply themselves to instruction.” Hence Saint Leo the Pope also says: “If ignorance seems intolerable in laypeople, how much more in those who preside is it neither worthy of excuse nor of pardon?”

Therefore, brothers, ignorance of the divine scriptures does not make you excused before God, but doubly guilty, since, in order that you may not have to do God’s will, you desire to be utterly ignorant of it. For man ought not to be ignorant of the divine will, since he is placed in this world for this purpose: that through the illumination of the understanding and the purity of affection,

27
visionis eius sempiternam fruitionem promereat. Utraque enim cognition, Dei videlicet, et sui, unicuique mortalium necessaria est ad salutem, quam nusquam inveniet sine notitia scripturarum. Enimvero sic ut ex cognitione sui venit in hominem timor Dei, et ex notitia Dei nascitur amor Dei, ita provenit ex ignorantia sui superbia, et ex neglecta Dei cognitione cum desperatione salutis contemptus. Nihil infelicius monacho indocto, qui studium sanctarum scripturarum vel ignavus omittit, vel contemnit, quia nunquam potest in vera cordis tranquillitate apud semetipsum purus consistere, sed compellitur inquietudine propria contra monasticae conversationis integritatem externis mentem, et inutilibus occupare. Videmus inter vos quosdam scripturarum ignaros, instabiles, mente dyscolos, et vagos, quibus eo magis imputamus ignorantiam, quo minus inclinantur ad disciplinam. Turpe quidem nescire, quod scire iuberis: turpius non discere: turpissimum vero contemnere.
