Et sunt inter vos quidam, qui scientiam salutarem nesciunt: sunt etiam, qui discere negligunt: quid si addam esse et alios, qui scientiam divinarum scripturarum penitus contemnant? Certe non mentior: vos scitis, quia verum est, quod dico. Nam studiis meis nonnulli vestrum usque ad invidiam graviter adversati sunt aratores se nalle habere praelatum, quam oratores cavillantes. Nonne et visitatores in suam trahere sententiam tentaverunt, cupientes me illorum hortatu in abnegationem traducere scripturarum, ut ruricolam facerent, et porcorum curatorem potius, quam animarum? Sed frustra conantur divinum impedire oraculum, quo impellente omnes mundi honores, atque divitias, quamdiu vixero, studio postponere decrevi scripturarum, Abbas sum vester, quamdiu voluerit ille qui me vocavit, si alterum e duobus operteat, abbatiam malo dimittere, quam sancto scripturarum studio renunciare. Scio enim vere, nihil in hac vita homini claustralii salubrius posse contingere, quam si divinas coeperit scripturas veraciter amare. Quisquis vestrum hanc institutionem meam sequi voluerit, me ducem itineris pariter, et comitem habebit. Qui autem sequi discentem contempserit, docentem nihilominus audire compelletur, vel invitus. Haec dixerim in eos, qui terrena sapientes, et caduca timorem a se domini abiiciunt, qui omnia pene ignorantes discere contemnunt. Ego novi pecoris mei vultum: et singularum inclinationes cordium vestrorum me credo non penitus ignorare. Idcirco non cessabo vos cohortari ad sancta studia scripturarum, scius, quod amator sacrae lectionis non potest carnalium operator esse vitiorum. Quanta enim monachus in perdiscendis scripturis fuerit studiosior, tanto minus carnalium voluptatum ardoribus inflammatur. Quamvis enim iuxta sententiam divini Hieronymi monachus non docens, sed plangentis, potius videatur habere officium: quia tamen Christi profitetur militiam, congruit, immo necessarium est, ut

may merit the eternal enjoyment of his vision. For both kinds of knowledge, namely of God and of oneself, are necessary for every mortal person’s salvation, and he will nowhere find them without knowledge of the Scriptures.

Indeed, just as from knowledge of oneself the fear of God comes into a person, and from knowledge of God the love of God is born, so from ignorance of oneself comes pride, and from neglect of the knowledge of God come contempt and despair of salvation. Nothing is more wretched than an unlearned monk, who either through sloth omits the study of the holy Scriptures or despises it; for he can never remain pure within himself in true tranquility of heart, but is forced by his own restlessness, contrary to the integrity of monastic life, to occupy his mind with outward and useless things.

We see among you certain men ignorant of the Scriptures, unstable, difficult in mind, and wandering; and we blame their ignorance the more because they are the less inclined toward discipline. It is shameful not to know what you are commanded to know; more shameful not to learn; but most shameful of all to despise it. And there are among you some who do not know saving knowledge; there are also some who neglect to learn. What if I add that there are others too who utterly despise the knowledge of the divine Scriptures? Certainly I am not lying; you know that what I say is true.

For some of you have opposed my studies bitterly, even to the point of envy, quibbling that they wanted ploughmen rather than men of prayer as their prelate. Did they not also try to draw the visitors over to their opinion, desiring, by their urging, to bring me to a renunciation of the Scriptures, so that they might make me a tiller of fields and a keeper of pigs rather than of souls? But they strive in vain to hinder the divine oracle; under its impulse I have resolved, as long as I live, to set the study of the Scriptures before all the honors and riches of the world.

I am your abbot for as long as he who called me shall will it. If one of the two must be done, I would rather give up the abbacy than renounce the holy study of the Scriptures. For I truly know that nothing more wholesome can befall a cloistered man in this life than if he begins truly to love the divine Scriptures. Whoever among you wishes to follow this instruction of mine will have me alike as guide on the way and as companion. But whoever scorns to follow me as a learner will nevertheless be compelled to hear me as a teacher, even against his will.

I have said these things against those who, minding earthly and perishable things, cast away from themselves the fear of the Lord, who, though ignorant of almost everything, despise learning. I know the face of my flock, and I believe that I am not wholly ignorant of the inclinations of each of your hearts. Therefore I shall not cease to exhort you to the holy studies of the Scriptures, knowing that a lover of sacred reading cannot be a worker of fleshly vices. For the more zealous a monk has been in thoroughly learning the Scriptures, the less he is inflamed by the burning desires of fleshly pleasures. For although, according to the judgment of the divine Jerome, a monk seems to have the office not of teaching but rather of lamenting, yet because he professes the soldiery of Christ, it is fitting, indeed necessary, that

28
Homilia IIII. 31 Dei omnipotentis, in cuius verba iuravit et arma, beneplacitam noverit voluntatem. Verum sicut miles voluntatem domini sui procul absentis scire non potest, nisi per nuncios, et epistolas, ita monachus aeterni Regis praecipit non intelligit, nisi per sacras lectiones, atque sermones, et Evangelicas scripturas. Ianuam salutis nescientibus lectio scripturarum aperit, studiosum lectorem recto tramite ad Dei notitiam introducit, amatorem sui facit omnia mundana contemnere, et nihil aliud, quam veram sapientiam amare. Nihil autem turpius, quam in spirituali conversatione monachum nolle proficere, et voluntatem Dei scienter velle ignorare. Nemo sibi de sua infirmitate, vel ignorantia blandiatur, quoniam, qui ignorat, ignorabitur, et, qui scientiam odiit salutarem, merito condemnatur. Missurus in omnem terram praedicatores Dominus praemonuit dicens. Prudentes estote sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbae, ne, vel supplanteris ab aliquo per ignorantiam, vel iniuriam struas alicui per fraudem. Parum nanque distat in vitio, vel decipere posse, vel decipi. Rogo vos igitur, fratres charissimi, ut in regulam divi patris nostri Benedicti velitis intendere, quae vos monet, in plerisque locis frequentibus lectionibus divinarum scripturarum insudare. In scripturis enim docemur ad omnem pietatem informari, quemadmodum in hac brevissima peregrinatione huius incolatus debeamus vivere, ut Domino Deo nostro possimus super omnia placere. Monachorum namque est mundum, et omnes voluptates praesentis vitae pro Dei amore contemnere, motus carnis illicitos viriliter comprimere, orationi quoque, lectioni, et meditationi scripturarum insistere, et mentem a terrenis ad coelestia iugiter elevare. Beatus ille monachus, qui non abiit in consilio impiorum, et in via peccatorum non stetit, et in cathedra hominum pestilentium non sedet, sed in lege Domini meditatur die, ac nocte, discens hic in scripturis Dei sapientiam, cuius fructum recepturus est post huius peregrinationis terminum vitam aeternam. De quotidiana renovatione sancti propositi. Homilia V. A udivimus, fratres charissimi, lectionem nobis recitatam de libro sancti Iob, in qua humani generis deplangit miseriam, et huius calamitatem vitae, simul ac instabilem brevitatem. Homo, inquit, natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore repletur multis miseris, qui quasi flos egreditur, et conteritur, et fugit velut umbra, et nunquam in eodem statu permanet. Ecce, inquit, breves anni transeunt, et semitam, per quam non revertar, ambulo. Deficit omnis caro simul: et homo in cinerem revertetur: Quid inter haec fratres animadvertitis, quidve cogitatis? Est ne in nobis homo, qui se nesciat esse mortale, qui cum veritate possit dicere, non movebor in aeternum? Heu, fratres mei, 32 De quotidiana renovatione sancti propositi.

Homily IV.

Let him know the gracious will of almighty God, to whose words and service he has sworn allegiance. But just as a soldier cannot know the will of his lord when he is far away except through messengers and letters, so a monk does not understand the commands of the eternal King except through sacred readings, sermons, and the writings of the Gospel. For those who do not know it, reading Scripture opens the gate of salvation; it leads the diligent reader by the straight path to the knowledge of God; it makes the one who loves it despise all worldly things and love nothing except true wisdom.

Nothing, however, is more shameful than for a monk in the spiritual life to refuse to make progress, and knowingly to wish to remain ignorant of the will of God. Let no one flatter himself on account of his weakness or ignorance, since he who is ignorant will be ignored, and he who has hated saving knowledge is justly condemned. When the Lord was about to send preachers into all the earth, he warned them beforehand, saying: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves,” lest either you be overthrown by someone through ignorance, or devise injury against someone through deceit. For there is little difference in fault between being able to deceive and being deceived.

Therefore I ask you, dearest brothers, to give your attention to the Rule of our holy father Benedict, which admonishes you in many places to labor diligently in frequent readings of the divine Scriptures. For in the Scriptures we are taught to be formed in every kind of piety: how we ought to live in this very brief pilgrimage of our sojourn, so that we may be able to please the Lord our God above all things. For it belongs to monks to despise the world and all the pleasures of the present life for the love of God, manfully to restrain the unlawful movements of the flesh, to devote themselves also to prayer, reading, and meditation on the Scriptures, and continually to lift the mind from earthly things to heavenly things.

Blessed is that monk who has not gone away in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the chair of pestilent men, but meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, learning here in the Scriptures the wisdom of God, whose fruit, eternal life, he will receive after the end of this pilgrimage.

On the Daily Renewal of the Holy Purpose. Homily V.

We have heard, dearest brothers, the reading recited to us from the book of holy Job, in which he laments the misery of the human race, the calamity of this life, and at the same time its unstable brevity. “Man,” he says, “born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state.” “Behold,” he says, “the brief years pass by, and I walk the path by which I shall not return.” “All flesh fails together, and man will return to ashes.”

What do you notice amid these things, brothers, or what do you think? Is there any man among us who does not know himself to be mortal, who can say with truth, “I shall not be moved forever”? Alas, my brothers,

29
quam sumus caeci, oculos tenentes apertos, quam obliviosi viatores sumus, et desides, qui nos certo certius novimus esse morituros, et ita in vanitate praesentis vitae confidimus, ac si non essemus mortales. Sed quis est homo, qui vivet, et non videbit mortem, eruat animam suam de manu inferi? Ecce ait scriptura, omnes morimur, et quasi aqua dilabimur super terram. Idcirco memorae estote fratres mei, quoniam mors non tardat, et breve computabitur omne, quod praeterit, quia, ut sanctus ait Christophilus Paulus, statutum est hominibus semel mori, quam legem necessitatis communem nemo poterit subterfugere. O si nunc venturae mortis horam, quam unusquisque nostrum necessario subbiet in brevi, quotidie ante mentis intuitum poneremus, taliterque vitam disponeremus, et mores, quo semper inveniremur parati, quam felix, et tuta fieri posset emigratio nostra. Nonne et rex virorum, et mortuorum ipse Christus Dominus noster ad mortem nos semper volens esse paratos, in Sancto Evangelio praemonuit dicens: Ideo, et vos estote parati, quia, qua hora non putabitis, Filius hominis veniet? Quantum vero prosit ad mentis puritatem frequens meditatio mortis, sapiens in ecclesiastico praemonuit dicens: In omnibus operibus tuis memorare novissima tua, et in aeternum non peccabis. Mortis futurae cogitatio timorem inducit: timor vero mentem necessario concutit, et quasi clavus malleo impulsum, omnes carnis motus superbae ligno crucis affigit. Huius consideratione opinionis plerique philosophorum gentilium omnem viri sapientis vitam quandam meditationem mortis continuam esse dicebant. Hinc et sanctus Hieronymus dicit: Nihil aequi tibi proficiet ad temperantiam omnium rerum, sicut frequens meditatio brevis vitae huius, et incertae, quae sicut folium, quod vento rapitur, defluit, et quando non timetur, in mortem cadit. Idcirco memento mortis tuae, quam nullo consilio potest evadere, et omnes motus carnis facile poteris superare. Nam qui se quotidie cogitat moriturum, praesentia despicit, et se, nisi desipiat peuitus, ad futura praeparabit. Scio enim, et partim me fato expertum, quod mentis humanae voluntas in sancto vitae spiritualis fervore diu uniformis non potest consistere, et propterea memoriam mortis vobis ante oculos placuit saepius revocare, quatenus, dum mens futurorum timore concutitur, sancti fervor propositi quotidie renovetur. Animus etenim humanus colligatus pro exercitio sui ad corpus nimium est fluxus, et instabilis, et nunc ad illud rapitur, nunc vero ad aliud movetur. Propterea dicit in Proverbii Dei sapientia per Salomonem: Praebe fili mi cor tuum mihi, et oculi tui vias measet custodiant. Ac si dicat: Nisi totum amorem cordis tui Divinae sapientiae mancipaveris, nunquam in custodia mandatorum Domini stabilis, et confirmatus eris. Sicut enim cor primum est principium motus in homine, ita maior est illius pro vitae conservatione custodia; quoniam si morborum incursu

How blind we are, though we keep our eyes open; how forgetful and sluggish travellers we are, who know most certainly that we are to die, and yet put our trust in the vanity of the present life as though we were not mortal. But what man is there who shall live and not see death, shall he deliver his soul from the hand of hell? Behold, Scripture says, we all die, and like water we flow away upon the earth.

Therefore be mindful, my brothers, that death does not delay, and everything that passes will be reckoned brief; for, as the holy Christ-bearing Paul says, it is appointed for men once to die, and no one will be able to escape this common law of necessity. O, if now we set daily before the sight of our mind the hour of approaching death, which each one of us must necessarily undergo shortly, and so ordered our life and conduct that we might always be found ready, how happy and secure our departure could become.

Did not Christ himself, our Lord, king of the living and the dead, wishing us always to be prepared for death, warn us beforehand in the Holy Gospel, saying: Therefore you also be ready, because at the hour when you do not think, the Son of Man will come? How much frequent meditation on death profits toward purity of mind, the wise man warned in Ecclesiasticus, saying: In all your works remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.

The thought of future death brings fear; fear necessarily shakes the mind and, like a nail driven by a hammer, fastens all motions of proud flesh to the wood of the cross. In view of this consideration, many of the pagan philosophers used to say that the whole life of a wise man was a kind of continual meditation on death. Hence also Saint Jerome says: Nothing will profit you so much toward temperance in all things as frequent meditation on this brief and uncertain life, which passes away like a leaf carried off by the wind, and, when it is not feared, falls into death.

Therefore remember your death, which you can escape by no plan, and you will easily be able to overcome all motions of the flesh. For he who thinks daily that he is going to die despises present things and, unless he is utterly foolish, will prepare himself for future things. For I know, and in part have learned by experience, that the will of the human mind cannot long remain uniform in the holy fervor of spiritual life; and therefore it has pleased me to recall the memory of death more often before your eyes, so that, while the mind is shaken by fear of things to come, the fervor of holy purpose may be renewed each day.

For the human soul, bound to the body for its exercise, is very changeable and unstable; now it is carried off to this, now moved to that. Therefore the Wisdom of God says through Solomon in Proverbs: My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes keep my ways. As if he were saying: Unless you have entrusted the whole love of your heart to divine wisdom, you will never be steady and confirmed in keeping the commandments of the Lord. For just as the heart is the first principle of motion in man, so the greater care must be taken to guard it for the preservation of life; because if by the assault of diseases

30
Homilia V. 33 percutitur, vita corporis iam tota periclitatur. Unde scriptum est: Omnis custodia serva cor tuum, quia ex ipso vita procedit. Cordis autem nomine aTectum intelligimus, quoties ad allicius rei declinat amorem: illi tantum inhaerens, ut totam implicet voluntatem. Hinc psalmista dicit: Divitiae si affluant, nolite cor apponere, id est, nolite illas ex voluntatis desiderio amare. Nihil humano corde mobilius est, quod ad singulas poene cogitationes alteratur, et in eodem proposito difficulter potest consistere, nisi violenta quadam intentione restringatur. Quod Sanctus David non ignorans ad Dominum dicebat: Ego autem dixi in abundantia mea, non movebor in aeternum. Domine in voluntate tua praestitisti decori meo virtutem. Avertisti faciem tuam a me, et factus sum conturbatus. Idcirco, fratres mei carissimi, si quis est vestrum, qui Domino, et Salvatori nostro in vera puritate cordis famulari desiderat, si quis monachus esse, et opere simul, et nomine optat, discat in primis non sibi, sed Deo confidere, et bonum sanctae conversationis propositum nova semper institutione curet, non solum quotidian, sed singulis quantum praevalet etiam horis, atque momentis renovare. Spiritualis etenim conversationis fervor, ad cuius operationem experimentalem claustralis vitae institutio omnis dignoscitur ordinata, diu in eodem puncto non potest consistere, quoniam si non semper in anteriore proficit, ad inferiorea, et quod est deterius, infirmiora necessario recurrit. Non est in palaestra spiritualis exercitii aliqua stationis morosae consistens, quoniam humani cordis proprietas est suo motu naturali semper, vel ad meliora proficere, vel ad id, quod malum est, recidivare. Unde si non proficis in conversatione spirituali, necessario deficis, si non ad sanctiora progrederis, certe retrocedis. Quod nobis cum experientia perspicuum fecerit, non cesso admonere charitates vestras, ut desiderium vestrum in bona conversatione semper ad ulteriora extendatis, ne ibi perniciosum incidatis deficiendi periculum, ubi proficiendi non innovatis appetitum. Fervor autem spiritualis propositi ad Dei amorem dirigitur, et non aliter, quam in ipso conservatur. Est enim Dei amor igni non absurde comparandus, quoniam sic ut ignis subtrato fomento lignorum, necessario extinguitur, sic amor Dei, si desint continuata bonorum operum exercitia, mox evanescens periclitatur. Hinc est illud Salvatoris in Evangelio, Ignem veni mittere super terram, et quid volo, nisi ut ardeat? O monachi foelix conscientia illa, in cuius pectore praeter Christi amorem nihil ardet, qui Deum diligit super omnia, qui vanitatis studia contemnit universa. Considerate nunc fratres, quam diligentissime conscientias vestras, et examussim pensiculate, si Deum super omnia diligitis, et si ardet in vobis iam ignis Divini amoris, quatenus fomentum adhibeatis necessarium, ne quando per vestram tepidatatem sancti fervoris igniculum sentiatis poenitus extinctum. Credite 34 De quotidiana renovatione sancti propositi.

when it is struck, the whole life of the body is already endangered. Hence it is written: “With all vigilance guard your heart, because from it life proceeds.” By the name “heart,” however, we understand affection or desire, whenever it inclines toward the love of some thing, clinging to it so much that it entangles the whole will. Hence the psalmist says: “If riches abound, do not set your heart on them,” that is, do not love them from the desire of the will.

Nothing is more changeable than the human heart, which is altered by almost every single thought and can scarcely remain fixed in the same purpose unless it is restrained by a certain forceful intention. Saint David, not ignorant of this, said to the Lord: “But I said in my abundance, I shall never be moved. Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled.”

Therefore, my dearly beloved brothers, if there is anyone among you who desires to serve our Lord and Savior in true purity of heart, if anyone wishes to be a monk both in deed and in name, let him learn first of all to trust not in himself but in God, and let him take care always to renew the good purpose of holy conduct by fresh instruction, not only daily, but, as far as he can, at every hour and moment.

For the fervor of spiritual conduct, toward whose practical exercise the whole institution of cloistered life is known to be ordered, cannot remain long at the same point; for if it does not always advance toward what lies ahead, it necessarily falls back to lower things and, what is worse, weaker things. In the arena of spiritual exercise there is no standing still in a lingering halt, because it is the property of the human heart, by its own natural motion, always either to advance toward better things or to fall back into what is evil. Hence, if you do not advance in spiritual conduct, you necessarily decline; if you do not go forward toward holier things, you certainly go backward.

Since experience has made this clear to us, I do not cease to admonish your charity to stretch your desire in good conduct always toward further things, lest you fall into the destructive danger of failing precisely where you do not renew the desire of advancing. The fervor of a spiritual purpose is directed toward the love of God and is preserved in no other way than in him. For the love of God is not absurdly compared to fire, because just as fire, when the fuel of wood has been removed, is necessarily extinguished, so the love of God, if the continual exercises of good works are lacking, soon fades away and is endangered.

Hence that saying of the Savior in the Gospel: “I came to send fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” O monk, happy is that conscience in whose breast nothing burns except the love of Christ, who loves God above all things, who despises all pursuits of vanity.

Now consider your consciences, brothers, most diligently, and weigh them with exactness: whether you love God above all things, and whether the fire of divine love is already burning in you, so that you may apply the necessary fuel, lest at some time through your lukewarmness you feel the little flame of holy fervor utterly extinguished. Believe [unclear].

31
mihi fratres, quoniam experientia me docuit: ignem in vobis Divini fervoris ardentem faciliori exercitio conservabitis, quam extinctum denuo succendatis. Quicumque igitur iam in se Dei experitur amorem, quicumque coelestem in corde suo recepit charitatem, summa cum sollicitudine caveat in prioris vitae negligentias recidere, sed fomenta adhibeat necessaria spiritualium exercitiorum, quatenus proficientem in se Dei fervorem queat conservare. Caveat non solum peccata grandia, sed etiam negligentias parvas, et quantum poterit minimas, quoniam qui minima spertit, paulatim decidit: et qui non semper metuit periculum, spiritualis fervoris, atque propositi cito sentient detrimentum. Dicit enim scriptura, Si non instanter tenueris te in timore Domini, cito subvertetur domus tua. Beatus igitur homo, qui semper est pavidus, qui de acceptis virtutibus non praesumit, qui certo existimat se deficere, quoties se non invenerit singulis momentis ad altiora profecisse. Sed vereor, fratres, et vehementer timeo, nisi me operum quorundam fallat aestimatio, nonnullis in vobis ignem huius sancti necdum adesse fervoris, quippe cum vera monachorum studia parum videantur diligere, quod, ex illorum conversatione cum sit manifestum, nullus vestrum poterit ignorare. Quos monere quidem non duxi penitus superfluum, quamvis parum hactenus videar profecisse, cum non sit abbreviata manus Domini, quo minus queat salvare poenitentes. Confito enim in misericordia Dei viventis, quoniam propter meam in eos charitatem, et exercitia pietatis illorum, qui ad puritatem regulae in vobis ambulant, dabit eis aliquando resipiscere, et studia sancti fervoris ardentius amare. Quid est, fratres, quod non monastice in monasterio vivitis, et professi conversationem spiritus secundum carnem ambulatis? An nescitis, quam sit periculosum in coenobio monachum seculariter vivere, et votum sanctae puritatis, quod emisimus omnes, tepida conversatione violare? Cognoscite, precor, quoniam novissima omnium claustralium extremis sunt proxima, ut boni, et zelosi amatores propriae salutis monachi, non vulgarium, sed maxima sanctorum in coelo premia reci- piant; et qui male, vel tepide in religione conversantur monastica, non mediocri, aut populari, sed gravissimo, et daemonum puniantur cruciatu. Quanto enim status, in quo quis peccat fuerit altior, tanto poena delinquentis in eo erit et gravior. Idcirco si quis inter vos iam viam divini amoris cum fervore spiritus ambulare didicit, progre- diatur, necesse est, ut amplius quotdie proficiat: qui vero adhuc iacet in torpore mentis ignavae, conetur quantocyus, ut resurgat; quoniam sicuti iacentibus poena promittitur, ita non perseverantibus corona victoriae denegatur. Cavete igitur, ne mentem subvertat perniciosa tepiditas, quae nimium est periculosa claustralibus, quia molestissima est, et plena miseriarum, et dolorum, ac plane inferno proxima, de cuius voragine

my brothers, because experience has taught me: you will preserve the fire of divine fervor burning within you by easier practice than you will kindle it again once it has been extinguished. Therefore whoever already experiences the love of God within himself, whoever has received heavenly charity in his heart, must take the greatest care not to fall back into the negligences of his former life, but must apply the necessary fuel of spiritual exercises, so that he may be able to preserve the advancing fervor of God within himself. Let him beware not only of great sins, but also of small negligences, and, as far as he can, the very least; for whoever despises small things gradually falls, and whoever does not always fear danger will quickly feel the loss of spiritual fervor and of his purpose. For Scripture says: If you do not hold yourself constantly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown.

Blessed, therefore, is the man who is always fearful, who does not presume upon the virtues he has received, who firmly judges that he is failing whenever he has not found himself advancing at every moment toward higher things. But I fear, brothers, and I am deeply afraid, unless my estimate of certain works deceives me, that in some of you the fire of this holy fervor is not yet present, since you seem to love the true pursuits of monks only a little. Since this is plain from their way of life, none of you can be ignorant of it. I have not thought it altogether superfluous to admonish them, although so far I seem to have made little progress, since the hand of the Lord has not been shortened so that he cannot save the penitent. For I trust in the mercy of the living God that, because of my charity toward them and the exercises of devotion of those among you who walk according to the purity of the rule, he will at some time grant them to come to their senses and to love the pursuits of holy fervor more ardently.

What is this, brothers, that you do not live monastically in the monastery, and, having professed a way of life of the spirit, you walk according to the flesh? Do you not know how dangerous it is for a monk to live secularly in a community, and to violate by a lukewarm way of life the vow of holy purity which we have all made? Know, I beg you, that the last things of all cloistered persons are close to the extremes: so that good monks, zealous lovers of their own salvation, receive in heaven not ordinary rewards, but the greatest rewards of the saints; and those who conduct themselves badly or lukewarmly in monastic religion are punished not with a moderate or common torment, but with the gravest torment, that of demons. For the higher the state in which someone sins, the heavier also will be the punishment of the offender in it.

Therefore, if anyone among you has already learned to walk the way of divine love with fervor of spirit, he must go forward, so that he may make greater progress every day. But whoever still lies in the torpor of a sluggish mind should strive as quickly as possible to rise again; for just as punishment is promised to those who lie fallen, so the crown of victory is denied to those who do not persevere. Beware, therefore, lest destructive lukewarmness overthrow the mind. It is exceedingly dangerous for cloistered persons, because it is most grievous and full of miseries and sorrows, and plainly near to hell, from whose abyss

32
Homilia V. 35 raro consurgit monachus, qui semel inciderit. Et heu quot inveniuntur hodie claustrales pusillanimes, remissi, et desides, qui sub onere spiri- tualis militiae frequentiter succumbunt, et raro ad verum spiritus fervo- rem resurgunt. Horum sane miseranda conditio, qui nomen habent, quod vivant, et mortui sunt: quos ad veram compunctionem cordis, nec memoria mortis potuit inducere, nec inferni recordatio proposita emollire. Huiusmodi vero monachi, posteaquam diu ita manserint in accidia torpentes, aut opprimuntur mala consuetudine, et succumbunt, aut fiunt quodammodo in inferno, ut nunquam ad plenum respirent in lucem miserationem Domini, nec in libertatem spiritus, quae sola est regno coelorum proxima, facitque iugum Domini suave, et onus leve, perveniant. Haec illis mala contingunt, propterea quod voluntas eorum a carnalibus nondum est purgata passionibus, nec bonum sic volunt, sicuti noverunt, a propria concupiscentia illecti, et abstracti. Amant enim periturae consolationes carnis, quas, et si interrupunt aliquando, nunquam tamet penitus rumpunt. Inde est, quod suas affectiones in Deum rarissime dirigunt, et si quando compunguntur, ad horam non diu perseverant, sed pigritia, et inertia fatigantur mox animo, bonum, quod inchoaverunt, ex tristitia, et melancholia subito fastidientes. Im- pleri autem fervore divini amoris non potest mens his agitata procellis, quoniam caro ad ignem posita, saepiusque remota, sicut nunquam bene coquitur, sic anima in accidiam saepius relapsa, divino spiritu nequa- quam veraciter illustratur. Dicit enim scriptura ad Dominum: Qui elon- gant se a te, peribunt, et perdidisti omnes, qui operantur iniquitatem. Quanto namque mens per accidiam longius a fervore divini amoris recesserit, tanto proximior inferno, et desperationi, rarius, et difficilis ad veram poenitentiam convalescit. Quicunque igitur ex vobis, fratres mei, fugere de medio Babylonis desiderat, quicunque venire ad internum fervorem spiritus optat, summo semper conatu torporem mentis, et accidiam a se studeat repellere, et sanctum Divini amoris propositum quotidie innovare. Grave nimis est, fateor, pravae consuetudini carnis resistere, et in corde veteri contra morem nova cogitare. Certe, fratres, nemo cum tepida voluntate de profundis inferni potest resurgere, nec malam quis consuetudinem sine magna violentia, et diurna consue- tudine contraria poterit superare. Nam et si nemo fiat sanctus viribus suis, sed Deus est, qui operatur omnia in omnibus: constat nobis tamen manifeste, quoniam Dei regnum vim patitur, et qui suis inferre mo- tibus carneis vim negligit, ad sanctorum Domini consortium non per- tingit. Audi nunc monache, quicunque tepidus es ad amorem Dei, et accidiosus, audi inquam, et contremisce, quoniam, nisi de mala con- suetudine torpentis vitae continuo surrexeris, nisi vim tibi metipsi per consuetudinem contrariam intuleris, nisi ad fervorem divini amoris cor 36 De quotidiana renovatione sancti propositi.

Homily V.

Rarely does a monk rise again who has once fallen. And alas, how many faint-hearted, lax, and idle cloisterers are found today, who frequently collapse under the burden of spiritual warfare and rarely rise again to the true fervor of the spirit. Their condition is indeed pitiable: they have a name that they are alive, and they are dead. Neither the memory of death has been able to lead them to true compunction of heart, nor has the recollection of hell, set before them, been able to soften them.

Monks of this sort, after they have long remained thus sluggish in accidia, are either oppressed by evil habit and collapse, or in a certain way become as though in hell, so that they never fully breathe again into the light of the Lord’s mercy, nor reach the freedom of the spirit, which alone is nearest to the kingdom of heaven, and makes the Lord’s yoke sweet and his burden light. These evils befall them because their will has not yet been cleansed from carnal passions, nor do they will the good as they know it, since they are enticed and drawn away by their own concupiscence. For they love the passing consolations of the flesh; and even if at times they interrupt them, they never wholly break them off. Hence it is that they very rarely direct their affections toward God; and if they are ever moved to compunction, they do not persevere long, even for an hour, but are soon wearied in soul by sluggishness and inertia, and suddenly grow disgusted, through sadness and melancholy, with the good they had begun.

But a mind tossed by these storms cannot be filled with the fervor of divine love; for as flesh placed by the fire and then repeatedly removed is never well cooked, so a soul that often relapses into accidia is by no means truly illumined by the divine Spirit. For Scripture says to the Lord: “Those who go far from you shall perish, and you have destroyed all who work iniquity.” For the farther the mind has withdrawn through accidia from the fervor of divine love, the nearer it is to hell and despair, and the more rarely and with greater difficulty does it grow strong again for true repentance.

Therefore, whoever among you, my brothers, desires to flee from the midst of Babylon, whoever longs to come to the inward fervor of the spirit, should strive always with the utmost effort to drive away from himself torpor of mind and accidia, and daily to renew the holy purpose of divine love. It is very hard, I admit, to resist the perverse habit of the flesh, and in an old heart, against custom, to think new thoughts. Certainly, brothers, no one with a lukewarm will can rise from the depths of hell, nor will anyone be able to overcome an evil habit without great violence and the daily practice of its contrary. For even if no one becomes holy by his own strength, but it is God who works all things in all, nevertheless it is plainly certain to us that the kingdom of God suffers violence, and he who neglects to do violence to his own carnal impulses does not reach the fellowship of the Lord’s saints.

Hear now, monk, whoever you are who are lukewarm toward the love of God and given to accidia; hear, I say, and tremble, because unless you immediately rise from the evil habit of a sluggish life, unless you do violence to yourself by the practice of the contrary habit, unless you [unclear] your heart to the fervor of divine love.

33
tuum instanter praeparaveris, numquam Dei faciem in gloria videbis. Radix desperationis est accidia, et non solum radix, sed et nutrix eius, et mater, quae si mentem hominis Deo dicati semel oppresserit, omnem viam ad salutem illico pracludit. Non enim dormientibus regnum coelorum promittitur, non ocio, et desidia torpentibus beatitudo aeternitatis praeparatur, sed his qui motibus carnis viriliter imperant, corona reponitur: et, qui spiritu, non carne vivunt, aeternae foelicitatis gloria donantur. Nulla sine labore virtus acquiritur; hostis sine congressu nullus superatur, si vis coronari, vince: si vincere cupis, necesse est, ut fortiter, ac perseveranter praelieris. Usquequo piger dormies, Salomon tibi clamat, quando consurges e somno tuo? Si impiger fueris, veniet, ut fons, messis tua, et egestas longe fugiet a te. Qui enim coligit in messe, filius sapiens est; et qui stertit aestate, filius confusionis. Nam, qui operatur terram suam, satiabitur panibus: qui autem sectatur ocium, replebitur egestate. Nunc tempus est operandi bonum, fratres; nunc opportunitas promerendi aeternam beatitudinem nobis a Domino Deo conceditur, quae subito in morte amputatur. Dicit enim scriptura: Quodcumque facere potest manus tua, instante operare; quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas. Si vos delectat bonum aeternae beatitudinis, quod promittitur, oportet ne labores pugnandi mentem deterrent, qui proponuntur. Nemo enim a Domino coronabitur, nisi qui legitime certaverit: nemo perveniet ad culmen aeternae celsitudinis, nisi qui fervore spiritus illicitos motus superaverit carnis. Semper est nobis pugnandum, fratres, contra tripli-cem aciem diaboli, quamdiu in hac peregrinatione vivimus; quoniam nemo hic insuperabilis usque adeo efficitur, qui non tepescens paulatim superetur. Hic sanctus proclamat Augustinus: Nemo securus esse debet in hac vita, quae tota tentatio nominatur, ut qui potuit fieri ex dete-riori melior, non fiat ex meliore quandoque deterior. Unde et Salomon in libro Proverbiorum, Desideria, inquit, occidunt pigrum; quoniam sic ut in unoquoque opere bono perfectionem tribuit constantia, ita om-nis religionis, et profectus animae spiritualis interempricx, et noverca est accidia. Nam, ut divus inquit Hieronymus, nihil in sancto proposito deterius est ocio; quoniam non solum non acquirit nova, sed etiam turpiter consumit prius acquisita. Sanctae spiritualis vitae ratio processu continuo gaudio proficit, et crescit; cessatione vero torpet, et deficit. Propterea, fratres, quotidianis, ac recentibus virtutum incrementis in-stauranda mens est, et vivendi hoc iter ratio non de transacto, sed eo, quod restat, metienda. Ociositatem igitur, quae mater, et nutrix est omnium vitiorum, in primis fugite: accidiam autem non fugiendo, sed resistendo fortiter, superate. Dicit autem scriptura: Multam malitiam docuit ociositas. In desideriis enim vanis, et perniciosis est omnis

Unless you urgently prepare your [heart], you will never see the face of God in glory. Acedia is the root of despair, and not only its root, but also its nurse and mother; if once it has oppressed the mind of a person dedicated to God, it immediately closes off every road to salvation. For the kingdom of heaven is not promised to sleepers, nor is the blessedness of eternity prepared for those who grow sluggish in leisure and idleness; rather, the crown is laid up for those who manfully rule the motions of the flesh, and those who live by the spirit, not by the flesh, are granted the glory of eternal happiness.

No virtue is acquired without labor; no enemy is overcome without battle. If you wish to be crowned, conquer; if you desire to conquer, you must fight bravely and perseveringly. “How long will you sleep, O sluggard?” Solomon cries to you; “when will you rise from your sleep?” If you are diligent, your harvest will come like a fountain, and poverty will flee far from you. For he who gathers in harvest is a wise son, and he who snores in summer is a son of confusion. For he who works his own land will be satisfied with bread; but he who pursues idleness will be filled with poverty.

Now is the time for doing good, brothers; now the opportunity of earning eternal blessedness is granted to us by the Lord God, an opportunity that is suddenly cut off in death. For Scripture says: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly; for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge will be in the underworld, to which you are hastening.” If the good of eternal blessedness that is promised delights you, then the labors of the struggle that are set before you must not frighten your mind. For no one will be crowned by the Lord unless he has competed lawfully; no one will reach the summit of eternal loftiness unless by fervor of spirit he has overcome the unlawful motions of the flesh.

We must always fight, brothers, against the devil’s threefold battle-line as long as we live in this pilgrimage; for no one here becomes so unconquerable that, if he grows lukewarm, he is not gradually overcome. Here Saint Augustine proclaims: “No one ought to feel secure in this life, which is wholly called temptation, lest one who was able to become better from being worse should at some time become worse from being better.” Hence Solomon too says in the book of Proverbs: “Desires kill the sluggard.” For just as constancy gives perfection in every good work, so acedia is the destroyer and stepmother of all religion and of the progress of the spiritual soul. For, as blessed Jerome says, nothing is worse in a holy purpose than idleness, since it not only fails to acquire new things, but also shamefully consumes what was previously acquired.

The order of holy spiritual life advances and grows by continual progress in joy; but by cessation it grows sluggish and fails. Therefore, brothers, the mind must be renewed by daily and fresh increases of virtues, and the measure of this path of life must be taken not from what has passed, but from what remains. Therefore flee idleness first of all, for it is the mother and nurse of all vices; but overcome acedia not by fleeing it, but by resisting it bravely. Scripture says: “Idleness has taught much evil.” For in vain and pernicious desires is every [unclear].

34
Homilia V. 37 ociosus. Semper itaque monachus, qui Christo in vera puritate mentis desiderat militare, sit in aliquo exercitio spirituali occupatus; ne oculum generet vitium, et inveniant perniciosae cogitationes, quo roborentur, locum. Quemadmodum rubigo consumit ferrum, et vestis a vermis corroditur; ita mentem enervat oculum, et virtus diu intermissa animi paulatim defuit, ac penitus enervatur. Oculum igitur fugite; accidiam vero superate. Verum cum non possimus in uno statu divini amoris firmiter, et sine mutatione mentis persistere, necessarium nobis est, ne defluamus penitus, quotdie sanctum propositum innovare, ut quoties per negligentiam humanae infirmitatis, quantumlibet parum torpescere a spirituali fervore incipimus, toties nosmetipsos discutientes memoria futurorum, et dominicae passionis intuitu ad pristinum mox proficiendi propositum conscientiam revocemus. Hoc autem summopere nobis ca- vendum est, ne hunc sanctum proficiendi conatum differamus in cra- stinum, quoniam saepe nocuit distulisse bonum in tempus futurum, quod fieri citius potuisset. Hinc sapiens in Ecclesiastico dicit, Ne tardes converti ad Dominum, et ne differas de die in diem. Subito enim veniet ira illius, et in tempore vindictae disperdet te. Augustinus quoque ait, Cur bonum differs in crastinum, dicens, adhuc vita longa erit? Quis enim scit, si longa erit? Et si bona non est, quid prodest, quod longa erit? Sine vita bona, mors dicenda est conversatio monachi potius, quam vita. Remedia igitur emendatoris vitae, nullis sunt cunctationibus dif- ferenda, ne tempus conversionis pereat tarditate, cum iam nulla dilatio conceditur poenitendi. Qui enim poenitenti indulgentiam promisit, diem crastinum non spopondit. Nemo Deum timens converti differt ad poe- nitentiam, nec in crastinum salutem prolongat hodiernam. Omnis au- tem homo sciens se in mentis tepiditate constitutum, qui differt emen- dationem vitae de die in diem, spe longioris aevi decipitur; quoniam si sciret se in crastino moriturum, hodie procul dubio mutaret propo- situm. Multos miserabiliter decepit spes vitae longioris: qui dum emen- dationem conversationis suae quotdie differunt, subito in mortis pro- fundum cadunt. Quis in vobis est, fratres, qui non statuat in animo suo emendatoris vitae assumere propositum, antequam moriatur? Credo enim, quod unusquisque vestrum adhuc maiorem intendat exercere pietatem ad Deum, priusquam mortis periculum incidat. Et quare tam diu expectatis? Quare de die in diem differtis? Ecce, qui nunc sani vivitis, et non datis vos ad spiritualia exercitia divini amoris, quando potestis, et Dominus patienter expectat, veniet dies unicuique vestrum extrema, et iam properat, in qua perurgente angelo mortis, auferetur a vobis potestas, cuius effectum tantundem distulistis. Unde iterum, atque iterum vos rogo, fratres, et qua possum sedulitate admoneo, con- vertite vos ad Dominum Deum nostrum in toto corde vestro, dum 38 De amore quietis, et solitudinis. vivitis sani, et incolumes, nec differatis ulterioris voluntatem; ne amit- tatis etiam concessam vobis potestatem. Cogitate, saepiusque recogitate, quoniam non sumus cives huius mundi, sed advenae, et peregrini; neque habemus hic manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus; et ad mor- tem quotidiane nescientes etiam properamus. De amore quietis, et solitudinis. Homilia VI.

Therefore the monk who desires to serve Christ in true purity of mind should always be occupied in some spiritual exercise, lest idleness give birth to vice and harmful thoughts find a place where they may gain strength. Just as rust consumes iron, and a garment is eaten away by worms, so idleness weakens the mind; and the virtue of the soul, long left unused, gradually fails and is utterly enfeebled. Flee idleness, then, and overcome acedia.

But since we cannot remain firmly and without any change of mind in one state of divine love, it is necessary for us, lest we fall away entirely, to renew our holy purpose every day. Thus, whenever through the negligence of human weakness we begin, however slightly, to grow sluggish from spiritual fervor, we should examine ourselves, and by the remembrance of things to come and by contemplation of the Lord’s Passion, immediately recall our conscience to its former purpose of making progress.

Above all, however, we must beware of putting off this holy effort to make progress until tomorrow, because it has often been harmful to postpone to a future time a good that could have been done sooner. Hence the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” Augustine also says: “Why do you put off the good until tomorrow, saying, ‘There will still be a long life’? For who knows whether it will be long? And if it is not good, what does it profit that it will be long?”

Without a good life, the conduct of a monk should be called death rather than life. Therefore the remedies of an amended life must not be delayed by any hesitation, lest the time for conversion perish through tardiness, when no further delay for repentance is granted. For he who promised forgiveness to the penitent did not promise tomorrow. No one who fears God delays turning to repentance, nor postpones today’s salvation until tomorrow. Every person who knows that he is set in tepidity of mind, and who puts off the amendment of life from day to day, is deceived by the hope of a longer age; for if he knew that he would die tomorrow, he would undoubtedly change his purpose today. The hope of a longer life has miserably deceived many, who, while they put off the amendment of their conduct each day, suddenly fall into the depth of death.

Who among you, brothers, does not resolve in his heart to take up the purpose of an amended life before he dies? For I believe that each of you still intends to exercise greater devotion toward God before the danger of death comes upon him. And why do you wait so long? Why do you put it off from day to day? Behold, you who now live in health, and do not give yourselves to the spiritual exercises of divine love when you can, while the Lord patiently waits: the final day will come for each one of you, and it is already hastening, when, as the angel of death presses hard, the power whose effect you have put off for so long will be taken away from you.

Therefore again and again I ask you, brothers, and with all the earnestness I can I admonish you: turn to the Lord our God with your whole heart while you live healthy and unharmed, and do not further delay your will, lest you lose even the power granted to you. Think, and often think again, that we are not citizens of this world, but strangers and pilgrims; we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one to come; and every day we are hastening toward death, though we do not know it.

35
Duo sunt intellectus ab initio creati: quod neminem vestrum scio lateris, fratres charissimi, angelicus videlicet, et humanus. Angel- licus vero quando fuerit creatus, sancta scriptura manifeste non aperit, sed Patrum sententia conditionem angelorum opus Dei esse, et inter opera sex dierum computavit. Sunt autem, qui scribunt, angelos fuisse creatos longe ante mundum istum visibilem, quod sicut probare testi- monio divinarum scripturarum non possumus, ita neque temere impu- gnamus. Sunt enim viri graves, et sancti complures, qui conditionem Angelorum principio mundi longe praetulerunt. Fuit autem intellectus Angelicus statim a principio in omnium scibilium actu factus: et omnia novit, quae scire potuit; nihilque ad sui perfectionem deinceps admi- sit. Creatus enim a Domino in sua perfectione naturali, quan habere potuit, nullius rationem incrementi, quo intelligeret, amplius requisivit. Enimvero cum sine medio sit Deo coniunctus, purus intellectus natura factus est, nec more nostro exercitatione ad intelligendum indiget, cuius esse nullam admittit corruptionem. Itaque suo adhaerens obiecto per affectum amoris, Deum, quem centrum suae beatitudinis esse intelligit, immediate, et immobiliter contemplatur, et diligit; beatus est, et nullam sui alterationem pertimescit. Humanus vero intellectus, quem nostri praeceptores animam vocaverunt, a principio quidem in omni ignorantia creatus est, et nihil eorum novit, quae angelicus intelligit a natura. Differunt autem isti duo intellectus, sicut actus et potentia, lux et tenebrae, scientia et ignorantia; habitus et privatio, principium et finis, simplex et compositum, substantia et accidentis, natura et ars, veritas et similitudo. Omnia namque, scriptura testante divina, quae angelico intellectui a natura insunt, et a principio, humanus conseque- tur per artem in fine, sicut Dominus Iesus in Sancto Evangelio dicit: In resurrectione mortuorum neque nubent, neque nubentur, sed erunt sicut Angeli Dei in Coelo. Ut enim mens exercetur ad intellectum per multos labores, quasi per artem, in ergastulo corporis ad breve tempus posita est; in quo si conversa ad Deum, artificium suum per amorem rite consummaverit, egrediens tandem hinc par Angelo evadit. Quod si carnis motibus consentiens, ordinem suum non custodierit, perturbata, et misera, ruentibus apostatis spiritibus, similis de corpore in aeternum

There are two intellects created from the beginning, which I know is hidden from none of you, dearest brothers: namely, the angelic and the human. Holy Scripture does not plainly disclose when the angelic intellect was created, but the judgment of the Fathers has counted the creation of the angels as a work of God and among the works of the six days. There are, however, some who write that the angels were created long before this visible world; and just as we cannot prove this by the testimony of the divine Scriptures, so neither do we rashly oppose it. For there are many weighty and holy men who placed the creation of the angels long before the beginning of the world.

The angelic intellect was made from the very beginning in act with respect to all knowable things: it knew everything that it could know, and thereafter admitted nothing further for its own perfection. For, created by the Lord in the natural perfection that it could have, it required no further means of increase by which it might understand. Indeed, since it is joined to God without intermediary, it was made a pure intellect by nature, and does not, as we do, need exercise in order to understand; its being admits no corruption. And so, cleaving to its object through the affection of love, it immediately and unchangeably contemplates and loves God, whom it understands to be the center of its blessedness; it is blessed, and fears no alteration of itself.

But the human intellect, which our teachers have called the soul, was indeed created from the beginning in complete ignorance, and by nature knows none of the things that the angelic intellect understands. These two intellects differ as act and potency, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, habit and privation, beginning and end, simple and composite, substance and accident, nature and art, truth and likeness. For all the things which, as divine Scripture testifies, are in the angelic intellect by nature and from the beginning, the human intellect will attain through art at the end, as the Lord Jesus says in the Holy Gospel: In the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God in heaven.

For as the mind is trained toward understanding through many labors, as though through art, it has been placed for a short time in the prison-house of the body; and if there, turned toward God, it has duly completed its craft through love, then at last, departing from here, it becomes equal to an angel. But if, consenting to the motions of the flesh, it has not kept its order, disturbed and wretched, like the falling apostate spirits, from the body into eternity

36
Homilia VI. 39 crucianda emigrabit. Cum enim mens nostra, sive anima in rerum omnium ignorantia, et privatione sit creata, necesse est, ut continua actione, motu, et arte in rerum notitiam perveniat. Finis quippe humanum intellectum aequat Angelico, eius potentiam commutans in actum: facietque de privatione habitum, de vacuo plenum, de imperfecto perfectum, de privato habentem, de tenebroso lucidum, de nocturno diurnum, de lunari solarem, et de terreno caelestem. Finis iste, fratres mei charissimi, salutis aeternae principium est: ad quem venire nemo foeliciter sufficit, qui non totis viribus ad apicem perfectionis tendit. Verum cum sit difficile in medio turbarum hunc necessarium proficiendi conatum semper infractum tenere, ubi mille peccandi praebentur occasiones, sancti patres ordinis monastici fundatores verbo, et exemplo nos docuerunt mundum fugere, et non solum animo, sed etiam corpore frequentiam declinare. Ex eis, qui fortiores erant animo, plures convolverunt ad eremum, ut eo mente fierent propinquiores Domino, quo corpore longius recesserunt a mundo. De quibus dictum Esaiae Prophetae legimus: Exultabit solitudo, et florebit quasi lilium, germinans germinabit, et exultabit laetabunda, et laudans. Alii vero cupientes prodesse multis instituerunt coenobia, in quibus multitudinem collocarunt monachorum, quorum conservatio segregata esset a populis, et nihilominus sibi mutuo fieret socialis. Non enim omnibus conuenit sedere in eremo, quibus in medio fratrum magis congruit Domino militare. Nam et monasteria nostra solitudinem habent suam, ut qui voluerit esse solitarius, possit in medio fratrum, dum cellae, in qua moratur, continuaverit secretum. Monachus enim secundum nominis sui interpretationem solitarius dicitur: propterea quod mente, et corpore a tumultu huius mundi segregatur. Unde sermonem hodiernum facturus ad charitates vestras, moneo vos paterna sollicitudine, et rogo, ne frustra tantundem fuerim locutus: qui nihil aliud quaero, nisi vestrum bonum: nihil magis cupio, quam vestrum in spirituali conversatione profectum. Rogo, inquam vos, et hortor in visceribus fraternalis caritatis, ut cellae quietem diligatis, tanquam salutis vestrae officinam, in qua pax est multa diligentibus Deum, et magna commoditas perficiendi ad cognitionem summae veritatis intellectum. Dicit enim propheta Esaias: In silentio, et spe erit fortitudo vestra. Qui non amat solitudinem cellae, et quietem silentii, mentis puritatem nequaquam diligit: sed corpore vagus, novas semper animo vanitates haurit. Hinc divus Hieronymus ait: Quid desideramus urbium frequentiam, qui de singularitate censemur? Mihi enim oppidum carcer est, solitudo paradisus. Si nos, fratres, eremus delectaret, ac solitudo, magnam locum iste proposito nostro commoditatem praestaret, ubi praeter pauperes rusticanos, hospes rarus occurrit, nemo turbat quietem nostram, nemo molestat, nemo spectacula, vel rumores introducit 40 De amore quietis, et solitudinis.

Homily VI.

…will depart to be tormented. For since our mind, or soul, was created in ignorance and privation of all things, it must necessarily come to knowledge of things by continual action, movement, and art. The end, indeed, makes the human intellect equal to the angelic, changing its potentiality into act; and it will make from privation a habit, from emptiness fullness, from the imperfect the perfect, from one deprived one possessing, from darkness light, from night day, from lunar solar, and from earthly heavenly.

This end, my dearly beloved brothers, is the beginning of eternal salvation; and no one can happily come to it who does not strive with all his strength toward the summit of perfection. But since it is difficult amid crowds always to keep unbroken this necessary effort of advancing, where a thousand occasions for sinning are offered, the holy fathers, founders of the monastic order, taught us by word and example to flee the world, and to avoid crowds not only in mind but also in body.

Of those who were stronger in spirit, many withdrew to the desert, so that they might become nearer to the Lord in mind the farther they had withdrawn in body from the world. Of these we read the saying of Isaiah the prophet: “The wilderness shall rejoice and shall blossom like the lily; budding, it shall bud, and shall rejoice with gladness and praise.”

Others, however, desiring to benefit many, established cenobitic houses, in which they placed a multitude of monks, whose way of life was separated from the peoples and nevertheless made social among themselves. For it is not suitable for all to sit in the desert, for whom it is more fitting to serve the Lord in the midst of brothers. For our monasteries too have their own solitude, so that anyone who wishes to be solitary can be so in the midst of brothers, if he keeps up the seclusion of the cell in which he dwells.

For a monk, according to the interpretation of his name, is called solitary, because in mind and body he is separated from the tumult of this world. Therefore, as I am about to deliver today’s sermon to your charity, I warn you with fatherly concern, and I beg that I may not have spoken so much in vain, since I seek nothing other than your good and desire nothing more than your progress in spiritual conduct. I ask you, I say, and exhort you in the bowels of brotherly charity, to love the quiet of the cell as the workshop of your salvation, in which there is great peace for those who love God, and great advantage for bringing the intellect to perfection in the knowledge of the highest truth.

For the prophet Isaiah says: “In silence and in hope shall be your strength.” Whoever does not love the solitude of the cell and the quiet of silence by no means loves purity of mind; rather, wandering in body, he always drinks in new vanities in spirit. Hence blessed Jerome says: “Why do we desire the crowds of cities, we who are reckoned from our singularity? For to me a town is a prison, solitude a paradise.”

If, brothers, the desert and solitude delighted us, this place would offer great convenience for our purpose, where, apart from poor country people, a guest is rarely met; no one disturbs our quiet, no one troubles us, no one introduces spectacles or rumors.

37
momentaneae novitatis. Sed paucos inter vos amatores internae quietis cerno; et doleo vehementer; propterea quod optime sciam monachum non posse in spirituali conversatione proficere, quem constat cellae quietem non amare. Qui autem novit, quantum animae conferat bonum, solitudinis secretum, cellam suam diligit, nec facile foras egressitatur, semper metuens, in tumultu perdere, quod magno in abdito labore congregavit. Nam, ut sanctus Augustinus dicit, minus voluptatibus stimulatur, qui non est, ubi frequentia est voluptatum: et minus avaritiae molestias patitatur, qui procul ab hominibus positus divitias non videt. Cum ergo sanctus Dei spiritus mentis amet secretum, horreat autem publicum, ad vos pertinet, fratres, cellarum solitudinem, et omnium ergasterium virtutum diligere, et ab eius habitaculo sine causa rationabili se nunquam alienare. Monachus enim secreti amorator non ociosus, qui didicit fortiter in cella consistere, multis interdum sanctis consolationibus fruitur, quibus vagus, et inquietus necessario privatur. Quemadmodum piscis, si diutius teneatur extra aquam, moritur; ita monachi omnis perit devotione, si crebrius extra cellam evagatur. Ioannem imitetur Baptizam, quem Chrysostomus principem dicit esse monachorum, qui monachus, statim ut natus est, in eremo vivit, in eremo nutritur, et Christum in solitudine monachus expectavit. Nam sicut difficile est arborem iuxta viam positam fructus usque ad maturitatem servare, sic difficile est monachum extra cellam suam crebro vagantem, et in actibus mundi occupatum, iustitiae fructus usque ad finem immaculatos custodire. Recedamus igitur de via secularis tumultus, et plantemus nos in secreto monasticae solitudinis; ut nec mundus habeat nobiscum quicquam commune, nec nos cum illo. Mens enim, quae curis, et sollicitudinibus mundi concutitur, raro in Dei amore veraciter radicatur. Motus etenim corporis statum frequenter alterat mentis: et homo, qui semper in externis mergitur, fervore divini spiritus nunquam illustratur. Quies nanque mentis ex solida consistentia corporis nascitur, et vir, qui solitudinem pro Dei amore diligit, fortior, et sibi unitus in sancto exercitio consistit. Quisquis igitur in vobis est, fratres, salutis propriae studiosus amator, discat quietus in cella consistere, et quantum potest, studeat se in operibus divini amoris cum desiderio iugiter occupare. Esto autem quietus in cella, non ociosus; tranquillus, non somnolentus; spirituali semper exercitio deditus, non torpore animi dissolutus. Instrumenta vero spiritualium in cella exercitiorum sunt quatuor, legere, scribere, orare, ac meditari: quintum vero paucis conceditur, qui post veram cordis puritatem in montem contemplationis Domini elevantur. Denique, quatuor ista monachorum exercitia in solitudine cellae manentium, ita sunt moderanda, ut neque taedium generent, neque mentis torporem, sed cuique actioni tempus congruum deputetur, ut dum vi-

of momentary novelty. But I see few among you who love inner quiet, and I grieve deeply, because I know very well that a monk cannot make progress in spiritual conduct if it is clear that he does not love the quiet of the cell. But he who knows how much good the secrecy of solitude brings to the soul loves his cell and does not readily go outside, always fearing that in the turmoil he may lose what he has gathered with great labor in hiddenness. For, as Saint Augustine says, he is less stirred by pleasures who is not where there is a crowd of pleasures; and he suffers less trouble from avarice who, placed far from men, does not see riches.

Since, therefore, the holy Spirit of God loves the secrecy of the mind and shudders at public exposure, it belongs to you, brothers, to love the solitude of your cells, the workshop of all virtues, and never to estrange yourselves from its dwelling without a reasonable cause. For the monk who loves secrecy and is not idle, who has learned to stand firm in his cell, sometimes enjoys many holy consolations, of which the wandering and restless man is necessarily deprived. Just as a fish dies if it is kept too long out of the water, so every monk perishes in devotion if he wanders too often outside his cell.

Let him imitate John the Baptist, whom Chrysostom calls the prince of monks: as a monk, as soon as he was born, he lived in the desert, was nourished in the desert, and as a monk awaited Christ in solitude. For just as it is difficult for a tree planted beside the road to preserve its fruits until maturity, so it is difficult for a monk who often wanders outside his cell and is occupied in the affairs of the world to keep the fruits of righteousness unstained to the end.

Let us therefore withdraw from the road of worldly tumult and plant ourselves in the secrecy of monastic solitude, so that neither the world may have anything in common with us, nor we with it. For a mind shaken by the cares and anxieties of the world is rarely truly rooted in the love of God. The movement of the body often alters the state of the mind, and a man who is always immersed in external things is never illumined by the fervor of the divine Spirit. For quiet of mind is born from the firm steadiness of the body, and the man who loves solitude for the love of God stands stronger and more united to himself in holy exercise.

Therefore whoever among you, brothers, is a zealous lover of his own salvation should learn to remain quietly in his cell and, as much as he can, should strive to occupy himself continually and with desire in the works of divine love. But be quiet in your cell, not idle; tranquil, not sleepy; always devoted to spiritual exercise, not slackened by torpor of soul. The instruments of spiritual exercises in the cell are four: to read, to write, to pray, and to meditate. A fifth is granted to few, those who, after true purity of heart, are raised to the mountain of contemplation of the Lord. Finally, these four exercises of monks remaining in the solitude of the cell must be so moderated that they produce neither weariness nor torpor of mind, but that a fitting time be assigned to each action, so that while

38
Homilia VI. 41 cissitudo mentem alleviat, ultra vires corpusculum non gravetur. Habeat igitur horam suam convenientem studio divinarum lectio scripturarum, quae cum senserit devotionis adesse desiderium, mox in orationem fervidam commutetur. Manualis autem labor, qui monacho commoranti sub tranquillitate solitudinis indicetur, utilis est valde, ne perniciosa in mente tepiditas oriatur. Nam lectio sanctorum scripturarum ad Dei charitatem monachum excitat; meditatio autem passionis dominicae, ac beneficiorum Dei mentem ad fervorem amoris ardentissimi inflammat; oratio vero infirmum animum confirmat, et manualis labor temperate continuatus a torpore, et taedio conservat. Cum oramus instanter, et devote, cum Deo nostro ubique praesente loquimur: dum vero in sanctis scripturis legimus, quid nobis sit appetendum, aut fugiendum, ab ipso Domino edocemur. Oratio, si fuerit ardens in Dei amore, mentem a peccatis, et vitiis purificat; lectio autem instruit, et informat, sancto dicente Isidoro: Orationibus, inquit, mundanur: lectionibus instruimur. Utrunque bonum est, si licet: si non licet utrunque, melius est orare, quam legere. Monachus ergo, qui tempus suum in cella cupit utiliter, et fructuose expendere, his iugiter exercitiis per vices studeat mentem, et corpus occupare: quoniam animus, qui tantis laboribus invigilat, nullum perversis cogitationibus aditum praestat. Hinc divus Hieronymus monachum admonens dicit: Semper aliquid boni facito, ut diabolus inveniat te occupatum; Minus enim pulsatur illecebris carnis, qui semper occupatus utiliter nullum admittit fastidium mentis. Enimvero dum cautus animae suae custos monachus quisque ab unius boni operis exercitio in aliud cum desiderio fervoris sancti per vicissitudinem rapitur, ad constantiam omnium virtutum roboratur, et tanto minus taedium incidit, quanto magis variari studium, et alternis contra fastidium uti consuevit. Unde rursum Hieronymus ait: Lectionem frequenter interrupat oratio, et animam iugiter adhaerentem grata vicissitudo sanctae operationis accendat. Monachus, qui non amat cellae secretum, verus Christi miles non est: quoniam nomen monachi, et habitum portat sine operibus: et qui solitarius esse pro Dei amore debuerat, mente reversus ad saeculum, vanitatis studium amat. Hinc divus Papa Gregorius ait: Qui corpore remotus ab hominibus vivit, sed tumultibus conversationis humanae, terrenorum se desiderio cogitatione immergit, non est solitarius, quamvis in solitudine commoretur. Si vero prematnr aliquis corporaliter popularibus turbis: et tamen nullos secularium cu- rarum tumultus in corde patiatur, non est in urbe, etiam si in medio hominum conversetur. Et hoc est, quod contra Iovinianum sanctus dicit Hieronymus: Sapiens, inquit, nunquam solus esse potest, Habet enim secum omnes, qui sunt, et qui fuerunt boni, et animum liberum, et quaecunque vult, profert, et transfert se, quocunque voluerit. Quod enim 42 De labore Monachorum manuali.

variety relieves the mind, so that the little body is not burdened beyond its strength. Therefore the reading of the divine Scriptures should have its own suitable hour for study; and when it senses that the desire for devotion is present, it should at once be changed into fervent prayer. Manual labor, too, which is appointed for a monk dwelling in the quiet of solitude, is very useful, lest harmful tepidity arise in the mind. For the reading of the holy Scriptures stirs the monk to the love of God; meditation on the Lord’s passion and on the benefits of God inflames the mind to the fervor of most ardent love; prayer strengthens the weak soul; and manual labor, continued temperately, preserves it from sluggishness and weariness.

When we pray earnestly and devoutly, we speak with our God, who is present everywhere; but when we read in the holy Scriptures, we are taught by the Lord himself what we should seek or avoid. Prayer, if it is ardent in the love of God, purifies the mind from sins and vices; reading instructs and forms it, as holy Isidore says: “By prayers,” he says, “we are cleansed; by readings we are instructed. Both are good, if both are possible; if both are not possible, it is better to pray than to read.”

Therefore the monk who desires to spend his time in the cell usefully and fruitfully should strive continually to occupy mind and body by turns in these exercises, because a spirit that keeps watch over such labors gives no entrance to perverse thoughts. Hence blessed Jerome, admonishing the monk, says: “Always do something good, so that the devil may find you occupied.” For he is less assailed by the enticements of the flesh who, always usefully occupied, admits no weariness of mind.

Indeed, when every monk, as a careful guardian of his soul, is carried by turn from the practice of one good work to another with the desire of holy fervor, he is strengthened in the constancy of all virtues; and he falls into weariness the less, the more he has been accustomed to vary his occupation and to use alternating tasks against weariness. Hence Jerome again says: “Let prayer frequently interrupt reading, and let a pleasing alternation of holy activity continually kindle the soul that clings to God.”

The monk who does not love the secrecy of the cell is not a true soldier of Christ, because he bears the name and habit of a monk without the works; and he who ought to have been solitary for love of God has turned back in mind to the world and loves the pursuit of vanity. Hence blessed Pope Gregory says: “He who lives bodily removed from men, but in thought plunges himself, through desire for earthly things, into the tumults of human intercourse, is not solitary, although he dwells in solitude. But if someone is physically pressed by the crowds of the people, and yet suffers no tumults of secular cares in his heart, he is not in the city, even if he lives in the midst of men.”

And this is what holy Jerome says against Jovinian: “The wise man,” he says, “can never be alone. For he has with him all good men, both those who are and those who have been; he has a free mind, and whatever he wishes he brings forth, and he carries himself wherever he wishes.” For what

39
corpore non potest, mente complectitur: et si hominum inopia fuerit, loquitur cum Deo. Nunquam ergo vir bonus solus erit. Itaque consistens in cella tua, semper ocium caveto: quoniam nihil ita vires mentis ener- vat omnes, sicut ocium; posteaquam ex se produxerit accidiam. Si Deum ardenter amaveris, nunquam eris ociosus, quia verus Christi amor non sinit in animo nasci torporem, sed impellit semper ad voluntatem dilecti amantem. Et sicuti quidam carnaliter sapiens veraciter dixit, qui non vult fieri desidiosus, amet, ita nos docuit experientia in amore spirituali, quia mentem, quam inhabitare coeperit, torpescere ocium, et ignavia non permittit. Semper enim ad meliora divinus amor impellit, et quanto plus ardendo profecerit, tanto sui maius incrementum sumit. Huius vero ergasterium amoris est conscientia mundi, quam si monachus, et quod habere, et conservare mundam desiderat, necesse in primis est, quod mundi vanitates, et rerum temporalium negotia contemnat. Non enim possibile est, quod geminus in uno residente pectore amor, nec prae- valet homo diligere Christum, qui non vult contemnere mundum. Deus nanque in Trinitate Personarum, cum sit in essentia substantiae unus, aut solus a nobis diligetur, aut cum socio non amatitur. Ut igitur con- scientia in omni puritate permaneat mundi, utque Deum amare mens valeat super omnia, secretum cellae monachus diligit, et nunquam ab interna dulcedinis exercitio recedat. In cella enim boni, et sapientis monachi summa tranquillitas est: et si uspiam est paradisus terrestris, in monasterio est eorum, qui ad puritatem institutionis coenobiticae conservantur. Est ibi pax, pietas, bonitas, lux, virtus, honestas: est ibi gaudium, puritas, dulcedo, et magna vitae tranquillitas: ubi monachus orator devotus cum Domino loquitur, et futura caelestis regni suavitas a contemplativo milite praegustatur. O cella monachorum Deo vera- citer servientium paradisus: tu certe hortulus es honestissimae voluptatis, in quo mens Deo per amore coniungitur, et per desiderium dulciter elevatur. Monachus, qui te diligit, veneratur, et colit, verus Christi miles est, et Domino in plenitudine virtutum deservit. Ille vero, qui cellae secretum abhorret, et deserit, salutis propriae officinam contemnit. Vos igitur, fratres mei charissimi, precor, ut secretum cellae incipiatis cum desiderio mentis incolere: sine cuius amore nullus ad perfectionem vir- tutum in coenobio poterit pervenire. De labore Monachorum manuali. Homilia VII. ABORES mānuum tuarum quia manducabis, inquit Propheta Domini, beatus es, et bene tibi erit. Si beati censentur on:nes, qui proprio manuum vicitant de labore: nemo certe panem manducat sine reatu, et crimen ociosus. Omnipotens nanque Deus hanc protoplasto Adae

What he cannot embrace with the body, he embraces with the mind; and if there is a lack of human company, he speaks with God. Therefore the good man will never be alone. And so, remaining in your cell, always beware idleness, because nothing so weakens all the powers of the mind as idleness, once it has produced listlessness from itself. If you have loved God ardently, you will never be idle, because the true love of Christ does not allow sluggishness to be born in the soul, but always impels the lover toward the will of the beloved. And just as a certain carnally wise man truly said, “Let him love who does not wish to become slothful,” so experience has taught us in spiritual love, because it does not permit the mind in which it has begun to dwell to grow sluggish through idleness and laziness. For divine love always impels one toward better things, and the more it advances by burning, the greater increase it takes to itself.

The workshop of this love is a clean conscience; and if a monk desires both to have it and to preserve it clean, it is necessary first of all that he despise the vanities of the world and the business of temporal things. For it is not possible that a double love should reside in one breast, nor can a man succeed in loving Christ if he is unwilling to despise the world. For God, though in the Trinity of Persons he is one in the essence of substance, will either be loved by us alone, or he is not loved with a partner. Therefore, so that conscience may remain clean in all purity, and so that the mind may be able to love God above all things, the monk loves the solitude of the cell and never withdraws from the inner exercise of sweetness.

For in the cell of a good and wise monk there is the highest tranquility; and if anywhere there is an earthly paradise, it is in the monastery of those who are preserved according to the purity of the cenobitic institution. There is peace, piety, goodness, light, virtue, honor; there is joy, purity, sweetness, and great tranquility of life, where the devout monk in prayer speaks with the Lord, and the future sweetness of the heavenly kingdom is tasted beforehand by the contemplative soldier. O cell, paradise of monks truly serving God: surely you are the little garden of most honorable delight, in which the mind is joined to God through love and is sweetly lifted up through desire. The monk who loves, reveres, and cherishes you is a true soldier of Christ and serves the Lord in the fullness of virtues. But he who abhors and deserts the solitude of the cell despises the workshop of his own salvation. Therefore I beg you, my dearest brothers, begin to inhabit the solitude of the cell with longing of mind; without love for it, no one in the monastery will be able to attain the perfection of virtues.

On the Manual Labor of Monks. Homily VII.

“Because you shall eat the labors of your hands,” says the Prophet of the Lord, “you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.” If all who live by the labor of their own hands are judged blessed, surely no one eats bread without guilt while idle, and the idle man is blameworthy. For almighty God [unclear] this to the first-formed Adam.

40
Homilia VII. 43 poenam pro mandati originalis transgressione inflixit, denuncians ei, quoniam in sudore vultus sui cibum de terra manibus operaturus esset. Cum autem in Adam peccaverimus omnes, eisdem necessario poenis subicimur, quibus illum constat fuisse suppositum. Manibus ille suis laborabat escam, unde viveret, nec panem oculos manducabat. Hinc divus pater noster Benedictus ocium detestans monachorum in regula, quam nobis tradidit, inquit: Ociositas inimica est animae, et ideo certis temporibus occupari debent monachi in labore manuum, certisque iterum horis in lectione divina. Tunc enim vere sunt monachi, si labore manuum suarum vivunt, sicut et patres nostri fecerunt, et apostoli. Unde et sanctus Christophilus Paulus in epistola dicit: Qui non laborat, non manducet.
