Erat in primordio monastici status ista consuetudo monachorum, ut nullum sine labore admitterent in sui consortium, non tam propter victus necessaria, quam propter animae salutem, ne perniciosis cogitationibus per ocium daretur occasio. Non erant monachis illo tempore census, non decimae, non reditus, non proventus ulli annuales: sed victum, et vestitum omnes in comuni conversantes manibus sibi procurabant, neminem debiti exatione gravantes. Sancti quoque Salvatoris nostri apostoli, cum haberent potestatem de praedicatione Evangelii vivendi, manibus suis laborare maluerunt, ne quem fidelium gravasse viderentur, et ut haberent, non solum unde ipsi viverent, sed etiam quo indigentibus necessaria ministrarent. Verum postea quam census monachi habere coeperunt, et reditus, pristina mox simplicitatis studia defecerunt, crevitque paulatim cum divitiis rerum temporalium superbia, intantum ut labores manuum omnes cum tempore monachi recusarent. Quandiu fuerunt pauperes monachi, et genere humiles, Deum in veritate coluerunt: postea vero quum divitiis abundare coeperunt, simplicitatem fugavit duplicitas, et elatio nobilium humilitatem monachorum extirpavit. Integritas nanque observantiae regularis abundantiām peperit rerum temporalium: sed paulatim divitiae monachorum puritatem ordinis funditus extinxerunt. Sublata vero integritate observantiae regularis, mox etiam in multis coenobiis divitiae rerum temporalium iusto Dei iudicio defecerunt. Ex eorum numero praesens monasterium fuit Spanhemense, neque ultimum, fratres mei, neque primum: quod multis annis in utroque statu miserabiliter mansit desolatum usque adeo, quod quinque in eo duntaxat monachi vitam agentes dissolutam non haberent, unde sibi vitae necessaria desumerent. Unde misericordia Dei tandem providente, Fredericus Dux Transilvanus invocato patrum ordinis reformati consilio, anno Christianorum sexagesimo nono supra quadrigentesimum, atque millesimum, deformatos vita monachos ex-pulit, abbatem nomine Ottonem de Colonia deposuit, et alias de ob- servantia Burssfeldensium ex coenobio Montis Speciosi nuncupatos,

Homily VII.

He inflicted punishment for the transgression of the original commandment, declaring to him that by the sweat of his face he would have to work his food from the earth with his hands. And since we all sinned in Adam, we are necessarily subject to the same penalties to which he is known to have been subjected. He labored with his hands for the food by which he might live, nor did he eat his bread in idleness.

Hence our holy father Benedict, detesting the idleness of monks in the Rule which he handed down to us, says: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul, and therefore at fixed times the monks ought to be occupied in manual labor, and again at fixed hours in divine reading. For then they are truly monks, if they live by the labor of their own hands, as our fathers and the apostles also did.” Hence Saint Paul also says in the epistle: “He who does not work, let him not eat.”

In the beginning of the monastic state this was the custom of monks: that they admitted no one into their fellowship without labor, not so much because of the necessities of food as because of the salvation of the soul, lest through idleness occasion be given to destructive thoughts. At that time monks had no rents, no tithes, no revenues, no annual proceeds of any kind; but all, living in common, procured food and clothing for themselves with their hands, burdening no one by the exaction of debt.

The holy apostles of our Savior also, although they had the power to live from the preaching of the Gospel, preferred to labor with their own hands, lest they should seem to have burdened any of the faithful, and so that they might have not only what they themselves could live on, but also something from which they could supply necessities to the needy.

But after monks began to have rents and revenues, the former zeal for simplicity soon failed, and pride gradually grew along with the wealth of temporal things, to such a degree that in time monks refused all manual labors. As long as monks were poor and humble in birth, they worshiped God in truth; but afterwards, when they began to abound in riches, duplicity drove out simplicity, and the arrogance of nobles uprooted the humility of monks. For the integrity of regular observance had produced an abundance of temporal goods; but little by little the riches of the monks utterly extinguished the purity of the order. And when the integrity of regular observance had been taken away, soon in many monasteries the riches of temporal goods also failed by the just judgment of God.

Among these was the present monastery of Spanheim, neither the last, my brothers, nor the first. For many years it remained miserably desolate in both respects, to such an extent that the only five monks living there, and living a dissolute life, did not have the means from which to obtain the necessities of life. Therefore, at last, by the providence of God’s mercy, Frederick, Duke of Transylvania, after invoking the counsel of the fathers of the reformed order, in the one thousand four hundred sixty-ninth year of the Christians, expelled the monks deformed in life, deposed the abbot, named Otto of Cologne, and called in others from the observance of Bursfeld, from the monastery called Mount Speciosus,

41
44 De labore Monachorum manuali. quatuor in hoc monasterio collocavit: quibus Abbatem praefecit Ioannem ex nobili familia de Budisbach, quam vulgo de Carbonaria domo nuncupant: virum qualis vidistis, et audistis aeterna memoria dignum, qui locum hunc in extrema paupertate reperit, et annis ferme quatuordecim in magna patientia praesidens in eum statum, quo nunc vivimus, revocavit. Unde cum nos inopia rerum temporalium adhuc graviter premat, opus continuo esset labore, quo nos victu aleremus necessario, et domum Dei, in qua versamur, ab aere solveremus alieno. Sed qui sunt vestri labores, aut quantum nobis ad tam grandia conducere possunt? Numero sumus pauci, et rusticanos ad labores inepti: nec permittit nos ordinis Sacerdotalis institutio totum in agro diem lapides manibus versare, et Divinam intermittere servitutem. Miseri sumus, et nimia paupertate, inopiaque omnium necessariorum depressi: et si multum laboraverimus, parum exinde proficimur: et si parum fuerimus operati, amplius certe animo deficiemus. Homo enim, scriptura testante, nascitur ad laborem (quemadmodum avis ad volandum). Ne igitur panem vestrum manducetis ociosi, semper vos aliquo labore honesto, et utili oportebit esse mancipatos, quo et mens a taedio relevetur observantiae regularis, et inopia gravis, vel in parvo saltem reparetur. Messis tempore ad foenum, et autumni diebus ad vindemiam vos duntaxat extra Monasterium consuevimus occupare, quando videlicet labor, et multum est necessarius, et mercenariorum charitas, precium, mercedemque adauget famulorum. Reliquo vos tempore in coenobio decrevimus continere, propterea quod labores vestri comparatione impensarum monasterii utilitatibus parum conducunt, et voluntarii ad rusticana studia paucissimi vestrum, ut nobis videtur, libenter occurrunt. Est et alia consideratio, quae animum concitat meum, ne vos externis operibus manuum de facili occupem sine causa rationabili, et necessitate manifesta: experior etenim, quod labores huiuscemodi operis non conveniunt in vobis observantiae regularis, sed integritatem monasticae disciplinae apud vos magis destruunt, quam promoveant. Erubesco dicere, et nihilominus effari ccmpellor, vestros labores extra Monasterium, et cellam plus destructionis afferre puritati animarum, quam salutis. Quid enim laboratis, et quae sunt studia vestra in laboribus? Nonne vagari, discurrere, comessionationibus indulgere, et pocolis, ac reliquum temporis sermonibus occupare vanis, et inutilibus? Non habetis in vobis illum spiritus Dei sanctum fervorem, quo priscos institutionis nostrae Monachos legimus quondam inflammatos; qui pro necessitate communi tanto desiderio, tanto studio, tantoque conatu omnes, et singuli manibus suis laborabant, ut putassetis omne Monasterii negotium in uniuscuiusque providentia locatum. Ita enim laborabant, ac si manibus suis singuli omnem enutrire congregationem debuissent. Inter haec tamen Divini

He placed four in this monastery, over whom he set as abbot John, from the noble family of Budisbach, commonly called “of the house of Carbonaria”: a man such as you have seen and heard, worthy of eternal memory. He found this place in extreme poverty and, presiding over it for almost fourteen years with great patience, restored it to the condition in which we now live.

Therefore, since lack of temporal goods still presses heavily upon us, there would be continual need of labor by which we might feed ourselves with necessary sustenance and free the house of God in which we dwell from debt. But what are your labors, or how much can they help us in such great matters? We are few in number and unfit for rustic labors; nor does the institution of the priestly order permit us to spend the whole day in the field turning stones with our hands and to neglect the divine service.

We are wretched, crushed by excessive poverty and by lack of all necessities. If we labor much, we gain little from it; and if we have worked little, we shall certainly fail still more in spirit. For man, as Scripture bears witness, is born to labor, just as a bird is born to fly. Therefore, lest you eat your bread in idleness, you must always be bound to some honest and useful labor, by which both the mind may be relieved from weariness in regular observance and our heavy poverty may be repaired, at least in some small measure.

In harvest time we have been accustomed to employ you outside the monastery only for haymaking, and in the days of autumn for the vintage, when, that is, the labor is both very necessary and the scarcity of hired men increases the price and wages of servants. At other times we have determined to keep you within the monastery, because your labors, in comparison with the monastery’s expenses, contribute little to its advantage, and, as it seems to us, very few of you willingly come forward of your own accord for rustic pursuits.

There is also another consideration that stirs my mind not to occupy you readily in external works of the hands without reasonable cause and evident necessity. For I find by experience that labors of this kind do not agree in you with regular observance, but rather destroy than promote the integrity of monastic discipline among you. I am ashamed to say it, and nevertheless I am compelled to utter it: your labors outside the monastery and the cell bring more destruction to the purity of souls than salvation.

For what do you labor at, and what are your pursuits in your labors? Are they not to wander about, run here and there, indulge in feasting and cups, and spend the rest of the time in vain and useless conversations? You do not have within yourselves that holy fervor of the Spirit of God with which we read that the monks of our ancient institution were once inflamed; for the common necessity they all and individually labored with their hands with such desire, such zeal, and such effort that you would have thought the whole business of the monastery rested in the foresight of each one. For they labored as though each one had to nourish the whole congregation with his own hands. Yet amid these things, the divine

42
Homilia VII. 45 cultus obsequium tanta cum alacritate die, ac nocte persolverunt, quasi laboribus manuum in nulla penitus fuissent occupati. Quis talium in vobis imitator est, fratres, ut inopiam communitatis nostrae totius, vel suam existimet, vel sudore vultus sui laborando pro viribus studeat revelare? Illi manibus laborantes continuis Deum cordibus exorabant: vos autem fabulis intenti, nec manibus officio satisfacitis, nec Monachi mentibus. Tempore quoque ieiunii regularis, illi statutum sibi abstinenceae modum, aut diligentiter custodiebant, aut si praemagnitudine laborum nequivissent, ideo manducabant, quatenus laboribus apti, et idonei redderentur. Vos autem non manducatis, ut laboretis, sed laboratis potius, ut manducetis. Quando ex regula fuerat ieiunandum, occasionem ex labore sumitis, ut ieiunium solvatis. Coeterum quam immunde, et viliissime nonnulli ex vobis tractent indumenta sua, quis regularis disciplinae studiosus amator aequanimiter ferat? Cuius nam sunt, fratres mei, quae dispendiose consumitis? Christi patrimonium est omne, quod pertinet ad Monasteria servorum Dei, totumque Deo dicatum est, nec rebus Christi cuicumque licet abuti, vel eas in usum alium commutare. An nescitis, quid vobis Sanctus Legislator noster Benedictus dicat in regula? Si quis sordide, aut negligentiter res Monasterii tractaverit, corripiatur: Si non emendaverit, disciplinae regulari subiaceat. Et in capite de cellario Monasterii dicit: Omnia vasa Monasterii, cunctamque substantiam ita servet, ac si altaris vasa sacra conspiciat. Denique tacere non possum, nec debo certe, quam sordide, ac negligentiter plerique vestrum tractent omnia, quasi vel non conspicientur a Deo, vel nullum eorum rebus coenobii pariat detrimentum ignavia. Scitote fratres, quoniam praenuncians annuncio vobis, quod pro his omnibus, sicut et pro aliis peccatis vestris Domino Deo rationem estis reddituri. Labores extra Monasterium propterea vobis minui, ne gravius male operando peccaretis, et inunxi vobis opus manuale, scribere, libros ligare, hisque similia: quae cum tranquillitate mentis, et corporis intra septa Monasterii potestis perficere. Utinam vel ista manuum vestrarum opera cum diligentia pro Dei Amore faceretis, ne panem in toto comedatis ociosi. Nullum est opus manuale, quod Monachum meo iudicio plus deceat, quam libros sacrae lectionis scribere, et sribentibus aliis necessaria praeparare. Hunc enim sanctum laborem oratione plerunque licebit interumpere, et pro cibo mentis non minus, quam corporis vigilare. Nec- cessitas etiam nos urget libris scribendis cum diligentia intendere, si cupimus habere ad manum, unde nos mutuo possimus in studio spiri- tuali utiliter occupare. Cernitis enim huius coenobii bibliothecam omnem, quae olim fuit insignis, et magna, per deformatos ante nos Monachos usque adeo distractam, venditam, et alienatam, ut ultra quatuordecim volumina non fuerint hinc a nobis inventa. Industria quidem impressio- 46 De labore Monachorum manuali.

they paid the service of worship day and night with such eagerness as if they had not been occupied at all in the labors of their hands. Which of you, brothers, is an imitator of such men, so that he regards the need of our whole community as his own, or strives, according to his strength, to relieve it by laboring in the sweat of his brow? They, while laboring with their hands, prayed to God with unceasing hearts; but you, intent on tales, satisfy neither the duty of your hands nor that of monks in your minds.

In the time of the regular fast, too, they either diligently kept the measure of abstinence appointed for them, or, if they could not do so because of the great extent of their labors, they ate for this reason: that they might be made fit and capable for their labors. But you do not eat in order to work, but rather work in order to eat. When, according to the Rule, you ought to fast, you take occasion from work to break the fast.

Moreover, how filthily and contemptibly some of you treat their clothing: what lover zealous for regular discipline could bear it calmly? Whose property is it, my brothers, that you wastefully consume? Everything that belongs to the monasteries of God’s servants is Christ’s patrimony, and all of it is dedicated to God; nor is it lawful for anyone to misuse the things of Christ, or to divert them to another use. Do you not know what our holy lawgiver Benedict says to you in the Rule? “If anyone treats the things of the monastery in a dirty or negligent way, let him be corrected. If he does not amend, let him be subjected to regular discipline.” And in the chapter on the cellarer of the monastery he says: “Let him keep all the vessels of the monastery and all its substance as if he were looking upon the sacred vessels of the altar.”

Finally, I cannot be silent, and certainly ought not to be, about how filthily and negligently many of you treat everything, as if you were either not seen by God, or as if the sloth of any of you caused no harm to the property of the community. Know, brothers, that I forewarn you and announce to you that for all these things, as also for your other sins, you will have to render an account to the Lord God.

I therefore reduced for you the labors outside the monastery, lest by working badly you should sin more gravely, and I enjoined on you manual work: writing, binding books, and things of this kind, which you can accomplish within the enclosure of the monastery with tranquility of mind and body. Would that you performed even these works of your hands diligently for the love of God, so that you may not eat your bread wholly idle. There is no manual work which, in my judgment, is more fitting for a monk than to write books of sacred reading and to prepare necessities for others who write. For this holy labor may very often be interrupted by prayer, and one may keep watch no less for the food of the mind than of the body. Necessity also presses us to devote ourselves diligently to writing books, if we wish to have at hand the means by which we may occupy ourselves together usefully in spiritual study. For you see that the whole library of this community, which once was distinguished and great, has been so scattered, sold, and alienated by the misshapen monks before us that no more than fourteen volumes were found here by us. The industry of printing...

43
riae artis nostris diebus nuper ad Moguntiam inventae multa quotidianie volumina producit in lucem, sed comparare nobis omnia nequaquam est possibile, qui adhuc maxima deprimimur egestate. Quo circa vos moneo, et hortor, qui ad externos manuum labores non satis libenter occurritis, quatenus ad honorem Dei scribendis voluminibus, quam diligenter laboretis; quia sicut ociositas inimica est animae, sic labor moderatus spiritualis conservator est vitae. Monachus enim, quia miles est regis aeterni, nunquam debet esse ociosus. Ociun nanque parit accidiam, et illa introducit animae perniciosae mortis egestatem. Labores autem Monachorum ita sunt moderandi, ut nunquam a Divinis vacent colloquis sed inter opera manuum in corde meditatio ferveat scripturarum: quae posteaquam in ardorem spiritus mentem perduxerit, mox in orationem devotissimam commutetur. Sit ergo Monachus Christi miles, sicuti animal Dei mundum, quod ruminat, habens semper in ore cordis sui sanctarum pabula scripturarum, ne vanis, et perniciosis cogitationibus mens pateat, aut verbum ex ore loquentis turpe, sive ociosum erumpat. Memor sit semper inter operandum scripturae dicentis: Beatus vir qui in lege Domini meditabitur die, ac nocte. Omnis enim, qui Dominum Iesum in veritate diligit, doctrinam simul, et passionem eius in corde suo cum lacrymis et orationibus quotidianie revolvit. Verus namque Dei amator non est, qui mandatorum eius, vel ad momentum Eccles. 2. Psal. 118. Obliviscitur. Enimvero, sicut ait scriptura, qui diligunt Dominum, requirunt, quae beneplacita sunt illi, et qui timent nomen sanctum eius, replebuntur lege ipsius. Hinc quidam sanctorum dixit ad Dominum: In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi. Excitandus ergo semper animus, et stimulis spiritualibus quotidianie renovandus, ne vel ignavia torpeat, vel inerti ocio languescat. Laboris Monasticae institutionis exercitium, lectionis, et orationis studium, et diligens custodia vigiliarum, vera sunt incitamenta virtutum. Nihil autem sancto proposito Monachi perniciosius ocio, quoniam et carnem excitat in libidinem, et mentis omnem enervat virtutem, extinguitque spiritus fervorem. Omnium enim fomes, et nutrimentum malorum in claustro est ocium. Ubicunque igitur fueris, sive in agro, sive in claustro semper ocium ut perniciosissimam animae pestem fugito, mentem ornans, et exercitans vel oratione, vel meditatione scripturarum. Cum bonis, et studiosis Dei amatoribus conversare libenter: negligentes vero, et salutis propriae contemptores devita. Qui enim picemi contingit, inquinabitur ab ea: et qui socium se facit peccatorum, non erit immunis a scelere. Sermones tuos diligenter considera, ut nulli detrahans omnino, nec alium auscultes detrahentem: quoniam detractor simul, et libens auditor, uterque daemoni famulator, alter loquendo, alter vero auscultando. Labora sicut bonus miles Christi Iesu: et diligenter operare manibus, quodcunque

The art recently invented at Mainz in our own days brings forth many volumes daily into the light; but it is by no means possible for us to purchase them all, since we are still weighed down by the greatest poverty. Therefore I warn and exhort you, who do not very readily turn to external labors of the hands, to labor as diligently as you can, for the honor of God, in writing books; for just as idleness is the enemy of the soul, so moderate labor is the preserver of the spiritual life.

For the monk, because he is a soldier of the eternal King, must never be idle. Idleness indeed gives birth to sloth, and sloth brings upon the soul the want of deadly destruction. But the labors of monks must be so moderated that they are never empty of divine converse, but that amid the works of the hands meditation on the Scriptures may burn in the heart; and after it has led the mind into the ardor of the spirit, it should at once be changed into most devout prayer.

Let the monk, therefore, be a soldier of Christ, like a clean animal of God, which chews the cud, always having in the mouth of his heart the food of the holy Scriptures, lest his mind lie open to vain and harmful thoughts, or a foul or idle word burst from the mouth of the speaker. Let him always remember, while he works, the saying of Scripture: Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.

For everyone who truly loves the Lord Jesus daily turns over in his heart, with tears and prayers, both his teaching and his passion. For he is not a true lover of God who forgets his commandments even for a moment. Indeed, as Scripture says, those who love the Lord seek the things that are pleasing to him, and those who fear his holy name will be filled with his law. Hence one of the saints said to the Lord: I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you.

The soul, therefore, must always be stirred up and daily renewed by spiritual goads, lest it grow dull through laziness or languish in sluggish idleness. The exercise of monastic discipline in labor, the pursuit of reading and prayer, and the careful keeping of vigils are true incentives to virtue. Nothing, however, is more destructive to the holy purpose of a monk than idleness, since it both stirs the flesh to lust, weakens every virtue of the mind, and extinguishes the fervor of the spirit. For idleness in the cloister is the tinder and nourishment of all evils.

Wherever, then, you may be, whether in the field or in the cloister, always flee idleness as the most destructive plague of the soul, adorning and exercising your mind either with prayer or with meditation on the Scriptures. Gladly keep company with good and zealous lovers of God; but avoid the negligent and those who despise their own salvation. For he who touches pitch will be defiled by it; and he who makes himself the companion of sinners will not be free from guilt.

Consider your words carefully, so that you do not disparage anyone at all, nor listen to another who disparages someone; for the slanderer and the willing listener alike are servants of the devil, the one by speaking, the other by listening. Labor like a good soldier of Christ Jesus, and diligently do with your hands whatever...

44
Homilia VII. 47 tibi ex obedientia iniungitur: nec tibi durum videatur alterius obedere imperio, pro quo spiritui tuo corona aeternae foelicitatis praeparatur in Coelo. Unde nullus labor gravis, nullum tempus longum, nulla Monacho dura videri observantia debet, quibus gloria aeternae beatitudinis acquiritur. Brevitatem huius vitae fratres mei perpendite, et agite bonum, quandiu licet: quoniam qui nunc parce seminat, post mortem quoque parce et metet: et pro suo unusquisque opere mercedem condignam recepturus est, non pro alieno. Laborandi tempus brevissimum est: mercedis vero, quae bonis debetur operibus, sempiternum. Considerate fratres mei homines mundo implicatos, et omnes huius seculi amatores, quam fortes sunt in rebus terrenis, atque caducis, in coelestibus vero debiles, et infirmi, ut vos intantum Deo placere curetis, quantum illi, ut mundo divites appareant, et gloriosi, continue laborant. Nam pro temporali gloria multi usque ad mortem desudare non refugunt: sed pro spe futurae foelicitatis etiam parum, vel agere, vel sustinere contemnunt. Pro terrenis lucris quaslibet injurias patientissime tolerant: et pro coelesti mercede substinere, vel tenuissimi verbi contumeliam recusant. Regi terreno, Principi, vel Iudici totidie fortes possunt assistere: in oratione autem coram omnipotente Domino ad unius horae spicium nequeunt perdurare. Multa pro acquirendis perituriis divitiis adversa libenter tolerant: superna vero bona quaerere tanto magis negligunt, quanto in amore terrestrium delectabilius occupantur. Horum vos conversatio, fratres charissimi, admoneat omnes huius mundi curas tanto amplius fugere, quanto iam vobis licet minus terrenarum rerum negotia pertractare. Omnem sollicitudinem vestram, et curam pro acquisitione celestium bonorum semper impendite, et pro mercede futurae beatitudinis omni tempore diligentissime laborate. Nam sicut scriptura testatur, militia est vita vestra super terram: et quaecumque homo seminaverit, haec et metet. Scitote, quia mors quotidianus properat, et singulis momentis pars vitae non amplius reversura extinguitur. Vigilate igitur fratres mei charissimi, vigilate: quia nescitis, quando Dominus Deus noster ad iudicium mortis uniuscuiusque venturus sit, sero, an media nocte, an galli cantu, an mane; ne cum venerit repente, inveniat vos dormientes. Vigilate itaque omni tempore orantes, ut digni habeamini fugere mala omnia, quae futura sunt, et stare cum fiducia ante conspectum Filii Dei omnia iudicantis. Omnes enim, divo testante Christophilo, stabimus ante tribunal Christi, ut referat unusquisque propriam corporis, prout gessit, sive bonum, sive malum. Beatus ille monachus, quem invenerit Dominus in bonis operibus vigilantem, qui se ad nuptias Agni coelestis in vera puritate cordis praeparaverit, qui occurrere iudici non formidabit. Semper sit illud in cordibus vestris memorabile verbum Divi Hieronymi super Evangelium sanctum Matthaeum 48 Quod sine intermissione sit orandum.

is enjoined upon you out of obedience; and let it not seem hard to you to obey the command of another, for in return for it a crown of eternal happiness is being prepared for your spirit in heaven. Therefore no labor should seem burdensome, no time long, no observance hard to a monk, by which the glory of eternal blessedness is acquired.

Consider, my brothers, the shortness of this life, and do good while it is permitted; for he who now sows sparingly will also reap sparingly after death, and each person will receive the fitting reward for his own work, not for another’s. The time for labor is very brief, but the reward owed to good works is everlasting.

Consider, my brothers, men entangled in the world and all lovers of this age: how strong they are in earthly and perishable affairs, but weak and feeble in heavenly ones. Take care to please God as much as they continually labor to appear rich and glorious in the world. For many do not shrink from sweating even to death for temporal glory; but for the hope of future happiness they scorn to do or endure even a little. For earthly gains they bear any injuries with the greatest patience, yet for a heavenly reward they refuse to endure even the insult of the slightest word. They can stand daily, strong and steadfast, before an earthly king, prince, or judge; but in prayer before the almighty Lord they cannot persist for the space of one hour. They willingly bear many adversities to acquire riches that will perish; but they neglect heavenly goods all the more, the more delightfully they are occupied in love of earthly things.

Let their way of life, dearly beloved brothers, warn you to flee all the cares of this world so much the more, now that it is permitted you to handle the business of earthly things so much the less. Always devote all your solicitude and care to the acquisition of heavenly goods, and labor most diligently at all times for the reward of future blessedness. For, as Scripture bears witness, your life on earth is warfare/service, and whatever a man has sown, that also he will reap.

Know that death hastens daily, and at every moment a part of life, never to return again, is extinguished. Watch, therefore, my dearly beloved brothers, watch, for you do not know when the Lord our God will come for the judgment of each one’s death: evening, midnight, cockcrow, or morning; lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping. Therefore watch at all times, praying that you may be deemed worthy to escape all the evils that are to come and to stand with confidence before the sight of the Son of God, who judges all things. For, as the blessed Christophilus testifies, we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is proper to the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil.

Blessed is that monk whom the Lord finds watching in good works, who has prepared himself for the wedding-feast of the heavenly Lamb in true purity of heart, who will not fear to meet the Judge. Let that memorable saying of Saint Jerome on the holy Gospel according to Matthew always be in your hearts:

45
dicentis: Sive comedam, sive bibam, sive aliud quid faciam, semper vox illa videtur sonare in auribus meis, Surgite mortui, et venite ad iudicium. Quoties diem illum cogito futuri examinis, totus corde, et corpore contremisco. Unde si qua praesentis vitae est laetitia, fratres mei, ita agenda est, ut amaritudo illius tremendi iudicii nuncquam recedat a memoria. O dies illa magna, terribilis, tremenda nimium, et amara valde: in qua Sol, et Luna obscurabuntur, non diminutione luminis, sed comparatione maiestatis: ubi cessabit omne argumentum excusationis: ubi omnia erunt manifesta: nihilque latere iudicem poterit: quoniam qui novit occultas cogitationes mentium, tunc palam iudicabit: qui nec gratia praevenitur, nec misericordia flectitur, muneribus, et donis non corrupitur, precibus non mitigabitur, nec satisfactio iam deinceps aliqua placabitur. In hac igitur vita positi, fratres, agat unusquisque vestrum pro anima sua, quantum potest: quoniam poenitentia peccatorum hic facta solum est utilis, et fructuosa, quandiu locus est veniae, et sententia adhuc differtur iustitiae. Qui bene facere, ac poenitentiam agere differt usque ad mortem, damnationi est proximus: quoniam bonum, quod sanus, et incolimus negligit, raro infirmus, et iam moriturus instaurabit. Dicit enim Sanctus Papa Gregorius: Quisquis poenitentiae fructus differre usque ad mortis horam non metuit, ipse sibi testis est, quod poenitere veraciter nunquam in eius mente fuit. Nunc ergo convertite vos ad Dominum nostrum in toto corde vestro poenitentiam agentes coram illo, et sic vivite, precor, ut cum hinc migrandum fuerit, apparere ante faciem eius non timeatis. Quod sine intermissione sit orandum. Homilia VIII. DOMINUS, ac Salvator noster Iesus Christus in Evangelio, fratres, sanctum Lucam, volens nos continuos esse in orationibus, ita praemonuit dicens: Oportet semper orare, et nunquam deficere. Hoc Domini consilium prae cunctis mortalibus maxime decet Monachos, et omnes in quacunque religione claustrales: quorum omnis actio, et tota vita, immo quicquid faciunt, aut oratio esse debet, aut saltem orationi conforme. Dicuntur enim non absque ratione spiritualis, quicunque militiam profitentur Monasticam, quatenus ipso moneantur vocabulo, carnis voluptates pro Dei amore contemnere, et per veram charitatem in ardore spiritus ambulare. Dicit nanque Sanctus Christi Apostolus. Qui in carne sunt, placere non possunt: quoniam, si secundum carnem vi- xeritis, moriēmini: si autem spiritu facta carnis mortificaveritis, vivetis. Sciens autem sine orationis instantia fervorem spiritu diu nobis non posse subsistere, iterum ad Thessalonicenses ait: Semper gaudete; sine intermissione orate; in omnibus gratias agite, quoniam haec est vo-

saying: “Whether I eat or drink, or whatever else I do, that voice always seems to sound in my ears: ‘Arise, you dead, and come to judgment.’ As often as I think of that day of the future examination, I tremble in my whole heart and body. Therefore, if there is any gladness in the present life, my brothers, it must be pursued in such a way that the bitterness of that dreadful judgment never withdraws from memory.

O that great day, terrible, exceedingly dreadful, and very bitter, on which the sun and moon will be darkened, not by any lessening of their light, but by comparison with his majesty; where every argument of excuse will cease; where all things will be manifest, and nothing will be able to lie hidden from the Judge; because he who knows the hidden thoughts of minds will then judge openly; he who is not anticipated by favor, nor bent by mercy, is not corrupted by gifts and presents, will not be softened by prayers, nor will any satisfaction thereafter appease him.

Therefore, placed in this life, brothers, let each of you do as much as he can for his soul, because repentance for sins performed here alone is useful and fruitful, so long as there is room for pardon and the sentence of justice is still deferred. He who puts off doing good and doing penance until death is near to damnation, because the good which he neglects when healthy and sound, he will rarely restore when sick and already about to die. For holy Pope Gregory says: Whoever does not fear to defer the fruits of repentance until the hour of death is himself a witness against himself that true repentance was never in his mind. Now, therefore, turn yourselves to our Lord with your whole heart, doing penance before him; and so live, I beg you, that when you must depart from here, you may not fear to appear before his face.

That one must pray without interruption. Homily VIII.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in the Gospel, brothers, according to Saint Luke, wishing us to be constant in prayers, gave this warning, saying: “One must always pray and never give up.” This counsel of the Lord befits monks above all mortals, and all cloistered persons in whatever religious life: their every action and their whole life, indeed whatever they do, ought either to be prayer or at least in conformity with prayer. For not without reason are all who profess the monastic warfare called spiritual, so that by the very word they may be reminded to despise the pleasures of the flesh for love of God and to walk through true charity in the ardor of the spirit.

For the holy Apostle of Christ says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God,” because “if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” And knowing that without persistence in prayer the fervor of the spirit cannot long remain in us, he again says to the Thessalonians: “Always rejoice; pray without interruption; give thanks in all things, because this is the [unclear].”

46
Homilia VIII. 49 luntas Dei in Christo Iesu in omnibus vobis. Quis autem sit modus orandi, Salvator nos docuit in Evangelio dicens: Tu autem, cum ora- veris, intra in cubiculum tuum, et clauso ostio ora patrem tuum in abscondito: et pater tuus, qui videt in abscondito, reddi tibi. Et in alio loco dixit ad mulierem Samaritanam: Mulier crede mihi: quia veniet hora, quando neque in hoc monte, neque Hierosolymis adorabitis pa- trem. Sed venit hora, et nunc est, quando veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu, et veritate. Nam et pater tales quaerit, qui adorent eum. Spiritus est Deus, et eos, qui adorant eum, in spiritu, et veritate oportet adorare. Orationem esse cordis, potius quam sermonem oris prolixum, ex Christi doctrina constat manifestum: quia cum Deus sit spiritus, non aliter quam intimo fervore spiritus venit adorandus. Ora- tionis enim cordis in fervore spiritus magna est virtus, multiplicationis vero sermonum sine attentione mentis nulla omnino utilitas. Hinc San- ctus Hieronymus ait: Non in verbis tantum, sed corde orandus est Deus. Quapropter melior est quinque psalmorum decantatio cum cordis puritate, ac serenitate, spiritualique hilaritate, quam totius psalterii modulatio cum anxietate cordis, atque tristitia. Et Divus Papa Gregorius: Vera postulatio est, non in oris vocibus, sed in cordis vocibus, hoc est in sanctis cogi- tationibus. Nam valentiores voces apud Dei aures non faciunt verba, sed desideria. Exceptis igitur his orationibus, quas dicere, vel ex decreto Ec- clesiae tenemur, vel ex institutione ordinis Monastici, prolixitas in reli- quis, et multiplicatione verborum nihil, aut parum conducunt ad veram, internamque devotionem mentis: quoniam ubi non est fervens in Dei amore desiderium, superflue extensio introducitur sermonum. Dicit enim sacer Au- gustinus: Absit ab oratione multa precatio, sed fervens perseveret intentio: quia multum loqui in orando est rem necessariam superfluis agere ver- bis. Oratio nanque paucis verbis res multipes comprehendit, ut cito simplicitas fidei sufficientiam suae salutis addisceret, et prudentia inge- nirosorum profunditate misteriorum stupesceret. Illis vero, quibus propter duritiam cordis, interni defuerit fervoris compunctio, cum se prosterrent ad orationem, sermone prolixiore, clamore, et lachrymis opus est, ut diuturna excitatione mentis, ignem divini amoris ferventem in semetipsis tandem excutiant, donec in affectum sanctae orationis in Dei spiritu consurgant. Postea vero quam fervor divini amoris, et compunctionis mentem penetraverit, iam deinceps non opus est exercitatione verborum, sed spiritualis fomenti continuatio requiritur, ne fervor spiritualis in- cendii extinguatur. In hunc finem sanctissimus pater noster orationem in conventu abbreviari voluit: ut si quis in spiritu voluerit orare, seor- sum possit. Sunt autem nonnulli, qui usque adeo sunt duri cordis, ut parum, vel nihil inter orandum spiritualis inveniant compunctionis: quibus libertas perniciem, et solitudo frequenter parit desperationem. 50 Quod sine intermissione sit orandum.

The will of God in Christ Jesus in all of you. But what the manner of praying is, the Savior taught us in the Gospel, saying: “But you, when you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” And in another place he said to the Samaritan woman: “Woman, believe me, the hour will come when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father. But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth. For the Father also seeks such as worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth.”

From Christ’s teaching it is plainly established that prayer is of the heart rather than lengthy speech of the mouth, because, since God is spirit, he must be worshiped only with the inward fervor of the spirit. For the prayer of the heart in the fervor of the spirit has great power, but the multiplication of words without attention of mind has no usefulness at all. Hence Saint Jerome says: “God must be prayed to not only with words, but with the heart. Therefore the chanting of five psalms with purity and serenity of heart and spiritual cheerfulness is better than the singing of the whole psalter with anxiety and sadness of heart.” And the blessed Pope Gregory says: “True petition is not in the sounds of the mouth, but in the voices of the heart, that is, in holy thoughts. For it is not words, but desires, that make stronger voices in the ears of God.”

Therefore, except for those prayers which we are bound to say either by decree of the Church or by the institution of the monastic order, in the rest, lengthiness and the multiplication of words contribute nothing, or little, to true and inward devotion of mind, because where there is no fervent desire in the love of God, an extension of words is introduced superfluously. For holy Augustine says: “Let much speaking be absent from prayer, but let fervent attention persevere; for to speak much in praying is to conduct a necessary matter with superfluous words.” Indeed, prayer comprehends many-sided realities in few words, so that the simplicity of faith might quickly learn the sufficiency of its salvation, and the wisdom of the gifted might be amazed at the depth of the mysteries.

But for those who, because of hardness of heart, lack the compunction of inward fervor, when they prostrate themselves for prayer, there is need of more prolonged speech, crying out, and tears, so that by a long stirring up of the mind they may at last strike forth within themselves the burning fire of divine love, until they rise up in the Spirit of God into the affection of holy prayer. But after the fervor of divine love and compunction has penetrated the mind, there is thereafter no need for the exercise of words; rather, the continuation of spiritual fuel is required, lest the fervor of the spiritual fire be extinguished. To this end our most holy father wished prayer in the community to be shortened, so that if anyone wished to pray in the Spirit, he could do so apart. There are, however, some who are so hard of heart that in praying they find little or no spiritual compunction; for such people liberty brings ruin, and solitude often gives birth to despair.

47
Attendite quaeso fratres charissimi his, quae dico vobis, et pensate, quam sitis ad sine intermissione orandum obligati. Non satis est monacho in schola Christi regis aeterni ad perfectionem tendenti orationes canonicas persolvere: nec sufficit homini, Deo per votum sollemniter dicato preces ordinis communes in conventu adimicere: quoniam qui semper orare sine intermissione praecipitur, ultra verbales etiam ad spirituales orationes obligatur. Nam orationes ab ecclesia, vel ordine institutae, sub merito sunt obedientiae, et lege necessitatis ratione praecpti, ille vero modus orandi, qui spiritualis dicitur, omni tempore monacho utilis, et necessarius ad perfectionem, in libertate spiritus roboratur. Unde notandum, quod ad orationes, quae sunt de praecerto ecclesiae, vel ordinis, prolatio verborum de necessitate requiritur, cum intentione satisfacendi statuto, quo ad orandum quispiam tenetur. Viderint illi, quomodo satisfaciant mandato ecclesiae, qui orationes septem canonicas verborum prolatione non exprimunt, sed ore clauso seriem precum sola cogitatione oculis ministrantibus percurrunt. In illis autem orationibus, quas non ex mandato, sed propria voluntate ex devotione sola dicendas assumimus, fervor mentis in Deum sine prolatione verborum sufficit; quia tales, qui adorent in spiritu, et veritate, Deus oratores, sicut diximus, requirit. Canonicas vero preces, quas nuncupant horas, dicere tenemur, et non soluim cogitare. Utrobique devotione mentis ad Deum est utilis; sine qua nullae preces creduntur efficaces. Itaque, fratres mei, quando stamus ad orationem, summo studio invigilare debemus, et intendere precibus, quas fundimus, ne sine fructu internae compunctionis oremus. Discedat igitur omnis cogitatio carnis: mentem nulla impediat occupatio rei familiaris: nec aliud quicquam tunc animus cogitet, nisi hoc solum, quod precatur. Ideo et sacerdos praefatione ante sacrificium de more praemissa, mentes fratrum parat dicens: Sursum corda: ut, dum respondet plebs, Habemus ad Dominum, admonetur nihil aliud cogitare debere, quam ipsum, quem invocat, Deum. Claudatur ergo contra adversarium pectus, et soli Domino patet: nec in tempore sanctae orationis quicquam occupationis mundanae penitus admittat. Magna enim orationis purae utilitas, quae veluti nuncius fidelis mandatum fervidae mentis peragit, volansque ascendit in caelum, quo caro non pertingit. Duabus etenim alis sustentatur oratio, quatenus in coelum evolet, quarum altera ieiunium dicitur, altera eleemosyna nominatur. Hinc sanctus Ioannes dicit Chrysostomus: Nihil potentius homine orante, qui orat cum ieiunio; quoniam duplices alas habet, et neque oberrat, neque torpet. Oremus igitur in summo fervore spiritus: et quanta possimus conscientiae puritate vivamus, quoniam illius est perfecta, et Deo placens oratio, cuius et causa clamat, et lingua, cuius actus, et sermo deprecationi consentiunt, cuius vita,

Pay attention, I beseech you, dearly beloved brothers, to what I say to you, and consider how greatly you are bound to pray without ceasing. It is not enough for a monk, striving toward perfection in the school of Christ the eternal King, to discharge the canonical prayers; nor is it sufficient for a man solemnly dedicated to God by vow to join in the common prayers of the order in choir, because he who is commanded always to pray without ceasing is bound, beyond vocal prayers, also to spiritual prayers.

For the prayers instituted by the Church or by the order fall under the merit of obedience and under the law of necessity by reason of the command. But that manner of praying which is called spiritual, useful to a monk at every time and necessary for perfection, is strengthened in the freedom of the spirit. Hence it must be noted that for the prayers which are prescribed by the Church or by the order, the utterance of words is required of necessity, together with the intention of satisfying the statute by which one is bound to pray.

Let those see how they satisfy the command of the Church who do not express the seven canonical prayers by uttering the words, but, with closed mouth, run through the sequence of prayers by thought alone, their eyes serving them. But in those prayers which we undertake to say not from command but by our own will and from devotion alone, the fervor of the mind toward God suffices without the utterance of words; for God seeks, as we have said, such worshipers as adore in spirit and in truth. But the canonical prayers, which they call the hours, we are bound to say, and not merely to think. In both, devotion of the mind toward God is useful; without it no prayers are believed to be effective.

Therefore, my brothers, when we stand for prayer, we must keep watch with the greatest care and attend to the prayers we pour forth, lest we pray without the fruit of inward compunction. Let every thought of the flesh depart; let no occupation with household affairs hinder the mind; nor let the soul then think of anything else at all except this alone, what it is praying. For this reason also the priest, after the customary preface before the sacrifice has been given, prepares the minds of the brethren, saying, “Lift up your hearts”; so that, when the people answer, “We have them lifted up to the Lord,” they are reminded that they ought to think of nothing other than God himself, whom they invoke.

Let the breast, then, be closed against the adversary and open to the Lord alone; and during the time of holy prayer let it admit absolutely no occupation of the world. For great is the usefulness of pure prayer, which, like a faithful messenger, carries out the charge of a fervent mind and, flying, ascends into heaven, where flesh does not reach. For prayer is sustained by two wings, so that it may fly up into heaven: one of these is called fasting, the other is named almsgiving. Hence Saint John Chrysostom says: “Nothing is more powerful than a person who prays, who prays with fasting; for he has double wings, and neither wanders nor grows sluggish.”

Let us therefore pray in the highest fervor of spirit, and live with as much purity of conscience as we can, since that prayer is perfect and pleasing to God whose cause cries out along with the tongue, whose deeds and speech agree with the petition, whose life,

48
Homilia VIII. et cogitatio patrocinium precibus ferunt. Nam sine iustitia veritatis omnis erit infructuosa oratio; quoniam scimus, quod Deus non exaudit peccatores, et quia longe a peccatoribus salus, dicente scriptura: Qui avertit aures suas, ne audiat legem, oratio eius erit execrabilis. Sanctus quoque? in psalmo prophetae dicit: Iniquitatem si aspexi in corde meo, non exaudiet me Dominus. Sicut enim in vulnere nullum proficit medicamentum, nisi prius extrahatur ferrum: ita nihil proficit illius oratio, cuius adhuc dolus in mente, vel odium manet in pectore. Ut autem Deus orationem exaudiat tuam, in primis oportet, ut conscientia mundetur ab omni macula peccati mortalis, et verum mens propositum subeat emendationis. Multum orare simul, et in multis offendere, quid est aliud quam Deum irridere? Duobus etenim modis oratio intercipitur, ne a Domino exaudiatur: altero, cum orator adhuc peccando committit malum; altero vero, si debitori suo propter Deum non dimitit debitum. Tu ergo, qui habere fructum orationum tuarum desideras; qui venire ad Dei miserationem cum poenitentibus optas, cave, ne quid mali contra Dei voluntatem peragas, et cura diligentè, ut omnia in te commissa hominibus ex corde veraciter dimittas. Scis enim dixisse Dominum: Dimittite, et dimittemini. Postea vero quam mundaveris conscientiam tuam a malo, et remiseris omne delictum proximo, iam eris ad orandum idoneus, si fueris fervore sancti propositi recte ad Deum ordinatus. Iam nunc accede confidenter ad precandum Dominum; prosterne te humiliter in conspectu eius; et ora cum puritate cordis, et fervore spiritus, nec deficias ab oratione, quandiu vivis in carne. Sit oratio tua pura, simplex, dilucida, et manifesta; sit plena gravitatis, et ponderis, et decore ornata verae humilitatis. Non postules quicquam in oratione saluti animae contrarium: neque pro re temporali nimis importune preceris; quoniam impudentia est, ut petas a Deo divitias, quae maximam occasionem praestant superbiae, et christianam puritatem frequentè commaculat. Non est impudentia, si petas panem quotidianum: quoniam aliud est materiam postulare, unde superbias; et aliud est petere alimentum necessarium, unde vivas. Non te iustifices orans, ne sicut Phariseus exes condemnatus: nec postules quicquam a Domino, quasi tuorum ex debito meritorum; sed humilia te in omnibus, ut gratiam recipere merearis. Memento humilitatis publicani, et cum tanta humilitate ora, ut veniam peccatorum, et animi iustificatió- nem cum illo invenias. Uberior enim est Dei gratia, quam oratio sup- plicantis; et plus orantibus nobis tribuit, quam rogamus. Non in cla- more vocis orabis ad eum, qui novit abscondita cordis: sed in fervore spiritus, et intimae clamore mentis aures pulsa divinae maiestatis. Neque longitudinem protrahas verborum ante eum, qui est spiritus, quia non in multiloquio, sed in pura mente orantis placabitur Deus. In tempore

and thought bring support to prayers. For without the justice of truth every prayer will be fruitless, since we know that God does not hear sinners, and that salvation is far from sinners, as Scripture says: He who turns away his ears so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be abominable. The holy prophet also says in the psalm: If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me. For just as no medicine does any good in a wound unless the iron is first drawn out, so the prayer of one in whose mind deceit still remains, or hatred in whose breast, does no good.

But in order that God may hear your prayer, first of all your conscience must be cleansed from every stain of mortal sin, and the mind must take on a true purpose of amendment. To pray much at the same time and offend in many things, what else is it than to mock God? For prayer is intercepted in two ways, so that it is not heard by the Lord: one, when the one praying still commits evil by sinning; the other, if he does not forgive his debtor the debt for God’s sake. Therefore you who desire to have fruit from your prayers, who long to come with the penitent to God’s mercy, beware lest you do any evil against God’s will, and take diligent care that you truly forgive from your heart all things committed against you by men. For you know that the Lord said: Forgive, and you shall be forgiven.

But after you have cleansed your conscience from evil and forgiven every offense to your neighbor, then you will be fit for prayer, if by the fervor of a holy purpose you have been rightly ordered toward God. Now then approach confidently to beseech the Lord; cast yourself humbly in his sight; and pray with purity of heart and fervor of spirit, and do not cease from prayer as long as you live in the flesh. Let your prayer be pure, simple, clear, and plain; let it be full of seriousness and weight, and adorned with the beauty of true humility. Do not ask anything in prayer that is contrary to the salvation of the soul; nor should you pray too importunately for a temporal thing, since it is shamelessness to ask God for riches, which provide the greatest occasion for pride and often stain Christian purity. It is not shamelessness if you ask for daily bread, since it is one thing to ask for material from which you may grow proud, and another to ask for the necessary food by which you may live.

Do not justify yourself when praying, lest like the Pharisee you go away condemned; nor ask anything from the Lord as though it were owed to your merits as a debt, but humble yourself in all things, that you may deserve to receive grace. Remember the humility of the publican, and pray with such great humility that with him you may find forgiveness of sins and justification of soul. For God’s grace is more abundant than the prayer of the suppliant, and he grants us more when we pray than we ask. You will not pray to him who knows the hidden things of the heart with a cry of the voice, but with fervor of spirit and with the cry of the inward mind knock at the ears of the divine majesty. Nor should you draw out a length of words before him who is spirit, because God will be appeased not by much speaking, but by the pure mind of the one praying. In time

49
52 Quod sine intermissione sit orandum. orationis omnem malitiam, et inquietudinem cordis projice abs te: et, quod saepe dicimus, remitte, si quid habes adversus proximum tuum. Nisi enim proximo tuo debitum omne pro Salvatoris amore dimiseris, nihil tuis orationibus a Domino impetrabis. Dicitur quoddam esse genus serpentis, quod cum ire voluerit in aquam ad bibendum, prius evomit omne venenum. Imitare et tu monache hunc serpente in hac parte, omneque venenum irae, et amaritudinis evome, remittens fratri tuo centum denarios, ut tibi remittat Dominus decem milia talentorum. Matt. 18. Qualis erga te cupis esse Dominum, talem te quoque exhibeas ad conservum. Invoca Dominum ex toto corde de tuo, et invenies eum. Sit oratio ardens, atque purissima, ut mens tua in eius amore sanctissimo copuletur. Hoc stude in omni vita tua, ut orationem puram offeras Domino Deo in omni tempore. Nunquam deficias in oratione, nec de misericordia Domini desperes. Deus enim, quod concessurus est, et si differt, non auffert. Non levitate utitur, nec facile sententia movetur, quod promisit est fixum, si oraveris instanter, videbis miraculum. Me- mento te sub Dei stare conspectibus, qui omnia cordium secreta intel- ligit, et mentis abdita novit. Vigilanter itaque assiste in conspectu eius, qui omnia cognovit, et, quanto poteris fervore spiritus, ora, ut mise- ricordiam consequi merearis. Nam oratione sancta mundatur conscientia poenitentis, et, qui cor suum in vera puritate ad Dominum erigit, eius orationi vacua non redit. O si sciretis fratres charissimi, quam gratae sint Deo pure mentis orationes, et quantam animae conferant utilitatem, nullum transire tempus sine precibus sineretis. Oratio enim nostra, si pura fuerit, et ardens in fervore spiritus, nuncius est fidelissimus ad Deum, pro nobis Deo loquitur, et omnia, quae saluti nostrae sunt ne- cessaria, obtinet, dum precatur. Quocirca vos admonco, et in vera charitate exhortor, ut sine intermissione oretis, nec a sancti spiritus fervore unquam cessetis. Non sit vobis ullum tempus vacuum, vel in torpore mentis ociosum. In timore Domini semper quaeso vigiles, et solliciti estote, quatenus tentationes imminentes fortiter possitis vincere, ac superare. Mox, ut cogitationes sordidae mentem pulsare coeperint, ad studium orationis recurrite, et minime vobis poterunt praevalere. Oratio nanque grandis munitio est animae; in cuius praesentia deficiunt omnes machinationes partis adversae. Per orationes enim purissimas omnia nobis a Deo tribuuntur utilia, et cuncta procil effugantur adversa. Mens orationibus puris in amore Dei valenter accenditur, et quicquid occurrerit levioris maculae, orando purgatur. Orationibus sanctis, et continuis mundus vincitur: animae pestes devotis precibus sanantur; lachrymis, et fletu superatur diabolus; et, cui mille cohortes ad pu- gnandum non sufficiunt, unius oratione pauperis infirmatur. Quemad- modum a facie ignis cera liquescens resolvitur, sic ad orationis purae

52

That one must pray without interruption.

Cast from yourself all malice and unrest of heart in prayer; and, as we often say, forgive if you have anything against your neighbor. For unless you forgive your neighbor every debt for love of the Savior, you will obtain nothing from the Lord by your prayers.

It is said that there is a certain kind of serpent which, when it wishes to go into the water to drink, first vomits out all its poison. You too, monk, imitate this serpent in this respect, and vomit out all the poison of anger and bitterness, forgiving your brother the hundred denarii, so that the Lord may forgive you the ten thousand talents. Matthew 18.

As you desire the Lord to be toward you, so also show yourself toward your fellow servant. Call upon the Lord with all your heart, and you will find him. Let your prayer be burning and most pure, so that your mind may be joined to him in his most holy love. Strive for this throughout your whole life: to offer pure prayer to the Lord God at every time. Never fail in prayer, nor despair of the Lord’s mercy. For what God is going to grant, even if he delays it, he does not take away. He does not act from fickleness, nor is he easily moved from his decision; what he has promised is fixed. If you pray persistently, you will see a miracle.

Remember that you stand under the gaze of God, who understands all the secrets of hearts and knows the hidden things of the mind. Therefore stand watchfully in the sight of him who knows all things, and pray with as much fervor of spirit as you can, so that you may deserve to obtain mercy. For by holy prayer the conscience of the penitent is cleansed, and the prayer of one who lifts up his heart to the Lord in true purity does not return empty.

O dearest brothers, if you knew how pleasing to God are the prayers of a pure mind, and how great a benefit they bring to the soul, you would allow no time to pass without prayers. For our prayer, if it is pure and burning in fervor of spirit, is a most faithful messenger to God; it speaks to God on our behalf, and obtains everything necessary for our salvation while it prays.

Therefore I warn you and exhort you in true charity to pray without interruption, and never to cease from the fervor of the Holy Spirit. Let no time be empty for you, or idle in sluggishness of mind. I beg you, always be watchful and attentive in the fear of the Lord, so that you may be able bravely to conquer and overcome the temptations that threaten you. As soon as foul thoughts begin to strike the mind, flee back to the practice of prayer, and they will by no means be able to prevail over you.

For prayer is a great fortification of the soul; in its presence all the contrivances of the opposing side fail. Through most pure prayers, all useful things are granted to us by God, and all adversities are driven far away. By pure prayers the mind is powerfully kindled in the love of God, and whatever stain of lighter fault occurs is cleansed by praying. By holy and continual prayers the world is conquered; the plagues of the soul are healed by devout petitions; by tears and weeping the devil is overcome; and he for whom a thousand cohorts are not enough for battle is weakened by the prayer of one poor man. Just as wax melts and dissolves before the face of fire, so at pure prayer [unclear].

50
Homilia VIII. 53 fervorem omnis daemonum potentia contrita enervatur. Si cogitatio turpis animo tuo per daemones immissa fuerit, impresso mox fronti signo crucis dicio: Salva me Iesu Christe, mediator Dei et hominum, et cunctam a me hostis antiqui depelle nequitiam per tuam innocentissimam passionem. Quid hac oratione brevius, quidve potentius esse potest? Nam statim, ut contra daemonum vel praesentiam, vel suggestionem cum fervore mentis proleta fuerit, omnis iniquitatis machinatio recedit. Orationis enim purae virtus est maxima, quoniam et caelum penetrat, et sua constantia debellat aereas potentates. Oratio mentem illuminat, affectum purificat, veniam delictorum impetrat, spiritum in Dei amore contra omnes adversarios confortat. Nihil sic mentem a terrenis ad coelestium amore elevat, nihil carnis voluptates tam cito, et valenter exterminat, nihil adeo illustrat intellectum, nihil quoque in tantum veritatis confundit adversarium: sicut oratio pura, quae cum fervore Divini amoris ad Deum funditur, et bonae testimonio conscientiae decoratur. Si daemonibus cupis esse terribilis, si Dei vis esse amicus, conscientiam habeto puram, et spiritualem nunquam intermittas orationem. Omnia enim devota potest oratio, si rectitudine fidei, et vitae puritate decoretur. Oratio daemones fugat, virtutem malignantium enervat, languescentem in tepiditate animam sanat, ac debilem, et infirmum in Dei timore spiritum confirmat. Oratio pura Deo facit proximum, et eum, quem acceperat, servum Dei facit esse amicum. Oratio pura, et fervens in amore Dei coelum penetrat, intellectum orantis mirabiliter illuminat, infernum claudit, Paradisum aperit, animas fidelium introducit. Veritas enim non mentitur, quae in sancto Evangelio promittit dicens: Petite, et dabitur vobis; quaerite, et invenietis; pulsate, et aperietur vobis. Omnis enim, qui petit accipit; et qui quaerit invenit, et pulsanti aperietur. Quis vestrum in toto corde suo conversus ad Dominum oravit unquam, et non est exauditus? Aut quis invocavit Dominum, et elongavit se ab eo? Dicit enim scriptura: Scitote, quoniam exaudiet Dominus preces vestras, si manentes permanseritis in ieiuniis, et orationibus in conspectu Domini. Memores estote Moysi servi Domini, qui Amalech confidentem in virtute sua, non ferro pugnando, sed precibus sanctis orando deiecit. Multum enim valet deprecatione iusti assidua, et oratio humilantis se penetrat nubes. Helias homo erat similis nobis passibilis, et oravit oratione, ut non plueret super terram, et non pluit annos tres, et menses sex. Et rursum oravit, et coelum dedit pluviam, et terra dedit fructum suum. Oratione, et lachrimis Rex Ezechias quindecim annos vitae longioris obtinuit, et Prophetae sententiam precibus mutavit. Orationibus viri sancti claruerunt miraculis, et supplicantes ad Dominum mortuos revocarunt ad vitam. Orationis etiam puritati subiecta sunt omnia; et nihil est in nobis tam difficile, quod

all the power of demons, crushed, is weakened by fervor. If a foul thought has been cast into your mind by demons, then, after making the sign of the cross upon your forehead, say at once: Save me, Jesus Christ, mediator of God and men, and drive away from me all the wickedness of the ancient enemy through your most innocent passion.

What can be shorter than this prayer, or more powerful? For as soon as it has been uttered with fervor of mind against either the presence of demons or their suggestion, every contrivance of iniquity withdraws. For the power of pure prayer is very great, since it both penetrates heaven and by its steadfastness defeats the powers of the air. Prayer enlightens the mind, purifies the affections, obtains pardon for sins, and strengthens the spirit in the love of God against all adversaries. Nothing so raises the mind from earthly things to the love of heavenly things; nothing so swiftly and powerfully exterminates the pleasures of the flesh; nothing so enlightens the understanding; nothing also so greatly confounds the adversary of truth as pure prayer, which is poured out to God with the fervor of divine love and is adorned by the testimony of a good conscience.

If you desire to be terrible to demons, if you wish to be a friend of God, keep your conscience pure, and never cease from spiritual prayer. For devout prayer can do all things, if it is adorned with uprightness of faith and purity of life. Prayer puts demons to flight, weakens the power of malignant spirits, heals the soul languishing in tepidity, and strengthens the spirit that is weak and infirm in the fear of God. Pure prayer brings one near to God, and makes him whom it had received as a servant of God to be his friend. Pure prayer, fervent in the love of God, penetrates heaven, wonderfully enlightens the understanding of the one who prays, shuts hell, opens Paradise, and brings in the souls of the faithful.

For Truth does not lie, who promises in the holy Gospel, saying: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and he who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it shall be opened. Which of you has ever turned to the Lord with his whole heart and prayed, and was not heard? Or who has called upon the Lord, and he withdrew himself from him? For Scripture says: Know that the Lord will hear your prayers, if you remain steadfast, continuing in fasts and prayers in the sight of the Lord.

Remember Moses, the servant of the Lord, who cast down Amalek, trusting in his own strength, not by fighting with the sword, but by praying with holy prayers. For the continual supplication of a righteous man avails much, and the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the clouds. Elijah was a man subject to suffering like us, and he prayed with prayer that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and heaven gave rain, and the earth gave its fruit. By prayer and tears King Hezekiah obtained fifteen years of longer life, and by prayers changed the sentence of the prophet. By prayers holy men became renowned for miracles, and, supplicating the Lord, called the dead back to life. All things are subject even to the purity of prayer; and there is nothing in us so difficult that

51
54 Quod sine intermissione sit orandum. oratio devota, et fervida nequeat impetrare. Tunc autem orantes fidu- ciam impetrandi, quod postulamus, a Domino accipimus; cum precibus nostris vitae pravitas nulla contradicit. Nam iustae precis exauditor est Dominus; quando videlicet orationem vitae commendat integritas, et reatus conscientiae nullus haesitare facit orantem. Inter dissimiles non stabit amicitia, et inter Deum, et peccatorem non poterit esse communio. Si vis exaudiri orans, cura in primis, ut a Dei voluntate non discordes. Vive spiritu persimilis Deo, et nullam patieris in ora- tione repulsam. Enimvero conscientiae puritas in fervore Divini amoris hominem Deo facit intellectu persimilem, similitudo causat amorem, amor vero introducit familiaritatem, familiaritas confidentiam, et con- fidentia petitionis consequitur facilem impetrationem. Nam sicut inter dissimilia non fit unio, ita inter Deum, et hominem malum nihil pro- ficit oratio. Quicunque igitur vestrum orationum suarum consequi desiderat effectum, in primis per veram poenitentiam cordis sui domi- ciliun ab omni mundet delicto, deinde sanctae compunctionis semet- ipsum studet inflammare exercitio, postea mentem continue pascat in Dei amoris studio, quatenus bonum, quod inchoat, nullo deinceps tem- pore intermittat. Postea vero quam crescente semper in eo Divini amoris desiderio, sanctae puritatis exercitium longo studio perduxerit in con- suetudinem; et mens in bono proposito necessariam conceperit firmi- tatem, tunc primum similitudo Divinae communionis paulatim intro- ducitur, et ad statum debitum oratio formatur. Nam quanto mens in Dei amore amplius excitata profecerit, tanto citius oratio, quod postu- lat, a Domino impetrabit. Solus etenim Dei amor facit orationem esse potentem, in quo mens quanto ferventius arserit, tanto facilius petitio- num suarum consequetur effectum. Nam si multum amas, multum potes. Deus enim charitas est, et, qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet, et Deus in eo. In quo vero manet Deus, nihil est illo fortius, nisi Deus ipse solus. Sunt inter vos quidam infirmi, et debiles animo, qui se iam fortes in via Domini existimant, atque perfectos, quorum est rara, et horaria devotio, qui sine veste nuptiali regno se appropinquasse glo- riantur coelorum, cum tamen adhuc longe in inferioribus iaceant. His ego, quod saepius dixi, iterum dico, quoniam nemo repente fit sum- mus, et nisi Monachus omnes passiones suas animales per carnis ma- cerationem domuerit, ad montem Divinae contemplationis altissimum non pertingit. Quisquis enim in coenobio sub potestate, et obedientia constitutus voluntatem suam contra Monasticam institutionem sequitur, dignus non est, ut in suis orationibus a Domino exaudiatur. Isti autem, de quibus loquimur, in oculis suis magni sunt, et sapientes, qui pro- priam voluntatem diligentcs ad omnia murmuran: et quicquid ipsi non ordinaverint, male factum putant. Actus fratrum suorum curiosa

That one must pray without ceasing.

...that devout and fervent prayer cannot obtain. But then, when we pray, we receive from the Lord confidence of obtaining what we ask, when no perversity of life contradicts our prayers. For the Lord is the hearer of a righteous prayer: that is, when integrity of life commends the prayer, and no guilt of conscience makes the one praying hesitate. Friendship will not stand between those who are unlike, and between God and a sinner there can be no communion.

If you wish to be heard when you pray, take care first of all that you do not differ from the will of God. Live in spirit most like God, and you will suffer no rejection in prayer. Indeed, purity of conscience in the fervor of divine love makes a person like God in understanding; likeness causes love, love introduces familiarity, familiarity confidence, and confidence easily obtains the granting of the petition. For just as union does not occur between unlike things, so between God and an evil person prayer avails nothing.

Therefore, whoever among you desires to obtain the effect of his prayers should first cleanse the dwelling of his heart from every fault through true repentance; then he should strive to inflame himself by the exercise of holy compunction; afterward he should continually feed his mind in the pursuit of the love of God, so that at no later time he interrupts the good that he begins. But afterward, when, with the desire of divine love always increasing in him, he has brought the practice of holy purity by long effort into habit, and his mind has conceived the necessary firmness in its good purpose, then for the first time a likeness of divine communion is gradually introduced, and prayer is formed into its proper state.

For the more the mind, stirred up in the love of God, has advanced, the more quickly prayer will obtain from the Lord what it asks. For the love of God alone makes prayer powerful; and the more fervently the mind burns in it, the more easily it will obtain the effect of its petitions. For if you love much, you can do much. For God is charity, and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him. But in the one in whom God abides, nothing is stronger than he, except God alone.

There are among you certain men weak and feeble in soul, who already think themselves strong and perfect in the way of the Lord; theirs is a rare and momentary devotion, and they boast that without the wedding garment they have come near to the kingdom of heaven, though in fact they still lie far below. To these I say again what I have often said: no one suddenly becomes the highest, and unless a monk has subdued all his animal passions by the mortification of the flesh, he does not reach the most lofty mountain of divine contemplation.

For whoever, placed in a monastery under authority and obedience, follows his own will against monastic discipline is not worthy to be heard by the Lord in his prayers. But those of whom we speak are great and wise in their own eyes; loving their own will, they grumble at everything, and whatever they themselves have not arranged they think badly done. The actions of their brothers with prying [unclear].

52
Homilia VIII. 55 inquisitione discutiunt, suas vero discernere negligentias contemnunt. In moribus sunt dissoluti, et incompositi, in verbis leves, et clamosi, ad obedientiam involuntarii, et semper in bonis operibus tardi, et accidia pleni. Communia ordinis exercitia negligentunt, privatis iuxta voluntatem propriam intendunt. Et quandiu in sua temeritate permanent, ad verum Dei amorem non consurgunt. Audiant, quid Dominus dicat, monachi propriae voluntatis amatores. Non veni, ut faciam voluntatem meam, sed eius, qui misit me, Patris. Hunc, fratres, praecipitem attendite, ad cuius imitationem nisi vixeritis, sine fructu orabitis. Eius nanque orationem libenter exaudit Dominus, qui mandata eius in veritate custodit. Qui vero Dei mandatum transgreditur, qui carnis voluptates, et mundi solatia cum desiderio sequitur, eius oratio non exauditur. Deus nanque iustus, et rectus tunc orationem tuam libenter exaudire creditur, quando mens, et vita bona simul deprecantur. Cuius autem conversatio Deo displaceit, oratio eius quomodo placebit? Deus enim spiritus est; et homo, qui non in spiritu, sed in carne ambulat, certe ad Deum minime appropinquit. Tu itaque, monache, qui ad puritatem Evangelii, et regulae non ambulas, qui propriam, non Dei voluntatem amas, scito, quoniam orationum tuarum non senties efficaciam, nisi prius emendaveris vitam. Nisi enim conversatio tuae vitae concordaverit orationi, non impetrabis, quod precaris. Tunc magna voce clamas ad Dominum, quando etiam lingua tacente bonis operibus clamas. Orationes enim bonae, et conversatio mala nihil boni merentur. Fac ergo, quod sapiens quidam monuit: Et si peccasti, non adiicias iterum: sed et pristinis deprecare, ut tibi dimittantur. Ante orationem praepara animam tuam, et noli esse quasi homo, qui tentat Deum. Sit mens pura, et ardens in amore Domini, sit conscientia munda, et in sanctae conversationis proposito roborata, et erit oratio divinis auribus grata. Si aliter oraveris, nihil impetrabis. Bene orat, qui bene vivit: et facile impetrat, qui sanctis operibus orat. Denique oratio multum redditur efficax, et grata in conspectu Dei, si fuerit omni tempore consonans passioni Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Christus enim Deus est et homo, mediator inter Deum, et nos, per quem tutum accessum habemus ad patrem, sicut ipse testatur in sancto Evangelio: Nemo, inquit, venit ad Patrem nisi per me. Unde nulla praeterea dies, in qua Christo, ad minus semel, orando gratias non agas, qui suorum dolore vulnerum animae tuae sanavit languores, qui sanguinem pro te suum effudit, et morte sua innocentissima de mortis perpetuae interitu te miserum redemit. Homo certe ingratisissimus est, et christiano vocabulo indignus, qui tantorum beneficiorum Christi usque adeo fuerit obliviosus, ut non quotidie, vel semel ad minus gratiarum illi referat actiones. Monachus autem, qui saeculo mortuus Deo soli vivere iubetur, dominicae passionis

they examine others by inquiry, but despise discerning their own negligences. In their morals they are lax and disorderly, in their words frivolous and noisy, unwilling for obedience, and always slow in good works and full of sloth. They neglect the common exercises of the order; they devote themselves to private ones according to their own will. And as long as they remain in their rashness, they do not rise up to the true love of God.

Let monks who love their own will hear what the Lord says: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.” Attend to this example, brothers; unless you live in imitation of him, you will pray without fruit. For the Lord gladly hears the prayer of the one who truly keeps his commandments. But the prayer of one who transgresses God’s command, who follows with desire the pleasures of the flesh and the consolations of the world, is not heard.

For God, just and upright, is believed to hear your prayer gladly when both mind and good life plead together. But if a man’s conduct displeases God, how will his prayer please him? For God is spirit; and the man who walks not in the spirit but in the flesh certainly draws very little near to God.

Therefore you, monk, who do not walk according to the purity of the Gospel and the rule, who love your own will and not God’s, know that you will not feel the efficacy of your prayers unless you first amend your life. For unless the manner of your life agrees with your prayer, you will not obtain what you ask. Then you cry to the Lord with a loud voice when, even with the tongue silent, you cry out by good works. Good prayers and an evil life merit no good.

Do, therefore, what a certain wise man advised: “And if you have sinned, do not add again; but also pray concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you.” Before prayer, prepare your soul, and do not be like a man who tempts God. Let the mind be pure and burning in love of the Lord; let the conscience be clean and strengthened in the purpose of holy conduct, and the prayer will be pleasing to divine ears. If you pray otherwise, you will obtain nothing.

He prays well who lives well; and he easily obtains his request who prays with holy works. Finally, prayer is rendered very efficacious and pleasing in the sight of God if at all times it is in harmony with the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. For Christ is God and man, the mediator between God and us, through whom we have safe access to the Father, as he himself testifies in the holy Gospel: “No one,” he says, “comes to the Father except through me.”

Therefore let there be no day on which, in prayer, you do not give thanks to Christ at least once, for by the pain of his wounds he healed the sicknesses of your soul, shed his blood for you, and by his most innocent death redeemed you, wretched man, from the destruction of everlasting death. Surely he is a most ungrateful man, and unworthy of the Christian name, who is so forgetful of such great benefits of Christ that he does not render thanks to him daily, at least once.

But the monk, who is commanded to be dead to the world and to live for God alone, [unclear] the Lord’s Passion.

53
56 Quod sine intermissione sit oranduin. memoriam in suo pectore iugiter portet, semper gratias agens suo Redemptori, semper benedicens, semper adorans, et quotdie, immo quantum fieri potest, singulis momentis amaritudinem vulnerum Christi cum lachrimis compatiendo revolvat.
