Omni die post orationes singulas regulares, quas Graeci appellant canonicas, flexis genibus, et elevata mente in coelum dicat: Gratias ago tibi, et benedicens adoro te, o mediator Dei, et hominum Christe Iesu dulcissime, Deus et homo pro Incarnatione tua sanctissima, pro Nativitate tua ex Virgine; pro Circuncisione, pro fuga in Aegyptum, et septenni exilio, quod pro nobis sustinuisti. Adoro te, Domine Salvator Iesu Christe pro laboribus tuis, pro fame, et siti, frigore, ac nuditate, pro itineribus tuis, pro doctrina, et praedicatione tua, pro miraculis tuis, pro vocatione gentium, et pro iustificatione peccatorum. Ago tibi gratias Domine Fili Dei vivi, pro dolore vulnerum tuorum, benedico te pro effusione sanctissimi Sanguinis tui: adoro te pro morte tua, quam innocentissime sustinuisti: et rogo te per omnem passionem, pietatem tuam, et clementiam miserere mei nunc, et in hora mortis meae. Hanc brevissimam orationem in die ad minus septies devotus Monachus perorabit, et quoties coram imagine Crucifixi transierit, simili modo cum fervore mentis Christum adorabit. Qui verus Christi amator est, Christum semper cogitat, Christum loquitur, et veneratur, Christum sibi non dubitat ubique esse praesentem. Eius memoriae passio Christi nunquam deest, et prae amoris magnitudine seipsum obliviscitur, et in Christo mente, et desiderio totus occupatur. In amore Christi quisquis fervet animo, terrena contemnit, carnem vincit, sola coelestia concupiscit. Christum vigilans semper cum desiderio cogitat, dormiens Christum somniat, et continue suspirans cum Divo Ignatio clamat: Amor meus crucifixus est. Suspirii coniungit suspiria, et Iesum, quem totid corde suo diligit, non oculis, sed spiritu praesentem cernit. Urgente amoris desiderio quoties crucifixum intuetur, mox in lachrymas resolvitur, et aestuans charitatis incendio vociferatur: O amor cunctis fortitudinibus fortior, quam dulciter ardet, qui Christi desiderio inflamatur? Recte locutus est, qui dixit: Fortis est, ut mors, dilectio. Quid enim fortius esse potest amore Christi, cuius ardore Sancti Martyres tot millia genera mortis contemnentes superaverunt? O amor crucifixe meus miserere mei, da mihi eam, de qua loquor, dilectionis tuae sentire dulcedinem, ut semper in corde meo circumferam tuam amarissimam Passionem. Scio, fratres mei, scio, quod non est efficacior modus orandi, nec utilior nobis, qui adhuc sumus infirmi, quam in memoria, et virtute Passionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Unde cum sit manifestum, quod sine mediatore non est ascensus mentis ad Deum, omne opus bonum in Christi nomine est inchoandum; quia tunc preces ad Deum utiliter effundimus, cum purificata conscientia per eius unigenitum Filium oramus.

That one must pray without interruption.

Let him continually carry his memory in his breast, always giving thanks to his Redeemer, always blessing, always adoring, and every day, indeed as much as possible at every moment, let him ponder with tears, in compassion, the bitterness of Christ’s wounds. Every day, after each of the regular prayers, which the Greeks call canonical, with knees bent and mind lifted up to heaven, let him say:

I give thanks to you, and, blessing you, I adore you, O mediator of God and men, sweetest Christ Jesus, God and man, for your most holy Incarnation, for your Nativity from the Virgin, for your Circumcision, for your flight into Egypt and the seven-year exile which you endured for us. I adore you, Lord Savior Jesus Christ, for your labors, for hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, for your journeys, for your teaching and preaching, for your miracles, for the calling of the nations, and for the justification of sinners. I give thanks to you, Lord, Son of the living God, for the pain of your wounds; I bless you for the shedding of your most holy Blood; I adore you for your death, which you endured in all innocence; and I ask you, through all your Passion, your goodness and mercy, have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death.

This very short prayer the devout monk shall say at least seven times in the day; and as often as he passes before an image of the Crucified, in like manner, with fervor of mind, he shall adore Christ. Whoever is a true lover of Christ always thinks of Christ, speaks of Christ, and venerates Christ; he does not doubt that Christ is present to him everywhere. The Passion of Christ is never absent from his memory, and because of the greatness of his love he forgets himself and is wholly occupied in Christ in mind and desire. Whoever burns in spirit with the love of Christ despises earthly things, conquers the flesh, and longs only for heavenly things. Waking, he always thinks of Christ with desire; sleeping, he dreams of Christ; and sighing continually, he cries out with Saint Ignatius: My love has been crucified.

He joins sighs to sighs, and Jesus, whom he loves with all his heart, he beholds present not with the eyes but with the spirit. Whenever, under the urgency of loving desire, he looks upon the crucified one, at once he melts into tears, and, burning with the fire of charity, cries aloud: O love stronger than all powers, how sweetly he burns who is inflamed with longing for Christ! He spoke rightly who said: Love is strong as death. For what can be stronger than the love of Christ, by whose ardor the holy martyrs, despising so many thousands of kinds of death, overcame them? O my crucified love, have mercy on me; grant me to feel that sweetness of your love of which I speak, so that I may always carry in my heart your most bitter Passion.

I know, my brothers, I know that there is no more effective way of praying, nor any more useful for us who are still weak, than in the memory and power of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, since it is clear that without a mediator there is no ascent of the mind to God, every good work must be begun in the name of Christ; for then we pour out our prayers to God profitably, when with a purified conscience we pray through his only-begotten Son.

54
Homilia IX. 57 De custodia, et origine cogitationum. Homilia IX. SALOMON rex ille ille quondam sapientissimus in libro, quem pro- verbiorum praenotavit, filium ad veram cohortans sapientiam, inter caetera dixit: Fili mi attende sapientiam meam, et prudentiae meae inclina aurem tuam, ut custodias cogitationes, et disciplinam labia tua conservent. Non enim minima sapientiae pars est, fratres charissimi, si sciat monachus cogitationes suas prudenter discernere, et earum motus omni tempore sollicitate custodire. Magna res est nihil cogitare mali, sed non minoris prudentiae malas ab exordio cogitationes posse repellere. Humani etenim cordis profunda sententia; mobilis, varia, multiplex, et instabilis semper; cuius observare principia, et refrenare motus, summa prudentia est, et magnum sapientiae signum. Molam si dixero perpetuo motu agitatam cor hominis, a veritate non aberravi, maxime si quis eius inquietudinem adamussim pensiculare voluerit. Quid nam aliud est cor humanum, quam mola quaedam in motu semper conterens aliquid? Nunquam est ociosum cor humanum, nun- quam sine motu quiescit, sed agit semper aliquid: et sicut mola se- metipsam consumit vacua motu proprio, ita cor hominis a semetipso turpiter defluit, dum illud boni cogitatio non constringit. Semper mo- vetur in aliud obiectum cum amoris sui desiderio, semper molit, semper agit, semper circa aliud occupatur delectabile, sive bonum sit, sive malum. Sicut corpus non movetur sine anima, sic mens ho- minis non manet fixa in bono, nisi continue restricta fuerit per sancta exercitia. Propterea dixit in Ecclesiastico vir sapiens: Iucunditas cordis haec est vita hominis, et thesaurus sine defectione sanctitatis, et exul- tatio viri est longaevitas. Miserere animae tuae placens Deo, et contine, et congrega cor tuum in sanctitate eius, et tristitiam longe expelle a te. Quid est congregatio cordis, nisi diligens custodia cogitationis; Cor etenim suum in sanctitate Domini congregat, qui motus cogitationum suarum in timore Dei iugiter observat. Et ideo scriptura dicit: Omni custodia serva cor tuum, quoniam ex ipso vita procedit. Sumunt au- ten cogitationes motuum suorum principia ex his, quae offeruntur a sensibus, quae tanto evagantur periculosius, quanto minus iudicio ra- tions ab exordio considerantur. Quisquis igitur cogitationum suarum vigilans esse desiderat, quisquis congregare cor suum in sanctitate Do- mini optat, sensus suos exterioros in prinis diligentissime costodiat, et frenum prudentiae singulis imponat. Hinc de auditu, et visu scri- ptura sic praeципit. Sepi aures tuas spinis, et linguam nequam noli audire, et ori tuo ostia, et seras auribus tuis. Beatus homo, qui obturat aures suas, ne audiat sanguinem, et claudit oculos suos, ne videat 58 De custodia, et origine cogitationum. Iob. 31. malum. In sancto quoque Iob sic legimus: Pepigi foedus cum oculis meis, ut ne cogitarem quid de virgine. In eos vero, qui ministerio sensuum corruerunt in foveam peccatorum, sic Dominus contestatur per Prophetam Hieremiam: Quia ascendit mors per fenestras vestras, ingressa est domos vestras disperdere parvulos deforis, et iuvenes de plateis. Mors per fenestras domos nostras ingreditur, quoties iniqua cogitatio per ministerium visus, vel auditus ad mentem intromittitur.

Homily IX.

On the guarding and origin of thoughts. Homily IX.

Solomon, that once most wise king, in the book which he entitled Proverbs, exhorting his son to true wisdom, said among other things: “My son, attend to my wisdom, and incline your ear to my prudence, that you may guard your thoughts, and that your lips may preserve discipline.” For it is no small part of wisdom, dearly beloved brothers, if a monk knows how to discern his thoughts prudently and to guard their movements carefully at all times. It is a great thing to think no evil; but it belongs to no less prudence to be able to repel evil thoughts from their very beginning. For the depths of the human heart are, by profound judgment, mobile, varied, manifold, and always unstable; to observe its beginnings and restrain its movements is the highest prudence and a great sign of wisdom.

If I call the heart of man a mill driven by perpetual motion, I shall not have strayed from the truth, especially if anyone wishes to weigh its restlessness exactly. For what else is the human heart than a kind of mill, always grinding something while in motion? The human heart is never idle, never rests without motion, but is always doing something; and just as an empty mill consumes itself by its own motion, so the heart of man shamefully runs away from itself when the thought of good does not bind it fast. It is always moved toward some other object with the desire of its own love; it is always grinding, always acting, always occupied with something else that gives delight, whether it is good or evil. As the body is not moved without the soul, so the mind of man does not remain fixed in the good unless it has been continually restrained by holy exercises.

Therefore the wise man said in Ecclesiasticus: “Gladness of heart is the life of man, and a treasure without failing of holiness, and the rejoicing of a man is long life. Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God, and restrain yourself, and gather your heart in his holiness, and drive sadness far from you.” What is the gathering of the heart, if not the diligent guarding of thought? For he gathers his heart in the holiness of the Lord who continually observes the movements of his thoughts in the fear of God. And therefore Scripture says: “With all watchfulness keep your heart, because life proceeds from it.”

Now thoughts take the beginnings of their movements from those things which are presented by the senses; and they wander the more dangerously, the less they are considered from the beginning by the judgment of reason. Therefore whoever desires to be watchful over his thoughts, whoever wishes to gather his heart in the holiness of the Lord, must first guard his outward senses most diligently and place the bridle of prudence upon each of them. Hence Scripture commands thus concerning hearing and sight: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue,” and, “Make doors for your mouth, and bars for your ears.” “Blessed is the man who stops his ears lest he hear bloodshed, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil.” In holy Job also we read thus: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I should not think about a virgin.” But against those who have fallen into the pit of sins through the service of the senses, the Lord bears witness thus through the prophet Jeremiah: “Death has come up through your windows; it has entered your houses, to destroy the little children outside and the young men from the streets.” Death enters our houses through the windows whenever a wicked thought is admitted into the mind through the service of sight or hearing.

55
Hier. 9. Domus enim conscientia est, de qua scriptura dicit: Nisi te instanter tenueris in timore Domini, cito subvertetur domus tua, quod est conscientia. Domus haec fragilis est multum, et cito subvertitur, nisi continuo exercitio timoris Domini muniatur. Nisi enim Dominus custodierit domum, frustra vigilat, qui custodit eam. Timore igitur Domini munienda est domus conscientiae. Sensus quoque diligentissime refrenandi sunt; quia custodire cogitationes suas non sufficit, qui aures, et oculos ab occasione mali non avertit. Itaque, si vis cogitationum tuarum custos esse prudentes, et verus congregator cordis in sanctitate Domini, sepel aures tuas spinis compunctionis timoris Dei, ne audiant malum, et oculos averte tuos, ne per visum introducant peccatum. Quod tibi non licet concupiscere, noli cum desiderio videre: et, quod habere non expedit, noli cogitare. Multi perierunt ministerio sensuum, et, qui videre incaute pergunt externa; saepius interiora sua bona turpiter amiserunt. Qui non timet periculum, iam certe prope interitum est: et, qui de sua virtute praesumit, ad ruinam peccati festinanter currit. Qui oculum vibrat in choruscationem fulguris, excaecabitur ad horam: et, qui considerat speciem mulieris, non erit immunis a periculo. Illius laudo prudentiam monachi, qui in medio turbarum est solus, et sensibus suis praeponit censorem, ne quid intromittat mali ad Dominam. Statuit iuxta portam custodes, qui gladio et fuste repellant in composite irruentes. Timor enim Domini sanctus nunquam deserit mentem viri sapientis, sed tanquam pugil fortis, et vigilans semper ad latus stat principis, ita custodit Dominam cordis. Avertit aures suas ab omni scurrilitate verborum, et claudit oculos suos, ne videant malum. Semper incedit iuxta duodecimum humilitatis gradum defixis in terram aspectibus, orans cum propheta ad Dominum: Averte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem, in via tua vivifica me Domine. Ita vos moneo, fratres, sensus vestros in timore Domini dirigite, ut cordis domicilium semper mundum, et inviolatum possitis custodire. Mementote scripturae dicentis: Mundamini, qui fertis vasa Domini. Considerate precor, quanta oporteat vos nitere munditia, et puritate mentis, qui non solum ratione ordinis sacerdotalis vasa Domini fertis, sed quod est amplius, etiam vos ipsi vasa Domini estis. Dicit enim sanctus Christophilus Paulus: Nescitis, quoniam corpora vestra membra sunt Christi; Et ite-

For the house is the conscience, of which Scripture says: Unless you steadfastly keep yourself in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown, that is, your conscience. This house is very fragile, and is quickly overthrown unless it is fortified by the continual exercise of the fear of the Lord. For unless the Lord guards the house, he who guards it keeps watch in vain. Therefore the house of conscience must be fortified by the fear of the Lord.

The senses also must be most carefully restrained; for it is not enough for a man to guard his thoughts if he does not turn his ears and eyes away from the occasion of evil. Therefore, if you wish to be a prudent guardian of your thoughts and a true gatherer of your heart in the holiness of the Lord, bury your ears with the thorns of compunction and fear of God, lest they hear evil, and turn away your eyes, lest through sight they bring in sin. What it is not lawful for you to desire, do not look upon with desire; and what it is not expedient to have, do not think about.

Many have perished through the service of the senses, and those who go on incautiously looking at external things have very often shamefully lost their inner goods. He who does not fear danger is surely already near destruction; and he who presumes upon his own virtue runs hastily toward the ruin of sin. He who flashes his eye at the gleam of lightning will be blinded for a time; and he who contemplates the beauty of a woman will not be free from danger.

I praise the prudence of that monk who is alone in the midst of crowds and sets a censor over his senses, lest he admit any evil to the mistress. He stations guards by the gate, who with sword and club drive back those rushing in disorderly. For the holy fear of the Lord never deserts the mind of a wise man, but, like a strong and watchful fighter always standing at the prince’s side, so it guards the mistress of the heart. He turns his ears away from all scurrility of words, and closes his eyes lest they see evil. He always walks according to the twelfth degree of humility, with his gaze fixed on the ground, praying with the prophet to the Lord: Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity; in your way give me life, O Lord.

Thus I admonish you, brothers: direct your senses in the fear of the Lord, so that you may always be able to keep the dwelling of the heart clean and inviolate. Remember the Scripture that says: Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord. Consider, I beg you, with how great a cleanness and purity of mind you ought to shine, you who not only, by reason of the priestly order, carry the vessels of the Lord, but, what is more, are yourselves also vessels of the Lord. For the holy Christophilus Paul says: Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? And again—

56
Homilia IX. 59 rum dicit: An nescitis, quoniam membra vestra templum sunt Spiritus Sanctus, qui in vobis est, quem habetis a Deo, et non estis vestri, ac alibi: Templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos. Et de ipso Paulo in Actibus Apostolorum: Dominus dixit ad Ananiam: Vade, quoniam vas electionis est mihi iste. Monachus, qui ordine sacerdotali in Dei ecclesia fungitur, duplici ratione ad sanctissimae puritatis observantiam tenetur. Oportet enim Christi militem propter votum, quod Deus fecit, esse purum, sanctum, et in bonis operibus iugiter infatigabilem, et ratione sacerdotalis ministerii circumspectum, ac diligentissime vigilantem. Scriptum est enim: Maledictus homo, qui facit opus Dei negligentemente. Vos ministri estis Dei omnipotentis, qui ad altare quotidianum filium eius immolatis, cuius opus in manibus vestris committitur, et magna propterea puritas mentis, et corporis in vestra conversatione postulatur. Ut ergo casta permaneat puritas mentis, necessitatem est, quod restringatur instabilitas cogitationis. Custodiendi sunt omni tempore sensus, per quos corrompitur integritas mentis. Mortui enim estis mundo, et coepistis iam vivere Christo, non licet vobis cogitare, nisi sanctum, nec decet vos Dei ministros aliquid amare terrenum. Deus est enim, cui servitis o monachi; omnipotens est, cui ministratis o fratres mei. Vivite puri, sancti, et innocentes, quia non decet vos occupari mundi negotiis, qui ad militiam Dei vocati estis. Crescat in vobis cum tempore amor Dei, et puritas cordis, ut quanto diutius in hoc mundo vivitis, tanto sanctiores evadatis. Visum ab omni malo semper avertite, ut possitis in bonis cogitationibus sine defectu permanere. Oculos mentis vestrae semper in coelum erigite; et visum carnis in rebus perituris nolite occupare. Auditum quoque vestrum ab omni sermone inutili, vano, et stulto semper claudite; et futurum Dei iudicium semper cum pavore cogitate. Manus vestras illicito, et turpi contactu quarumlibet rerum nolite polluere, ut Dei filium mundo corpore, et pura conscientia possitis immolare. In cibo, et potu non est monachorum sapores discernere, nec decet milites Christi corporales delicias amare. Natura paucia requirit, et, quibus alatur, rusticana, cibaria: appetitus autem, nisi restringatur imperio rationis, ad illicita rapitur, per quem naturae simplicitas violatur. Crapulam in omnibus fugite, et in victu regulari temperantiam servate. Nemo vestrum patienter audiat detrahentem fratri suo, aut male de proximo loquentem. Linguam suam unusquisque vestrum ab inutili sermone cohibeat, et male loqui de hominibus christianis bonus monachus erubescat. Nunquam recedat a memoria vestra illa comminatio Domini in sancto Evangelio dicentis: Ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. Bonus homo de bono thesauro profert bona, et malus homo de malo thesauro profert mala. Dico autem vobis, quoniam omne verbum ociosum, quod locuti fuerint homines, 60 De custodia, et origine cogitationum.

Homily IX.

He says: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?” And elsewhere: “For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.” And concerning Paul himself, in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Lord said to Ananias: Go, for this man is a vessel of election for me.”

The monk who serves in priestly order in the Church of God is bound for two reasons to the observance of most holy purity. For a soldier of Christ, because of the vow that he has made to God, must be pure, holy, and always tireless in good works; and by reason of the priestly ministry he must be circumspect and most diligently watchful. For it is written: “Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently.”

You are ministers of almighty God, who daily offer his Son upon the altar; his work is committed into your hands, and therefore great purity of mind and body is required in your manner of life. Therefore, so that the chaste purity of the mind may remain, the instability of thought must be restrained. The senses, through which the integrity of the mind is corrupted, must be guarded at all times.

For you have died to the world, and have now begun to live for Christ. It is not lawful for you to think anything except what is holy, nor is it fitting for you, ministers of God, to love anything earthly. It is God whom you serve, O monks; it is the Almighty whom you minister to, my brothers. Live pure, holy, and innocent lives, because it is not fitting for you to be occupied with the business of the world, you who have been called to the service of God. Let love of God and purity of heart grow in you with time, so that the longer you live in this world, the holier you may become.

Always turn your sight away from every evil, so that you may be able to remain without failing in good thoughts. Always lift the eyes of your mind to heaven, and do not occupy the sight of the flesh with perishable things. Close your hearing also at all times against every useless, vain, and foolish word, and always think with fear upon the future judgment of God. Do not defile your hands with unlawful and shameful contact with any things whatsoever, so that you may be able to offer the Son of God with a clean body and a pure conscience.

In food and drink it is not for monks to distinguish flavors, nor is it fitting for soldiers of Christ to love bodily pleasures. Nature requires few things, and simple, rustic foods by which it may be nourished; but appetite, unless it is restrained by the command of reason, is carried off toward unlawful things, and through it the simplicity of nature is violated. Avoid gluttony and drunken excess in all things, and keep temperance in your regular diet.

Let none of you patiently listen to one slandering his brother or speaking evil of his neighbor. Let each one of you restrain his tongue from useless speech, and let a good monk be ashamed to speak evil of Christian people. Never let that warning of the Lord in the holy Gospel depart from your memory, where he says: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. A good man brings forth good things from a good treasure, and an evil man brings forth evil things from an evil treasure. But I say to you that every idle word that men have spoken…”

57
reddent rationem de eo in die iudicii. O nimis metuenda sententia. Si de ocioso sermone ratio exigitur, detractio, scurrilitas, et turpiloquium quid merentur; aut si verbum inutile rationi districti examinis censetur obnoxium, quid respondebit, qui tam facile loquitur malum, et perniciosum? Ocio sum verbum quid. frateres considerate sermones vestros; et nemo loquatur verbum ad rem non pertinens, vel iustae utilitatis, vel necessariae rationis. Audivistis enim formidabilem Domini sententiam, et Divi legislatoris nostri praeceptum non ignoratis in regula dicentis: Scurrilitates, verba ociosa, et risum moventia, aeterna clausura in omnibus locis damnamus, et ad tale eloquium discipulum aperire os non permittimus. Tria hic verborum genera sanctus Pater Benedictus monachis interdixit, et aeterna clausura in omnibus locis damnavit. Scurrilitas videlicet, ociosa, et risum moventia. Quid autem sit scurrilitas, grammaticorum nobis interpretatio declaravit. Est enim scurrilitatis vitium urbanitati, et modestiae oppositum, et iocularitas quaedam lasciva risum provocans auditorum sine verecundia, vel honestate immoderatum per verba, et gestus, qui non congruunt rationi, nec virum decent bonum, nec sapienti conveniunt. Dicitur autem scurrilitas a scurra, qui domos sequitur divitum, lascivis, et inhomestis verbis, et gestibus auditores praemitt, vel stipis gratia provocans ad risum. Et hoc genus verborum monachis Divus Pater Benedictus interdixit, et penitus damnavit, quoniam, qui Deo serviant, merito abstinere in conspectu eius perpetuo a verbis turpis, et inhomestis iubentur. Inter scurrilitatem vero, et multiloquium hoc interesse videtur, quod illa excedit ratione inhomestatis, et ista causa superfluitatis. Illa est turpis, et inhomesta, ista vero sine utilitate superflua. Stultiloquium his recte coniungitur, quoniam non solum monachis, verum etiam omnibus interdicitur christianis. Hinc sanctus Christi apostolus dicit: Fornicatio autem, et omnis immunditia, aut avaritia, nec nominetur in vobis, sicut decet sanctos, aut turpitudo, aut stultiloquium, aut scurrilitas, quae ad rem non pertinet, sed magis gratiarum actio. Verbum ociosum similiter monachis cunctis interdictur, quoniam a Domino, sicut audivistis, in sancto Evangelio prohibetur. Risum quoque moventia verba non decent homines christianos, et multo minus conveniunt claustralibus. Monachus enim, qui mortuus est mundo, sua novissima semper cogitare praecipitur, risum vero, et omnem praesentis vitae insolentiam pro Dei amore ubique locorum contemnere iubetur. Est autem risus vox confusa, internam animi laetiam immoderata denuncians. Nihil autem, quod modestiam, et temperantiam excedit, monachis adesse permittitur, quorum vita, et conversatio non carni, et sanguini, sed angelicae puritati

they will render an account of it on the day of judgment. O sentence greatly to be feared. If an account is demanded for an idle word, what do slander, buffoonery, and foul speech deserve? Or if a useless word is judged liable to the reckoning of a strict examination, what will he answer who so readily speaks what is evil and destructive?

Consider, brothers, what an idle word is; consider your speech, and let no one speak a word that does not pertain to the matter, or to rightful usefulness, or to necessary reason. For you have heard the fearful sentence of the Lord, and you are not ignorant of the command of our holy lawgiver in the Rule, when he says: “Scurrilities, idle words, and words provoking laughter we condemn everywhere to perpetual exclusion, and we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth for such speech.”

Here the holy father Benedict forbade monks three kinds of words, and condemned them everywhere to perpetual exclusion: namely buffoonery, idle words, and words provoking laughter. What buffoonery is, the explanation of the grammarians has made clear to us. For the vice of buffoonery is opposed to courtesy and modesty; it is a kind of wanton joking that shamelessly and dishonorably provokes immoderate laughter in hearers by words and gestures that do not accord with reason, do not befit a good man, and are not fitting for a wise man.

Buffoonery is so called from the buffoon, who follows the houses of the rich, provoking his hearers to laughter with wanton and indecent words and gestures, either [unclear] or for the sake of a gift. This kind of speech the holy father Benedict forbade to monks and utterly condemned, since those who serve God are rightly commanded to abstain perpetually in his sight from shameful and indecent words.

Between buffoonery and much speaking there seems to be this difference: the former goes beyond measure by reason of indecency, the latter by reason of superfluity. The former is shameful and indecent; the latter is superfluous and without usefulness. Foolish talk is rightly joined to these, since it is forbidden not only to monks but also to all Christians. Hence the holy apostle of Christ says: “But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not even be named among you, as befits saints; nor filthiness, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery, which is not fitting, but rather thanksgiving.”

Likewise an idle word is forbidden to all monks, since it is prohibited by the Lord, as you have heard, in the holy Gospel. Words that provoke laughter also do not befit Christian men, and much less are they suitable for those in the cloister. For the monk, who is dead to the world, is commanded always to think on his last things, and is commanded everywhere, for the love of God, to despise laughter and every insolence of this present life.

Laughter is a confused sound, immoderately announcing the inward gladness of the soul. Nothing that exceeds modesty and temperance is permitted to be present in monks, whose life and conduct belong not to flesh and blood, but to angelic purity.

58
Homilia IX. 61 comparatur. Risus autem intempestivus, et immoderata levitate profusus dissolutae mentis indicium est, et ostendit hominem moderatae honestatis, et modestiae oblitum. Monachus vero, qui Christum imitari iubetur, et ea conditione saeculo renunciat, ut maiore puritate vivere possit, ab omnibus cavere debet, quae statum mentis virilem subvertunt, et vana huius mundi gaudia pro caelestis patriae desiderio cuncta despicere, seque in omni maturitate mentis, et corporis perpetuo insuperabilem conservare. Et quemadmodum risus immoderatus monachis in omni tempore, et loco interdicitur, ita et loqui verba risum auditoribus moventia prohibetur. Hic iam fratres charissimi vosmetipsos attendite, et quomodo refrenare linguas beatis vestras, sedulo cogitate. Quid propheta dicat in psalmo, ad memoriam saepius revocate: Psal. 38. Dixi, custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea. Posui ori meo custodiam, obmutui, et humiliatus sum, et silui a bonis. Recogitate vos in omni loco astante Domino. Deo, qui ubique est praesens, omnia audit, omnia videt, omnia novit, omnia intelligit, a cuius notitia nihil absconditur, cuius districto examini omnia reservantur: in cuius aspectu sic vivite, ut venire ad eius iudicium secure valatis. Quoties de licentia nostri, vel prioris convenitis ad colloquium, a verbis scurrilibus, ociosis, et risum concitantibus iuxta praecipsum Legislatoris nostri summopere caveatis. Sint eloquia vestra modestiae plena, non clamosa, non frivola, non temeraria, non contentiosa, ne rationi exactae reddantur obnoxia. Multiloquium similiter fugite, quoniam non est sine peccato, et Monachum facit cunctis hominibus onerosum. Seniores loquuntur non quaelibet, sed verba doctrinae salutaris, quibus animos iuniorum ad semitam Iustitiae instruant, et ad Dei amorem peramplius incendant. Nam Sancto Legislatore nostro dicente, loqui, et docere magistrum condecedet; tacere, et audire discipulum. Et ideo seniores loquuntur utilia, et doceant; iuniores autem tacendo audiant, et discant. Et si quae requirenda sunt a priore, cum omni humilitate, reverentia, et subiectione requirantur, ne quis videatur plus loqui, quam expedit. Ex verbis suis cognoscitur vir, et, qui multiplicat locutiones in ore suo, insipiens est corde. Conscientiae testis est sermo viri, et, qui pudicitiam et innocentiam cordis diligit, illius pudicos, et sine vanitate opportet esse sermones. Dei nanque viventis ministri estis o fratres mei, omnis sermo vanus, inutilis, et ociosus non exeat de ore vestro, sed si quis bonus est ad aedificationem auditorum, ut charitatem augeat mentibus ad illustrationem cordis in cognitionem, et amorrem summae veritatis. Preciosa lingua Monachi, quae nihil omnino loquitur, nisi sanctum, et os benedictione dignum, de quo nihil profertur, nisi Divinum. Cor suum unusquisque mundum custodiat ab omni cogitatione iniqua, quoniam, qui bonus est corde, malum non lo- 62 De custodia, et origine cogitationum.

Homily IX.

...is compared. But untimely laughter, poured out with immoderate levity, is a sign of a dissolute mind, and shows a man forgetful of proper honor and modesty. A monk, however, who is commanded to imitate Christ and renounces the world on this condition, that he may live in greater purity, must beware of everything that overturns a manly state of mind; and, out of desire for the heavenly homeland, he must despise all the vain joys of this world and preserve himself always unconquered in every maturity of mind and body.

And just as immoderate laughter is forbidden to monks at every time and place, so too speaking words that move the hearers to laughter is prohibited. Here now, most dear brothers, pay attention to yourselves, and carefully consider how you ought to restrain your tongues. Often recall to memory what the prophet says in the psalm: “I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue. I set a guard over my mouth; I was mute and humbled, and kept silence even from good things.”

Think of yourselves in every place as standing before the Lord God, who is present everywhere, who hears all things, sees all things, knows all things, understands all things, from whose knowledge nothing is hidden, and to whose strict examination all things are reserved. Live in his sight in such a way that you may be able to come securely to his judgment.

Whenever, by permission of us or of the prior, you come together for conversation, you must with the greatest care avoid scurrilous, idle, and laughter-provoking words, according to the command of our Lawgiver. Let your speech be full of modesty, not loud, not frivolous, not rash, not contentious, lest it become liable to an exact accounting. Likewise flee much speaking, because it is not without sin and makes a monk burdensome to all people.

Let the elders speak not just anything, but words of saving doctrine, by which they may instruct the minds of the younger men in the path of righteousness and kindle them more fully to the love of God. For, as our holy Lawgiver says, speaking and teaching belong to the master; keeping silence and listening belong to the disciple. Therefore let the elders speak useful things and teach; but let the younger men listen in silence and learn. And if anything must be asked of the prior, let it be asked with all humility, reverence, and subjection, lest anyone seem to speak more than is fitting.

A man is known by his words, and he who multiplies utterances in his mouth is foolish in heart. A man’s speech is the witness of his conscience; and he who loves modesty and innocence of heart must have modest speech, without vanity. For you are ministers of the living God, my brothers. Let no vain, useless, or idle word come from your mouth, but only what is good for the building up of the hearers, so that it may increase charity in their minds and enlighten the heart unto the knowledge and love of the highest truth.

Precious is the tongue of the monk that speaks nothing at all except what is holy; and worthy of blessing is the mouth from which nothing is brought forth except what is divine. Let each one keep his heart clean from every wicked thought, because he who is good in heart does not speak evil.

On the guarding and origin of thoughts.

59
quitur verbum: et, qui Deum veraciter diligit, sermonem non profert ociosum. Omnem sollicitudinem, et considerationem adhibete cogitatio- nibus vestris, quoniam ibi praecipua intentione observandum est malum, ubi suorum processuum sumit exordium, quatenus mox, ut oriri coe- perit, radicitus amputetur. Nulla enim tam debilis cogitatio mali, quae tempore non crescat, si consensu nutriatur cogitantis. Mox igitur a principio vincendum est adhuc debile malum, quia dum mora interpo- nitur, vires accipit malum, quantunlibet parvum in exordio videatur. Magnum ex parva scintilla saepe oritur incendium, et de minuta co- gitatione grande nonunquam surgit peccatum. Cogitatio dum parit de- lectationem, mox in consensum solet irrumpere, et consequenter in opus etiam, si potest, semetipsam praecipitem dare. Dum autem co- gitationi mala in opus per delectionem praestiterit voluntas consen- sum, etiam si non perficiatur, quod concupiscit animus, iam tamen consummatum est coram Deo peccatum. Sed quid dicit scriptura? Pe- ccatum, cum fuerit consummatum, generat mortem. Omnipotens etenim Deus voluntatem hominis respicit, sive bonum, sive malum velit. Pro- pterea in Sancto Evangelio dicit: Qui viderit mulierem ad concupi- scendum eam, iam moechatus est eam in corde suo. Voluntatem Deus pro facto computat, quoties homo non potest in effectum deducere, quod volebat. Idcirco iterum, atque iterum moneo fratres, et quanta possum sedulitate contestor, ut iuxta Sanctum Apostolum caute am- buletis, non quasi insipientes, redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt. Insidias daemonis mali cautissime observate, malisque, et im- mundis cogitationibus statim a principio resistite, quoniam sero nimis cogitatetur de remedio, cum morbus invaluit tempore diurno. Assue- scite omni tempore bonis, et sanctis cogitationibus insistere, et mala- rum insolentiam facile poteritis superare. Nam sicut vasa bonis liquo- ribus plena, nihil corruptionis externae suscipiunt, ita mentes repletae cogitationibus bonis, malarum intemperantiam non admittunt. Mundi cordis oculus est, quo Deus cernitur, et per puritatem conscientiae, ad gloriam aeternae foelicitatis pervenitur. Dicit enim in Sancto Evan- gelio Dominus: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Cor mundum Spiritus Sancti habitaculum est, et ubi mala cogitatio non ad- mittitur, Deus procul dubio moratur. Cor mundum sedes est sapientiae, et ubi custoditur puritas mentis, nulla nocebunt pericula adversitatis. Memores estote scripturae dicentis; Perversae cogitationes separant a Deo, probata autem virtus corripit insipientes. Quoniam in malevolam animam non introbit sapientia, nec habitabit in corpore subdito pec- catis. Spiritus enim sanctus disciplinae effugiet fictum, et auferet se a cogitationibus, quae sunt sine intellectu. Perversa vero cogitatio est, quaecunque admittitur Evangelicae puritati contraria, cuius commercio

And who truly loves God does not utter an idle word. Apply every care and attention to your thoughts, because evil must be watched with chief intent there where it takes the beginning of its progress, so that as soon as it begins to arise it may be cut off at the root. For there is no thought of evil so weak that it does not grow with time, if it is nourished by the consent of the one thinking it. Therefore evil, while still weak, must be conquered at once from the beginning, because when delay is interposed, evil gains strength, however small it may seem at its outset.

A great fire often arises from a small spark, and from a tiny thought a great sin sometimes rises up. When thought gives birth to delight, it is soon accustomed to break out into consent, and consequently even into deed, if it can, and to cast itself headlong. But when the will has given consent through delight to an evil thought for the deed, even if what the soul desires is not carried out, nevertheless the sin has already been consummated before God. But what does Scripture say? Sin, when it has been consummated, begets death.

For almighty God looks upon the will of man, whether he wills good or evil. Therefore he says in the holy Gospel: Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. God counts the will as the deed whenever a man cannot bring into effect what he wished. For this reason again and again I admonish you, brothers, and with as much diligence as I can I urge you, that according to the holy Apostle you walk cautiously, not as the unwise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

Watch most carefully for the snares of the evil demon, and resist evil and unclean thoughts immediately from the beginning, because remedy is thought of far too late when the sickness has gained strength by the course of time. Accustom yourselves at all times to dwell on good and holy thoughts, and you will easily be able to overcome the insolence of evil ones. For just as vessels filled with good liquids receive nothing of external corruption, so minds filled with good thoughts do not admit the excess of evil thoughts.

The eye of the heart is pure, by which God is seen, and through purity of conscience one comes to the glory of eternal happiness. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. A pure heart is the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, and where an evil thought is not admitted, God beyond doubt abides. A pure heart is the seat of wisdom, and where purity of mind is guarded, no dangers of adversity will do harm.

Be mindful of Scripture when it says: Perverse thoughts separate from God, but proven virtue rebukes the foolish. For wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor will it dwell in a body subject to sins. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit and will withdraw itself from thoughts that are without understanding. But a perverse thought is any thought that is admitted contrary to evangelical purity, by whose intercourse

60
Homilia IX. mens cogitantis polluitur, quoties in his, quae Deo adversantur, cogitando, et revolvendo delectatur. Et istae cogitationes perversae mentem cogitantis a Deo separant, et paulatim in profundum malorum praecipitant. Mala enim, atque perversa cogitatio mentem, quam penetraverit, primo per delectationis venenum intoxicat, deinde rationem obnubilat, postea voluntatem ad consentiendum suggestioni malae pertrahit, postremo peccatum in opere consumat. Iam deinceps malum semel praesumptum licentius agitur, et omnis verecundia, seu timor per consuetudinem auffertur. Peccatum peccato coniungitur, et paulatim consuetudini malefaciendi roboratur. Dum vero consuetudini malae tempus conceditur, quaedam mox peccandi necessitas generatur. Hic durissimum mortis imperium, hic extrema profunditas malorum, Quicunque hanc semel, abyssum peccatorum intraverit, sine speciali Dei gratia, et maximo labore poenitendi ad puritatem cordis raro, immo non facile consurgit. Voluntate sua peccator in hac foveam mortis cecidit, resurgere autem sine Dei miseratione non valebit. Durissimum est iugum consuetudinis malae, cui si quis collum semel submisserit, ad pristinam libertatem spiritus raro convalescit. Haec omnia operatur cogitatio per versa, cum ad mentem intrumittitur, et per delectationem in consensum, et opus commutatur. Nulla enim cogitatio tam parva est, quae paulatim non crescat, si a mente non repellitur. Beatus igitur ille Monachus, qui omne cogitatum suum iactat in Dominum, qui pravis cogitationibus semper, et ubique denegat locum, qui omnes mundi perituras divitias despicit, qui cuncta corporis solita contemnit. Cordis munditiam sui Domino praeparat; nihil in hoc mundo praeter Dominum amat; omnes cogitationes suas ad gloriam salvatoris ordinat, et mandata illius diligentissime observat. Quid illo foelicius monacho, qui se non civem, sed peregrinum exhibet mundo? In mundo vivit, quasi non sit in mundo: immo maior est mundo, cuius conversatio tota in coelo. Considerate nunc igitur fratres charissimi huius brevitatem temporis, et semper mementote quia mortales, et cito transituri estis. Non enim habemus hic manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus; et qui tot millia hominum per mortem nos praecessisse cognoscimus, quam cito simus necessario et ipsi morituri, cogitemus. Tempus nunc quidem breve, sed acceptabile nobis multum conceditur, in quo fructus aeternae vitae operemur. Nunc enim laborandi est tempus: nunc hiora seminandi bonum, quia post mortem unusquisque mercedem laborum suorum recepturus est, cum laborandi iam facultas nulla conceditur. Idcirco fratres mei hanc mortis horam sanctis praevenite operibus, et nolite nunc in semine laboris deficere, ut in aeterna retributione pos sitis sine fine gaudere. Nulla praetereat dies, in qua unusquisque ve strum se melior non evaserit, et ad ea, quae praemisit opera bona,

Homily IX.

The mind of the thinker is defiled whenever, by thinking about and turning over those things that are opposed to God, it takes delight in them. And these perverse thoughts separate the mind of the thinker from God and gradually hurl it down into the depth of evils. For an evil and perverse thought, when it has penetrated the mind, first poisons it with the venom of delight; then it darkens reason; afterward it draws the will into consenting to the evil suggestion; finally it completes the sin in deed. From then on, an evil once presumed is committed with greater license, and all shame or fear is taken away through habit. Sin is joined to sin, and little by little the habit of doing evil is strengthened. But when time is granted to an evil habit, there soon arises a certain necessity of sinning. Here is the hardest rule of death; here is the utmost depth of evils. Whoever has once entered this abyss of sins rarely, indeed not easily, rises again to purity of heart without the special grace of God and the greatest labor of repentance. By his own will the sinner has fallen into this pit of death; but he will not be able to rise again without the mercy of God. Most hard is the yoke of evil habit; if anyone has once submitted his neck to it, he rarely regains his former freedom of spirit. All these things perverse thought brings about when it is admitted into the mind and, through delight, is changed into consent and deed. For no thought is so small that it does not gradually grow if it is not driven away from the mind.

Blessed, then, is that monk who casts every thought of his upon the Lord; who always and everywhere denies a place to wicked thoughts; who despises all the perishable riches of the world; who scorns all the customary comforts of the body. He prepares purity of heart for his Lord; he loves nothing in this world except the Lord; he orders all his thoughts to the glory of the Savior and observes his commandments most diligently. What is happier than that monk who shows himself to the world not as a citizen but as a pilgrim? He lives in the world as though he were not in the world; indeed, he is greater than the world, for his whole way of life is in heaven.

Consider now, therefore, most beloved brothers, the brevity of this time, and always remember that you are mortal and soon to pass away. For we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come; and since we know that so many thousands of people have gone before us through death, let us consider how soon we too must necessarily die. A short time is now granted to us, yet a very acceptable one, in which we may work the fruits of eternal life. For now is the time for labor; now is the hour for sowing good, because after death each person will receive the reward of his labors, when no further opportunity for labor is granted. Therefore, my brothers, anticipate this hour of death with holy works, and do not now fail in the sowing of labor, so that in eternal recompense you may be able to rejoice without end. Let no day pass in which each one of you has not become better, and toward those good works which he has sent ahead,

61
64 De quotidiano certamine tentationis. novum aliquid non addiderit. Semper cogitate futurae precium messis, et nulla vos terrebit magnitudo laboris. De quotidiano certamine tentationis. Homilia X. Hesterno sermone admonui charitates vestras, dilectissimi fratres, principis malarum cogitationum obsistere, et vos bonis, ac sanctis operibus ad futurae mercedis praemium totis viribus praeparare. Sed cum, scriptura testante, tentatio sit vita hominis super terram, necessarium duxi de hac ipse materia, quantum dederit Dominus, in auribus vestris disserere, ut praemoniti fortius contra adversarium in- visibilem possitis dimicare. Verba non ignoratis viri sapientis, qui in Eccles. 2. Ecclesiastico dicit: Fili accedens ad servitutem Dei, sta in iustitia, et in timore, et praepara animam tuam ad tentationem. Nemo se liberum a tentatione existimet, fratres, quandiu in hac mortali conversatione gra- ditur, sed quanto in Dei timore quisque amplius profecerit, tanto sibi no- verit cautius esse vivendum. Dicit enim sanctus Papa Gregorius: Hostis noster, quanto magis rebellari sibi conspicit, tanto amplius expugnare con- tendit. Eos enim pulsare negligit, quos quieto iure se possidere sentit. Fu- gientem a se diabolus persequitur, et eum, qui rebellat suo imperio, sub- vertere conatur. Vos o viri quanto amplius in spirituali conversatione pro- ficitis, tanto maiore instantia contra adversarium salutis vestrae oportet vigiletis. Nam ut sanctus Ioannes Chrysostomus ait: Nunquam dormit no- ster adversarius, sed in perniciem semper vigilat generis humani, cui nemo nostrum potest resistere, nisi qui omni tempore in timore Domini di- dicit vigilare. Et sanctus Leo Papa urbis Romae, in quodam sermone dicit. Non desinit antiquus hostis tentationum laqueos ubique praetendere, ut quoquo modo fidem credentium corrupiendo valeat denigrare. Novit enim, cui illecebras carnis ingenerat, cui vires invidiae infundat, cui incitamenta luxuriae apponat. Novit, quem moerore conturbet, quem gaudio fallat, quem metu opprimat, quem admiratione seducat. Omnium discutit mores, omnium scrutatur affectus. Et ibi quaerit causas nocendi, ubi viderit quenquam studiosius occupari. Nulla sunt sine tentationum experimento opera virtutis; nullum sine hoste certamen; nulla sine con- gressione victoria. Hinc sanctus Iacobus Apostolus in epistola dicit: Beatus vir, qui suffert tentationem, quoniam, cum probatus fuerit, ac- cipiet coronam vitae, quam repromisit Deus diligentibus se. Hinc ite- rum dicit scriptura: Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines iustos ten- tatio tribulationis. Sed ne quis putaret diabolo permissum tentare ho- mines, quantum desiderat, sanctus Christophilus clamat: Fidelis autem Deus est, qui non patietur vos tentari supra id, quod potestis, sed fa- cit etiam cum tentatione proventum, ut possitis sustinere. if he has not added anything new. Always keep in mind the value of the harvest to come, and no greatness of labor will terrify you.

On the Daily Struggle of Temptation. Homily X.

In yesterday’s sermon, dearly beloved brothers, I warned your Charity to resist the beginnings of evil thoughts, and to prepare yourselves with all your strength, by good and holy works, for the reward of the future recompense.

But since, as Scripture bears witness, the life of man upon earth is temptation, I have thought it necessary to speak in your hearing, as far as the Lord grants, about this very subject, so that, forewarned, you may be able to fight more strongly against the invisible adversary. You know the words of the wise man, who says in Ecclesiasticus: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.” Let no one think himself free from temptation, brothers, as long as he walks in this mortal way of life; rather, the more each one has advanced in the fear of God, the more cautiously he should know that he must live. For the holy Pope Gregory says: “Our enemy, the more he sees that he is being resisted, the more he strives to attack. For he neglects to strike those whom he feels he possesses by undisturbed right.” The devil pursues the one who flees from him, and tries to overthrow the one who rebels against his rule.

O men, the more you advance in the spiritual life, the more earnestly you must keep watch against the adversary of your salvation. For, as Saint John Chrysostom says: “Our adversary never sleeps, but is always awake for the destruction of the human race; and none of us can resist him except the one who has learned to keep watch at all times in the fear of the Lord.” And Saint Leo, pope of the city of Rome, says in a certain sermon: “The ancient enemy does not cease to spread everywhere the snares of temptations, so that in whatever way he can he may darken the faith of believers by corrupting it. For he knows in whom to implant the enticements of the flesh, into whom to pour the strength of envy, before whom to set the incitements of lust. He knows whom to trouble with sorrow, whom to deceive with joy, whom to crush with fear, whom to seduce with admiration. He examines the conduct of all, he searches the affections of all. And there he seeks occasions for doing harm, wherever he sees anyone to be occupied with particular zeal.”

There are no works of virtue without the trial of temptations; no contest without an enemy; no victory without conflict. Hence Saint James the Apostle says in his epistle: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.” Hence again Scripture says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men.” But lest anyone should think that the devil is permitted to tempt men as much as he desires, Saint Christophilus cries out: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also make a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.” And Saint

62
Homilia X. 65 Augustinus. Tantum, inquit, permittitur diabolus tentare, quantum tibi prodest, ut exercearis, ut proberis, ut qui te nesciebas, a te ipso inveniaris. Potest enim diabolus, permittente Deo, excitare tentationis motum, sed in tua est liberrima potestate, si velis tentanti dare, vel negare consensum. Unde, cum tentaret in deserto Dei filium, non impulit, non tetigit, non coegit, sed tantum dixit, Mitte te deorsum, ut intellegas, quoniam non potest vincere, nisi volente. Idcirco divus Christi archiapostolus dixit: Resistite diabolo, et fugiet a vobis. Potest enim suggerere malum diabolus, cogere non potest, nec superare, nisi consentias. Vita nostra, sancto testante Augustino, in hac peregrinatione non potest esse sine peccato, et tentatione: quia profectus noster per tentationes augeitur; nec sibi quisquam innotescit, nisi tentatus; nec potest coronari, nisi vicerit; nec potest vincere, nisi certaverit; nec potest certare, nisi inimicum, et tentationes habuerit. Dicit nanque scriptura: Qui non est tentatus, qualia scit? Nemo enim coronabitur, nisi qui legitime certaverit. Accedentes igitur ad servitutem Dei, fratres charissimi, state in iustitia et timore, et quandiu potestis vinci ab adversario, et subiici, de securitate nolite gloriarri. Semper vigilate, semper timete, quoniam hostis, cum quo inistis certamen, nunquam dormit, non quiescit, non cessat a persecutione: vobisque insidians semper, nunquam fatigatur. Quod si aliquando superatus fuerit, mox ad novum certamen consurgit, nec desistit ab impugnatione bonorum, donec victus omnino succumbat, aut certe importuna perseverantia concertantem vincat. Unde et sanctus Papa Gregorius dicit: Antiquus hostis ex primo certamine, dum se succumbere considerat, alia tentationum bella restaurat. Intuetur humani generis cautelosus adversarius, uniuscuiusque mores, et cui sint vitio propinquiores, illa ponit ante faciem cordis, magnisque utitur viribus, ut subvertat statum mentis. State in timore Domini firmiter radicati, et cunctas facile superabitis tentationes inimici. Scriptum est enim in libro proverbiorum. In timore Domini fiducia fortitudinis. Et iterum: Per misericordiam et fidem, purgantur peccata, per timorem autem Domini declinat omnis a malo. In Ecclesiastico vero sapiens dixit: Timor Domini expellit peccatum. Nam, qui sine timore est, non poterit iustificari. Iracundia enim animositatis illius subvertit eum. Idcirco, Salomonis testimonio, beatus ille dicitur homo, qui semper est pavidus: qui vero mentis est durae, corruet in malum. Animas quoque vestras per studium sanctae conversationis praeparate ad tentationem, ut cum venerit possitis resistere, et eo fortiores stare. Nam facile superabitis diabolum, si praeparati semper accesseritis ad bellandum. Ecce adversarius vester tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quaerens quem devoret, cui vos oportet in fide Domini nostri Iesu Christi resistere, si victoriam cupitis obtinere. Nullus hic fugiendi locus

Augustine says: The devil is permitted to tempt only so far as benefits you, so that you may be exercised, so that you may be tested, so that you, who did not know yourself, may be discovered by yourself. For the devil, if God permits it, can stir up the impulse of temptation; but it is in your own completely free power whether you wish to give consent to the tempter or to refuse it. Hence, when he tempted the Son of God in the desert, he did not drive him, did not touch him, did not compel him, but only said, “Cast yourself down,” so that you may understand that he cannot conquer unless one is willing. Therefore the divine chief apostle of Christ said: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” For the devil can suggest evil; he cannot compel, nor can he overcome unless you consent.

Our life, as Saint Augustine bears witness, cannot in this pilgrimage be without sin and temptation, because our progress is increased through temptations; nor does anyone come to know himself unless he is tempted; nor can he be crowned unless he has conquered; nor can he conquer unless he has fought; nor can he fight unless he has had an enemy and temptations. For Scripture says: “He who has not been tempted, what does he know?” For no one will be crowned except the one who has fought lawfully.

Therefore, as you approach the service of God, dearly beloved brothers, stand in justice and fear; and so long as you can be overcome and subdued by the adversary, do not boast of security. Always keep watch, always fear, because the enemy with whom you have entered into combat never sleeps, does not rest, does not cease from persecution; and as he is always laying snares for you, he is never wearied. But if at any time he has been overcome, at once he rises up to a new battle, and he does not desist from attacking the good until, utterly defeated, he gives way, or else by troublesome perseverance he conquers the one who is fighting against him.

Hence Saint Pope Gregory also says: The ancient enemy, when he sees himself giving way in the first contest, renews other wars of temptations. The crafty adversary of the human race observes each person’s character, and whichever vices they are nearer to, these he sets before the face of the heart; and he uses great strength to overthrow the condition of the mind.

Stand in the fear of the Lord, firmly rooted, and you will easily overcome all the temptations of the enemy. For it is written in the book of Proverbs: “In the fear of the Lord is confidence of strength.” And again: “By mercy and faith sins are purged; but by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil.” In Ecclesiasticus, too, the wise man said: “The fear of the Lord drives out sin. For he who is without fear will not be able to be justified; for the wrath of his temper overthrows him.” Therefore, by Solomon’s testimony, that man is called blessed who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil.

Prepare your souls also for temptation through the practice of holy conduct, so that when it comes you may be able to resist and stand all the more strongly. For you will easily overcome the devil if you always come prepared to fight. Behold, your adversary, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; you must resist him in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ if you desire to obtain the victory. There is no place here for fleeing.

63
66 De quotidiano certamine tentationis. conceditur, nulla securitatis morula pugnantibus indulgetur, sed con- grediaris necessē est, superaturus hostem, si fortiter steteris; aut vin- cendus ab eo, si male pugnaveris. Hac lege mundum intravimus omnes, ut pugnando vincamus; hac sumus conditione homines facti, ut, super- ratis illecebris carnis, pares angelis sanctis evadere debeamus. Nun- quam desunt monachis certamina, quoniam, quandiu versamur in carne, Psal. 33. tentationibus necessāri sumus expositi. Dicit enim scriptura: Multae tribulationes iustorum, et de omnibus his liberabit eos Dominus. In omnibus autem tentationibus nostris illud Esaiae prophetae ad memo- riam sedulo revocemus dicentis: Qui ablactati estis a lacte, qui abstracti ab ubere, tribulationem super tribulationem expectate, spem super spem adhuc pusillum propter malitiam labiorum, propter linguam malignam. Ablactati et abstracti ad ubere sunt viri aetate provecti, quorum est tribulationem super tribulationem propter Deum suscipere, ut super Rom. 5. spem mereantur reportare, sacra dicente scriptura. Sed et gloriamur in tribulationibus nostris, scientes, quod tribulatio patientiam operat, pa- tientia autem probationem, probatio vero spem. Spes autem non con- fundit: quia charitas Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Per multas enim tribulationes oportet nos Act. 14. intrare in regnum Dei. Tentationibus nanque nobismetipsis innotesci- mus, et experimur, si Deum veraciter timeamus. Hinc Dominus per Deut. 13. Moysen ad populum loquitur dicens: Tentat vos Dominus Deus vester, Mundus ut sciat, si diligatis eum de toto corde vestro, et de tota anima vestra. hic fornax Mundus iste, fratres charissimi, fornaci comparandus est, in qua con- quaedam est tinue ardet ignis tentationis, et adversitatis, per quam necessario nobis iustis. est transeundum. In hac fornace tribulationis palea comburitur, aurum vero et argentum ab omni macula purgantur; Palea in cinerem verti- tur, aurum ad ornatum et decorum regalis palatii reservatur. Fornax, inquam, est mundus, ignis tentatio, sive tribulatio, aurum homines iusti, palea vero iniusti, et peccatores: artifex, qui purgat aurum, ipse est Omnipotens Deus, qui nostris profectibus favet, et ad virtutis meritum cooperatur per gratiam. Quod ergo vult Deus, faciamus; quod imponit, patienter pro eius amore toleremus, quoniam, ut sacer Christophilus inquit, Non sunt condignae passiones huius temporis ad superventuram Rom. 8. gloriam, quae revelabitur in nobis. Hinc sanctus Hieronymus ait: Quis non tribulari velit, quis se maledici non desideret, ut merēatur Christi voce laudari, et coelesti, copiosaque mercede munerari? Utinam propter Domini mei nomen, atque iustitiam, cuncta infidelium turba me perse- quatur, et tribulet. Utinam in opprobrium meum totus hic mundus con- surgat, tantum ut merear a Christo laudari, et ad suae polllicitatio- nis properare mercedem. Et sapiens in ecclesiastico dicit. Vasa figuli Eccles. 27. probat fornax, et homines iustos tentatio tribulationis. Quisquis igitur

no respite of security is granted, no little delay is allowed to those who fight; rather, you must necessarily engage, either to overcome the enemy if you have stood firm bravely, or to be conquered by him if you have fought badly. On this law we all entered the world: that by fighting we should conquer. On this condition we were made human beings: that, having overcome the enticements of the flesh, we should become equal to the holy angels.

Combats are never lacking to monks, since, as long as we live in the flesh, we are necessarily exposed to temptations. For Scripture says: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them.” But in all our temptations let us diligently call to mind that saying of the prophet Isaiah: “You who have been weaned from milk, you who have been drawn away from the breast, expect tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope, yet a little while, because of the malice of lips, because of the malignant tongue.” Those weaned and drawn away from the breast are men advanced in age, whose part it is to undergo tribulation upon tribulation for God, so that they may deserve to receive hope upon hope, as sacred Scripture says: “But we also glory in our tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience, and patience proof, and proof hope. And hope does not confound, because the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” For through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.

Indeed, through temptations we become known to ourselves, and we discover whether we truly fear God. Hence the Lord speaks through Moses to the people, saying: “The Lord your God tests you, that he may know whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul.”

This world, dearly beloved brothers, must be compared to a furnace, in which the fire of temptation and adversity burns continually, through which we must necessarily pass. In this furnace of tribulation the chaff is burned up, but gold and silver are cleansed from every stain. The chaff is turned into ashes; the gold is reserved for the ornament and beauty of the royal palace. The furnace, I say, is the world; the fire is temptation or tribulation; the gold is righteous men; the chaff is the unrighteous and sinners. The craftsman who purifies the gold is almighty God himself, who favors our progress and cooperates by grace toward the merit of virtue.

Therefore let us do what God wills; what he lays upon us, let us endure patiently for love of him, since, as holy Christophilus says, “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which shall be revealed in us.” Hence Saint Jerome says: Who would not wish to be troubled, who would not desire to be spoken ill of, so that he may deserve to be praised by the voice of Christ and rewarded with a heavenly and abundant recompense? Would that, because of the name and justice of my Lord, the whole multitude of unbelievers might persecute and afflict me. Would that this whole world might rise up to my reproach, provided only that I may deserve to be praised by Christ and hasten to the reward of his promise.

And the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men.” Therefore, whoever...

64
Homilia X. 67 vestrum, o fratres mei, ad regnum coelorum pervenire desiderat; quisquis Deo placere super omnia curat, pro eius amore tribulationes tentatio- num libenter discat suscipere, et quicquid occurrerit adversi, gaudenter sustineat. Nemo enim est nostrum, qui purgatione quotidiana non in- digeat, nemo qui singulis momentis ferme non delinquat. Si ergo pro- priam salutem diligimus, si nobis remittit nostra delicta, et purgari ab omni cordis macula flagitamus, patienter sustineamus, quicquid adversi nobis acciderit; quoniam plus animam purgant mala tribulationis, quae pro Dei amore patienter tolerat, quam opera bona, quae nunc in hoc mundo sua sponte patrat. Magna nobis in hoc loco patiendi materia relicta est, quos inopia graviter premit, paupertas deprimit, aeris quoque alieni debitum constringit. Quid in hoc monasterio non experimur ad- versi? quas non procellas, et tempestates patimur, fratres? quibus non exagitamur incommodis? Quam fuerint omnia desolata huius coenobii bona, cum ante annos quindecim observantia introduceretur regularis, nullus vestrum ignorare potest. Sed in me gravius debacchatur inopiae communis tribulatio, qui vobis vitae necessaria providere debo: et saepius, unde reddam, non satis scio. Consolatur autem spiritum meum patientia vestra, et spes, quam in Domino salvatore humilium conce- pistis, ut non dubitem eius misericordiam cum tempore affuturam, et audio mihi dicentem per Esiam prophetam. Ecce excoxi te, sed non quasi argentum, elegi te in camino paupertatis. Libenter autem habebo patientiam in paupertate, quam, Deo sic ordinante, nunc patimur, ut venire post mortem ad aeternitatis divitias mereamur. Quanto enim in hac peregrinatione nostra iam persecutionibus, paupertate, inopia, labo- ribus, et tribulationibus fuerimus afflicti, tanto in futura remuneratione iustorum, Domino largiente, maiora praemia consequemur. Mecum ita- que, fratres mei, tolerate patienter, quicquid omnipotens Deus pati nos praordinavit, quoniam, sicut divus Papa Gregorius ait: In omnipotente Deo tunc certa est fiducia, quando pro opere bono adversitas additur, et in hoc mundo flagellum Dei cum gudio recipitur, ut pulchrior merces in retributione sanctorum futura servetur. Iterum quoque dicit. De spe sempiternae haereditatis gaudium sumunt, quos adversitas vitae temporalis humilitat, quia non salvandos in perpetuum cerneret, si eru- diendos sub disciplinae regimine Divina dispensatio non frenaret. Af- flicti terrena perdimus, sed afflictionem humiliter sustinentes bona nobis caelestia multiplicamus. Via quippe est vita praesens, qua ad patriam tendimus, et idcirco frequenter in ea perturbationibus tangimur, ne hic esse patriam arbitremur. Gaudeat ergo in adversitate sua Monachus, laetetur tentatus, cui crucifixus est mundus: ad Dei se confidat per- tinere consortium, qui pura conscientia bonum semper operat, et re- cipit in tribulatione contrarium. Verissimum enim Divinae miserationis 68 De quotidiano certamine tentationis.

Homily X.

Whoever of you, my brothers, desires to reach the kingdom of heaven, whoever takes care above all things to please God, let him learn willingly, for love of him, to accept the trials of temptations, and let him joyfully endure whatever adversity may befall him. For there is none of us who does not need daily purification, none who does not offend almost at every moment. Therefore, if we love our own salvation, if we ask that our offenses be forgiven us and that we be cleansed from every stain of heart, let us patiently endure whatever adversity happens to us; for the evils of tribulation, which the soul patiently bears for love of God, purify it more than the good works which it now performs of its own accord in this world.

A great occasion for suffering has been left to us in this place: need presses us heavily, poverty weighs us down, and debt also binds us. What adversity do we not experience in this monastery? What squalls and storms do we not suffer, brothers? By what hardships are we not shaken? None of you can be ignorant how desolate all the goods of this monastery were when regular observance was introduced fifteen years ago. But the tribulation of our common need rages more fiercely against me, since I must provide you with the necessities of life, and often I do not sufficiently know from where I shall pay.

Yet your patience consoles my spirit, and the hope which you have conceived in the Lord, the savior of the humble, so that I do not doubt that his mercy will be present in time; and I hear him saying to me through Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I chose you in the furnace of poverty. Gladly, then, will I have patience in the poverty which, God so ordaining, we now suffer, so that after death we may deserve to come to the riches of eternity. For the more, in this our pilgrimage, we have been afflicted by persecutions, poverty, need, labors, and tribulations, the greater rewards, by the Lord’s bounty, we shall obtain in the future recompense of the just.

Therefore, my brothers, patiently endure with me whatever almighty God has foreordained that we should suffer, since, as the blessed Pope Gregory says: Trust in almighty God is certain when adversity is added to a good work, and when the scourge of God is received with joy in this world, so that a more beautiful reward may be kept for the future recompense of the saints. Again he also says: Those whom the adversity of temporal life humbles take joy from the hope of an everlasting inheritance, because divine dispensation would not restrain under the rule of discipline those whom it did not see were to be saved forever. When afflicted, we lose earthly things; but by humbly sustaining affliction, we multiply heavenly goods for ourselves. For the present life is a road by which we journey toward our homeland, and therefore we are often touched in it by disturbances, lest we think that our homeland is here.

Let the monk, then, rejoice in his adversity; let him be glad when tempted, he to whom the world has been crucified. Let him trust that he belongs to the fellowship of God, who with a pure conscience always does good and receives the contrary in tribulation. For it is the truest [unclear] of divine compassion.

65
indicium est, si homo Christianus variis adversitatibus in hoc mundo percutitur, qui pura conscientia Deo serviens in vera humilitate sine offensione conversatur. Frequenter enim misericors Deus eos, quos diligit, variis modis in hoc mundo percutit, quibus aeterna praemia in coelo praeparavit. Quosdam vero, sciens multum posse peccare, ne peccent, infirmitate corporis praoccupat, et in salutem eorum misericorditer flagellat, cernens eorum animabus utilius esse languoribus frangiri ad salutem, quam vivere incolumes ad damnationem. Alios vult esse pauperes, quos praenovit divititis uti non posse ad salutem. Multis enim huius mundi opes, atque divitiae causam aeternae damnationis praebuerunt. Unde sanctus Papa Gregorius iterum dicit. Multos sua peius foelicitas stravit, multos diurna pax victos reddidit: eoque illos inopinatus hostis gravius percellit, quo longo quietis usu negligentes invenit. Unde sancti viri cum multa se proficere virtutum prosperitate considerant, quodam supernae dispensationis moderamine exerceri se etiam tentationibus exultant, quia tanto robustius acceptam virtutum gloriam custodunt, quanto tentationis impulsu concussi infirmitatem suam humilis agnoscent. Compendiosum iter ad Christum est via tribulationis, et citius, quam in tranquillitate, in eo reperitur. Dicit enim sanctus praesul Ambrosius. Multi sunt, qui in ocio quaerunt Christum, et non inveniunt: et sunt, qui quaerunt in persecutionibus, et cito inveniunt. In periculis fidelium suorum adest, quemadmodum in psalmo de iusto loquitur dicens. Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum. Custodiatur in adversitate conscientiae puritas, servetur vitae inviolata semper integritas, et erit nobis proculdubio ad salutis meritum quaecunque adversitas. Neminem antiquus hostis concertando potest deficere, nisi quem invenerit prius a semetipso defecisse. Ocio quaerit torpentem, incautum supplantat militem, illumque prostrernit facillime, quem armis invenerit denudatum. Propterea fratres mei semper vigilate in orationibus sanctis, semper instate operibus bonis, ut quoties tentator accesserit, nunquam inveniat ociosos. Mementote verborum salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi in sacro Evangelio dicentis. Sint lumbi vestri praecincti, et lucernae ardentes in manibus vestris, et vos similes hominibus expectantibus Dominum suum, quando revertatur a nuptiis, ut cum venerit, et pulsaverit, confestim aperiant ei. Vigilat, qui solidus in timore Domini consistens nunquam torpore mentis dormitat. Vigilat, qui animam suam contra qualibet huius mundi adversa per sancti constantiam propositi infatigabilem conservat. Vigilat, quisquis proficere quotidie in amore Domini non cessat. Lucernam in manibus baiulat, quisquis sanctitatis propositum condignis operationibus exornat. Lucernam quoque tenet in manibus, quisquis mente, et corpore purgatus proximo lucet operibus sanctae pietatis. Hinc sanctus Christi

It is a sign if a Christian man is struck by various adversities in this world, one who, serving God with a pure conscience, lives in true humility without offense. For the merciful God often strikes in various ways in this world those whom he loves, for whom he has prepared eternal rewards in heaven. Some, indeed, knowing that they are very capable of sinning, he forestalls by bodily illness so that they may not sin, and mercifully scourges them for their salvation, seeing that it is more useful for their souls to be broken by sickness unto salvation than to live unharmed unto damnation. Others he wills to be poor, whom he foreknew would not be able to use riches for salvation. For the wealth and riches of this world have provided many with a cause of eternal damnation.

Hence holy Pope Gregory again says: Their own prosperity has laid many low more grievously; long-lasting peace has rendered many conquered; and the unexpected enemy strikes them the more severely because he finds them negligent through long habit of quiet. Hence holy men, when they consider that they are making great progress by the prosperity of virtues, rejoice that by a certain moderation of heavenly dispensation they are also exercised by temptations, because they guard the glory of the virtues they have received so much more sturdily, the more, shaken by the assault of temptation, they humbly acknowledge their own weakness.

The way of tribulation is a short road to Christ, and he is found in it more quickly than in tranquillity. For the holy bishop Ambrose says: There are many who seek Christ in leisure and do not find him; and there are those who seek him in persecutions and quickly find him. He is present in the dangers of his faithful, just as he speaks of the righteous man in the psalm, saying: I am with him in tribulation; I will deliver him and glorify him. Let purity of conscience be guarded in adversity; let the inviolate integrity of life always be preserved; and whatever adversity there is will undoubtedly be for us a merit of salvation.

The ancient enemy, by contending, can overcome no one except one whom he has first found to have fallen away from himself. He seeks one sluggish in leisure; he trips up the unwary soldier; and he most easily casts down the one whom he finds stripped of arms. Therefore, my brothers, always keep watch in holy prayers; always be intent upon good works, so that whenever the tempter comes, he may never find you idle. Remember the words of our Savior Jesus Christ, saying in the holy Gospel: Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands, and be like men waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once.

He keeps watch who, standing firm in the fear of the Lord, never dozes in sluggishness of mind. He keeps watch who, through the tireless constancy of a holy purpose, preserves his soul against any adversities of this world. He keeps watch, whoever does not cease daily to advance in the love of the Lord. He carries a lamp in his hands, whoever adorns the purpose of holiness with fitting works. He also holds a lamp in his hands, whoever, purified in mind and body, shines before his neighbor with works of holy devotion. Hence the holy [unclear] of Christ

66
