Homilia X. 69 amator Paulus in epistola dicit: Obsecro vos, charissimi, per miseri- Rom. 12. cordiam Dei, ut exhibeatis corpora vestra hostiam viventem, sanctam, Deo placentem. Qui corpus suum per sanctae abstinentiae studia ca- stigans in servitutem spiritui redigit, viventem Domino hostiam con- secravit. Quisquis autem cor suum ab omni pollutione peccati mund- dum, et purum conservare iam didicit, sanctam proculdubio hostiam Domino immolavit. Quisquis vero in sanctitatis proposito persevera- verit usque ad finem, hostiam sine dubio obtulit placentem. Lumbos autem praecingimus, dum nos ab omni specie libidinis pueros, et im- maculatos corpore, et mente custodimus. Magni apud Deum meriti virtus est sanctae castitatis, et pro magnitudine certaminis singulari praemio in retributione iustorum donanda, dicente Domino per Esiam Prophetam. Haec dicit Dominus eunuchis. Qui custodierint sabbata mea, Esa. 56. et elegerint, quae ego volui, et tenuerint foedus meum: dabo eis in domo mea, et in muris meis locum, et nomen melius a filiis, et fi- liabus. Nomen sempiternum dabo eis, quod non peribit. Et de his in Sancto Evangelio dicit Dominus. Sunt enim eunuchi, qui de matris utero sic nati sunt, et sunt eunuchi facti ab hominibus, et sunt eunu- chi, qui se ipsos castraverunt propter regnum coelorum. Qui potest capere, capiat. Quare autem dixit, qui potest capere, capiat? Puto, quod ista eunuchorum illatio, qui seipsos castrant amore regni coelorum, non ad excisionem genitalium referenda sit membrorum, quod plerique existimantes erraverunt a veritate Evangelii, sed potius ad mentis im- perium, quo castitas servatur integra, Christi amore concepta. Seipsos enim propter regnum Dei castrant, qui veram mentis, et corporis ca- stitatem pro Dei amore inviolabilem observant. Et sicut corporaliter nemo facile castratur sine magni cruciati doloris, ita nemo sine ma- ximo laboris studio pervenire sufficit ad perfectionem castitatis. Et certe nemo castus viribus suis; nemo pudicus meritis propriis. Deus est, qui dat bonam voluntatem, ipse est etiam, qui voluntati, ut possit, con- nectit virtutein. Quoniam vero non est multorum caelibes vivere, suo relinquit unumquenque arbitrio, dicens: Qui potest capere capiat. Ab- scissio membrorum castam non efficit mentem, quoniam radix luxuriae interior est, quam ut pudendorum amputatione possit auferri. Mens vero si casta, et integra fuerit, facile membrorum insolentiam refre- nabit. Nihil enim fortius mente hominis Deum puro corde super omnia dulciter amantis. Cogitate nunc fratres charissimi futura praemia pul- chritudinis, et non gravabit vos labor castitatis. Ad magna enim pra- emia celsitudinis ardui pervenitur instantia laboris. Quicunque igitur la- borem subterfugit certaminis, nunquam perveniet ad celsitudinem li- noris. Breve nunc tempus est, in quo laboramus resistentes diabolo, sed veniet quantocyus aeternum, quo regnantes sine fine exultabimus 70 De quotidiano certamine tentationis.

Paul, the lover, says in the epistle: I beseech you, dearly beloved, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living, holy, God-pleasing sacrifice. Whoever chastens his body by the exercises of holy abstinence and brings it under the service of the spirit has consecrated a living sacrifice to the Lord. Whoever has now learned to keep his heart clean and pure from every pollution of sin has beyond doubt offered a holy sacrifice to the Lord. And whoever perseveres in the purpose of holiness to the end has without doubt offered a pleasing sacrifice.

We gird our loins when we keep ourselves pure from every form of lust, unstained in body and in mind. The virtue of holy chastity is of great merit before God, and because of the greatness of the struggle it is to be given a singular reward in the recompense of the righteous, as the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my sabbaths, and choose the things that I have willed, and hold fast my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that shall not perish.

And of these the Lord says in the holy Gospel: There are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs made by men; and there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the kingdom of heaven. He who can receive it, let him receive it.

But why did he say, He who can receive it, let him receive it? I think that this mention of eunuchs, who castrate themselves for love of the kingdom of heaven, must not be referred to the cutting off of the genital members, as many have thought and so have strayed from the truth of the Gospel, but rather to the command of the mind, by which chastity, conceived from the love of Christ, is kept whole. For those castrate themselves for the kingdom of God who, for the love of God, preserve true chastity of mind and body inviolate. And just as no one is easily castrated in body without the pain of great torment, so no one is able to attain the perfection of chastity without the greatest application of labor.

And certainly no one is chaste by his own strength; no one is modest by his own merits. It is God who gives the good will; it is he also who joins virtue to the will, so that it may have power. But because it is not for many to live unmarried, he leaves each one to his own judgment, saying: He who can receive it, let him receive it. The cutting off of members does not make the mind chaste, because the root of lust is within, and cannot be removed by the amputation of the private parts. But if the mind is chaste and whole, it will easily restrain the insolence of the members. For nothing is stronger than the mind of a man who with a pure heart sweetly loves God above all things.

Now consider, most beloved brothers, the future rewards of beauty, and the labor of chastity will not burden you. For the great rewards of exaltation are reached by the persevering effort of arduous labor. Therefore whoever shrinks from the labor of the contest will never come to the height of honor. The time is short now in which we labor, resisting the devil; but very soon the eternal time will come, in which, reigning, we shall rejoice without end.

67
cum Christo. Castigetur corpus abstinentia discreta, ne mentis imperio recalcitret; frangatur concupiscentia carnis sanctis exercitiis, ut semper obediatur consiliis rationis. Si quando lascivis mentem pulsare motibus ceperit, etiam coerceatur verberibus, quia melius est, ut livor plagarum humilitet dorsi, quam carnis petulantia animam praecepit in infernum. Dicit enim scriptura. Qui delicatae a pueritia sua nutrit servum suum, postea sentiet eum contumacem. Caro servus est mentis, quae semper imperio debet obediae rationis. Quod si caro nimis licenter nutrita fuerit, ferre spiritus imperium iam voluptatibus assueta recusabit. Servus enim Domino suo contumax efficitur, quoties delicatae ab eo per consuetudinem nutritur. Difficile autem est servum rebellem, et contumacem ad humilem obedientiam reducere, postea quam longo tempore consuevit recalcitratae. Scriptum est enim. Servus verbis non potest erudiri, quia, quod dicit, intelligit, et respondere contemnit. Propterea sapiens in ecclesiastico dicit. Cibaria, et virga, et onus asino; panis, et disciplina, et opus servoe. Operatur in disciplina, et quaerit requiescere: laxa manus illi, et quaerit libertatem. Iugum, et lorum curvant collum durum, et servum inclinant operationes assidue. Si haec scripturarum testimonia ad moralem sensum a literali mutare ceperimus, omnia, quae de servoe, et asino sunt dicta, quam recte conveniant carni pigrae, ac delicatae, inveniemus. Vere etenim caro servus est animae, quae semper contra Dominam erigitur, nisi disciplina, et opere quotidianae fatigetur. Hanc enim, qui in ocio, et voluptatibus omni tempore delicatae nutrit, contra spirituales instinctus necessario sentient contumacem, quia dum caro in superbiaem erigitur, spiritus ocio languescens, et tepidus infirmatur. Nisi ergo hunc servum tuum, videbit carnum, o frater monachae, per opus, et abstinentiam continue humilaveris, nisi motibus eius illicitis frenum continentae, ac sobrietatis imposueris, totus, illo praeceente, in praecipitium ibis. Scimus enim, sancto dicente Apostolo, quoniam caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, et nisi spiritu mortificaverimus opera carnis, in eius corruptione moriemur. Nihil amplius praecepit animam in foveam peccati, quam insolentia carnis, quae dum suo vivere arbitrio permittitur, Domino servus contumax reluctatur. Caro infelix, quae concupiscentia vanitatis praecepit animam, non tibi cedet impune, si quid te suggerente mali commiserit, quoniam Deus utranque iudicabit. Vae tibi, cum illa peccaverit, quia dum Adam de paradiso transgressor mandatorum expellitur, Eva incaetrix malorum necessario miserum comitatur. Esto consentiens spiritui caro, quia dicit Apostolus: Qui autem sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis, et concupiscentiis. Et vos, o viri fratres, qui Christi militiam profitebimini, qui in legem monasticae conversationis voluntarie iurasti, qui salvatoris imitari vestigia promisistis, attendite vocationem vestram,

with Christ. Let the body be chastened by discerning abstinence, lest it kick against the rule of the mind; let the concupiscence of the flesh be broken by holy exercises, so that it may always obey the counsels of reason. If ever it begins to assail the mind with wanton impulses, let it even be restrained with blows, because it is better that the bruise of stripes should humble the back than that the insolence of the flesh should cast the soul down into hell.

For Scripture says: He who rears his servant delicately from his youth will afterward find him rebellious. The flesh is the servant of the mind, and must always obey the command of reason. But if the flesh has been reared too indulgently, being now accustomed to pleasures, it will refuse to bear the rule of the spirit. For a servant becomes rebellious against his lord whenever he is habitually reared by him in softness. And it is difficult to bring back a rebellious and insolent servant to humble obedience after he has long been accustomed to kick against the goad. For it is written: A servant cannot be instructed by words, because he understands what is said and disdains to answer.

Therefore the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: Fodder and a rod and a burden are for an ass; bread and discipline and work are for a servant. He works under discipline and seeks to rest; slacken your hand toward him, and he seeks liberty. The yoke and the strap bend a stiff neck, and continual tasks bow down a servant. If we begin to turn these testimonies of Scripture from the literal sense to the moral sense, we shall find how rightly everything said of the servant and the ass applies to lazy and delicate flesh.

For truly the flesh is the servant of the soul, and it always rises up against its mistress unless it is wearied by daily discipline and work. He who at all times rears it delicately in idleness and pleasures will necessarily find it rebellious against spiritual promptings, because while the flesh is lifted up in pride, the spirit, languishing in idleness and lukewarm, is weakened. Therefore unless you continually humble this servant of yours, namely the flesh, O brother monk, by work and abstinence, unless you place upon its unlawful impulses the bridle of continence and sobriety, you will go wholly, with it leading, into the abyss.

For we know, as the holy Apostle says, that the flesh lusts against the spirit, and unless by the spirit we mortify the works of the flesh, we shall die in its corruption. Nothing casts the soul more deeply into the pit of sin than the insolence of the flesh, which, when it is permitted to live by its own will, struggles rebelliously, a servant against its lord. Unhappy flesh, which by the concupiscence of vanity casts down the soul: it will not go unpunished for you if, at your prompting, it commits any evil, since God will judge both. Woe to you when it has sinned, because when Adam, the transgressor of the commandments, is expelled from paradise, Eve, the instigator of evils, necessarily accompanies the wretched man.

Be consenting to the spirit, O flesh, because the Apostle says: Those who are Christ’s have crucified their flesh with its vices and concupiscences. And you, O men and brothers, who profess the warfare of Christ, who have voluntarily sworn yourselves to the law of monastic life, who have promised to imitate the footsteps of the Savior, consider your calling.

68
Homilia X. 71 ut caute ambuletis, non quasi insipientes, qui omni vento agitantur, sed tanquam veri amatores Iesu Christi, qui spiritu facta carnis mortificarunt. Vos, inquam, commilitones mei amantissimi semper in bonis operibus vigilate, mortificantes pro Christi amore corpora vestra, quae sunt super terram, in ieiuniis, et orationibus assidui, et in meditatione divinarum scripturarum iugiter occupati. Semper vos in anteriora extendite, quotdie fervorem sancti propositi novo studio reformate. Ociun, et omnem desidiam fugite, et quam breve sit huius vitae tempus, sedulo cogitate. Non vos terreat brevis, et modicus labor duri certaminis, non reddat pusillanimis improbitas hostis, quoniam labor omnis importunitate voluntaria cito vincitur, et diabolus quantumlibet saeviat, mox, ut Christum invocaveritis, superatur. Mementote verborum Domini, et salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi in sancto Evangelio dicentis. Qui vult venire post me, abneget semet ipsum, et tollat cruxem suam quotdie, et sequatur me. Crux autem nostra, fratres mei, quid est, nisi vita tentationibus, et adversitatibus plena, et onus disciplinae regularis, sub quo die fatigamur, et nocte? Sed congregemus corda nostra, fratres charissimi, et sustineamus pro Dei amore gaudenter quicquid ille nos voluerit sustinere, ut dicere in eius iudicio mereamur: Transivimus per ignem, et aquam, et induxisti nos in refrigerium. O quam gloriosa merces in regno coelorum servis Dei reponitur, qui in hoc brevi stadio certantes, nunc pro eius amore fatigantur. Oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit illius immensitas boni, quod omnipotens Deus suis amatoribus in aeterna foelicitate praeparavit sine fine perpetuo mansurum. Huius autem boni summa foelicitas humilitate acquiritur, puritate cordis, et divini fervore amoris possidetur. Illo festinemus, fratres charissimi, illo, quanta possumus devotione mentis, curramus, ubi creatori suo per fruitionem dulcedinis coniungitur spiritus, ubi in cognitione summi boni, quod est Deus, perficitur intellectus. Ibi est gaudium sempiternae foelicitatis, quod non minuitur; ibi laetitia, quae non terminatur; ibi laborum omnium perpetua requies; ibi tribulationum, et iniuriarum pro Christo gloria merces. Quicquid boni nunc agimus, ibi procul dubio inveniemus reposi- tum: quicquid pro amore Christi patienter sustinuerimus adversi, ibi recipiemus praemio copiosissimo remuneratum. O monache, monache, qui tempus infructuose expendis tibi ad bene operandum a Domino Deo misericorditer concessum, quid metes, aut quid mercedes recipies in illa terribili hora, qui nunc tam piger, et involuntarius es ad seminandum; An scriptum de sanctorum laboribus non legisti? Euntes ibant, et flebant, mittentes semina sua: Venientes autem venient cum exultatione portantes manipulos suos. Iam tempus est operandi agrum cordis tui, o monache, nunc hora seminandi bonum semen cum hilaritatis benedi- 72 De fugiendo pravorum consortio. ctione, quoniam qui parce nunc seminat, in illa quoque futurae mercedis retributione parce et metet. Laborandum nunc est, et nunquam a bono opere cessandum, quoniam quicquid iam hic operati fuerimus, ibi procul dubio recipiemus. Si quis ergo fidelis inter vos est monachus, si quis propriae salutis studiosus amator, semper horam futurae mercedis, quam nemo potest subterfugere, cogitet, semper ad reddendum villicationis suae rationem se paret. Nulla dies unquam praetereat, in qua non fecerit aliquod opus bonum singulariter, quod ad futuram retributionem praemittat. Illum se diem expendisse inutiliter existimet, in quo non praemisit bonum opus, quod remunerandum expectet. Agrum cordis sui monachus bonus omni tempore studet excolere, et omnes sentes, ac tribulos malarum affectionum paenitus, quantum praevalet, extirpare. Discat Dominum Iesum super omnia pura mente diligere, et quicquid mandavit ille, diligentissime custodire. Seminet in lachrymis devotionis, et constantiae, quod metat cum omnibus sanctis in exultatione. Non deterret mentem laborandi difficultas assidua, non frangat animum carnis decertatio dura, quoniam qui parum laborat, parum fructus in messe colligit: et qui nunc multum pro Christi amore in lachrymis seminat, fructum in illo die copiosissimum reportat. Haec enim destinatio nostri est itineris, fratres, quod in praesenti peregrinatione agimus, ut continua laborum, et adversitatum exercitatio purgati, hinc mundi, et puri ad patriam exeamus. De fugiendo pravorum consortio. Homilia XI.

Homily X

that you walk cautiously, not as fools, who are tossed about by every wind, but as true lovers of Jesus Christ, who by the Spirit have mortified the deeds of the flesh. You, I say, my most beloved fellow-soldiers, always keep watch in good works, mortifying your bodies, which are upon the earth, for love of Christ; be constant in fasts and prayers, and continually occupied in meditation on the divine Scriptures. Always stretch yourselves forward to what lies ahead; every day renew with fresh zeal the fervor of your holy purpose. Flee idleness and every sluggishness, and diligently consider how brief is the time of this life.

Let not the short and moderate toil of the hard contest terrify you; let not the wickedness of the enemy make you faint-hearted, because every labor is quickly overcome by willing perseverance, and the devil, however much he rages, is defeated as soon as you have invoked Christ. Remember the words of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who says in the holy Gospel: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. But what is our cross, my brothers, except a life full of temptations and adversities, and the burden of regular discipline, under which we are wearied day and night?

But let us gather our hearts, dearest brothers, and gladly bear for the love of God whatever he wishes us to bear, so that at his judgment we may deserve to say: We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment. O how glorious a reward is laid up in the kingdom of heaven for the servants of God, who, contending in this brief course, are now wearied for love of him. Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, the immensity of that good which almighty God has prepared in eternal happiness for those who love him, to remain without end forever.

The highest happiness of this good is acquired by humility, and possessed by purity of heart and the fervor of divine love. Let us hasten there, dearest brothers; let us run there with as much devotion of mind as we can, where the spirit is joined to its creator through the enjoyment of sweetness, where the intellect is perfected in the knowledge of the highest good, which is God. There is the joy of everlasting happiness, which is not diminished; there is gladness which has no end; there is perpetual rest from all labors; there is the glorious reward for tribulations and injuries suffered for Christ. Whatever good we now do, there without doubt we shall find laid up; whatever adversity we have patiently borne for the love of Christ, there we shall receive it rewarded with most abundant payment.

O monk, monk, you who fruitlessly spend the time mercifully granted you by the Lord God for doing good, what will you reap, or what wages will you receive in that terrible hour, you who are now so lazy and unwilling to sow? Have you not read what is written about the labors of the saints? Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves. Now is the time to work the field of your heart, O monk; now is the hour to sow good seed with the blessing of cheerfulness, because he who now sows sparingly will also reap sparingly in that future repayment of reward.

Now we must labor, and never cease from good work, because whatever we have done here now, there without doubt we shall receive. Therefore if anyone among you is a faithful monk, if anyone is a zealous lover of his own salvation, let him always think of the hour of the future reward, which no one can escape; let him always prepare himself to render an account of his stewardship. Let no day ever pass in which he has not done some particular good work, to send ahead for future repayment. Let him judge that he has spent uselessly the day on which he has not sent ahead a good work for which he may expect to be rewarded.

A good monk strives at all times to cultivate the field of his heart, and to root out completely, as far as he can, all the thorns and thistles of evil affections. Let him learn to love the Lord Jesus above all things with a pure mind, and to keep most diligently whatever he has commanded. Let him sow in the tears of devotion and constancy what he may reap with all the saints in exultation. Let not the continual difficulty of laboring frighten his mind; let not the hard struggle of the flesh break his spirit, because he who labors little gathers little fruit at harvest; and he who now sows much in tears for the love of Christ will carry back most abundant fruit on that day.

For this is the destination of our journey, brothers, which we undertake in the present pilgrimage: that, purified by continual exercise in labors and adversities, we may depart from here clean and pure to our homeland.

On fleeing the company of the wicked. Homily XI.

69
PRAVORUM consortia multos a via Domini, et salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi retraxerunt. Propterea, fratres mei amantissimi, non cessamus admonere vos, quatenus cum bonis, et sanctis in via Domini ambuletis, quorum institutione, et exemplo quotidiane meliores evadatis. Nam sicut divus ait Christi Apostolus, Menandri cuiusdam graeci senarium imitatus, corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava. Bonus esse vera- citer non desiderat, quem pravorum conversatio delectat. Nemo enim prava loquitur, nisi qui prius in corde suo contra puritatem evangelicae traditionis corruptus, et depravatus invenitur. Qualis unusquisque est, et qualia in secreto cordis sui ruminando, et cogitando peragit, talis ab eius ore sermo frequentius procedit. Cordis enim testis veracissimus est sermo loquentis, Domino, ac Salvatore nostro in sancto Evangelio dicente: Quoniam ex abundancia cordis os loquitur. Nam bonus homo de thesauro cordis sui profert bona; et malus profert similiter mala. Cum ergo bonus non sit, qui male loquitur, cavendi nobis sunt omnes, qui pravis, scurrilibus et perniciosis utuntur sermonibus, in quorum locutione turpiora quaedam frequenter resonant; sanctitatis autem verba, Homilia XI. 73 aut nunquam, aut rarissime audiuntur. Turpis sermo impudici cordis indicium est, etiam si opera non sequuntur. Vos igitur, fratres mei charissimi, qui non solum in opere castitatem, et omnimodam pudici- tiam servare usque ad mortem implicita professione simul, et expressa secundum regulam, et statuta divorum patrum ecclesiastica promisistis, verum etiam ab omni cogitatione immunda longe debetis esse alieni, consortia pravorum hominum fugite, et conventus malignantium: et, qui loquuntur iniqua, turpia, seu ociosa, omni tempore declinate. Me- mentote scripturae dicentis. Qui tetigerit picem, inquinabitur ab ea, et qui communicaverit superbo, induet superbiam. Hinc sanctus Papa Gregorius dicit. Infirmi vitare debent societatem pravorum: ne mala, quae frequentiter aspicunt, et corriger non praevalent, delectentur imi- tari. Et divus Ioannes episcopus: Bonus, inquit, malo si connectitur, aut pares redduntur, aut cito ab invicem separantur. Amicitiae enim pares aut quaerunt, aut faciunt. Rerum etenim natura sic est, ut quoties bonus malo coniungitur, non ex bono malus melioretur, sed ex malo bonus contaminetur. Diversitas enim rerum nunquam potest habere concordiam, et multos sollicitat nefanda societas. Sunt inter vos quidam, fratres, gemens dico, regularis disciplinae multum obliviosi professores, quibus cella carcer est, chorus obsidium, oratio nausea, silentium poena, scripturarum lectio fastidium. Amor Dei corda eorum aut nunquam, aut raro sursum erigit, quorum conversatio tota in inferioribus consistit. Quotiescunque me contingit esse absentem, mox inter se conveniunt, non de Christo, neque de dulcedine regni coelestis, neque de integri- tate observantiae regularis, sed longum de vanis, et inutilibus huius mundi negotiis sermonem proferunt, et de quibus monacho non licet cogitare, fabulis, regumque bellis se, colloquendo, intromittunt. Quic- quid autem his loquor, quicquid dico, quicquid iniungo poenitentiae, nihil proficit, quos mala consuetudo ab initio suae institutionis depra- vavit. Nihil autem deterius consuetudine mala; Monachus enim, qui novitius, et iuvenis negligitur, omnibus vitae sua diebus in torpore, et ignavia conversatur. Dicit nanque scriptura. Adolescens ambulans iuxta viam suam, etiam cum senuerit, non recedet ab ea. Propterea vobis dico, venerandi senes, vos precor, vos moneo, et per Dei mis- ericordiam, qua possum instantia rogo, ita iam deinceps vivite, ita con- versamini, ita ambulate, quatenus annis conveniant mores senectutis, et qui iam longe processistis in senium, exemplum sanctitatis institutioni praestetis iuniorum. Vobis procul dubio ascribitur, quicquid deesse iunio- rum moribus invenitur. Vos enim iuniores in omni sanctitate, in verbo, et in opere debetis praecedere; vos illis exemplum totius perfectionis iubemini exhibere, ut dum omnium in vobis opera virtutum perfecta conspiciunt, quasi verecundiae quodam impulsu provocari, ad imitatio- Eccles. 13. Prov. 12. Adhortatio ad senes. 74 De fugiendo pravorum consortio.

The company of the wicked has drawn many back from the way of the Lord and of our Savior Jesus Christ. Therefore, my most beloved brothers, we do not cease to admonish you to walk with the good and holy in the way of the Lord, so that by their teaching and example you may daily become better. For as the divine Apostle of Christ says, imitating the verse of a certain Greek named Menander, bad conversations corrupt good morals. He does not truly desire to be good who takes pleasure in the company of the wicked. For no one speaks wicked things unless he is first found in his heart to have been corrupted and depraved against the purity of the evangelical tradition. As each person is, and as the things are which he turns over and considers in the secrecy of his heart, so the speech that proceeds from his mouth is more often. For speech is the truest witness of the speaker’s heart, as our Lord and Savior says in the holy Gospel: “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” For a good man brings forth good things from the treasure of his heart, and an evil man likewise brings forth evil things.

Since, therefore, he who speaks evilly is not good, we must beware of all who use wicked, scurrilous, and destructive speech, in whose talk shameful things often resound, while words of holiness are either never heard or heard very rarely. Foul speech is the sign of an unchaste heart, even if deeds do not follow. Therefore, my dearest brothers, you who promised, by a profession both implicit and explicit according to the rule and the ecclesiastical statutes of the divine fathers, to preserve chastity in deed and every kind of modesty even to death, and who ought also to be far removed from every unclean thought, flee the company of wicked men and the gatherings of the malicious, and at all times avoid those who speak unjust, shameful, or idle things.

Remember the Scripture which says: “He who touches pitch will be defiled by it, and he who has fellowship with the proud will put on pride.” Hence holy Pope Gregory says: “The weak ought to avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take pleasure in imitating the evils which they often see and are unable to correct.” And the divine Bishop John says: “If a good man is joined to a bad one, either they are made alike, or they are quickly separated from one another. For friendships either seek equals or make them.” For the nature of things is such that, whenever a good man is joined to a bad one, the bad man is not made better by the good, but the good man is contaminated by the bad. For diversity of things can never have concord, and wicked company tempts many.

There are some among you, brothers, I say it with groaning, professors greatly forgetful of regular discipline, for whom the cell is a prison, the choir a siege, prayer nausea, silence a punishment, and the reading of the Scriptures a weariness. The love of God either never or rarely lifts upward the hearts of those whose whole way of life consists in lower things. Whenever I happen to be absent, they soon come together among themselves, not to speak of Christ, nor of the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, nor of the integrity of regular observance, but they bring forth a long discourse about the vain and useless affairs of this world; and by conversing they involve themselves in tales and in the wars of kings, matters about which it is not lawful for a monk to think. Whatever I say to them, whatever I declare, whatever penance I impose, it profits nothing for those whom evil custom has depraved from the beginning of their instruction.

Nothing is worse than an evil custom; for the monk who is neglected as a novice and a young man spends all the days of his life in torpor and sloth. For Scripture says: “A young man walking according to his way, even when he has grown old, will not depart from it.” Therefore I say to you, venerable elders, I beg you, I warn you, and by the mercy of God I ask you with all the urgency I can: live henceforth in such a way, conduct yourselves in such a way, walk in such a way, that the habits of old age may correspond to your years, and that you who have already advanced far into old age may provide an example of holiness for the instruction of the younger men. Without doubt, whatever is found lacking in the conduct of the younger men is ascribed to you. For you ought to go before the younger men in all holiness, in word and in deed; you are commanded to show them an example of all perfection, so that when they behold in you the perfect works of all the virtues, they may be stirred, as if by a certain impulse of shame, toward imitation [unclear].

70
nem sanctitatis vestrae concitentur. Mores etenim seniorum, iunioribus vivendi praebent exemplum, sicuti proverbio dicitur: Quod cecinere senes, hoc et iuvenes didicerunt. Vos autem iuniores reverentiam cum humilitate senioribus illorum considerando caniciem exhibete, et, quos in observantia regularis disciplinae ferventiores cognoscitis, eorum vos consortio habere praecceptores gaudeatis. Cavete illos, qui vel inquiete ambulant, vel puritatem regularis disciplinae negligentius observant. Non omnes, qui dicuntur seniores, iuniorum imitatione sunt digni: nec monachum anni faciunt venerabilem, sed mores in Dei amore cum prudentia constitunt venerandum. Propterea quicunque in vobis, fratres charissimi, verus Dei cupit esse amator, quicunque proficere in sancta conversatione monastica desiderat, quam profitetur, indisciplinatorum fratrum consortia semper fugiat, et suo proposito consentientes in bonum commilitones quaerat. Dicit nanque prophet a in psalmo. Cum sancto sanctus eris, et cum viro innocentе innocens eris, et cum electo electus eris, et cum perverso perverteris. Multis enim nocuit societas mala: et, qui delectatur habitare cum reprobis, non erit immunis a contagione peccati. Omnis quippe, qui cum malis conversatur, et reprobis, necesse est, ut eorum perversitate aliquantulum eis vitietur integritas. Aut enim diligit illos, et similis eorum efficitur malus, aut odio habebit, et erit inimicus multorum, et ob id necessario inquietus. Quod si multitudine pravorum devictus eorum delectari consortio semel ceperit, iam et ipse depravatus est, et paulatim amplius depravabitur. Si vero malorum opera detestatus fuerit, gravi mentis inconmmodo laborabit, et erit in proficiendo ad melius tanto tardius in ipso desiderium, quanto inquietatur amplius consortio perversorum. Ago tamen gratias Omnipotenti Deo pro vobis, quoniam, et si non omnes in Dei charitate, ut optarem, estis fervidi, a magnis tamen, ut confido, peccatis, et superbiae temeritate omnes procul vivitis alieni. Exhortationes meas, et paternas admonitiones, quas vobis facio, ut teneor, quotidi libenter suscipitis, quamvis illas in opere nec dum perfecte omnes exhibeatis. Spero autem in Domino Iesu, quoniam perficiet in vobis bonum, quod cepit, ut impleatur gaudium meum, et videam vos omnes uno studio, uno proposito, uno sancti fervoris incendio flagrantès in ergasterio delectari, et exerceri divini amoris. Cum autem hoc desiderium meum non nulli vestrum differant, animum plenioris emendationis necdum assumentes, quem cupio, iusta necessitate compellor admonere proficientes, quatenus consurgentes animo virili, sociates privatas, et nocentes fugiant tepidorum. Adhuc enim parvus in eorum cordibus est ignis divini amoris, adhuc novitium, et debile sancti fervoris ardet in cendium, et nisi quotidianis fomentetur augmentis, facile sentiet detrimentum. Idcirco iterum, atque iterum admoneo vos, qui amoris interni

[unclear] may be stirred by your holiness. For the morals of elders furnish the younger with an example of living, as the proverb says: What the old have sung, the young too have learned. But you who are younger, considering their gray hair, show reverence with humility to your elders; and rejoice to have as your instructors those whose company you know to be more fervent in the observance of regular discipline. Beware of those who either walk restlessly or observe the purity of regular discipline too negligently.

Not all who are called elders are worthy of imitation by the young; nor do years make a monk venerable, but morals grounded in the love of God with prudence make him worthy of reverence. Therefore whoever among you, dearest brothers, desires to be a true lover of God, whoever desires to advance in the holy monastic way of life that he professes, let him always flee the company of undisciplined brothers, and seek good fellow-soldiers who agree with his purpose. For the prophet says in the Psalm: With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverted.

For evil company has harmed many; and he who delights to dwell with the reprobate will not be free from the contagion of sin. Indeed, everyone who keeps company with the wicked and the reprobate must have the integrity of his life somewhat corrupted by their perversity. For either he loves them and becomes evil like them, or he will hate them and be the enemy of many, and for that reason necessarily restless. But if, overcome by the multitude of the wicked, he once begins to delight in their company, then he too has already been depraved, and little by little he will be depraved still more. But if he detests the works of the wicked, he will labor under a grave trouble of mind, and his desire will be so much slower in advancing toward the better, the more he is disturbed by the company of the perverse.

Yet I give thanks to Almighty God for you, because, even if not all of you are fervent in the love of God as I would wish, nevertheless, as I trust, you all live far removed and estranged from great sins and from the rashness of pride. My exhortations and fatherly admonitions, which I give you as I am bound to do, you willingly receive every day, although you do not yet all display them perfectly in deed. But I hope in the Lord Jesus that he will bring to perfection in you the good that he has begun, so that my joy may be fulfilled and I may see you all, with one zeal, one purpose, one blaze of holy fervor, delighting and exercising yourselves in the workshop of divine love.

But since some of you delay this desire of mine, not yet taking up the spirit of fuller amendment that I desire, I am compelled by just necessity to admonish those who are making progress, that, rising up with a manly spirit, they flee the private and harmful associations of the lukewarm. For the fire of divine love is still small in their hearts; the flame of holy fervor that burns in them is still new and weak, and unless it is fostered by daily increases, it will easily suffer loss. Therefore again and again I admonish you who [unclear] of inward love.

71
Homilia XI. 75 cepistis experiri fervorem, pergite constanter animo, quo Domino inspirante destinastis, et, si quos in hoc itinere sancto vobis opere, vel sermone inveneritis contrarios, ut pestiferum virus declinate. Nam sicuti aqua extinguit ignem, cui infunditur, sic novitiorum sanctum propositum exemplis tepidorum violatur. Cavete illorum interesse colloquis, quos in observantia mandatorum Dei, et monasticae puritatis conspicitis negligentes; quia cum sint passionibus agitati carnalibus, ex abundantia cordis nihil aliud, quam vana, et carnalia loquuntur. Corruptunt enim mores iuvenum bonos senum colloquia prava. Vana sunt cuncta illorum studia, et inutiles, immo pestiferi sermones, qui carnaliter divini amoris exercitia non noverunt. Enimvero sic ut una ovis morbida paulatim universum corruptit ovile, ita unus in congregatione monachus acidiosus, et perversus, multarum saepe fit causa transgressionum. Quemadmodum, sancto Christophilo testante, modicum fermentum totam farinae massam, cui miscetur, suo corruptit odorem, ita monachi iuvenes, atque novitii, qui cum tepidis, et acidiosis conversantur senioribus, illorum pravis moribus imbuuntur, et nunquam deincepts ad sancti fervoris integritatem reformantur. Quocirca vobis seni-ribus dico: Estote bonis operibus, castisque, et semper pudicis sermonibus iuvenum forma vivendi, ut quoties pro suis emendantur delictis, seniorum se non tueantur exemplis. Turpissimum est enim seniores in illis esse culpabiles, pro quibus merito corripiuntur iuniores. Ita, precor, senes vivite, ut coram vobis nihil, quod videatur esse reprehensibile, iuniores aut loqui praesumant, aut facere. Iudices vos timeant malorum, non patronatus vicem agentes; quoniam quotquot exemplo vestri pec- caverint, vestro periisse magisterio reputantur. Non sit inter vos tepidus quisquam, aut desidiosus, quoniam, et desideria occidunt pigrum, et perimit vanitas omnem monachum oculosum. Non sit in vobis homo verbosus, girovagus, circumcellio, murmurans, et inquietus, quoniam quisquis talibus delectatur studiis, et se malo perdit opere, et fratem suum occidit exemplis. Non sit inter vos irrisor simplicium, non humilium contemptor, aut temerarius quisquam taxator; quoniam, qui ad ridendum est promptulus, in stultitia sua consumabitur, et non erit gloriosus. Os suum aperit contra humilem, semper querit iurgia, et gaudet se factis aliorum esse loquacem. Non prosperabitur in consilio suo, et si fuerit aliquo sublimatus honore, cito corruet in profundum. Odibilis est Deo superbia eius, quoniam, cum sit stultus, et fatus, eruditum se gloriatur, et sapientem. Cito denudabitur insipientia eius, et gravis eum occupabit interitus. Cor eius meditabitur stultitiam, et non est pax in circuitu eius. Odio erit proximis, atque vicinis, et nullus illum fidelis prosequetur amicus. Vitam ducit in hypocrisi assumptae simulationis, et multos sua stultitia trahet in aversionem. Pacem odit,

you have begun to experience fervor, go on steadfastly in the spirit to which, by the Lord’s inspiration, you have set yourselves; and if in this holy journey you find any men opposed to you in deed or in word, shun them as deadly poison. For just as water extinguishes the fire into which it is poured, so the holy purpose of novices is damaged by the examples of the lukewarm. Beware of taking part in the conversations of those whom you see to be negligent in the observance of God’s commandments and of monastic purity; for since they are driven by carnal passions, out of the abundance of the heart they speak nothing but vain and carnal things. For the evil conversations of old men corrupt the good morals of the young. Vain are all their pursuits, and useless, indeed poisonous, are the words of those who, being carnal, do not know the exercises of divine love.

Indeed, just as one diseased sheep gradually corrupts the whole sheepfold, so one slothful and perverse monk in a congregation is often the cause of many transgressions. As Saint Christophilus testifies, a little leaven corrupts with its odor the whole mass of flour with which it is mixed; so young monks and novices who associate with lukewarm and acedia-ridden elders are imbued with their depraved habits, and thereafter are never restored to the integrity of holy fervor.

Therefore I say to you elders: be, by good works and by chaste and always modest speech, a model of life for the young, so that whenever they are corrected for their faults, they may not defend themselves by the examples of their elders. For it is most shameful that elders should be guilty in those matters for which juniors are deservedly rebuked. Live, I pray, you old men, in such a way that in your presence the younger men presume neither to say nor to do anything that seems blameworthy. Let them fear you as judges of evils, not as men acting the part of patrons; since all who have sinned by your example are reckoned to have perished through your instruction.

Let there be among you no one lukewarm or idle, for desires kill the lazy man, and vanity destroys every wandering-eyed monk. Let there be among you no talkative man, no roving monk, no gadabout, no murmurer and restless man, because whoever delights in such pursuits both ruins himself by evil conduct and kills his brother by his examples. Let there be among you no mocker of the simple, no despiser of the humble, no rash critic; for he who is quick to laugh will be consumed in his own folly and will not be glorious. He opens his mouth against the humble, always seeks quarrels, and rejoices that he is talkative about the deeds of others. He will not prosper in his counsel, and if he has been raised to some honor, he will quickly fall into the depths. His pride is hateful to God, because, though he is foolish and stupid, he boasts that he is learned and wise. His foolishness will soon be laid bare, and a grievous destruction will seize him. His heart will meditate folly, and there is no peace around him. He will be hated by those near him and by his neighbors, and no faithful friend will attend him. He leads his life in the hypocrisy of an assumed pretense, and by his folly he will draw many into estrangement. He hates peace,

72
76 De fugiendo pravorum consortio. discordiam diligit, in ignavia mentis sua capietur, et non erit, qui condoleat. Afflictione duplici conteretur pro eo, quod habentibus pacem non permisit. Diabolus in lingua eius nidum composuit, et satanas in mente illius fixit domicilium. Propterea non est amor fratum in corde ipsius, quoniam disseminat inter pastorem, et oves discordiam. Amicum se Dei gloriatur, et similem in observantia regulari neminem accipit, sed maximum ornamentum monachi humilitatem non intelligit. Os suum ad verba spiritualis aedificationis non aperit, et ex corde illius nihil aliud, quam vanitas, procedit. Diem totam mente dissolutus, et corpore vagus discurrit in coenobio, sermoni vacat inutili, et paenitus ocioso, nihil de salute animae cogitat, ventrem pro Deo curat. Custodi mentem tuam ab eius eloquio, et in viam sermonum eius pedem tuum ne posueris. Quisquis te monachum, et Dei ministrum exhibere desideras, quisquis Dominum Iesum in toto corde veraciter amas, esto cautus, et vigilans in omnibus operibus tuis, et consortia semper eorum fugito, in quorum vita nihil doctrinae coelestis conspicitur. Humilium, et perfectionem sectantium monachorum comes esto, et socius; et eum, quem in Dei timore cognoveris esse fundatum, libenter admitte praceptorem, atque magistrum. Cum his, qui amant disciplinam, et mentis puritatem, libenter ambula, et noli esse quasi homo, qui omni vento cedit agitatus, sed confirma in bono proposito animam tuam, ne pravorum decipiaris consilio. Optimum est enim gratia stabilire cor, et nec posse decipi, nec velle decipiere. Fratrem disciplinatum habeas tibi amicum, et eum, qui te verbo corrigit a malo, et exemplo instruit ad bonum, ama, et venerare ut patrem. Cum fratre inquieto non habeas aliquod familiaritatis commercium, ne quando eius confortatus pravo exemplo in rebellionem incidas superborum. Monachus iracundus, et murmuratione plenus non sit in latere tuo: et eum, qui maioribus recalcitat, nunquam arbitris amicum. Quem videris sine benedictione senioris canonem violare ieiunii, ut hostem fuge salutis: et, qui loquacitate velox est, non existente causa, subvertit pacem, et suscitat lites. Quasi a facie colubri fuge monachum rebellem, et inobedientem senioribus: quoniam veneno malitiae plenus aestuat, et in elatione mentis perdidit animam suam. Qui non obedit mandato senioris; perversus est: et, qui corruptus non humiliatur, apostata est. Qui fratri suo detrahens obloquitur, non sit in colloquio tuo, quoniam longe est fure deterior. Quem omni studio in observantia regulari videris sollicitum, ut patrem amabis, et veneraberis ut amantissimum praceptorem. Eius familiaritate confidenter utaris, cuius amicitia semper in Dei amore te faciat meliorem. Viros toto studio imitare bonos, et illorum sequere mores, qui vivunt monasticae perfectioni conformes. Fratrem bonae voluntatis habe amicum: ab eo autem, qui duri cordis est, averte aures

He loves discord; he will be caught in the sloth of his own mind, and there will be no one to grieve with him. He will be crushed by a double affliction, because he did not allow peace to those who possessed it. The devil has made a nest in his tongue, and Satan has fixed his dwelling in his mind. Therefore there is no love of the brethren in his heart, because he sows discord between the shepherd and the sheep. He boasts that he is a friend of God and accepts no one as his equal in regular observance, yet he does not understand humility, the greatest ornament of a monk. He does not open his mouth for words of spiritual edification, and from his heart nothing proceeds except vanity. All day long, dissolved in mind and wandering in body, he runs about the monastery, gives himself to useless and entirely idle talk, thinks nothing of the salvation of his soul, and cares for his belly as his god.

Guard your mind from his speech, and do not set your foot on the path of his words. Whoever you are who desire to show yourself a monk and minister of God, whoever you are who truly love the Lord Jesus with your whole heart, be cautious and watchful in all your works, and always flee the company of those in whose life no heavenly teaching is seen. Be the companion and associate of humble monks who pursue perfection; and the one whom you have known to be grounded in the fear of God, gladly accept as instructor and master. Walk gladly with those who love discipline and purity of mind, and do not be like a man who, shaken, yields to every wind, but strengthen your soul in a good purpose, lest you be deceived by the counsel of the wicked. For it is best for the heart to be strengthened by grace, and neither to be able to be deceived nor to wish to deceive.

Have as your friend a disciplined brother; and love and venerate as a father the one who corrects you from evil by word and instructs you toward good by example. Have no familiar dealings with a restless brother, lest, strengthened by his wicked example, you ever fall into the rebellion of the proud. Let no monk who is angry and full of murmuring be at your side; and never consider as a friend the one who kicks against his superiors. When you see someone violating the rule of fasting without the blessing of an elder, flee him as an enemy of salvation; and one who is quick to chatter, when there is no cause, overturns peace and stirs up quarrels.

Flee a rebellious monk, disobedient to elders, as from the face of a serpent, because he burns full of the poison of malice, and in the pride of his mind he has lost his soul. He who does not obey the command of an elder is perverse; and he who, being corrupt, is not humbled, is an apostate. Let one who disparages his brother with slander not be in conversation with you, because he is far worse than a thief. The one whom you see wholly zealous in regular observance you shall love as a father and venerate as a most loving instructor. Confidently enjoy the familiarity of the one whose friendship always makes you better in the love of God. Imitate good men with all zeal, and follow the conduct of those who live in conformity with monastic perfection. Have as a friend a brother of good will; but from the one who is hard of heart, turn away your ears.

73
Homilia XI. 77 tuas. Qui levis est animo, et moribus dissolutus, sit tibi quasi homo, qui sepes in agro dissipat. Noli socius esse illius, qui regulam, et si- lentium contemnit, qui loca non discernit, nec tempora, qui sine be- nedictione prioris ubique verba multiplicat: Monachum vino, et po- tationibus communem monasterii canonem crebrius excedentem, ut fomentum luxuriae, et scaturigenem devita omnium vitiorum. Monachus, qui consilio capitis sui contra senioris mandatum innititur, perditioni est proximus, et festinus anhelat in periculum animae suae. Ne com- municaveris operibus monachii pertinacis, et ne habeas illius amicitiam, qui sua temeritate maiorum factis cachinnans obloquitur. In medio di- sciplinatorum esto continuus, et libenter cum humilibus ambulet anima tua. Qui enim viris coniungitur bonis, virtutem illorum participat: et, qui cum malis graditur, cadet in foveam. Monachus autem perversae voluntatis seducit plurimos, et, qui contemnit obedientiam, nunquam exaltabitur. Qui vocem loquens extollit, et clamat in altum vociferans, stultitiam cordis sui non potest abscondere, et in vanitate sua gloria- bitur. Amicitia bonorum virorum firma salus est animae, et in societate pravorum, simplicium innocentia corrumpitur. Societas illorum est optima, quorum Dei timor confirmavit bonorum operum exempla. Nihil preciosius amico timente Deum; et nihil periculosius socio, qui pravae est voluntatis. Frater timens Deum in toto corde suo, pro muro for- titudinis erit amico suo: et, qui tali cum sanitate mentis coniungiur, benedictione Dei spiritus omni tempore sanctificatur. Qui in medio timentium Deum graditur, quasi muro in circuitu fortissimo, ne defi- ciat, sustentatur. Ex verbis suis cognoscitur servus altissimi, et mona- chum bonum opera indicant sanctitatis. Omne verbum turpe, scurrile, et ociosum ab ore timentis Dominum non egreditur: et, qui verus amator est Iesu nihil, quod offendat bonitatem, operatur. In ore monachi Deum amantis semper Christus resonat: et, qui verus est Dei cultor; sermonem iustitiae in ore simul, et in opere demonstrat. Qui timet Deum, consiliarius est optimus: et, qui ad canonem ambulat, iudex est prudens cogitationum. Senior timens Deum, et in observantia re- gulari multo tempore probatus, et expertus, director est iuvenum: et, qui non habet in veste maculam, bonus institutor sit novitiorum. Qui divinarum est intelligens doctor, et explanator scripturarum custodiens in humilitate animam suam, omnia verba oris eius, tanquam sint aurea, libenter excipe, quoniam nervos habent, et soliditatem futurae foeliciti- tatis aeternae. Qui vere doctus est, infirmanti compatitur, et, qui Iesum diligit, fluctuantem animo ad fortitudinem cohortatur. Qui cum homine verboso graditur, non evadet contentionem: et, qui delectatur mendacio, nunquam erit sapientiae amicus. Qui assiduus est in externis, non erit proficiens, et sine causa gloriatur se monachum. Cito propositum san- 78 De fugiendo pravorum consortio.

Homily XI.

your [unclear]. One who is fickle in mind and dissolute in conduct should be to you like a man who tears down hedges in a field. Do not be the companion of one who despises the rule and silence, who does not distinguish places or times, who without the prior’s blessing multiplies words everywhere. Avoid the monk who often exceeds the common canon of the monastery in wine and drinking, as fuel for lust and a spring of all vices.

A monk who relies on the counsel of his own head against the command of an elder is near to destruction and hastens breathlessly into danger for his soul. Do not share in the works of an obstinate monk, and do not have friendship with one who, in his own rashness, laughingly speaks against the deeds of his superiors. Be continually in the midst of disciplined men, and let your soul gladly walk with the humble. For he who is joined to good men shares in their virtue; and he who walks with the wicked will fall into the pit.

A monk of perverse will leads very many astray, and he who despises obedience will never be exalted. He who raises his voice when speaking and cries out with loud shouting cannot hide the folly of his heart, and he will glory in his vanity. The friendship of good men is the firm salvation of the soul, and in the company of the wicked the innocence of the simple is corrupted. The company of those is best whose fear of God has confirmed examples of good works. Nothing is more precious than a friend who fears God, and nothing more dangerous than a companion who is of perverse will.

A brother who fears God with his whole heart will be like a wall of strength for his friend; and he who is joined to such a man in soundness of mind is sanctified at all times by the blessing of the Spirit of God. He who walks in the midst of those who fear God is upheld, lest he fail, as though by a very strong wall round about. From his words the servant of the Most High is known, and works of holiness reveal a good monk. No foul, buffoonish, or idle word comes from the mouth of one who fears the Lord; and he who is a true lover of Jesus does nothing that offends goodness.

In the mouth of a monk who loves God, Christ always resounds; and he who is a true worshiper of God shows the speech of righteousness both in his mouth and in his work. He who fears God is the best counselor; and he who walks according to the canon is a prudent judge of thoughts. An elder who fears God, and who has been tested and proved for a long time in regular observance, is a guide of the young; and he who has no stain on his garment should be a good instructor of novices.

Receive gladly all the words of the mouth of one who is an understanding teacher of divine things and an interpreter of the Scriptures, keeping his soul in humility, as though they were golden, because they have the sinews and solidity of future eternal happiness. He who is truly learned has compassion on the weak, and he who loves Jesus exhorts the wavering in mind to strength. He who walks with a talkative man will not escape contention; and he who delights in falsehood will never be a friend of wisdom. He who is constantly occupied with outward things will not make progress, and boasts without cause that he is a monk. The holy purpose [unclear] quickly.

On fleeing the company of the wicked.

74
ctitatis corrumpitur, quando monachus extra cellam cum desiderio fre- quentius evagatur. Qui secretum cellae suae sine mandato senioris deserit, ad perfectionem sancti propositi non contendit. Bonorum vi- rorum, ac Deum timentium pulchra societas: et, qui consuevit habitare cum eis, non sentiet confusionem. Tabula munda est cor monachi juvenis, in qua seniorum conversatio nunquam delenda inscribitur. Cordis pulchri scriptor est pessimus senior, qui turpia coram iuvene vel agit, vel loquitur. Qui sermone temerario mentes iuvenum inficit, quasi Herodes impius, qui pueros interfecit. Malum, quod iuvenis a sene stulto, et negligentie recipit, etiam presbyter factus non emendabit. Omne vas, quod impletur aceto, corrumpitur: et monachus, qui in novitiatu negligitur, cum senuerit, non emendatur. Maledictus senex, cuius mala conversatione pereunt iuvenes, quoniam, qui sequentibus relinquit mala vestigia, quasi qui caecum sua manu praecipitavit in foveam. Apud internum iudicem tot quisque mortibus dignus est, quot innocentes pravo exemplo eius perierunt. Senem vitae moderatorem tuae requirito iuvenis: non qui multos complevit annos in sua conver- satione dissoluta, et tepida, sed quem timor Domini, et scripturarum Dei scientia commendat. Melior est societas monachi adolescentis, qui timet Dominum, quam senis doctoris contubernium, cuius vita non habet lumen amoris divini, et regularis observantiae integritatem. Senex moribus incompositus, indigens munditia mentis, et carens disciplina, quasi qui laesus in tibia claudus ducitur ad sepulcrum. Monachus senex, et dissolutus similis est homini fatuo, qui, nesciens finem, cum latro- nibus in convivio potantium capitur. Senior sine maturitate, quasi fistula sambuci contrita pedibus ludentium. Vane gloriatur se multis diebus exititisse monachum, qui conversationis internae non percepit initium. Qui cordis sui munditiam diligit, a consortio indisciplinatorum fratrum se omni tempore custodit. Sicut adhaerens vestibus saltantium macula picis contristat virgines, ita, qui bonus est iuvenis, ad turpia verba seniorum erubescit. Lascivus sermo non est hominis Deum timentis, quoniam ex abundantia cordis os loquitur: et qui turpia profert eloquia, non est mundus coram altissimo. Si odire te coeperint peccatores, pro- pter timorem Dei, non contristeris, quia nisi malis displaceas, bonorum perfectionem non apprehendes. Malis enim displaceere propter iustitiam laudabile est, et divini amoris manifestum indicium. Si diligis animam tuam, fuge consilia indisciplinatorum, et cum derisoribus ne commu- nicaveris. Cum bonis ambula, et qui timet Dominum, fiat consilia- rius tuus.

Chastity is corrupted when a monk too often wanders outside his cell with desire. He who leaves the privacy of his cell without the elder’s order does not strive toward the perfection of his holy purpose. Beautiful is the fellowship of good men who fear God; and he who has become accustomed to dwell with them will not feel confusion. The heart of a young monk is a clean tablet, on which the conduct of elders is written, never to be erased.

A very bad elder is a writer on a fair heart when he either does or says shameful things before a young man. He who infects the minds of the young with rash speech is like wicked Herod, who killed the children. The harm that a young man receives from a foolish and negligent old man he will not amend even when he has become a priest. Every vessel that is filled with vinegar is spoiled; and a monk who is neglected in his novitiate is not amended when he has grown old.

Cursed is the old man by whose evil conduct the young perish, since he who leaves evil footsteps for those who follow is like one who has cast a blind man with his own hand into a pit. Before the inward Judge each person is worthy of as many deaths as the innocent who have perished by his depraved example. Young man, seek an old man to be the guide of your life: not one who has completed many years in his lax and lukewarm way of life, but one whom the fear of the Lord and knowledge of God’s Scriptures commend.

Better is the fellowship of a young monk who fears the Lord than the company of an old teacher whose life lacks the light of divine love and the integrity of regular observance. An old man disordered in morals, lacking cleanness of mind and without discipline, is like one injured in the leg, led lame to the grave. An old and lax monk is like a foolish man who, not knowing the end, is caught with robbers at a drinking banquet. An elder without maturity is like an elderwood pipe crushed under the feet of those playing. Vainly does he boast that he has been a monk for many days, if he has not perceived the beginning of inward conversion.

He who loves the cleanness of his heart guards himself at all times from the company of undisciplined brothers. As a pitch stain clinging to the garments of dancers saddens virgins, so a good young man blushes at the shameful words of elders. Wanton speech does not belong to a man who fears God, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; and he who utters shameful words is not clean before the Most High.

If sinners begin to hate you because of the fear of God, do not be saddened, because unless you displease the evil, you will not attain the perfection of the good. For to displease the evil for righteousness’ sake is praiseworthy, and a clear sign of divine love. If you love your soul, flee the counsels of the undisciplined, and do not associate with scoffers. Walk with the good, and let one who fears the Lord become your counselor.

75
Homilia XII. 79 De monachis in viam directis. Homilia XII. Monachorum est mundum fugere, et hominum turbas, amore solitudinis, quantum praevalent, omni tempore declinare. A solitudine monachus dicitur, sicut ab unitate unus nominatur. Monachus esse non potest, qui frequentiam sectatur populum: et, qui delectatur in urbis, monasticam necdum gustavit dulcedinem. Qui monachus es, coenobii solitudinem sine causa rationabili non debes deserere: et qui obligaris ad silentium, noli colloquiiis oblectari mundanorum. Quisquis amat vagos in urbe discursus, conscientiam suam deseruit: et qui frequens est extra monasterium suum, puritatem interni profectus non custodit. Qui domos parentum circum, et epulis delectatur proximorum, se non considerat monachum: et qui pergit ad convivia potantium, interficit animam suam. Qui dormit in domo cognati sui, quaerit solatia: et qui declinat religiosorum conventus, perniciosam sequitur libertatem. Monachus in domo patris, et matris quasi agnus in medio luporum, et quasi lepus, qui venatorum circumdatus est canibus. Si monachus es, si Dei servus, et miles, quid facis in domo parentum? aut quid requiris in medio populum? Monachus extra coenobium diu manens in medio secularium, quasi homo, qui sub aquarum profundo sepelivit unigenitum suum. Nam sicuti piscibus non est vita in arido, ita monachis non est salus animae in saeculo. Extra flumen piscis moritur, et monachi conscientiae puritas cito extra monasterium violatur. Monachorum vita in coenobio, et mors animorum in medio negotiorum secularium. Magna virtus animi est turbas hominum fugere, aut quibus interesse fuerit omni necessarium, mente tamen declinare. Compellimur necessitate iter nonnunquam per mundum agere, sed tanto minus ex hominum occursu puritas conscientiae polluitur, quanto mentis desiderium a cellae secreto minus elongatur. Monendus igitur nobis est monachus quisque bonus, ut, quoties pro cuiusque rei necessitate praecepto senioris in viam dirigitur, nunquam foris animo evagetur. Qui sensus suos non custodit, obiecto malo cito corruptitur: et qui timorem Domini abiicit, ad monasterium impurus necessario revertetur. Cum affuit Rhenus, limositate sua pulchritudinem patentium in circuitu pratorum commaculat: et dum fabulis secularium intendit monachus, puritatem conscientiae deturbat. Antequam ergo de monasterio ponas pedem tuum, sanctis te orationibus munias; et priusquam egrediaris, viam Domino precibus commendare non omittas. Deinde, quod legislator mandavit, exequere, et orationibus tam abbatis, quam fratrum omnium tuendum te committe. Canonem severitatis observantiae regularis tibimetipsi praescribito, sub cuius memoria stabili ab omni animum defluxu occurren- 80 De monachis in viam directis.

Homily XII.

On monks sent out on the road. Homily XII.

It belongs to monks to flee the world and the crowds of men, and, out of love for solitude, to avoid them at all times as far as they are able. A monk is so called from solitude, just as one is named from unity. He cannot be a monk who follows after throngs of people; and he who takes delight in cities has not yet tasted monastic sweetness. If you are a monk, you ought not to leave the solitude of the monastery without reasonable cause; and if you are bound to silence, do not take pleasure in the conversations of worldly people.

Whoever loves wandering about in the city has abandoned his conscience; and he who is often outside his monastery does not preserve the purity of inward progress. He who delights in going around the homes of his relatives and in the banquets of his neighbors does not regard himself as a monk; and he who goes to the feasts of drinkers kills his own soul. He who sleeps in the house of his kinsman is seeking comforts; and he who avoids the assemblies of the religious follows a destructive freedom.

A monk in the house of his father and mother is like a lamb in the midst of wolves, and like a hare surrounded by hunters’ dogs. If you are a monk, if you are God’s servant and soldier, what are you doing in your parents’ house? Or what are you seeking in the midst of the people? A monk who remains long outside the monastery among secular people is like a man who has buried his only-begotten son beneath deep waters. For just as fish have no life on dry land, so monks have no salvation of soul in the world. Outside the river a fish dies, and the purity of a monk’s conscience is quickly violated outside the monastery.

The life of monks is in the monastery, and the death of souls is in the midst of secular business. It is a great virtue of the soul to flee the crowds of men, or, if it is wholly necessary to be among them, nevertheless to withdraw from them in mind. We are sometimes compelled by necessity to make a journey through the world; but the purity of conscience is polluted so much less by encounters with men, the less the desire of the mind is drawn away from the secrecy of the cell.

Therefore every good monk must be admonished by us that, whenever by command of his superior he is sent on the road for the necessity of some matter, he should never wander outward in spirit. He who does not guard his senses is quickly corrupted when evil is set before him; and he who casts away the fear of the Lord will necessarily return impure to the monastery. When the Rhine overflows, by its muddy waters it stains the beauty of the meadows lying open all around; and when a monk gives his attention to the tales of worldly people, he disturbs the purity of his conscience.

Before, then, you set your foot out of the monastery, arm yourself with holy prayers; and before you go forth, do not fail to commend your way to the Lord with prayers. Then carry out what the lawgiver commanded, and entrust yourself to be protected by the prayers both of the abbot and of all the brothers. Prescribe for yourself a rule of severity in regular observance, under the steady remembrance of which you may meet every flowing-away of the mind [unclear].

76
tium custodias vanitatum. De coenobio nusquam progrediaris sine benedictione abbatis, quia, cum debes esse mortuus, atque sepultus huic seculo, non licebit tibi quicquam ulterioris absque senioris imperio. Militem te Regis Iesu Christi agnoscito, tuum imperatorem sequaris opertet, sine quo non est salus. Ille cruci affixus, non suis, sed aliorum manibus deponitur: et tu si cupis salvari, necesse est, tua voluntas abbatis imperio gubernetur. Monachus enim, qui coenobium sine permissione abbatis quoquam egressitur, quasi ovicula in tenebris, qua domus incendio concrematur. Verus autem Christi monachus etiam extra coenobium existens corpore, in claustro mente remanet, et non minus est solus cum multis, quam in cella consuevit esse solitarius. Amator Christi etiam in medio multitudinis Iesum cogitat: et, qui verus est operator virtutum, in omni loco cor suum in Dei timore solidum conservat. Nam et si corpore non sit in monasterio, corde tamen propter vigorem animi semper consistit stabilis, quasi solus in claustro. Corporis motu spiritus non pollutur, quando mentis solitudo custoditur. Eadem tibi sanctitate vivendum est in itinere, o monache, qua conversari iuberis in coenobio, et maiore quadam gradiendum cautela, ne quempiam remissiore scandalizes exemplo, ubi tot monachorum sunt iudices, quot inspectores adesse videntur. Omnium oculi secularium in monachos suspiciunt, et sanctitatem, quam illos audiunt professos, in operibus exquirunt. Plus offendit monachus in uno temerario verbo, quam homo seculo deditus in decem millibus. Quantumlibet enim levis, et scurrilis homo videatur mundanus, monachorum tamem insolentiam aequanimiter tolerare non didicit, quoniam omnes claustrales non quales sunt, sed quales esse debent, rustica simplicitate credit. Unde malum verbum, aut factum apud illos monacho damnationem ascribitur, quod mundano homini ad veniam imputatur. Nec immerito. Monachus enim, qui sanctum, et approbatum canonem professus est, omnem conatum suum tenet ad perfectionem dirigere, et conversationem hominum secularum verbo, et opere in omni puritate mentis, et corporis longe superare. Verbum etenim levis, seu oiciosum, quod secularibus ad veniam conceditur, claustralibus ad interitum aestimatur. Omnibus metallis aurum praeciosius est, et amplius a mortalibus concupiscitur, et in nullo citius macula, vel corruptio falsitatis accusatur. Et vitium, quod in auro iudiciaire severitate discernitur, in caeteris metallis pro vilitate naturae dissimulatur. Aurum sua pulcritudine laetificat oculos, et confortat in virtute sua praecordia vitae. Aurum conflatum in igne non minuitur: et verus Dei monachus in tribulatione persecutionis a sanctitatis proposito non mutatur. Parva in aureo vase macula multum in conspectu potentis disiplcit: si curvum sit fictile, nemo detestatur. Monacho delinquenti in modicis, clamor multorum contra illum ingens

[unclear] watches of vanities. Do not leave the monastery anywhere without the abbot’s blessing, because, since you ought to be dead and buried to this world, nothing further will be lawful for you without the command of your superior. Know yourself a soldier of King Jesus Christ; you must follow your commander, without whom there is no salvation. He, fastened to the cross, is taken down not by his own hands but by the hands of others; and you, if you desire to be saved, must have your will governed by the abbot’s command.

For a monk who goes out anywhere from the monastery without the abbot’s permission is like a little sheep in the darkness, when the house is consumed by fire. But the true monk of Christ, even when he is outside the monastery in body, remains in the cloister in mind; and he is no less alone among many than he is accustomed to be solitary in his cell. The lover of Christ thinks of Jesus even in the midst of a crowd; and he who is a true worker of virtues keeps his heart firm in the fear of God in every place. For even if he is not in the monastery in body, yet in heart, because of the vigor of his spirit, he always stands firm, as though alone in the cloister. The spirit is not polluted by the movement of the body when the solitude of the mind is preserved.

You must live with the same holiness on the road, O monk, with which you are commanded to conduct yourself in the monastery, and you must walk with a certain greater caution, lest you scandalize anyone by a more lax example, where there seem to be as many judges of monks as there are observers present. The eyes of all secular people look up to monks, and they seek in their works the holiness which they hear them profess. A monk gives more offense by one reckless word than a man given to the world does by ten thousand. For however frivolous and buffoonish a worldly man may seem, still he has not learned to tolerate calmly the insolence of monks, because with rustic simplicity he believes all cloistered men to be not what they are, but what they ought to be. Hence an evil word or deed is ascribed by them to a monk as condemnation, while in a worldly man it is counted as pardonable.

And not without reason. For the monk who has professed the holy and approved rule must hold all his effort directed toward perfection, and must far surpass the conduct of secular men, in word and deed, in all purity of mind and body. For a light or idle word, which is granted pardon among secular people, is judged ruinous among cloistered men.

Gold is more precious than all metals, and is more desired by mortals, and in nothing is a stain or corruption of falseness more quickly charged. And the defect which is discerned in gold with judicial severity is overlooked in the other metals because of the baseness of their nature. Gold gladdens the eyes by its beauty, and strengthens the inner parts of life by its virtue. Gold melted in the fire is not diminished; and the true monk of God is not changed from his purpose of holiness in the tribulation of persecution. A small stain on a golden vessel greatly displeases in the sight of a powerful man; if an earthen vessel is crooked, no one detests it. Against a monk who sins in small matters, the great outcry of many against him is immense.

77
Homilia XII. 81 oritur, quoniam auro conversatio eius comparatur. Aureum est speculum, canonica ita monachorum. Aurum in medio luti nullam naturae suae maculam recipit, sed omnem pulchritudinem suam inviolabilem custodit. Monachus quoque verus Christi amator, qualis in secreto cellulae suae conversari didicit, talis etiam directus in viam cum hominibus consistit, quia purus tam mente, quam corpore coram Domino incedit. Nam, si verus est monachus, pulvere alienae conversationis non pulluitur, nec a rectitudine sancti propositi, cuiusquam vel praesentia, vel colloquio mutatur. Inter mundanorum tumultuarias fabulationes aliunde cogitat; et aliorum dissoluta conversatio eius mentem non oblectat. Qui secum est corde, etiam in medio tumultuantium non dividitur. Idcirco monache, qui cupis esse bonus, mentem ad te tuam collige, et priusquam egrediaris cellam, ad iter cor tuum dispone. Timor Domini semper tui sit comes itineris, et custodia monasticae disciplinae nunquam discedat de latere tuo. Sepi aures tuas novissimorum memoria, ne sermonis vani auditus mentis tuae integritatem polluat. Oculos humiliter in terram deprimie, ne inspicient quod concupiscere Dei servum non deceat. Colloquiis noli interesse carnalium, quorum si nequiveris declinare praesentiam, caveto ne accommodes mentem. Etiam in medio improborum tuum non transgrediaris canonem, et consuetam ne deseras maturitatem. Contumelias, et opprobria petronum ne timeas, et a verbis tenebrionum non turbetur cor tuum. Conservatio monasticae disciplinae, iustitia; et qui despiciunt simplicem, risu persequuntur innocentem. Sanctum in omnibus conserva propositum, et altissimus vindicabit iniuriam. Non dicas in corde tuo, vim patior, neque verecunderis ad verba deridentium. Gloria monachi sustineo contumeliam: et corona pulchritudinis gaudere in opprobriis. Qui patiens est ad iniurias, Atlante est fortior: et qui non contristatur irrisus, maior est omnibus. Si in coelo fixeris desiderium tuum, nihil te con-turbabit in terra: et si monachus es verus, ad iniurias exultabit cor tuum. Est iudex in coelis, qui novit omnia, et est altissimus Deus, qui curat universa. Iustus retributor est meritorum; et pauperum suorum recordabitur. Quanto animam tuam nunc in hac vita pro eius amore deieceris in profundum humilitatis, tanto in futura gloria super caeteros exaltaberis. Patientia enim ascenditur in coelum, et humilitate pervenitur ad regnum. Nam, et ipsum oportuit pati Christum, et sic intrare in gloriam suam. Delicatus est miles, qui, contumelias et irrisiones patiente imperator, quaerit delicias: et illo pendente in patibulo crucis pro suo exercitu, sequitur voluptates. Miles, qui sine armis ad bellum nudus egreditur, et monachus, qui patientiam, et humilitatem in contumeliis amplecti dedignatur, velox amborum interitus. Qui sincerus Christi amator est monachus, ad iniurias non irascitur, inferentibus 82 De monachis in viam directis.

arises, because his way of life is compared to gold. The canonical life of monks is a golden mirror. Gold in the midst of mud receives no stain upon its nature, but keeps all its beauty inviolate. So too the true monk, a lover of Christ, remains the same when sent onto the road among men as he has learned to live in the secrecy of his cell, because he walks before the Lord pure in mind as well as in body. For if he is a true monk, he is not polluted by the dust of another way of life, nor is he changed from the uprightness of his holy purpose by anyone’s presence or conversation. Amid the disorderly talk of worldly people he thinks of other things, and the dissolute conduct of others does not delight his mind. He who is with himself in heart is not divided even in the midst of those who are making an uproar.

Therefore, monk, you who desire to be good, gather your mind back to yourself, and before you leave your cell, set your heart in order for the journey. Let the fear of the Lord always be your companion on the way, and let the guard of monastic discipline never depart from your side. Fence in your ears with the memory of the last things, lest the hearing of vain speech pollute the integrity of your mind. Lower your eyes humbly to the ground, lest they look upon what it is not fitting for a servant of God to desire. Do not take part in the conversations of carnal men; and if you cannot avoid their presence, take care not to lend them your mind. Even in the midst of the wicked, do not transgress your rule, and do not abandon your customary seriousness. Do not fear the insults and reproaches of [unclear], and let not your heart be troubled by the words of men of darkness. The preservation of monastic discipline is justice; and those who despise the simple persecute the innocent with laughter. Preserve your holy purpose in all things, and the Most High will avenge the injury. Do not say in your heart, “I am suffering violence,” nor be ashamed at the words of those who mock you. It is the glory of a monk to endure insult, and the crown of beauty to rejoice in reproaches.

He who is patient under injuries is stronger than Atlas; and he who is not saddened when mocked is greater than all. If you have fixed your desire in heaven, nothing on earth will disturb you; and if you are a true monk, your heart will exult at injuries. There is a judge in heaven who knows all things, and there is the Most High God who cares for all. He is the just rewarder of merits, and he will remember his poor ones. The more you cast down your soul now in this life, for love of him, into the depth of humility, the more in future glory you will be exalted above the rest. For by patience one ascends into heaven, and by humility one comes to the kingdom. For Christ himself also had to suffer, and so enter into his glory. A delicate soldier is one who, while his emperor is enduring insults and mockeries, seeks pleasures; and while he hangs on the gibbet of the cross for his army, pursues delights. Swift is the destruction of both: the soldier who goes out naked to war without weapons, and the monk who disdains to embrace patience and humility amid insults. The monk who is a sincere lover of Christ is not angered by injuries, against those who inflict them.

78
contumeliam non comminatur, in sancto stat fixus proposito, et quantumlibet irruant improbi, non movetur. Quemadmodum in pratis auget opportuna pluvia foenum, ita monacho crescit meritum ex humili tolerantia iniuriarum.
