Omnium nervus virtutum humilitas; et minera bonorum operum constans ad iniurias pro Dei amore patientia. Egressurus itaque in viam de monasterio praepara cor tuum ad tolerantiam iniuriarum, et mentem corrobora adversum insolentias derisorum. Cum inclamaverint post tergum tuum nebulones, nomen ingeminantes monachi, Christum memento irrisum, et consputum ante praesidem, qui non respondit verbum, sed tacitus conservabat patientiam. Hunc imitare Ducem o monache: hunc semper ausculta praecptorem, qui mitis extitit, et humiliis corde. Non respondeas te irridentibus verbum, non intorqueas faciem tuam retrorsum, sed dicio cum prophetā: Qui inquirebant mala mihi, locuti sunt vanitates, et dolos tota die meditabant: Ego autem tamquam surdus non audiebam, et sicut mutus non aperiens os suum: Et factus sum sicut homo non audiens, et non habens in ore suo redargutiones. Hoc Christus fecit, hoc Iesus docuit: hoc Rex omnium praecipit, cuius si vis esse discipulus, ad omnes iniurias semper oportet sis paratus. Constitutus in itinere, qua potes devotione, orationes tuas canonicas dicere non negligas, et semper aliquid boni tecum in mente, vel orando, vel meditando revolvas. Dominus tecum graditur, et sancti angeli eius te ambulantem comitantur. Et ideo cor mundum conserva in omnibus, ne tantorum offendas comitum maiestatem. Dominus oculus est totus, et auris, a cuius notitia nihil absconditur. Sermonibus tuis iugem adhibe custodiam, et praeveniat omne verbum oris deliberatio cordis, ut nihil, de quo poenitere possis, omnino loquaris. Os monachi loquitur, et paucā, et rationabilia, et labia eius nunquam excedunt in sermone. Omnis conversatio eius in aedificatio- nem ponitur proximorum; et, qui moribus docet plurimos, etiam tacens utilia loquitur. Qui amator verus est Dei, humillime in via graditur: et, qui timet altissimum, os suum a cachinno temperat. In omni vita tua mortalem te cogita, et quasi qui iam ultimum emittit spiritum, moriens vivito. Felix regnum, et dives apud Deum provincia, in quibus cum Boote consurgunt monachi, quoniam ubi non est timor Dei, replentur theatra claustralibus. Monachus in via quasi vir, qui dormiens loquitur; cum evigilaverit de somno, nihil eorum, quae somniaverat, meminit. Sic enim canon monasticus praecipit. Nec praesumat quisquam aliis referre, quacumque foris monasterium viderit, aut audierit, quia plurima destructio est. Quod si quis praesumpserit, vindictae regulari subiaceat. Similiter, et qui praesumpserit claustra monasterii egredi, vel quocunque ire, vel quicquid quamvis parvulum sine iussione abatis facere. Hanc vitae normam voluntarie suscipientes in eius verba

He does not threaten insult; he stands fixed in his holy purpose, and however much the wicked may rush upon him, he is not moved. Just as timely rain increases the hay in the meadows, so a monk’s merit grows from humble endurance of injuries. Humility is the sinew of all virtues, and steadfast patience under injuries for the love of God is the mine of good works.

Therefore, when you are about to go out on the road from the monastery, prepare your heart to endure injuries, and strengthen your mind against the insolence of mockers. When scoundrels shout after your back, repeating the name “monk,” remember Christ mocked and spat upon before the governor, who did not answer a word, but kept patience in silence. Imitate this Leader, O monk; always listen to this Teacher, who was meek and humble of heart.

Do not answer a word to those who mock you; do not turn your face back toward them, but say with the prophet: “Those who sought evils for me spoke vanities, and all day long they meditated deceits. But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute man not opening his mouth. And I became like a man who does not hear, and who has no rebukes in his mouth.” This Christ did; this Jesus taught; this the King of all commands. If you wish to be his disciple, you must always be prepared for every injury.

When you are on the road, do not neglect to say your canonical prayers with whatever devotion you can, and always turn over something good with yourself in your mind, either by praying or by meditating. The Lord walks with you, and his holy angels accompany you as you walk. Therefore keep your heart clean in all things, lest you offend the majesty of such great companions. The Lord is wholly eye and ear, and nothing is hidden from his knowledge.

Keep constant watch over your words, and let deliberation of the heart precede every word of your mouth, so that you say absolutely nothing for which you might have to repent. The mouth of a monk speaks few things, and reasonable things, and his lips never go beyond measure in speech. All his conduct is set toward the edification of his neighbors; and he who teaches many by his character speaks useful things even when silent.

He who is a true lover of God walks most humbly on the road; and he who fears the Most High restrains his mouth from loud laughter. In your whole life consider yourself mortal, and live as one dying, as though already breathing out your last breath. Happy is the kingdom, and rich before God the province, in which monks rise with Boötes, since where there is no fear of God, the theaters are filled with cloistered men.

A monk on the road is like a man who speaks while sleeping; when he has awakened from sleep, he remembers none of the things he had dreamed. For thus the monastic canon commands. Nor should anyone presume to report to others whatever he has seen or heard outside the monastery, because it is very destructive. But if anyone has presumed to do so, let him be subject to the regular punishment. Likewise also he who has presumed to leave the cloisters of the monastery, or to go anywhere, or to do anything, however small, without the abbot’s command. Those who voluntarily take up this rule of life in its words...

79
Homilia XII. 83 iuravimus: non licet alicui nostrum retrocedere, vel aliquid in contrarium attentare. Quae foris vel audisti, vel vidisti, foris maneant; noli reversus de via fratribus inferre novitatem, ne mentium parias distractionem. Qui timet Dominum, regulae mandata custodit: et, qui amator est disciplinae, semper maturus incedit. Stultus in via gradiens verba multiplicat, et omnium montium vocabula inquirit. Frater humilis cum Deo loquens in abscondito cordis, tacenti est similis, et in sua simplicitate exultans graditur. Quicquid patrum constitutio mandavit, diligentissime considerat; et ubicunque fuerit, omnia studiose conservat. Monachus, qui directus in viam, se mundum, et purum custodivit ab omni macula culpae, laetus ad monasterium reverterit, et quasi maris evaserit periculum, ad portum quietis suspirans festinat. Qui autem perdidit verecundiam, insolens factus est, et quasi iturus ad carcerem, tristis, moerensque regreditur. Amicitiam secularium hominum verus Christi monachus non quaerit, nec amat, sed despicit: qui autem familiaritatem dissimilium multiplicat, paulatim decidit a proposito sanctitatis. Maledictus homo claustralis, qui ponit in hominibus confidentiam suam, et recessit a Domino Deo cor eius. Non quaeras amicitias hominum, sed cura, ut invisibilium consequaris consortium angelorum. Non conveniunt monacho frequentes amicitiae mortalium, per quas, et vigor mentis resolvitur, et vanae occupationes ingeruntur. Nam sicut stillicidium longo tempore cavat lapidem, quamvis durum, et solidum; sic nimia secularium hominum familiaritas paulatim rigorem emollit monasticum. Charitatem habeto ad omnes, familiaritatem vero ad paucos. Qui Deum habet amicum, facile hominum contemnit familiaritatem: et, qui cum angelis loquitur, mortalium colloquiis minime delectatur. Quoties in via signum dominicae passionis, aut crucifixi conspexeris, non praeteras, nisi dicas. Ago tibi gratias, Domine Iesu Christe, pro dolore vulnerum tuorum, pro sanctissimi sanguinis tui effusione, et pro morte tua innocentissima, quam in ara crucis sustinuisti pro nobis: et rogo te per amaram passionem tuam, miserere mei nunc, et in tremenda hora mortis meae. Hanc orationem brevissimam saepius inter eundum replica, et nunquam praeteres imaginem crucifixi, nisi gratias egeris salvatori. Non contendas cum eo, qui tecum in via graditur, ne contra te reversus ad monasterium mali quicquam mentiatur. Qui socium itineris ad impatiens provocat, quasi qui canem furiosum verbere compellit ad latrandum. Mansuetudine vincitur improbus, et qui humilis est corde, mitigat animo concitatum. In medio secularium hominum non effundas sermonem, ne forte contra te sumant irrisiōnem. Mesopolium loqui bona concedimus inter iuvenes, qui autem minor est ordine, audiat illum. Arator lassus festinat ad requiem, et monachus integer animo, currens de via ad cel-

we have sworn: none of us may turn back or attempt anything contrary. What you heard or saw outside, let it remain outside; when you return from the road, do not bring novelty among the brothers, lest you cause distraction of minds.

He who fears the Lord keeps the commandments of the rule; and he who is a lover of discipline always walks with maturity. A fool, walking on the road, multiplies words and asks the names of all the mountains. A humble brother, speaking with God in the hidden place of his heart, is like one silent, and walks rejoicing in his simplicity. Whatever the constitution of the fathers has commanded, he considers most diligently; and wherever he may be, he carefully preserves all things.

The monk who, when sent on the road, has kept himself clean and pure from every stain of fault, will return joyful to the monastery, and, as though he had escaped the danger of the sea, hastens with longing to the harbor of rest. But he who has lost modesty has become insolent, and returns sad and sorrowful, as though going to prison.

The true monk of Christ does not seek or love the friendship of worldly people, but despises it; but he who multiplies familiarity with those unlike himself gradually falls away from the purpose of holiness. Cursed is the cloistered man who places his confidence in human beings, and whose heart has departed from the Lord his God. Do not seek the friendships of men, but take care to obtain the fellowship of the invisible angels. Frequent friendships with mortals do not suit a monk; through them both the vigor of the mind is dissolved and vain occupations are brought in. For just as dripping water over a long time hollows out a stone, however hard and solid it may be, so excessive familiarity with worldly people gradually softens monastic rigor. Have charity toward all, but familiarity with few. He who has God as a friend easily scorns familiarity with men; and he who speaks with angels takes little delight in the conversations of mortals.

Whenever on the road you see the sign of the Lord’s Passion, or of the crucified one, do not pass by unless you say: I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, for the pain of your wounds, for the pouring out of your most holy blood, and for your most innocent death, which you endured for us on the altar of the cross; and I ask you, through your bitter Passion, have mercy on me now and in the fearful hour of my death. Repeat this very brief prayer often as you go, and never pass by an image of the crucified one unless you have given thanks to the Savior.

Do not quarrel with the one who walks with you on the road, lest on returning to the monastery he falsely say something evil against you. He who provokes his traveling companion to impatience is like one who drives a mad dog to bark by beating it. The wicked man is overcome by gentleness, and he who is humble of heart calms the one stirred up in spirit. In the midst of worldly people do not pour out speech, lest perhaps they take up mockery against you. We permit [unclear] to speak good things among the young; but let the one who is lower in rank listen to him. The tired plowman hastens to rest, and the monk whole in spirit, running from the road to his cel

80
84 De monachis in viam directis. iam suam cum desiderio revertitur. Comprimatur in ore verbum, do- nec ratio sententiam aequitatis proferat, et sermo, qui potest instruere audientes, non abscondatur. Non credideris carminibus palponum, quo- niam cum exbalistraverint innocentem, aures mulcent sermonibus in- compositis. Mancipiti similis est monachus, qui contentionibus alitur, et quasi homo spaticus, qui sub nomine religionis iurgia suscitat. Coram eruditis non adiicias loqui, ne forsitan cum non intelligas pa- rabolam, irridearis a circumstantibus. Qui monachum se recognoscit, profundo sermone non utitur: et, qui docet parvulos, enodem facit quaestionem. Cum vadis ad homines proposito tuo dissimiles, non glorieris in aliquo, sed si fueris interrogatus, paucis responde humiliter. Constitutus in itinere semper Deum cogita, et senioris tui reverentiam existima comitantem. Nihil facias omnino, quod illi velis non esse manifestum, quoniam, ut sacer inquit Hierodulus, Christi vices in coe- nobio agere creditur, et ideo ab omnibus merito honoratur. Sic ergo vive, quasi eum semper habeas ante oculos praesentem, et quod agere, vel dicere, illo inspectante, non praesumeres, neque absente, ullatenus at- tentes. Stulta enim consolatio est, conscientiam mordente reatu homi- nis lateri peccatum, et iudicium fugere pastoris, qui se ad mortem novit aegrotantem. Monachus, qui facit malum, quod suum cupit la- tere praelatum, monastici canonis integritatem violavit, et in quintum humilitatis gradum enormiter deliquit. Sic enim praecipit: Quintus humilitatis gradus est, si omnes cogitationes malas cordi suo advenien- tes, et mala a se in abscondito facta, per humilern confessionem abbatì non celaverit suo. Haec Benedicti Patris sunt monita; haec sancta mo- nasticae institutionis documenta, quae si tu monache contempseris, vel neglexeris, immemor salutis propriae convinceris. Certum humilitatis indicium est, si monachus aperire seniori cor suum non recusaverit, nihilque malorum, quae commisit, suum cupiat lateri pastorem. Qui confitetur delictum suum cum humilitate, contra adversarium salutis suae confortabitur: et qui abscondit cogitationes, proficiet in malum. Nulla enim tam parva cogitatio malorum, quae paulatim non crescat neglecta, et nullum tam exile vitium, quod vires non sumat, si fuerit dissimulatum. Statim igitur a principio cogitationes malae sunt repel- lendae, quia cum prava non subito extinguitur cogitatio, parit delecta- tionem, delectatio vero consensus, consensus autem praecipitat in ope- rationem. Deinceps actio mali saepius iterata generat consuetudinem, consuetudo necessitatem, necessitas autem inducit desperationem, de- sparatio contemptum, contemptus obstinationem, et illa mortem ani- mae parit aeternam. Dicit nanque scriptura: Impius, cum venerit in profundum malorum, contennit. Nonne abbas tuus, o monache, pastor, et medicus est animae tuae? Nonne, fratres mei charissimi, ego post Homilia XII. 85 Deum ille sum, qui pascit mortalia corpora vestra necessario alimento? Nonne verbum salutis ministrare vobis ego compellor? Si oves pastorem fugitis, quae sunt pascua spiritus, quae a nobis expectatis? Qui medicum fugit infirmus, propriam alutem despicit, et animam suam voluntarie occidit. Monachus ergo ambulans in via malitiae, et declinans a semitis iustitiae, morti est proximus, et tanto magis in profundum vitiorum labitur, quanto minus iudicium corrigitis reveretur. Ille autem vere est monachus, qui ab omni iniquitate custodit animam suam, et nihil agit paenitius, quod suum vellet ignorare pastorem. Qui occultat viam suam, non est purus: et qui fugit praesentiam iudicis, auget suspicionem. Quasi ovis in deserto ambulans, quae a lupo rapitur, monachus negligens, et impurus, qui se a notitia subtrahit pastoris, et a demonibus devoratur. Ovis morbida currens in interitum, et monachus abscondens omne peccatum, non est salus eorum, nisi revertantur ad medicum. Revertentes de via monachi statim ipso die, iuxta monasticum canonom fratum omnium provolvantur conspectibus, quatenus communibus orationibus expietur, quicquid in via per negligentiam delinquitur. Multum enim valet ad diluendum peccata communis oratio plurimorum, si fuerit cum devotionis fervore profusa ad Dominum. De quotidiana peccatorum expiatione. Homilia XIII.

Concerning monks sent on the road.

Let the word be restrained in the mouth until reason brings forth a judgment of equity, and let not speech that can instruct the hearers be hidden. Do not trust the songs of flatterers, for when they have shot down an innocent man, they soothe the ears with disordered words. A monk who feeds on quarrels is like a slave, and like a swaggering man who stirs up disputes under the name of religion.

In the presence of learned men do not be eager to speak, lest perhaps, when you do not understand the parable, you be laughed at by those standing by. He who recognizes himself as a monk does not use profound speech; and he who teaches little ones makes the question plain. When you go to men unlike you in your way of life, do not boast in anything; but if you are asked, answer humbly in few words.

When you are set upon a journey, always think of God, and consider the reverence owed to your elder as accompanying you. Do absolutely nothing which you would not wish to be made known to him, since, as the holy Hierodulus says, he is believed to act in Christ’s place in the monastery, and therefore is deservedly honored by all. Live, then, as though you always had him present before your eyes; and what you would not presume to do or say while he looked on, do not in any way attempt while he is absent. For it is foolish consolation, when conscience is gnawed by guilt, for a man’s sin to lie hidden and for one who knows himself sick unto death to flee the judgment of his shepherd.

The monk who does evil which he wishes to hide from his prelate has violated the integrity of the monastic rule and has grievously sinned against the fifth degree of humility. For it commands thus: “The fifth degree of humility is this: if, by humble confession, he does not conceal from his abbot all the evil thoughts that come into his heart, and the evil things done by him in secret.” These are the admonitions of Father Benedict; these are the holy teachings of the monastic institution. If you, monk, despise or neglect them, you are proved forgetful of your own salvation.

It is a sure sign of humility if a monk does not refuse to open his heart to his elder, and does not wish any of the evils he has committed to be hidden from his shepherd. He who confesses his fault with humility will be strengthened against the adversary of his salvation; and he who conceals his thoughts will advance in evil. For there is no thought of evils so small that it does not gradually grow if neglected, and no vice so slight that it does not gain strength if it is dissembled.

Therefore evil thoughts must be driven back at once from the beginning, because when a depraved thought is not immediately extinguished, it gives birth to delight; delight to consent; and consent hurls one into action. Thereafter the action of evil, repeated often, begets habit; habit, necessity; necessity brings in despair; despair, contempt; contempt, obstinacy; and that gives birth to the eternal death of the soul. For Scripture says: “When the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises.”

Is not your abbot, O monk, the shepherd and physician of your soul? Am I not, my dearest brothers, after God, the one who feeds your mortal bodies with necessary food? Am I not compelled to minister the word of salvation to you? If you, the sheep, flee the shepherd, what pastures of the spirit do you expect from us? The sick man who flees the physician despises his own salvation and willingly kills his soul. Therefore the monk who walks in the way of malice and turns aside from the paths of justice is near to death, and he slips so much more deeply into the abyss of vices the less he reveres the judgment of correction. But he is truly a monk who guards his soul from all iniquity and does nothing at all which he would wish his shepherd not to know.

He who hides his way is not pure; and he who flees the presence of the judge increases suspicion. Like a sheep wandering in the wilderness and seized by the wolf is the negligent and impure monk who withdraws himself from the knowledge of his shepherd and is devoured by demons. A diseased sheep running to destruction, and a monk hiding every sin, have no salvation unless they return to the physician.

Monks returning from the road, on that very day, according to the monastic rule, are to be prostrated before the eyes of all the brothers, so that whatever has been committed through negligence on the road may be expiated by the common prayers. For the common prayer of many greatly avails to wash away sins, if it has been poured out to the Lord with the fervor of devotion.

Concerning the daily expiation of sins. Homily XIII.

81
Quandiu in hac vita corruptibili sumus constituti, fratres charissimi, quotidie in multis offendimus, et quantunilibet sancte conversari videamur, peccato non caremus. Corpus enim, quod corruptur, aggravat animam; et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensum multa cogitante. Dicit nanque scriptura: Non est homo iustus in terra, qui faciat bonum, et non peccet. Divus quoque evangelista Ioannes: Si dixerimus, inquit, quoniam peccatum non habemus, ipsi nos seducimus, et veritas in nobis non est. Commercio nempe carnis nimium delectata peccat anima, et fortitudo imminuitur desperatione spiritus. Mens enim obiectione sensibilium decipitur, et delinquendi promptitudo longa consuetudine robatur. Infirmitas carnis, fervorem spiritus debilitat, et sancto nementis proposito voluntatis fragilitas repugnat. Hinc Salomon rex sapientissimus in libro Proverbiorum dicit: Septies in die cadet iustus, et resurget, impii autem corruent in malum. Huius sententiae testimonio admonemur in sanctitatis proposito non tepescere, etiam si nos contingere septies in die cecidisse. Quoties, Monache, per peccatum a sanctitatis proposito cecideris, toties resurgere ad fervorem pristinum non pigriteris. Humanae fragilitatis est cadere, sed pertinacae diabolicae deiectum in luto sceleris permanere. Semel peccaverunt daemones, et facti sunt in sua obstinatione indurati et pertinaces, ad poenitentiam 86 De quotidiana peccatorum expiatione. deinceps nunquam reversuri. Homines autem quotiescunque ceciderint, semper ad poenitentiam possunt resurgere, et Dei gratiam, quam per- diderant peccando, lachrymis et orationibus impetrare. Cor etenim ho- minis flexibile in utranque partem mov- ri potest: quia nunquam homo in carne tam malus fieri posse credendus est, quin valeat, si velit a ma- litia sua resipiscere, et, Deo largiente, ad bonitatem mentem suam refor- mare. Rursus quoque nemo tam bonus in hac vita mortali efficitur, qui non fieri malus possit, si gratia Domini abutatur. Quae cum ita se habeant, fratres mei, hodierna mihi cohortatione fueritis admonendi, quatenus caute ambuletis, ut qui conscientia testante, iam in semitis iustitiae graditur, in ipsa proficiendo quotidiie perseveret: et qui reum se coram Domino intelligit, vitam quantocyus emendet. Si te humana fragilitas quotidiie impellit, sive, ut proprius dicam, praecipitat, facit- que delinquere, incitet etiam te amor Dei, et propriae salutis, quotidiie culpam tuam per veram contritionem humiliter expiare. Sic enim septies in die cadit iustus, et resurgit, quoniam et si ex humana fragilitate labitur, semper tamen in sanctitatis perseverans proposito, magis, ac magis animo in Dei amore confortatur. A gravibus nanque peccatis conscientiam suam conservans immunem, quotidianis negligentiis invi- tus polluitur; et cum se vivere sine delictis non posse conspicit, suam humiliter infirmitatem agnoscens, amplius ingemiscit. Quod si etiam graviore delicto praecuppatus fuerit, mox ad emendationem per poe- nitentiam resurgit. Unde considerantes humanae fragilitatis conditio- nem prisci monasticae disciplinae moderatores, varia expiationis genera instituerunt, quibus et bonae voluntatis monachi quotidiie proficiant in melius, et improbi ad observantiam regularis vitae compellantur. In regula nanque sanctus Pater Benedictus sic praecipit dicens: Omni sol- licitudine curam gerat abbas circa delinquentes fratres, quia non est opus sanis medicus, sed male habentibus. Quamobrem primi observ- vantiae regularis principes provida consideratione instituerunt, ut quo- tidie post primas in loco deputato conventus celebretur culparum, in quo praesidente, vel Abbate, vel Priore, omnium actus fratrum aequa discussione proferantur in medium. Locus iste, fratres mei typum ge- rit purgatorii animarum, quoniam hic non soluui peccata expiantur praeterita, sed etiam praemunimur contra futura. In hoc etenim loco, quem vocamus capitularem, quicquid in aperto deliquistis, corrigitur, et per salutarem poenitentiam expiatur. Hic quotidiie legem vestram monasticam, ad cuius integritatem vivere promisistis, paraphraste pro- nunciante cognoscitis; hic verbum salutis exhortatorium diebus sin- gulis auditis; hic martyrum Christi victorias, multimodasque pro fide orthodoxa passiones breviter recitatas auscultatis. Haec est monachorum schola pro consideratione disciplinae regularis necessaria, in qua totum

As long as we are placed in this corruptible life, dearly beloved brothers, we offend daily in many things, and however holy our way of life may seem, we are not without sin. For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and this earthly dwelling depresses the mind as it thinks on many things. Scripture says: “There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin.” Likewise the blessed evangelist John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

The soul, indeed, too much delighted by commerce with the flesh, sins, and its strength is diminished by despair of spirit. The mind is deceived by the assault of sensible things, and readiness to sin is strengthened by long habit. The weakness of the flesh weakens the fervor of the spirit, and the frailty of the will resists the holy purpose of the mind. Hence Solomon, that most wise king, says in the book of Proverbs: “Seven times in a day the righteous man will fall and rise again, but the wicked will fall into evil.”

By the testimony of this saying we are warned not to grow lukewarm in the purpose of holiness, even if it happens that we have fallen seven times in a day. As often, monk, as you fall through sin from the purpose of holiness, so often do not be slow to rise again to your former fervor. It belongs to human frailty to fall, but to stubborn diabolical obstinacy to remain cast down in the mire of wickedness. The demons sinned once, and in their obstinacy were made hardened and stubborn, never thereafter to return to repentance. But human beings, as often as they have fallen, can always rise again to repentance and obtain by tears and prayers the grace of God which they had lost by sinning.

For the heart of man is flexible and can be moved in either direction, because no man in the flesh should ever be believed able to become so evil that he cannot, if he wills, come to his senses from his wickedness and, by God’s gift, reform his mind toward goodness. Again, no one becomes so good in this mortal life that he cannot become evil, if he misuses the grace of the Lord. Since this is so, my brothers, you must be admonished by today’s exhortation to walk carefully, so that he who, as his conscience bears witness, is already walking in the paths of justice may persevere daily in them by making progress, and he who knows himself guilty before the Lord may amend his life as quickly as possible.

If human frailty daily drives you on, or, to speak more properly, hurls you down and makes you sin, let the love of God and of your own salvation also urge you daily to expiate your fault humbly through true contrition. For in this way the righteous man falls seven times in a day and rises again, because even if he slips through human frailty, nevertheless, always persevering in the purpose of holiness, he is strengthened more and more in soul in the love of God. For while he preserves his conscience free from grave sins, he is unwillingly defiled by daily negligences; and when he sees that he cannot live without faults, humbly acknowledging his own weakness, he groans all the more. But if he has even been overtaken by a graver fault, he at once rises again to amendment through repentance.

Therefore the ancient governors of monastic discipline, considering the condition of human frailty, established various kinds of expiation, by which monks of good will might daily advance toward what is better, and the wicked might be compelled to the observance of regular life. For in the Rule the holy Father Benedict commands thus, saying: “With all solicitude let the abbot take care of offending brothers, because it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are sick.”

For this reason the first leaders of regular observance, with provident consideration, established that every day after Prime, in the place appointed, a convent of faults should be held, in which, with either the abbot or the prior presiding, the actions of all the brothers should be brought into the open by fair examination. This place, my brothers, bears the figure of the purgatory of souls, because here not only are past sins expiated, but we are also fortified against future ones. For in this place, which we call the chapter-house, whatever you have done wrong openly is corrected and expiated through salutary penance. Here daily, as the paraphraser pronounces it, you learn your monastic law, according to whose integrity you have promised to live; here each day you hear the exhortatory word of salvation; here you listen to the victories of Christ’s martyrs and their many kinds of sufferings for the orthodox faith briefly recited. This is the school of monks, necessary for the consideration of regular discipline, in which the whole...

82
Homilia XIII. 87 discitur, quod observandum claustralibus mandatur. Duo sunt, fratres mei dilectissimi, quae a vobis iste locus exigit; alterum, ut in corre- ptione humilem semper teneatis patientiam: alterum vero, ut nostram qualemcumque libenter suscipiatis exhortationem. Ad primum cupientes vos esse paratos sancti legislatores nostri fortia martyrum gesta, quo- rum imitatores fieri debeatis, legenda praecipiant: ac deinde, ut sitis dociles animo, passum ex regula unum subiungere mandaverunt. Ita- que, ut sitis imitatione sanctorum martyrum fortes, et patientes ad increpationes necessarias, series passionis eorum in auribus vestris hic legitur: et quatenus ad salutarem doctrinam praeparetis animos, lectio vobis de regula, quam profitemini, una recitatur. Sancti martyres Chri- sti, exemplo vos suo cohortantur ad patientiam, et ut sitis etiam ad iniurias parati, divus vos admonet Benedictus per doctrinam. Nemo igitur vestrum, amantissimi fratres, in hoc loco poenitentiam recuset pro suis negligentiis quotdie humiliter suscipere, nemo dedignetur. Hic locus est publicum expiandi peccatum, in quo sic iudicii temperatur severitas, ut pietas discretionis non violetur. Medicus enim esse cupio animatorum vestrarum, non peremptor: idcirco ad iudicii nostri examen securi accedite, et vosmetipsos de commissis in aperto negligentiis hu- milliter proclamate. Nolo vos gravare supra regulam, ut secretissima conscientiae delicta de confessione sacramentali ad publicum transferam examen culparum, quod novimus fecisse quosdam in grave animarum detrimentum suorum subditorum. Sic enim dicit legifer noster Bene- dictus in regula: Si vero animae peccati causa fuerit latens, tantum abbati, aut spiritualibus senioribus patefaciat, qui sciant curare sua, et aliena non detegere vulnera, seu publicare. Duo sunt in monasterio loca expiationis peccati, alter eorum, quae sunt manifesta: et alter eo- rum, quae sunt occulta. Manifesta enim peccata in proclamatione cul- parum quotidiana publice coram omnibus expianda sunt: occulta vero, et quorum manifestatio scandalizaret infirmos, ad confessionem sunt remittenda. Nam, cuius peccatum est manifestum, oportet, ut publice quoque puniatur: et, qui deliquit in occulto, etiam in secreto emen- detur. Sunt quidam claustralium rectores, qui latentia subditorum pec- cata ad publicum examen referre non verentur, qui iudicio quidem meo non satis prudenter iura praelationis exequuntur sua, dum subditis viam pracludunt salutis, et confessionem liberrimam constringunt sub vinculo malae voluntatis: quod quam sit periculosum, nemo, vel me- diocriter sapiens, qui non intelligat. Hanc enim pastoris temeritatem sanctus institutor monachorum ita redarguit dicens: Magnopere solli- citudinem gerat abbas, et omni sagacitate, et industria curet, ne ali- quam de ovis suis creditis perdat. Noverit se infirmarum curam su- scepisse animarum, non super sanas tyrannide. Ordinavimus vobis ex 88 De quotidiana peccatorum expiatione.

There are two things, my most beloved brothers, which this place requires of you: one, that in correction you always maintain humble patience; the other, that you willingly receive our exhortation, such as it is. Desiring you to be ready for the first, our holy lawgivers commanded that the brave deeds of the martyrs, whose imitators you ought to become, be read; and then, so that you may be teachable in spirit, they ordered one passage from the Rule to be added. Therefore, so that you may be strong by imitating the holy martyrs, and patient under necessary rebukes, the account of their passion is read here in your ears; and so that you may prepare your minds for saving doctrine, one reading is recited to you from the Rule which you profess. The holy martyrs of Christ, by their example, exhort you to patience; and blessed Benedict admonishes you by his teaching to be ready even for injuries.

Therefore let none of you, most beloved brothers, refuse in this place humbly to accept penance daily for his negligences; let no one disdain it. This place is the public expiation of sin, in which the severity of judgment is so tempered that the kindness of discretion is not violated. For I desire to be the physician of your souls, not their destroyer. Therefore come without fear to the examination of our judgment, and humbly accuse yourselves openly of the negligences you have committed. I do not wish to burden you beyond the Rule, so as to transfer the most secret offenses of conscience from sacramental confession to the public examination of faults, as we know certain men have done to the grave harm of the souls of their subjects. For thus says our lawgiver Benedict in the Rule: “But if the cause of the soul’s sin is hidden, let him reveal it only to the abbot or to spiritual elders, who know how to heal their own wounds and those of others, not to expose or make them public.”

There are two places in the monastery for the expiation of sin: one for those sins that are manifest, and the other for those that are hidden. Manifest sins are to be expiated publicly before all in the daily proclamation of faults; hidden sins, however, and those whose disclosure would scandalize the weak, are to be referred to confession. For the one whose sin is manifest must also be punished publicly; and the one who has sinned in secret must also be corrected in secret. There are certain rulers of cloistered men who do not fear to bring the hidden sins of their subjects to public examination; in my judgment, they do not carry out the rights of their office with sufficient prudence, since they close off the way of salvation to their subjects and constrain the freest confession under the bond of ill will. How dangerous this is, no one of even moderate wisdom fails to understand. For the holy founder of monks rebukes this rashness of a shepherd when he says: “Let the abbot show the greatest concern, and with all shrewdness and diligence take care not to lose any of the sheep entrusted to him. Let him know that he has undertaken the care of weak souls, not tyranny over healthy ones.” We have appointed for you from

83
senioribus quatuor spirituales confessores, ut si quis vestrum aliqua fuerit occulta tentatione praecupatus, et nostram habuerit inexpertam iuventutem suspectam, ad illos pro consolatione sui securum possit habere recursum. Quamvis neminem in tota congregatione hactenus invenerimus ista, quem nobis fidem tam in confessione, quam extra detraxisse notaverimus. Omnes enim cognoscitis, et aperte videtis, quod nihil in vobis amplius quaero, nihil plus desidero, quam vestrarum salutem, et spiritualis profectus quotidianum incrementum. Vos enim corona mea, vos honor meus, vos gaudium meum: quia, tunc me foelicem existinio, cum vos in Dei profecisse amore cognosco. Magnam proficiendi opportunitatem consecuti estis fratres charissimi, quoniam, et locus, in quo militamus Domino, ab omni strepitu remotus est et quotidiana vos admonitione ad meliora promovere non cessamus. Quoties vero quispiam vestrum in aliquod peccatum per humanam fragilitatem ceciderit, iacere in delectione animi diutius non permittitur, ubi alter ab altero in vera caritate fraterna pro suis negligentiis quotidianie proclamatitur. Haec est officina salutis, in qua mens pabulo coelestis doctrinae pascitur, et anima satisfactione publica quotidie a delictorum maculis emundatur. Hic locus est purgatorii terrestris, in quo monachus pro suis negligentiis discrete corripitur, et per humilem patientiam pro Christi amore quotidie longo martyrio creatori suo immolatur. Nostrum est fratres, in hoc consistorio culparum proclamatos discrete corripere: vestrui est omnia patientissime sufferre. Oportet enim, ut pro nostris satisfaciamus peccatis: quod, si facere in hac vita neglexerimus, in futura compulsi necessario faciemus. Sunt inter vos nonnulli correctiones graviter ferentes, quibus denuntiamus quod saepe diximus; quoniam necesse est ut in futuro gravissima sustineant, qui parva hic sustinere, ac levia recusant. Ego autem considerans eorundem infirmitatem et ignorantiam, penes meipsum graviter crucior, quia mentes eorum saucias video, et tamen adhibere necessaria medicamina pertimesco. Nam, si convenientia morbis applicavero remedia, vereor, ne pusillanimes effecti in desperationem incidunt, vel certe in reprobum sensum dati paenitus a sancto proposito recedant. Quanta igitur possim discretionie utor, sic vos omnes mibi testimonium perhibebitis, malens infirmos per patientiam cum charitate mittere ad purgatorium, quam ex iusta severitate desperatos descendere ad infernum. Quis enim in hac mortalitate satisfacere pro peccatis unquam potuit, qui bonam poenitentiae non adhibuit voluntatem? Sola nanque voluntas bona poenitentium opera commendat. Cum autem plures puniantur inviti, adhuc sunt remoti a perfecta satisfactione: Credite milii fratres mei dilectissimi, quoniam patiendo magis, quam agendo commendatur satisfactio pro peccatis. Nam, et ipse Dominus, ac salvator omnium nostrum Iesus Christus patiendo

spiritual confessors from the four elders, so that if any of you has been overtaken by some hidden temptation, and has suspected our inexperienced youth, he may have safe recourse to them for his consolation. Yet thus far in the whole congregation we have found no one whom we have observed to have withdrawn his trust from us either in confession or outside it.

For you all know, and plainly see, that I seek nothing more in you, desire nothing more, than your salvation and the daily increase of your spiritual progress. For you are my crown, you my honor, you my joy; because I count myself happy when I know that you have advanced in the love of God.

You have obtained a great opportunity for progress, dearest brothers, since the place in which we serve the Lord as soldiers is removed from all noise, and we do not cease to move you toward better things by daily admonition. And whenever any one of you has fallen into some sin through human frailty, he is not allowed to lie long in the delight of his mind, where one brother is daily proclaimed by another, in true brotherly charity, for his negligences.

This is the workshop of salvation, in which the mind is fed with the nourishment of heavenly doctrine, and the soul is daily cleansed from the stains of sins by public satisfaction. This place is an earthly purgatory, in which the monk is discreetly corrected for his negligences, and through humble patience, for the love of Christ, is daily offered to his Creator in a long martyrdom.

It is our part, brothers, in this court of faults, to correct discreetly those who have been proclaimed; it is yours to endure all things with the greatest patience. For we must make satisfaction for our sins; and if we neglect to do this in this life, in the life to come we shall necessarily be compelled to do it.

There are some among you who take corrections hard. To them we declare what we have often said: that in the future they must endure very grievous things, who here refuse to endure small and light ones. But I, considering their weakness and ignorance, am grievously tormented within myself, because I see their minds wounded, and yet I am afraid to apply the necessary medicines. For if I apply remedies suited to their diseases, I fear that, becoming fainthearted, they may fall into despair, or certainly, given over to a reprobate sense, may wholly withdraw from the holy purpose.

Therefore I use as much discretion as I can, as you all will bear witness for me, preferring to send the weak, through patience with charity, to purgatory, rather than through just severity to make them despair and descend to hell. For who in this mortality was ever able to make satisfaction for sins, who did not apply a good will to penance? For only a good will commends the works of the penitent. But since many are punished unwillingly, they are still far from perfect satisfaction.

Believe me, my most beloved brothers, that satisfaction for sins is commended more by suffering than by acting. For even the Lord himself, and the Savior of us all, Jesus Christ, by suffering

84
Homilia XIII. 89 totius mundi peccatum in ara crucis expiavit. Utinam sciretis quam sit efficax animae peccatis sauciatae medicina, proclamations, et cor- reptiones cum humili patientia susciperet, et etiam in augmentum per- fectae satisfactionis iniurias, et contumelias aequanimiter tolerare? Cer- tus sum, quod omnia satisfactionis genera procul excedit humilis in adversitate patientia: et quanto mens ad tolerandas pro Christi amore contumelias, et iniurias promptior fuerit, tanto facilius, et citius omnium peccatorum suorum veniam, et plenorem indulgentiam a Domino con- sequetur. Locus enim iste, in quo nunc loquimur, purgationis, et ex- piationis ergasterium est, in quo zelus disciplinae regularis principatum- obtinet, discretio examini praesidet, charitas omnia dirigit, et complet. Unde in hoc ipso loco patientia vobis multum est necessaria, sine cuius praesentia nulla erit satisfactio consummata. Qui salutis suae studiosus amator est monachus, hunc locus ut officinam expiationis diligit, et nunquam seipso non melior factus inde procedit. Locus enim iste dae- monibus metuendus est, atque terribilis, sanctis autem Dei angelis charus, et multum venerandus, in quo humilium monachorum culpa diluitur, et quicquid in aperto delinquitur, etiam publice coram omnibus expiatur. Si quid vero latentis culpae a quoquam vestrum commissum fuerit, occulta similiter confessio poenitentis expurgabit. Utrobique pura confessio cum humilitate requiritur, et tam hic, quam illic pa- tientia vobis necessaria iudicatur. Quisquis igitur monachus cupis esse bonus, in omni patientia praepara animam tuam, ut tam in adversis, quam in prosperis constantissimam teneas mentis tranquillitatem. Cum pro negligentiis tuis ab aliquo confratre proclamatus fueris, patienter feras cum omni humilitate, fideliter inducens ad memoriam, quam in- nocenter Dei pro te filius fuerit accusatus. Nam si passus est ille con- tumelias iustus, et innocens, qui peccatum non fecit; quare tu non feras patienter increpationes a seniore, qui in multis quotdie offendis? Innumeras ille pro salute tua patientissime sustinuit iniurias, et tu pro tuis peccatis cur non sufferas humiliter, patienterque, breves et pauculas admonitiones? Nam si iuste proclamaris in iudicio culpam, necessario es patiens, quoniam, quod sustines, ipse meruisti, et imputabitur tibi humilis increpationum tolerantia in satisfactionem peccatorum. Quod si non meruisti proclamationem in iudicio, sustineas tamen pro Christi amore patienter: nam non solum reputabitur tibi ad satisfactionem praecedentium peccatorum, sed multo amplius ad iustificationem. Sive ergo iuste proclamatur monachus, sive iniuste, causam non habet iustae defensionis, quoniam si deliquit, merito suo patitur: si vero est inno- cens, magis ad patientiam obligatur. Nemo enim nisi patiens, et hu- milis Christum poterit imitari: sed cum monachus Christi maxime te- neatur esse discipulus, et imitator, maxime illum convenit esse pa- Multum no- bis prodest, si Christum amamus, si- ve iuste sive iniuste de- ferri. 90 De quotidiana peccatorum expiatione.

[He] expiated the sin of the whole world on the altar of the cross. Would that you knew how effective a medicine it is for a soul wounded by sins to receive public accusations and corrections with humble patience, and even, for the increase of perfect satisfaction, to bear injuries and insults with equanimity. I am certain that humble patience in adversity far surpasses every kind of satisfaction; and the readier the mind is to endure insults and injuries for love of Christ, the more easily and swiftly it will obtain from the Lord pardon for all its sins and a fuller indulgence.

For this place in which we now speak is a workshop of purification and expiation, in which zeal for regular discipline holds primacy, discretion presides over examination, and charity directs and completes all things. Therefore in this very place patience is greatly necessary for you; without its presence no satisfaction will be complete. The monk who is a zealous lover of his own salvation loves this place as a workshop of expiation, and never leaves it without having been made better than he was before.

For this place is fearful and terrible to demons, but dear and greatly venerable to the holy angels of God; in it the fault of humble monks is washed away, and whatever is committed openly is also expiated publicly before all. But if some hidden fault has been committed by any one of you, the penitent’s secret confession will likewise cleanse it away. In both cases pure confession with humility is required, and both here and there patience is judged necessary for you.

Therefore, whoever you are who desire to be a good monk, prepare your soul in all patience, so that in adversities as well as in prosperity you may keep a most constant tranquillity of mind. When you have been publicly accused by some brother for your negligences, bear it patiently with all humility, faithfully bringing to mind how innocently the Son of God was accused for you. For if he, just and innocent, who committed no sin, suffered insults, why should you not patiently bear rebukes from a senior, you who offend in many things every day?

He most patiently endured countless injuries for your salvation; and why should you not, for your sins, bear humbly and patiently a few brief admonitions? For if you are justly accused of a fault in judgment, you must necessarily be patient, since you yourself have deserved what you suffer, and your humble endurance of rebukes will be reckoned to you as satisfaction for sins. But if you did not deserve the public accusation in judgment, nevertheless bear it patiently for love of Christ; for it will be reckoned to you not only as satisfaction for former sins, but much more as justification.

Therefore, whether a monk is accused justly or unjustly, he has no cause for just self-defense, since if he has sinned, he suffers by his own deserving; but if he is innocent, he is all the more bound to patience. For no one unless patient and humble will be able to imitate Christ; but since a monk is especially bound to be Christ’s disciple and imitator, it especially befits him to be patient.

It profits us greatly, if we love Christ, whether we are accused justly or unjustly.

85
tientem. Sine ferro, et igne martyr esse potest monachus, si veram ubique patientiam in animo pro Dei amore custodierit. Verus etenim monachus nec laudibus extollitur, nec vituperio contristatur, ad injurias patientem se exhibit, ad contumelias, et opprobria laetus humiliter tacet. Nemo fortior patiente, qui novit semet ipsum vincere, et quaelibet contraria pro Dei amore tranquilla mente humiliter tolerare. Omnis autem impatiens, superbus, et arrogans est, quoniam praecptorem humilitatis Iesum non sequitur, et idcirco ad iustas increpationes, quas meruit, indignatur. Quemadmodum fornax probat aurum, ita contumeliae, et iniuriae probant monachum, si veraciter diligit Christum. Humilitas, et patientia in adversis vera sunt insignia monachorum: quorum ornatu quicunque non induitur, frustra de nomine gloriatur. Qui humilis non est, monachus veraciter esse non potest: et qui patientiam non custodit in adversis, verus Christi non potest esse discipulus. Hinc Salomon rex in libro Proverbiorum dixit: Melior est patiens virg fortis, et qui dominatur animo suo, expugnator urbium. Doctrina enim viri per patientiam dignoscitur, et gloria eius est iniqua praetergredi. Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines iustos tentatio tribulationis. Ad omnes iniurias patiens est monachus, qui Christum in veritate sequitur: et qui Dominicae passionis meditator est non obli viosus, in contumeliis exultat animo, et laetatur. Omnes enim, ut sacer Christophilus inquit, qui pie volunt vivere in Christo Iesu, persecutionem patientur: et quicquid eis acciderit mali, summa constantia per vincunt. Et quamvis patientia monacho in omni loco, et tempore sit necessaria, in quotidiano tamen examine culparum praecipua est intentione diligentius custodienda, ubi de correctione morum agitur, et quicquid fuerit contra normam monasticae puritatis commissum, in unoquoque per seniorem emendatur. Prius, ergo, quam hunc locum ingrediamur, mane cogitanda sunt omnia, et animus adversus ea, quae possunt evenire, firmandus est, ut, si durior forsitan increpatio evenerit, mentem a statu tranquillitatis non subvertat. Nam, et si nulli vestrum contumeliam inferre, sive iniuriam facere statuerimus unquam, fieri posse non negamus, ut ultra demeritum se correpsum existimet, quisquis paternam in nobis correptionem verbis potius, quam animo pensat. Vestram salutem, sicut Deus novit, in omnibus, et nihil aliud quaerimus: amputare vitia radicibus iuxta religionis nostra instituta, non laedere quenquam sincere cogitamus. Non possumus omnibus complacere in omnibus, sed illis disiplicere maxime compellimur, qui peccantes in canonem, quotdie impunitatem sibi scelerum pollicentur: de quibus rex Salomon dixit: Doctrina mala deserentium viam vitae, et qui odit increpationes, morietur. Non amat pestilens eum, qui se cor ripit, nec ad sapientes graditur. Qui male operatur, ex proposito fugit

A monk can be a martyr without sword and fire, if for the love of God he everywhere keeps true patience in his soul. For the true monk is not puffed up by praise nor saddened by blame; he shows himself patient under injuries; amid insults and reproaches he joyfully and humbly keeps silence. No one is stronger than the patient man, who knows how to conquer himself and humbly to endure every adversity with a tranquil mind for the love of God.

Every impatient man, however, is proud and arrogant, because he does not follow Jesus, the teacher of humility, and therefore he is indignant at the just rebukes that he has deserved. As the furnace tests gold, so insults and injuries test the monk, whether he truly loves Christ. Humility and patience in adversities are the true marks of monks; whoever is not clothed with their adornment boasts of the name in vain. He who is not humble cannot truly be a monk; and he who does not keep patience in adversities cannot be a true disciple of Christ.

Hence King Solomon said in the book of Proverbs: “A patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than one who storms cities.” For a man’s learning is known through patience, and his glory is to pass over wrongs. The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous men.

The monk who follows Christ in truth is patient under all injuries; and he who is not forgetful in meditating on the Lord’s passion exults and rejoices in his soul amid insults. For all, as holy Christophilus says, who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution; and whatever evil befalls them, they overcome it with the greatest constancy.

And although patience is necessary for a monk in every place and time, still in the daily examination of faults it must be guarded with especial care and more diligent attention, where the correction of morals is at issue, and whatever has been committed against the standard of monastic purity is amended in each person by the senior. Therefore, before we enter this place, all things must be considered in the morning, and the soul must be strengthened against what may happen, so that, if perhaps a harsher rebuke should occur, it may not overthrow the mind from its state of tranquillity.

For even if we have resolved never to bring insult upon any of you or do injury to anyone, still we do not deny that it can happen that someone may think himself rebuked beyond his desert, if he weighs our fatherly correction by the words rather than by the spirit. As God knows, we seek your salvation in all things, and nothing else; we sincerely intend to cut out vices by the roots according to the statutes of our religion, not to harm anyone. We cannot please everyone in all things, but we are compelled especially to displease those who, sinning against the rule, daily promise themselves impunity for their crimes. Of these King Solomon said: “Evil teaching belongs to those who abandon the way of life, and he who hates rebukes will die.” The pestilent man does not love the one who corrects him, nor does he go to the wise. He who does evil deliberately flees.

86
Homilia XIII. 91 lucem, et odit corpectionem, quia stultus est: qui autem sensatus est animo, gratias aget suo correctori. Propterea in hac parte non vereor odia murmurantium subditorum, sciens me curam infirmarum suscepisse ovium, quibus, et volentibus et nolentibus, salutis teneor adlibere remedia. Si fieri posset, fratres, optarem summopere neminem vestrum, in aliquo vel tenuiter perturbare, sed in medio vestri cum summa tranquillitate conversari, et Domino Deo nostro in pace mentis, et corporis hilariter deservire. Sed quia non omnes, quae Dei sunt, in veritate quaeritis, oportet me corripere, et aliando turbare inquietos, ne imputitas parvorum scelerum audaciam praebat graviorum. Scio enim, quam patiar necessitatem periculi curae pastoralis, et ideo silere nec possum, nec debo vobis peccantibus, ne ab aliquibus iudicer consentiens. Libenter suffero, si me propterea contingat odio haberi: quod cum fieri sine gravissimo animarum vestrarum periculo nequeat, rogamus vos per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum pro nobis crucifixum, ut paternas, et necessarias increpationes nostras pro Dei amore in remissionem peccatorum vestrorum omni tempore patienter, et cum vera humilitate sustineatis. Cogitet unusquisque apud se nullum esse diem, in quo omnia bene faciat, et non offendat in aliquo; sciatque se mercedem suorum operand in brevi recepturum, pro bonis bona, et pro malis similiter mala. Studeat ergo, quantumcunque potest, in hac vita pro delictis satisfacere, et omnes iniquitates suas quotidianae castigatione corporis humiliter expiare. Scitote fratres mei, quia non est aliquid peccatum tam parvum, quod Omnipotentis Dei iustitia dimittat impunitum. Propterea cum nemo sit nostrum, qui non offendit in multis, armate vos precor patientia, et humilitate, ut quoties pro peccatis correcti fueritis, cum omni mansuetudine sustineatis. Nam in hoc tempore libertatis arbitrii cum parva expiatione satis potestis facere pro debitis multis, quando post mortem in purgatorio anima etiam pro parvis diu, et gravissime cruciabitur. Enimvero multum valet satisfactio voluntaria: quae autem fit ex necessitate, minus promeretur ad gratiam: Omnino, fratres, convenit, et oportet animam purgari a delicto, si debit in caelis regnare, et gaudere cum Christo. Anima vero, quae purgationem delictorum in praesenti vita neglexerit, gravius in futuro punietur. Nemo vestrum dicat, fratres mei charissimi, quod plures imperiti homines dicere consueverunt. Sufficit mihi, si anima mea purgatorii poenas consecuta fuerit: Credite mihi fratres, quicumque hoc verbum ex animo dixerit, quid futurum sit purgatorium, non perpendit. Nescit enim, quid petat, qui purgatorium desiderat. Quemadmodum stultus est, qui cum posset solvere debitum liber, contemnit, et libens vadit ad carcerem; ita stultissimus omnium hominum est merito iudicandus, qui satisfacere in hac vita, cum possit Deo pro peccatis, differt 92 De quotidiana peccatorum expiatione.

the light and hates correction, because he is foolish; but the sensible man will thank his corrector. Therefore in this matter I do not fear the hatred of murmuring subjects, knowing that I have taken on the care of sickly sheep, to whom, whether they wish it or not, I am bound to apply the remedies of salvation.

If it were possible, brothers, I would greatly prefer to disturb none of you in anything, even slightly, but to live among you in the greatest tranquility and cheerfully serve the Lord our God in peace of mind and body. But because not all of you truly seek the things that are God’s, I must rebuke and at times disturb the restless, lest impunity for small offenses provide boldness for graver ones. For I know what dangerous necessity I undergo in the pastoral office, and therefore I neither can nor ought to be silent when you sin, lest I be judged by some to have consented.

I willingly endure it if on this account I happen to be hated. But since this cannot happen without the gravest danger to your souls, we beseech you through our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us, that for the love of God and for the remission of your sins you always endure our fatherly and necessary rebukes patiently and with true humility. Let each one think within himself that there is no day on which he does all things well and does not offend in something; and let him know that he will shortly receive the reward of his works: good things for good deeds, and likewise evil things for evil deeds.

Therefore let him strive, as much as he can, to make satisfaction for his faults in this life, and humbly expiate all his iniquities by daily chastisement of the body. Know, my brothers, that there is no sin so small that the justice of Almighty God lets it go unpunished. Therefore, since there is none of us who does not offend in many things, arm yourselves, I pray, with patience and humility, so that whenever you are corrected for your sins, you may bear it with all meekness. For in this time of free will you can make satisfaction for many debts with a small expiation, whereas after death in purgatory the soul will be tormented for a long time and most grievously even for small sins.

Indeed, voluntary satisfaction is worth much; but that which is made from necessity earns less toward grace. Altogether, brothers, it is fitting and necessary for the soul to be cleansed from fault if it ought to reign in heaven and rejoice with Christ. But the soul that has neglected the cleansing of its faults in the present life will be punished more severely in the life to come. Let none of you, my dearest brothers, say what many ignorant people are accustomed to say: “It is enough for me if my soul reaches the punishments of purgatory.” Believe me, brothers: whoever says this from the heart has not considered what purgatory will be. For he does not know what he asks who desires purgatory. Just as a man is foolish who, when he could pay his debt while free, despises this and willingly goes to prison, so he must deservedly be judged the most foolish of all men who, when he can make satisfaction to God for his sins in this life, delays.

87
ad futuram. Huius vitae fructuosa est poenitentia, et voluntaria satisfactio, multum quoque meritoria: post mortem vero non erit locus poenitendi, sed unusquisque tunc recipiet, prout gessit in corpore suo, sive bonum, sive malum. Haec fratres cogitate, dum sani vivitis, ne mortis imperio praecoccupati sero tandem doleatis. Dubium non expe-ctet crastinum salus hodierna, et, qui debitum potest cum gratia in libertate solvere, non se patiatur ad carcerem trahi cum tortura. Quantum quisque potest in omni vita sua, tantum curet satisfacere pro pec- catis, quoniam securus ad Dominum spiritus revertitur, qui adhuc in corpore existens per ignem Divini amoris quotidianie purgatur. Habetis hic locum, in quo publicorum reatum quotidiana expiatio agitur; si veram et humilem tenueritis in animo patientiam, certam procul dubio consequemini omnium remissionem. Pro secretis vero, et occultis quid agere debeatis, non solum regula vos admonet, sed etiam quotidiana confessio sacramentalis ad omnia informat. Ad altare nanque Dei filium quotidianie singuli devote immolare consuevimus, ad quod sacrosanctum mysterium nemo nostrum accedit, nisi prius ex more confessus, quo- niam summa puritas requiritur, ubi salus per missam totius mundi re- novatur. Quis inter haec nostrum, fratres amantissimi, quotidianie in Dei amore non proficiat, nisi omnem proficiendi appetitum turpiter, ac paenitus deponat? Audeo namque dicere, quia Monachus, qui in hac sancta congregatione non proficit, salutis propriae paenitus convincitur oblitus. Credite mihi fratres, neminem Deus salvabit invitum: si vos profectum neglexeritis proprium, non illi, sed vobis imputabitur. Deus enim lumen est intellectuale, quod illuminat omnem hominem venien- tem in hunc mundum, sicut altivolans inquit Ioannes: qui autem lu- men non recipiunt, in tenebris necessario permanserunt. Qui mentem suam avertit a fide, quae est in filio Dei, manet in tenebris: et, qui non facit opera lucis, nihil fides ei proderit ad salutem. Extra fidem Domini nostri Iesu Christi non est salus: et qui aliter sentit, non est Christianus. Non te seducat o homo pietatis stultae consideratio, ut credas aliquem extra fidem Christi in qualibet religione salvandum, quantumlibet vivat innocenter, vel ad legem naturae: quoniam sicut extra Noe arcani non fuit hominibus vita, sic extra fidem Christianam non est alicui salus ad vitam aeternam. Christus enim Dei filius unicus, et solus salvator est mundi, in quem quicumque non crediderit, ira Dei manet super illum, et cum diabolo condemnabitur. Vos autem, fratres mei, qui iam in Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum creditis, ita precor, deinceps vivite, ut nomine, et opere Christiani, ad eius con- sortium pervenire valeatis, qui vivit, et regnat cum Deo Patre in uni- tate spiritus santi, Deus, per omnia saecula saeculorum.

In this life repentance is fruitful, and voluntary satisfaction also highly meritorious; but after death there will be no place for repentance, and then each person will receive according to what he has done in his body, whether good or evil. Think on these things, brothers, while you live in health, lest, overtaken by the command of death, you at last grieve too late. Present salvation should not wait for an uncertain tomorrow; and he who can pay his debt with grace while free should not allow himself to be dragged to prison with torment.

As much as each person can in his whole life, so much let him take care to make satisfaction for his sins, since the spirit returns securely to the Lord when, while still existing in the body, it is daily purified by the fire of divine love. Here you have a place in which daily expiation is made for the guilt of public offenses; if you keep true and humble patience in your soul, you will without doubt obtain certain remission of all. As for secret and hidden sins, what you ought to do is taught to you not only by the Rule, but also by daily sacramental confession, which instructs you in all things.

For each day we are accustomed devoutly, one by one, to offer the Son of God at the altar; and none of us approaches that most holy mystery unless he has first, according to custom, made confession, because the greatest purity is required where the salvation of the whole world is renewed through the Mass. Amid these things, dearly beloved brothers, who among us would not daily make progress in the love of God, unless he disgracefully and utterly laid aside every desire for progress? For I dare to say that the monk who does not make progress in this holy congregation is plainly proved to have utterly forgotten his own salvation.

Believe me, brothers: God will save no one unwillingly. If you neglect your own progress, it will be imputed not to him but to you. For God is the intellectual light that enlightens every man coming into this world, as high-flying John says; but those who do not receive the light necessarily remain in darkness. He who turns his mind away from the faith that is in the Son of God remains in darkness; and if he does not do the works of light, faith will profit him nothing for salvation.

Outside the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ there is no salvation; and whoever thinks otherwise is not a Christian. Do not let the consideration of foolish pity seduce you, O man, into believing that anyone outside the faith of Christ, in any religion whatever, will be saved, however innocently he may live, even according to the law of nature; for just as outside the ark of Noah there was no life for human beings, so outside the Christian faith there is no salvation for anyone unto eternal life. For Christ, the only Son of God, is the sole savior of the world; whoever does not believe in him, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he will be condemned with the devil.

But you, my brothers, who now believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, I beg you: henceforth live in such a way that, Christians in name and in deed, you may be able to come to fellowship with him who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever.

88
Homilia XIII. 93 De vera poenitentia monachorum. Homilia XIII. QUAMVIS tota conversatio nostra, fratres mei charissimi, recte poenitentia nominari possit, quippe qui et nobis mortui, et mundo iam sepulti videmur; quia tamen carne mortali sumus circumdati, et peregrinamur in medio nationis peccatricis, fieri non potest, quin, fragilitatis propriae impulsu, quotdie in aliquo delinquamus, pro cuius expiatione non solum generaliter, sed etiam specialiter fuerit poenitendo satisfaciendum: Est enim poenitentia cunctis mortalibus necessaria, qua et commissa mala deplangant cum emendationis proposito, et deinceps, quantum fieri potest, vivere statuant sine peccato. Monachorum est proprium, sine intermissione poenitentiam agere, et tam pro suis, quam pro alienis peccatis iugiter orare. Non enim docentis officium habet monachus, ut sacer Hieronymus inquit, sed plangentis, qui vel se lugeat infirmus, vel mundum perfectus, et Domini pavidus praestoletur adventum. Si perfectus es monachus, poenitentiam agito pro peccatis alienis: si vero infirmus, oportet ut amplius poeniteas pro propriis. Semper itaque poenitendum est monacho, qui non solum pro suis, sed etiam pro delictis aliorum intercessor ad Deum constituitur. Sed quis in vobis est fratres, qui proprio non gravetur delicto? Quis inquam, est vestrum, qui non indigeat poenitentia? Video vos in multis quotidianie offendere, et doleo: cerno, quam praeteritorum negligatis poenitentiam, et contremisco. Nunquid non agnoscitis vos esse mortales? Et quare vocabulo monachi non satisfacitis, ut poenitentiam in tempore necessarium agatis? Mementote quaeso comminantis scripturae dicentis. Ne tardes converti ad Dominum, et ne differas de die in diem. Subito enim veniet ira illius, et in tempore vindictae disperdet te. Non enim praeteribit mortem, quae vobis, o senes, in ianua est, et iunioribus latet in insidiis: sed, quando minus cogitatis, de corpore compulsum exiet spiritus. Unde si vos esse peccatores recognoscitis, si venire ad Dei misericordiam desideratis, amodo iam poenitentiam, precor, assumite, et mores vestros in omnibus secundum regulae puritatem emendate. Satis sit hactenus veram negligisse poenitentiam, et nimis tepidam tanto continuasse tempore conversationem. Deus etenim, qui dissimulat peccata hominum propter poenitentiam, differentibus poenitere non promisit vitae prolongationem. Considerate longanimitatem Dei, qui vos peccantes quotidianie tam diu misericorditer distulit, et agite poenitentiam, quatenus optatam inveniatis remissionem. Dicit enim Dominus per Prophetam: Nolo mortem impii, sed ut convertatur a via sua mala, et vivat. In Sancto quoque Evangelio dicit. Poenitentiam agite, appropinquavit enim Regnum Coelorum. Magnum est bonum poeni- 94 De vera poenitentia monachorum.

Homily XIII.

On the True Penance of Monks. Homily XIII.

Although our whole way of life, my most beloved brothers, may rightly be called penance, since we seem both dead to ourselves and already buried to the world, nevertheless, because we are surrounded by mortal flesh and live as pilgrims in the midst of a sinful nation, it cannot happen that, driven by our own frailty, we do not offend daily in some matter. For the expiation of this, satisfaction must be made by penance not only generally but also specifically.

For penance is necessary for all mortals: by it they both lament the evils they have committed, with a purpose of amendment, and resolve thereafter, as far as can be done, to live without sin. It is proper to monks to do penance without interruption and continually to pray both for their own sins and for those of others. For a monk does not have the office of one who teaches, as Saint Jerome says, but of one who laments: either, if weak, he mourns himself, or, if perfect, the world, and in fear awaits the coming of the Lord.

If you are a perfect monk, do penance for the sins of others; but if you are weak, you must do penance all the more for your own. Therefore a monk must always do penance, for he is appointed before God as an intercessor not only for his own sins but also for the offenses of others.

But who among you, brothers, is not weighed down by his own fault? Who among you, I ask, does not need penance? I see you offending daily in many things, and I grieve; I perceive how you neglect penance for past sins, and I tremble. Do you not recognize that you are mortal? And why do you not live up to the name of monk, so that you do the necessary penance while there is time?

Remember, I beg you, the threatening Scripture, which says: “Do not delay to be converted to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” For death will not pass you by; it is at the door for you old men, and lies hidden in ambush for the younger. But when you least expect it, the spirit, driven from the body, will depart.

Therefore, if you acknowledge that you are sinners, if you desire to come to the mercy of God, from now on, I beg you, take up penance, and amend your conduct in all things according to the purity of the rule. Let it be enough that until now you have neglected true penance and have continued for so long in a way of life that is far too lukewarm. For God, who overlooks the sins of men for the sake of penance, has not promised a prolonging of life to those who defer repentance.

Consider the long-suffering of God, who has mercifully put up with you for so long while you sin daily, and do penance, so that you may find the remission you desire. For the Lord says through the prophet: “I do not will the death of the wicked, but that he be converted from his evil way and live.” He also says in the holy Gospel: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Penance is a great good [unclear].

89
tentia mortalibus, quae sordidas purgat animas, et mentes ab interitu revocat destinato. Hinc Divus dicit Augustinus; Poenitentia languores sanat, leprosos curat, et mortuos suscitat, sanctitatem auget, gratiam conservat. Poenitentia claudis gressum, coecis visum, aridis copiam, debilibus restituit firmitatem, vitia fugat, virtutes exornat, mentem munit, et corroborat. Illa autem vera est poenitentia, fratres, quam necessariae partes, ut totum, veracitater commendant; ubi contritio mentem penetrat, ubi latens peccatum humilis, et pura confessio referat, ubi pro viribus satisfacit obedientia, ubi sic poenitens dolet de praeteritis, ut veraciter omni tempore caveat a futuris. Vera poenitentia est, quam Dei amor gemitibus exornat, et lachrymis: ubi plus dolet peccator de offensa Dei, quam timeat de cruciatu inferni. Et quis nostrum non doleat, fratres amantissimi, quis non ingemiscat monachorum, in legem se deliquisse altissimi, a quo habemus non solum vivere, sed etiam expectamus promissionem foelicitatis aeternae? Vae nobis, fratres, si veram agere poenitentiam in hac vita neglexerimus, quam ut semper ageremus, monachi facti sumus. Nostra enim conversatio in solo crucifixo Iesu Christo debet esse occupata, et a mundi solatii paenitus aliena. Non decent te mundi solatia o monache, non voluptates, non deliciae, non risus, non cachinni, non aliqua consolatio carnis, sed moeror, et amaritudo cum lachrymis: quibus si non indulseris continue, monachi vocabulum amisisti. Non licet tibi gaudere cum saeculo, qui mortuus es mundo: nec debes aliqua praesentis vitae solatia quaere, qui Domino promisisti secundum regulam monasticam in solitudine servire. Tuum est, monache, universa huius mundi gaudia pro Dei amore semper, et ubique contemnere, et nulla adversa, vel dura subire pro honore salvatoris tui recusare. Sic enim te canon monet, sic institutio monastica iubet, sic ratio salutis necessaria suadet. Omni vilitate, et extremitate iuberis esse contentus, et semper ad omnia pavidus. Sed video plerosque vestrum regulam salutis pervertere, et aliter, quam oportet in coenobio conversari. Delicias monachi nunc quaerere in coenobiis non metuunt, qui ad conversionem pauperes, et mendici de saeculo venerunt. Nam quae foris habere non poterant, iam si defuerint in monasterio, quasi contumeliam passi gravissimam, contra humilitatem rebellis sunt. Vae monachis, quos non Dei amor, sed inopia fecit claustrales, quorum Deus venter est, et nihil minus quam paupertatem cogitant. Non est vestrum, o monachi, delicias in monasterio deinceps quaerere, quas regula praecipit omnino abnegare. Vobis convenit omnes voluptates praesentis vitae spernere, et praeter Deum nihil in hoc mundo paenitus amare. Tota enim conversatio vestra divinis semper debet esse mancipata obsequiis, qui vivere spiritu, et non secundum carnem promisistis. Nunquam sine poenitentia vivit, qui verus

Penance for mortals cleanses filthy souls and calls minds back from the destruction destined for them. Hence Saint Augustine says: Penance heals sicknesses, cures lepers, raises the dead, increases holiness, preserves grace. Penance restores walking to the lame, sight to the blind, abundance to the barren, firmness to the weak; it drives away vices, adorns virtues, fortifies and strengthens the mind.

But that is true penance, brothers, whose necessary parts truly commend it as a whole: where contrition pierces the mind; where humble and pure confession discloses hidden sin; where obedience makes satisfaction according to its powers; where the penitent so grieves for past things that he truly guards himself at all times against things to come. True penance is that which the love of God adorns with groans and tears, where the sinner grieves more over the offense against God than he fears the torment of hell.

And who among us would not grieve, most beloved brothers? Who among the monks would not groan that he has sinned against the law of the Most High, from whom we have not only life, but also await the promise of eternal happiness? Woe to us, brothers, if in this life we have neglected to do true penance, for the continual practice of which we became monks. For our way of life ought to be occupied in Jesus Christ alone, crucified, and altogether alien to the consolations of the world.

Worldly consolations do not befit you, O monk; not pleasures, not delights, not laughter, not guffaws, not any comfort of the flesh, but sorrow and bitterness with tears. If you do not continually give yourself to these, you have lost the name of monk. It is not lawful for you to rejoice with the world, you who are dead to the world; nor ought you to seek any consolations of the present life, you who promised the Lord to serve in solitude according to the monastic rule. It is your part, monk, always and everywhere to despise all the joys of this world for the love of God, and to refuse to undergo no adversity or hardship for the honor of your Savior. For so the canon admonishes you, so the monastic institution commands, so the necessary reasoning of salvation advises.

You are commanded to be content with every vileness and extremity, and always fearful toward all things. But I see very many of you perverting the rule of salvation and living in the monastery otherwise than you ought. Monks now do not fear to seek delights in monasteries, though they came from the world to conversion poor and beggars. For the things they could not have outside, if they are now lacking in the monastery, they become rebellious against humility, as though they had suffered a most serious insult. Woe to the monks whom not the love of God but poverty has made cloistered, whose god is the belly, and who think of nothing less than poverty.

It is not for you, O monks, henceforth to seek delights in the monastery, which the rule commands you wholly to renounce. It befits you to despise all the pleasures of the present life and to love absolutely nothing in this world except God. For your whole way of life ought always to be bound to divine services, you who promised to live by the spirit and not according to the flesh. He who is a true [unclear] never lives without penance.

90
Homilia XIII. 95 est monachus; sed quotidiē corpus suum per abstinentiam macerat, quisquis ad aeternae foelicitatis epulas veraciter anhelat. Non enim fieri potest, ut praesentis vitae deliciis utatur monachus, et aeternis, sed necesse est, si ad illas anhelat, istas contemnat. Christi nanque salva- toris esse discipulus iubetur monachus, qui canonem profitetur coeno- biticum: cui si placere in veritate desiderat, necesse est, ut eius imitator fiat. Sic enim in sancto Evangelio dicit: Qui vult meus esse discipulus, me sequatur. Quid vero sit, me sequatur, sanctus Ioannes Apostolus in epistola quadam edocet dicens: Qui dicit se in Christo manere, debet sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambulare. Et ipse Dominus iterum in Evan- gelio dicit: Qui vult venire post me, abneget semet ipsum, et tollat crucem suam quotidiē, et sequatur me. Qui amat patrem, aut matrem plus quam me, non est me dignus. Et: qui amat filium, aut filiam super me, non est me dignus. Et: qui non accipit crucem suam, et sequitur me, non est me dignus. Non est obscurē locutus magister tuus, o monache, neque sententiam aenigmatibus involvit, sed enōdem protulit sermonem, quo nullam praetendere quas excusationem.
