Ipse nanque Christus est exemplar, et norma conversationis bonae, et per- fectae omni Christiano, et praecipie monacho, quem homo claustralis, qui pro viribus in toto corde non sequitur, de fidei professione frustra gloriatur. Nam sicut a Christo dicitur Christianus, ita nominatur ab imitatione magistri discipulus. Moribus igitur imitare magistrum, ut verum te Christi probes discipulum. Dominus enim Iesus Christus, cuius te profiteris discipulum o monache, cum esset dives, pro nobis pauper factus est: tu autem cum sis vilis, et inops in schola pauper- tatis omnium rerum abundantiam quaeris: et, quem praecceptor iubet omnia pro sui amore contemnere, rursus omnia cupis in monasterio possidere. Dominus, et magister tuus Patri usque ad mortem crucis obediens pro nobis extitit; tu vero, superbia et impatiēntia plenus, obe- dire maiōribus pro eius amore, aut renuis, aut invitus, et cum indi- gnatione obedis. Ille propter salutem tuam non solum verba, et opprobria improborum hominum patientissime in omni vita sua sustinuit, sed etiam verbera, plagasque lividas, et horrenda vulnera tui amore toleravit. Mor- tem quoque subiere turpissimam non renuit, ut animam tuam ab errore mortis ad vitam lucis aeternae revocaret. A die nativitatis suae in mundo pauper vixit, et humilis, multisque tribulationibus saturatus, et oppro- briis, ut te perditissimum hominem ad Dei cognitionem, et amorem doctrina, et beneficiis repararet. Quid enim essēmus, si Dei filius non apparuiisset homo, nisi perditissimi? et quid sumus, si non imitemur magistrum pro viribus, nisi ingrati? Vae nobis ingratis mortalibus, qui Dominum, et salvatorem nostrum humillimum sequi contemnimus. In- tuemur conversationem nostram, frātres, et comparemus discipulos ad 96 De vera poenitentia monachorum.

is a monk; but whoever truly longs for the banquets of eternal happiness daily chastises his body through abstinence. For it cannot be that a monk should enjoy both the delights of the present life and the eternal ones; rather, if he longs for those, he must despise these.

For the monk who professes the cenobitic rule is commanded to be a disciple of Christ the Savior; and if he desires to please him in truth, he must become his imitator. For thus he says in the holy Gospel: “He who wishes to be my disciple, let him follow me.” And what “let him follow me” means, the holy apostle John teaches in one of his letters, saying: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked.” And the Lord himself again says in the Gospel: “He who wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And he who loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. And he who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.”

Your teacher has not spoken obscurely, O monk, nor wrapped his meaning in riddles, but has set forth a plain saying, by which you can put forward no excuse. For Christ himself is the example and rule of good and perfect conduct for every Christian, and especially for the monk; and the cloistered man who, with all his powers and with his whole heart, does not follow him, boasts in vain of the profession of faith. For just as a Christian is so called from Christ, so a disciple is named from imitation of his master. Therefore imitate your master in your conduct, so that you may prove yourself a true disciple of Christ.

For the Lord Jesus Christ, whose disciple you profess yourself to be, O monk, though he was rich, became poor for our sake; but you, though you are lowly and needy in the school of poverty, seek abundance of all things, and though your teacher commands you to despise everything for love of him, you in turn desire to possess everything in the monastery. Your Lord and teacher was obedient to the Father for our sake, even to the death of the cross; but you, full of pride and impatience, either refuse to obey your superiors for love of him, or obey unwillingly and with indignation.

For the sake of your salvation, he not only endured with the utmost patience throughout his whole life the words and insults of wicked men, but also for love of you bore blows, livid wounds, and dreadful injuries. He did not refuse even to undergo a most shameful death, so that he might call your soul back from the error of death to the life of eternal light. From the day of his birth he lived in the world poor and humble, filled with many tribulations and insults, so that by his teaching and benefits he might restore you, a most ruined man, to the knowledge and love of God.

For what would we be, if the Son of God had not appeared as man, except utterly lost? And what are we, if we do not imitate our master with all our powers, except ungrateful? Woe to us ungrateful mortals, who disdain to follow our most humble Lord and Savior. Let us look at our conduct, brothers, and compare the disciples to...

91
magistrum, cuius nomen invocatum est super nos, et, quam longe re- cesserimus a semitis benignissimi praecessoris nostri, manifeste intelli- gemus. Sed revertamur ad eum in toto corde, precor, et agamus, Poe- nitentiam, quia procul a via salutis recessimus, carni potius, quam spiritui servientes. Nemo semetipsum spei vanitate decipiat, nullus ul- timam huius vitae horam, quando iam nequeat peccare, pro poenitentia expectet, quia nec vitae quantitas habet certitudinem, nec dilatio poe- nitendi securitatem. Qui sanus non poenitet, stultus est: et qui non emendat vitia, cum potest, iusto Dei iudicio dilatam amittit potestatem. Tunc enim fructuosa est poenitentia, cum arbitrii libertate fuerit vo- luntaria: sed mortis iam instante periculo videtur potius esse necessaria, quam propria poenitentis electione assumpta. Nemo dicat in corde suo, fratres mei, nemo cogitet durum esse poenitendi laborem, et idcirco usque in ultimam huius vitae particulam differendum. Nimis est peri- culosa ista cogitatio, quoniam vitae certum terminum, quem unicum divina providentia statuit, sicuti latere omnes voluit, ita nulli poeniten- tiam di"erenti ex intentione prolongabit. Si volumus esse conscientia tuti, atque securi, agamus poenitentiam, dum sani sumus, dum peccare possimus, dum adhuc nulla mortis necessitate instantis urgemur. Valde nanque dubia res est poenitentiam agere, cum iam necessitas compellit, et mortis te instantia facit non amplius posse peccare, quando videlicet non tu peccata, sed illa impotentem te sui dimiserunt. O quam multi spe vitae longioris decepti ad barathrum damnationis aeternae descen- dunt, qui poenitentiam agere sani contemperunt. Quanto enim diutius poenitentiam distuleris, tanto semper ad poenitentiam minus dispositus invenieris. Sumit nanque malitia cum tempore vires, et nullum est peccatum tam parvum, quod non crescat neglectum. Poenitentiam igitur amplectere, dum sanus es, nec differas de die in diem, quoniam quid hodie possis, intelligis: quid autem futurum sit crastino, ignoras. Affert enim sua quaeque nova incommoda dies, et qui hodie ad poenitentiam non est dispositus, cras forsitam minus aptus erit. Nemo autem dicat vestrum, quid peccavi, ut mihi necessaria videatur poenitentia, cum vita mea tota nihil sit aliud, quam dura quaedam, et prolixa poenitendi necessitas? Audistis, scriptura testante, quoniam non est homo super terram, qui benefaciat, et non peccet, cum nemo sit mundus coram Deo. Nam, et si non committatis grandia humanae impietatis scelera, ut sunt homicidium, furtum, adulterium, fornicationes, et his similia, quia tamen in ea estis vocatione constituti, in qua viribus totis ad statum perfectionis omnem debetis elevare conatum, peccata, quae mortalibus in mundo viventibus parva sunt, vobis certe graviora imputantur. Ca- venda sunt enim claustralibus, quantum fieri potest, omnia peccata, non solum, quae salutem impediunt, sed etiam, quae commaculant indictam

the master, whose name has been invoked over us, and we shall clearly understand how far we have withdrawn from the paths of our most kindly predecessor. But let us return to him with our whole heart, I beg you, and do penance, because we have withdrawn far from the way of salvation, serving the flesh rather than the spirit.

Let no one deceive himself with empty hope; let no one wait for the final hour of this life, when he can no longer sin, as the time for penance, because neither the length of life is certain nor delay in repenting safe. He who does not repent while healthy is foolish; and he who does not amend his vices when he can, by the just judgment of God loses the power he had put off using. For penance is fruitful when it has been voluntary, by freedom of choice; but when the danger of death is already pressing, it seems to be necessary rather than undertaken by the penitent’s own choice.

Let no one say in his heart, my brothers, let no one think that the labor of repentance is hard and therefore to be put off until the very last particle of this life. That thought is exceedingly dangerous, since the certain limit of life, the one which divine providence has fixed, just as it has willed it to lie hidden from all, so it will prolong it for no one who deliberately defers repentance. If we wish to be safe and secure in conscience, let us do penance while we are healthy, while we are able to sin, while we are not yet pressed by any necessity of approaching death.

For it is a very doubtful matter to do penance when necessity already compels, and the pressure of death makes you no longer able to sin: that is, when it is not you who have left your sins, but they that have left you powerless over them. O how many, deceived by the hope of a longer life, go down to the pit of eternal damnation, who in health despised doing penance. For the longer you put off penance, the less disposed to penance you will always be found. For malice gains strength with time, and there is no sin so small that it does not grow when neglected.

Therefore embrace penance while you are healthy, and do not put it off from day to day, because you understand what you can do today, but you do not know what tomorrow will bring. For each new day brings its own troubles, and he who today is not disposed to penance will perhaps be less fit for it tomorrow. But let none of you say, “What have I sinned, that penance should seem necessary for me, when my whole life is nothing other than a certain hard and prolonged necessity of doing penance?”

You have heard, with Scripture as witness, that there is no man upon earth who does good and does not sin, since no one is clean before God. For even if you do not commit the great crimes of human impiety, such as murder, theft, adultery, fornications, and the like, nevertheless, because you have been placed in that vocation in which you ought with all your strength to raise every effort toward the state of perfection, sins which are small for mortals living in the world are certainly imputed to you as more serious. For cloistered men must avoid, as far as possible, all sins, not only those that hinder salvation, but also those that stain the prescribed [unclear].

92
Homilia XIII. 97 perfectionem. Et quis vestrum tanta puritate vivit, quantum perfectio monastica requirit? Grande peccatum est monacho, si a perfectione conatum suum deposuerit, si negligentiter in monasterio vixerit, si vel unum canonis, et Evangelii mandatum transgressus fuerit. Et quis in vobis est, fratres, qui Dominum Deum tanta sinceritate, tanta charitate, tantoque diligit fervore amoris, sicut homo factorem, et redemptorem suum tenetur diligere? Aut quem dabitis mihi ex omnibus vobis, qui non excedat aliquando vel in cibo sumendo, vel in potu plus, quam integritati congruit monachorum? Quis vestrum non offendit in verbo? aut quis non vexatur aliquando cogitationibus malis? Quem in vobis non percussit acidia? et quem tristis non turbavit pigritia? Quis est ille, quem in hac parva congregatione vestrum non tangat elatio, et quem non facit impatiens frequentius murmurantem? Consideret unus- quique vestrum semitas conversationis suae, et inveniet se in multis quolibet etiam momento delinquere. Quid enim si nihil mali commi- serit monachus? Quid si mundum se custodierit ab hoc saeculo nequam? Perfectus esse non poterit, nisi, et a malo declinaverit, et bonum fe- cerit, quod eius perfectione requirit. Alterum enim sine altero non sufficit, sed ex utroque perfectione in homine consurgit. Summo igitur studio nobis semper invigilandum est fratres, ut satisfaciamus institutioni san- ctorum patrum, secundum quam vivere nos professione publica so- lemniter obligavimus, quatenus ad perfectionem nobis propositam co- natum nostrum sine intermissione dirigamus. Non retrahat nos a sancto conatu propriae infirmitatis nostrae consideratio, quia non minus adiu- vamur gratia creatoris, quam nostro curramus desiderio. Sicuti quotidi- in multis quidem negligentius conversando qualibet occasione delinqui- mus, ita singulis quoque momentis a torpore mentis resurgentes, san- ctum conatum in bono proposito renovemus. Coniungamus sanctis ora- tionibus lachrymas, et Dei semper auxilium devotis supplicationibus invocemus. Charitatem in omnibus custodiamus inviolabilem, quoniam ipsa est, quae multitudinem operit peccatorum. Singulis diebus bonus Christi miles, qui Domino suo cupit esse fidelis, conscientiam suam ad minus semel discutiendo examinet, et quantum in sancto profecerit desiderio, vel defecerit eo die, diligentius penset. Quoties vero depre- henderit se deliquisse in aliquo, confestim agat poenitentiam, et cum lachrymis a Domino postulet miserationem. Non dubium expectet cra- stinum salus hodierna, et qui statim potest invenire veniam, nullatenus interponat dilationem. Corde mox doleat se peccasse contra Dominum, sanctum quoque novo fervore innovet propositum, illumque diem se perdidisse paenitus existimet, in quo se melior proficiendo non evaserit. Semper in ore Monachi versetur oratio, in corde sit iugis compunctio, ab oculis lachrymae devotionis continue defluant, et interni amoris 98 De vera poenitentia monachorum.

And which of you lives with such purity as monastic perfection requires? It is a grave sin for a monk if he abandons his effort toward perfection, if he lives negligently in the monastery, if he transgresses even one commandment of the rule and of the Gospel. And who among you, brothers, loves the Lord God with such sincerity, such charity, and such fervor of love as a man is bound to love his maker and redeemer? Or whom will you give me from among all of you who does not sometimes go too far either in taking food or in drink, beyond what befits the integrity of monks? Which of you does not offend in word? Or who is not sometimes troubled by evil thoughts? Whom among you has acedia not struck? And whom has gloomy sloth not disturbed? Who is there in this small congregation of yours whom pride does not touch, and whom impatience does not more often make a murmurer?

Let each one of you consider the paths of his manner of life, and he will find that in many things, even at any moment, he is at fault. For what if a monk has committed no evil? What if he has kept himself unstained from this wicked age? He will not be able to be perfect unless he has both turned away from evil and done the good that his perfection requires. For one without the other is not enough, but from both together perfection arises in a man.

Therefore, brothers, we must always keep watch with the greatest zeal, so that we may satisfy the institution of the holy fathers, according to which we solemnly bound ourselves by public profession to live, in order that we may direct our effort without interruption toward the perfection set before us. Let not the consideration of our own weakness draw us back from holy effort, because we are helped no less by the grace of the Creator than we run by our own desire. Just as every day, by living rather negligently in many things, we fall into fault on any occasion, so also at every moment, rising again from the sluggishness of mind, let us renew our holy effort in our good purpose.

Let us join tears to holy prayers, and always call upon the help of God with devout supplications. Let us keep charity inviolate in all things, since it is charity that covers the multitude of sins. Each day the good soldier of Christ who desires to be faithful to his Lord should examine his conscience by searching it at least once, and should weigh carefully how much he has advanced in holy desire, or fallen short in it, on that day. And whenever he finds that he has sinned in anything, let him at once do penance, and with tears ask mercy from the Lord. Let today’s salvation not wait for the uncertain morrow; and he who can immediately find pardon must in no way insert delay. Let him at once grieve in heart that he has sinned against the Lord; let him also renew his holy purpose with new fervor, and let him judge that he has utterly lost that day on which, by making progress, he has not become better.

Let prayer always be on the monk’s lips; let continual compunction be in his heart; let tears of devotion flow continually from his eyes, and [unclear] of inward love.

93
exercitia nunquam ab eius memoria recedant. Crebro sit in mente hominis claustralis Dominicae Passionis amarissimae recordatio, et omnes preces, quas facit ad patrem, in virtute sanguinis, et vulnerum Domini nostri Iesu Christi porrigamus. Semper in ore sint verba compunctae mentis indicium pra se ferentia, et vel oratio porrigatur ad Deum, vel sermonum eius meditatio revolvatur. Declinet a malo devotus Mo- nachus, et faciat bonum, quod potest, cum hilaritate et discretione spiritus Dei, quoniam, sicut est dictum, ad poenitentiam agendum non sufficit mores commutare in melius, et a malefactis recedere, nisi etiam bonis operibus conscientiam suam studeat exornare. Ad veram igitur poenitentiam quatuor, ut scitis fratres mei, requiruntur. Primum est contritio vera pro peccatis, quae est dolor cordis voluntarie assumptus in eorum detestationem malorum, quae commisit. De qua scriptura dicit: Cor contritum, et humiliatum Deus non despiciet. Et iterum: Qui seminant in lachrymis, in exultatione metent. Comes enim poen- itentiae dolor est contritionis, qui quanto maior fuerit, tanto poenitentia fructuosior erit. Contritio nanque vera est, quam et dolor mentis com- mendat, et lachrymarum mundatio continua testatur. Magna est utilitas lachrymarum, quia nullum est tam grave peccatum, quod contritio lachrymis non deleat comitata. Hinc Sanctus Doctor Augustinus dicit: O humilis lachryma quam potens es, et virtuosa, quia tuum est regnum, tua est potentia. Aspectum iudicis non vereris: inimicis accusantibus silentium imponis: sola intras ad regem, sed sola non recedis: vincis invincibilem, et ligas omnipotentem. Idem quoque ait: Quanto est qui- libet sanctior, et desiderii sancti plenior, tanto est, in orando, fletus uberior. Vera compunctio dolorem habet, dolor autem lachrymis ostent- ditur, et his poenitentia quasi quibusdam ornamentis decoratur. Vera compunctio facit animum horrescere peccatum, quae cum ceperit a timore, suis aucta incrementis paulatim consurgit in amorem, cuius magna est virtus, et vere admiranda potestas, ut cui mox cedit omnis peccatorum enormitas. Quemcumque enim vera cordis compunctio sup- plicare fecerit, mox hunc misericors Dominus exaudit. O felices la- chrymae, o salutaris afflicto, et vere dulcis amaritudo, quam diabolus metuit, per quam anima compuncta ad Dei misericordiam consurgit. Nam, ut sanctus inquit Papa Gregorius, quo uberioris culpa defletur, eo altior cognitio veritatis attingitur, quia ad videndum internum lumen polluta dudum conscientia lachrymis baptizata renovatur. Secundum, quod ad poenitentiae veritatem pertinet, est firmum emendationis pro- positum, quoniam quisquis verbum confessionis in ore habet, et in corde non habet emendationis propositum, aut dolosus est, aut vanus. Qui vero in corde, et non in ore, aut superbus est, aut timidus, et ne- Rom. 10. quaquam ad veram poenitentiam idoneus. Dicit enim scriptura: Corde

Let these exercises never depart from his memory. Let the most bitter remembrance of the Lord’s Passion often be in the mind of the cloistered man, and let us offer all the prayers that he makes to the Father in the power of the blood and wounds of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let there always be on his lips words bearing before them the mark of a contrite mind, and let either prayer be offered to God or meditation on his words be turned over in the mind. Let the devout monk turn away from evil and do the good he can, with cheerfulness and with the discernment of the Spirit of God, since, as has been said, for doing penance it is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also strives to adorn one’s conscience with good works.

For true penance, then, four things are required, as you know, my brothers. The first is true contrition for sins, which is a sorrow of heart voluntarily undertaken in detestation of the evils one has committed. Of this Scripture says: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.” And again: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in rejoicing.” For the companion of penance is the sorrow of contrition, and the greater it is, the more fruitful the penance will be. True contrition, indeed, is that which both sorrow of mind commends and continual cleansing by tears bears witness to.

Great is the usefulness of tears, because there is no sin so grave that contrition, accompanied by tears, does not blot it out. Hence the holy teacher Augustine says: “O humble tear, how powerful you are, and how full of virtue, for yours is the kingdom, yours is the power. You do not fear the gaze of the judge; when enemies accuse, you impose silence. Alone you enter to the king, but alone you do not depart. You conquer the unconquerable and bind the omnipotent.” The same man also says: “The holier anyone is, and the fuller of holy desire, the more abundant is his weeping in prayer.”

True compunction has sorrow; sorrow, however, is shown by tears, and by these penance is adorned as though with certain ornaments. True compunction makes the soul shudder at sin; and when it has begun from fear, increased by its own growth it gradually rises into love. Great is its virtue, and truly admirable its power, since all enormity of sins soon yields to it. For whomever true compunction of heart has made a suppliant, the merciful Lord at once hears him. O happy tears, O saving affliction, and truly sweet bitterness, which the devil fears, through which the pierced soul rises up to the mercy of God. For, as the holy Pope Gregory says, the more abundantly guilt is wept over, the higher is the knowledge of truth that is reached, because a conscience once polluted, baptized anew with tears, is renewed for seeing the inward light.

The second thing that belongs to the truth of penance is a firm purpose of amendment, since whoever has the word of confession in his mouth and does not have the purpose of amendment in his heart is either deceitful or empty. But whoever has it in his heart and not in his mouth is either proud or fearful, and is by no means fit for true penance. For Scripture says: “With the heart…”

94
Homilia XIII. 99 creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Quae Christophili sententia, et si de fide Domini nostri Iesu Christi principali- ter intelligenda sit, recte nihilominus ad veram poenitentiam videtur applicanda. Nam, sine confessione oris, non sufficit ad poenitentiam sola contritio cordis, ex eo maxime tempore, quo statutum ecclesiae confessionem decrevit necessariam ad salutem. Tertium igitur oris con- fessio est ad veritatem poenitentiae necessarium, sine qua nec contri- tio sufficit, nec emendationis futurae propositum. Qualis vero debat esse haec salutaris confessio, neminem vestrum latere scio. Dico ta- men, quia fortassis non erit inutile, quoniam oportet confessionem esse propriam, integram, liberam, humilem, spontaneam, et verecun- dam. Dicit enim praesul sanctus Ambrosius, quoniam plurimum suf- fragatur Deo ad remittendum peccata hominibus verecunda confessio, et poenam, quam evitare defensione non possimus, pudore humili relevamus. Magna res est confessio debita peccatorum, quoniam et sauciam delictis animam confitentis mox ad sanitatem reformat spir- tualem, mentem quoque humiliatam iustificat, et veniam peccatis donat. Omnis enim spes nostra post lapsum peccati. consistit in humilitate confessionis, quoniam culpa non dimittitur, nisi Deo scienti omnia per sacerdotem in confessione reveletur. In confessione namque locus est misericordiae, sicut Salamon dicit in libro Proverbiorum: Qui ab- scondit scelera sua, non dirigetur: qui autem confessus fuerit, et re- liquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur. In psalmo quoque scriptum est: Dixi, confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino: et tu remi- sisti impietateim peccati mei. Sanctus etiam Evangelista Ioannes in epi- stola prima dicit: Si confiteamur peccata nostra, Deus fidelis est, et iustus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, et emundabit nos ab omni iniquitate. Et sanctus praesul Augustinus ait: Confessio est salus ani- marum, dissipatrix vitiorum, restauratrix virtutum, expugnatrix daemo- num, et cumulatrix omnium bonorum. Os claudit inferni, et portas coelestis aperit Paradisi. Cassiodorius quoque virtutem commendans verae confessionis, ita dicit: O beata confessio, quae sempiternum tol- lit opprobrium, quoniam quicquid reatum invenerit poenitentia, per- petuis seculis reddit absolutum. Quartum ad veram poenitentiam neces- sarium satisfactio est, qua videlicet omnes causas peccatorum excidentes auferimus, et pro his, quae commisimus perperam, sanctis operibus Dominum placamus. Hinc Divus Papa Gregorius ait: Nequaquam sa- tisfacimus, si ab iniquitate cessamus, nisi voluptates quoque, quas di- leximus, oppositis e contrario lamentis insequamur. Sanctissimus etiam Papa Leo in sermone dicit: Oratione Dei propitiatio quaeritur, ieiu- nio concupiscentia carnis extinguitur, eleemosynis peccata redimuntur, simulque per omnia Dei imago in nobis renovatur. Est autem confessio 100 De abstinence, et ieiunio monachorum. delinquentis voluntaria accusatio ex erubescentia, et per claves ecclesiae satisfactoria pro peccatis cum obligatione per poenitentiam ea, quae protulit, castigandi in semetipso, iussione Sacerdotis. Oportet autem confessionem esse simplicem, humilem, puram, fidelem, frequentem, nudam et apertam, discretam, voluntariam, propriam, verecundam, integram, secretam, lachrymis plenam, debitis temporibus factam, fortem, et seipsum ex animo veraciter accusantem, quoniam haec omnia requirit vera poenitentia, quae sic peccata deflet praeterita, ut deinceps non committat amplius plangenda. De abstinence, et ieiunio monachorum. Homilia XV.

Homily XIII.

With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Although this saying of the lover of Christ is to be understood chiefly of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, nevertheless it seems rightly applicable to true penitence. For without confession of the mouth, contrition of the heart alone is not sufficient for penitence, especially from that time when the statute of the Church decreed confession to be necessary for salvation.

Therefore the third thing necessary for the truth of penitence is confession of the mouth; without it neither contrition nor the purpose of future amendment is sufficient. I know that none of you is ignorant what this saving confession ought to be like. Yet I say it, because perhaps it will not be useless: confession must be one’s own, entire, free, humble, spontaneous, and shamefaced. For the holy bishop Ambrose says that a shamefaced confession greatly helps God in forgiving sins to men, and that the punishment which we cannot avoid by defense we lessen by humble shame.

A great thing is the due confession of sins, because it quickly restores to spiritual health the soul of the one confessing, wounded by offenses; it also justifies the humbled mind and grants pardon for sins. For all our hope after the fall of sin consists in the humility of confession, because guilt is not dismissed unless it is revealed in confession, through the priest, to God who knows all things.

For in confession there is place for mercy, as Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: He who hides his crimes will not be directed; but he who has confessed them and abandoned them will obtain mercy. It is also written in the Psalm: I said, I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin. The holy evangelist John also says in his first epistle: If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, so that he forgives us our sins and cleanses us from all iniquity.

And the holy bishop Augustine says: Confession is the salvation of souls, the scatterer of vices, the restorer of virtues, the conqueror of demons, and the heaper up of all good things. It closes the mouth of hell and opens the gates of the heavenly Paradise. Cassiodorus too, commending the power of true confession, speaks thus: O blessed confession, which takes away everlasting disgrace, because whatever guilt penitence finds, it renders absolved for endless ages.

The fourth thing necessary for true penitence is satisfaction: by it, namely, we cut off and remove all the causes of sins, and for those things which we have wrongly committed we appease the Lord with holy works. Hence the divine Pope Gregory says: We by no means make satisfaction if we cease from iniquity, unless we also pursue, with contrary lamentations, the pleasures which we loved. The most holy Pope Leo also says in a sermon: By prayer God’s favor is sought; by fasting the concupiscence of the flesh is extinguished; by alms sins are redeemed; and at the same time, through all these things, the image of God is renewed in us.

Confession, moreover, is the voluntary accusation of the offender arising from shame, and, through the keys of the Church, making satisfaction for sins, with the obligation, by penance and at the command of the priest, of chastising in oneself those things which one has brought forth. Confession must be simple, humble, pure, faithful, frequent, bare and open, discreet, voluntary, one’s own, shamefaced, entire, secret, full of tears, made at the proper times, strong, and truly accusing oneself from the heart; for true penitence requires all these things, which so laments past sins that thereafter it commits no more things that must be lamented.

On the abstinence and fasting of monks. Homily XV.

95
MAGNUM, et necessarium bonum est monacho, fratres charissimi, abstinence cum ieiunio, ut mente videlicet non delinquat in concupiscentia carnis, et cogitationibus malis, et corpore abstineat ab escis, et potibus lasciviam animi generantibus. Cito enim concupiscentia mentis in libidinem accenditur, si corpus nimis accurate nutriatur. Huius boni utilitatem maximam considerantes olim sanctissimi Patres, qui monachis vivendi praecerta tradiderunt, una omnes sententia ieiuniorum nobis certam statuere mensuram, sub cuius moderamine tantum corpus ciborum refectionem sumeret, quantam natura requireret, non quantam intemperies concupisceret voluntatis. Sancta quoque scriptura ieiunium nobis multipliciter commendat, cuius toties cum laude facit mentionem. Dicit enim Dominus Deus per os Prophetae sui Iohelis: Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro, in ieiunio, planctu et fletu. In libro quoque Iudith sic legitur. Scitote, quoniam exaudiet Dominus preces vestras, si manentes permaneritis in ieiunii, et orationibus in conspectu Domini. In Tobia similiter legimus. Bona est oratio cum ieiunio, et eleemosyna magis quam thesauros auri recondere: quoniam eleemosyna a morte liberat, et ipsa est, quae purgat peccata. Dominus quoque noster Iesus Christus in sancto Evangelio dixit ad discipulos: Beati, qui nunc esuritis, quoniam saturabimini. Optimum vero Monachorum ieiunium est abstinere a cunctis, quae animum polluere possunt, hoc est ociosum non proferre sermonem, vanas, inutiles, seu turpes nullas admittere cogitationes, nihil committere, quod Dei non deceat servum et nihil omittere, quod ad iustitiae pertinet consummationem. Nisi enim mens a vitiis, et peccatis ieiunaverit, corporalis abstinentia nihil ad animae proficiet salutem. Hinc divus Presbyter Hieronymus ait: Abstinence tua, atque ieiunium eo magis Deo grata sunt, quo cum moribus sanctis offerentur, ut, quae in aliis sunt umbracula vitiorum, in te fiant ornamenta virtutum. Nam quid prodest attenuari corpus abstinentia, si animus intumescit superbia? aut quid virtutis habet vinum

Abstinence with fasting is a great and necessary good for a monk, dearly beloved brothers: namely, that in mind he not sin through desire of the flesh and evil thoughts, and that in body he abstain from foods and drinks that beget wantonness of soul. For the desire of the mind is quickly kindled into lust if the body is nourished too carefully.

Considering the very great usefulness of this good, the most holy Fathers of old, who handed down fixed rules of life to monks, all with one judgment established for us a definite measure of fasting, under whose moderation the body should take only so much refreshment from foods as nature required, not as much as the excess of the will desired. Holy Scripture also commends fasting to us in many ways, and mentions it so often with praise. For the Lord God says through the mouth of his prophet Joel: “Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, lamentation, and weeping.” In the book of Judith also it is read thus: “Know that the Lord will hear your prayers, if you remain steadfast in fastings and prayers before the Lord.” Likewise we read in Tobit: “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good, more than storing up treasures of gold, because almsgiving delivers from death, and it is this that purges sins.” Our Lord Jesus Christ also said to his disciples in the holy Gospel: “Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be filled.”

But the best fasting of monks is to abstain from everything that can pollute the soul: that is, not to utter idle speech, to admit no vain, useless, or foul thoughts, to commit nothing unbecoming to a servant of God, and to omit nothing that belongs to the perfection of righteousness. For unless the mind fasts from vices and sins, bodily abstinence will profit nothing toward the soul’s salvation. Hence the holy priest Jerome says: “Your abstinence and fasting are the more pleasing to God, the more they are offered together with holy conduct, so that things which in others are coverings for vices may in you become ornaments of virtues.” For what good is it for the body to be made thin by abstinence, if the soul swells with pride? Or what virtue is there in wine...

96
Homilia XV. non bibere, et ira, luxuria, odio, atque invidia inebriari? Aut quid nobis conducet ad aeternam salutem, fratres, quod iuxta regulam Divi Patris nostri Benedicti carnes non comedimus, si carnis vitia non domamus? Dicit enim ter sanctus Papa Gregorius: Incassum corpus per abstinentiam atteritur, si inordinatis motibus divisa mens vitiis dissipatur. Unde bene dicit scriptura: Sanctificate ieiunium. Ieiunium sanctificare, est adiunctis aliis bonis operibus dignam Deo carnis abstinentiam ostendere. Enimvero si abstinentia sola ciborum hominem virtuosum efficeret, non opus fuisset adiungere, sanctificate: sed quia ieiunium ad sanctificati- onem animae solum sufficit, necessarium est, ut virtutum ornatu omnium decoretur. Nam, qui a cibis abstinent, et mala peragunt, dae- mones imitantur, quibus et semper est ieiunium, et nunquam deest peccatum. Acceptabile Deo ieiunium est corpus per abstinentiam a concupiscentia malorum restringere, et facta carnis per spiritum compu- ctionis pro Christi amore iugiter mortificare. Sit mens ieiunantis in Dei charitate fervida, sit conscientia semper a vitiis munda, et placebit altissimo servorum humilium ieiunia. Sint monachis quotidiana ieiunia, sicut canon sancti praecessoris Benedicti instituit: sint munda corda, sicut Dominus Iesus in sacro Evangelio praecepit: sit moderata reffectio satietatem fugiens, quoniam sicut ex nimia saturitate corpus diversis, et variis morbis corrumpitur, ita libidinis incompositus motus in eo concitatur. Modicus namque, ac moderatus cibus, et corpori est medicina, et animae virtutis adminiculum. Dicit enim sanctus Ioannes, os aureum, episcopus: Nihil sic iuncundum est, sicut cibus bene digestus, atque de- coctus; nihil sic salutem, nihil sic acumen operatur sensuum, nihil sic aegritudinem fugat, sicut moderata reffectio. Sufficientia enim cum nu- trimento moderata sospitatem simul procreat, et voluptatem. Abundantia vero, morbum facit, molestiasque ingerit, et aegritudines varias generat. Quod enim fames nimia facit, hoc etiam plenitudo immoderata ciborum consuevit operari. Fames quidem in paucis diebus auffert hominem, et liberat eum de hac vita poenali; excessus vero ciborum consumit, et computrescere facit corpus humanum, et macerat aegritudine diuturna, tandemque morte crudeli consumit. Ut ergo mente vivatis, et corpore sani, fratres mei dilectissimi, hanc normam vivendi tenete, quam vobis sancti Patres verbo praescripserunt, et vivo praemonstrarunt exemplo, ut omnem ciborum, potuvmque luxuriam fugientes, corpori tantum indulgeatis, quantum, requirente natura, bonae valetudini satis est. Cibus famem sedet, non corpus incitet ad libidinem: potus extinguat sitim, non mentein subvertat, aut sensum: vestis arceat frigus, non fa- ciat in vanitatis amore mollescere animum. Memores semper estote, fratres, quoniam gula primos parentes nostros de regno paradisi, et inocentiae turpiter expulit, qui non avem, non piscem, non vitulum de- De abstinentia, et ieiunio monachorum.

Homily XV.

What good is it not to drink, and yet to be drunk with anger, lust, hatred, and envy? Or what will it profit us for eternal salvation, brothers, that according to the Rule of our holy father Benedict we do not eat meat, if we do not tame the vices of the flesh?

For the thrice-holy Pope Gregory says: “The body is worn down in vain by abstinence, if the mind, distracted by disordered impulses, is scattered among vices.” Hence Scripture rightly says: “Sanctify the fast.” To sanctify the fast is to show abstinence of the flesh worthy of God by joining it with other good works. For if abstinence from food alone made a man virtuous, there would have been no need to add, “Sanctify”; but because fasting alone does not suffice for the sanctification of the soul, it must be adorned with the beauty of all the virtues. For those who abstain from foods and do evil imitate the demons, who always fast and are never without sin.

A fast acceptable to God is to restrain the body by abstinence from desire for evil things, and continually to mortify the deeds of the flesh by the spirit of compunction for love of Christ. Let the mind of the one fasting be fervent in the love of God; let his conscience always be clean from vices, and the fasts of humble servants will please the Most High. Let monks have daily fasts, as the rule of our holy predecessor Benedict established; let their hearts be clean, as the Lord Jesus commanded in the holy Gospel; let their refreshment be moderate, fleeing satiety, because just as the body is corrupted by many and various diseases from excessive fullness, so the disordered motion of lust is stirred up in it. For modest and moderate food is both medicine for the body and a support of virtue for the soul.

For Saint John, the golden mouth, the bishop, says: “Nothing is so pleasant as food well digested and cooked; nothing so works health, nothing so sharpens the senses, nothing so drives away sickness, as moderate refreshment. For sufficiency with moderate nourishment produces both soundness and pleasure. But abundance causes disease, brings troubles, and generates various illnesses. For what excessive hunger does, immoderate fullness of foods is also accustomed to do. Hunger indeed carries a man off in a few days and frees him from this penal life; but excess of foods consumes and makes the human body rot, wastes it with long illness, and at last destroys it by a cruel death.”

Therefore, in order that you may live in mind and be healthy in body, my dearly beloved brothers, keep this rule of living which the holy Fathers prescribed for you by word and showed beforehand by living example: fleeing all luxury in foods and drinks, indulge the body only so much as is enough for good health, as nature requires. Food should allay hunger, not incite the body to lust; drink should quench thirst, not overthrow the mind or the senses; clothing should ward off cold, not make the soul grow soft in love of vanity. Always remember, brothers, that gluttony shamefully drove our first parents from the kingdom of paradise and innocence; they did not desire a bird, or a fish, or a calf.

97
voraverunt, aut porcum, ut cibum aestimaretis in culpa, sed vilissimum pomum contra Dei mandatum praesumpserunt, quo non escam, sed appetitum sciatis obnoxium esse vitio peccati. Saepe namque fieri potest, ut aliquis homo lautiores cibos sine culpa sumat, dum appetitum regulat, qui viliores non sine conscientiae reatu percipit, cum temperantiae modum per immoderantiam excedit. Unde nemo vestrum se a vitio gulae propterea existimet securum, quia nec lauta cibaria comedit, nec delicata, cum non cibus, sed appetitus cibi habeatur in culpa. Valde namque possibile est manducantem fabas, et olera peccatum reatus contrahere, et aves in cibo sumentem alium delicatissimas non peccare. Hinc quidam sanctorum patrum dicit: Quibuslibet escis repletus venter seminaria luxuriae parit: nec praevalet mens discretionum gubernacula moderari ciborum pondere praefocata. Non enim sola crapula vini mentem inebriare consuevit, verum etiam cunctarum escarum nimietas vacillantem, ac nutabundam eam reddit, omnique integritatis, ac puritatis contemplatione omnino despoliat. Propterea magna discretione opus est, ut et corpori cibus duntaxat impendatur ad vitae sustentationem necessarius, et nullus indulgentiae fiat excessus. Hinc ait Divus Papa Gregorius: Magnus discretionis labor est exactori ciborum corpori, et aliquid impendere, et aliquid denegare, et non dando naturam enutrire. Per abstinentiam quippe, vitia extinguenda sunt, non caro; et per cibum corpus alendum est, non peccata. Sic ergo necessit est, ut artem continentiae monachus in victu teneat, quatenus non carnem, sed vitia occidat. Saepe enim dum in carne hostem persequimur, spiritum devotionis, quem diligimus, per immoderatam abstinentiam severe trucidamus. Saepius etiam dum carne nimium compatientes, quasi concivi parcimus, ad praelium contra nos hostem enutrimus. Dominante autem gulae vitio, omne, quod homines fortiter egerunt, perdunt, quia, dum venter non restringitur, simul omnes virtutes obruuntur. Nam ad conflictum spiritualis agonis non assurgitur, si non intra nosmetipsos positus hostis, gulae videlicet appetitus, per nos, iuvante Deo, prius edometur: quoniam, nisi ea, quae nobis sunt viciniora, superaverimus, inaniter ad ea, quae sunt longius posita, pugnaturi festinamus. Incassum namque contra extraneos inimicos bellum in campo geritur, dum intra urbis moenia civis insidians habeatur. Daemonum insultus nunquam vincimus, nisi gulam prius in nobismetipsis supereremus. Nemo se, fratres, inani persuasione seducat, ut inter fabas, et olera credat non esse peccatum, si animus nimia laxet voluptate percipiendi appetitum. Nam ubique potest in sumendo esse reatus, dum ultra naturae normam extenditur appetitus. Ecce carnem sive in monasterio, sive extra nunquam comedimus: pisces hic in rure campestri rarissime videntur: nemo inter nos unquam lautiora vidit cibaria; delicata habere, nec possumus, nec

they devoured, or a pig, so that you might think the food was at fault; rather, they presumed to take the vilest fruit against God’s command, so that you may know that not food, but appetite is liable to the fault of sin.

For it can often happen that a person takes richer foods without fault, while he governs his appetite, whereas another takes poorer foods not without guilt of conscience, when through immoderation he exceeds the measure of temperance. Therefore let none of you think himself safe from the vice of gluttony merely because he eats neither rich nor delicate foods, since it is not the food, but the appetite for food, that is held at fault. For it is quite possible for someone eating beans and vegetables to incur the guilt of sin, and for another taking the most delicate birds as food not to sin.

Hence one of the holy fathers says: “A belly filled with any foods at all produces the seedbeds of lust; nor can the mind prevail in managing the rudders of discretion when it has been choked by the weight of foods. For not only drunkenness from wine is accustomed to intoxicate the mind, but also excess in all foods makes it unsteady and wavering, and utterly strips it of every contemplation of integrity and purity.”

For this reason great discretion is needed, so that only the food necessary for sustaining life is given to the body, and no excess of indulgence occurs. Hence the divine Pope Gregory says: “It is a great labor of discretion both to give something and to deny something to the body that demands food, and by not giving to nourish nature.” For through abstinence the vices are to be extinguished, not the flesh; and through food the body is to be nourished, not sins. Thus it is necessary that a monk maintain the art of self-restraint in his diet, so that he kills not the flesh but the vices.

For often, while we pursue the enemy in the flesh, we severely slaughter, through immoderate abstinence, the spirit of devotion that we love. Very often too, while we show too much sympathy to the flesh and spare it as though it were a fellow-citizen, we nourish an enemy for battle against ourselves. But when the vice of gluttony rules, people lose everything they have done bravely, because when the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are at once overwhelmed. For one does not rise up to the struggle of the spiritual contest unless the enemy placed within ourselves, namely the appetite of gluttony, is first subdued by us with God’s help; since unless we overcome the things that are nearer to us, we hasten in vain to fight against those set farther away. For war is waged uselessly in the field against foreign enemies while a citizen plotting within the city walls is present. We never conquer the assaults of demons unless we first overcome gluttony in ourselves.

Brothers, let no one deceive himself with empty persuasion, so as to believe that there is no sin among beans and vegetables if the mind, with excessive pleasure, loosens the appetite for receiving them. For guilt can be present everywhere in taking food, when appetite is extended beyond the rule of nature. See: we never eat meat, whether in the monastery or outside it; fish are very rarely seen here in this rural countryside; no one among us has ever seen richer foods; we neither can have delicacies, nor...

98
Homilia XV. 103 quidem debemus, esculenta. Cibaria autem nostra sunt ordeum, avena, fabae, pisa, et olera, lac quoque, caseus, et ova. Ex his vitae nostrae quotidiana percipimus sustentacula, quorum ne consurgat fastidium, fames incitat appetitum. Pisces extra tempus ieiunii quadragesimalis nobis usque adeo sunt rari, ut vix in mense semel pauci afferantur ex Nabo flumine, atque minutissimi. Nullum est in tota Bursfeldensium reformatione coenobium minus in piscium necessitate provisum. Sed nun- quid propterea non possimus in gulae vitium incidere, quoniam lautora cibaria non possimus invenire? Enimvero cum non cibus in vitio sit, sicut iam dictum est, sed appetitus; non minus pisorum, aut fabarum comestor in edendo potest delinquere, quam ille, qui cibos lautissimos, et exquisitos consuevit manducare. Non facit nos inopia paenitus a gula securos, quamvis causas minuat in delicatioribus delinquendi. Habemus quidem victum simplicem, et rusticum, quoutcunque su- stentetur natura: hoc precor, fratres mei, curemus, ne illo, quod nau- seam delicatis generat, conscientia nostra per excessum polluatur. Su- mamus cum patientia, et gratiarum actione de eo, quod Dominus donavit, quantum necessitas ipsa requirit; nec putemus diaboli nobis non posse nocere insidias, qui primos in paradiso homines non lau- tiore cibo, sed modico, et vili pomo supplantavit. Non enim in cibo vi- tium est, sed in appetitu, cum aut interdicta nobis concupiscimus, aut concessis avide inhiantes aliter utimur, quam debemus. Neminem plus decet abstinentia, quam monachum, qui cum sit ad Christi mili- tiam specialiter vocatus, non convenit eius professioni quibuslibet va- care deliciis. Paupertas nostra abstinentiae nobis quandam necessitatem indicit, quia tanto nos facilius ad temperantiam possimus restringere quanto nos, quo defluamus, deliciarum minus possimus invenire. Ver- tamus itaque, precor, gravamina egestatis in arma salutis, ut quo minus lautioribus reficimur cibariis, eo purius in sanctitate animi ieiunemus. Facilius enim in paupertate servatur temperantia, quae in divitiis quidem periclitatur citius. Qualis autem debeat esse cibus monachorum, beatus manifestat Hieronymus dicens in epistola quadam ad Paulinum: Sit vils, et vespertinus tibi cibus, olera videlicet, et legumina, interdum- que pisciculos edere paucos pro summis ducas deliciis. Qui Christum desiderat, et illo caelesti pane vescitur, non quaerit magnopere, quam de preciosis cibis stercus conficiat. Amator Christi abstinentiam diligit, ieiunium, ut unicum animae, corporisque remedium colit, summo cavet studio, ne cor eius gravetur crapula, nec plus sumit ciborum, quam contenta paucis expostulat natura. Monachus autem, qui ieiunium abiicit, qui nutricem virtutum abstinentiam odit, qui cibos cum aviditate, ingur- gitat, qui vinum, aut siceram, et quicquid inebriare potest, ad satie- tatem potat, ipso monachi nomine indignus est, et Christi non potest 104 De abstinentia, et ieiunio monachorum.

Our foods are barley, oats, beans, peas, and vegetables, also milk, cheese, and eggs. From these we receive the daily supports of our life; and lest disgust at them arise, hunger stirs up appetite. Outside the season of the Lenten fast, fish are so rare for us that scarcely once in a month are a few, and very tiny ones, brought from the river Nabe. In the whole Bursfeld reform there is no monastery less provided with fish in time of need. But can we therefore not fall into the vice of gluttony, because we cannot find more sumptuous foods? Indeed, since the vice lies not in the food, as has already been said, but in the appetite, the eater of peas or beans can sin no less in eating than one who is accustomed to eat the most sumptuous and choice dishes. Poverty does not make us wholly secure from gluttony, although it lessens the occasions of sinning in more delicate fare.

We do indeed have simple and rustic food, by which nature is somehow sustained. This, my brothers, I beg us to take care over: that by excess our conscience not be polluted by that which produces nausea in the delicate. Let us take with patience and thanksgiving from what the Lord has given as much as necessity itself requires; and let us not think that the snares of the devil cannot harm us, since he overthrew the first human beings in Paradise not with richer food, but with a small and common apple. For the vice is not in the food, but in the appetite, when either we desire what is forbidden to us, or, greedily gaping after what is permitted, we use it otherwise than we ought.

Abstinence befits no one more than a monk, who, since he has been specially called to the warfare of Christ, ought not by his profession to be free for any pleasures whatever. Our poverty imposes on us a certain necessity of abstinence, because we can restrain ourselves to temperance all the more easily, the less we can find delights into which to flow away. Let us therefore, I beg, turn the hardships of want into weapons of salvation, so that the less we are refreshed with richer foods, the more purely we may fast in holiness of soul. For temperance is more easily preserved in poverty, while in riches it is more quickly endangered.

What the food of monks ought to be, blessed Jerome makes clear, saying in a certain letter to Paulinus: Let your food be cheap and taken in the evening, namely vegetables and legumes, and sometimes count it the highest delicacy to eat a few little fish. He who desires Christ and feeds on that heavenly bread does not greatly seek from what precious foods he may make dung. The lover of Christ loves abstinence, honors fasting as the one remedy of soul and body, and with the greatest care guards against his heart being weighed down with excess; nor does he take more food than nature, content with little, demands.

But the monk who casts aside fasting, who hates abstinence, the nurse of virtues, who gulps down food greedily, who drinks wine or strong drink, and whatever can intoxicate, to satiety, is unworthy of the very name of monk, and cannot be Christ’s [unclear].

99
esse discipulus. Vae temporibus nostris, in quibus iam clerici, et monachi complures virtutem abstinentiae turpiter abiecerunt, et qui populo Dei non minus exemplo, quam verbo iter salutis praemonstrare debuerant, comensationibus dediti, continuisque potationibus, et voluptatibus contra omne honestatem clericorum immersi, eum in perditionem acernea mortis praecedere festinant. Dicit autem scriptura: Initium vitae hominis panis, et aqua. At nunc monachi et claustrales nostri quicquid preciosius venditur, quicquid lautiis invenitur, sibi magnis sumptibus comparant, suis ventribus ingurgitando sepelunt, animam simi, et corpus per intemperantiam corrumpunt. Inter epulas de ieiunio disputant, et cum inebrati fuerint, temperantiam laudant. Ibi unusquisque victorem se gloriat vitiorum, cum a gula, et ebrietate iam fuerit superatus. Videte, inquit Dominus noster Iesus Christus in sancto Evangelio secundum Lucam, ne graventur corda vestra in crapula. Non decet hominem Deo dicatum ad satietatem comedere, vel bibere, nec licet monacho plus, quam natura exigit, manducare. Sedet famem co- mestio, non inducat repletionem: absint procul ructus, quos epulonibus consuevit generare satietas: vomitus, et indigeries nunquam inter monachos audiantur. Magno discretionis moderamine omnes utamur clau- strales oportet, quatenus ita corpus nutriatur esculentis, et poculis, ut spiritui subserviens possit vivere, non autem ut incrassatum contra mentis imperium incipiat lascivire. Procul semper absit satietas, quo- niani nihil sic inflammat corpus, et concitat membra genitalia, sicut indigestus cibus, et venter aestuans vino, sive cervisia. Hinc divus Hieronymus monens Eustochium ad virtutum omnium conservatricem temperantiam in quadam epistola dicit: Sponsa Christi vinum fugiat pro veneno, quoniam adversus adolescentiam arma sunt vinum, et ipsa iuventus proclivior ad gulam. Non sic avaritia quatit adolescentiam, nec inflat superbia, neque delectat ambitio, sicut illa, quae nobis vi- dentur concreta voluptati, vitia carnis. Facile aliis carebimus vitiis, si in timore Domini vel mediocriter vigilemus. Hic autem hostis noster intus est semper inclusus: quocunque pergimus, hunc nobiscum adversarium portamus. Vinum, adolescentia, duplex incendium voluptatis. Quid oleum flammae adiicimus, aut quare ardenti corpusculo fomenta ignea ministramus? Multos caste ambulantes in medio itinere prostra- vit ingluvies, et quos suis instinctibus vincere diabolus non potuit, in profundum luxuriae vini potatio nimia proiecit. Idcirco sanctissimus vitae nostrae institutor Benedictus instrumenta bonorum enumerans operum, inter praecipua reposuit, corpus castigare, vigilias amplecti, ieiunium amare. Nemo enim Christum in veritate sequitur, qui carnem suam delicate nutriens sine quotidiana abstinentia in monasterio con- versatur. Abstinentia quippe moderata, ac Deo placens multa in nobis

to be a disciple. Woe to our times, in which many clerics and monks have now shamefully cast aside the virtue of abstinence; and those who ought to have shown the people of God the way of salvation no less by example than by word, given to feasting and continual drinking, and sunk in pleasures contrary to all clerical honor, hasten to go before them into the perdition of eternal death.

Scripture says: “The beginning of man’s life is bread and water.” But now our monks and cloistered men buy for themselves, at great expense, whatever is sold most dearly and whatever is found most luxurious; they bury it by gorging it into their bellies, and through intemperance corrupt both soul and body. Amid banquets they debate fasting, and when they are drunk they praise temperance. There each man boasts that he is the conqueror of vices, although he has already been overcome by gluttony and drunkenness.

“Take heed,” says our Lord Jesus Christ in the holy Gospel according to Luke, “lest your hearts be weighed down in gluttonous excess.” It does not befit a man dedicated to God to eat or drink to satiety, nor is it lawful for a monk to eat more than nature requires. Let eating calm hunger, not bring on fullness. Let belches, which satiety is accustomed to produce in banqueters, be far away; let vomiting and indigestions never be heard of among monks. It is fitting that all we cloistered men use a great moderation of discretion, so that the body is nourished with foods and drinks in such a way that, serving the spirit, it can live, but not so that, fattened, it begins to grow wanton against the command of the mind. Let satiety always be far away, since nothing so inflames the body and stirs the generative members as undigested food and a belly heated with wine or beer.

Hence blessed Jerome, admonishing Eustochium to temperance, the guardian of all virtues, says in a certain letter: “Let the bride of Christ flee wine as poison,” since wine and youth itself are weapons against adolescence, which is more inclined to gluttony. Avarice does not so shake youth, nor does pride puff it up, nor ambition delight it, as do those vices of the flesh which seem to us bound together with pleasure. We shall easily lack other vices if we keep watch even moderately in the fear of the Lord. But this enemy of ours is always shut up within; wherever we go, we carry this adversary with us. Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure. Why do we add oil to the flame, or why do we supply fiery fuel to a little body already burning? Gluttony has overthrown many who were walking chastely in the middle of the road, and those whom the devil could not conquer by his own incitements, excessive drinking of wine has cast down into the depth of lust.

Therefore Benedict, the most holy founder of our way of life, when listing the instruments of good works, set among the chief ones: “to chastise the body, to embrace vigils, to love fasting.” For no one truly follows Christ who, nourishing his flesh delicately, lives in a monastery without daily abstinence. For moderate abstinence, pleasing to God, does many things in us.

100
Homilia XV. 105 bona operatur, si usque ad finem vitae religiosa intentione fuerit continua. Auget enim in primis meritum, et nutrit in nobis omnium generas virtutum. Quaenam fuit causa, ut primis parentibus nostris omnipotens Deus esum pomi sub interminatione mortis interdiceret, nisi ut eis meritorum causam per obedientiae bonum ostenderet? Creavit enim, testante Scriptura, duos intellectus ab initio, angelicum videlicet, et humanum, quibus ad fruitionem aeternae felicitatis per gratiam communicaret semet ipsum. Quamvis tamen utrumque ex gratiae sua dono condidit, fieri perpetuo felices etiam ex merito eorum proprio rectissime ordinavit: quatenus in eis, et miseratio locum, et conversio necessarium ad salutem consequeretur meritum. Angelicus vero intellectus statim bifariam divisus est, cum aliis per elationem suam sponte corruentibus, aliis suo per amore Principio humiles, et subjecti adhaerent. Et illi quidem apostatantes a suo Principio, infelices recesserunt, isti autem pro adhaesionis merito sempiterna beatitudine sunt donati. Humanus vero intellectus in carnem demissus est, qui mox, persuadente diabolo, mandatum Dei transgreditur, et de interdicto sibi cibo epulatur. Hinc totius humani generis perditio sequitur, quam auferre alius, quam Dei filius homo factus ex virgine pro nobis, potuit nemo. Quid enim damnavit protoparentes nostros, nisi mandati transgressio; quoniam non fuit Deo cura de cibo, sed de obedientia. Nam si abstinuisset homo, sicut ei praeceperat omnipotens Deus, certe per hanc obedientiam meruisset in sua innocencia fruitionem aeternae felicitatis. Constat enim traditione Scripturarum hominem sine merito libero arbitrii non posse salvare, quoniam et si gratia Dei omnia operatur in omnibus, neminem tamet salvabit sine cooperatione propriae voluntatis, exceptis duntaxat in Trinitatis nomine baptizatis infantibus, et qui liberum habere nequeunt usum rationis. Nam sicut arbitrium liberum nihil operatur ad salutem sine gratia salvatoris, sic Dei gratia non salvabit adultum sine merito bonae voluntatis. Primus autem homo in Paradiso positus, mandatumque Dei per temperantiam transgressus, meritum obedientiae in bona voluntate non habuit, propterea miser, et infelix proiectus fuit. Sed omnipotens Dei miseratio collapsum ex infirmitate reformare ab aeternitate statuit, quem deceptum invidii suggestione serpentis potius, quam propria malitia, non ignoravit. Condonavit hunc reatum passioni, et morti unigeniti filii sui, in tempore nascentis de virgine, ut qui propria temeritate perit, mediatoris obedientia reformaretur ad salutem. Impossibile namque fuit perditum per inobedientiam genus humanum ad misericordiam creatoris pervenire, nisi per obedientiam talis mediatoris, qui Deus esset, et homo, in quo et virtus esset potentiae, et innocentia naturae. Eramus enim caeci per ignorantiam, et muti per taciturnitatem. Venit mediator Dei, et 106 De abstinence, et ieiunio monachorum.

Homily XV.

It works good things, if it continues with a religious intention until the end of life. For above all it increases merit, and nourishes in us every kind of virtue.

What was the reason that almighty God forbade our first parents to eat the fruit, under threat of death, except to show them the occasion of merit through the good of obedience? For, as Scripture bears witness, he created two intellects from the beginning, namely the angelic and the human, to whom, through grace, he might communicate himself for the enjoyment of eternal happiness. Yet although he created both by the gift of his grace, he most rightly ordained that they should become forever blessed also by their own merit, so that in them both mercy might have its place, and conversion might obtain the merit necessary for salvation.

But the angelic intellect was immediately divided in two: some, falling of their own accord through pride, while others, humble and subject through love of their Principle, cleaved to him. Those who apostatized from their Principle departed in misery; but these, for the merit of their cleaving to him, were endowed with everlasting blessedness.

The human intellect, however, was sent down into flesh; and soon, at the devil’s persuasion, it transgressed the command of God and feasted on the food forbidden to it. From this followed the ruin of the whole human race, which no one could take away except the Son of God, made man from the Virgin for our sake. For what condemned our first parents except the transgression of the command? God was not concerned about the food, but about obedience. For if man had abstained, as almighty God had commanded him, surely by this obedience he would have merited, in his innocence, the enjoyment of eternal happiness.

For it is established by the tradition of the Scriptures that man cannot be saved without the merit of free will, since, even if the grace of God works all things in all, nevertheless he will save no one without the cooperation of his own will, except only infants baptized in the name of the Trinity, and those who cannot have the free use of reason. For just as free will does nothing toward salvation without the grace of the Savior, so the grace of God will not save an adult without the merit of a good will.

But the first man, placed in Paradise, transgressed the command of God through intemperance, and did not have the merit of obedience in a good will; therefore he was cast out, wretched and unhappy. Yet the mercy of almighty God determined from eternity to restore the one who had fallen through weakness, knowing that he had been deceived rather by the suggestion of the envious serpent than by his own malice. He pardoned this guilt through the passion and death of his only-begotten Son, born in time of the Virgin, so that the one who perished by his own rashness might be restored to salvation by the obedience of the mediator.

For it was impossible for the human race, lost through disobedience, to come to the mercy of the Creator except through the obedience of such a mediator, who would be God and man, in whom there would be both the power of divinity and the innocence of nature. For we were blind through ignorance, and mute through silence. The mediator of God came, and

101
hominum Christus Iesu, destinatus ut illuminaret omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, Dei mortalibus cognitionem tradidit, mortuusque pro perditis maximam causam amoris redemptis consignavit. Intellectum erudivit per fidem, qua Deus cognoscimus; affectum concitavit per passionem, quo ipsum super omnia merito diligamus. Itaque, si Dominum, et Redemptorem nostrum integra sinceritate diligimus, dignum est plane, ut corpus nostrum pro eius amore castigemus. Conducet enim nos abstinence nostra duplici ratione ad meritum: dum videlicet ieiunantes per obedientiam statutis patrum satisfacimus: et abstinentes per charitatem Dei, nos redemptori nostro, qui nostri causa mortem sustinuit, gratos exhibemus. Abstinence meritum auget, obedientiam commendat, sapientiam, et eruditionem praestat, affectum purgat, intellectum illuminat, victoriam contra daemones tribuit, religionem perficit, veniam peccatorum impetrat, motus carnis illicitos domat, orationibus efficaciam conciliat, exemplum virtutis proximo declarat. Abstinence mentem purificat, animam virtutibus ornat, infirmum corpusculum sanat. Qui diligit abstinenceam, sapiens est: qui ieiunium amat, dominator fortis. Mens sobria domicilium sapientiae: qui autem sectatur convivia, in egestate animi morietur. Difficile est hominem evadere sapientem, qui vitam agit in deliciis. Paucis contentatur natura: et in modicis vitae sanitas conservatur. Multis nocuit diutius continuata voracitas, et plures crapula, quam gladio perierunt. Consuetudo enim naturam alterare videtur, et quanto diutius convaluerit, tanto iam fortior in quolibet negotio erit. Est apud Helvetios homo Nicolaus nomine, cuius abstinence totius Germaniae homines convertit in admirationem, et hodie, sicut audivistis, in ore omnium cum sanctitatis titulo nominatur. Is quondam ruricola in quodam Helvetiorum vico existens, more paganorum inter quatuordecim ius dicere consuevit altercantibus villanis. Contigit eum quodam tempore sententiam non posse revocare sociorum, quam putabat iniquam, metuensque salutis animae suae periculum, relictis domo, uxore, filiis, et cunctis mundi negociis, ac rebus, solus in vicinum nemus pro Dei secessit amore, in quo vitam solitarius agit. Et ecce annus hodie vigesimus, ex quo solitudinem ingressus cibum non sumpsit humanum. Omnibus notissima loquor; nec hominem in Germania vivere puto, qui famam huius miraculi non audiverit. Et ne quis forsitan in posterum simulatione deceptos nos credat, Helvetianos una cum praesule Constantiensis ecclesiae in testimonium citamus, qui mores, et vitam eius curiosissime observant. Acutissimus ingenio vir est, qui cum sit literarum paenitus ignarus, tamen quasi alter eremita quondam Antonius sensum optime callet Scripturarum. Vidimus, quae disertissime cum quodam disputavit magistro de sacramento altaris, quae satis mirari non poterit, qui caelestia per

Christ Jesus, appointed to enlighten every man coming into this world, gave mortals knowledge of God; and, dying for the lost, he sealed for the redeemed the greatest cause for love. He instructed the intellect through faith, by which we know God; he stirred the affection through his passion, so that we may deservedly love him above all things.

Therefore, if we love our Lord and Redeemer with unbroken sincerity, it is altogether fitting that for love of him we should discipline our body. For our abstinence will lead us to merit in a twofold way: namely, when by fasting we satisfy the statutes of the fathers through obedience, and when by abstaining out of charity toward God we show ourselves grateful to our Redeemer, who endured death for our sake.

Abstinence increases merit, commends obedience, bestows wisdom and learning, purifies affection, enlightens the intellect, grants victory against demons, perfects religion, obtains pardon for sins, subdues the unlawful motions of the flesh, wins efficacy for prayers, and displays to one’s neighbor an example of virtue. Abstinence purifies the mind, adorns the soul with virtues, and heals the weak little body. Whoever loves abstinence is wise; whoever loves fasting is a strong ruler. A sober mind is the dwelling place of wisdom; but whoever pursues banquets will die in poverty of spirit. It is hard for a man to become wise who lives a life of pleasures.

Nature is content with few things, and the health of life is preserved in moderation. Long-continued voracity has harmed many, and more have perished by drunken excess than by the sword. For habit seems to alter nature, and the longer it has grown strong, the stronger it will then be in any undertaking.

There is among the Swiss a man named Nicholas, whose abstinence has turned the people of all Germany to admiration; and today, as you have heard, he is named by everyone with the title of holiness. He was once a peasant in a certain Swiss village, and according to the custom of the pagans he used to pronounce judgment among fourteen for quarrelling villagers. It happened at one time that he could not revoke a sentence of his associates which he thought unjust; and fearing danger to the salvation of his soul, he left house, wife, children, and all the business and possessions of the world, and withdrew alone into a neighboring wood for love of God, where he lives a solitary life.

And behold, today it is the twentieth year since, entering solitude, he has taken no human food. I am saying things very well known to all; nor do I think there is any man living in Germany who has not heard the fame of this miracle. And lest anyone perhaps in the future believe that we have been deceived by simulation, we call as witnesses the Swiss, together with the bishop of the church of Constance, who observe his habits and life with the utmost care. He is a man of very keen intelligence, and though he is utterly ignorant of letters, nevertheless, like another Antony the hermit of old, he understands the sense of the Scriptures extremely well. We saw the things which he most eloquently debated with a certain master concerning the sacrament of the altar, things at which he who [unclear] heavenly matters by [unclear] will not be able to marvel enough.

102
Homilia XV. 107 contemplationis studium minime gustavit. Haec ideo introduxerim, frātres, quo intelligatis nihil esse tam difficile, quod consuetudo multo tempore continuata non efficiat leve. Sanctus iste homo, sicut ipse con- fitetur, non subito ad huius abstinentiae celsitudinem pervenit, sed cum tempore successively per gradus, paulatim videlicet sibi de cibo subtra- hens modicum, quousque tandem abstinere potuit per totum. Abstinuit enim, sicut diximus, ab omni corruptibili cibo iam in annum ferme vigesimum. Huius viri exemplo, frātres mei, unusquisque vestrum discat sibi quotidiē aliquid de cibo, et potu pro Dei amore subtrahere, et assue- scat corpori suo, non quantum potest, sed quantum satis est ad naturae sustentationem, ministrare. Paucis enim minimisque, Boetio testante, Natura con- tenta paucis. multas aegri- tudines multa fercula pariunt, et ventris ingluvies mentem hebetat, et vitam cruciat. Dicit enim vir sapiens: Dulcis est somnus operanti, sive Eccles. 5. parum, sive multum comedat; saturitas autem divitis non sinit eum dormire. Sine satietate implendus est venter, et sine fastidio de mensa surgendum, ut videretur edamus, non quantum possimus, sed quantum, postulante natura, debemus. Monachis autem maxime vitanda est ci- borum varietas: nam, qui esculentis variis utitur, plus quam natura exigit, ingerere stomacho tentans, non sine gulae vitio epulatur. Vires enim corporis nostri moderato, et simplici sunt cibo reficiendae, non autem variis, et multis turpiter opprimendae, quia non corpus propter escam, sed esca propter corpus creata est. Quod enim variis corpori morbos afferat ciborum varietas, antiquorum temperantia probamus, quos uniformis esculentorum simplicitas in hac vita diutissime con- servavit. Sanctissimus autem institutor noster, principum monachorum omnium modestissimus hierophantes Benedictus canonem nobis pra- scripsit summa discretione decoratum, in quo mensuram ciborum cupiens ostendere monachis, dicit. Sufficere credimus ad refectionem quotidia- nam tam sextae, quam nonae omnibus mensis cocta duo pulmentaria, propter diversorum infirmitates, ut, qui forsan ex uno non potuerit edere, ex alio reficiatur. Ergo duo pulmentaria cocta omnibus fratribus sufficiant. Et, si fuerint ibi poma, aut nascentia leguminum, addatur et tertium. Si mentem legislatoris nostri sane intelligo, monachis duo pulmentaria cocta indulsit, ubi necessitas expositulat infirmitatis, non ad sanorum repletionem appetitus. Monachus enim, qui sanus est, ab hac indulgentia merito excipitur, ut uno dumtaxat pulmentario cocto reficiatur. Infirmus autem refici de utroque mea sententia iure permit- titur, cum excessus in nullo timeatur. Verum cum non omnia possim- simus aequaliter omnes, et unus plus indigeat ciborum, aliis vero minus, impossibile est unam abstinentiae formam praescribere cunctis, sed re- 108 De abstinence, et ienunio monachorum.

Homily XV.

He has by no means tasted the zeal for contemplation. I have introduced these things, brothers, so that you may understand that nothing is so difficult that habit, continued over a long time, does not make it easy. This holy man, as he himself confesses, did not suddenly arrive at the height of this abstinence, but gradually over time, by degrees, little by little subtracting a little from his food, until at last he was able to abstain altogether. For, as we have said, he had abstained from every perishable food for almost twenty years.

By the example of this man, my brothers, let each of you learn daily to subtract something from his food and drink for the love of God, and accustom himself to give his body not as much as it can take, but as much as is sufficient to sustain nature. For nature, as Boethius testifies, is content with few and very small things. Many dishes produce many illnesses, and gluttony of the belly dulls the mind and torments life. For the wise man says: “The sleep of the laboring man is sweet, whether he eats little or much; but the fullness of the rich man does not allow him to sleep.”

The belly should be filled without satiety, and one should rise from table without disgust, so that we eat not as much as we can, but as much as, at nature’s demand, we ought. Monks especially must avoid variety of foods; for whoever uses varied dishes, trying to put into his stomach more than nature requires, feasts not without the vice of gluttony. The strength of our body must be restored by moderate and simple food, not shamefully oppressed by varied and many foods, because the body was not created for food, but food for the body. That variety of foods brings diseases upon the body we prove from the temperance of the ancients, whom a uniform simplicity of foods preserved for a very long time in this life.

Our most holy founder, Benedict, the most modest sacred teacher of all the leaders of monks, prescribed for us a rule adorned with the highest discretion; in it, wishing to show monks the measure of foods, he says: “We believe that for the daily meal, whether at the sixth or at the ninth hour, two cooked dishes are sufficient for all tables, on account of the different infirmities, so that anyone who perhaps cannot eat from one may be refreshed from the other. Therefore two cooked dishes should suffice for all the brothers. And if there are fruits there, or fresh vegetables, let a third be added.”

If I understand our lawgiver’s mind soundly, he allowed monks two cooked dishes where the necessity of infirmity requires it, not for the filling of the appetite of the healthy. For a monk who is healthy is rightly excepted from this indulgence, so that he is refreshed by only one cooked dish. But in my judgment the sick man is rightly permitted to be refreshed from both, since no excess is to be feared in him. Yet since we cannot all do all things equally, and one person needs more food while others need less, it is impossible to prescribe one form of abstinence for all, but [unclear].

103
linquitur uniuscuiusque discretionis iudicio, ut tantum sumat, quantum expositulat necessitas, non quantum imperat appetentiae voluptas. Hoc maxime cavendum, ne subrepat immoderata ciborum satietas, quae tune animam commaculat, cum aut fastidium refectionem sequitur, aut gravis acidia mentem. Vomitus de saturitate procedens, canum est potius, quam monachorum. Religio christiana virum maxime detestatur epulonem, quoniam deliciae servorum Dei, non esca et potus; sed pietas, et iustitia sunt, quia et Deus fidei puritate colitur, et unicuique quod suum est, iuste ministratur. Quisquis igitur Deo placere in toto corde tuo desideras, quicunque pervenire ad aeternae felicitatis gaudia festinas, ieiunandi modum tibi iuxta mensuram virium tuarum indicito, et curam adhibe maximam, ut ieiunans sis in oratione continuus, in iudiciis iustus, in fraterna dilectione praecipuus, in iniuriis patiens, in increpationibus humilis, in sermone circumspectus, in conscientia mundus, in amore Dei fervidus, et in cunctis actionibus tuis, comitante prudentia, timoratus. Verba inutilia, et otiosa fugito, et esto perseverans in operibus bonis omni tempore, habens in adversis constantiam, in tentationibus vigilantiam, in refectione continentiam, et simplicem in corde puritatem. Sint moderata, et sancta in omni mentis humilitate ieiunia, quae ita corpus attenuent, ut mentem in superbiam non elevent, ne humilitatis exercitium materia fiat vitiorum. Ieiunium otium detestatur, verbositatem non amat, secretum diligit, orationibus et lacrymis intendit. Ieiunium, sancto testante Ambrosio, mors culpae est, excidium delictorum, remedium salutis, radix gratiae, fundamentum castitatis. Hoc gradu iustus ad Deum Moyses pervenit: hoc munere Helias in caelum, priusquam moreretur, curru ascendit. Qui spiritu ambulant, ieiunium diligunt: et qui castitatem profitentur, affluentiam necessario fugiunt deliciarum. Fames enim amica virginitati est, inimica lasciviae. Saturitas vero prodit castitatem, et nutrit lasciviam. Ardentes enim diaboli sagittas ieiunium extinguit, orationis instantia reprimit, et vigiliarum in Christi amore continuatio omnes daemonum insidias repellit.
