Let us therefore separate our minds from all troublesome earthly affairs; let us cleanse our consciences from all enticements of the flesh; let us put on the fervor of the Holy Spirit, and drive far from us all laziness and cowardice. For just as a heavy burden weighs down the back of a slothful man, so drowsiness during psalmody is accustomed to oppress the minds of monks. Nothing harms monks more than acedia, or sloth, which little by little weakens all the powers of the mind and extinguishes the whole fervor of the spirit. For as soon as a monk begins to fall away from the fervor of holy devotion, countless evil thoughts creep into his mind; and he is now able to repel them so much the less, the farther he is shown to have withdrawn from his former fervor.

From this arises drowsiness in the performance of the divine offices; the mind is weighed down excessively by sadness and melancholy, and the monk, growing lukewarm in spirit, strives with all his effort to relieve it not by spiritual consolations, but by earthly and carnal little comforts. And when he goes on longer in this estrangement of mind, he is hardened, as though insensible, against the exercise of compunction; and the more he pants after the consolations of the flesh, the farther he wanders from the inward fervor of the spirit. For what makes you drowsy during psalmody except acedia? For the mind that falls into sluggishness soon makes the body doze.

But again I warn you, brothers, as I have been accustomed to do very often: above all, flee laziness and drowsiness in the time of prayer, because just as drunkenness brings forgetfulness upon the soul, so too drowsiness makes the mind senseless and foolish before God. Beware this vice of drowsiness, O you young men, with which we sorrow to see some of the older men already infected by long habit; for in choir dozing is familiar to them, and compunction of mind toward God is very rare. Beware, I say, this evil habit of sleeping, which, once it has led a monk away captive, rarely lets him go free. Therefore at the very beginning of conversion, young men especially must fight against this most destructive enemy of religion, as someone said in verse:

Resist at the beginnings: medicine is prepared too late, When evils have grown strong through long delays. But make haste, and do not put yourself off to the coming hours; He who is not ready today will be less ready tomorrow.

On the sleep and wakefulness of monks.

117
Difficile namque est longam, et diurnitate inveteratam curare in- firmitatem. Regibus, et principibus terrenis quanta diligentia, et sedu- litate famuli assistant, videamus, ut, quemadmodum coram Deo, qui solus est Rex omnium, et Dominus universorum, in orationibus astare nos deceat, non ignoremus. Oculi omnium in Dominum respiciunt, et ad nutum eius omnes et singuli diligentissime pendent, ne quid, illo iubente, per negligentiam fugiat assistentes. Hinc igitur conside- remus, quanta nos oporteat Domino Deo puritate in orationis synaxi die, nocteque assistere, a quo regnum cupimus aeternae felicitatis im- petrare. Non vox, non clamor; sed fervens in Dei charitate intentio meretur exauditionem. Somnolentiam ergo, et torporem mentis, ut letale venenum fugite, quia somnus, et oculi scaturigo sunt omnium vitiorum. Oculus autem vigilans minister est internae devotionis, et monachus, qui Iesum Christum veraciter diligit, ab omni immoderantia se custodit. Qui vigilans est, mentem acuit intelligentia, multum vero dormiens monachus turpiter excaecat animam suam. Vigilans in ora- tione, et ieiunio monachus, formidabilis est diabolus: qui autem cibo satiatur, et somno, a spiritu fornicationis non permittitur quiescere. Vigilia enim orationibus dicata fervorem frangit luxuriae, ignem quoque valenter extinguit concupiscentiae, intima cordis purificat, mentem illu- minat, affectum ad amorem caelestium inflammat. Vigilia est bonarum cogitationum pares, nutrix, atque custodia, tentationum antiqui hostis certa victoria, phantasmatum fuga, mors vitiorum, vita, et fons omnium virtutum. Somnus autem multus comes, et fotor libidinis, raptor vitae hominis, imago mortis, oblivionis conciliator, inertiae coniunx. Somnus immoderatus stomachum corrumpit, cerebrum laedit, corpus simul, et animam dissolvit. Monachus frequenter somno deditus, sapientiam spernit, castitatem prostituit, animae salutem negligit, tempus preciosum perdit, mentem interficit, vitia nutrit. Quisquis igitur vestrum, aman- tissimi fratres, ad supernae foelicitatis requiem pervenire desiderat, omnem a se torporem, et ignaviam mentis fortiter repellat, discat in primis semetipsum vincere, ut hostem salutis suae diabolum deinceps valeat superare. Enimvero nisi malum, quod in te est, prius extermini- naveris, illud, quod adventitium est, quando superabis? Disce passio- nibus imperare tuis, et omnia, quae foris accidentunt, adiuvante Domino, facile superabis. Purga mentem ab omni concupiscentia inordinata, ut solum Iesum in veritate super omnia diligas, cum quo gaudere in ae- ternum speras. Nemo autem cum Christo regnabit in coelis, qui eum sanctis moribus non imitatur in terris, sancta dicente Scriptura: Qui dicit se in Christo manere, debet, sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambu- lare. Dominus etenim Iesus, qui sua nos morte ab interitu damnationis aeternae liberavit, ipse mediator Dei, et hominum voluntarie Homilia XVII. 123 factus est, ipse via, per quam nobis vitae trames est continuandus, ipse Dux potens itineris, ipse norma, et regula Christianis est salutaris conversationis. Nemo venit ad Deum nisi per Christum Patrem, nemo videbit nisi per Filium. Unde, si vultis venire ad salutem, oportet, ut transeatis per Salvatorem. Ipse namque in sancto Evangelio dixit: Nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Et illud, Ego sum ostium: per me si quis introierit, pabulum vitae aeternae inveniet. Ac iterum: Ego sum via, veritas, et vita. Per hanc viam piis, et sanctis moribus vivendo, precor, fratres mei semper incedite, hanc veritatem puro corde ferventer diligite: ad hanc vitam, quae sola est permanens, ardenter festinate. Doctrina Christi nunquam de cordibus vestris recedat, sed omni tempore in memoria permaneat, quoniam verus imitator eius fieri renuit, qui non die, ac nocte in meditatione verborum eius exercitatus fuit. Semper itaque in orationibus vigilantes tanta puritate mentis vivite, quatenus vocantem vos in mortis hora cum laetitia mereamini audire Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, qui vivit, et regnat cum Deo Patre in unitate Spiritus sancti, Deus, omnipotens, unus, per omnia secula seculorum. Amen. De patientia, et mansuetudine. Homilia XVIII.

For it is difficult to cure an illness that is long and has become inveterate through length of time. Let us consider with how great diligence and attentiveness servants stand before earthly kings and princes, so that we may not be ignorant of how it befits us to stand in prayer before God, who alone is King of all and Lord of the universe. The eyes of all look to the Lord, and all together and each one singly depend most carefully upon his nod, lest, when he commands, anything escape those who attend him through negligence. From this, therefore, let us consider with how great purity we ought to stand before the Lord God, day and night, in the assembly of prayer, from whom we desire to obtain the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

Not voice, not shouting, but an intention fervent in the love of God merits being heard. Therefore flee drowsiness and sluggishness of mind as a deadly poison, because sleep and the [unclear] of the eyes are the source of all vices. But the watchful eye is the servant of inward devotion, and the monk who truly loves Jesus Christ guards himself from every excess. He who is watchful sharpens his mind with understanding; but the monk who sleeps much shamefully blinds his own soul. A monk watchful in prayer and fasting is formidable to the devil; but one who is sated with food and sleep is not permitted to rest by the spirit of fornication.

For a vigil dedicated to prayers breaks the heat of lust, powerfully extinguishes the fire of desire, purifies the inward parts of the heart, enlightens the mind, and inflames the affection toward love of heavenly things. Vigil is the parent, nurse, and guardian of good thoughts, the sure victory over the temptations of the ancient enemy, the flight of phantasms, the death of vices, the life and fountain of all virtues. But much sleep is the companion and fosterer of lust, the robber of a man’s life, the image of death, the bringer of forgetfulness, the spouse of sloth. Immoderate sleep corrupts the stomach, harms the brain, and weakens both body and soul. A monk often given over to sleep despises wisdom, prostitutes chastity, neglects the salvation of his soul, loses precious time, kills the mind, and nourishes vices.

Therefore, whoever among you, most beloved brothers, desires to reach the rest of heavenly blessedness, let him vigorously drive away from himself all sluggishness and cowardice of mind. Let him learn first of all to conquer himself, so that thereafter he may be able to overcome the devil, the enemy of his salvation. For truly, unless you first root out the evil that is in you, when will you overcome that which comes from outside? Learn to rule your passions, and with the Lord’s help you will easily overcome everything that happens outwardly. Cleanse your mind from every disordered desire, so that in truth you may love Jesus alone above all things, with whom you hope to rejoice forever.

But no one will reign with Christ in heaven who does not imitate him on earth by holy conduct, as holy Scripture says: “He who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked.” For the Lord Jesus, who by his death freed us from the destruction of eternal damnation, himself willingly became mediator between God and men; he himself is the way by which the path of life must be continued for us; he himself is the powerful guide of the journey; he himself is the pattern and rule of saving conduct for Christians. No one comes to God the Father except through Christ; no one will see the Father except through the Son.

Therefore, if you wish to come to salvation, you must pass through the Savior. For he himself said in the holy Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” And also: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will find the pasture of eternal life.” And again: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” By this way, living with pious and holy conduct, I beg you, my brothers, always walk; love this truth fervently with a pure heart; hasten ardently toward this life, which alone is lasting.

Let the teaching of Christ never depart from your hearts, but remain in memory at all times, since he refuses to become a true imitator of him who has not been exercised day and night in meditation on his words. Therefore, always watchful in prayers, live with such purity of mind that at the hour of death you may deserve to hear with joy our Lord Jesus Christ calling you, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God almighty, one, forever and ever. Amen.

118
INTER omnes fidei Christianae professores nullum hodie genus est hominum, cui virtus patientiae magis videatur esse necessaria, quam coetui monachorum. Nam refrigescente his nostris diebus charitate mul- torum, ut Pauli utamur eloquio, spectaculum facti sumus mortalibus, ut, quocunque monachus inter homines mundanos devenerit, digitis ferme omnium, a quibus cernitur, subsannandus, et irridendus denotetur. Cur hoc dixerim, scitis: quid factum in oppido nuper Bingionum non ignoratis. Excepti juvenum, ac puerorum ebria turba monachum quempiam via transeuntem publica, et quasi pluviae causam praestitisset itinerans, proiecit in lutum, tractansque iniuria virum, impudentiae sua miserandum effinxit spectaculum. Nemo, qui conpesceret insolentes, adfuit: vicit tamen patientia monachi furentes, et Christi plenus amore, nihil aliud, cum male tractaretur, quam Deo gratias, respondit. Unde quanto se magis exhibuit mente, et animo tranquillum, tanto plus nebulones in fontem traxerunt, vino illum aestuare putantes, quem amor Christi iucundum fecerat, et laetum. Reliquit monachis cunctis magnum patientiae documentum: qui cum posset se vindicare, non voluit, iniuriatum. Utinam fratres mei tam patientes pro Dei amore, peccatisque nostris essemus in minimis, quam ille bonus vir in maximis fuit. Sunt inter vos quidam, invitus loquor, nimium protervi, et impati- tientes qui verbo, quamvis non iniurioso, moventur ad iram: atque, dum pro suis negligentiis juste corriguntur, iniuste murmuran, peccatum per impatienciam peccato adiicientes. Sed in quem finem patientiam 124 De patientia, et mansuetudine.

Among all professors of the Christian faith today, there is no class of men to whom the virtue of patience seems more necessary than to the company of monks. For, as the charity of many grows cold in these our days, to use Paul’s expression, we have become a spectacle to mortals, so that wherever a monk comes among worldly people, he is marked out to be mocked and derided by the fingers of almost all who see him.

You know why I have said this; you are not unaware of what recently happened in the town of Bingen. A drunken crowd of youths and boys accosted a certain monk passing along the public road, and, as though he, by traveling, had caused the rain, threw him into the mud; and by treating the man outrageously, it made him a pitiable spectacle of its own shamelessness. No one was there to restrain the insolent men. Yet the monk’s patience overcame their frenzy, and, full of the love of Christ, when he was being badly handled, he answered nothing else but “Thanks be to God.”

Therefore, the more he showed himself tranquil in mind and spirit, the more those worthless men dragged him into the fountain, thinking that he was heated with wine, when the love of Christ had made him glad and joyful. He left to all monks a great lesson in patience: although he could have avenged himself when wronged, he would not.

Would that we, my brothers, were as patient for the love of God and for our sins in the smallest things as that good man was in the greatest. There are some among you, I say it unwillingly, too insolent and impatient, who are moved to anger by a word, even one that is not insulting; and while they are justly corrected for their negligences, they murmur unjustly, adding sin to sin through impatience. But to what end patience...

119
illis memorati hominis propono in medium, qui omnium virorum patientissimum non attendunt Iesum Christum? Enimvero quisquis exemplo Regis coelorum patientiam, et humilitatem non amplexitur, nullius imitazione hominis ad mansuetudinem revocatur. Summum namque, et supremum patientiae, et humilitatis exemplar est Dei filius, cuius recordatione passionis quisquis ad sufferentiam non flectitur, induratus, et daemonum socius, merito censetur. Verba Domini nostri Iesu Christi esse vera bonus nemo dubitat christianus: dicit autem in sancto Evangelio Matt. 5. Christus: Beati mites, quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram. Si mites beati Luc. 22. sunt dicendi: quid prohibet ne rancorosi, iracundi, et immites nominentur maledicti? Certe, nihil. Et si, testante ipso Domino, et Salvatore nostro Iesu Christo, animas nostras in patientia possidemus, non est dubium, quin eas per impatientiam amittamus. Maxime igitur convenit monachos esse mites, mansuetos, et patientes, qui se Christi, et Apostolorum imitationi solemniter devoverunt. Christus autem omnium mitissimus suis in Evangelio discipulis, et imitatoribus praecipit dicens: Matt. 11. Discite a me, quia mitis sum et humilis corde, et invenietis requiem animabus vestris. Hinc sanctus praesul Augustinus: Si cum Christo vis regnare in coelis, discie prius ab eo, ut sis mitis, patiens, humilis, et mansuetus, quoniam nisi ad eius imitationem vitae in hoc mundo conversatus fueris, nullatenus cum eo in perpetuum regnabis. Divus quoque Ambrosius dicit: Cum deposuero omne peccatum, et exuero omnem malitiam, et simplicitate contentus fuero inops, malorum, superest, ut mores temperem. Quid enim mihi prodest carere sceleribus, nisi fuero mitis, atque mansuetus? Ille autem mitis est: qui cedit improbitibus, et non resistit in malo, sed vincit in bono malum. Mansuetus est autem, testante Chrysostomo, qui cum iniuriis provocatus fuerit, nec malum cogitat facere, nec facit. Cassiodorius vero dicit: Mansuetos appellamus manu consuetos, id est patientes, et mites, qui alienas iniquitates tolerant, nec aliquem gravare praesumunt, de quibus in psalmo dicitur: Psal. 33. In Domino laudabitur anima mea, audiant mansueti et laetentur. Non dixit in lege periti, non ieiunantes, non psallentes, sed mansueti laetentur, qui cum charitate praecipue habere omnium rerum temperantiam consueverunt. Illi autem vere sunt mites, mansueti et patientes, qui neminem laedunt, neminí iniuriantur, neminem poenitus offendunt, sed in sua simplici humilitate consistentes omnes iniurias, contumeliás, et irrisiones, pro Christi amore, semper aequanimiter tolerant, et contra laedentes nullo animi dolore moventur, quemadmodum fuisse monachum illum iam diximus, quem apud Bingiones pueri furentes nimis contumeliose tractaverunt. Facile autem est esse imitem, patientem, et mansuetum, quandiu nihil dicitur, vel agitur nisi pro voluntate et arbitrio patientis. Patebit autem quam sit longe a vera mansuetu-

I set before them the example of the man already mentioned, who do not heed Jesus Christ, the most patient of all men. For indeed, whoever does not embrace patience and humility after the example of the King of heaven will not be recalled to gentleness by the imitation of any man. For the Son of God is the highest and supreme model of patience and humility; whoever is not bent toward endurance by the remembrance of his passion is rightly judged hardened and a companion of demons.

No good Christian doubts that the words of our Lord Jesus Christ are true. Now Christ says in the holy Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” If the meek are to be called blessed, what prevents the rancorous, the wrathful, and the unmeek from being called accursed? Certainly nothing. And if, as our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself bears witness, we possess our souls in patience, there is no doubt that through impatience we lose them.

It is therefore especially fitting that monks be meek, gentle, and patient, since they have solemnly devoted themselves to the imitation of Christ and the apostles. But Christ, the meekest of all, commands his disciples and imitators in the Gospel, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.”

Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: If you wish to reign with Christ in heaven, first learn from him to be meek, patient, humble, and gentle, since unless you have lived in this world in imitation of his life, you will by no means reign with him forever.

Saint Ambrose also says: When I have laid aside every sin, stripped off every malice, and, content with simplicity, have been poor in evils, it remains that I temper my conduct. For what does it profit me to be free of crimes, unless I am meek and gentle? But he is meek who yields to wickedness and does not resist in evil, but overcomes evil with good.

And, as Chrysostom bears witness, he is gentle who, when provoked by injuries, neither thinks of doing evil nor does it.

Cassiodorus, moreover, says: We call the gentle “accustomed to the hand,” that is, patient and meek, those who bear the wrongs of others and do not presume to burden anyone. Of them it is said in the psalm: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the gentle hear and rejoice.” He did not say, “let those skilled in the law rejoice,” nor “those who fast,” nor “those who sing psalms,” but “let the gentle rejoice,” those who, together with charity, have especially been accustomed to possess temperance in all things.

But those are truly meek, gentle, and patient who harm no one, wrong no one, offend no one at all, but, standing firm in their simple humility, always bear with evenness of mind all injuries, insults, and mockeries for the love of Christ, and are moved by no grief of heart against those who harm them, just as we have already said that monk was, whom the raging boys at Bingen treated with great insult.

It is easy, however, to be meek, patient, and gentle so long as nothing is said or done except according to the will and judgment of the one who is patient. But it will become clear how far he is from true gentleness

120
Homilia XVIII. 125 dine, si levis oriatur occasio. Magna est virtus, si non laedas, a quo laesus es: magna fortitudo animi, si pro Dei amore iniuriam remittas inferenti: magna gloria si Christi mandatum observas, et preces pro iniuriantibus fundis. Nemo vires animi cognovit sui, quem contumelia necdum adussit insignis. Nemo se glorietur mitem, vel patientem, qui non fuit saturatus opprobriis. Non est sine adversitate patientia, nec sine improprio mansuetudo, quoniam si debitas tolerantiae metas custodire volueris, oportebit in primis contumeliam adesse inferentem. Si fuisset, inquit monachus piger, et animalis, in diebus martyrum, nulla poenarum genera subire pro Christi amore timuissem, corpus voluntarie obiecisset torturibus, ut coroñam martyrii reportassem. Magna stultitiae temeritas. Verbum pro Dei amore patienter sufferre nunquam potuisti, et constantiam sanctorum martyrum polliceris? Levem correptionem metuis, qui corpus te daturum pro Christo promittis. Si martyrium te delectat, audi, quid beatissimus Papa Gregorius dicat: Si, adiuvante nos Christo, virtutem patientiae servare contendimus, et in pace ecclesiae vivimus, et martyrii palmam tenemus. Nam sine ferro et flamma martyres esse possimus, si patientiam in animo veraciter custodiamus. Mori a persequente, martyrium in aperto opere est: ferre autem contumelias, et odientem diligere, martyrium est in occulta cogitatione. Patientia vero est aliena mala aequanimiter perpeti, et contra eum, qui malum intulit, nullo dolore morderi. Quid nunc piger dices o monache, qui martyrium verborum sufferre levisimum impotens, de constantia fundendi sanguinis tam proterve gloriaris? Disce miser in levibus habere patientiam, et considera, quoniam, dicente Scriptura, qui in modo infidelis est, ei, quod maius est, quis credere? Ad omnia, quae fiunt in coenobio, murmuras, increpatus quantumlibet leniter pro gravibus delictis, et negligentiis tuis, impatientissime toleras, nemo tibi recte in monasterio graditur, nemo praeter te in tua aestimatione religiose conversatur. Tu, quantum tibi videtur, solus in coenobio sanctus, tu omnium doctissimus neminem scire consentis, quod tu solus ignoras. Super omnes te honoribus cunctis existimas dignum, quia non solum patientia cares, sed neque humilitatem veram, neque obedientiam retines. Non est haec via, per quam itur ad regnum coelorum, quando in schola humilitatis superbit monachus, et moribus Christo vivit contrarius christianus. Monachus autem Iesu Christi solemniter iuratus minister, ut Dominum possit imitati suum, non debet esse superbus, sed humilis: obediens, non rebellis: mansuetus, non crudelis, neque protervus, sed mitis. Monachus vero superbus, iracundus, contentiosus, et proprie voluntatis amator, quales, proh dolor, ut frequenter sunt in temporalibus constituti, quos apud nos cellerarios secundum regulam nuncupamus, quorum elatio multis 126 De patientia, et mansuetudine. Superbus quidam mo- nachus foe- de lapsus est.

[unclear], if even a slight occasion arises. Great is the virtue if you do not harm the one by whom you were harmed; great is the courage of soul if, for the love of God, you forgive the one inflicting injury; great is the glory if you observe Christ’s command and pour out prayers for those who wrong you. No one has known the strength of his own soul whom no notable insult has yet burned. Let no one boast that he is meek or patient who has not been sated with reproaches. There is no patience without adversity, nor meekness without insult, because if you wish to keep the proper bounds of endurance, an insult-inflicter must first be present.

“If I had lived,” says the lazy and fleshly monk, “in the days of the martyrs, I would have feared to undergo no kind of torment for the love of Christ; I would willingly have exposed my body to tortures, so that I might have gained the crown of martyrdom.” Great rashness of folly. You have never been able patiently to endure a word for the love of God, and you promise the constancy of the holy martyrs? You fear a slight correction, you who promise that you will give your body for Christ. If martyrdom delights you, hear what the most blessed Pope Gregory says: “If, with Christ helping us, we strive to preserve the virtue of patience, then we live in the peace of the Church and hold the palm of martyrdom. For we can be martyrs without sword and flame, if we truly preserve patience in the soul. To die at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in open deed; but to bear insults and love one who hates you is martyrdom in hidden thought.”

True patience is to endure another’s evils with equanimity, and not to be gnawed by any grief against the one who has inflicted the evil. What will you say now, O lazy monk, who, unable to endure the very light martyrdom of words, boast so insolently of constancy in shedding blood? Learn, miserable man, to have patience in small things, and consider that, as Scripture says, “He who is unfaithful in little, who will trust him with what is greater?”

You murmur at everything done in the monastery; when rebuked, however gently, for your grave faults and negligences, you bear it most impatiently. No one in the monastery walks rightly in your eyes; no one besides you, in your estimation, lives religiously. You alone, as it seems to you, are holy in the monastery; you, the most learned of all, allow no one to know what you alone do not know. You judge yourself worthy of all honors above everyone, because you not only lack patience, but possess neither true humility nor obedience.

This is not the road by which one goes to the kingdom of heaven, when a monk is proud in the school of humility and a Christian lives in conduct contrary to Christ. But the monk, the solemnly sworn servant of Jesus Christ, so that he may imitate his Lord, must not be proud, but humble; obedient, not rebellious; gentle, not cruel; not insolent, but meek. But a monk who is proud, wrathful, contentious, and a lover of his own will, such as, alas, those placed in charge of temporal affairs often are, whom among us according to the Rule we call cellarers, whose arrogance to many

121
viam ad interitum fecit. Compellit me dolor ad loquendum, et prohibet verecundia, quamvis casum noveritis omnes, quo nos in fratre diabolus pridem confudit. Quis illo in tota congregatione nostra superior? quis maiores protervia plenus incescit? Quia vero maiorem inter nos rerum temporalium experientiam habere videbatur, cunctis ob id se praestan- tiorem existimavit. Permisit Omnipotens, ut caderet, quatenus qui suam infirmitatem reputatus agnoscere noluit, confusus tandem non sine mul- torum scandalio adversarium intelligeret Deum superborum. Doleo vehe- menter, et plus quam dici potest, culpa ruentis mihi gravior videtur, quoniam, illo ruente, confundimur omnes. Det illi Deus poenitentiam agere veram, ut qui eius lapsu scandalizati fuerant, satisfactione coram Deo, et hominibus aedificentur. Semper monachis perniciosa fuit elatio, et, mentem hominis quam semel invaserit, in foveam vitiorum omnium demergit. Cavete superbiam, fratres mei, quoniam ipsa est omnis pec- cati exordium; ipsa est, quae per invidiam diaboli mortem introducit in orbem terrarum. Superbia virtutum est mors omnium, et cunctorum fons, et scaturigo vitiorum. Humilitas autem virtutum nutrix maxime decet monachos, quoniam et mites facit, et mansuetos. Omnis enim superbus impatiens, et omnis arrogans mansuetudinis inimicus. Qui humilis est corde, habet in adversis pro Dei amore patientiam: et, qui ad iniurias animo tranquillus est, duplicem meretur coronam. Vir pa- tiens in adversis Deo proximus: qui autem superbus, et immitis est, Prov. 16. laetificat inimicos. Dicit namque scriptura: Melior est patiens viro forti, et qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatorc urbium, Sanctus quoque praesul Augustinus. Paratus debet esse homo iustus, et pius, patienter eorum malitiam sustinere, quos fieri bonos cupit, ut potius numerus crescat bonorum, et non pari malitia se quis numero addat malorum. Est enim nobis patientia multum necessaria, fratres, ut voluntatem Dei facientes, Hebr. 16. sanctam in Christo reportemus promissionem. Nobis quotdie adsunt, quibus exercitemur adversa, propterea sicuti tolerantiae nunquam deest causa, ita precor, necessaria semper adsit patientia. Inopia et pauper- tate necessariarum rerum opprimitur, carnis infirmiae commercio gra- vamur, tentat praeterea nos mundus, ut alliciat, tentat diabolus, ut se- ducat. Inter tot salutis nostrae adversarios necessarium est, fratres, ut in omni patientia, et humilitate vigilemus, quoniam in hac peregrina- tione quandiu vivimus, in medio, ut ita dixerim, malorum positi sumus. Sufficiat nobis paupertas nostra oportet, quia non est monasticae reli- gionis in temporalibus exaltari, sed potius deprimi, ut monachi pau- peres Christum imitantes pro nobis pauperem factum, in perpetuum cum eo in coelis mereamur gloriarri. Quid si malos et peccatores quos- dam in saeculo videamus abundare divitiis? Si boni homines, et iusti in hoc mundo sunt divites, eorum non fortitudini, sed infirmitati per

made a path to destruction. Grief compels me to speak, shame restrains me, although you all know the misfortune by which the devil lately confounded us in our brother. Who was higher than he in our whole congregation? Who went about filled with greater insolence? Because he seemed to have greater experience than we in temporal affairs, he therefore judged himself superior to all. The Almighty permitted him to fall, so that the man who, through self-regard, refused to acknowledge his own weakness might at last, confounded and not without the scandal of many, understand that God is the adversary of the proud. I grieve deeply, more than can be said, and the fault of the one who fell seems heavier to me because, when he falls, we are all confounded. May God grant him true repentance, so that those who had been scandalized by his fall may be built up by his satisfaction before God and men.

Pride has always been destructive to monks, and once it has invaded a man’s mind, it plunges him into the pit of every vice. Beware pride, my brothers, for it is the beginning of every sin; it is pride which, through the devil’s envy, brings death into the whole world. Pride is the death of all virtues, and the fountain and source of all vices. But humility, the nurse of the virtues, most befits monks, because it makes them gentle and meek. For every proud man is impatient, and every arrogant man is an enemy of meekness. He who is humble of heart has patience in adversity for the love of God; and he who remains calm in spirit under insults deserves a double crown. A patient man in adversity is near to God; but one who is proud and harsh gladdens his enemies. For Scripture says: “A patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than a conqueror of cities.” The holy bishop Augustine also says: “A just and devout man must be ready to endure patiently the malice of those whom he wishes to become good, so that the number of the good may rather increase, and no one by equal malice add himself to the number of the wicked.”

Patience is greatly necessary for us, brothers, so that, doing the will of God, we may receive the holy promise in Christ. Each day adversities are present to us by which we may be exercised; therefore, just as a cause for endurance is never lacking, so, I pray, may necessary patience always be present. We are oppressed by want and poverty in necessary things; we are burdened by the commerce of the flesh’s weakness; besides this the world tempts us, to allure us, and the devil tempts us, to seduce us. Among so many adversaries of our salvation it is necessary, brothers, that we keep watch in all patience and humility, because in this pilgrimage, as long as we live, we are placed, so to speak, in the midst of evils. Our poverty ought to be enough for us, because it does not belong to monastic religion to be exalted in temporal things, but rather to be brought low, so that poor monks, imitating Christ, who was made poor for us, may deserve to glory with him forever in heaven. What if we see certain wicked men and sinners in the world abounding in riches? If good and just men are rich in this world, it is granted through [unclear] to their weakness, not to their strength.

122
Homilia XVIII. 127 Dei providentiam consultur, ut beneficiis ad meliora provocentur. Iunior fui, dicit prophetā, et senui, et non vidi iustum derelictum, nec semen eius mendicans. Iacta, inquit, cogitatum tuum in Domino, et ipse te enutriet, non dabit in aeternum fluctuationem iusto. Novit Dominus Iesus, quid unīcuique servulorum suorum ad salutem conveniat, et ideo munera praesentis vitae pro captu singularum inaequaliter dispensat. Non enim omnibus omnia conveniunt; propterea iustorum in hoc mundo rebus temporalibus aliī sunt pauperes, aliī vero locupletes. De pauperibus Dominus Iesus in sancto evangelio dicit. Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum. Et per Prophetam loquitur dicens. Ecce excoxi te, sed non quasi argentum, elegi te in camino paupertatis. Non enim conductit ad aeternam salutem omnibus huius mundi possidere divitias, sed quosdam expedit esse pauperes, quosdam vero locupletes, prout Dominus universorum cuique providit esse utilius. De iustis, et bonis divitibus Salomon dicit in libro Proverbiorum; Benedictio Domini divites facit, nec sociabitur ei afflictio. Si autem mali, et reprobī divitīs abundaverint in hoc saeculo, non debent bonōs movere ad indignationem: sed magis timeant eum, qui nullum bonum dimitit irremuneratum, et nullum malum impunitum. Malos enim, quos propter iniquitatem eorum remunerare in caelis non potest, pro eorum bonis in hac vita remunerat: et bonis, quos hic in paupertate nutrit, pro iustitiae merito, aeterna in coelis praemia conservat. Verum sicut non omnes in hoc mundo pauperes sunt iusti, et boni, ita non omnes rerum temporalium divites in hac vita sunt mali. Malorum remuneratio in terris merito sine indignatione ferenda est, quam non amor Dei, sed iustitia voluit esse praesentem. Unde sicut mali nihil habent in Coelo, ita vos, qui Monasticam paupertatem estis professi, nihil habere debetis in terra, sed spe illius boni, ad quod tenditis, quicquid in via contigerit adversi, tolerare patientissime debetis. Nam, ut sanctus Christi amator Paulus, ait, non sunt condignae passiones huius temporis ad superventuram gloriam, quae revelabitur in nobis. Qui divites sunt in Christo, coniungant humilitati misericordiam: qui vero sunt pauperes, sumant cum innocentia pro Dei amore patientiam. Miles etenim Christi, nec paupertate deiicitur, nec divitiis elevatur, sed in se firmus consistens animo, Regi Coelorum tranquillus militat, et nihil de rebus transitoriis curat. Ita, qui verus est Monachus, nec laudibus extollitur, nec vituperatione frangitur, non intumescit necessariarum rerum affluentia, nec contrahitur paupertate, laeta simul contemnit, et tristia: quoniam, sicut Prophetā dixerat, Sol eum non uret per diem, nec luna per noctem. Nos autem, frātres charissimi, faciamus de necessitate virtutem, et voluntatem bonam; et de paupertatis incommodo, quod necessario patimur, bonum nobis, et utile ma- 128 De patientia, et mansuetudine.

God’s providence is consulted, so that by benefits they may be stirred toward better things. “I was young,” says the prophet, “and now am old, and I have not seen the just man forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.” “Cast,” he says, “your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you; he will not allow the just man to waver forever.”

The Lord Jesus knows what is fitting for the salvation of each one of his little servants, and therefore he distributes the gifts of the present life unequally, according to the capacity of each individual. For not everything is suitable for everyone; therefore among the just in this world some are poor in temporal goods, while others are wealthy. Concerning the poor the Lord Jesus says in the holy Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And through the prophet he speaks, saying: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.”

For it is not conducive to eternal salvation for everyone to possess the riches of this world; rather, it is expedient for some to be poor and for others to be wealthy, according as the Lord of all has provided what is more useful for each. Concerning just and good rich men Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: “The blessing of the Lord makes men rich, and affliction will not be joined to it.” But if evil and reprobate rich men have abundance in this age, good men ought not be moved to indignation, but should rather fear him who leaves no good unrewarded and no evil unpunished.

For the evil, whom because of their iniquity he cannot reward in heaven, he rewards in this life for their good deeds; and for the good, whom he nourishes here in poverty, he preserves eternal rewards in heaven for the merit of their justice. Yet just as not all the poor in this world are just and good, so not all who are rich in temporal things in this life are evil. The reward of the evil on earth is rightly to be borne without indignation, since not the love of God but his justice willed it to be present.

Therefore, just as the evil have nothing in heaven, so you, who have professed monastic poverty, ought to have nothing on earth; but in hope of that good toward which you are hastening, you ought to bear most patiently whatever adversity befalls you on the way. For, as Paul, the holy lover of Christ, says, “the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which shall be revealed in us.” Let those who are rich in Christ join mercy to humility; but let those who are poor take up patience with innocence for the love of God.

For the soldier of Christ is neither cast down by poverty nor lifted up by riches, but, standing firm in himself in spirit, serves the King of heaven in tranquility and cares nothing for transitory things. So too, he who is a true monk is neither puffed up by praises nor broken by blame; he does not swell with an abundance of necessary things, nor is he constricted by poverty; he despises both joyful and sorrowful things alike, because, as the prophet had said, “the sun shall not burn him by day, nor the moon by night.”

But we, dearest brothers, let us make virtue and a good will out of necessity; and from the hardship of poverty, which we suffer of necessity, let us make for ourselves something good and useful [unclear].

123
gnum comparemus, quod tunc demum fieri potest, si pro Dei amore hanc ipsam viriliter, et animo tranquillo toleremus inopiam. Anteces- sorum nostrorum deformata conversatio eam, quam patimur egesta- tem, huic Monasterio induxit, quam omnipotentis Dei miseratio, si mandata eius corde perfecto custodierimus, cum tempore procul dubio relevabit. Ab annis retro ferme ducentis, quemadmodum coniectura simul, et literis praecedentium assequi possumus, puritas Monasticae institutionis in hoc Spanhemensi Monasterio, sicuti et in alis pene omnibus defecit, et inordinatio vitae Monachorum omnem terrenarum rerum substantiam penitus dissipavit. Enimvero cum anno Christiano- rum nono, et sexagesimo supra quadringentesimum, atque millesimum FridericuS Bavariae dux Spanhe- mense mo- nasterium repurgavit. that we may gain the kingdom, which can only then be done if, for the love of God, we bear this poverty manfully and with a tranquil mind. The disordered conduct of our predecessors brought upon this monastery the want that we suffer; the mercy of almighty God, if we keep his commandments with a perfect heart, will in time without doubt relieve it. For almost two hundred years past, as we can gather both by conjecture and from the writings of those before us, the purity of monastic observance in this monastery of Spanheim, as in almost all others, failed, and the disorderly life of the monks utterly squandered all temporal substance. For indeed, when in the year of the Christians 1469 [unclear].

Frederick, duke of Bavaria, reformed the monastery of Spanheim.

124
Homilia XVIII. 129 lectabilium huius seculi, in conscientia pura, et humilitate cordis. Attendite nunc igitur vocationem vestram, o Monachi, et nolite propositum sanctitatis corrumpere, si ad Dei gloriam cupitis pervenire. Vae tibi Monache infidelis, qui vocationis tuae contemptor, ac voti transgressor factus in Monasterio non monastice vivis: qui ad tribulationem patienter tolerandam vocatus es Dei pro amore, et de refrigerio percunctaris. Iubet enim te tua professio in omni vilitate, et extremitate vestimentorum humiliter contentum incidere, et tu curiositati vestium non metuis studium adhibere. In sitim vocatus es, et tu, aquam bibere contemnens, vinum usque ad satietatem potare contra monasticum canonem delectaris. Ad dimicandum contra salutis tuae adversarium fortiter Monachus factus es, et tu, proiectis a te virtutum armis, piger, iners, et nudus, immo, quod gravius est, caterva vitiorum comitante, incedis. Ad vigilandum in orationibus sanctis invitatus es, et tu somno inerti, et ignavia turpi resolveris. In subjectionem humilis obedientiae vocatus es, et tu inflatus superbia seniorum praecptis obtemperare contemnis. In charitatem vocatus es, et tu contra fratrem tuum odium in pectore gestare non formidas. In fletum, et lachrymas vocatus es, et tu risus cum inordinato profundis cachinno. Ad poenitentiam te Dominus vocavit in Monasterio, et tu resolutus in lasciviam peccato coniungis peccatum. Ad meditandum die, ac nocte in lege Domini nostri Iesu Christi vocatus es, et tu, post vanitatem ambulans, fabulis, et rebus caducis intendis. Ad coelum vocatus es, et tu, mundum diligens, terrena sectaris. In mansuetudinem humilitatis vocavit te Dominus, et tu rancore, et superbia plenus incedis. Ad perfectionem purissimae conversationis Monasticae a Domino vocatus es, et tu, ut iumentum in stercore vanitatis, et negligentiae computrescis. Ad observantiam mandatorum Dei vocatus es, et tu voluptatibus carnis deditus nihil minus, quam Christum cogitas. Ad amandum Dominum Iesum super omnia invitatus es, et tu ambulas post desideria cordis tui mala ingratum te exhibens redemptori tuo. Qui spiritu vivere debueras, terrena sapis, et omnia spiritualis conversationis sancta exercitia, submersus in superbia, contemnis. Et quid in illa die Iudicii responsurus es Iudici, qui ingratisimo tibi dicturus est: Ego, qui Dominus sum universorum, propter te humiliavi, me metipsum, formam servi accipiens, et habitu, inventus ut homo, sanguinem pro te meum effudi, pro te verbera sustinui, et mortem pro te nimis amaram spontanea voluntate subivi. Ego te, o Monache, in toto corde meo dilexi; ego te in sanguine meo de morte perpetua redemi: ego te, si mandata custodivisses mea, ad coeleste regnum ex amore vocavi. Tu autem vixisti praecptis meis contrarius, et, quod gravius est, in verba mea iuratus, cum esses, apostatam, et impium te traditorem contra me Dominum tuum exhibere non timuisti. Nunc 130 De patientia, et mansuetudine.

Consider now, therefore, your calling, O monks, and do not corrupt your purpose of holiness, if you desire to arrive at the glory of God. Woe to you, faithless monk, who, having become a despiser of your calling and a transgressor of your vow, live in the monastery not as a monk: you who were called to endure tribulation patiently for the love of God, and yet ask about refreshment.

For your profession commands you to be humbly content with all mean and very poor clothing, and you are not afraid to devote your zeal to finery in dress. You were called to thirst, and you, despising the drinking of water, delight in drinking wine to satiety, against the monastic rule. You were made a monk to fight bravely against the enemy of your salvation, and you, throwing away from yourself the weapons of the virtues, go about lazy, idle, and naked; indeed, what is worse, with a troop of vices accompanying you. You were invited to watch in holy prayers, and you are dissolved in sluggish sleep and shameful idleness. You were called into the subjection of humble obedience, and you, swollen with pride, despise obedience to the precepts of your elders. You were called into charity, and you do not fear to carry hatred against your brother in your breast. You were called to weeping and tears, and you pour out laughter with disorderly guffawing.

The Lord called you to repentance in the monastery, and you, loosened into wantonness, join sin to sin. You were called to meditate day and night on the law of our Lord Jesus Christ, and you, walking after vanity, devote yourself to tales and perishable things. You were called to heaven, and you, loving the world, pursue earthly things. The Lord called you into the meekness of humility, and you go about full of rancor and pride. You were called by the Lord to the perfection of the purest monastic way of life, and you rot away like a beast in the dung of vanity and negligence. You were called to the observance of God’s commandments, and you, given over to the pleasures of the flesh, think of nothing less than Christ. You were invited to love the Lord Jesus above all things, and you walk after the evil desires of your heart, showing yourself ungrateful to your Redeemer. You who ought to have lived by the Spirit savor earthly things, and, drowned in pride, you despise all the holy exercises of the spiritual life.

And what will you answer on that day of judgment to the Judge, who will say to you, most ungrateful one: I, who am Lord of all things, humbled myself for your sake, taking the form of a servant, and, being found in appearance as a man, poured out my blood for you; for you I endured scourges, and for you I underwent a most bitter death of my own free will. I, O monk, loved you with my whole heart; I redeemed you by my blood from everlasting death; I called you out of love to the heavenly kingdom, if you had kept my commandments. But you lived contrary to my precepts, and, what is worse, though you had sworn yourself to my words, you were not afraid to show yourself against me, your Lord, as an apostate, impious traitor. Now

125
igitur da rationem villicationis tuae. Quid tunc responsurus es, o Mo- nache piger, et deses, qui tempus nunc acceptabile tam infructuose consumis, et vivere in vera puritate monastica secundum regulam con- temnis? Quid, inquam, respondebis? Negabisne pravitatis opera, quae commisisti, ostensurus per fallaciam bona, quae nunc operari spernis, quatenus, mendacio circumveniens Iudicem, sicque debitam evadas tuis demeritis poenam? Sed ignorare non debes, quoniam omnia, quae fe- cisti, dixisti, vel cogitasti per omnem vitam tuam, bona, et mala in conspectu Iudicis sunt manifesta, et nihil eum latere potest, qui solus omnia novit. Omnia enim in libro Dei scripta sunt: et conscientia tua omnium adversum te male gestorum apertum perhibebit testimonium: ita quod nec minima quidem cogitatio poterit latere. Dicit enim ad Psal. 75. Deum scriptura prophetarum: Quoniam cogitatio hominis confitebitur tibi. Ad tribunal omnia scientis iudicandus es, ante cuius terrible Iu- dicium omnis creatura cum metu nimio, et tremore stabit, ubi nulla penitus admittitur excusatio, sed singuli recepturi sunt debitam suis meritis, semota appellazione, sententiam. Millia millium, et decies cen- tena millia sanctorum spirituum assistent ei, et tu mendacio te fallere Iudicem posse confidis? Sed audi consilium meum, et surgens ab inertia tua perniciosa tandem expergiscere, et per veram poenitentiam ad Dei misericordiam in tempore, a iustitia recurre. Non differas de die in diem, quoniam nimis est periculosum in peccatis manenti confidere, et salutis remedium, quod offertur, refutare. Memento, quoniam moriturus es, et quando non cogitas, ad iudicium vocaberis. Cogita, precor, du- bium vivendi tempus, quomodo labitur, et omnia, quae mortalia sunt, quam cito corrumpuntur. Nihil in humanis stabile, nihil fixum, nihil firmum, sed omnia, quae cernimus, corruptibilia sunt, et cum tempore mutantur. Considera etiam, ubinam sunt fratres nostri Valentinus, Mar- tinus, et Ioannes, qui anno praesenti nobiscum viventes sani, incolumes, ac laeti fuerunt, nobiscum pariter loquebantur, manducabant, bibebant, et laborabant, nihil minus, quam hoc anno se morituros cogitantes. Ecce, quando non putabant, venit mors, rapuit eos, statuique animas eorum ad tribunal tremendi iudicis, qui reddidit unicuique secundum opera manuum suarum. Ecce nunc iam disce fratrum tuorum exemplo, quoniam et tu moriturus es, et forsan multo transibis ab hoc mundo citius, quam poteris aestimare. Resipiscito miser, quando iam potes, age poenitentiam in tempore sanitatis tuae, quando iudex pollicetur misericordiam, et noli differre bonum hodiernum in dubium crastinum. Consurge, vel nunc sero tandem ab ignavia negligentioris transactae conversationis, in qua hactenus turpiter computruisti; et expurga con- scientiam tuam ab omni macula peccati; lachrymis exterge, quod com- misisti malum, et iam deinceps vive innocenter, ut condecat monachum. Homilia XVIII. 131

Therefore give an account of your stewardship. What then will you answer, O lazy and idle monk, who now spends the present acceptable time so fruitlessly, and despises living in true monastic purity according to the rule? What, I ask, will you answer? Will you deny the works of wickedness that you have committed, intending by deceit to show good works that you now disdain to perform, so that, deceiving the Judge by a lie, you may thus escape the punishment due to your demerits?

But you must not be ignorant that everything you have done, said, or thought throughout your whole life, good and evil alike, is manifest in the sight of the Judge, and nothing can be hidden from him who alone knows all things. For all things are written in the book of God, and your conscience will bear open testimony against you concerning all the evils you have done, so that not even the smallest thought will be able to lie hidden. For the Scripture of the prophets says to God in Psalm 75: “For the thought of man shall confess to you.”

You are to be judged before the tribunal of the all-knowing one, before whose terrible judgment every creature will stand in great fear and trembling, where no excuse whatever is admitted, but each person will receive the sentence due to his merits, with appeal set aside. Thousands of thousands and ten hundred thousand holy spirits will stand beside him, and do you trust that you can deceive the Judge by a lie?

But hear my counsel, and, rising from your destructive inertia, at last wake up, and by true repentance flee in time from justice to the mercy of God. Do not put it off from day to day, because it is extremely dangerous for one remaining in sins to be confident, and to reject the remedy of salvation that is offered. Remember that you are going to die, and when you do not expect it, you will be summoned to judgment.

Consider, I beg you, how the uncertain time of life slips away, and how quickly all mortal things decay. Nothing among human affairs is stable, nothing fixed, nothing firm; rather all things that we see are corruptible and change with time. Consider also where our brothers Valentinus, Martinus, and Ioannes are, who in the present year were living with us healthy, safe, and joyful; they spoke with us, ate, drank, and labored together with us, thinking of nothing less than that they would die this year. Behold, when they did not think it, death came, snatched them away, and set their souls before the tribunal of the dreadful Judge, who rendered to each one according to the works of his hands.

Behold, now learn from the example of your brothers that you too are going to die, and perhaps you will pass from this world much sooner than you can estimate. Come to your senses, wretched man, while you still can; do penance in the time of your health, while the Judge promises mercy, and do not defer today’s good into tomorrow’s uncertainty. Rise up, even now, late though it is, at last from the sloth of your more negligent past way of life, in which until now you have shamefully rotted away; cleanse your conscience from every stain of sin; wipe away with tears the evil you have committed, and from now on live innocently, as befits a monk.

126
Perfectum emendationis capesse propositum, et intellige quoniam non incipientibus bonum, sed perseverantibus usque in finem repromittitur regnum coelorum. Scito etiam, quod non pervenitur inertia, et torpore ad coelum, sed labore magno, conatu voluntatis proficiendi maximo, et studio exercitii spiritualis indefesso. Volens igitur Domino servire, ac placere, in veritate semper consiste apud temetipsum pavidus in timore, et praepara animam tuam ad tentationem. Resistendum est fortiter inordinatis motibus, et concupiscentiis carnis: reluctandum est animo constantissimo blandimentis, et vanitatibus seculi cunctis: per orationes et magnanimitatem spiritus, fugandus est daemon nostraee adversarius salutis. Nemo somnolentus, piger, acidiosus unquam Dei pervenit ad regnum: nemo sine labore continuo, et multis sudoribus obtinuit coelum. Dicit enim in sancto Evangelio Dominus: Regnum Dei vim patitur, et violenti, hoc est qui malis concupiscentiis carnis noverunt resistere constanter, rapiunt illud. Revolvite omnium gesta sanctorum, et nusquam invenietis aliquem sine magno, et continuo labore sanctificatum. Nam et si nemo fiat sanctus viribus suis, tamen omnipotentis Domini gratiosa miseratio, quae, et voluntatem benefaciendi certantibus praestat et vires, neminem sanctificat sine operibus bonae, et rectae voluntatis. Cum ergo Deus velit salvos fieri omnes homines, et nemo perire, nobis fratres mei, summopere cavendum est, ne gratiam eius in vacuam recipiamus, sed entendum potius viribus totis, quatenus tanti satoris gratuitis donis veluti ager fertilis, ex operibus bonae voluntatis fructibus semper respondeamus condignis. Armemus nos igitur scuto fidei, et induamus loricam constantiae, ac patientiae salutaris, ut praeparati adversus omnia, quae nobis accidere possunt, per humilitatem, et fervorem sancti spiritus, adiuvante Domino nostro Iesu Christo, vincamus. In omnibus his patientia nobis multum est necessaria, sine cuius admiciculo nulla unquam fuit, vel esse potuit in operibus bonis, et sanctis perseverantia. Neque enim via sanctis ad coelum fuit alia, quam patientia: neque sanctificari unquam potuit, qui patientiam abiecit. Enimvero quotquot omnipotenti Deo placuerunt ab exordio mundi usque in hanc nostram aetatem, non aliter, quam per patientiam contra mundi principem triumpharunt. Unde illud psalmistae omnes dicere quam rectissime potuerunt: Propter te mortificamur tota die, aestimati sumus sicut oves occasionis. Sanctissimus quoque Apostolus Christi Paulus veterum commemorans patientiam sanctorum, inter caetera dicit: Circumierunt in melotis, in pellibus caprinis, egentes, angustiati, afflicti, quibus dignus non erat mundus, in solitudinibus errantes, in montibus, in speluncis, et in cavernis terraee. Omnes enim, qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patiuntur, quoniam, sicut ait prophetae, multae sunt tribulationes iustorum, et de omnibus his liberabit eos Dominus. 132 De patientia, et mansuetudine.

Take up a firm purpose of complete amendment, and understand that the kingdom of heaven is promised not to those who begin well, but to those who persevere to the end. Know also that heaven is not reached by idleness and sluggishness, but by great labor, by the strongest effort of the will to make progress, and by tireless zeal in spiritual exercise.

Therefore, wishing to serve and please the Lord, always stand in the truth within yourself, fearful in awe, and prepare your soul for temptation. The disordered impulses and desires of the flesh must be strongly resisted; all the enticements and vanities of the world must be fought against with a most steadfast spirit; through prayers and greatness of soul the devil, the adversary of our salvation, must be driven away.

No sleepy, lazy, slothful person ever reached the kingdom of God; no one without continual labor and much sweat has obtained heaven. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent,” that is, those who have learned steadfastly to resist the evil desires of the flesh, “seize it.” Review the deeds of all the saints, and nowhere will you find anyone sanctified without great and continual labor. For even if no one becomes holy by his own powers, nevertheless the gracious mercy of the almighty Lord, which grants to those who strive both the will to do good and the strength, sanctifies no one without the works of a good and upright will.

Since, then, God wills all men to be saved and no one to perish, we, my brothers, must take the greatest care not to receive his grace in vain, but rather strive with all our strength, so that, like fertile soil, we may always answer the free gifts of so great a sower with fitting fruits from the works of a good will.

Let us therefore arm ourselves with the shield of faith, and put on the breastplate of steadfastness and saving patience, so that, prepared against everything that can happen to us, through humility and the fervor of the Holy Spirit, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we may overcome. In all these things patience is very necessary for us; without its support there never has been, nor could there ever be, perseverance in good and holy works. For there was no other way to heaven for the saints than patience; nor could anyone ever be sanctified who cast patience aside.

Indeed, all who have pleased almighty God from the beginning of the world down to this our age have triumphed over the prince of the world in no other way than through patience. Hence all of them could most rightly say that verse of the psalmist: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been reckoned as sheep for slaughter.” The most holy apostle of Christ, Paul, also recalling the patience of the saints of old, says among other things: “They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves, and in the caverns of the earth.” For all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution, because, as the prophet says, “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them.”

132

On patience and gentleness.

127
Necessaria est igitur cunctis mortalibus patientia, et maxime decet claustrales, quoniam sicuti nunquam desunt iustis in hoc mundo contraria, ita nemo justificabitur sine patientia. Sunt autem gradus patientiae principales, quemadmodum veterum distinxit industria, tres. Primus quidem, ac infimus illorum est hominum, qui adversa neque inquirunt, neque libenter sufferunt, sed cum acciderint, gravantur animo, et deicientur moerore, conqueruntur etiam, quandoque, et murmurant contra inferentes ad horam, sed postquam inflammatā transierit concitatio mentis, ad se redeunt, et irrogatam sine vindicta contumeliām patienter tolerare videntur. Horum tamen non magnae virtutis patientia semper vitio inquietae mentis est proxima, et propterea saepe nullius, interdum vero minoris meriti aestimanda. Et quamvis hi nostris temporibus virtute patientiae dicantur insignes, comparati tamen veteribus sanctis hoc venerabile nomen Christianae longanimitatis, et tolerantiae non merentur. Non enim patientia videtur esse vera, quae amaritudine, et indignatione mentis concitatae fuerit obfuscata. Secundus patientiae gradus illorum esse hominum dicitur, qui licet mala perpeti non quaerant, attamen, cum venerint, ultro benigně suscipiunt, et quasi donum a Deo missum patientissime amplexantur. Et hi tales veraciter dicendi sunt patientes, qui divino succensi amore, quicquid adversi provenerit, aequanimiter tolerant, et eadem, quam prius habebant in prosperis, animi tranquillitatem, etiam in tribulatione conservant. Horum ex numero fuisse sanctissimum illum Job Idumaeum non dubitaverim, qui non solum adversitate percussus extrema patienter omnia tulit, sed, etiam in voragine malorum positus, gratias agens Domino benedixit. Dominus, inquiens, dedit, Dominus abstulit: sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est, sit nomen Domini benedictum. Hunc patientiae gradum omnes custodire convenit Christianos, et praeceteris maxime claustrales. Dicit enim vir sapiens: Doctrina viri per patientiam dignoscitur. Nam quanto unusquisque in lege Domini, et cognitione institutionis naturae rationalis doctior fuerit, tanto in adversis patientior erit. Quid si audentius loquar veritatis amator, quoniam plus nobis prosum adversa, quam prospera, si docti sumus, et propriae conditionis non oblivivosi pensiculatores? Tertius vero patientiae gradus reliquorum certe, et supremus, et perfectissimus illis merito conceditur, qui contraria non solum, cum opus fuerit, pro Dei amore, et utilitate fratrum aequanimiter tolerant, sed etiam ferventiore spiritu charitatis inflammati ultro se ingerentes ad contumelias, et iniurias suscipiendas alacriter festinant. Et hoc genus patientiae bifariam dividitur, sicuti duplex ratio martyrii sanctorum invenitur. Nam quidam, cum latere potuissent in persecutione credentium, ardente in eis charitate Christi, nemine compellente, sed spontanea se voluntate tribunalibus persequentium inges-

Patience, therefore, is necessary for all mortals, and it especially befits those who live in the cloister, since, just as adversities are never lacking to the righteous in this world, so no one will be justified without patience. Now the principal degrees of patience, as the diligence of the ancients distinguished them, are three.

The first and lowest is that of those people who neither seek out adversities nor bear them willingly, but when they befall them are weighed down in spirit and cast down with sorrow; they also sometimes complain and murmur for a time against those who inflict them. But after the agitation of their inflamed mind has passed, they return to themselves, and seem patiently to endure the insult inflicted on them without revenge. Yet the patience of these people, not being of great virtue, is always very near the fault of an unquiet mind, and therefore is often to be reckoned of no merit, and sometimes of lesser merit. And although in our times such people are called distinguished by the virtue of patience, nevertheless, compared with the holy men of old, they do not deserve this venerable name of Christian long-suffering and endurance. For that does not seem to be true patience which has been darkened by bitterness and indignation of an agitated mind.

The second degree of patience is said to belong to those people who, although they do not seek to suffer evils, nevertheless, when they come, receive them freely and kindly, and embrace them most patiently as though they were a gift sent by God. Such people are truly to be called patient: inflamed with divine love, they bear with equanimity whatever adversity has occurred, and preserve, even in tribulation, the same tranquillity of mind that they formerly had in prosperity. I would not doubt that that most holy Idumaean Job was of their number: struck not only by extreme adversity, he bore all things patiently, but even when placed in the whirlpool of evils, he gave thanks and blessed the Lord, saying: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

All Christians ought to keep this degree of patience, and especially, before others, those who live in the cloister. For the wise man says: “A man’s learning is known through patience.” For the more learned anyone is in the law of the Lord and in the knowledge of the ordering of rational nature, the more patient he will be in adversities. What if I, as a lover of truth, speak more boldly: that adversities profit us more than prosperities, if we are learned and not forgetful weighers of our own condition?

The third degree of patience, surely the highest and most perfect of the remaining ones, is rightly granted to those who not only, when there is need, bear adversities with equanimity for the love of God and the benefit of the brethren, but who also, inflamed with a more fervent spirit of charity, willingly thrust themselves forward and hasten eagerly to receive insults and injuries. And this kind of patience is divided in two ways, just as a twofold manner of martyrdom of the saints is found. For some, when they could have lain hidden during the persecution of believers, with the charity of Christ burning in them, with no one compelling them, but of their own free will, presented themselves to the tribunals of their persecutors [unclear].

128
Homilia XVIII. 133 serunt, et Iesum publice confitentes Redemptorem mundi, illata sibī tormenta cum gaudio susceperunt. Alii vero, quamvis se ultro non ingesserint, martyrium tamen gaudenter susceperunt oblatum, parati sempre sustinere pro fide Christi, quicquid crudelitas tyrannorum in- ferre potuisset. His gradum obtinent lucidissimi Confessores merito vi- ciniorem, quos et si crudelitas impiorum persequendo non abstulit, gloriam tamen martyrii nullatenus amiserunt. Enimvero crucifigens pro Christi nomine carnem suam in hoc mundo, et voluntarium, et diuturnum martyrium pertulerunt: qui per abstinentiam, et humilitatem glori- rosi facti sunt, animo constantes, ac patientissimi semper existentes, et ad martyrium corporaliter suscipiendum paratissimi. Quorum vos, o Monachi pro viribus imitatores esse curate, ut, quoniam hostes, qui corpus interimant pro Christo, iam desunt, concupiscentiis carnis reluc- tantes, et adversa patienter pro Dei amore sustinentes vos martyres mente, et spiritu exhibeatis. Martyrii genus in pace sanctorum est opti- mum, carnem pro Dei nomine per abstinentiam affligere, nihil in hoc mundo concupiscere, in operibus bonis semper proficere, et, si quid acciderit mali, cum hilaritate mentis gratanter, ac patienter in omnibus tolerare. Ad hanc normam patientiae fratres charissimi deinceps vivite, si cum Christo in aeternum cupitis regnare. Alter alterius onera port- tate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi, ut, quod sibi fieri quisque de- siderat, etiam fratri suo hilariter impendat. Isto modo Christianī omnes martyrium debemus Christo. De vera humilitate Monachorum. Homilia XIX. Omnium ferme doctorum sententia est, fratres charissimi, summam, et praecipuam monachorum virtutem, non aliam esse, quam humilitatem; propterea quod ipsa mater, et nutrix sit omnium virtutum. Humilitas namque monachum facit, superbia destruit, et corruptit. Hinc Dominus per Esaiam dicit: Ad quem respiciam, nisi ad pauperculum, et contritum spiritu, et trementem sermones meos? Deus enim superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam: quia initium omnis peccati su- perbia est, et sine vera humilitate nemo salutem consequi potest. Quod cum ita sit, necessarium mihi fore existimo, fratres, sine intermissione cohortari vos, ut superbia fugientes in omnibus operibus vestris pro- fundam semper custodatis humilitatem. Nullum quippe opus bonum Domino Deo placere creditur, quod sine condimento humilitatis praes- sentatur. Humilitas enim medicina est animabus fidelium saluberrima, quae omnibus consultit, quoniam tumentia spiritus viscera comprimit, tabescentia reficit, depravata corrigit, excrecentia tollit. O mater, et parens omnium virtutum humilitas, tu patientiam confirmas, compunctio- nem excitas, charitatem illuminas, castitatem ornas, orationem foecun-

Homily XVIII.

[unclear], and, publicly confessing Jesus as Redeemer of the world, they received the tortures inflicted on them with joy. Others, although they did not offer themselves of their own accord, nevertheless willingly received the martyrdom offered to them, always ready to endure for the faith of Christ whatever the cruelty of tyrants could have inflicted.

The most radiant Confessors rightly hold a rank nearer to these; even if the cruelty of the impious did not take them away by persecution, still they in no way lost the glory of martyrdom. For by crucifying their flesh in this world for the name of Christ, they endured a voluntary and long-lasting martyrdom: through abstinence and humility they were made glorious, steadfast in soul, always most patient, and most ready to undergo martyrdom bodily.

Take care, O monks, to be imitators of them according to your strength, so that, since enemies who kill the body for Christ are now lacking, you may show yourselves martyrs in mind and spirit by resisting the desires of the flesh and patiently enduring adversities for the love of God. In the peace of the saints, the best kind of martyrdom is to afflict the flesh for God’s name through abstinence, to desire nothing in this world, always to advance in good works, and, if any evil happens, to bear it in all things gladly and patiently with cheerfulness of mind.

Live henceforth according to this rule of patience, dearest brothers, if you desire to reign with Christ forever. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ, so that each one may cheerfully give to his brother what he desires to be done for himself.

In this way all Christians owe martyrdom to Christ.

On the True Humility of Monks. Homily XIX.

It is the judgment of almost all the teachers, dearest brothers, that the highest and chief virtue of monks is no other than humility, because it is itself the mother and nurse of all virtues. For humility makes the monk; pride destroys and corrupts him. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “To whom shall I look, except to the poor little one, and the contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my words?”

For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, because pride is the beginning of every sin, and without true humility no one can attain salvation. Since this is so, I think it necessary, brothers, to exhort you without ceasing that, fleeing pride, you always preserve deep humility in all your works. Indeed, no good work is believed to please the Lord God if it is presented without the seasoning of humility.

For humility is a most healthful medicine for the souls of the faithful, helping all, because it presses down the swollen inward parts of the spirit, restores what is wasting away, corrects what is depraved, and removes what has grown excessive. O humility, mother and parent of all virtues: you strengthen patience, stir up compunction, illumine charity, adorn chastity, make prayer fruitful [unclear].

129
134 De vera humilitate monachorum. das, ieiunium, et abstenientiam commendas. O sancta, et vere Deo dilecta humilitas, tu per poenitentiam iustificas impium, tu in sanctitatis proposito conservas iustum, tu amatoribus tuis potenter aperis coelum, tu poenitentibus claudis infernum. O veneranda, et nimium Deo grata humilitas, tu filium patris aeterni de coelis in uterum Mariae castissimae, atque perpetuae virginis compulisti descendere, tu illum nobis fecisti visibilem apparere, tu, pannis involutum vilibus, reposuisti in praesepio, ut nos ornamentis perpetuae foelicitatis decoraret in coelo. Tu Dei filium circumcisionem carnis impulisti suscipere, ut mente circumcisi nos ad promissam haereditatem sanctorum possemus introire. O magnae potentatis humilitas, quae regem coeli, et terrae a facie unius vilissimi homuncionis fecisti recedere, et septenni exilio in terra Aegyptiorum habitare. Tu Christum Iesum unigenitum Dei filium, quem corpus humanum pro salute nostra compulisti assumere, amarisimam quoque passionem, et mortem fecisti spontanea voluntate subire. Magnum est imperium tuum, o veneranda sanctitatis humilitas, quoniam tibi regnum coelorum promittitur, tuis cultoribus beatitudinis sempternae munus conceditur, et quisquis tua custodit vestigia, ad angelorum celsitudinem sublimatur, dicente in sancto Evangelio Christo: Omnis qui se exaltat, humiliabitur: et qui se humiliat, exaltabitur. Te Rex coelorum docuit, qui suis imitatoribus dixit: Discite a me, quia mitis sum, et humilis corde, et invenietis requiem animabus vestris. Beatissima quoque genitrix intacta virgo Maria, in suo cantico laudis dulcissimo de Domino Deo sic loquitur. Deposuit potentes de sedibus, et exaltavit humiles. Et propheta dicit in psalmo: Respexit Dominus in orationes humilium, et non sprevit preces eorum. Oratio nanque humilantis se nubes penetrat, et donec propinquet, non consolabitur, et non discedet, donec altissimus aspiciat. Monachum in conscientia sua purum humilitas Deo facit gratissimum, et quanto se pro Dei honore amplius humiliando deiecerit, tanto gloriosior in regno apparebit. Monachus, qui veraciter se humiliat, filius altissimi per gratiae participationem efficitur, et cum rege coelorum Iesu Christo in aeternum laetabitur. Qui vere Christum imitari desiderat, humilitatem quoque veram assumat, qua circumaminctus, et munitus quasi lorica fortitudinis magna faciat, de se non nisi humilia sentiens vanae gloriae maculam non incurrat. Haec enim vera monachorum perfectio est, propriam semper imperfectionem humiliter recognoscere, et potius, quid ei desit boni, quam quid habeat, sedulo cogitare. Vera namque humilitas in anteriora per desiderium charitatis semper extenditur, et praeteritorum causa memoratrix, ne perdat habita, metuit, et cupiens nondum habita per studium devotionis acquirere, in sanctitatis fervore non tepescit. In quantis adhuc deficiat, studiosissime considerat, et in quibus profe-

You give [unclear], and commend fasting and abstinence. O holy humility, truly beloved of God, through repentance you justify the ungodly; you preserve the just man in his resolve of holiness; you powerfully open heaven to those who love you; you close hell to the penitent.

O venerable humility, exceedingly pleasing to God, you compelled the Son of the eternal Father to descend from heaven into the womb of Mary, the most chaste and perpetual Virgin. You made him appear visible to us; you laid him, wrapped in poor cloths, in a manger, so that he might adorn us in heaven with the ornaments of everlasting happiness. You drove the Son of God to undergo circumcision of the flesh, so that we, circumcised in mind, might be able to enter the promised inheritance of the saints.

O humility of great power, you made the King of heaven and earth withdraw before the face of one most contemptible little man, and dwell in seven years’ exile in the land of Egypt. You made Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, whom you compelled to assume a human body for our salvation, undergo also his most bitter passion and death by his own free will.

Great is your dominion, O venerable humility of holiness, since the kingdom of heaven is promised to you, the gift of everlasting blessedness is granted to your worshipers, and whoever keeps to your footsteps is raised up to the height of the angels, as Christ says in the holy Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled; and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” The King of heaven taught you, when he said to his imitators: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” The most blessed Mother of God also, the untouched Virgin Mary, speaks thus of the Lord God in her sweetest song of praise: “He has cast down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble.” And the prophet says in the psalm: “The Lord has regarded the prayers of the humble, and has not despised their petitions.” For the prayer of one who humbles himself pierces the clouds; until it draws near, he will not be comforted, and he will not depart until the Most High looks upon him.

Humility makes a monk who is pure in his conscience most pleasing to God; and the more he casts himself down by humbling himself for God’s honor, the more glorious he will appear in the kingdom. The monk who truly humbles himself becomes a son of the Most High through participation in grace, and will rejoice forever with the King of heaven, Jesus Christ.

He who truly desires to imitate Christ should also take up true humility; girded and protected by it as by a breastplate of strength, he will do great things, thinking nothing of himself except what is humble, and will not incur the stain of vainglory. For this is the true perfection of monks: always humbly to recognize their own imperfection, and diligently to consider rather what good is lacking to them than what they possess.

For true humility always stretches forward toward the things ahead through the desire of charity; mindful of what is past, it fears lest it lose what it has, and, desiring to acquire through the zeal of devotion what it does not yet have, it does not grow lukewarm in the fervor of holiness. It considers most carefully how greatly it is still deficient, and in what respects it has made progress [unclear].

130
Homilia XIX. 135 cerit, non pensat. Enimvero quisquis se iam esse aliquid existimat, adhuc longius a vera humilitate distat, quoniam vera humilitas magna facit, et de se sentit minima, et quanto amplius profecerit, tanto in- firmitatem suam profundius recognoscit. Sic etenim Scriptura praecepit dicens. Quanto maior es, humilia te in omnibus, et coram Deo invenies gratiam. Iterumque dicit: Humilia valde spiritum tuum, quoniam vin- dicta carnis impii ignis, et vermis. Humilitatem igitur fratres mei as- sumite veram, non illam, quae foris in gestu, et voce coram hominibus a simulatoribus quandoque ostenditur, sed Christianam, quae puro cor- dis affectu possidetur. Aliud est enim virtutem habere humilitatis, et aliud imaginem similitudinis. Vera humilitas ad omnes iniurias, et contumelias tranquillo corde semper est patiens, ad praecepta quoque non solum maiorem, sed etiam aequalium est sine disceptatione obe- diens, in adversis servat constantiam, in corporis necessitate moderan- tiam, in moribus conscientiam, in convictu honestatem. Hilaris est, non dissoluta: gravis est, non melancholica: larga in miserationibus, non prodiga: infirmis compatiens, non remissa. Humilitas Christiana sine intermissione in amore Dei compungitur, in spiritu devotionis fervens jugiter lachrymis rigatur, suum principem Iesum Christum videre sem- per desiderat, cuius monita sequens in spiritu, prae dolore suspirat. Dolet enim se peccatorem, quicunque humilitatem veram complectitur; ingemiscit se non posse tantum proficere, quantum cupit, quisquis Dei filium imitatur. Nihil excellentius humilitate Christiana, nihil pra- clarius cognitione propria, quae semper in eminentiori posita nunquam extollitur: et subiecta omnibus universis dominatur. Qui enim parvus est in oculis suis, magnus coram Deo efficitur: et qui se magnum ali- quid esse in hoc mundo existimat, coram Deo nullius momenti iu- dicatur. Nam tanto erit quisque apud internum iudicem preciosior, quanto bene faciens, et nunquam deficiens, fuerit in aestimatione sua despectior. Humilitas enim stabile fundamentum est omnium virtutum, quoniam omne spirituale aedificium, quod in altum Christianae per- fectionis erigitur, sola humilitatis petra sustinetur.
