Be ready at all times to obey the commands of your shepherd, and however much progress you have made in the struggle of holy combat, do not lift up your soul in any estimation of your progress. For what are our righteousnesses before the Lord? Or what good can we do that he has not given? Since God, who is sufficient to himself in all things and alone perfect, has no need of our good deeds, for he is the highest and unchangeable good, in comparison with whom all our justifications are less than nothing.

Therefore a monk placed under an abbot, in the humility of one truly obedient, walks securely; and if he perseveres to the end, fighting and conquering, he will be gloriously rewarded. Truly, brothers, the humility of your obedience delights me, which you show faithfully to the almighty Lord. In this respect I do not regard myself as your prelate, but as your companion and the humble minister of you all, though a more useless one. Therefore, in those matters that concern your salvation, I beg you, do not look at my person as I speak, but rather at the common Lord of all, for love of whom you have set me, an unworthy man, over you as abbot. For I will not be troublesome to you while you are running well; but if anyone turns aside from the way of truth, I am compelled, even unwillingly, to oppose him as far as I can.

Let a monk always remember his entrance into the monastery, and never forget the first resolve of his training. In all your works too, O monk, always remember that you are not lasting long upon the earth, but will shortly depart from this life, and that you will die perhaps when you do not expect it. Therefore keep inviolate your purpose of holiness, and always be watchful in good works, so that when the Lord comes and calls you, he may find you prepared. Remember that you are a pilgrim on earth, and have here no abiding city; but just as a traveler hastens quickly toward the end of his journey, so death approaches you daily without interruption.

Therefore, while you are healthy, set the house of your conscience in order, so that you may not fear death, since he rarely dies well who is not prepared as one who will die each day. O how securely that monk departs from this life who, keeping his conscience clean in all purity, conducts himself at all times, without reproach, according to the full integrity of the rule of our most holy lawgiver, even to death. Let your mind continually [keep before it] our Lord Jesus Christ as present, indeed as nowhere absent.

143
Homilia XX. 149 habeat in memoria; et non transeat hora, in qua patientem pro te cum gratiarum actione non cogites. Sta in humilitate, et vera obedientia, et nulla tibi unquam praevalebunt contraria. Quemadmodum arbor multas, et magnas radices in terra mittens non facile de loco suo evellitur, sic monachus charitatem, et obedientiam in humilitate cum caeteris virtutibus possidens, nequaquam a daemonibus superatur. Obedientia magna virtus est, fratres, quae menti caeteras virtutes insertis, insertasque per humilitatis ministerium custodit. Ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus, qui factus est pro nobis obedientis usque ad mortem crucis, corda vestra per gratiam suam illuminet, et mentes vestras ad observantiam regularis vitae omni tempore dulciter inflammet, qui vivit, et regnat cum Deo patre in unitate Spiritus sancti Deus per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen. De continentia et vera castitate. Homilia XXI. Maxime optarem, fratres mei charissimi, eam me gratiam consequentum a Deo, qua vobis pastor dignus, ed idoneus opere simul esset, et sermone. Scio enim, nec me fugit, quam periculosa res sit homini iuveni, et inexperto, qualis ego sum, regimen animarum, quando is, qui necdum semetipsum dirigere, et gubernare ad iustitiae normam didicit, accedere ad aliorum magisterium praesumit. Erubesco in medio vestrum os meum aperire ad docendum, qui breve tempore discipulus, ante maturitatem cogor esse didascalus. Verum, quoniam ita placuit vobis, et voluistis me iuvenem habere magistrum, parcite mihi, quoniam necessitas me compellit commissum pro viribus adimplere officium. Vestris mihi subvenite orationibus, precor fratres, ut vires, quas aetatis imperitia denegat, Dei miseratio impendat. Cupio enim vos coram Deo ambulare in omni puritate mentis, et corporis, ut ei complacatis, cui vos ab initio tradidistis. Ducem itineris assumpti ad coelum intueamini Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, qui natus de virgine Maria semper pudicissima, mentis, et corporis perfectissimam castitatem perpetuo conservavit. Hunc sequamini praecceptorem, in cuius militiam manus consecrasti, ut non solum corpore servetis vobis continentiam, sed etiam mente lucidam super saphirum, et carbunculum custodiatis perpetuo castitatem. Castitas enim virtus pulcherrima praecipue decet claustrales, per quam sub iugo rationis impetus omnis refroenetur libidinis, et furia extincta vitiorum habitudo corporis servetur totius honestatis. Monachus incontinentis, et lascivus, qui spurcam carnis libidinem sequitur, cum daemonibus, qui recesserunt a Domino, computatur. Tria sunt enim, sine quorum observatione perpetua, nemo inter monachos censetur nominandus. Horum primum, est humilis, et verae subiectionis obedientia; et secundum, omnis abdication propriae. 150 De continentia et vera castitate.

Let him keep it in memory, and let no hour pass in which you do not think with thanksgiving of him suffering for you. Stand in humility and true obedience, and no adversities will ever prevail against you. Just as a tree that sends many great roots into the earth is not easily torn from its place, so a monk who possesses charity and obedience in humility, together with the other virtues, is by no means overcome by demons. Obedience is a great virtue, brothers; it plants the other virtues in the mind, and, once planted, guards them through the ministry of humility. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who was made obedient for us unto the death of the cross, enlighten your hearts by his grace, and sweetly inflame your minds at all times for the observance of the regular life; he who lives and reigns with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

On Continence and True Chastity. Homily XXI.

I would greatly wish, my dearest brothers, that I had obtained from God that grace by which I might be a worthy and suitable pastor for you in deed as well as in word. For I know, and it does not escape me, how dangerous a thing the governance of souls is for a young and inexperienced man such as I am, when one who has not yet learned to direct and govern himself according to the rule of justice presumes to undertake the teaching of others. I blush to open my mouth among you to teach, since after only a short time as a disciple I am compelled, before maturity, to be a teacher. Yet since it has so pleased you, and you have wished to have me, a young man, as your master, spare me, for necessity compels me to fulfill, according to my strength, the office entrusted to me. Help me with your prayers, I beg you, brothers, so that the mercy of God may supply the strength that the inexperience of age denies.

For I desire you to walk before God in all purity of mind and body, so that you may please him to whom you gave yourselves from the beginning. Look to our Lord Jesus Christ as the guide of the journey you have undertaken toward heaven: born of the ever most chaste Virgin Mary, he preserved forever the most perfect chastity of mind and body. Follow this teacher, into whose service you have consecrated your hands, so that you may preserve continence for yourselves not only in body, but also perpetually guard in mind a chastity brighter than sapphire and carbuncle. For chastity is a most beautiful virtue, especially fitting for those in the cloister; through it every impulse of lust is curbed under the yoke of reason, and, the madness of vices being extinguished, the body’s disposition is preserved in complete honorableness.

An incontinent and wanton monk, who follows the filthy lust of the flesh, is counted with the demons who withdrew from the Lord. For there are three things without whose perpetual observance no one is to be reckoned worthy of being named among monks. The first of these is the obedience of humble and true subjection; and the second, the renunciation of everything of one’s own.

144
tatis, ut praecipit regula; tertium, perpetuae continentiae, et castitatis inviolata custodia. Quodlibet istorum violaverit monachus, ordinis sui propositum corruptit. Duobus castitas sustentatur comitibus, ieiunio vi- delicit, ac temperantia, quibus si aliquando destituta fuerit, cito procul dubio labascit. Castitas monachorum ornamentum est maximum, qua decorati ad consortium introducentur angelorum. Castitate nihil est pulchrioris, quae conceptum de immundo semine facit mundum, de hoste quoque efficit domesticum, et de homine terrestri angelum. Castitas virtus est omnium virtutum speciosissima, quae dum pro Christi amore usque ad mortem servanda promittitur, inaestimabili praemio remuneratur. Castitas angelorum societati est proxima, et summa christianae mentis medicina. Castitas est Iesu Christi aeterni regis amabile domicilium, et futurae incorruptionis mirabile principium. Castitas est plenitudo coelestis gratiae, per quam redintegratur omnis corruptio naturae. Castitas est virtus omnium potentissima, per quam in vase fragili mirabili certamine vincitur natura. Castitas vitam imitatur angelicam, et nescit in medio luti aliquam maculae conspersionem. Beatus homo, qui vere donum castitatis a Domino Deo suscipe promeruit, et ipsum inviolatum usque ad mortem in humilitate christianae custodivit. Castus est, qui amore Iesu Christi mente, et corpore purus, ab omni carnis coinquinatione se abstinet, qui fervore sancti Spiritus in charitate Dei dulciter ardet, qui nihil omnino concupiscit in hoc saeculo, qui esse, et vivere semper desiderat cum Christo. Castus est, qui memor professionis militiae spiritualis motus carnis ratione comprimit, et omnes prurientes libidinis scintillas mox a principio fortiter restringit. Castus est, qui mox, ut cogitatio carnalis mentem pulsare cepert, divinum cum lacrymis implorat auxilium, nec quiescit a precibus, donec incendium prurientis ardoris penitus senserit extinctum. Castus est, qui fugit omnem materiam, et occasionem luxuriae, qui pepigit foedus cum oculis suis, ne quid cogitet de foemina, et ponit custodiam sensibus suis, ne qua ingerantur foeda, vel impudica. Castus est, qui lascivorum declinat consortia, et semper avertit oculos suos, ne conspiciat vana. Castus est, qui omnium mulierum detestatur frequentiam, et qui suam fragilitatem cum timore, et vigilantia omni tempore habet suspectam. Castus quidem est, qui mente et corpore naturam imitatur angelicam, et qui sanctis moribus nullam admittit corruptionem. Castitas donum est gratiae, et non opus naturae, vel industriae humanae. Castitas monachum humilem Deo facit esse gratissimum, quoniam, qui vivit in carne mortali sine corruptione, socius est angelorum. Qui castitatem assecutus est veram, semper est humilis: et qui naturam eius intelligit, non sibi eius possessionem arrogat, sed Domino, qui dedit. Nemo enim castus viribus suis, quoniam naturam vincere homo fragilis non

of [unclear], as the Rule commands; the third vow, perpetual continence and the inviolate custody of chastity. If a monk violates any one of these, he corrupts the purpose of his order.

Chastity is supported by two companions, namely fasting and temperance; if it is ever deprived of them, it very quickly, without doubt, begins to totter. Chastity is the greatest adornment of monks; adorned with it, they will be brought into the company of the angels. Nothing is more beautiful than chastity: it makes clean what was conceived from unclean seed, it makes a member of the household out of an enemy, and an angel out of an earthly man.

Chastity is the most beautiful virtue of all virtues; when it is promised to be kept even until death for the love of Christ, it is rewarded with an inestimable prize. Chastity is nearest to the fellowship of angels, and is the highest medicine of the Christian mind. Chastity is the beloved dwelling place of Jesus Christ, the eternal King, and the wondrous beginning of future incorruption. Chastity is the fullness of heavenly grace, through which every corruption of nature is restored. Chastity is the most powerful virtue of all, through which, in a fragile vessel, nature is conquered in a wondrous contest. Chastity imitates the angelic life, and knows no sprinkling of stain in the midst of the mire.

Blessed is the man who has truly deserved to receive from the Lord God the gift of chastity, and has kept it inviolate until death in Christian humility. He is chaste who, pure in mind and body for the love of Jesus Christ, abstains from every defilement of the flesh; who, with the fervor of the Holy Spirit, burns sweetly in the love of God; who desires absolutely nothing in this world; who always longs to be and to live with Christ.

He is chaste who, mindful of his profession in spiritual warfare, restrains the movements of the flesh by reason, and at once, from the very beginning, firmly checks all the itching sparks of lust. He is chaste who, as soon as a carnal thought has begun to strike the mind, implores divine help with tears, and does not cease from prayers until he feels that the fire of itching ardor has been utterly extinguished.

He is chaste who flees every matter and occasion of lust; who has made a covenant with his eyes that he should think nothing about a woman, and sets a guard over his senses, lest any foul or immodest things be thrust upon them. He is chaste who avoids the company of the wanton, and always turns his eyes away lest he behold vain things. He is chaste who detests the frequent company of all women, and who at all times regards his own frailty with fear and vigilance as suspect.

He indeed is chaste who in mind and body imitates the angelic nature, and who admits no corruption in holy conduct. Chastity is a gift of grace, not a work of nature or of human effort. Chastity makes a humble monk most pleasing to God, since he who lives in mortal flesh without corruption is a companion of the angels. He who has attained true chastity is always humble; and he who understands its nature does not arrogate its possession to himself, but to the Lord who gave it. For no one is chaste by his own strength, since frail man cannot conquer nature.

145
Homilia XXI. 151 sufficit, nisi dederit ille, qui naturam et omnia creavit. Nam quoties natura per castitatem vincitur, Deus homini manifeste cooperatur. Habet autem ipsa castitas in pubescentibus difficile principium, quousque motus illicitae cogitationis ducatur in contemptum. Castitas fornicationem fu- giendo potius, quam concertando, exsuperat, quoniam tot subtilibus armis luxuria circumcingitur, ut ul tro sit declinanda priusquam con- grediatur. Quotiescunque ergo animus luxuriae motibus tangitur, di- vinum sine mora auxilium invocetur, non detur immundae cogitationi deliberacionis spacium, sed mox ut sentiri ceperit, per oblivionis reme- dium ducatur in contemptum. Cum hoste fraudulento, et qui semper utitur insidiis, nulla sunt penitus commiscenda colloquia, et cum im- mundis cogitationibus carnis non sunt tractanda consilia. Enimvero nisi caput serpentis conteras, labitur: et nisi motus luxuriae mox com- primas a principio, roborantur. Monet sanctus Christi Apostolus Paulus contra quaelibet vitia pugnandum, fornicationem solam praecipit fu- giendam. Materiam contra nos victoriae circumferimus, propterea vult, quod hostem fugiamus. Castitas ieiunio alitur, gula naufragatur. Unde si castitatem diligis, ama ieiunium, ut necessarium habeat alimentum. Qui castus est, apis industriae sequitur: et qui vere est monachus, quasi omnibus floribus exornatus, cunctis virtutibus decoratur. Castus est non omnis, qui nescit luxuriam, sed qui in carne pura, et munda pro Christi amore solius, etiam mentis obtinet sanctitatem. Alioquin quid prodest domicilii puritas, si habitator sit foedus, et immundus? Habuit et virgines suas quondam Vestae sacrificantes caeca gentilitas, sed quia non Deo vero pudicitiam corporum immolarunt, nec fidem rectam mente tenuerunt, cum suis daemonibus, quos coluerunt, in pro- fundum inferni descenderunt. Castus est enim, qui amore creatoris et carnem ab omni cohibet luxuria, et mentem sanctis virtutibus ipsi Deo immolat omnifariam decoratum. Extra fidem Iesu Christi hodie non est castitas vera, neque ad salutem aeternam meritoria. Vive castus o monache, conversare purus, et sanctus, et quandiu manet in corpore spiritus, de luto non praesumas confidentiam habere castitatis. Cibus castitatis est ieiunium, et abstinentia, et in omni actione salubris con- tinentiae firmamentum. Sed cum omnia fueris assecutus, noli confidere, quia de coelo lapsus est, quem scimus nihil manducasse. Maceratio corporis ad conservandam pulchritudinem castitatis necessaria est valde, et utilis; sed quantumcumque in utraque profeceris, noli tibimetipsi confidere, sed vigilans semper, et sperans in auxilium Domini time. Nisi enim continue et instantissime tenueris te in timore Domini, cito subvertetur domus conscientiae tuae. In vanum currit, qui castitatem suis viribus custodire praesumit. Nisi enim Dominus aedificaverit ca- stitatis domicilium, frustra laborat, qui abstinentiae construit murum. Vincenda libido om- nis, non pu- gna, sed fuga. r. Cor. 6. Amans ca- stitatem, ama et iei- unium. Eccles. 27. 152 De continentia et vera castitate. Castitas maxime dom- num Dei. Et nisi tu viribus totis gratiae divinae cooperator extiteris, castitatis pulchritudinem nullatenus obtinebis. Neque enim castum te faciet Deus sine tua voluntate, neque tu donum hoc magnum consequeris, nisi succurrat ille per suam miseracionem tuae infirmitati. Tuum ergo fuerit o monache in bona voluntate castitatis offerre desiderium, et in humili confidentia certum a Domino expectare incrementum. Adhibe tuum, et non deerit Domini auxilium. Castitas donum est gratiae, non naturae, et praeter carnem, in carne vivere, angelicae fortitudinis est, non humanae. Veruntamen non est difficile servare castitatem homini bonae voluntatis, qui maxime segregatur a tumultu saecularium, et vivit solitarius in medio monachorum. Monachus etiam, qui iuvenis, et innocens bonae reformationis caenobium ingreditur, si mentem suam in timore Domini continue occupaverit, minus a luxuria impugnatur. Perniciosa enim est libidinis experientia, quoniam sicut quidam veraciter dixit: Vincere vult animos non satiare venus.

Homily XXI.

It is not enough unless he who created nature and all things has given it. For whenever nature is overcome by chastity, God is manifestly working together with man. Chastity itself has a difficult beginning in the young, until the movement of unlawful thought is brought into contempt. Chastity overcomes fornication by fleeing rather than fighting, because lust is girded about with so many subtle weapons that it must be avoided before it is engaged.

Therefore, whenever the soul is touched by the movements of lust, let divine help be invoked without delay. Let no time for deliberation be given to an unclean thought, but as soon as it begins to be felt, let it be brought into contempt by the remedy of forgetfulness. With a deceitful enemy, one who always uses ambushes, no conversations at all are to be mingled; and with the unclean thoughts of the flesh no counsels are to be discussed. For unless you crush the serpent’s head, it slips away; and unless you immediately repress the movements of lust from the beginning, they grow strong.

The holy apostle of Christ, Paul, warns that one must fight against every vice, but he commands that fornication alone be fled. We carry about with us the material for victory against ourselves; therefore he wills that we flee the enemy. Chastity is nourished by fasting; by gluttony it suffers shipwreck. Therefore, if you love chastity, love fasting, so that it may have its necessary nourishment.

He who is chaste follows the diligence of the bee; and he who is truly a monk, as if adorned with every flower, is adorned with all virtues. Not everyone is chaste who does not know lust, but he who, in pure and clean flesh, for the love of Christ alone, also obtains holiness of mind. Otherwise, what does the purity of the dwelling profit, if the inhabitant is foul and unclean?

Blind paganism once had its virgins sacrificing to Vesta; but because they did not offer the chastity of their bodies to the true God, nor hold right faith in their mind, they went down into the depth of hell with their demons, whom they worshiped. For he is chaste who, for love of the Creator, restrains the flesh from every lust, and offers the mind, adorned in every way with holy virtues, to God himself. Outside faith in Jesus Christ today there is no true chastity, nor any that merits eternal salvation.

Live chastely, O monk; conduct yourself pure and holy; and as long as the spirit remains in the body, do not presume to have confidence in the chastity of clay. The food of chastity is fasting and abstinence, and in every action the strengthening of wholesome continence. But when you have attained all things, do not trust in yourself, because he fell from heaven whom we know to have eaten nothing. The mortification of the body is very necessary and useful for preserving the beauty of chastity; but however much you have advanced in both, do not trust in yourself, but always keep watch, hope in the help of the Lord, and fear.

For unless you continually and most urgently keep yourself in the fear of the Lord, the house of your conscience will quickly be overthrown. He runs in vain who presumes to guard chastity by his own strength. For unless the Lord has built the dwelling of chastity, he labors in vain who builds the wall of abstinence. And unless you have become, with all your strength, a co-worker with divine grace, you will by no means obtain the beauty of chastity.

For God will not make you chaste without your will, nor will you attain this great gift unless he comes to the aid of your weakness through his mercy. Therefore, O monk, it will be yours, with a good will, to offer the desire for chastity, and with humble confidence to await sure increase from the Lord. Apply what is yours, and the Lord’s help will not be lacking. Chastity is a gift of grace, not of nature; and to live in the flesh as though beyond the flesh belongs to angelic strength, not human.

Yet it is not difficult for a man of good will to preserve chastity, especially one who is separated from the tumult of secular people and lives solitary in the midst of monks. A monk also who, young and innocent, enters a monastery of good reform, if he continually occupies his mind in the fear of the Lord, is less attacked by lust. For experience of desire is destructive, since, as someone has truly said:

Venus wants to conquer souls, not satisfy them.

146
Monachus autem propriae salutis studiosus, amator libidinis ardorem de facilis potest extinguere, si otium, et saturitatem fugiens, in spirituali exercitio se continue voluerit occupare. Inter omnia quippe vita, nullum amplius, et periculosius castitatem impugnat, quam saturitas, et otium. Si haec duo mala superaverit monachus, castitatem facile custodiet. Hinc sanctissimi principes monachorum, cupientes amputare libidinis causas, victum nobis parcum, ac tenuem constituerunt ad certam mensuram, quo corpus sustentetur ad necessitatem, et non incrassetur ad libidinem. Somni quoque parcitatem monachis utillem sanxerunt, quia requies immoderata carnem non minus extendit, quam gula. Otium vero tanquam animae perniciosissimam pestem longe voluerunt esse a claustralibus, partientes sapientissime tempus, ut monachus nunquam inveniretur otiosus. Audite haec fratres, et mente percipite, qui thesaurus magnum in fragili corpusculo portatis. Otium fugite, semper aliquid boni facite, ut quoties tentator diabolus accesserit, utiliter vos inveniat occupatos. Enimvero qui otiosus est, insidiis patet tentantis: qui autem occupatur in opere bono, aditum clausit omnem insidiis. Continua igitur exercitazione occupandus est animus, ut nunquam inveniatur otiosus. Beatus ille monachus, qui mentem suam in omni tempore in bonis exercitiis occupat, et nunquam in somno torporis et ignaviae dormit. Beatus est miles Christi spiritualis, qui semper in timore Domini vigilat, et omnes inordinatos motus carnis statim a principio refroenat. Veram enim castitatem illaesam custodire non sufficit, quisquis cum immundis cogitationibus quasi deliberans ludit. Primis motibus iniquarum cogitationum reluctandum est, quoniam ubi mora generat periculum, statim fortiter est pugnandum. Semper est vigilandum contra salutis

But a monk zealous for his own salvation can easily extinguish the fire of lust, if, fleeing idleness and repletion, he is willing to occupy himself continually in spiritual exercise. For among all the vices, none attacks chastity more greatly or more dangerously than repletion and idleness. If a monk has overcome these two evils, he will easily guard chastity. Hence the most holy fathers of monks, wishing to cut away the causes of lust, established for us a sparing and scanty diet in fixed measure, so that the body may be sustained for necessity and not fattened for lust. They also ordained restriction of sleep as useful for monks, because immoderate rest inflames the flesh no less than gluttony. But they wished idleness, as the most destructive plague of the soul, to be far from cloistered men, most wisely dividing the time so that a monk would never be found idle.

Hear these things, brothers, and grasp them in your mind, you who carry a great treasure in a fragile little body. Flee idleness; always do some good thing, so that as often as the devil the tempter approaches, he may find you usefully occupied. For truly, he who is idle lies open to the snares of the tempter; but he who is occupied in good work has closed every entrance to snares. Therefore the mind must be occupied with continual exercise, so that it may never be found idle.

Blessed is that monk who occupies his mind at all times in good exercises, and never sleeps in the slumber of torpor and sloth. Blessed is the spiritual soldier of Christ who always keeps watch in the fear of the Lord, and immediately restrains from the beginning all the disordered movements of the flesh. For it is not enough to preserve true chastity unharmed if one plays, as though deliberating, with unclean thoughts. One must resist the first stirrings of wicked thoughts, since where delay gives rise to danger, one must immediately fight bravely. One must always keep watch against [unclear] of salvation.

147
Homilia XXI. 153 nostrae adversarium, qui nunquam citius vincitur, quam si mox a principio sufocetur. Continua exercitazione opus est fratres, quia mens in sanctis studiis semper occupata est quasi turris altissima fortitudinis, in qua constitutus miles Iesu Christi vigilantissimus, nullas metuit insidias hostilitatis. Obsecro vos igitur, fratres mei charissimi, ne otio tempus consumatis, ne materiam in vobis vitiorum auxeritis, qui maligni spiritus astutias non ignoratis. Continentiam servate in omnibus, et directricem virtutum temperantiam adhibete cunctis operibus vestris. Semper cogitate, quemadmodum oporteat vos in omni religione, et sanctitate ambulare coram Domino Deo, in cuius verba iurastis, et sic vivite, ut comparere in eius iudicio non timeatis. Monachi estis in ministerium Domini nostri Iesu Christi voluntaria promissione segregati de mundo, unde oportet sub necessitate salutis altorem, et sanctiorem vos caeteris conchristianis ducere vitam, et omnem carnis, et animae devincere pravitatem. Oportet enim vos mente simul, et corpore semper esse castissimos, et nulla corruptibilis carnis spurcitia maculatos. Monachus incontinentis apostata est: et qui carnem suam coinquinat spurcitia mulierum, similis est violanti iuramentum. Lacus inferni luxuria, et desperatio semper incontinentiae est proxima. Monachus, qui semel in foveam carnis labitur, raro ad veram compunctionem cordis inflammatur. Nam fornicationis vitium consuetudine diuturna convalescens, de facili non vincitur, nisi contrariis remediis per violentiam emendetur. Maioris difficultatis est post lapsum carnis ad veram castitatem resurgere, quam in habita continenti permanere. Facilius est a statu rectitudinis in quodlibet vitium cadere, quam roboratum consuetudine peccatum emendare. Nam, ut veraciter quidam ait gentilis, Facilis descensus Averni: Sed revocare gradum superasque evadere ad auras, Hoc opus, hic labor est. Consideremus illos, qui foveam hanc turpissimam inciderunt, et postea maiorum auctoritate ad poenitentiam compulsi sunt, quemadmodum in medio fratrum conversantur. Verae compunctionis non habent signa, sed in ariditate cordis vitam agunt inquietam. Nulla mentis devotio apud eos conspicitur, sed carnis ubique solita sequuntur. O quam raro ad interni amoris dulcedinem convertitur, quiquis in lacum fornicationis semel precipitat. Nisi enim, priusquam in hanc miseriam deveniat, fundatus in timore Domini fuerit lapsus, difficillime ad veram compunctionem recurrit. Sobrie igitur vivite fratres charissimi, et semper vigilate in orationibus sanctis, quoniam nisi cautissime in omnibus ambulaveritis, laqueos daemonum nequaquam poteritis evadere. Abstinentiam dilegitte, humilitatem super omnia custodite. Nemo enim carnis suae motus potest deprimere, qui gulam, et superbiam contemptserit edomare. For- 154 De continentia et vera castitate.

our adversary [unclear], who is never overcome more quickly than if he is choked off at once from the beginning. Constant practice is needed, brothers, because a mind always occupied in holy studies is like a very high tower of strength, in which the most watchful soldier of Jesus Christ, once stationed, fears no hostile ambushes.

Therefore I beseech you, my dearest brothers, do not waste your time in idleness; do not increase within yourselves the material of vices, since you are not ignorant of the cunning of the evil spirit. Preserve continence in all things, and apply temperance, the guide of the virtues, to all your works. Always consider how you ought to walk before the Lord God in all religion and holiness, into whose words you have sworn, and live in such a way that you do not fear to appear at his judgment.

You are monks, separated from the world by voluntary promise for the service of our Lord Jesus Christ; therefore, under the necessity of salvation, you must lead a higher and holier life than the rest of your fellow Christians, and overcome every depravity of flesh and soul. For you must always be most chaste in mind and body alike, and stained by no filth of corruptible flesh. An incontinent monk is an apostate; and one who defiles his flesh with the filth of women is like one who violates an oath. Lust is a pit of hell, and despair is always very near to incontinence.

A monk who once slips into the pit of the flesh is rarely kindled to true compunction of heart. For the vice of fornication, growing strong through long habit, is not easily overcome unless it is corrected by force with contrary remedies. It is more difficult after a fall of the flesh to rise again to true chastity than to remain in continence once possessed. It is easier to fall from the state of uprightness into any vice than to correct a sin strengthened by habit. For, as a certain pagan truly says:

Easy is the descent to Avernus; but to recall the step and escape to the upper airs, this is the task, this is the labor.

Let us consider those who have fallen into this most foul pit and afterward, by the authority of their superiors, have been compelled to do penance: how do they live among the brothers? They do not have the signs of true compunction, but pass an unquiet life in dryness of heart. No devotion of mind is seen in them, but everywhere they follow the accustomed ways of the flesh. How rarely is anyone converted to the sweetness of inward love who has once plunged into the pit of fornication. For unless, before he comes into this misery, he has been grounded in the fear of the Lord, once fallen he returns with the greatest difficulty to true compunction.

Therefore live soberly, dearest brothers, and always keep watch in holy prayers, because unless you walk most cautiously in all things, you will by no means be able to escape the snares of demons. Love abstinence; guard humility above all things. For no one can suppress the impulses of his flesh who has neglected to tame gluttony and pride.

148
nicationis insolens daemonium nunquam melius vincitur, quam si vera cordis humilitas in plenitudine virtutum omnium conservetur. Nam sicut omnipotens Deus superbis resistens, humilibus dat gratiam, ita diabolus fugiens humiles, superbos praecipitat in fornicationem. Qui ergo gulosus ad satietatem, manducans et bibens, vincere spiritum for- nicationis desiderat, quasi oleum ad incendium portat. Et, qui cum sola abstinentia luxuriae motus contendit extinguere, similis est homini, qui cum una manu in medio flunctuum cernitur natare. Coniungatur absti- nentiae continua ad Deum oratio, et in navi sanctae humilitatis secure navigabitur. Semper sit in ore monachi oratio, et memoria passionis, et mortis Domini Iesu nunquam ab eius meditatione recedat. Nihil enim sic mentem adversus daemonem fornicationis confortat, et animam, sicut devota meditatio passionis Domini, et salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Quoties ergo motum carnis inordinatum senseris, quoties hostem adesse invisibilem ad nocendum perceperis, mox ad pendentem in cruce filium Dei confugito, flexisque in terram genibus, talis ad eum formetur oratio. O Iesu crucifixe amor meus, per dolorem vulnerum tuorum miserere mei, per sanctissimi sanguinis tui effusionem adiuva me in isto certa- mine, et per virtutem innocentissimae mortis tuae libera me ab omni mentis, et corporis contagione. Nihil hoc orationis modo salubrius, in qua passionis Christi memoria colitur, et in virtute salvatoris omnium petitiones solidantur. Nihil antiqui hostis insidias magis extenuat, nihil vires malignitatis eius citius infirmat, quam si devotus Christi servus in meditatione amarissimae passionis Domini humiliter perseverat. Quemadmodum fur quispiam fugit ante faciem iudicis persequentis, sic diabolus velociter evanescit a conspectu monachi meditantis cum atten- tione passionem et mortem salvatoris. Cito motus iniquae cogitationis extinguitur, ubi passionis Christi amaritudo ad mentem revocatur. Quem- admodum nix incalescente sole resoluitur, ita diabolus a meditatione passionis dominicae fugatur. Maximum castitatis praesidium est, au- xilium semper invoke divinum. Et nisi mox a principio tentationis recurras ad Dominum, senties paulatim ex mora detrimentum. Nam si moram in cogitationibus perniciosis admiseris, insensibilem mox dae- mones ingerunt caecitatem mentis. Nisi enim mens prius excaecata fuerit, voluntas daemoni non succumbit. Fornicationis vero spiritus mentem in primis graviter obtenebrat, postea, donec praecipitaverit in peccatum, obcoecatum pugnat. Postea vero quam monachum in lutum nefandi sceleris praecipitaverit, ne consurgat iterum ad poenitentiam, duobus se modus interponit. Aut enim peccati gravitatem subtiliter al- leviare conatur, ut poenam grandem non metuat: aut distinctionem iu- dicii lapso reducit ad memoriam, ut desperationis foveam incurrat. His laqueis capitur peccatrix anima, et quanto diutius iacuerit in profundo

The insolent demon of fornication is never better conquered than when true humility of heart is preserved in the fullness of all virtues. For just as almighty God, resisting the proud, gives grace to the humble, so the devil, fleeing the humble, hurls the proud down into fornication. Therefore anyone who is gluttonous, eating and drinking to satiety, and desires to conquer the spirit of fornication, is carrying oil to the fire. And anyone who strives to extinguish the impulses of lust by abstinence alone is like a man seen swimming with one hand in the midst of the waves. Let continual prayer to God be joined to abstinence, and he will sail securely in the ship of holy humility.

Let prayer always be in the monk’s mouth, and let the memory of the passion and death of the Lord Jesus never depart from his meditation. For nothing so strengthens the mind against the demon of fornication, and the soul, as devout meditation on the passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Therefore, as often as you feel a disordered movement of the flesh, as often as you perceive that the invisible enemy is present to do harm, at once flee to the Son of God hanging on the cross, and, with your knees bent to the ground, let such a prayer be formed to him:

O Jesus crucified, my love, through the pain of your wounds have mercy on me; through the shedding of your most holy blood help me in this struggle; and through the power of your most innocent death free me from every defilement of mind and body.

Nothing is more wholesome than this manner of prayer, in which the memory of Christ’s passion is honored and all petitions are strengthened in the power of the Savior. Nothing more weakens the snares of the ancient enemy, nothing more quickly enfeebles the forces of his malice, than if the devoted servant of Christ humbly perseveres in meditation on the most bitter passion of the Lord. Just as some thief flees before the face of the pursuing judge, so the devil swiftly vanishes from the sight of a monk meditating attentively on the passion and death of the Savior. The movement of wicked thought is quickly extinguished where the bitterness of Christ’s passion is recalled to mind. Just as snow melts when the sun grows warm, so the devil is put to flight by meditation on the Lord’s passion.

The greatest safeguard of chastity is always to invoke divine aid. And unless you run back to the Lord at once from the beginning of temptation, you will gradually feel the harm caused by delay. For if you allow delay amid pernicious thoughts, the demons soon introduce an imperceptible blindness of mind. For unless the mind has first been blinded, the will does not succumb to the demon. But the spirit of fornication first heavily darkens the mind; afterward, until it has hurled it down into sin, it fights against the blinded one. And after it has hurled the monk into the mire of unspeakable crime, lest he rise again to repentance, it sets itself in the way in two ways. For either it subtly tries to lessen the gravity of the sin, so that he may not fear a great punishment; or it brings back to the fallen man’s memory the strictness of judgment, so that he may fall into the pit of despair. By these snares the sinful soul is caught, and the longer it has lain in the deep...

149
Homilia XXI. 155 miseriae, tanto redditur magis obdurata. Fugite o claustrales ocium, et gulam, satietatemque ventris summopere declinate, quoniam monachus, qui ventrem cibo, et potu satiat, fornicationis daemoni materiam no- cendi praestat. Cordis veram contritionem assumite, et illicitos motus carnis per lachrymas orationis refroenate. Nemo enim corpus suum recte vincere sufficit, qui contritionis aculeum prius non assumpsit. Ad sanctae autem contritionis gratiam non potest pertingere, qui seipsum perfecte contempserset abnegare. Quisquis autem seipsum pro Christi amore per- fecte abnegaverit, iam carnis impetum superans gratiam contritionis fa- cilius consequetur. Nam qui voluntate mortificatus est, nihil carnale, nihil turpe concupiscit. Sed quis est nostrum frater, qui ad hanc mort- ificationis gratiam dicere se audeat pervenisse? Quis nostrum se nesciat infirnum? In stadio spiritualis militiae currimus, et quotidiano certa- mine contra vitia pugnamus. Fiduciam pacis nullam accepimus, etiam si pacem interdum habeamus. Quanto nobis familiarior est infirmitas carnis, tanto sunt duriora praelia castitatis. Hinc nobis maxime vigi- landum est, quando hostem familiarem circumferimus, et quasi domes- ticum impulsum malum sustinemus. Quousque igitur in hac mortali- tate vivimus, corruptorem castitatis semper timeamus. Caveamus omnia, quae libidinem excitant, et quantum possimus, accidiam, et ocium fu- giamus. Sunt enim vere castitatis fortissimi hostes saturitas panis, et ocium, qui nisi per abstinentiam, et operationem salutaris exercitii procul expulsi fuerint, proximum castitati minantur naufragium. Omni custodia servate corda vestra charissimi fratres mei, et contra nunquam dormientem adversarium vestrum semper animo vigilate. Armate vos lo- rica perfectae fidei Iesu Christi, quatenus opere, et credulitate sitis veri christiani. Omnes in fraterna charitate semper estote unanimes, et in vera regularis disciplinae observantia sine fictione concordes. Ieiunium, et continentiam diligite, sine intermissione semper orate. Ociun velut animae pestem perniciosam fugite, et in sanctis operibus vos iugiter exercete. Amate silentium, et solitudinem monasticam nolite fugere, si veram mentis et corporis munditiam cupitis obtinere. Oculorum, aurium, et sermonum continuam habete custodiam, ne per fenestras mors in- grediatur ad animam. Mulierum alloquia fugite, et contactus etiam sanctorum velut ignis incendium declinate. Nemo tuto libenter intuetur, quod mortis affert aculeum cupitum. Dominum nostrum Iesum Chri- stum morientem pro vobis in cruce fidelibus oculis mentis per amorem semper aspicite, in eius doctrina evangelica vos salubriter quotidie oc- cupate, passioni eius simul, et morti gratias humiliter agite. Haec si continuata perseverantia in vera simplicitate cordis usque ad mortem feceritis, confidimus, quod sanctorum consortio eritis praemiandi. 156 De fraterna charitate monachorum. De fraterna charitate monachorum. Homilia XXII.

Homily XXI.

of misery, the more hardened it becomes. Flee idleness, O cloistered ones, and shun gluttony and fullness of the belly with all your strength, because the monk who fills his belly with food and drink gives the demon of fornication material for doing harm. Take on true contrition of heart, and restrain the unlawful motions of the flesh through the tears of prayer. For no one is able rightly to conquer his body unless he has first taken up the goad of contrition. But he cannot attain the grace of holy contrition who has not perfectly despised and denied himself. Yet whoever has perfectly denied himself for the love of Christ, already overcoming the assault of the flesh, will more easily obtain the grace of contrition. For one who has been mortified in will desires nothing carnal, nothing shameful. But which of us, brother, is there who would dare to say that he has reached this grace of mortification? Which of us does not know himself to be weak? We run in the arena of spiritual warfare, and in daily struggle we fight against vices. We have received no assurance of peace, even if at times we have peace. The more familiar to us the weakness of the flesh is, the harder are the battles of chastity. Therefore we must be especially watchful, since we carry about with us a familiar enemy and endure an evil impulse as though it were domestic. Therefore, as long as we live in this mortality, let us always fear the corrupter of chastity. Let us beware of everything that stirs up lust, and as much as we can, let us flee sloth and idleness. For the strongest enemies of true chastity are fullness of bread and idleness; unless they are driven far away by abstinence and by the work of salutary exercise, they threaten chastity with imminent shipwreck. Guard your hearts with every care, my dearly beloved brothers, and always keep watch in mind against your adversary, who never sleeps. Arm yourselves with the breastplate of perfect faith in Jesus Christ, so that in deed and in belief you may be true Christians. Always be of one mind in brotherly charity, and without pretense be united in the true observance of regular discipline. Love fasting and continence; always pray without ceasing. Flee idleness as a deadly plague of the soul, and continually exercise yourselves in holy works. Love silence, and do not flee monastic solitude, if you desire to obtain true purity of mind and body. Keep continual guard over your eyes, ears, and speech, lest death enter the soul through the windows. Flee conversations with women, and avoid even the touch of holy women as a blazing fire. No one safely looks willingly at what, when desired, brings the sting of death. Always behold with the faithful eyes of the mind, through love, our Lord Jesus Christ dying for you on the cross; occupy yourselves each day for your salvation in his evangelical teaching; humbly give thanks for his passion and death alike. If with continued perseverance and in true simplicity of heart you do these things until death, we trust that you will be rewarded with the fellowship of the saints.

On the Fraternal Charity of Monks.

On the Fraternal Charity of Monks. Homily XXII.

150
A udivimus fratres mei charissimi Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum in sancto Evangelio praecipentem: Quaecunque vultis, ut faciant vobis homines, et vos facite illis similiter. Brevis quidem, sed solida fraternae charitatis commendatio, sine qua nemo ad Dei amorem potest ascendere. Nemo enim potest Deum diligere, qui conchristianum suum convincitur non amare. Hinc beatus Ioannes dicit Apostolus: Omnis, qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est, et scitis, quoniam omnis homicida non habet vitam aeternam in se manentem. Unde si quis dixerit quoniam diligo Deum, et fratrem suum odit, mendax est. Propter sanctus hortatur nos Christophilus Paulus dicens: Alter alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi. Et princeps Apostolorum ita nos admonuit Petrus: Ante omnia, inquit, mutuam in vobismetipsis charitatem continuam habentes, quia charitas operit multitudinem peccatorum. Quam sit necessaria fraterna charitas ad salutem, Dominus universorum Iesu Christus aperuit dicens: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, et in toto anima tua, et in toto mente tua. Hoc est primum, et maximum mandatum. Secundum similis est huius: Diliges proximum tuum sicut temetipsum. In his duobus mandatis universa lex pendet, et prophetae. Quicquid enim in toto serie scripturarum usquam praecipitur, ac haec duo mandata sine dubio refertur. Proximum hic non sanguinis necessitudine iunctum intelligimus, sed omnem hominem societate rationis, maxime vero christianum, quem unusquisque tamquam seipsum iubetur diligere, cum quo aeternam salutem cernitur expectare. Vos autem fratres maxime decet alterutrum in vera charitate salvatoris Iesu Christi diligere, quibus professio indicit monastica totis viribus ad perfectionis culmen anhelare. Nam sicut radix omnium malorum est cupiditas, ita radix omnium bonorum est charitas. Deum in primis propter seipsum, quia summum bonum est, super omnia corde puro debetis diligere, ac deinde proximum sincera charitate propter Dominum amare. Haec duo charitatis praecelta Christi auctoritate coniuncta sunt, ut alterum impleri sine altero nullatenus possit. Nam qui Deum veraciter diligit, proximum suum odire non potest. Si odet proximum, non vere diligit Deum. Parit enim Dei amor dilectionem proximi, et per amorem proximi nutritur amor Dei. Si alter amorum defuerit, alter minime convalescit. Nam qui proximum suum perfecte non diligit, se Dei amore vacuum ostendit. Tunc ergo Deum veraciter diligitus, quando proximum nostrum, hoc est omnem hominem christianum sincera intentione diligentius amamus. Charitas namque fraterna est vinculum pacis, quae sola nutrit in habitazione con-

We have heard, my dearest brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ commanding in the holy Gospel: “Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do likewise to them.” It is indeed a brief, but solid commendation of brotherly charity, without which no one can ascend to the love of God. For no one can love God who is proved not to love his fellow Christian. Hence the blessed apostle John says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.” Therefore, if anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar.

For this reason holy Paul, the lover of Christ, exhorts us, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” And Peter, the prince of the apostles, admonished us in this way: “Before all things,” he says, “have constant mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins.”

How necessary brotherly charity is for salvation, Jesus Christ, the Lord of all, made clear when he said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.” For whatever is commanded anywhere in the whole sequence of the Scriptures is without doubt referred to these two commandments.

Here we understand “neighbor” not as someone joined by kinship of blood, but as every human being joined by the fellowship of reason, and especially a Christian, whom each person is commanded to love as himself, since he is seen to await eternal salvation together with him.

But it especially befits you, brothers, to love one another in the true charity of Jesus Christ the Savior, since the monastic profession enjoins you to strive with all your strength toward the summit of perfection. For just as covetousness is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all goods. First you must love God for his own sake, because he is the highest good, above all things with a pure heart; and then you must love your neighbor with sincere charity for the Lord’s sake.

These two precepts of charity have been joined together by Christ’s authority, so that neither can in any way be fulfilled without the other. For one who truly loves God cannot hate his neighbor. If he hates his neighbor, he does not truly love God. For the love of God brings forth love of neighbor, and through love of neighbor the love of God is nourished. If one of the two loves is lacking, the other does not grow strong. For one who does not perfectly love his neighbor shows himself empty of the love of God. Therefore we truly love God when we love our neighbor, that is, every Christian human being, more earnestly with sincere intention.

For brotherly charity is the bond of peace, which alone nourishes in the dwelling of

151
Homilia XXII. 157 cordiam, et conservat inter fratres christianam unitatem. Charitas est genitrix mansuetudinis, et generosa mater catholicae pietatis. Charitas fraterna daemonibus est formidabilis, quoniam victoriosos facit omnes, quorum circumpectitur atrium cordis. Charitas extinguit libidinis incen- dium, et omnem multitudinem operit peccatorum. Charitas hominem Deo reddit charissimum, et sanctorum socium facit angelorum. Cha- ritas in unitate sanctorum conservat ecclesiam, extra quam salutem nullus consequitur aeternam. Charitas fraterna mores componit clau- stralium, et Deum habitare facit in medio monachorum. Charitas nulli facit iniuriam, sed omnibus ministrat auxilium per miserationem. Cha- ritas exterminat omne vitium, quia nutrix est unica omnium virtutum. Charitas fraternitatis reformationem in vigore conservat claustralium, et magnam operatur salutem animarum. Charitas mutua confirmat obe- dientiam, et fructuosam facit fraternalm correctionem. Charitas veram inter fratres nutrit concordiam, et tam mentium, quam corporum bene redolentem conservat castitatem. Charitas monachos in domo Dei facit esse unanimes, et in omni bono opere laudabiliter concordes. Charitas mutua rigorem ordinis alleviat, et omnia, quae dura, et aspera videntur carnalibus, per consuetudinem, quasi levissima quaedam, in naturam commutat. Charitas pulchritudo est monachorum pulcherrima, quae cunctis est virtutibus adornata. Charitas odium, et invidiae de coenobiis servorum Dei penitus exterminat, et reliqua mortis crimina procul sua praesentia fugat. Charitas fratrum est spiritus sancti decens habitacu- lum, et serenae conscientiae fortalitium. Charitas est ministra iustitiae, et unica in monasterio conservatrix regularis disciplinae. Charitas men- tem a crudelitate servat innoxiam, et placidam cunctis subministrat animi lenitatem. Charitas fraterna salutem quaerit omnium, et non sinit habentem se torpescere oculosum. Charitas non detestatur inopiam, sed parata est fratrum amore omnem sufferre paupertatem. Charitas est aqua caelestis dulcedinis, quam si quis in fervore spiritus sancti potaverit, inferni perpetuam sitim non expavescit. Charitas fraterna carnis non quaerit illecebras, sed affectiones dirigit in proximum puras, sanctas, et impollutas. Charitas nomen habet castae pulchritudinis, quod com- municari non potest rebus, vel actionibus impurissimae voluptatis. Cha- ritas puritatem diligit, atque munditiam, et non admittit aliquam im- puritatem. Charitas in operatione dilectionis non carnem proximi con- siderat, sed animam, quam ad imaginem Dei non dubitat esse creatam. Charitas fraterna piis admonitionibus delinquentem proximum erigit, et omnes actiones suas ab omni malitia puras, et innoxias costodit. Charitas in pace, et tranquillitate mentis ambulat, et neque verbo, neque facto, neque signo, proximum contristat. Charitas, quantum potest, se in cunctis humiliat, et infirmanti proximo, quasi Dei filio diligentissime 158 De fraterna charitate monachorum.

mercy, and preserves Christian unity among the brothers. Charity is the begetter of meekness and the noble mother of catholic piety. Brotherly charity is formidable to demons, since it makes victorious all whose courtyard of the heart it surrounds. Charity extinguishes the fire of lust and covers the whole multitude of sins. Charity makes a man most dear to God and makes him a companion of the holy angels. Charity preserves the Church in the unity of the saints; outside it no one obtains eternal salvation. Brotherly charity orders the conduct of cloistered men and causes God to dwell in the midst of monks. Charity does injury to no one, but ministers help to all through compassion. Charity drives out every vice, because it is the one nurse of all virtues. Charity keeps the reform of brotherhood in vigor among cloistered men and works great salvation for souls. Mutual charity strengthens obedience and makes brotherly correction fruitful. Charity nourishes true concord among the brothers, and preserves a sweet-smelling chastity of both minds and bodies. Charity makes monks of one mind in the house of God and praiseworthily harmonious in every good work. Mutual charity lightens the rigor of the order, and all things that seem hard and rough to carnal people it changes through habit into nature, as though they were very light. Charity is the most beautiful beauty of monks, adorned with all virtues. Charity utterly drives hatred and envy from the monasteries of God’s servants, and by its presence drives far away the other crimes of death. The charity of the brothers is a fitting dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and a fortress of serene conscience. Charity is the servant of justice and the sole preserver of regular discipline in the monastery. Charity keeps the mind harmless from cruelty and supplies to all a peaceful gentleness of spirit. Brotherly charity seeks the salvation of all and does not allow the one who possesses it to grow sluggish [unclear]. Charity does not loathe want, but is ready, for love of the brothers, to endure every poverty. Charity is the water of heavenly sweetness; if anyone drinks it in the fervor of the Holy Spirit, he does not fear the everlasting thirst of hell. Brotherly charity does not seek the enticements of the flesh, but directs pure, holy, and undefiled affections toward one’s neighbor. Charity bears the name of chaste beauty, which cannot be shared with the things or actions of most impure pleasure. Charity loves purity and cleanness, and admits no impurity. In the work of love, charity does not consider the flesh of one’s neighbor, but the soul, which it does not doubt was created in the image of God. Brotherly charity raises up a sinning neighbor with pious admonitions, and keeps all its actions pure and harmless from every malice. Charity walks in peace and tranquility of mind, and saddens one’s neighbor neither by word, nor by deed, nor by sign. Charity humbles itself in all things as far as it can, and most diligently [unclear] for a neighboring brother who is weak, as for a son of God.

152
ministrat. Charitas neminem temere iudicat, sed peccantem proximum mansuetissimis admonitionibus humiliter emendat. Charitas terribilis, et metuenda est reprobis, sed pia, et benigna mansuetis. Charitas aliena incommoda, veluti propria computat, et pro fratribus tribulatione, quasi patiatur ipsa, plorat. Charitas omnibus in necessitate positis compatitur, et non minus pro malis alienis, quam pro suis contristatur. Charitas proximo nihil improparet, sed infirmitates omnium pro Dei amore semper aequanimititer portat. Charitas in bonis operibus est assidua, et quandiu manet in corde, nunquam est ociosa. Charitas nihil eorum, ad quae obligatur, negligit, sed omnia quam diligentissime custodit. Charitas fraterna legis est consummatio, quoniam quicquid post Dei cultum praecipitur, ad dilectionem proximi refertur. Hinc sanctus Christi amator dicit: Qui diligit proximum, legem implevit. Nam non adulterabis, non occides, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, non concupisces rem proximi tui, et si quod est aliud mandatum, in hoc verbo instauratur, diliges proximum tuum, sicut teipsum. Dilectio proximi malum non operatur. Plenitudo ergo legis est dilectio. Itaque fratres mei charissimi, rogamus vos per Dominum, et Salvatorem nostrum Iesum Christum; qui iudicaturus est vivos, et mortuos, quatenus fraternalam charitatem semper custodiatis illaesam, sine qua nec Deum veraciter potestis diligere, nec aliquod mandatum eius adimplere. Tam enim necessaria est vobis ad salutem fraternalae charitatis custodia, quam corporibus ad vitam conservandam ciborum, et potus alimenta. Corpus namque sine nutrimento necessario moritur, et omnes animae virtutes sine fraternali charitate dissipantur. Charitas etenim fraternala multitudinem monachorum conservat in unitate spiritus, quoniam sine vinculo dilectionis mutuae nullus claustralium perseverat sine perturbatione conventus. Monachus, qui fratrem suum odio prosequitur, a Dei charitate procul elongatur. Dicit enim sanctus Evangelista Ioannes: Qui odit fratrem suum, in tenebris est, et in tenebris ambulat, et nescit quo eat, quia tenebrae obcaecaverunt oculos eius. Amator autem proximi castus, et prudens in lumine spiritus sancti securus ambulat, et nec ipse perturbatur ab aliquo, nec quemquam alium perturbat. Est enim proximi verus amor mitis, dulcis, ac piissimus, et in omni convictu suo mansuetus, pacificus, atque tranquillus. Dirigit tamen vigor disciplinae apud rectores mansuetudinem, et clementia fraternalae considerationis pulchre temperat vigorem. Oportet enim, ut sic alterum temperetur ex altero, quatenus nec vigor sit rigidus, nec amor dissolutus. Amator fraternalae charitatis viam iustitiae non deserit: et qui recte diligit proximum suum, nihil corruptionis interponit. Verus namque proximi amor nec aurum concupiscit, nec ministrantium requirit obsequia, sed contemptis omnibus, quae animi statum subvertere possunt,

serves. Charity judges no one rashly, but humbly corrects a sinning neighbor with the gentlest admonitions. Charity is terrible and fearsome to the reprobate, but kind and gracious to the meek. Charity counts others’ troubles as its own, and weeps for brothers in tribulation as though it itself were suffering. Charity has compassion for all who are in need, and is saddened no less by the misfortunes of others than by its own. Charity reproaches a neighbor with nothing, but for the love of God always bears the weaknesses of all with equanimity. Charity is constant in good works, and so long as it remains in the heart, it is never idle. Charity neglects none of the things to which it is bound, but keeps all things as diligently as possible.

Fraternal charity is the fulfillment of the law, since whatever is commanded after the worship of God is referred to love of neighbor. Hence the holy lover of Christ says: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, You shall not covet your neighbor’s property, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love of neighbor works no evil. Therefore love is the fullness of the law.”

And so, my dearest brothers, we beseech you through our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, that you always preserve fraternal charity unharmed; without it you can neither truly love God nor fulfill any commandment of his. For the preservation of fraternal charity is as necessary for your salvation as the nourishment of food and drink is for bodies to preserve life. For the body dies without necessary nourishment, and all the virtues of the soul are scattered without fraternal charity.

Indeed, fraternal charity preserves a multitude of monks in unity of spirit, because without the bond of mutual love no cloistered man perseveres without disturbance of the community. The monk who pursues his brother with hatred is driven far away from the charity of God. For the holy Evangelist John says: “He who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.”

But the chaste and prudent lover of his neighbor walks securely in the light of the Holy Spirit, and is neither disturbed by anyone himself nor disturbs anyone else. For true love of neighbor is gentle, sweet, and most dutiful, and in all its common life meek, peaceable, and tranquil. Yet among rulers the vigor of discipline guides meekness, and the clemency of fraternal consideration beautifully tempers vigor. For one must be so tempered by the other that vigor is not harsh, nor love lax. The lover of fraternal charity does not abandon the way of justice; and he who rightly loves his neighbor admits no corruption.

For true love of neighbor covets no gold, nor seeks the services of attendants, but, despising all things that can overthrow the state of the soul,

153
Homilia XXII. 159 solius animae sectatur incrementa. Non enim sincera est charitas proximorum, dona corruptionis appetere, aut more puerorum propter musculorum distributiones concurrentem affectu similitudinis amare. Monachorum amicitia inter bonos eiusdem propositi zelatores debet esse communis, et procul remota ab omni affectione carnis. Sit pura, simplex, recta, et sine cuiusquam iniuria durabilis, nec habeat in se quicquam suspectae conspirationis. Non est haec norma fraternalis charitatis, privata consolationis interdictae conventicula quaerere, et, sine benedictione prioris, furtivis, immo prohibitis locutionibus vacare. Amorem vestrum proximo non recte, sed potius perniciose impenditis, quoties contra normam regularis observantiae ad carnis solatia convenitis. Dilectio monachi debet esse solida, et ab omni transgressione disciplinae regularis remotissima, quoniam nisi charitas muta fuerit a colloquiis carnalibus, ignem in se non habet divini amoris. Examineate nunc fratres vestra colloquia, et si corda habeatis etiam in vera charitate radiata. Charitas enim, quae consolationes spiritui nocentes vel dat proximo, vel recipit, nunquam sincera fuit. Curate igitur mentis oculum non ad carnis pulchritudinem, sed potius ad animae contemplationem dirigere, si recte vultis proximum, et laudabiliter amare. Caro enim cum sine respectu animae diligitur, non sincera, sed carnalis, et impura dilectio generatur. Considera fratrem tuum animam tibi habere consimilem, et semper cogita, quoniam foelicitatem ambo expectatis aequalem. Mente, sive anima intelligimus; anima, non corpore immortales sumus. Quod immortale est, alter iubetur in altero diligere, et ad animam potius, quam ad corpus respectum charitatis ordinare. Nam sicuti ratione, et intellectu a brutis animalibus discernimus, ita dilectionis nostrae intuitus ad mentem, qua intelligimus, non ad corpus, quod cum bestiis habemus commune, referatur. Procul sint a monachis sanctis omnes affectiones carnis, qui mutuam, et sinceram non ignorant regulam charitatis. Sit amor in alterutrum purus, rectus, et Dei solius timore conceptus, quatenus nullum interveniat commodum rei corruptibilis, sed permaneat simplex intentio charitatis. Charitas vero simplex, et pura malae conspirationis non quaerit diverticula, nec se armat contentionis murmure ad iniquitatis machinamenta. Qui veram charitatem fraternitatis in corde suo possidet, pacem custodit in omnibus, et nul lam excitat materiam, vel causam perniciosae dissensionis. Charitas uniu cuique ius suum impendens, nulli facit iniuriam, et omne, quod sibi non vult fieri, nunquam in alterius transfundit personam. Non existimetis vos veram charitatem habere fraternal, quando alterutrum dili gitis intuitu carnis, vel commodi rei cuiuslibet temporalis, quoniam ubi causa dilectionis non est Dominus, semper affectus diligentis est vel in parte, vel in toto vitiosus. Recte autem diligit fratrem suum, qui di 160 De fraterna charitate monachorum.

Homily 22.

pursues only the soul’s growth. For it is not sincere charity toward one’s neighbors to seek gifts of corruption, or, in the manner of boys, to love with an affection of likeness someone who comes running because of distributions of little dainties. The friendship of monks, among good men who are zealous for the same purpose, ought to be common, and far removed from every carnal attachment. Let it be pure, simple, upright, lasting without injury to anyone, and let it have in itself nothing of suspicious conspiracy. This is not the rule of brotherly charity: to seek private forbidden meetings for consolation and, without the prior’s blessing, to spend time in furtive, indeed prohibited, conversations. You bestow your love upon your neighbor not rightly, but rather ruinously, whenever you come together, contrary to the rule of regular observance, for the comforts of the flesh. The monk’s love ought to be solid and most remote from every transgression of regular discipline, since unless charity is mute with regard to carnal conversations, it does not have in itself the fire of divine love.

Now examine your conversations, brothers, and see whether your hearts are also radiant with true charity. For charity that either gives to a neighbor, or receives from him, consolations harmful to the spirit was never sincere. Therefore take care to direct the eye of the mind not toward the beauty of the flesh, but rather toward contemplation of the soul, if you wish to love your neighbor rightly and praiseworthily. For when the flesh is loved without regard for the soul, a love is generated that is not sincere, but carnal and impure. Consider that your brother has a soul like your own, and always remember that you both await an equal happiness. By mind we mean soul; by soul, not by body, we are immortal. What is immortal is what each is commanded to love in the other, and to order the regard of charity toward the soul rather than toward the body. For just as we are distinguished from brute animals by reason and understanding, so the gaze of our love should be referred to the mind by which we understand, not to the body, which we have in common with beasts.

Let all carnal attachments be far from holy monks, who are not ignorant of the mutual and sincere rule of charity. Let love for one another be pure, upright, and conceived from fear of God alone, so that no advantage of any corruptible thing may intervene, but the simple intention of charity may remain. But simple and pure charity does not seek the byways of evil conspiracy, nor does it arm itself with the murmur of contention for the contrivances of iniquity. Whoever possesses true brotherly charity in his heart preserves peace in all things, and stirs up no matter or cause of ruinous dissension. Charity, giving each one his due, does injury to no one, and whatever it does not wish done to itself, it never transfers onto the person of another. Do not think that you have true brotherly charity when you love one another with regard to the flesh, or for the advantage of any temporal thing whatever, since where the cause of love is not the Lord, the affection of the one who loves is always faulty either in part or in whole. But he rightly loves his brother who

154
ligt cum amore Dei, et propter communem, quam expectamus, participationem regni. Propterea, ut sanctus Ioannes dicit episcopus, in unum corpus baptizati sumus ecclesiae, quatenus non dissolvamur, sed in ea, quae adinvicem est, convenientia, et amicitia corporis unius charitatem, et convenientiam mutuam perpetuo conservemus. Quemadmodum nemo extra unitatem ecclesiae catholicae salutem potest consequi, ita nullus sine fraterna charitate posse creditur salvari. Charitas ergo vobis ante omnia est ad salutem necessaria, sine qua reliqua virtutum opera penitus sunt infructuosa. Nihil enim boni esse potest, nihil meriti salutaris ad vitam, quod ex illa non duxit originem. Charitas via quaedam est ad virtutis compendium, per quam si quis recto ingreditur tramite itineris, nulla egebit directione ducis. Charitas pura, simplex, et recta non proximum consuevit laedere, nec malum alicui inferre. Charitas affectum, quem commodis praestat propriis, impendere consuevit omnibus: et quicquid sibi ad salutem sperat conducere, hoc universis hominibus in Christo Iesu cupit esse commune. Charitas absque ulla perturbatione officio dilectionis utitur, et cum omnes homines maxime diligit, pro nullo tamen ad zelum amaritudinis provocatur. Semper est solida, semper constans, semper stabilis, et firma, quia nec passionibus tangitur, nec motibus inquietudinis agitatur. Communem se praebet omnibus, et ita suam dilectionem impendit singulis, ut tamen proxima videatur universis. Charitas in his, quae pertinent ad rationem mentis, et animae, seipsam non negligit: in illis vero, quae commodum respi ciunt corporis, saepe causas aliorum propriis utilitatibus praeponit. Magnum est verae charitatis imperium, quod alienum incommodum com pellit hominem facere suum. Vos itaque fratres mei, qui vos solemniter ad Christi praecinxitis militiam, qui per arduum iter obedientiae ad vitam anhelatis aeternam, si non vultis in tam laboriosi certaminis stadio frustra currere, curetis ante omnia, hortamur, fraternam in vobis charitatem semper inviolabilem custodire. Nisi enim sinceram, et perfectam charitatem adinvicem habueritis, sine fructu in observantia regulari laboratis. Nihil vobis abstinentia ab esu carnium, ad animarum salutem conferet, nihil abdicatio peculii omnis ad aeternae foelicitatis adoptionem proficiet, si locum in cordibus vestris fraterna dilectio non tenet. Cupientes ergo salvari cum Christo, in veritate vos mutuo dilit gite, et sicut Christus dilexit vos, ita precamur, alterutrum amate. Quod sibi fieri unusquisque vestrum desiderat, hoc ipsum fratri suo sine invidia propter Dei amorem omni tempore impendat. Vincat in vobis omnia carnis iurgia, et qualisbet contentiones amor divinus, nec inveniat locum perniciosa carnis dissensio, ubi commorari iugiter debet fraternae charitatis plenitudo. Nam si omnes in monasterio secundum legem christianae institutionis vivitis, alter ab alterius laesione neces Homilia XXII. 161 sario semper abstinetis. Si vero per contentiones, et iniurias mutuo vos laeditis, nec monachi certe, nec veri christiani estis. Decet enim claustrales, et monachos omnes in observantia charitatis esse praecipuos, ab invidiae, odiique rancore longius esse remotos. Sit ergo monachus in proposito sanctitatis usque ad mortem stabilis, sit in Dei ministerio fidelis, quatenus, et in amore creatoris dulciter ferveat, et nunquam a puritate conscientiae recedat. Quisquis enim Dominum Deum ex toto corde suo perfecte diligit, et conscientiam suam ab omni pollutione peccati mundam conservat, et puram, et sinceram proximo suo semper exhibet charitatem. Eum vero, quem vel invidia urit, vel odium contra fratrem excitat, manifestum est, nec Deum veraciter diligere, nec puram a peccato conscientiam habere. Omnis ergo, qui fratrem suum odio, et indignatione prosequitur, nec monachus est verus, nec dignus nomine christiani, sed merito, et conversatione daemonum minister, et socius. Procul igitur hinc a sancta congregatione vestra cedant odia, nulla sint in medio vestrum contentionis perniciosae certamina, non reperiatur isthic zelus amaritudinis, sermo nullus audiatur displicentis elationis. Iugiter hic vigeat fraternae unitatis concordia, singularum conscientias exornet christianae puritatis innocentia, ut sic vivamus in hoc brevi tempore, quatenus post mortem cum Christo gloriemur in aeternitate. De charitate hominis in Deum. Homilia XXIII.

...binds with love of God, and because of the common participation in the kingdom which we await. Therefore, as the holy bishop John says, we have been baptized into one body of the Church, so that we may not be dissolved, but may preserve forever, in that harmony which exists toward one another and in the friendship of one body, charity and mutual concord. Just as no one outside the unity of the catholic Church can obtain salvation, so no one is believed able to be saved without brotherly charity.

Charity, therefore, is necessary for you before all things for salvation; without it the remaining works of the virtues are utterly fruitless. For there can be nothing good, no saving merit for life, which has not taken its origin from it. Charity is a certain short path to virtue; if anyone enters upon it by the right track of the journey, he will need no direction from a guide. Charity, pure, simple, and upright, is not accustomed to harm one’s neighbor, nor to inflict evil on anyone. Charity is accustomed to bestow on all the affection which it gives to its own advantages; and whatever it hopes will conduce to its own salvation, it desires this to be common to all people in Christ Jesus. Charity exercises the office of love without any disturbance, and although it loves all people greatly, nevertheless for no one is it provoked to a zeal of bitterness. It is always solid, always constant, always stable and firm, because it is neither touched by passions nor shaken by movements of unrest. It shows itself common to all, and so bestows its love on each one that nevertheless it seems nearest to all. Charity does not neglect itself in those things which pertain to the reason of the mind and soul; but in those things which regard the advantage of the body, it often places the causes of others before its own benefits. Great is the command of true charity, which compels a person to make another’s disadvantage his own.

You, therefore, my brothers, who have solemnly girded yourselves for the warfare of Christ, who through the arduous way of obedience pant after eternal life, if you do not wish to run in vain in the arena of so laborious a contest, take care, we exhort you, before all things always to keep brotherly charity inviolate among you. For unless you have sincere and perfect charity toward one another, you labor without fruit in regular observance. Abstinence from eating meat will contribute nothing to the salvation of your souls; the renunciation of all private property will profit nothing toward the adoption of eternal happiness, if brotherly love does not hold a place in your hearts. Therefore, desiring to be saved with Christ, love one another in truth, and, as Christ loved you, so we beg you, love one another. Whatever each one of you desires to be done to himself, let him bestow that very thing on his brother without envy, for the love of God, at all times. Let divine love overcome in you all quarrels of the flesh and every kind of contention; and let no pernicious dissension of the flesh find a place where the fullness of brotherly charity ought continually to dwell. For if all of you in the monastery live according to the law of Christian instruction, you necessarily always abstain from injuring one another. But if through contentions and wrongs you injure one another, you are certainly neither monks nor true Christians.

For it befits cloistered men and all monks to be outstanding in the observance of charity, and to be far removed from the rancor of envy and hatred. Therefore let the monk be stable in his purpose of holiness even to death; let him be faithful in the service of God, so that he may both sweetly burn in love of the Creator and never depart from purity of conscience. For whoever perfectly loves the Lord God with his whole heart both preserves his conscience clean from every pollution of sin and always shows pure and sincere charity to his neighbor. But the one whom either envy burns or hatred stirs up against his brother, it is clear that he neither truly loves God nor has a conscience pure from sin. Therefore everyone who pursues his brother with hatred and indignation is neither a true monk nor worthy of the name of Christian, but by merit and conduct a servant and companion of demons.

Therefore let hatreds depart far from this holy congregation of yours; let there be no contests of pernicious contention among you; let no zeal of bitterness be found here; let no speech of displeasing pride be heard. Let the concord of brotherly unity flourish here continually; let the innocence of Christian purity adorn the consciences of each one, so that we may live in this brief time in such a way that after death we may be glorified with Christ in eternity.

On the Charity of Man toward God. Homily XXIII.

155
Nihil tam iustum, nihil tam sanctum, nihil in humanis actionibus tam potest esse honestum, quam Deum ex toto corde, et in tota mente, et in tota virtute super omnia semper diligere, et pro eius amore nec mortem, nec poenarum quaelibet genera formidare. Nullius actionis maior in nobis est causa, quam divini amoris, quia cum Deus sit auctor omnium, nihil eo diligitur iustius: et cum bonorum cunctorum sit maximum, eo nihil amatur fructuosius. Prior Deus dilexit nos, infimos summus, maximus parvulos, omnipotens infirmos. Nos igitur fratres mei, Dominum Deum toto corde, tota anima, totaque virtute diligamus, a quo suavissime diligimus, qui nos non solum ad imaginem, et similitudinem suam condidit, sed quod indicium est amoris maximi, per doctrinam, et mortem unigeniti filii sui Domini nostri Iesu Christi ad regnum aeternae felicitatis misericorditer vocavit. Nunquam sic tenerime, dulciter, et fortiter aliqua mater carnalis dilexit unigenitum filium suum, quemadmodum nos dilexit omnipotens Deus, qui non solum homo fieri ad nostram eruditionem voluit, sed etiam mortem subire in assumpta carne pro salute nostra dignatus fuit. Nulla dilectio maior unquam extitit, si recte pensiculemus, quis fuerit, qui tanta pro nobis 162 De charitate hominis in Deum. toleravit. Nostri quippe amore liber a mortis debito voluntarie moritur, et qui ab omni peccato semper immunis exitit, innocens, et iustus pro nostris peccatis volens condemnatur. Iustissima ergo ratione nobis praecipitur, ut Dominum Deum nostrum ex toto corde diligamus, qui nos cum non essemus, ex sola bonitate condidit: et cum periissemus, misericorditer liberavit.
