170 De ad mortem praeparatione continua. mines iudicatur, qui auro praefert scoriam; sed insipientissimus apud Deum habetur, qui bonis sempiternis temporalem anteponit voluptatem. Eccles. 33. Qui serenam conscientiam diligit, ocium fugiat; quoniam, sicut scri- ptura dicit, in desideriis est omnis ociosus, et multam malitiam docuit ociositas. Occupandus est bonis exercitiis animus, et sanctae conversa- tionis, qui charitate ferveat ignis, usu continuo nutriendus. Ocius enim nec sibi vivit, nec proximo, sed ventri semper est deditus, aut somno: mentem aperit vitiis, et clausam, vacuamque tenet virtutibus. Ociositas incentrix libidinis cito extinguit fervorem spiritualis devotionis. Abstinentia quoque monacho valde in primis est necessaria, ut con- scientia permaneat munda. Nain, ut divus Hieronymus ait, repletus venter facile despumat in libidinem: et qui servum suum nutrit deli- cate, sentiet eum contumacem. Amator serenitatis conscientiae, in sanctis orationibus sit continuus; quoniam sicut canis lapidem, ita daemones fugiunt devotam, et continuam orationem. Accidiam quoque diligenter caveat, simul et mentis tristitiam; moxque ut aliquam serpere tenta- tionem senserit, ad consolationem scripturarum habeat recursum. Enim- vero mentem, quam Dei sermo repleverit, turpis cogitatio non intrabit. Quicquid agimus, quicquid cogitamus, quicquid operamur, Dei semper sciamus adesse praesentiam, et inordinatam facile superabimus delecta- tionem. Conscientia bona Dei praesentiam nunquam obliviscitur, sed iudicem semper adesse suum meditatur. Agite nunc fratres mei, ut con- scientias habeatis puras ab omni scelere: et si quis gravatum se in aliquo delicto senserit, per veram poenitentiam sine mora revertatur ad ne- cessariam puritatem. Nisi enim conscientias omni tempore mundas, et bonas habueritis, apostatae, non monachi vivitis. De ad mortem praeparatione continua. Homilia XXV. SUMMA claustralium philosophia, fratres mei charissimi, continua est meditatio mortis. Hinc quidam sapiens utilitatem considerans huius philosophiae, quemlibet admonuit mortalem dicens: Memorare novis- simà tua, et in aeternum non peccabis. Meditatio mortis hominem a voluptatibus carnis rethrahit, et contemptum omnium corruptibilium in- ducit. Meditatio mortis, praesentia voluntaria paupertate despicit, et mentem ad futurorum desiderium impellit. Meditatio mortis superbiam procul eliminat, et veram humilitatem in corde meditantis plantat. Me- ditatio mortis monachum circa observantiam regularis disciplinae facit sollicitum, et nunquam permittit esse ociosum. Meditatio mortis omnes mundi vanitates amputat, et mentem in summa temperantia conservat. Meditatio mortis vanos, et transitorios mundi honores facit contemnere, et nihil aliud, quam futurum Dei iudicium cogitare. Meditatio mortis

On Continual Preparation for Death.

A man is judged foolish among men who prefers dross to gold; but he is considered most foolish before God who places temporal pleasure before everlasting goods. Ecclesiasticus 33.

He who loves a serene conscience should flee idleness; for, as Scripture says, every idle man is in desires, and idleness has taught much evil. The mind must be occupied with good exercises, and the fire of holy conduct, which burns with charity, must be nourished by continual practice. For an idle man lives neither for himself nor for his neighbor, but is always given over to his belly or to sleep: he opens his mind to vices, and keeps it closed and empty of virtues. Idleness, the kindler of lust, quickly extinguishes the fervor of spiritual devotion.

Abstinence also is especially very necessary for a monk, so that his conscience may remain clean. For, as Saint Jerome says, a full belly readily foams over into lust; and he who feeds his servant delicately will find him rebellious. The lover of serenity of conscience should be constant in holy prayers; for as dogs flee a stone, so demons flee devout and continual prayer. He should also carefully beware of sloth, and likewise sadness of mind; and as soon as he feels some temptation creeping in, he should have recourse to the consolation of the Scriptures. Indeed, a foul thought will not enter a mind which the word of God has filled. Whatever we do, whatever we think, whatever we undertake, let us always know that God’s presence is at hand, and we shall easily overcome disordered delight. A good conscience never forgets the presence of God, but always meditates that its judge is present. Act now, my brothers, so that you may have consciences pure from every crime; and if anyone feels himself burdened by some fault, let him return without delay, through true repentance, to necessary purity. For unless you have clean and good consciences at all times, you live as apostates, not as monks.

On Continual Preparation for Death. Homily 25.

The highest philosophy of cloistered men, my dearest brothers, is continual meditation on death. Hence a certain wise man, considering the usefulness of this philosophy, admonished every mortal, saying: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. Meditation on death draws a man back from the pleasures of the flesh and brings in contempt for all corruptible things. Meditation on death despises present things through voluntary poverty, and drives the mind toward desire for future things. Meditation on death removes pride far away and plants true humility in the heart of the one meditating. Meditation on death makes a monk attentive to the observance of regular discipline and never allows him to be idle. Meditation on death cuts off all the vanities of the world and preserves the mind in the highest temperance. Meditation on death makes one despise the vain and passing honors of the world, and think of nothing other than the future judgment of God. Meditation on death

164
Homilia XXV. 171 paupertatem huius vitae non metuit; quoniam sempiternas divitias tota desiderio concupiscit. Meditatio mortis omnia huius mundi adversa pro Christi amore patientissime tolerat; quia nihil aliud, quam supernam retributionem sperat. Meditatio mortis monachum facit humilem, et in cunctis mandatis rectitudinis obedientem. Meditatio mortis monachum quietum facit, et in congregatione stabilem, et cum omnibus in Christo bene concordantem. Meditatio mortis monachum quietum facit, atque pacificum, et sine mentis perturbatione aliqua tranquillum. Meditatio mortis omnes dissolutiones, et levitates exterminat, et monachum ma- turum, et salubriter tristem in omnibus praeservat. Meditatio mortis monachum facit solitarium, et in sanctis orationibus continue devotum. Meditatio mortis accelerat poenitentiam, et veram inducit compunctio- nem. Meditatio mortis desiderium ab omni vanitate subtrahit, et con- scientiam serenam, et purissimam custodit. Meditatio mortis hominem facit omnia huius mundi solitia contemnere, et ad exitum se quotidie praeparare. Meditatio mortis ocium docet fugere, et facit hominem in timore Domini iugiter vigilare. Meditatio mortis nulli facit iniuriam, quia districtam semper metuit iudicii rationem. Meditatio mortis ira- cundiam, et omnes motus inordinatos mitigat; quia, dum se homo cito moriturum cogitat, mentem nihil extrinsecum perturbat. Meditatio mortis cor contritum facit, et humile; quia futurorum intenta memoria nemi- nem permittit superbire. Meditatio mortis continua tutam in extremis facit exitum; quoniam ex multo tempore meditantem constituit pra- paratum. Meditatio mortis claustrales maxime decet, ac monachos, quos omnium terrenorum abdicatio, et ipsa professio regularis mundo iam fecit mortuos, atque sepultos. Meditatio mortis monachum facit in stadio spiritualis militiae prudenter currere, et propositum sancti fervoris quo- tidie innovare. Meditatio mortis continua valde utilis est claustralibus; quoniam et carnis vitia potenter reprimit, et nullum perversis cogita- tionibus mentis aditum concedit. Dicit enim sanctus praesul Augustinus. Timor de futura morte mentem necessario concutit, et quasi clavus carnis omnes motus superbiae ligno crucis affigit. Et sanctus Ecclesiae pugil Hieronymus dicit: Nihil aequa tibi proficiet ad temperantiam omnium rerum, quam frequens cogitatio brevis vitae, cuius finis certus est, hora vero incertius nihil est. Meditatio igitur mortis omne in- temperatiam corrigit, et mores meditantis pulchra varietate stabiles componit. Meditatio mortis veram praestat homini sapientiam, et sum- mam in claustralibus perficit philosophiam. Nam et Platonis sententia fuit, omnem sapientum vitam meditationem esse mortis, propterea quod ea conditione omnes nascimur, ut hinc rursus per mortem egressiamur. Dicit enim scriptura. Omnes morimur; et quasi aquae in terram dila- bimur, quae amplius non revertuntur. Et sanctus Christi Apostolus 172 De ad mortem praeparatione continua.

Homily XXV.

He does not fear the poverty of this life, because with his whole desire he longs for eternal riches. Meditation on death endures all the adversities of this world most patiently for love of Christ, because it hopes for nothing other than the recompense from above. Meditation on death makes the monk humble and obedient in all the commandments of righteousness. Meditation on death makes the monk quiet, stable in the congregation, and in good concord with everyone in Christ. Meditation on death makes the monk calm and peaceable, and tranquil without any disturbance of mind. Meditation on death exterminates all dissoluteness and levity, and preserves the monk mature and healthfully sorrowful in all things. Meditation on death makes the monk solitary and continually devoted to holy prayers.

Meditation on death hastens penitence and brings in true compunction. Meditation on death withdraws desire from every vanity, and keeps the conscience serene and most pure. Meditation on death makes a man despise all the comforts of this world, and prepare himself daily for his departure. Meditation on death teaches him to flee idleness, and makes a man keep continual watch in the fear of the Lord. Meditation on death does injury to no one, because it always fears the strict accounting of judgment. Meditation on death mitigates anger and all disordered impulses, because, while a man considers that he will soon die, nothing external disturbs his mind. Meditation on death makes the heart contrite and humble, because attentive remembrance of things to come permits no one to be proud.

Continual meditation on death makes one’s departure safe at the end, because it has made the meditator prepared over a long period of time. Meditation on death is especially fitting for cloistered men and monks, whom the renunciation of all earthly things and the very profession of the rule have already made dead and buried to the world. Meditation on death makes the monk run prudently in the course of spiritual warfare, and renew daily the purpose of holy fervor. Continual meditation on death is very useful for cloistered men, because it both powerfully restrains the vices of the flesh and grants no entrance of the mind to perverse thoughts.

For the holy bishop Augustine says: Fear of future death necessarily shakes the mind, and, like a nail of the flesh, fastens all the motions of pride to the wood of the cross. And the holy champion of the Church, Jerome, says: Nothing will help you as much toward temperance in all things as frequent thought of this brief life, whose end is certain, while nothing is more uncertain than its hour. Therefore meditation on death corrects all intemperance, and arranges the habits of the one who meditates in stable order with beautiful variety. Meditation on death gives a man true wisdom, and perfects the highest philosophy among cloistered men. For Plato too held the opinion that the whole life of the wise is meditation on death, because we are all born on this condition: that from here we must depart again through death.

For Scripture says: We all die, and like waters we flow down into the earth, which do not return again. And the holy Apostle of Christ

165
Paulus: Statutum est, inquit, hominibus semel mori. Meditatio necessariae mortis continua facit hominem nuncquam in terrenis rebus confidere, sed exitum suum in omni loco, et tempore cum providentia expectare. Meditatio mortis terminum vivendi semper in omni loco expectat, propterea quod moriendi punctum penitus ignorat. Qui mortis futurae quotidian meditatur adventum, quanta potest diligentia omni tempore se disponit ad moriendum. Nihil enim morte nobis certius est, quamvis horam moriendi omnes ignoramus. Unde charitates vestras, fratres, qua possimus instantia, monemus, ut vos semper cogitatis moriuros, talique vos providentia ad moriendum sedulo praeparetis, ut cum venerit hora, egressi non timeatis. Nemo vitam sibi polliceatur in hoc mundo prolixam; quia nihil sic decipit mortales, quomodo spes aevi longioris. Quid enim operatur in hominibus prolixior aetas, nisi quod pluribus delictis facit obnoxios, et ad moriendum semper minus dispositos? Quanto vivimus in hoc mundo diutius, tanto mortem amplius formidamus. Accumulat longior aetas maiora spiritualis obligationis debita; et tanto venire ante conspectum districti iudicis homo senex amplius metuit, quanto se in pluribus ad reddendam rationem obligatum coram Domino recognoscit. Animus enim de corpore suo invitus egreditur, qui conscientiae sua gravioribus stimulis agitatur. Qui autem ab omni malitia iniquitatis est purus, et necessariarum decore virtutum ad salutem ornatus, mori non metuit, quia per mortem ad vitam sempiternam vadit. Qualis ergo mori vis o monache, talis nunc vive; quia mala moris esse non poterit, quam vitae bonae integritas praecessit. O quam secure moritur, quisquis Dominum Iesum super omnia diligit, et omnia huius mundi bona pro illius amore contemnens, eius sermones vera citer custodit. Securus ab hac vita egreditur, qui sine macula conscientiae semper in Dei amore conversatur. Secure moritur, cuius vita nullis huius mundi voluptatibus inquinatur. Mors enim sanctorum, somnus est dulcissimus, et ad vitam aeternam tranquillus introitus. Mors autem peccatorum pessima, quorum vita mala, et divinis institutionibus praecessit contraria. Qui vivit in peccatis Deo contrarius, fit illi mors ad infernum horrendus introitus. Male non moritur, qui bene vixit: et raro bene moritur, qui semper male vixisse demonstratur. Securus moritur, qui Deum pura mente super omnia diligit, et se ab hoc seculo nequam mundum omni tempore custodit. Mors bonis, et rectis corde optabilis, quia terminum imponit exilio, et vitam reddit in coelo. Mors est relictio corporis, eversio tenebrosi carceris, et depositio sarcinae gravis. Mors est praesentium malorum terminus, tristitiae finis, et omnis sepulchrum terrenae voluptatis. Mortem bona vita in fide, et charitate Iesu Christi facit preciosam et Dei servo maxime optabilem. Curate nunc igitur fratres mortem sanctis praevenire operibus, et vobis facite

Paul says: “It is appointed for human beings to die once.” Continual meditation on necessary death makes a person never trust in earthly things, but await his departure in every place and time with foresight. Meditation on death always expects the end of life in every place, because it is wholly ignorant of the moment of dying. Whoever meditates daily on the coming of future death prepares himself for dying at every time with all the diligence he can. For nothing is more certain for us than death, although we all are ignorant of the hour of dying.

Therefore, brothers, with all the urgency we can, we admonish your charity always to think that you are going to die, and with such foresight diligently to prepare yourselves for dying that, when the hour comes, you may not fear to depart. Let no one promise himself a long life in this world, because nothing deceives mortals as much as the hope of a longer span. For what does a longer age produce in human beings except that it makes them liable to more sins and always less prepared for dying? The longer we live in this world, the more we fear death. A longer age piles up greater debts of spiritual obligation; and an old man fears all the more to come before the sight of the strict judge, the more he recognizes that he is bound before the Lord in many matters to render an account. For the soul departs unwillingly from its body when it is tormented by the heavier stings of its conscience.

But whoever is pure from every evil of iniquity and adorned for salvation with the beauty of the necessary virtues does not fear to die, because through death he goes to everlasting life. Therefore, O monk, live now as you wish to die; for the death which has been preceded by the integrity of a good life cannot be evil. O how securely he dies, whoever loves the Lord Jesus above all things and, despising all the goods of this world for love of him, faithfully keeps his words. He departs securely from this life who always lives in the love of God without stain of conscience. He dies securely whose life is defiled by no pleasures of this world. For the death of the saints is a most sweet sleep and a peaceful entrance into eternal life. But the death of sinners is worst, whose evil life has gone before it, contrary to the divine ordinances. For one who lives in sins, opposed to God, death becomes for him a dreadful entrance into hell.

He does not die badly who has lived well; and rarely does he die well who is shown always to have lived badly. He dies securely who loves God above all things with a pure mind and at all times keeps himself from this wicked world. Death is desirable for the good and upright in heart, because it sets an end to exile and restores life in heaven. Death is the leaving of the body, the overthrow of the dark prison, and the laying down of a heavy burden. Death is the end of present evils, the finish of sadness, and the grave of every earthly pleasure. A good life in the faith and charity of Jesus Christ makes death precious and especially desirable to the servant of God. Therefore now, brothers, take care to anticipate death with holy works, and make for yourselves

166
Homilia XXV. 173 virtutum studio iucundum, quod natura cunctis voluit esse necessarium. Mementote, quoniam omnes necessario sumus mortales, et quando non putamus, ex hoc mundo transibimus. Nam, ut praesul quidam dixit venerandus, Tollimur e medio fatis urgentibus omnes, Et trahimur, quo nos vita peracta vocat. Quocumque igitur possimus bonum, operemur fratres mei, dum tempus habemus, ne mortis praeveniente imperio, nos fuisse negligentes nimium sero doleamus. Tempus solum est nostrum, caetera vero aliena sunt omnia. Labor militiae nostrae spiritualis, et si durus aliquantulum tepidis mentibus videatur, tamen brevissimus est, et cum vita cito terminabitur: sed merces bonorum operum, quae dabitur nobis, manet in aeternum. Meditatio cito futurae mortis nunquam vos deserat; sed consideratione districti iudicii, quod nemo subterfugere potest, mentes vestras in Dei amore iugiter compungat. Ecce quot monachi nos in hoc Spanhemensi coenobio per annos ferme quadringentos a prima fundatione sui vivendo, et moriendo praecesserunt, quorum apud nos hodie nulla penitus superest memoria. Quod nos sumus, illi fuerunt: quod illi sunt, post breve tempus erimus. Homines fuerunt mortales, quod sumus, mortui sunt, et reversi in pulverem terrae, quod erimus. Abbas ego sum huius monasterii Spanhemensis quintus atque vigesimus nisi quatuor et viginti praecessissent ad mortem, ego certe vigesimus quintus non pervenisset ad hanc abbatiam. Locum alteri quoque brevi daturus sum, ut sextus atque vigesimus abbatum numerus impleatur. Post illum rursus ordinabitur alius; et mors unius institutio fit alterius; et dum alter succedit alteri, mortis imperio subiciuntur universi. Ubi sunt ergo, fratres, qui nos in hoc monasterio praecesserunt? Quemadmodum nulla eorum memoria est apud nos, qui praecesserunt: ita et nos in oblivione erimus sempiterna apud illos, qui sequentur. Haec praecogitemus, fratres charissimi, dum vivimus, ne imparati mortem incidamus. Sicuti quotidiane properamus ad mortem, ita quotidiane pro viribus praeparemur: quoniam securus moritur, qui bonis, et sanctis operibus in vita decoratur. Non vos decipiatur spes vitae longioris; quoniam quanto diutius in hoc mundo vivitis, tanto brevius victuri estis. Ecce quotidiane ad mortem tendentes morimur; quotidiane una pars vitae nobis amputatur; et quanto vita nostra diutius protrahitur, tanto reliquum vivendi tempus abbreviatur. Omne quod viximus, tempus, totum amnisimus, quia praeterit: quod hodie vivimus momentaneum, cum morte dividimus: quantum vivendi de futuro restet nobis temporis, ignoramus. Quid igitur in vanitate huius vitae confidimus, qui cito morituri sumus? Itaque assidue cogitemus, fratres, eo nos cito perventuros, quo nos omnes maiores nostri dudum praecesserunt. Omnes hac lege 174 De ad mortem praeparatione continua.

pleasant through the pursuit of virtues, which nature willed to be necessary for all. Remember that we are all necessarily mortal, and when we do not expect it, we shall pass from this world. For, as a certain venerable prelate said:

We are all taken from the midst as the fates press on, and we are drawn where life, once completed, calls us.

Therefore, wherever we can do good, my brothers, let us do it while we have time, lest, when death’s command forestalls us, we grieve too late that we have been negligent. Time alone is ours; all other things are another’s. The labor of our spiritual warfare, even if it seems somewhat hard to lukewarm minds, is nevertheless very brief, and will soon be ended with life; but the reward of good works, which will be given to us, remains forever.

Let meditation on death soon to come never leave you; but by consideration of the strict judgment, which no one can escape, let it continually pierce your minds with love of God. Behold how many monks in this monastery of Sponheim have gone before us, living and dying, through almost four hundred years from its first foundation; of them no memory at all remains among us today. What we are, they were; what they are, we shall soon be. They were mortal men, as we are; they died and returned to the dust of the earth, as we shall.

I am the twenty-fifth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim; unless twenty-four had gone before me to death, I certainly would not have come as the twenty-fifth to this abbacy. I too shall shortly give place to another, so that the number of the twenty-sixth abbot may be fulfilled. After him another again will be appointed; and the death of one becomes the institution of another; and while one succeeds another, all are subjected to the command of death.

Where, then, brothers, are those who went before us in this monastery? Just as there is no memory among us of those who went before, so we too shall be in everlasting oblivion among those who follow. Let us think on these things beforehand, dearly beloved brothers, while we live, lest we fall upon death unprepared. As daily we hasten toward death, so daily let us prepare ourselves according to our strength; for he dies secure who in life is adorned with good and holy works.

Do not let the hope of a longer life deceive you; for the longer you live in this world, the shorter is the time you will still live. Behold, daily tending toward death, we die; daily one part of our life is cut away from us; and the longer our life is drawn out, the more the remaining time for living is shortened. All the time that we have lived we have wholly lost, because it has passed away; the present moment in which we live today we share with death; how much time for living remains to us in the future, we do not know. Why, then, do we trust in the vanity of this life, we who are soon to die? And so, brothers, let us constantly consider that we shall soon come to that place where all our forefathers long ago went before us. All by this law

167
nascimur, ut brevi moriamur. Mors illis videatur terribilis, quorum vita in carnis voluptate tota polluitur, et nihil in coelo bonorum reservatur. Nos, qui spem nostram in Dominum Iesum Christum salvatorem omnium collocantes, mundi voluptates pro eius amore contemptimus, mortem quare timeamus? Veruntamen, cum omnium terribilium terribilissimum sit mors, indiscretum moriendi timorem, ita propulsare poterimus, si nos quotidianus quasi iam morituros praeparemus. Aliud tamen est pavorem mortis habere, aliud tremorem. Nam et Dominus Iesus pavorem mortis praesensit, non tremorem, ut duarum proprietates naturarum ostenderet. Meditatio igitur mortis continua nobis infirmis omnino est necessaria, ut mens necdum in charitate Christi perfecta, quasi violento quodam impulso ad compunctionis gratiam excitetur. Memoria enim futurae mortis, quasi clavus qui ligno infigitur, ita mens pavore utili penetratur. Memoria mortis arduam introducit poenitentiam, et veram mentis sobrietatem. Memoria mortis necessaria est insipientibus; quorum conversatio a servili timore incipit, ut per filialem successively in charitatem elevetur. Memoria mortis, et districti examinis futuri iudicis Dei maxime illis est necessaria, qui mala consuetudine, ac diurna trahuntur ad peccandum. Et sunt inter vos quidam in militia spirituali nimis tepidi, et negligentes, quos monentes exhortamur paternae, quatenus se recordentur esse mortales, taliterque vivant deinceps, ut mori non timeant. Valde enim periculosum est in eo statu vivere, in quo mori quis formidaret. Ita vivendum est, ut mortem exspectemus securi: quod tunc demuin fieri potest, si nos in omni puritate mentis, et corporis conservantes, in exercitiis Divinae charitatis iugiter serveamus. Vivamus, quantum fieri potest innocenter, secundum divi Patris Benedicti regulam, quam professi sumus, et spem habebimus bonam, quoniam miserebitur nostri omnipotens Deus, qui perire hominem non permittit bonae voluntatis. Deum semper cogitemus nobis ubique praesentem, qui omnia videt, omnia novit, omnia intelligit, omnia remunerat: et ea puritate vivamus, qua nos suae Maiestatis Sanctissimae militare polliciti sumus. FINIS. Libri primi exhortationum ad Monachos finis adest manu mei propria Ioannis Tritemii Abbatis Spanhemensis scripti 9 die mensis Iunii, Anno Christianorum 1486 Indict. 4 Anno aetatis meae 24. Hoc opus dicavi antecessori meo nunc Abbati Selgenstatensi charissimo. EPISTOLA I OANNES Tritemius Abbas Monasterii Spanhemensis licet indignus, Reverendo Patri Domino Ioanni de Colenhausen Abbati Selgenstatensi, quondam vero Spanhemensi, antecessori meo charissimo cum orationibus animi complacendi promptum, atque paratum. Miseram nuper ad te praecessor venerande librum meum exhortationum ad monachos primum quinque et viginti continentem Homilias, quem posteaquam tuo examine comprobatum intellexi, etiam hunc secundum, quem nunc mitto, nomini tuo duxi confidenter inscribendum. In illum ad institutionem fratrum Homilias XXV quas coram eis habueram, comportavi: in isto sermones numero septem, secundum ordinem, quo dicti sunt in eorundem praesentia, ordinavi. Examen paternitatis tuae subire non vereor, quoniam te praecessorem semper mansuetum habui, et veritatis sincerum amatorem dudum expertus sum. Ingenio quippe viges, et mili, et profundo, qui facile inter verum, et falsum potest discernere, et tibi requirit necessitas, omnia sufficienter emendare. Unde secundum immatam tibi mansuetudinem patienter feras ingenii mei ruditatem, precor, qui et in scientia scripturarum sum parvulus, et in ordine praelatorum novitus. Dabit mibi, sicuti conjido, in scripturis exercitatio usum, et continuata scribendi sollicitudo profectum. Occupatio rei familiaris, et inopia loci saepius me a salutari studio retrahunt, et animum contra voluntatis propositum aliorsum transponunt. Diebus tantummodo festis, atque dominicis mihi ad scribendum conceditur ocium, in quibus ob Dei reverentiam nullas soleo admittere causas rusticorum. Interdum etiam post decantatas ex consuetudine laudes matutinas, quod reliquum est noctis, studio literarum soleo impendere, et aliquid pro fratribus meorum institutione, prout possim, lucubrare. Cupio tua in omnibus sequi vestigia, et laudabilem docendi subditos consuetudinem, quam introduxisti, perpetuo, si possim, observare. Scio me ad hoc obligatum

We are born so that we may shortly die. Let death seem terrible to those whose whole life is defiled in the pleasure of the flesh, and for whom no good things are reserved in heaven. But we, who have placed our hope in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of all, and for love of him have despised the pleasures of the world, why should we fear death?

Nevertheless, since death is the most terrible of all terrible things, we shall be able to drive away an indiscreet fear of dying if each day we prepare ourselves as though we were already about to die. Yet it is one thing to have dread of death, another to have trembling fear. For the Lord Jesus too felt the dread of death in advance, but not trembling fear, so that he might show the properties of the two natures. Therefore continual meditation on death is altogether necessary for us who are weak, so that the mind, not yet perfected in the charity of Christ, may be stirred, as though by a certain violent impulse, to the grace of compunction.

For by the remembrance of future death the mind is pierced with a useful dread, like a nail driven into wood. The remembrance of death introduces arduous repentance and true sobriety of mind. The remembrance of death is necessary for the unwise, whose conversion begins from servile fear, so that through filial fear it may be raised by degrees into charity. The remembrance of death, and of the strict examination of God, the judge to come, is especially necessary for those who by evil habit and daily practice are drawn into sin.

And there are among you some who are too lukewarm and negligent in the spiritual warfare; admonishing them, we exhort them paternally to remember that they are mortal, and to live henceforth in such a way that they do not fear to die. For it is very dangerous to live in that state in which a man would dread to die. We must live so that we await death securely; and this can be done only if, preserving ourselves in all purity of mind and body, we continually burn with the exercises of divine charity. Let us live, as far as possible, innocently, according to the rule of the holy Father Benedict, which we have professed, and we shall have good hope, because almighty God, who does not allow a man of good will to perish, will have mercy on us. Let us always think of God as present with us everywhere: he sees all things, knows all things, understands all things, rewards all things. And let us live in that purity in which we have promised to serve his most holy Majesty.

THE END.

Here ends the first book of exhortations to monks, written by my own hand, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the ninth day of the month of June, in the year of Christians 1486, in the fourth indiction, in the twenty-fourth year of my age. I dedicated this work to my predecessor, now abbot of Seligenstadt, most dear to me.

LETTER

Johannes Trithemius, though unworthy, abbot of the monastery of Sponheim, to the reverend father and lord Johannes de Colenhausen, abbot of Seligenstadt, formerly of Sponheim, my most dear predecessor: with prayers, ready and prepared to please him in spirit.

Recently, venerable predecessor, I sent you my first book of exhortations to monks, containing twenty-five homilies. After I learned that it had been approved by your examination, I judged that this second book also, which I now send, should confidently be inscribed with your name. Into the former I gathered twenty-five homilies for the instruction of the brothers, which I had delivered before them; in this one I have arranged seven sermons, according to the order in which they were spoken in their presence.

I do not fear to undergo the examination of your paternity, because I always had you as a gentle predecessor, and long ago found you to be a sincere lover of truth. For you flourish with a keen, gentle, and deep intellect, which can easily discern between true and false, and necessity requires you to correct all things sufficiently. Therefore I pray that, according to the gentleness innate in you, you patiently bear the rudeness of my talent, since I am both a little child in the knowledge of the Scriptures and a novice in the order of prelates.

Practice in the Scriptures, as I trust, will give me experience, and continued diligence in writing will give me progress. The occupation of household affairs and the poverty of the place often draw me back from salutary study, and turn my mind elsewhere against the purpose of my will. Only on feast days and Sundays is leisure granted me for writing, on which, out of reverence for God, I am not accustomed to admit any business of the peasants. Sometimes also, after the customary singing of matins and lauds, I am accustomed to spend what remains of the night on the study of letters, and, as far as I can, to compose something by lamplight for the instruction of my brothers. I desire in all things to follow in your footsteps, and, if I can, to observe forever the praiseworthy custom of teaching subjects which you introduced. I know that I am bound to this.

176 Epistola. ex officio; et, quamvis sim rudis, et indoctus, libenter tamen volo pro viribus in discendo simul, et docendo esse sollicitus. Sermones istos examini tuo subiicio, quos ut magisterii tui lima corrigat, humili supplicatione expositulo. Paucos e pluribus comportavi in ordinem, quoniam nec omnes commendavi litteris, nec videbatur mihi nimia libri extensio, vel necessaria, vel utilis. Festis enim diebus, quando feriamur a tumultu negotiorum mundialium, lectioni vacamus iuxta regulam scripturarum. Et ne frustra locum videar occupare pastoris, quod noctibus lucubravi, solem post nonas loco regularis studii dicere, et coram fratribus in conventu ex chartula recitare. Experior enim, quod haec sollicitando mea non solum fratribus ad aedificationem proficit, sed etiam mihi ad dictandi peritiam conducit. Vale, praceptor venerande, et ora pro nobis. Ex Spanheim duodecimo die mensis Septembris, anno Christianorum millesimo quadringentesimo octuagesimo sexto. IN NOMINE DOMINI NOSTRI IESU CHRISTI INCIPIT SECUNDUS LIBER EXHORTATIONUM AD MONACHOS IOANNIS TRITEMII ABBATIS SPANHEMENSIS, POSTEA PEAPOLITANI. Quod caute sit monachis vivendum. Sermo I. ULTA quidem sunt, fratres dilectissimi, vobis ad considerationem in hac vita necessaria, si ad aeternae salutis gloriam cupitis pervenire. Scitis enim, scriptura testante, quoniam adversarius vester diabolus, sicut leo rugiens circum, quaerens, quem devoret, cui magna vigilantia in fide Domini nostri Iesu Christi per charitatis opera novimus resistendum. Nemo igitur de suis viribus praesumat, ne in vanitate confidat: quoniam, nisi vos in timore Domini humiliter continueritis, cito in laqueum diaboli cadetis. Quanto magnus es (scriptura praecipit) humilia te in omnibus: quoniam Deus resistit superbis, et gratiam concedit humilibus. Monachum etenim decet esse humilem, et verum huius mundi contemptorem, Monachum oportet in observantia regularis disciplinae semper esse sollicitum, et in timore Domini continuo studiosum. Monachum oportet castum, et pudicum esse mente, simul et corpore, ut Deo serviat, quemadmodum promisit, in omni puritate. Monachus non debet vivere secundum voluntatem propriam, sed secundum regulam, et pastoris sui conformem normae institutionis coenobiticae directionem. Monachus negociosus et sanctum debet amare silentium, et mentem suam occupare utiliter in lectione scripturarum. Monachus omni tempore usque ad mortem debet esse sollicitus, quatenus in observantia mandatorum Dei, et regulae sit perfectus. Ut autem sciatis, quae vobis in sancta religione conversantibus ad perfectionem sint necessaria, describam vobis quendam virtutum tramitem, per quem ad Regnum Coelorum viam oportet dirigere. Virtutes autem omnes mutuo cohaerent necessitudinis glutino, ut, qui unam perfecte possidet, omnes habere videatur: et qui vel una caret, nullam penitus dicatur possidere. Omnium virtutum prima ad salutem necessaria est sanctissima fides catholica, ab omni errorum, et haeresum pollutione segregata, et doctrina Domini nostri Iesu Christi originaliter radicata. Nam, scriptura testante, sine fide impossibile est placere Deo: et qui non credit in unigenitum filium Dei, iam iudicatus est, et ira Dei manet Quod caute sit monachis vivendum.

by duty; and, although I am unskilled and unlearned, I nevertheless gladly wish, according to my powers, to be diligent both in learning and in teaching. I submit these sermons to your examination, and with humble supplication I earnestly ask that the file of your mastery may correct them. I have arranged a few out of many in order, since I neither committed them all to writing, nor did an excessive length of the book seem to me either necessary or useful. For on feast days, when we are free from the turmoil of worldly business, we devote ourselves to reading according to the rule of the Scriptures. And lest I seem to occupy the place of shepherd in vain, what I have labored over by night I am accustomed, after None, in place of the regular study, to speak and to recite from a little sheet before the brothers in chapter. For I find that this care of mine not only profits the brothers for edification, but also helps me toward skill in composition. Farewell, venerable teacher, and pray for us.

From Spanheim, on the twelfth day of the month of September, in the year of the Christians one thousand four hundred eighty-six.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the second book of exhortations to monks by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, afterward of [unclear].

That monks must live cautiously. Sermon I.

Many things indeed, most beloved brothers, are necessary for your consideration in this life, if you desire to attain the glory of eternal salvation. For you know, as Scripture bears witness, that your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; and we know that he must be resisted with great watchfulness in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ through works of charity. Therefore let no one presume on his own strength, lest he trust in vanity; for unless you humbly keep yourselves in the fear of the Lord, you will quickly fall into the snare of the devil. “The greater you are,” Scripture commands, “humble yourself in all things,” for God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.

For it befits a monk to be humble and a true despiser of this world. A monk ought always to be diligent in the observance of regular discipline and continually zealous in the fear of the Lord. A monk ought to be chaste and modest in mind and body alike, so that he may serve God, as he promised, in all purity. A monk must not live according to his own will, but according to the rule and according to the direction of his shepherd, conforming to the norm of cenobitic instruction. A monk [unclear] ought also to love holy silence and to occupy his mind usefully in the reading of the Scriptures. A monk ought at all times, even until death, to be diligent, so that he may be perfect in the observance of the commandments of God and of the rule.

But so that you may know what things are necessary for you, who live in holy religion, for perfection, I shall describe for you a certain path of virtues, by which you must direct your way to the kingdom of heaven. All the virtues, however, cling together by the bond of mutual connection, so that whoever perfectly possesses one seems to have them all; and whoever lacks even one is said to possess none at all.

The first of all the virtues necessary for salvation is the most holy catholic faith, separated from every pollution of errors and heresies, and rooted originally in the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as Scripture bears witness, without faith it is impossible to please God; and whoever does not believe in the only-begotten Son of God is already judged, and the wrath of God remains.

169
Hebr. 1. super eum. Omnium ergo virtutum origo fides est, de qua omnia salutis studia oriuntur. Fides in Deum vera, et recta timorem Domini generat: quoniam si Deum credimus iustum, merito confitebimur esse timendum. Fides recta spem parit, et confidentiam; quia, dum misericordem Deum credimus, mox de bonitate illius salutem nos posse consequi speramus. Fides charitatem generat; quia, si Deum esse sumnum bonum credimus, ipsum sine dubio amamus. Quis enim non amaret, quod summe bonum non dubitat? Fides est substantia rerum sperandarum, argumentum non apparentium, et unicum salutis nostrae fundamentum. Fides Deo coniungit animam, et facit eam in medio charitatis aeterni regis amicam. Dicit enim sanctissimus praesul Augustinus: Nullae maiores divitiae, nulli thesauri, nulli honores, nulla huius mundi maior est substantia, quam est fides catholica; quae peccatores homines salvat, caecos illuminat, infirmos curat, catechumenos baptizat, fideles iustificat, poenitentes reparat, iustos augmentat, martyres coronat, virgines, viduas, et coniugales casto pudore conservat, clericos ordinat, sacerdotes consecrat, credentes cum sanctis angelis in aeterna haereditate coelorum collocat. Ubi autem sana fides non est, non potest esse iustitia, quia injustus ex fide vivit; et qui caret iustitiae merito, portio- nem nullam habebit cum Christo. Fides est humanae salutis initium, sine qua nemo ad numerum filiorum Dei potest pertingere, nec partem aliquam in regno Dei possidere. Fides fundamentum virtutum est omnium: quicquid extra fidem agitur; procul dubio ad gehennam aedificatur. Fides christiana lampas est pulcherrima, illuminans animam, et per observantiam mandatorum introducens eam ad foelicitatem aeternam. Fides in primis mentem reducit ad Dei scientiam, postea dat praecerta vivendi ad obedientiam: et cum homo Dei mandata custodierit, spes consequendae salutis erigitur, deinde charitas in cordibus firmatur. Fides cognitionem dat animae; cognitio parit actionem in charitate; et his duobus beatitudo repromittitur in aeternitate. Cavendum summopere, ne sit error in cognitione; quia, dum fides recta haeresum falsitate corrompitur, ad salutis portum actione nulla pervenitur. Sit ergo in fide rectitudo, et veritas; in actione iustitia, et sinceritas, et nulla dominabitur iniquitas. Fides enim sine operibus mortua est, et nihil meretur ad salutem felicitatis aeternae. Fidem habere sine operibus charitatis, est imitari daemones, qui cum ab omni charitate prorsus sint alieni, Deum tamen esse iustum et credunt, et contremiscunt. Hinc de credulis, qui opera non exhibent charitatis, Dominus loquitur per prophetam Esaiam, et postea per semetipsum in sancto Evangelio dicens. Populus hic labiis me honorat; cor autem eorum longe est a me. Qui Christum ore laudat sine opere, quasi vir, qui dubitat in fide. Nam si veraciter crederet, Deum utique timeret. Fides

Hebrews 1: concerning him. Therefore faith is the origin of all virtues, from which all pursuits of salvation arise. True and right faith in God begets fear of the Lord, since if we believe God to be just, we shall rightly confess that he is to be feared. Right faith produces hope and confidence, because, when we believe God to be merciful, we at once hope that we can obtain salvation from his goodness. Faith begets charity, because if we believe God to be the supreme good, we undoubtedly love him. For who would not love what he does not doubt to be supremely good?

Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen, and the one foundation of our salvation. Faith joins the soul to God and, in the midst of charity, makes it the friend of the eternal King. For the most holy bishop Augustine says: There are no greater riches, no treasures, no honors, no greater substance of this world, than the catholic faith, which saves sinful men, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores penitents, increases the just, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins, widows, and married people in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, and places believers with the holy angels in the eternal inheritance of heaven.

But where sound faith is not present, there can be no justice, because the just man lives by faith; and whoever lacks the merit of justice will have no share with Christ. Faith is the beginning of human salvation; without it no one can reach the number of the children of God or possess any part in the kingdom of God. Faith is the foundation of all virtues: whatever is done outside faith is without doubt built for Gehenna. Christian faith is a most beautiful lamp, enlightening the soul and, through observance of the commandments, leading it to eternal happiness.

Faith first brings the mind back to the knowledge of God; afterward it gives the precepts of living for obedience. And when a person has kept God’s commandments, hope of obtaining salvation is raised up; then charity is strengthened in the heart. Faith gives knowledge to the soul; knowledge brings forth action in charity; and to these two blessedness is promised in eternity. One must take the greatest care that there be no error in knowledge, because when right faith is corrupted by the falsehood of heresies, no action brings one to the harbor of salvation. Therefore let there be rectitude and truth in faith, justice and sincerity in action, and no iniquity will have dominion.

For faith without works is dead and merits nothing toward the salvation of eternal happiness. To have faith without the works of charity is to imitate the demons, who, though they are wholly estranged from all charity, nevertheless both believe that God is just and tremble. Hence the Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, and afterward through himself in the holy Gospel, concerning believers who do not show the works of charity, saying: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Whoever praises Christ with his mouth without works is like a man who doubts in faith. For if he truly believed, he would surely fear God. Faith

170
Sermo I. 179 sine operibus, quasi corpus sine spiritu mortuum, quod a vivorum sublatum conspectibus absconditur in sepulchrum. Si bene credis, et male vivis, proprio te gladio perimis: quia scienti bonum et non facienti, peccatum est illi. Cavete fratres mei, ne quem errorem admittatis in fide, et curate summopere, ut nulla sit nequitia in operatione. Sequamini fidem, quam nobis sancta commendat ecclesia; agite vitam, sicut Evangelium praecipit, et norma coenobitica. Deinde spem habeatis in Dei miserationem omni tempore certissimam, sed nunquam a timore Domini alienam. Spes, est futurorum bonorum certa per gratiam miserentis Dei expectatio, et merendi per charitatis exercitium iustitiae coronam, sollicitudo. Spe est certa expectatio futurae beatitudinis: quam gratia Dei operatur in nobis comitante rectitudine bonae voluntatis. Spes est, qua quis venire ad vitam aeternae felicitatis sperat, quam desiderat, et mediente gratia Dei, suam etiam voluntatem in occursum componit, et aptat. Spes est bonorum arduorum futurorum, et possibilium, quibus nemo sperat contrarium. Neque enim malum quis sperat, neque leve, neque quod praesens est, sive praeteritum; nec ignoramus spem non esse impossibilium. Spes moderatrix laborum est omnium, et unica consolatrix in medio tribulationum. Spes enim futurorum bonorum laborantibus pro Christo in hac vita parit requiem, sicut in agone certantibus mitigat dolorem vulnerum coronae expectatio per continuam victoriam. Spes in tormentis roboravit martyres, et fecit eos in virtute Christi omnibus persecutoribus fortiores. Spes aeternae beatitudinis conservat ecclesiam, et dedit sanctis confessoribus, atque virginibus veram in Christo charitatem. Spes deiectum moerore fortiter erigit animum; et quanto se per amorem altius sustulerit, tanto minus contraria huius mundi sentit: Beatus vir, qui confidit in Domino, quia spes non confundit, sicut sanctus promisit Apostolus, qua salvi facti sumus. Ut autem spes non erumpat in praesumptionem, timor Domini ad salutem nobis est necessarius; ut quem, pium, et misericordem credimus, iustum etiam, et rectum non dubitemus. Dicit enim beatissimus Papa Gregorius. Nobis nihil securius, quam sub spe timere, ne incauta mens, vel desperando se in profundum vitiorum deiicit, vel extollendo de donis praesumptuosa ruat. Nam, quanto ante oculos districti iudicis sub spe humiliter trepidat, tanto in illo robustius stat. Timor Dei mentem corrigit, et puram ab omni malitia custodit. Timor Domini initium est sapientiae; quoniam in via Dei a timore incipitur, ut paulatim ad charitatis fortitudinem perveniatur. Timor Domini componit monachum, et facit eum in observantia regularis disciplinae studiosum. Timor Domini custodit regulam, et servat veram mentis, et corporis puritatem. Timor Domini nihil eorum, quae praecerta sunt, negligit, sed omnia sollicitate custodit. Timor Domini nullum admittit ocium, sed continuo occupatur 180 Quod caute sit monachis vivendum.

without works, like a body dead without the spirit, which is removed from the sight of the living and hidden in the tomb. If you believe rightly and live badly, you destroy yourself with your own sword, because for one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin.

Take care, my brothers, not to admit any error in faith, and strive with the utmost care that there be no wickedness in your conduct. Follow the faith which holy Church commends to us; live as the Gospel commands, and as the monastic rule commands. Then have at all times a most certain hope in the mercy of God, yet never one estranged from the fear of the Lord.

Hope is the certain expectation, through the grace of the merciful God, of future goods, and a solicitude to merit, through the exercise of charity, the crown of righteousness. Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, which the grace of God works in us, accompanied by the uprightness of a good will. Hope is that by which a person hopes to come to the life of eternal happiness, which he desires, and, through the mediation of God’s grace, also arranges and adapts his own will to meet it. Hope is of good things, difficult, future, and possible, for no one hopes for the contrary. For no one hopes for evil, nor for what is slight, nor for what is present or past; nor are we unaware that hope is not concerned with impossibilities.

Hope is the moderator of all labors and the sole consoler in the midst of tribulations. For hope of future goods brings rest to those who labor for Christ in this life, just as, for those contending in the arena, the expectation of the crown through continual victory lessens the pain of wounds. Hope strengthened the martyrs amid torments and made them, in the power of Christ, stronger than all their persecutors. Hope of eternal blessedness preserves the Church, and gave to the holy confessors and virgins true charity in Christ. Hope powerfully raises up a spirit cast down by grief; and the higher it lifts itself through love, the less it feels the adversities of this world. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, because hope does not confound, as the holy Apostle promised, by which we have been saved.

But so that hope may not break out into presumption, the fear of the Lord is necessary for our salvation, so that, while we believe him to be kind and merciful, we may not doubt that he is also just and upright. For the most blessed Pope Gregory says: Nothing is safer for us than to fear under hope, lest an unwary mind either cast itself down into the depth of vices by despairing, or fall presumptuously by exalting itself over gifts received. For the more it trembles humbly under hope before the eyes of the strict judge, the more firmly it stands in him.

The fear of God corrects the mind and keeps it pure from all malice. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, because in the way of God one begins from fear, so that little by little one may come to the strength of charity. The fear of the Lord orders the monk and makes him zealous in the observance of regular discipline. The fear of the Lord guards the rule and preserves true purity of mind and body. The fear of the Lord neglects none of the things that have been prescribed, but guards them all with care. The fear of the Lord admits no idleness, but is continually occupied.

171
circa bonum, ut excludat peccatum. Monachus, qui abiecit timorem Domini, quasi civitas in medium deveniens hostium, cuius omnes destructi sunt muri. Urbs sine murorum custodia cito ab inimicis capitur; et monachus, qui non habet Dei timorem, facile a daemonibus superatur. Solus enim Dei timor est, qui mentes corrigit, fugat crimina, innocentiam servat, et facit monachum in sanctitatis proposito perseverantem. Ex timore paulatim oritur caritas, quae cum, iuvante Deo, veraciter in mente radicata fuerit, servilem timorem superans iam foras mittit. Radix omnium bonorum est caritas; quoniam quicquid in hac vita boni agitur, ut Deo placeat, per solam caritatem temperatur. Caritas omnium virtutum est maxima, sine qua nihil sunt cuncta mortalia facta. Dicit enim sanctissimus Christi Apostolus. Si linguis hominum loquar, et Angelorum, caritatem autem non habuero, factus sum velut aes sonans, aut cymbalum tinniens. Et si habuero prophetiam, et noverim mysteria omnia, et omnem scientiam, et si habuero omnem fidem, ita ut montes transferam, caritatem autem non habuero, nihil sum. Et si distribuero in cibos pauperum omnes facultates meas; et si tradidero corpus meum, ita ut ardeam, caritatem autem non habuero, nihil mihi prodest. Considerate diligentem iam nunc fratres mei vosmetipsos, et conscientias vestras interrogate, si veram habeatis caritatem Dei, sine qua nihil caetera omnia proficiunt ad salutem. Audistis enim sententiam Apostoli manifestam, qua caritatem dicit ad salutem esse necessariam. Nemo in sapientia huius mundi confidat; nemo de acceptis donis naturalibus inaniter se extollat; nemo de continenti corporali praesumat, quoniam, si caritas defuerit, nihil ad salutem reliquorum observantia conducit. Verum, ne quis falsam de se aestimationem praesumeret, sanctus Apostolus signa quaedam, et operationes caritatis exposuit, dicens: Charitas patiens est, benigna est; caritas non aemulatur, non agit perperam, non inflatur, non est ambitiosa, non quaerit, quae sua sunt, non irritatur, non cogitat malum, non gaudet super iniquitate, congaudet autem veritati. Omnia suffert, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet. Charitas nunquam excidit. Habete caritatem Dei in vobis fratres mei; quam nisi custodieritis, frustra certando laboratis. Humilitatem vobis saepius diximus omnem esse necessariam, quae non solum virtus est magna, sed reliquarum quoque virtutum nutrix, et custos omnium praecipua. Dicit enim mag nus Papa Gregorius: Qui sine humilitate virtutes congregat, quasi pulverem in ventum portat. Maxima enim monachorum virtus humilitas est; quoniam, tanto esse humiliores tenentur cacteris in mundo vitam agentibus, quanto ex professione ad maiorem perfectionem conari, et tendere sunt adstricti. Virtutum stabile fundamentum est humilitas; super quo quicquid constructum fuerit, nullo tempestatis turbine subvertetur. Per

about the good, so as to exclude sin. The monk who has cast off fear of the Lord is like a city that has come into the midst of enemies, all of whose walls have been destroyed. A city without the protection of walls is quickly captured by enemies; and a monk who does not have fear of God is easily overcome by demons.

For fear of God alone corrects minds, drives away crimes, preserves innocence, and makes a monk persevering in his purpose of holiness. From fear charity gradually arises; and when, with God’s help, it has been truly rooted in the mind, overcoming servile fear, it now casts it out. Charity is the root of all good things, because whatever good is done in this life in order to please God is governed by charity alone. Charity is the greatest of all virtues; without it all mortal deeds are nothing.

For the most holy Apostle of Christ says: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my goods as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.

Consider yourselves carefully now, my brothers, and question your consciences, whether you have true charity of God, without which all other things avail nothing for salvation. For you have heard the clear judgment of the Apostle, in which he says that charity is necessary for salvation. Let no one trust in the wisdom of this world; let no one vainly exalt himself over natural gifts received; let no one presume upon bodily continence, because, if charity is lacking, the observance of the rest contributes nothing to salvation.

But lest anyone should presume a false estimation of himself, the holy Apostle set forth certain signs and works of charity, saying: Charity is patient, is kind; charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.

Have the charity of God within you, my brothers; unless you keep it, you labor in vain by struggling. We have often told you that humility is wholly necessary for you: it is not only a great virtue, but also the nurse of the other virtues and the chief guardian of all. For the great Pope Gregory says: He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.

For humility is the greatest virtue of monks, because they are bound to be humbler than others living their life in the world in the same measure as, by profession, they are obliged to strive and tend toward greater perfection. Humility is the stable foundation of the virtues; whatever is built upon it will be overturned by no whirlwind of storm. Through

172
Sermo I. 181 superbiam diabolus de coelo cecidit; per humilitatem homo ascendit. Frustra nominamur monachi, si non fuerimus humiles: quoniam sicut ignis, si fomento careat lignorum, extinguitur: ita monachus sine humilitate suo nomine valde indignus iudicatur. Humilitate Christiana diabolus vincitur, et quasi clavo percussus fugiens superatur. Nulla splendidior gemma in ornatu monastico humilitate cernitur: quam si monachus contempserit, et professionem suam, et Christum humilem negavit. Humilitati succedit prudentia; quae omnia semper ad normam rationis dirigit, et nihil praeter rectum, honestum, et laudabile facit. Prudentia novit, quid virtuose debeat appetere, et probe scit, quae secundum rectum rationis iudicium debeat vitare. Prudentia vera, et perfecta est, qua summum illud incommutabile bonum appetimus, et omnia ad finem debitum, et rectum ordinamus. Prudentia regularis disciplinae observantiam in vigore conservat stabilem, et reducit aberrantes Monachos ad amissi propositi integram reformationem. Prudentia Monachum in recta salutis via dirigit, et in neutram partem declinare sinit. Prudentia inter fratres pacem conservat, et concordiam, et rectam ordinat in singulis actionem. Prudentia vobis, o fratres mei, valde est necessaria; qua noveritis in omni actione, quae vobis assumenda sint, et quae rursus fugienda. Vera prudentia non carnis, sed spiritus docet vos mundum contemnere, et solum ea, quae futura, et aeterna sunt, desiderare. Prudentia docet hominem in semetipso stabilem consistere, et neque in prosperis, neque in adversis a sanctitatis proposito declinare. Prudentia docet pulchre ordinare praesentia, ad memoriam pro informatione reduct praeterita, et ne quid inopinate accidat, providet futura. Prudentia delinquentes utiliter, et fructuose corripit, omnia, quae vel agit, vel dicit, aut cogitat, secundum rationis iudicium ad finem debitum componit. Estote igitur prudentes sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbae: quia prudentia sine bonitate malitia est; et simplicitas sine prudentia rationali, stultitia nominatur. Dicit enim sanctissimus Paulus Christi Apostolus: Prudentia carnis mors est. Prudentes estote, ne fraude aliorum circumveniamini: simplices vero, ne quem circumveniatis. Hoc enim prudentis officium est, nec falli posse, nec aliquem velle decipere. Vir prudentis iudicium rationis non deserit, et nihil, de quo sit poenitendum, agit. A providendo enim prudentis dicitur. Prudentiam comitatur iustitia: quae omnium virtutum est splendidissima. Nam sine iustitia nihil sunt reliquae virtutes omnes. Iustitia est conservatrix religionis, mater gratiae, observantiae nutrix, veritatis altrix, genitrice pacis, et origo pietatis. Iustitia est virtus, quae distribuit, et conservat unicuique, quod suum est; quae propriam utilitatem neglit, ut communem servet utilitatem, et acquitatem, sine qua nulla Respublica diu in pace potest subsistere. Dicit enim in Ecclesiastico 182 Quod caute sit monachis vivendum.

Through pride the devil fell from heaven; through humility man ascends. We are called monks in vain if we have not been humble, since, just as fire is extinguished if it lacks the fuel of wood, so a monk without humility is judged utterly unworthy of his name. By Christian humility the devil is conquered, and, as though struck by a nail, is overcome and flees. No jewel is seen more splendid than humility in the adornment of monastic life; if a monk despises it, he has denied both his profession and the humble Christ.

After humility comes prudence, which always directs all things according to the rule of reason, and does nothing except what is right, honorable, and praiseworthy. Prudence knows what it ought virtuously to seek, and it knows well what, according to the right judgment of reason, it ought to avoid. True and perfect prudence is that by which we seek that highest, unchangeable good, and order all things to their due and right end. Prudence preserves the observance of regular discipline stable in its vigor, and brings wandering monks back to the complete reform of the purpose they have lost. Prudence directs the monk on the right way of salvation, and does not allow him to turn aside in either direction. Prudence preserves peace and concord among the brothers, and orders right action in each matter.

Prudence is very necessary for you, my brothers, so that in every action you may know what you should undertake and what, in turn, you should flee. True prudence, not of the flesh but of the spirit, teaches you to despise the world and to desire only those things that are future and eternal. Prudence teaches a man to stand firm within himself, and not to turn aside from his purpose of holiness either in prosperity or in adversity. Prudence teaches him to order present things well, brings past things back to memory for instruction, and provides for the future, lest anything happen unexpectedly. Prudence corrects offenders usefully and fruitfully; all that it either does, says, or thinks, it arranges according to the judgment of reason toward its due end.

Be therefore prudent as serpents and simple as doves, because prudence without goodness is malice, and simplicity without rational prudence is called folly. For the most holy Paul, Apostle of Christ, says: The prudence of the flesh is death. Be prudent, lest you be circumvented by the deceit of others; but be simple, lest you circumvent anyone. For this is the office of the prudent man: neither to be capable of being deceived, nor to wish to deceive anyone. A prudent man does not abandon the judgment of reason, and does nothing for which he must repent. For “prudent” is so called from foreseeing.

Justice accompanies prudence, and it is the most splendid of all the virtues. For without justice all the other virtues are nothing. Justice is the preserver of religion, the mother of grace, the nurse of observance, the fosterer of truth, the begetter of peace, and the source of piety. Justice is the virtue that distributes and preserves to each person what is his own; it neglects its own advantage in order to preserve the common advantage and equity, without which no commonwealth can long subsist in peace. For he says in Ecclesiasticus:

173
vir sapiens: Regnum a gente in gentem transvertur propter iniusticias, et iniurias, et contumelias, ac diversos dolos. Ordo iustitiae primum respicit Deum, deinde patriam, exinde parentes, postea omnes in communi secundum distinctiones graduum, et merita dignitatum. Deo in primis iustitia dictante debemus religionem, fidem, cultum, devotionem, et gratiarum actiones, et veram ex toto corde sub obedientia dilectionem. Nobis deinde puritatem mentis, et corporis, continentiam cum studio perfectionis; quo ad illum nobis per obedientiam redire liceat, a quo creati sumus. Tertio loco, patriae debemus commodum, honorem, et defensionem, eiusque, quantum possumus, cum ipsa iustitia procurare utilitatem. Quarto, parentibus tenemur exhibere honorem, et obedientiam, et in eorum necessitate curam, et omnimodam sustentationem. Quinto, praelatis, et superioribus nostris debemus obedientiam, et humilem pro amore Christi subjectionem. Sexto, debemus praelati doctrinam, et pabulum subditis, correctionemque delinquentibus. Septimo, autem loco, debemus maioribus, et principibus honorem, et sine crimine pro Dei amore subjectionem. Octavo, debemus venerabilibus personis reverentiam, et sacerdotibus honorem. Consequentur aequalibus tenemur praestare amicitiam, inferioribus dignationem, benefactoribus vicissitudinem, amicis communitatem, inimicis patientiam, pauperibus misericordiam, miseris consolationem, omnibus charitatem. Haec autem est vera iustitia, qua Deum ex toto corde propter seipsum diligimus, et proximum nostrum in Deo, sicut nosmetipsos, inimicus autem propter Deum; distribuientes unicuique quod sibi iure debetur, omnium utilitati providentes. Sed cum nimia iustitia facile incurrat peccatum, temperantia omnibus vobis necessaria est, quae sola perfectos facit. Est autem temperantia virtus ratione discernens, et vincens animi motus, et omnem libidinem, ne impetus in agendo excedat legis aequitatem. Temperantia virtus optima voluptatibus imperat, et omnia in ordine debito conservat. Omnibus in actionibus, verbis quoque et cogitationibus vestris adhibete temperantiam, et necessariam virtutibus discretionem. Quicquid boni cum discretione feceritis, virtutis merito vocabulum accipit: quod autem fit sine discretione, vitium est dicendum. Discretio moderatrix virtutum est omnium, et maximum prudentiae, ac iustitiae ornamentum. Discretio non solum praelatis, sed etiam subditis est necessaria; quoniam ipsa virtutibus dat ordinem, affectionibus confert modestiam, et cunctis hominum consiliis tribuit decorum pulcherrimum, et honestatem. Hinc quidam sapiens dixit: Est modus in rebus: sunt certi denique fines, Quos ultra citraque nequit consistere rectum. Ad hoc animi fortitudo vobis necessaria est, fratres; per quam non solum constantes efficiamini in adversis, sed etiam prompti, et alacres

The wise man says: A kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, injuries, insults, and various deceits. The order of justice first regards God, then one’s country, thereafter one’s parents, and afterward all people in common according to distinctions of rank and the merits of their dignities. To God, first of all, at the dictation of justice, we owe religion, faith, worship, devotion, thanksgiving, and true love from the whole heart under obedience. Next, to ourselves we owe purity of mind and body, continence with zeal for perfection, so that through obedience we may be permitted to return to him by whom we were created. In the third place, to our country we owe advantage, honor, and defense, and, as far as we can, the promotion of its welfare together with justice itself. Fourth, we are bound to show honor and obedience to our parents, and in their need care and every kind of support. Fifth, to our prelates and superiors we owe obedience and humble subjection for the love of Christ. Sixth, prelates owe teaching and nourishment to their subjects, and correction to those who do wrong. In the seventh place, we owe honor to elders and princes, and subjection without sin for the love of God. Eighth, we owe reverence to venerable persons, and honor to priests. Thereafter we are bound to offer friendship to equals, condescension to inferiors, requital to benefactors, fellowship to friends, patience to enemies, mercy to the poor, consolation to the wretched, and charity to all.

This is true justice: that we love God with the whole heart for his own sake, and our neighbor in God as ourselves, and our enemy for God’s sake, distributing to each person what is owed to him by right and providing for the benefit of all. But since excessive justice easily falls into sin, temperance is necessary for you all, and it alone makes people perfect. Temperance is a virtue that discerns by reason and conquers the movements of the soul and every lust, so that impulse in action may not exceed the equity of the law. Temperance, an excellent virtue, rules pleasures and preserves all things in due order. In all your actions, and also in your words and thoughts, apply temperance, and the discretion necessary to the virtues. Whatever good you do with discretion receives the name by merit of virtue; but what is done without discretion must be called vice. Discretion is the moderator of all virtues, and the greatest adornment of prudence and justice. Discretion is necessary not only for prelates but also for subjects, because it gives order to virtues, bestows modesty upon affections, and grants to all human counsels a most beautiful seemliness and honesty. Hence a certain wise man said:

There is a measure in things; there are, in short, fixed limits, beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.

For this, brothers, strength of soul is necessary for you, through which you may not only become steadfast in adversities, but also ready and cheerful.

174
Sermo I. 183 in arduis. Quis enim sine animi fortitudine maxima hunc mundum cum suis voluptatibus possit contemnere, et in sancta religione monastica sub obedientiae legibus usque ad mortem perseverare? Fortitudo animi vires de charitate Christi suscipit, et constans non minus in adversis, quam in prosperis virtutis desiderio consistit. Fortitudo viam rectitudinis absque timore graditur, et hostibus quadam sancta superbia terribilis, et formidanda videtur. Fortitudo animi parvulorum contemnit iniurias, et omnes facile superat carnis voluptates. Fortitudo in prosperis latet, in adversitate ostenditur, et manifeste per patientiam declaratur. Animo fortis est, non qui vindicat iniurias sibi illatas, sed qui patienter tolerat, et si acceperit in potestatem adversarium, potuisse vindicatam putat. Monachorum fortitudo est mundum contemnere, carnem vincere, omnes mundi honores, et voluptates spernere, et in solum Deum spem omnem, et confidentiam collocare. Mensura fortitudinis est nec timidum esse, nec audacem; quoniam recta incendis via, neque ad dexteram declinat, neque ad sinistram. Monachus ille fortis est iudicandus, qui temperans est in omnibus, moderatusque, et iustus. Hinc dicit sanctissimus Papa Gregorius: Iustorum fortitudo est carnem vincere, propriis voluptatibus contraire, delectationem vitae praesentis extinguere, huius mundi aspera pro aeternis praemiis amare, prosperitatis blandimenta contemnere, adversitatis metum in corde superare. Fortes facti sunt in bello, quia carnem domant, virtutibus coruscant, spiritum roborant, terrena despiciunt, coelestia appetunt, occidi possunt, flecti non possunt, nec sustinere falsa, per infirmitatem metuunt, nec laesi unquam a veritate conticescunt. Monachus ergo, qui vera virtute fortis est, nec temere audet, nec inconsulte timet. Regia enim via est fortitudo simul, atque constantia: a qua temerarius, et pertinax declinat ad dexteram, timidis vero, pusillanimis, pavidusque ad sinistram. Monachus animo constans, et fortis nunquam recidit a sanctitatis proposito, sed nec adversis deprimitur, nec prosperis elevatur. Unde, et sanctissimus praesul Ambrosius, Stultus, inquit, ut Luna mutatur: sapiens autem metu non frangitur, potestate non mutatur, non extollitur prosperis, non mergitur tristibus. Ubi enim sapientia, et virtus, ibi constantia est, et fortitudo animi. Sapiens ergo semper idem est animo, non minuitur, nec augetur mutationibus rerum, nec, ut parvulus, fluctuat, ut circumferatur omni vento doctrinae, sed manet perfectus in Christo, fundatus charitate, radicatusque in fidei perfectione. Postremo, fratres mei charissimi, perseverantia vobis in omni opere bono, et virtuoso necessaria est; sine qua nemo unquam pervenit ad gloriae coronam. Dicit enim in sancto Evangelio Dominus: Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, salvus erit. Tolle perseverantiam, et neque virtus habebit praemium, nec mercedem obsequium, nec gratiam meretur bene-

in difficult matters. For who without the greatest courage of soul could despise this world with its pleasures, and persevere in holy monastic religion under the laws of obedience even until death? Courage of soul receives its strength from the love of Christ, and stands firm in the desire for virtue, no less in adversity than in prosperity. Courage walks the path of uprightness without fear, and to its enemies, by a certain holy pride, appears terrible and formidable. Courage of soul despises the injuries of the little and easily overcomes all the pleasures of the flesh. Courage lies hidden in prosperity, is shown in adversity, and is plainly manifested through patience. Strong in soul is not the man who avenges injuries inflicted on him, but the man who patiently endures them; and if he has brought his adversary into his power, he counts it vengeance enough that he could have taken revenge.

The courage of monks is to despise the world, conquer the flesh, spurn all the honors and pleasures of the world, and place all hope and confidence in God alone. The measure of courage is to be neither timid nor rash, since it advances on the straight way and declines neither to the right nor to the left. That monk is to be judged courageous who is temperate in all things, moderate, and just. Hence the most holy Pope Gregory says: The strength of the just is to conquer the flesh, to resist their own pleasures, to extinguish delight in the present life, to love the hardships of this world for the sake of eternal rewards, to despise the allurements of prosperity, and to overcome in the heart the fear of adversity. They became strong in battle, because they tame the flesh, shine with virtues, strengthen the spirit, despise earthly things, seek heavenly things; they can be killed, but they cannot be bent; nor do they, through weakness, fear to endure falsehoods, nor, when injured, are they ever silent about the truth.

Therefore the monk who is strong with true virtue neither dares rashly nor fears without judgment. For courage together with constancy is the royal road; from it the rash and obstinate man declines to the right, but the fearful, fainthearted, and timid man to the left. The monk constant and strong in soul never falls away from his purpose of holiness, but is neither crushed by adversities nor lifted up by prosperity. Hence also the most holy bishop Ambrose says: The fool is changed like the moon; but the wise man is not broken by fear, not changed by power, not puffed up by prosperity, not sunk by sorrows. For where wisdom and virtue are, there is constancy and courage of soul. Therefore the wise man is always the same in soul; he is neither diminished nor increased by changes of circumstances, nor, like a little child, does he waver, so as to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but remains perfect in Christ, founded in charity and rooted in the perfection of faith.

Finally, my dearly beloved brothers, perseverance is necessary for you in every good and virtuous work; without it no one ever reaches the crown of glory. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: He who perseveres to the end will be saved. Take away perseverance, and virtue will have no reward, obedience no recompense, nor does [unclear] merit grace.

175
184 Quod caute sit monachis vivendum. ficiun. Sola etenim perseverantia bonorum operum coronam laudis meretur accipere; sine qua nihil prodest bonum inchoasse. Nullum virtus habet meritum, cui perseverantia non dedit incrementum. Non incipientibus bonum, sed perseverantibus in bono usque ad mortem, regnum aeternae felicitatis repromittitur; quia, non mane, non meridie, sed cum sero factum esset, laborantibus in vinea denarius reddetur. Non enim, qui bene caepit laudandus est; sed, qui bene continuavit usque ad finem, honorandus est. Quo circa, fratres mei, sedulo vos admonere solem; nec unquam debco cessare, quatenus diligentem attendatis vocacionem vestram, et caute ambuletis in omni religione, et sanctitate, quemadmodum iuratos decet milites Christi. Nunc enim tempus est benefaciendi; quia, cum mortis hora advenerit, omnem facultatem operandi funditus amputabit. Et ideo, quandiu vivitis sani, et incolumes, benefacite; futuram retributionem semper cogitate; et quotdie in profectu spirituali crescite. Quaerite Dominum, dum inveniri potest. Christi Salvatoris vita sit imitatio vestra; quem sequi pro viribus, non gressibus pedum, sed similitudine affectionum, ex institutionis vestrae fundamento tenemini. Caute in omnibus ambulate: timorem Dei in vera humilitate semper ante mentis intuitum ponite. Magna enim puritate vobis est opus, qui mente, et corpore in sanctam Christi militiam consensistis. Ad vos nunc pertinet, o fratres, mundum, et omnia, quae in mundo sunt propter Deum perpetua fortitudine contemnere, omnes carnalium voluptatum motus vincere peccatum fugere, in bonis, et sanctis operibus vos iugiter occupare. Vita quoque vestra quantum fieri humana infirmitas sinit, puritatem imitari angelicam, et omnem fugere, ac detestari pravitatem. Angeli autem sancti nunquam sunt otiosi, sed in laudibus Dei semper absque fatigacione, vel taedio solliciti. Angeli sancti Deum super omnia diligunt, et ab eius charitate nec momentanee quidem recedunt. Horum imitatione monachus in obsequio Christi debet esse assiduus, et semper in bonis operibus secundum Evangelium, et regulam occupatus. Monachus Dei charitatem debet habere ferventissimam, et proximi veram, ordinatamque, et sinceram dilectionem. Amor etenim fervens in Deum perficit monachum, et non sinit esse otiosum. Dicit enim quater sanctissimus Papa Gregorius. Amor Dei nunquam est otiosus. Operatur enim magna, si est: qui si operari renuit, verus Dei amor nunquam fuit. Nam si de carnali amore verum poeta dixit insanus, qui non vult fieri desidiosus, amet: quanto fortius castissimus Dei amor mentem ad ardua impellit, quam possidet. Amate Deum fratres in toto corde, quantum se desiderii fortitudo potest extendere; et omnia, quae vobis praecerta sunt facillime potestis observare. Nihil enim amanti difficile; sed omnia dura, omnia gravia, et ardua, ardens facillia facit amor.

That monks must live cautiously.

For perseverance alone in good works deserves to receive the crown of praise; without it, it profits nothing to have begun well. Virtue has no merit where perseverance has not given increase.
