The arrogance of monks is hateful both to God and to men, and is always liable to sin.

The twenty-seventh sign of humility is perfectly attained by him who, out of love for regular discipline, delights more in being silent than in speaking. The humble lover of Christ loves silence, and, lest he offend in speech, is accustomed to say very little. Humility is rarely found among the talkative, and he who is quick to speak casts down his own soul. A talkative and chattering monk is not without pride, and he who is foolish multiplies words. Whoever desires in spiritual combat to overcome his adversary through humility should not fail to restrain his tongue from much speaking and from every idle word. It is written in the book of Proverbs that in much speaking sin will not be lacking.

Whoever has attained the twenty-eighth sign of perfect humility will avoid laughter and all the disordered gestures of those who guffaw. Mourning chiefly befits a monk, not laughter, since he is one who has died to all the frivolities of the world. And the wise man says: The fool raises his voice in laughter, but the wise man will scarcely laugh quietly.

The twenty-ninth mark of perfect humility takes its beginning from the fear of the Lord,

189
pro cuius honore, quantum praevalet, omne fugit, et detestatur peccatum. Omnis enim, qui peccare non metuit, humilis veraciter non fuit. Monachus autem, qui Christum pro viribus in vera humilitate sequitur, omne peccatum consuevit fugere, et quantum potest, se in virtutum studio exercere. Confitetur peccatum suum humilitas, et quoties etiam in minimis offendit, donec emendaverit omnia per veram poenitentiam, non quiescit. Qui veraciter est humilis, pro servanda conscientiae munditia semper etiam invenitur studiosus. Humilitatis enim nutrimentum est charitas, quae habentem non permittit oculosum. Trigesimum verae humilitatis signum confirmatum in proposito sanctitatis ostendit monachum, et facit eum cunctis fratribus etiam iunioribus subiectum. Quicquid mandaverit pastor, obedit simpliciter: et nunquam praeccepta senioris discutit: causam, cur ita iubeat, non requirit. Ad impossibilia, si praecipientur, animo est promptulus; ad quaecunque dura, et ardua sine contradictione paratus. Consilio pastoris sui dirigitur; illi credit, illi confidit; illi obsequitur; illius imperio volens gubernatur. Audistis iam fratres mei charissimi triginta verae humilitatis indicia; o bone Deus, ubi sunt opera? Quis nostrum gloriabitur veram se habere humilitatem, ut in his signis nullum patiatur defectum? Haec, proh pudor, sunt nostra tempora, in quibus charitas multorum refriguit, perit sanctae religionis integritas, devotio pene omnium expiravit. Monachi nostri sanctitatem quaerunt sine virtutum merito: meritum habere voluit sine laboris exercitio; propterea sanctus hodie non reperitur in monasterio. Fervor sanctae compunctionis in multis nimium est aut rarus, aut tepidus, quoniam, ubi carni, et sanguini vivitur, fervor internae charitatis non habetur. Non satis est tibi, o monache, qui de observantia gloriaris, nihil habere proprium, foeminam non tangere, sub obedientia pastoris in monasterio residere, non manducare carnes, et in caeteris, quae sunt exteriora disciplinae regularis, iuxta monasticam institutionem vivere, nisi cum summa diligentia studeas etiam interiora tua per veram charitatem Dei, et proximi exornare. Charitas enim finis est observantiae regularis, ad cuius acquisitionem caetera omnia sunt principaliter instituta. Unde sine charitate Dei nihil tibi prosunt omnia; quoniam ipsa, et unica est, et sola, quae discernit inter opera bona, et mala. O monache, monache, quicunque sine fervore charitatis tepide conversaris in monasterio, putasne, quod exterior apparatus disciplinae salvum te facere possit? Charitas est, quae habentem sanctificat, charitas reliquas Deo virtutes, et omnia bona commendat: Habeto charitatem, et erunt grata Deo cuncta, quae facis opera pietatis.

for whose honor, as far as he is able, he flees and detests every sin. For everyone who does not fear to sin has not truly been humble. But the monk who, according to his strength, follows Christ in true humility is accustomed to flee every sin and, as much as he can, to exercise himself in the pursuit of virtues. Humility confesses its sin, and whenever it offends even in the smallest matters, it does not rest until it has amended everything through true penitence. Whoever is truly humble is always found zealous to preserve the purity of his conscience. For charity is the nourishment of humility, and it does not allow the one who has it to be prying.

The thirtieth sign of true humility shows a monk confirmed in the purpose of holiness, and makes him subject to all the brothers, even the younger ones. Whatever his superior commands, he obeys simply, and he never debates the commands of his elder; he does not ask the reason why he orders it so. If impossible things are commanded, he is ready in spirit; for whatever is hard and arduous, he is prepared without contradiction. He is directed by the counsel of his superior; he believes him, trusts him, obeys him; he is willingly governed by his command.

You have now heard, my dearly beloved brothers, the thirty marks of true humility. O good God, where are the works? Which of us will boast that he has true humility, so that he suffers no defect in these signs? These, shame to say, are our times, in which the charity of many has grown cold, the integrity of holy religion is perishing, and the devotion of almost all has breathed its last. Our monks seek holiness without the merit of virtues; they wish to have merit without the exercise of labor; therefore today no saint is found in the monastery. The fervor of holy compunction in many is either very rare or lukewarm, because where one lives for flesh and blood, the fervor of inward charity is not possessed.

It is not enough for you, O monk, who boast of observance, to have nothing of your own, not to touch a woman, to reside in the monastery under obedience to your superior, not to eat meat, and in the other outward matters of the discipline of the Rule to live according to monastic institution, unless with the greatest diligence you also strive to adorn your inner life through true charity toward God and neighbor. For charity is the end of regular observance, for the acquisition of which all the other things were principally instituted. Therefore without the charity of God all things profit you nothing, since it alone, and no other, distinguishes between good and evil works. O monk, monk, whoever you are who live lukewarmly in the monastery without the fervor of charity, do you think that the outward apparatus of discipline can save you? It is charity that sanctifies the one who has it; charity commends the other virtues and all good things to God. Have charity, and all the works of piety that you do will be pleasing to God.

190
Sermo IV. 199 De ardua via quae ducit ad vitam. Sermo IV. A udistis, fratres charissimi, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum ho- dierna lectione in sancto evangelio dicentem: Quam angusta est Matt. 7. porta, et arcta via, quae ducit ad vitam, et pauci sunt, qui inveniunt Matt. 11. eam. Nonne ipse Christus est via, qui dixerat: Ego sum via, veritas, Ioan. 14. et vita? Et quo modo nunc dicit, eam arctam esse, et augustam, cum ipse sit, qui dixerat; Tollite iugum meum super vos: et discite a me, quia mitis sum, et humilis corde. Iugum enim meum suave est, et onus meum leve. Quid aliud est iugum Christi, quam arcta via, et angusta ad regnum Dei? Quomodo ergo et levis, et angusta? Audiat charitas vestra. Iugum Domini Iesu suave est bonis, durum, et importabile re- probis. Via Christi ad vitam lata est, et iucunda exercitatis in chari- tate humilibus, angusta vero, et amara superbis. Nihil est enim tam durum, nihil tam terribile, nihil tam arduum, quod amanti Deum non sit facile, et iucundum. Rursus nihil est tam lene, nihil tam facile, nihil tam parvum, quod malae voluntati non sit grave, et onerosum. Idecirco dixit Dominus: Discite a me, quia mitis sum, et humilis corde. Si vultis portare iugum meum super vos, primo mansuetudinem, et humilitatem cordis mei discite; quoniam nisi mites, et humiles fueritis, sarcinam meam quasi grave pondus, et importabile onus portare minime sufficietis. Humilis sum via, superbo: angusta sum porta, tumidos non admitto. Nisi omnia, quae mundana sunt animo spreveritis; nisi carnis voluptatibus vim necessariam intuleritis, quasi onustum pec- catis animal, per me ad regnum intrare non potestis. Via sum humilis: et mites, humilesque recipio. Ianua sum arcta; pauperes spiritu, et corde mundos intromitto. Ad vitam aeternam, fratres, per viam veri- tatis angustam tendimus; oportet, ut nobis omnia, quae ad tam arduum iter sunt necessaria, in tempore procuremus. Sunt autem viatoribus quatior in primis necessaria, sine quibus periculosum est iter, et ad scopon raro pervenitur. Primum, quod viatoribus dicimus esse neces- sarium, cognitionem esse credimus viarum. Nam, qui sine cognitione viarum praevia procul ambulare nititur, periculosis quandoque erroribus implicatur. Aut ergo viam prius discat prudens viator, aut peritum sibi assumat comitem itineris, ne vel in manus latronum incidat, vel a recto itineris tramite recedat. Ad patriam igitur coelestis regni cupientes re- dire per viam nimis angustam, et paucis cognitam, ipsum, necessè est, itineris habeamus ducem, et comitem, Iesum Christum, qui se viam nominavit, et veritatem. Extra Christum non est vera scientia: et qui Christum sui comitem itineris habere negligit, in vanum et sine fructu currit. Discamus ergo viam vitae, charissimi fratres, sine cuius scientia 200 De ardua via quae ducit ad vitam.

Sermon IV.

On the difficult way that leads to life. Sermon IV.

You have heard, dearly beloved brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ saying in today’s reading from the holy Gospel: “How narrow is the gate and confined the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.” Is not Christ himself the way, who had said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”? And how does he now say that it is confined and narrow, when he is the same one who had said, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light”? What else is the yoke of Christ but the confined and narrow way to the kingdom of God? How then is it both light and narrow? Let your charity hear.

The yoke of the Lord Jesus is sweet to the good, but hard and unbearable to the reprobate. The way of Christ to life is broad and pleasant to the humble who are trained in charity, but narrow and bitter to the proud. For there is nothing so hard, nothing so terrible, nothing so difficult, that it is not easy and pleasant to one who loves God. Again, there is nothing so gentle, nothing so easy, nothing so small, that it is not heavy and burdensome to an evil will.

Therefore the Lord said, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.” If you wish to carry my yoke upon you, first learn the meekness and humility of my heart; for unless you are meek and humble, you will by no means be able to carry my pack as if it were a heavy weight and an unbearable burden. I am a humble way to the proud; I am a narrow gate; I do not admit the swollen with pride. Unless you despise in your mind all things that are worldly, unless you bring necessary force against the pleasures of the flesh, you cannot enter through me into the kingdom like an animal loaded with sins. I am the humble way, and I receive the meek and humble. I am the narrow door; I admit the poor in spirit and the pure in heart.

To eternal life, brothers, we make our way by the narrow way of truth; therefore we must procure in due time all the things necessary for so difficult a journey. Now there are four things especially necessary for travelers, without which the journey is dangerous and the goal is rarely reached. The first thing that we say is necessary for travelers, we believe to be knowledge of the roads. For one who tries to walk far without prior knowledge of the roads is sometimes entangled in dangerous errors. Therefore let the prudent traveler either first learn the way, or take for himself an experienced companion for the journey, lest he either fall into the hands of robbers or depart from the right path of the journey.

Therefore, since we desire to return to the homeland of the heavenly kingdom by a way exceedingly narrow and known to few, it is necessary that we have as guide and companion of the journey Jesus Christ himself, who called himself the way and the truth. Outside Christ there is no true knowledge; and whoever neglects to have Christ as the companion of his journey runs in vain and without fruit. Therefore let us learn the way of life, dearly beloved brothers, without knowledge of which [unclear].

191
nemo pertingit ad patriam, ad vitam nemo perveniet aeternam. Credamus firmiter Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum unicum mediatorem Dei, et hominum, verum Deum, et hominem, extra cuius fidem nemo salvabitur, quantunlibet innocenter conversari videatur. Ipse quippe in sancto Evangelio dicit: Qui credit in unigenitum filium Dei, habet vitam aeternam in seipso manentem. Qui autem non credit in filium, manet ira Dei super eum. Quid est, manet ira super eum: nisi quod non removetur ab eo primum originale peccatum? Nam post institutionem novi testamenti per solam Christi fidem removetur originale peccatum a credentibus in eum. Circumcisio patribus data fuit in signum futurae salutis; nullus tamen eorum prius intrare ad regnum coelorum potuit, quam Christus salvator a mortuis resurrexit. Extra fidem ergo Christi non est salus, quoniam, sicut ipse dixit, qui non crediderit, iam iudicatus est, et condemnabitur. Maneamus in Christo per fidem, et amore; quoniam ipse via salutis est, ipse veritas sine errore, ipse vita sine morte. Si Dominum Iesum itineris nostri ducem habuerimus, confidenter ambulamus. Secundo, viatoribus necessarium est, ut per terras sui itineris transeant sine cuiusquam iniuria; quoniam, si aut furtum, aut latrocinium, vel simile quodcunque aliud peccatum in rem publicam commiserint, ultimo venirent plectendi supplicio, et non pertingerent ad propositam itineris destinationem. Nos autem in via positi, fratres, qua tendimus ad patriam regni coelestis, diligentissime caveamus, ne quid committamus verbo, facto, vel cogitatu iustitiae Dei contrarium: sed tribuamus unicuique ius, et debitum suum: Deo in primis pietatem, cultum, et charitatem: proximo dilectionem; nobis perfectae puritatis sanctimoniam. Enimvero, si aliter, quam Christus docuit, vixerimus, in recta via salutis, quae ducit ad regnum, non manemus. Manebimus autem in via, si mandata Dei custodierimus. Ambulabimus in veritate, si ipsum Dominum Deum nostrum in tota fortitudine mentis dilexerimus. Perveniemus ad vitam, si declinantes a malo, in exercitio boni continue perseveramus. Tertio, sumptum itineris habere necessarium est; quia, si viaticum defecerit ambulantibus, ad propositum locum non poterunt pervenire. Viator autem prudentis, priusquam domum exeat suam, tempus, et magnitudinem itineris apud se computat, et secundum quod requirit necessitas, viaticum, et sumptus parat. Iter nobis et magnum restat, et arduum: oportet ergo ut sumptus praeparemus plures in annos, ne deficiamus in hac via, qua pergimus. Viaticum huius itineris nostri ad patriam super coelestem, non aarum est, non argentum, non fallaces divitiae seculi, sed fides Christi, et amor Dei. Sanctae virtutes ad regnum coelorum viaticum indeficiens sunt animae, quibus confortata viam Dei ambulat in hilaritate. Anima Christo fidelis, et sanctis comitata virtutibus, arduam viam hilariter peragit huius longae peregrina-

No one reaches the homeland, no one will attain eternal life. Let us firmly believe that our Lord Jesus Christ is the one mediator between God and human beings, true God and true man; outside faith in him no one will be saved, however innocently he may seem to live. For he himself says in the holy Gospel: “He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life abiding in himself. But he who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him.” What does “the wrath remains upon him” mean, except that the first original sin is not removed from him? For after the institution of the New Testament, original sin is removed from those who believe in him through faith in Christ alone. Circumcision was given to the fathers as a sign of future salvation; yet none of them could enter the kingdom of heaven before Christ the Savior rose from the dead. Therefore outside faith in Christ there is no salvation, since, as he himself said, whoever does not believe is already judged and will be condemned.

Let us remain in Christ through faith and love, for he is the way of salvation, he is truth without error, he is life without death. If we have the Lord Jesus as the guide of our journey, we walk with confidence. Secondly, it is necessary for travelers to pass through the lands of their journey without injury to anyone; for if they commit theft, robbery, or any other similar sin against the commonwealth, they would at last come to be punished with the ultimate penalty and would not reach the intended destination of their journey. But we, brothers, placed on the road by which we strive toward the homeland of the heavenly kingdom, must most carefully beware lest we commit anything by word, deed, or thought contrary to the justice of God; rather, let us render to each his right and his due: first to God, piety, worship, and charity; to our neighbor, love; to ourselves, the holiness of perfect purity. Indeed, if we live otherwise than Christ taught, we do not remain on the right way of salvation, which leads to the kingdom. But we shall remain on the way if we keep the commandments of God. We shall walk in truth if we love the Lord our God himself with the whole strength of our mind. We shall attain life if, turning away from evil, we continually persevere in the practice of good.

Thirdly, it is necessary to have provision for the journey, because if travelers’ supplies fail, they will not be able to reach the place intended. A prudent traveler, before he leaves his house, calculates for himself the length and difficulty of the journey, and according as necessity requires, prepares provisions and expenses. A great and arduous journey remains for us; therefore we must prepare supplies for many years, lest we fail on this road by which we are going. The provision for this journey of ours to the super-heavenly homeland is not gold, not silver, not the deceptive riches of the world, but faith in Christ and love of God. The holy virtues are an unfailing provision of the soul for the kingdom of heaven; strengthened by them, it walks the way of God in gladness. The soul faithful to Christ, and accompanied by the holy virtues, joyfully completes the arduous road of this long pilgrimage.

192
Sermo IV. 201 tionis. Deum super omnia diligere, in bonis se operibus iugiter exercere, in omni puritate servare conscientiam, nulli facere iniuriam, verum praestat animae viaticum ad patriam in coelum sempiternam. Quarto, viatoribus necessarium consultur, ne priusquam perveniant ad finem itineris, coepti propositi obliviscantur. Stultus etenim viator dicendus est, qui puerorum ludis revocatur ab itinere, et obliviscitur, quo tendebat ire. Et nos, fratres charissimi, qui viam religionis monasticae arripuimus, necesse est, ut semper finem nostrum cogitemus; quoniam nobis etiam non advertentibus quotdie mors properat, et imparatos simul, et paratos iudicio praesentat. Agamus interea bonum, dum licet, quantum possimus; et converti ad Dominum in toto corde non tardemus: Christus est via, per quam ad regnum Dei pergimus. Christus est veritas, in qua manentes non erramus. Christus vita est, quam speramus. Audite, fratres, quid ipse dicat in sancto evangelio: Qui vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam, et sequatur me. Haec est via, quam a principio monasticae professionis estis ingressi; quam si vultis recte, et laudabiliter pergere, oportebit vos in observantia regulari pure conversantes, Christum super omnia amare. Vestrum est, fratres, nihil in hoc mundo diligere, et carnem pro amore Dei castigare. Monachorum est omnes delicias, et voluptates praesentis vitae contemnere, et nihil aliud, quam sempiternas epulas desiderare. Monachorum est Christum pro viribus imitari, et vitam suam ae evangelicam instituere puritatem. Imitari Christum summa perfectio est. Minister Christi fidelis Dominum suum sequitur; et ubi Christus est, illic et minister eius erit. Quicunque igitur vestrum propriae salutis amator, ad regnum coelorum venire post Christum desiderat: quicunque custodire, et servare usque in finem ea, quae promisit in religionis ingressu, optat, etiam ista custodiat. In primis quantum praevalet, monachus discat per fidem, et devotionem Deum in sinceritate mentis cognoscere, et se omni tempore in scripturis sanctis pie, et sobrie occupare. Ea, quae sancta fidelium mater ecclesia vel credenda, vel servanda statuit, fideliter, firmiterque, et credit, et custodiat, nec ab eius determinatione ulla tenus recedat. Omnes, remanerant extra arcam, diluvium quondam perdidit; solus Noe cum iis, qui fuerunt in arca, salvus evasit. Arca figuram ecclesiae praestitit; et res facta mysterium figuravit. Unde non est hominibus salus extra ecclesiam, quam Dominus noster Iesus Christus aedificavit supra petram firmissimam. Infidelis quisque non est in ecclesia, ergo peribit necessario, sicut illi quondam, qui non fuerunt in arca. Omnes enim, qui non credunt in Dominum, et Salvatorem mundi Iesum christum, Iudaei, Pagani, Gentiles, Saraceni, item Haeretici, atque Schismatici, qui se ab unione Ecclesiae catholicae subtraxerunt, extra salutis arcam sunt positi; 202 De ardua via quae ducit ad vitam. et si perseveraverint in errore, proculdubio cum daemonibus perpetuo damnandi. Cum ergo fides sit fundamentum salutis, sine qua impossibile est placere Deo, sciat monachus oportet, quid credere debat: et ne contingat eum errare, evangelium, et constitutiones ecclesiae concernentes eum discat. Nam, qui ignorat, ignorabitur. Turpissimum est monacho fidei regulas nescire christianae: et quid teneatur credere ad salutem, penitus ignorare. Non dicimus, quod ea, quae vobis proponuntur credenda, curiose argumentando debeatis discutere, cum, ut sanctus dicit Papa Gregorius, fides non habeat meritum, cui humana praebet ratio experimentum. Hoc autem monemus, quod monachus in divinis scripturis debet esse studiosus, ut sciat quid eum sancta mater ecclesia iubeat credere, ac possit omnes errores fidei contrarios praecavere. Sit ergo miles Iesu Christi monachus omnis in fide catholica firmus, et stabilis; sit in scripturis sobrius, et studiosus, et in bonis operibus continuus.

To love God above all things, to exercise oneself continually in good works, to keep one’s conscience in all purity, and to do injury to no one provides the soul with true provision for the journey to its everlasting homeland in heaven.

Fourth, travelers are necessarily advised not to forget the purpose they have undertaken before they reach the end of the journey. For he must be called a foolish traveler who is called back from his road by children’s games and forgets where he had meant to go. And we, dearest brothers, who have taken up the way of monastic religion, must always keep our end in mind, because even when we do not notice it, death hastens daily and presents both the unprepared and the prepared alike for judgment.

Meanwhile let us do good, while we may, as much as we can, and let us not delay turning to the Lord with our whole heart. Christ is the way by which we go to the kingdom of God. Christ is the truth, in which, if we remain, we do not go astray. Christ is the life for which we hope. Hear, brothers, what he himself says in the holy Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” This is the way upon which you entered from the beginning of your monastic profession. If you wish to proceed on it rightly and praiseworthily, you must live purely in regular observance and love Christ above all things. It is yours, brothers, to love nothing in this world and to chastise the flesh for the love of God. It belongs to monks to despise all the delights and pleasures of the present life and to desire nothing but the eternal banquet. It belongs to monks to imitate Christ with all their strength and to shape their life according to evangelical purity. To imitate Christ is the highest perfection. The faithful minister of Christ follows his Lord; and where Christ is, there also will his minister be. Therefore whoever among you loves his own salvation and desires to come after Christ to the kingdom of heaven, whoever wishes to guard and preserve to the end the things he promised on entering religion, let him also keep these things.

First of all, as far as he is able, let the monk learn through faith and devotion to know God in sincerity of mind, and at all times to occupy himself piously and soberly in the holy Scriptures. Whatever holy mother Church of the faithful has established either to be believed or to be observed, let him faithfully and firmly both believe and keep, and let him in no way depart from her determination. The flood once destroyed all who had remained outside the ark; Noah alone, with those who were in the ark, escaped safe. The ark presented the figure of the Church, and the deed that was done prefigured a mystery. Hence there is no salvation for men outside the Church, which our Lord Jesus Christ built upon the firmest rock. Every unbeliever is not in the Church, and therefore will necessarily perish, as once did those who were not in the ark. For all who do not believe in the Lord and Savior of the world, Jesus Christ, Jews, pagans, Gentiles, Saracens, likewise heretics and schismatics, who have withdrawn themselves from the unity of the Catholic Church, are placed outside the ark of salvation; and if they persevere in error, they are without doubt to be damned forever with the demons.

Since, then, faith is the foundation of salvation, without which it is impossible to please God, the monk must know what he ought to believe; and lest he happen to go astray, let him learn the Gospel and the constitutions of the Church that concern him. For he who is ignorant will be unknown. It is most shameful for a monk not to know the rules of the Christian faith, and to be utterly ignorant of what he is bound to believe for salvation. We do not say that the things proposed to you for belief should be examined by curious argument, since, as the holy Pope Gregory says, faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof for it. But we admonish you in this: that a monk ought to be studious in the divine Scriptures, so that he may know what holy mother Church commands him to believe, and may be able to guard against all errors contrary to the faith. Therefore let every monk, as a soldier of Jesus Christ, be firm and steadfast in the Catholic faith; let him be sober and studious in the Scriptures, and constant in good works.

193
Secundum, quod ambulanti monacho in via salutis aeternae credimus esse necessarium, est, ut studet cognoscere semet ipsum. Cognitio enim sui ipsius omnium scientiarum est optima: et ideo cunctis mortalium studiis merito praeferenda. Huius tamen scientiae salutaris nimium est difficile principium; propterea quod pauci sunt valde, qui non diligent mundum. Omnis enim, qui mundum sequitur, et diligit vanitates, quae transunt, sui ipsius cognitor esse non potest. Et nihil plus impedit hominem a cognitione sui, quam ipse homo. Qui voluptatibus carnis sua pascitur; qui vana scientia huius mundi, sive divitiis, sive honoribus in superbiam elevatur, venire ad cognitionem sui ipsius non permittitur. Veruntamen multa scire, et seipsum negligere, non sapere est, sed potius insanire. Ad gravioris damnationis cumulum pertinet multa discere, et semet ipsum turpiter ignorare. Cogitet igitur quisque vestrum, quid sit, unde sit, et quid futurus sit. Homo per se ipsum certe nihil est; sed quicquid est, ex Deo est, et propter Deum. Quid est homo, nisi viator, et peregrinus quasi unus diei super terram; qui hodie vivus in mundo cernitur, sed mane raptus per mortem amplius non videtur? Omnis vita nostra, omnis actio, omnis dies, omnis hora, quam nihil sumus, ostendit; qui vivendo morimur, agendo corruptimur, cum tempore extinguimur, et mutamur. O lachrymosum genus hominum, instabile, miserum, et infirmum, quam ventosum caecum et vanum te conspicio, dum ex illis, qui nos praecesserunt ad mortem, ad praesentes nos comparationem facio. Verum dixit, qui te folio arboris comparavit. Ventus de arbore rapiens folium in terram proiicit, in cuius locum aliud novum postea simili subiectum casui succrescit. Quod autem in terram cecidit, in terram resoluitur, et nunquam deinceps ad arborem revertitur. Hinc quidam Graecorum sapiens dicit: Quale genus folium, tale est genus atque virorum. Sermo IV. 203 Hominum genus foliorum generi simillimum est, quia virescit ad tempus, et in terram resoluitur: et nec folium ad arborem, nec homo ad vitam revertitur.

The second thing which we believe to be necessary for a monk walking on the way of eternal salvation is that he strive to know himself. For self-knowledge is the best of all sciences, and therefore deservedly to be preferred to all the pursuits of mortals. Yet the beginning of this saving knowledge is exceedingly difficult, because there are very few who do not love the world. For everyone who follows the world and loves the vanities that pass away cannot be one who knows himself. And nothing hinders a man more from knowledge of himself than man himself. He who is fed on the pleasures of his flesh, who is lifted up into pride by the vain knowledge of this world, or by riches, or by honors, is not permitted to come to knowledge of himself. Nevertheless, to know many things and to neglect oneself is not wisdom, but rather madness. It belongs to the heap of a heavier damnation to learn many things and shamefully to be ignorant of oneself.

Let each of you therefore consider what he is, whence he is, and what he is going to be. Man, certainly, of himself is nothing; but whatever he is, he is from God and for God. What is man but a traveler and a pilgrim, as it were of one day upon the earth, who today is seen alive in the world, but in the morning, snatched away by death, is seen no more? All our life, every action, every day, every hour, shows how nothing we are: we die by living, are corrupted by acting, are extinguished with time, and are changed. O tearful race of men, unstable, miserable, and weak, how windy, blind, and vain I see you to be, when I make a comparison between ourselves in the present and those who have gone before us to death. He spoke truly who compared you to the leaf of a tree. The wind, snatching a leaf from the tree, casts it to the ground; in its place another new leaf afterwards grows up, subject to a like fall. But what has fallen to the ground is resolved into the earth, and never thereafter returns to the tree. Hence a certain wise man of the Greeks says:

As is the race of leaves, so also is the race of men.

The race of men is very like the race of leaves, because it grows green for a time and is resolved into the earth; and neither does the leaf return to the tree, nor man to life.

194
Sequitur iam tertium, quod monacho in via Dei ambulanti valde puto necessarium. Omnis homo, qui semetipsum viatorem huius vitae brevissimi temporis intelligit, se humilem in omnibus veraciter ostendit. Ad quid enim terra superbiret, et cinis? Elatus esse non poterit, qui seipsum veraciter cognoscit. Nullam fratres mei causam habemus elationis et superbiae, sed humilitatis multam, atque continuam: quippe qui terra sumus, et pulveris quaedam compactio, atque post paucos dies iterum in pulverem reversuri. Sed, quia paucorum est vera humilitas, idcirco via salutis angusta dicitur, et a paucis inventur: Humilitate pervenitur ad regnum; quoniam, dicente in sancto Evangelio Domino, omnis, qui se propter Deum humilitat, exaltabitur, et qui se exaltat, humiliabitur. Quarto, viatori monacho ad coelum summe est necessarium, quatenus ab omni peccato se faciat alienum; quoniam ad regnum Dei nemo intromittitur, nisi qui summa conscientiae puritate commendatur. Unde sanctis virtutibus, ac bonis operibus continue ornanda est conscientia; quia illis dumtaxat aperitur coelum, qui pro Dei amore despiciunt mundum. Hinc Petrus Christi sanctissimus archiapostolus in epistola secunda dicit: Vos autem omnem curam subinferentes ministrate in fide vestra virtutem; in virtute scientiam; in scientia autem abstinentiam; in abstinentia patientiam; in patientia autem pietatem; in pietate amorem fraternitatis, in amore autem fraternitatis charitatem. Haec autem, si vobiscum adsint, et superent, non vacuos, nec sine fructu vos constituent in cognitione Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Una est, Firmiano testante, virtus, ac via bonorum, quae animas exutas a carne ducit, ac vehit non in fabulosos poetarum Elysios campos, sed in angelicos choris, fides scilicet christiana per opera verae charitatis decorata, quae omne fugit peccatum. Quinto, viatori per arduum iter coelestis regni praecipitur, ut Dei voluntatem servando, mandata in omnibus sequatur. Quicquid vel dicturus, vel acturus est, prius dilerentem examinet, si cum Dei, et ecclesiae ordinationibus concordet. Quod si vel Deo, vel ecclesiae invenerit esse contrarium, fugiat subito, ne incidat in peccatum, Sapientis enim est viri nihil inexaminatum committere, sed omnia, per providentiae consilium, antequam agat, diligenter cogitare. Qui autem in hoc itinere arduo vult esse tutus, atque securus, vitam et mores pro viribus imitetur Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui lux est omnibus in vitam aeternam. Sextum, quod viatori nostri judicamus necessarium, est ut salutare diligat studium scripturarum. Non sit curiosus in lectione, nec vanis superstitionibus deditus, sed animo simplex, purus, et rectus: Monachum non decet scripturis inhaerere 204 Quemadmodum sit fugiendum peccatum.

Now follows the third thing, which I think very necessary for a monk walking in the way of God. Every man who understands himself to be a traveler in this life of very brief duration truly shows himself humble in all things. For why should earth and ashes be proud? He who truly knows himself cannot be exalted. My brothers, we have no cause for exaltation and pride, but much and continual cause for humility, since we are earth, a certain compacting of dust, and after a few days are to return again into dust. But because true humility belongs to few, therefore the way of salvation is called narrow and is found by few. By humility one comes to the kingdom, because, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel, everyone who humbles himself for God’s sake will be exalted, and he who exalts himself will be humbled.

Fourth, for the monk traveling to heaven it is supremely necessary that he make himself a stranger to every sin, because no one is admitted into the kingdom of God unless he is commended by the highest purity of conscience. Therefore the conscience must continually be adorned with holy virtues and good works, because heaven is opened only to those who despise the world for love of God. Hence Peter, the most holy chief apostle of Christ, says in his second epistle: Applying all care, minister virtue in your faith; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, abstinence; in abstinence, patience; in patience, godliness; in godliness, love of brotherhood; and in love of brotherhood, charity. If these things are present with you and abound, they will make you neither empty nor without fruit in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. There is one virtue, as Firmianus testifies, and one way of the good, which leads and carries souls stripped of the flesh not into the fabulous Elysian fields of the poets, but into the choirs of angels: namely, the Christian faith adorned by works of true charity, which flees every sin.

Fifth, the traveler on the steep road of the heavenly kingdom is instructed that, by keeping God’s will, he should follow the commandments in all things. Whatever he is about to say or do, let him first examine diligently whether it agrees with the ordinances of God and of the Church. But if he finds it contrary either to God or to the Church, let him flee from it at once, lest he fall into sin. For it belongs to a wise man to commit nothing unexamined, but to consider all things diligently by the counsel of foresight before he acts. But whoever wishes to be safe and secure on this steep journey should, to the best of his strength, imitate the life and conduct of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the light for all unto eternal life.

The sixth thing that we judge necessary for our traveler is that he love the saving study of Scripture. Let him not be curious in reading, nor given to vain superstitions, but simple, pure, and upright in soul. It does not befit a monk to cling to writings.

195
gentilium, nec fabulis studium accommodare turpium poetarum. Qui sectatur vana, nunquam erit sapiens: et qui curiosa quaerit, cito defluet in peccatum. Omnem vanae superstitionis lectionem semper fugiat monachus; et quicquid non conducit ad divinarum scientiam scripturarum, viatori nostro omni tempore est contemnendum. Septimo, viatoris nostro iudicamus valde necessarium, quatenus et sensus, et cogitationes suas prudenter dirigat, et ab omni concupiscentia inordinata custodiat. Asellus noster protervus freno disciplinae coercendus est, ne sessorem spiritum praecepit in infernum. Qui se ambulare in conspectu videntis omnia semper cogitat, conscientiam suam puram, et mundam summa diligentia conservat. Semper in timore Domini vigilat; semper in ieiunio, et abstinentia corpusculum pro amore coelestis patriae castigat. Monachus, qui se peregrinum agnoscit, et advenam in hoc mundo, coelestis patriae nuncupam obliviscitur, quoniam nihil cernit in via praesentis vitae, in qua animus delectetur. Viator etenim prudens nulla viarum spectacula considerat, nihil eum in sua peregrinatione rerum transeuntium delectat, sed ad finem itineris omni tempore suspirat. Dulcem semper cogitat patriam, graviter fert suam prolongari, vel retardari peregrinationem; et idcirco nihil in hoc mundo, praeter Dominum Iesum habere desiderat, in cuius apparere conspectu sedulo festinat. Octavum viatori nostro necessarium est divinae charitatis exercitium indefessum. Nemo enim ad caelestem patriam venire poterit, qui a charitatis itinere discedit. Charitas Dei ad Deum via est: quam si quis in se ardentem habere neglexit, a vero itinere coelestis patriae miserabiliter erravit. Deus, inquit scriptura, charitas est et qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet, et Deus in eo. Qui autem in charitate non est, iam procul recessit a via salutis, et ambulans in tenebris peccatorum, nunquam perveniet ad regnum. Quemadmodum sit fugiendum peccatum. Sermo V. Audistis, fratres mei charissimi omnes, quid de peccatoribus dixit sanctus Ioannes Apostolus: Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est, quoniam ab initio diabolus peccat. Metuenda, et nimium formidanda sententia. Si omnes, qui faciunt peccatum, ex diabolo sunt, et in multis offendimus omnes, quantos inveniemus a peccato immunes? Dicit nihilominus consequenter: Omnis, qui natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit; quoniam semen ipsius in eo manet; et non potest peccare, quoniam ex Deo natus est. Praemiserat autem dicens: Si dixerimus, quoniam non habemus peccatum, ipsi nos seducimus et veritas in nobis non est. Quid sibi vult haec ipsa contradictio, ut nemo filiorum Dei sit absque peccato, et peccatum non faciat, qui est natus ex Deo?

of the gentiles, nor devote his study to the fables of shameful poets. He who follows vain things will never be wise; and he who seeks out curious matters will quickly fall into sin. The monk should always avoid every reading of vain superstition; and whatever does not contribute to knowledge of the divine Scriptures must at all times be despised by our traveler.

Seventh, we judge it very necessary for our traveler that he prudently direct both his senses and his thoughts, and guard them from every disordered desire. Our stubborn little ass must be restrained by the bridle of discipline, lest it cast its rider, the spirit, headlong into hell. He who always considers that he walks in the sight of him who sees all things preserves his conscience pure and clean with the greatest diligence. He always keeps watch in the fear of the Lord; always, in fasting and abstinence, he chastises his poor little body for love of the heavenly homeland. The monk who knows himself to be a pilgrim and a stranger in this world never forgets the heavenly homeland, because he sees nothing on the road of this present life in which his soul may take delight. For the prudent traveler pays no attention to the spectacles along the roads; nothing among passing things delights him in his pilgrimage, but at all times he sighs for the end of the journey. He always thinks of the sweet homeland, he bears it heavily that his pilgrimage is prolonged or delayed, and therefore he desires to have nothing in this world except the Lord Jesus, into whose presence he eagerly hastens to appear.

Eighth, tireless practice of divine charity is necessary for our traveler. For no one will be able to come to the heavenly homeland who departs from the path of charity. The charity of God is the way to God; if anyone has neglected to have it burning within himself, he has miserably strayed from the true road of the heavenly homeland. God, says Scripture, is charity, and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. But he who is not in charity has already withdrawn far from the way of salvation, and, walking in the darkness of sins, will never come to the kingdom.

How Sin Must Be Fled. Sermon V.

You have all heard, my dearly beloved brothers, what Saint John the Apostle said about sinners: He who commits sin is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning. A sentence to be feared and greatly dreaded. If all who commit sin are of the devil, and we all offend in many things, how many shall we find immune from sin? Nevertheless he says immediately after: Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. But he had said before: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. What is the meaning of this contradiction: that none of the sons of God is without sin, and yet he who is born of God does not commit sin?

196
Sermo V. 205 Nulla istic invenitur contradictio, quoniam utrumque verum est, quia et nemo sine peccato est in eo, quod nemo est sine lege peccati, et qui est natus ex Deo, peccatum non facit; quia per legem mentis, id est per charitatem, quae Dei semen est, peccatum non facit. Charitas enim operit multitudinem peccatorum, sine qua nullum est opus bonum, et ipsa sola potens est delere omne peccatum. Hinc sanctus dicit praesul Augustinus. Nullus sanctus, et iustus caret peccato, nec tamen ex hoc desinit esse iustus, vel sanctus, si cum affectu teneat sanctitatem. Sed ista peccata iustorum non sunt mortalia, vel enormia putanda, sed parva, et venialia, sine quibus vita praesens vix agitur, quoniam procul a iusto sit omne peccatum mortale, si nomen iustitiae debet retinere, necesse est. Peccatum namque mortale hominem a Deo separat, animam necat, et cum daemonibus in aeternum damnat. Hoc perniciosum genus peccati mortalis cavere per dei gratiam possimus, et per arbitrii recti- tudinem sollicite debemus. Propterea enim facti sumus monachi, ut cautissime viventes sub obedientiae salutaris imperio, mortalis non inci- deremus foveam peccati. Semper itaque vigilandum est monacho in operibus bonis, ut a mortali scelere vivat immunis. Quisquis autem in via Dei carnem sibi molestam sentit, atque contrariam, necesse est, ut eam per poenalium memoriam faciat spiritui subiectam, et quasi per metum obedientem. In primis ergo monachus propriae salutis amator fallacem huius mundi statum, deceptionemque semper attente consi- deret, et quam cito transeat omnis delectatio carnis, penset. Ille a pec- catis animum suum facile potest trahere, qui voluptatem carnis brevis- simam, poenam vero peccantibus debitam sedulo cogitaverit aeternam. Mundus transit simul, et concupiscentia eius; homines quoque mo- riendo transeunt omnes; et nemo diu in hac vita manere permittitur. Quid enim est mundus, nisi mare magnum, profundum, et inquietum? in quo tot sunt malorum reptilia, quot hominum desideria mala ad bonum ordinata. O mundo fallax, deceptor, et iminunde, qui tibi ad- haerentes turpiter decipis, sequentes te omnes in profundum inferni submergis, quam felices sunt illi, qui te pro Christi amore despiciunt, divisionemque facientes utilem a tuis vanitatibus in tempore discedunt. Quicquid in mundo cernimus, vanum est, et omnis mundi amator vanus efficitur, et in brevi corrumpetur. Cogitate vos in brevi morituros; quoniam nihil sic hominem a peccato rethrahit, quemadmodum frequens, et intenta mortis meditatio facit. Dicit enim scriptura: Memorare no- vissima tua, et in aeternum non peccabis. Necessitas moriendi cogitata mentem timore concutit, et a vitio compescit. Secundum, quod pec- catum persuadet fugere, est futuri metus iudicii, in quo necesse est omnes homines praesentari. Hoc tremendum iudicium nemo potest eva- dere, sed oportet nos omnes in eo comparere. Duo nobis metuenda

Sermon V.

There is no contradiction found here, since both statements are true: no one is without sin, in that no one is without the law of sin; and he who is born of God does not commit sin, because through the law of the mind, that is, through charity, which is the seed of God, he does not commit sin. For charity covers a multitude of sins; without it there is no good work, and it alone has power to blot out every sin. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: No saint and no just man is without sin; yet on account of this he does not cease to be just or holy, if he holds fast to holiness with affection. But these sins of the just are not to be regarded as mortal or enormous, but as small and venial sins, without which the present life is scarcely lived; for every mortal sin must be far from the just man, if he is to retain the name of justice.

For mortal sin separates man from God, kills the soul, and condemns it eternally with the demons. By the grace of God we can avoid this destructive kind of mortal sin, and through uprightness of will we must do so diligently. For this is why we have been made monks: that, living most cautiously under the command of saving obedience, we might not fall into the pit of mortal sin. Therefore a monk must always keep watch in good works, so that he may live free from mortal crime.

But whoever, on the way of God, feels his flesh troublesome and contrary to him must make it subject to the spirit through remembrance of punishments, and obedient, as it were, through fear. First of all, then, a monk who loves his own salvation should always attentively consider the deceitful condition of this world and its deception, and should weigh how quickly every delight of the flesh passes away. He can easily draw his soul away from sins who has carefully considered that the pleasure of the flesh is very brief, but the punishment owed to sinners is eternal.

The world passes away, and its desire with it; all human beings too pass away by dying, and no one is permitted to remain long in this life. For what is the world but a great sea, deep and restless? In it there are as many creeping things of evils as there are evil desires of human beings [unclear]. O deceitful, deceiving, and unclean world, you shamefully deceive those who cling to you; you plunge all who follow you into the depth of hell. How happy are those who despise you for love of Christ, and, making a useful separation from your vanities, depart from you in time.

Whatever we see in the world is vain, and every lover of the world becomes vain and will soon be corrupted. Think that you will soon die, for nothing draws a person back from sin as frequent and intent meditation on death does. For Scripture says: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. Thought of the necessity of dying shakes the mind with fear and restrains it from vice.

The second thing that persuades one to flee sin is fear of the future judgment, at which all human beings must necessarily be presented. No one can escape this terrible judgment; rather, we must all appear at it. Two things must be feared by us.

197
206 Quemadmodum sit fugiendum peccatum. iudicia imminent; quorum neutrum poterimus subterfugere, sed necessitas nos compellit in utroque comparere. Alterum particularis dicitur, in quo statim post mortem anima pro meritis, vel ad gratiam, vel ad poenam iudicatur. Alterum vero generale nominatur, quod erit in fine seculi; ubi omnes publice iudicabimus a filio unigenito Dei. Utrumque nimis terribile iudicium, et cunctis mortalibus valde metuendum. Hinc prophetam Ioelem dicit: Magnus dies Domini, et terribilis valde, et quis sustinebit eum? in concionatore quoque rex Salomon dicit: Cuncta, quae fiunt sub sole, adducet Deus in iudicium, pro omni errato iudicaturus, sive bonum sit, sive malum. In Esaia quoque sic legitur: Dominus ad iudicium veniet cum senibus populi sui, et principibus eius. Et in libro Amos prophetae sic scribitur; Vae desiderantibus diem Domini. Ad quid eam vobis? Dies enim Domini ista tenebrae, et non lux. Sophonias quoque prophetam Domini, amaritudinem futuri iudicii praenuncians dixit: Vox diei Domini amara, tribulabitur ibi fortis. Dies irae dies illa: dies tribulationis, et angustiae, dies calamitatis, et miseriae; dies tenebrarum, et caliginis; dies nebulae, et turbinis. In igne zeli Domini devorabitur omnis terra; quia consummationem cum festinatione faciet in cunctis habitantibus terram. Hunc diem terribilem nimis, et cunctis tremendum mortalibus, quem certo venturum creditis, in memoria, fratres, charissimi semper habeatis. Dicit enim sanctissimus praesul Ambrosius: Nihil est, quod magis proficiat ad vitam honestam, quam ut cum credamus iudicem futurum, quem nec occulta mentium fallunt, nec inhonesta delectant. Omnes enim nos, ut sanctus Christophilus inquit, manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi, ut referat unusquisque propria corporis, prout gessit, sive bonum, sive malum. Quam sit metuenda illa dies futura, terribilisque iudicii, sanctus presbyter Hieronymus insinuat dicens: Sive comedam, sive bibam, sive aliquid aliud faciam, semper vox illa videtur sonare in auribus meis: Surgite mortui, venite ad iudicium. Quoties diem iudicii cogito, totus corde, et corpore contremisco. Unde si qua praesentis vitae est letitia, ita agenda est, ut nunquam amaritudo futuri iudicii recedat a memoria. Quid nos miseris dicemus in illa die, vel quomodo stabimus ante districtum iudicem, si, ut divus Petrus dicit apostolus, vix iustus salvabitur? Si Hieronymus vir iustus, atque sanctissimus iudicium futurum timuit, o bone Deus, quomodo Tritemius peccator infelix comparebit? Si iustus metuit, peccator quomodo stabit? Quid enim dicemus, aut quid respondebimus undique, graviter accusati? Omnia elementa stabunt adversum nos in testimonium; accusabunt terra simul, et coelum: quod si etiam tacerent omnia, gravis erit unicuique conscientia propria. Nihil ignorat, qui novit omnia; quoniam ibi manifesta erunt iudicanti universa. Erunt ibi, quae fecimus mala nos graviter accusantia; aderunt circumcirca pro testi-

Two judgments are impending, neither of which we shall be able to escape; rather, necessity compels us to appear at both. One is called the particular judgment, in which, immediately after death, the soul is judged according to its merits, either to grace or to punishment. The other is named the general judgment, which will be at the end of the age, where we shall all be judged publicly by the only-begotten Son of God.

Both judgments are exceedingly terrible and greatly to be feared by all mortals. Hence the prophet Joel says: “Great is the day of the Lord, and very terrible; and who shall endure it?” Likewise in Ecclesiastes King Solomon says: “All things that are done under the sun God will bring into judgment, judging every error, whether it be good or evil.” In Isaiah also it is read thus: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes.” And in the book of the prophet Amos it is written: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord. What is it to you? For that day of the Lord is darkness and not light.” Zephaniah also, the prophet of the Lord, foretelling the bitterness of the future judgment, said: “The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be troubled there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind. In the fire of the Lord’s zeal the whole earth will be devoured, because he will make a consummation with haste upon all who dwell on the earth.”

This day, exceedingly terrible and fearful to all mortals, which you believe will certainly come, dearest brothers, you should always keep in memory. For the most holy bishop Ambrose says: “There is nothing that profits more toward an honorable life than that we believe there will be a judge whom neither the hidden things of minds deceive nor shameful things delight.” For all of us, as holy Christophilus says, must be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil.

How much that future day of terrible judgment is to be feared, the holy priest Jerome indicates, saying: “Whether I eat, or drink, or do anything else, that voice always seems to sound in my ears: Rise, you dead, come to judgment. Whenever I think of the day of judgment, I tremble in my whole heart and body.” Therefore, if there is any joy in the present life, it must be carried on in such a way that the bitterness of the future judgment never withdraws from memory.

What shall we wretches say on that day, or how shall we stand before the strict judge, if, as the divine apostle Peter says, scarcely will the just man be saved? If Jerome, a just and most holy man, feared the future judgment, O good God, how will Trithemius, an unhappy sinner, appear? If the just man fears, how will the sinner stand? For what shall we say, or what shall we answer, accused heavily on every side? All the elements will stand against us as witnesses; earth and heaven together will accuse us. But even if all things were silent, each one’s own conscience will be a heavy accuser. He who knows all things is ignorant of nothing, for there all things will be manifest to the judge. The evil things we have done will be there, accusing us heavily; they will be present all around as witnesses [unclear].

198
Sermo V. 207 monio contra nos infinita daemonia; apertum videbimus chaos infra nos horridum; iudicem super nos conspiciemus iratum; et ex omni parte extremum nobis imminere periculum. Haec fratres mei futuri examinis pericula semper in memoria cordis revolvite; et quam sit hor- rendum futuram sententiam iudicis incidere, sedulo cogitate. In illa ter- ribili hora plus valebunt pura corda; quam astuta rhetorum verba: plus conducet homini conscientia mundia, quam totius orbis pecunia; quo- niam, qui iudicaturus est omnia, non fallitur, immo nec precio, nec precibus immutatur. O quam incredibilis horror invadet impios omnes, Matt. 25. quam metuendam sunt audituri sententiam. Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum, qui praeparatus est diabolo, et angelis eius. O malorum omnium pessimum; o tristitia profundissima omnium tristitiarum, a consortio sanctorum. dividi, et cum daemonibus in aeternum cru- ciari. Vere dies Iudicii horrida, omnibusque metuenda; quia nimis amara; ubi synderesis conscientiae vermis non moritur, ubi semel damnatus ad supplicium nunquam liberatur. Monachus ergo salutem cu- piens assequi sempiternam, se quanta potest ab omni peccato mund- dum semper custodiat, et illa vox: Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum, nunquam ab eius memoria recedat. Unde tertium, quod ad declinandum a peccato, multum aestimamus conducere, est amaritudinem poenarum aeternae damnationis sedulo cogitare. Nulla enim tam vehemens est car- nalis voluptatis tentatio, quae non subito victa deficiat, si tentatus, quid iam patiantur in inferno damnati, studiosa meditatione recogitat. Gehen- nae infero- rum forma. Quid nunc divitiae quondam habitae prosunt damnatis? quid conferunt voluptates transactae positis in inferno luxuriosis? quid vanissimi ho- nores tumidis? quid potestas quondam lata superbis? Cogitate fratres, quid iam damnati patiantur apud inferos, et ne vos contingant similia, in bonis, et sanctis operibus iugiter perseverate. Si timetis infernum, fugite peccatum. Nihil enim nocebit infernum, si homo in fide Christi permanserit a peccatis alienus: nec ardebit in poena, qui prius hic non arserit in culpa. Metuendus inferni locus, in quo non est ulla redemptio; sed quisquis illuc damnatus semel intraverit, ad salutem amplius non exhibit. Clamant in tormentis, in angustia miseri, in horrore sempiterno positi, dicentes: quid nunc prodest nobis superbia nostra, divitiae, ho- nores, dignitates, luxuria, gula, et omnes transactae voluptates carnales? quid nobis iam prosunt in aeternum damnatis? Ecce omnia transierunt velut umbra, et tanquam unius noctis breve somnium cuncta evanue- runt. Nos autem cruciatibus aeternis deputati sumus, in quibus nullam esse redemptionem certissime scimus. In inferno, sicut Augustinus te- statur, et si erit stimulus poenitundinis, nulla tamen erit in damnatis correctio voluntatis, a quibus ita culpabitur iniquitas, ut nullatenus ab eis possit diligi, vel desiderari iustitiae acquisitas. Ibi tunc edax inferni

Sermon V.

We shall see countless demons around us as witnesses against us; below us we shall see the horrible open chaos; above us we shall behold the judge, angry; and on every side the utmost danger will be hanging over us. My brothers, always turn over in the memory of your heart these dangers of the examination to come, and diligently consider how dreadful it is to fall under the future sentence of the judge. In that terrible hour pure hearts will have more power than the crafty words of rhetoricians; a clean conscience will help a man more than the money of the whole world, because he who is to judge all things is not deceived, indeed is changed neither by price nor by prayers.

O what incredible horror will seize all the wicked, what fearful sentence they will hear: “Depart, accursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” O worst of all evils; O deepest sorrow of all sorrows, to be separated from the fellowship of the saints and to be tormented with demons forever. Truly the day of judgment is horrible and to be feared by all, because it is exceedingly bitter: there the worm of conscience does not die; there one once damned to punishment is never set free.

Therefore the monk who desires to attain eternal salvation should always keep himself, as far as he can, clean from every sin, and that voice, “Depart, accursed, into eternal fire,” should never depart from his memory. Hence the third thing which we judge to be of great help in turning away from sin is to think diligently on the bitterness of the punishments of eternal damnation. For no temptation of fleshly pleasure is so violent that it will not at once fail, overcome, if the person tempted recalls in earnest meditation what the damned are now suffering in hell.

What profit now to the damned are the riches they once possessed? What do past pleasures bring to the lustful who have been placed in hell? What do the emptiest honors bring to the proud? What does the power once so broad bring to the arrogant? Think, brothers, what the damned are now suffering in the lower world, and lest similar things befall you, persevere continually in good and holy works. If you fear hell, flee sin. For hell will do no harm if a man has remained in the faith of Christ, free from sins; nor will he burn in punishment who has not first burned here in guilt.

The place of hell must be feared, where there is no redemption; but whoever, once damned, has entered there will no longer go out to salvation. They cry out in torments, wretched in anguish, placed in everlasting horror, saying: “What does our pride profit us now, our riches, honors, dignities, luxury, gluttony, and all past fleshly pleasures? What do they profit us now, damned forever? Behold, all things have passed like a shadow, and everything has vanished like the brief dream of a single night. But we have been assigned to eternal torments, in which we know most certainly that there is no redemption.”

In hell, as Augustine bears witness, even if there will be the sting of repentance, nevertheless there will be no correction of the will in the damned; by them iniquity will be blamed in such a way that justice [unclear] can in no way be loved or desired by them. There then the devouring [unclear] of hell...

199
208 Quemadmodum sit fugiendum peccatum. flamma comburit, quos nunc carnalis delectatio polluit: et tanto amplius quisque in tormentis uritur, quanto hic in carne contra Deum magis delectatur. Apud inferos, contestante Gregorio, frigus erit intolerabile, ignis inextinguibilis, vermis conscientiae immortalis, foetor intolerabilis, tenebrae palpabiles, dolores inaestimabiles, flagella sine intermissione caelentium, horrenda visio daemonum, confusio commissorum criminum, desperatio omnium bonorum: sed omnium in inferno poenarum longe gravissima illa existimanda est, quod illi damnati lucis aeternae visione perpetuo sunt privati. Hinc beatissimus praesul Ioannes Chrysostomus ait: Intolerabilis res est gehenna, et omnes homines abhorrent eam. Quis enim nesciat illud supplicium inferni esse multum horribile? Verum si mille quisquam, immo si decem millia ponat gehennas, nihil est totum, quod dicit, comparatum ad illud, animam exosam Christo repelli a gloria sanctorum, et illam audire terribilem vocem ex ore iudicis omnium: Discedite a me operarii iniquitatis, quoniam nescio vos: et: ite maledicti in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est vobis, et diabolo. O vox omnium terribilium longe terribilissima, o sententia metuenda, et nimium horrenda cunctis mortalibus, odiri pro demeritis a Christo, exprobari a iudice, separari a consortio gloriae, et nullam spem recuperationis amplius retinere. Cogitate nunc fratres, certissime futuras impiorum poenas; et comparete quoscunque transuentis aevi cruciatus, omniaque cogitabilia huius mundi tormenta ad illa sempiterna damnatorum supplicia, et erunt sic ut nihil ad aliud, imaginatio ad veritatem, somnium ad vigiliam. Tentationes carnis, et legem peccati facile superabitis, si harum rerum cogitationem in memoria continue retinetis. O aeternum, quam inexcogitabile tempus, aevum sine fine, seculum sine tempore. Beatus, qui nunc praevidet in tempore, quomodo post hanc brevissimam vitam bene habeat in aeternitate. Quartum, quod hominem a peccato potest retrahere; est futurae, sempiternaque felicitatis continuam in corde memoriam habere. Vere non sunt condignae passiones huius temporis ad superventuram gloriam, quae revelabitur in sanctis; ubi nulla erit discordia, nulla penitus dissonantia; sed erit summa pax omnium, et sempiterna concordia laetantium sanctorum. In coelesti sanctorum beatitudine gaudium est verum sine tristitia, pax sine discordia, bonitas sine malitia, laetitia sine fine, lux sine tenebris, vita sine dolore perennis. Ibi est dulcedo sine amaritudine, requies sine labore, laus sine vituperio, amor sine vitio, claritas sine nubilo, satietas sine fastidio. Sine taedio manet aeternitas; sine defectu exuberat bonitas; sine miseria continuatur felicitas. Nam ubi Deus est omnia in omnibus, perfectum et plenum gaudium aderit universis. Ibi anima, sive mens sancta principio suo per amorem coniungitur, intellectus ad cognitionem summi boni perfecte illuminatur;

208

How sin is to be fled.

The flame burns those whom carnal pleasure now defiles; and each person is burned all the more in torments, the more he takes delight here in the flesh against God. In hell, as Gregory bears witness, there will be intolerable cold, inextinguishable fire, the immortal worm of conscience, unbearable stench, palpable darkness, immeasurable pains, scourges of those who strike without intermission, the dreadful sight of demons, confusion over crimes committed, and despair of all good things. But of all the punishments in hell, by far the gravest must be judged to be this: that those damned ones are forever deprived of the vision of eternal light.

Hence the most blessed bishop John Chrysostom says: “Gehenna is an intolerable thing, and all men shrink from it. For who does not know that the punishment of hell is very dreadful? Yet if someone should set down a thousand, indeed ten thousand gehennas, all that he says is nothing in comparison with this: for a soul hated by Christ to be driven away from the glory of the saints, and to hear that terrible voice from the mouth of the Judge of all: ‘Depart from me, you workers of iniquity, for I do not know you’; and: ‘Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for you and for the devil.’”

O voice by far the most terrible of all terrible things; O sentence to be feared, and exceedingly dreadful to all mortals: to be hated by Christ for one’s deserts, to be reproached by the Judge, to be separated from the fellowship of glory, and to retain no further hope of recovery. Think now, brothers, on the punishments of the wicked that most certainly will come; and compare all the torments of this passing age, and every imaginable torture of this world, with those everlasting punishments of the damned, and they will be as nothing compared with something else, imagination compared with truth, a dream compared with waking. You will easily overcome the temptations of the flesh and the law of sin if you continually keep the thought of these things in memory.

O eternity, what an inconceivable span of time; an age without end, a world without time. Blessed is he who now foresees in time how he may fare well in eternity after this very brief life.

The fourth thing that can draw a person back from sin is to keep continual remembrance in the heart of future and everlasting happiness. Truly, the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in the saints, where there will be no discord, no disharmony at all, but the highest peace of all and the everlasting concord of the rejoicing saints. In the heavenly blessedness of the saints there is true joy without sadness, peace without discord, goodness without malice, gladness without end, light without darkness, everlasting life without pain. There is sweetness without bitterness, rest without labor, praise without blame, love without fault, brightness without cloud, satiety without disgust. Eternity remains without weariness; goodness abounds without defect; happiness continues without misery. For where God is all in all, perfect and full joy will be present to everyone. There the soul, or holy mind, is joined to its beginning through love; the intellect is perfectly enlightened for the knowledge of the highest good;

200
Sermo V. 209 et ex duobus istis frutio aeternae felicitatis exultantibus infunditur. Deum in regno aeternitatis cognoscere, et diligere, est ipsam felicitatis gloriam fruendo possidere. Ad hoc quippe conditus est homo, ut Deum creatorem suum summum bonum intelligat, intelligendo super omnia diligit; amando in aeternum fruatur, atque possidet. Hic finis est institutionis monasticae; haec destinatio fidei Christianae, quatenus Deum, quem nunc per fidem cognoscimus, et in toto corde per charitatis opera diligimus, in beata vita perfecte intelligentes, objectum nostrae fruitionis perpetuum habeamus. Pro huius sempiternae felici- tatis adieptione, fratres charissimi, omnia etiam cum maximo labore facienda sunt bona, omnia patientissime toleranda adversa, quoniam brevisimum virtutis exercitium, praemium nobis parit aeternum. Au- dite, quid ad haec sanctus Ioannes dicat episcopus. Si quotdie, inquit, oporteret nos tormenta perferre, si ipsum denique gehennam parvo tempore tolerare, ut Christum videre possimus in gloria regnante aeterna, sanctorumque eius numero in perpetuum sociari, non erit pari ratione condignum, omne, quod nobis triste potest accedere, ut tanti boni gloriam inereamur possidere. Ad summum vero bonum non perve- nitur, nisi per summos labores; quoniam, sicut in sancto Evangelio Dominus dicit, regnum coelorum vim patitur, et violenti rapiunt illud. Quintum, quod hominem debet a peccato retrahere, est humanae con- ditionis honestatem considerare; quae naturali ductu rationis detestatur vitium, et virtutis diligit bonum. Virtutis amator est omnis homo, qui vivit secundum imperium rationis, qui autem in stercore vitorum sor- descens volitur, ut bestia, non ut homo conversatur. Vobis autem, fratres mei, maxime detestanda sunt vita, virtutes amandae; quippe qui propterea contempseritis mundum, ut in coenobio vitam ageretis a peccatis alienam, et sanctis virtutibus decoratam. Virtutes igitur vobis colendae sunt, non imagines virtutum colendae, dico, non thure, non sacrificio; sed amore, et proposito integerrimae voluntatis. Virtutes etenim colere, nihil est aliud, nisi eas animo comprehendere, et pro Dei amore usque ad mortem inviolatas retinere. Nam, sicut Lactantius ait; omne virtutis officium est non peccare: et ideo non est vera virtus, nisi quae per fidem Christi ad eum finem tendit, ubi est bonum ho- minis summum, quo melius esse non potest. Virtuosus autem non est, qui Deum non diligit, cum omnium virtutum summa sit charitas. Unde si Deum ex toto corde super omnia diligitis, virtuosi veraciter estis. Una igitur est virtus, ac via bonorum, qua per fidem, et dilectionem Iesu Christi pervenitur ad regnum. Qui Deum veraciter amat, virtutis amore non peccat. Considerate vestram dignitatem fratres mei, et fu- gite peccatum: quoniam omnis, qui superbia inflatur, qui luxuria sor- didatur, qui caeteris animae pestibus inficitur, non vivit ut homo, sed

and from these two there is poured into the exultant the enjoyment of eternal happiness.

To know God in the kingdom of eternity and to love him is to possess, by enjoyment, the very glory of happiness. For man was created for this: that he should understand God his creator as the supreme good; that, understanding him, he should love him above all things; and that, loving him, he should enjoy and possess him forever. This is the end of the monastic institution; this is the destination of the Christian faith: that God, whom we now know through faith and love with all our heart through works of charity, we may, in the blessed life, understand perfectly and have as the everlasting object of our enjoyment.

For the attainment of this eternal happiness, most beloved brothers, all good things must be done even with the greatest labor, and all adversities must be endured with the greatest patience, since the very brief exercise of virtue brings forth for us an eternal reward. Hear what holy Bishop John says on these matters: If every day, he says, it were necessary for us to endure torments, indeed if we had to tolerate even gehenna itself for a short time, so that we might see Christ reigning in eternal glory and be joined forever to the number of his saints, would it not, by equal reasoning, be fitting to endure everything sorrowful that can befall us, so that we may deserve to possess the glory of so great a good? But one does not arrive at the supreme good except through the greatest labors; for, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.

The fifth thing that ought to draw a man back from sin is to consider the dignity of the human condition, which, by the natural guidance of reason, detests vice and loves the good of virtue. Every man who lives according to the command of reason is a lover of virtue; but he who, becoming filthy in the dung of vices, rolls about in it, conducts himself as a beast, not as a man. But for you, my brothers, vices must especially be detested and virtues loved, since you have despised the world for this reason: that in the monastery you might lead a life estranged from sins and adorned with holy virtues.

Virtues, therefore, are to be cultivated by you. I say virtues are to be cultivated, not images of virtues; not with incense, not with sacrifice, but with love and with the purpose of a wholly upright will. For to cultivate virtues is nothing other than to embrace them in the soul and, for the love of God, to keep them inviolate even to death. For, as Lactantius says, the whole duty of virtue is not to sin; and therefore there is no true virtue except that which, through faith in Christ, tends toward that end where the supreme good of man is, than which nothing better can exist. But he is not virtuous who does not love God, since charity is the sum of all virtues. Therefore, if you love God with all your heart above all things, you are truly virtuous. Thus there is one virtue and one way of the good, by which, through faith and love of Jesus Christ, one arrives at the kingdom. He who truly loves God does not sin, because of his love of virtue.

Consider your dignity, my brothers, and flee sin; for everyone who is swollen with pride, who is defiled by lust, who is infected by the other plagues of the soul, does not live as a man, but ...

201
210 Quemadmodum sit fugiendum peccatum. in semetipso confunditur, et in perditionem aeternae mortis progre- ditur. Quanto enim quisque amplius in peccatum labitur, tanto longius recedit a Deo, et magis appropinquit inferno. Cum autem omnes ho- mines naturaliter appetant bonum, turpissimum est amare peccatum; quoniam omnis peccator bonum deserit, et ad malum se convertit. Sextum, mentem a peccato fortiter retrahit, si in meditatione Domi- nicae passionis ex consuetudine semper occupata persistit. Quis enim voluptatibus carnis operam navare poterit, si mundi rectorem Iesum Christum pendentem pro se in cruce cogitaverit? Mors Christi mund- dum liberavit a morte perpetua: quod beneficium quisquis in memoria secum portaverit, facile ab omni scelere vitiorum abstinebit. Denique, si quis Deum in omni loco sibi praesentem, omniaque scientem, et in- telligentem tota mentis intentione cogitaverit, omne peccatum procul- dubio semper abhorrebit. Est autem nobis Deus ubique; non solum praesens, sed vere intimus, ac praesentissimus: quem nullum latet se- cretum: cui nihil manet absconditum sed totum ei patet manifestum. Corda scrutatur omnium; secretissima novit cogitationum qui veram co- gnitionem solus habet universorum. Quis enim mortalium in praesentia tantae maiestatis, quam videre omnia credit, peccare sine maximo rubore audet, si, quis sit, et quantus, qui videt, pensat? Quoties ergo molestat iniqua cogitatio mentem; quoties inordinati motus carnis inquietant ani- mam, Dominum Deum, qui malorum est vindex, praesentem cogita; pas- sionis Iesu Christi amaritudinem ad memoriam revoca; auxilium gratiae caelestis devotus implora. Durior est lapide, quem ista diligentius cogitata nequierunt a peccandi proposito revocare. Septimum, quod mentem studiosi monachi a peccandi desiderio revocat, est, ut lectione continua passiones sanctorum martyrum percurrat. Enimvero quisquis invinci- bilem constantiam sanctorum martyrum Christi saepius ad memoriam revocat, fieri non potest, quin ad resistendum peccatis fortior, et ro- bustior fiat. Propterea namque fortia sanctorum gesta literis demandata sunt, ut, quoties nos infirmi talia legimus, ad imitationem praecedentium consurgamus. Non respiciatis in eos fratres, qui sanctorum historiis fidelis superba temeritate denegant: et ea, quae de beatissimis Christi amicis gloriosa narrantur, fabulas putant. Nam virtutes, et bona, quae in semetipsis non inveniunt, sanctos habuisse Dei credere contemnunt. Sunt enim plures, et inter eos potissime, qui de sua eruditione se magnos existimant, historias sanctorum patrum temere nimis refutantes: et cum ipsi arduum virtutis iter aggregi nequeant, neminem, aut raras potuisse ventosa loquacitate confingant. Quicquid coram eis de conver- sationibus sanctorum vel ardui, vel magni legitur, confictum, et fabu- losum clamitant: et quales ipsi vivunt in tenebris vitiorum positi, ta- liter eos, quorum derident historias, arbitrantur praecessisse. Monachus

How sin is to be fled.

He is confounded in himself and goes forward into the destruction of eternal death. For the more one falls into sin, the farther he withdraws from God, and the nearer he approaches hell. Since, however, all men naturally desire the good, it is most shameful to love sin, because every sinner abandons the good and turns himself to evil.

Sixth, it strongly draws the mind back from sin if it remains always occupied, by habit, in meditation on the Lord’s Passion. For who will be able to devote himself to the pleasures of the flesh, if he has thought of Jesus Christ, the ruler of the world, hanging for him on the cross? The death of Christ freed the world from perpetual death; whoever carries this benefit with him in memory will easily abstain from every crime of vice.

Finally, if anyone considers with the whole attention of his mind that God is present to him in every place, and knows and understands all things, he will without doubt always abhor every sin. For God is everywhere with us: not only present, but truly inward and most present. No secret is hidden from him; nothing remains concealed from him, but everything lies open and manifest to him. He searches the hearts of all; he knows the most secret thoughts, he who alone has true knowledge of all things. For what mortal dares to sin in the presence of such majesty, which he believes sees all things, without the greatest shame, if he considers who and how great he is who sees?

Therefore, whenever an evil thought troubles the mind, whenever the disordered movements of the flesh disturb the soul, think of the Lord God, the avenger of evils, as present; recall to memory the bitterness of the Passion of Jesus Christ; devoutly implore the help of heavenly grace. Harder than stone is the man whom these things, if carefully considered, cannot call back from the intention of sinning.

Seventh, what recalls the mind of a studious monk from the desire of sinning is that by continual reading he should go through the accounts of the martyrs’ sufferings. Indeed, whoever often recalls to memory the invincible constancy of the holy martyrs of Christ cannot fail to become stronger and more robust in resisting sins. For this reason the brave deeds of the saints were committed to writing: so that, whenever we who are weak read such things, we may rise up to imitate those who have gone before.

Do not pay regard, brothers, to those who, with proud rashness, deny faith to the histories of the saints, and think that the glorious things narrated about the most blessed friends of Christ are fables. For the virtues and good things which they do not find in themselves, they disdain to believe that the saints of God possessed.
