Their minds, indeed, longing for the practice of virtues, flee the more serious sins; but, weighed down by the weakness of evil habit, they pay no heed to the smallest ones. Hence they more often fall through frailty into the pit of mortal sin, because they have not guarded against venial sins as occasions of graver ones. For no sin is so small that it does not become greater when neglected. For even if we cannot wholly guard against venial sins, nevertheless with all our strength we must strive that they not multiply in [unclear].

215
224 De novem ascensionis gradibus. nobis, attendere debemus. Qui autem, miserante domino, in isto gradu quotidie ad meliora proficiunt, rarius in peccatum cadunt. Quoties vero ceciderint, toties per poenitentiam resurgunt. Status tamen eorum periculo est proximus; quoniam sicut vestis lacerata saepius, tandem inutilis redditur: sic homo, qui crebrius peccando labitur, mala consuetudine frequenter suffocatur. Si qui tamen ex isto gradu in miserationibus Domini ex hac vita decesserint, non sine gravissimis purgatorii poenis salvabuntur. Ad sublimiora igitur properandum est, quo non solum mortalia, sed etiam venialia pro viribus caveantur. Secundum gradum illi creduntur ascendere, qui venialia simul, et mortalia scelera, quantum praevalent, conantur evitare: verum nimio corporis infirmati commercio, non perseverant in proposito, sed frequenter in varia huius vitae negligentias incidunt, quamvis mortalia non committant. Hunc gradum nos tepidi ascendisse utcumque confidimus, qui sub regularis disciplinae observantia constituti, mentes nostras a gravioribus peccatis, adiuvante Domino, custodimus. Quoniam vero nimium sumus tepidi, multum negligentem vivimus et ad operandum sanctarum virtutum exercitia tardi sumus. Sunt autem plures in climate huius secundi gradus constituti, quos timor servilis occupat; qui solus si fuerit; regno Dei minime appropinquit. Ad consequendum nempe supernae felicitatis gloriam, timor servilis fine charitate non sufficit; quoniam servus est, qui non peccat metu supplicii; filius autem malum non facit amore Dei. Bonum est tamen a servili timore incipere, ut homo paulatim ad filialem, qui castus dicitur, valeat pervenire. Nam et si metu poenarum recedere a malo, ad consequendum Dei regnum minime sufficit, operantem tamen ad timorem filialem parat. Unde proficientium gradus est infimus, timore supplicii non delinquere, et ne damnetur perpetuo, non peccare. Sola enim charitas merita discernens omnium, ut apta ingredi ad regnum Dei intromittitur: et, quicquid factum extra illam fuerit, indignum Dei regno iudicatur. Quisquis ergo secundum hunc gradum meruisti ascendere: quisquis metu poenarum didicisti non peccare, si vis ad gaudium aeternae felicitatis pertingere, cura quantocuyus ad sublimiora properare. Quoniam vero (testante proverbio) nemo repente fit summus, ut ab inferioribus incipias, recte quidem permittemus; sed stare in valle tenebrarum diu, periculosum iudicamus. Ascende igitur quantum potes quotidie; et noli cum bestiis in stercoribus foentium actionum persistere, quoniam, si non proficis, deficis: si non ascendis, descendis. Tertius gradus ab illis comprehenditur, qui in bono proposito perseverantes, se ab omni peccato mortali custodunt, et a venialibus quoque pro viribus recedunt. Conscientiae puritatem diligunt: et nihil, quod eam maculare possit, ullanus committunt. In uno tamen inferiores sunt sequentibus, quia non simpliciter propter amorem Dei

224

On the nine degrees of ascent.

We must attend to ourselves. But those who, by the Lord’s mercy, daily make progress toward better things in this degree fall into sin more rarely. Yet whenever they have fallen, so often do they rise again through repentance. Still, their state is close to danger, because just as a garment often torn is at last rendered useless, so a person who slips by sinning more frequently is often smothered by evil habit. Yet if any from this degree depart this life in the Lord’s mercies, they will be saved, but not without the very grievous pains of purgatory. We must therefore hasten to higher things, so that not only mortal sins but also venial sins may be avoided as far as our strength allows.

Those are believed to ascend the second degree who strive, as much as they can, to avoid venial sins as well as mortal crimes; but because of too much commerce with the body’s weakness, they do not persevere in their purpose, but frequently fall into the various negligences of this life, although they do not commit mortal sins. We, the lukewarm, trust that we have in some measure ascended this degree, who, being placed under the observance of regular discipline, guard our minds, with the Lord’s help, from the more serious sins. But because we are exceedingly lukewarm, we live very negligently and are slow to perform the exercises of holy virtues.

There are many placed in the region of this second degree whom servile fear possesses; and if this fear stands alone, it by no means draws near to the kingdom of God. For to obtain the glory of heavenly blessedness, servile fear without charity is not enough, since he is a servant who does not sin from fear of punishment, but a son does no evil from love of God. Yet it is good to begin from servile fear, so that a person may gradually be able to arrive at filial fear, which is called chaste. For even if withdrawing from evil through fear of punishments is by no means enough to obtain the kingdom of God, still it prepares the one who acts for filial fear. Hence the lowest degree of those making progress is not to offend through fear of punishment, and not to sin lest one be condemned forever.

For charity alone, discerning the merits of all, is admitted as fit to enter the kingdom of God; and whatever has been done outside it is judged unworthy of God’s kingdom. Therefore, whoever you are who have deserved to ascend to this second degree, whoever you are who have learned not to sin through fear of punishments, if you wish to reach the joy of eternal blessedness, take care to hasten as quickly as possible to higher things. But since, as the proverb bears witness, no one suddenly becomes highest, we shall indeed rightly allow you to begin from the lower things; but we judge it dangerous to stand long in the valley of darkness. Ascend, therefore, as much as you can each day, and do not persist with the beasts in the dung of stinking deeds, because if you do not advance, you fall back; if you do not ascend, you descend.

The third degree is attained by those who, persevering in a good purpose, keep themselves from every mortal sin and also withdraw from venial sins as far as their strength allows. They love purity of conscience, and in no way commit anything that could stain it. Yet in one respect they are lower than those who follow, because they do not simply act for the love of God.

216
Sermo VII. 225 recedentes a malo benefaciunt, sed ideo, quod recepturos se regnum Dei pro suis meritis, confidunt. Non sunt in statu perfectionis, qui Deo propter mercedem serviant, sed cum infirmis adhuc longe a cul- mine sanctitatis in inferioribus consistunt. Qui Deum pura mente ve- raciter diligit, neque timore poenarum, neque intuitu mercedis, sed amore ipsius tantum illi famulatur, et servit. Et propterea gradus praescripti omnes proponuntur incipientibus, per quos paulatim ascen- dentes, tandem coniungentur perfectis. Bonum est metu poenarum a malo recedere; bonum est amore mercedis bonum facere; et quamvis nequaquam ad perfectionem sufficiat, initium tamen, et viam proficiendi cupientibus praestat. Timor etenim servilis continuatus filialem, et ca- stum generat; de cuius scaturigine perfecta charitas emanat. Charitas autem posteaquam mentem semel accenderit, omnem deinceps timorem servilem, et metum foras mittit. Quartus gradus viam perfectionis ma- nifestare ascendentibus nititur, et ideo maior praescriptis merito iudi- catur. Quicquid non in illis boni cernitur, in isto perfectius habetur. Ascensores nanque huius quarti gradus omni se studio non solum a mortalibus peccatis, sed etiam a venialibus, quantum est eis possibile, custodunt, bonis, et sanctis operibus diligentissime insistunt, et Deo placere super omnia cupiunt. In uno praecedentes superant; quoniam neque metu poenarum declinant a malo, neque spe mercedis bonum operantur: sed amore Dei solius omnia faciunt, et nihil aliud, quam Dei honorem quaerunt. Haec est via conantibus ad perfectionem pro- posita; haec est vera sanctae iustitiae regula, ut Deum pura mente diligamus super omnia, et pro eius honore faciamus cuncta opera no- stra. Amator etenim Dei verus nec poenam metuit, nec praemium co- gitat; sed in amplitudine cordis ambulans, voluntatem suam divinae ordinationi commendat. Deus enim quia summe bonus, non propter mercedem regni coelestis, nec propter aliquid aliud, sed propter semet- ipsum diligendus est, et semper in omni opere bono principaliter in intentione habendus. Festinate fratres mei charissimi hunc gradum spi- ritualis scalae quantocyus ascendere, quatenus ad perfectionis culmen possitis aliquando pervenire. Etenim si vos, qui sub obedientia mona- sticae perfectionis estis constituti, ad hunc quartum gradum profeceritis, iam sine labore quintum ascendetis. Nam, qui in quarto sunt positi gradu, opera iustitiae bona ex voluntate propria faciunt; quoniam nec voto, nec professione monasticis se constitutionibus submiserunt. Et in hoc uno sunt inferiores sequentibus; propterea quod opus bonum tanto est Deo acceptabilius, quanto magis obedientiae merito commen- datur. Quintum igitur gradum illi ascendunt, qui se totis viribus a pec- catis custodunt, et sub obedientia constituti, fortes semper, et constantes in sanctitatis proposito persistunt. Deum pura mente super omnia dili- 226 De novem ascensionis gradibus.

Those who withdraw from evil do good, but for this reason: because they trust that they will receive the kingdom of God for their merits. Those who serve God for the sake of reward are not in the state of perfection, but, together with the weak, still stand far from the summit of holiness in lower things. Whoever truly loves God with a pure mind serves and waits upon him neither from fear of punishments nor with a view to reward, but only from love of him. And therefore all the degrees set forth above are proposed to beginners, so that, ascending gradually through them, they may at last be joined to the perfect.

It is good to withdraw from evil through fear of punishments; it is good to do good from love of reward; and although this is by no means sufficient for perfection, nevertheless it provides a beginning and a way of advancing for those who desire to make progress. For servile fear, if continued, begets filial and chaste fear; from its spring perfect charity flows forth. But after charity has once kindled the mind, it thereafter casts out every servile fear and dread.

The fourth degree strives to show the way of perfection to those ascending, and therefore it is rightly judged greater than those previously described. Whatever good is not seen in them is possessed more perfectly in this one. For those who ascend this fourth degree guard themselves with all zeal not only from mortal sins but also from venial sins, as far as is possible for them; they apply themselves most diligently to good and holy works, and above all desire to please God. In one respect they surpass those who came before: they turn aside from evil neither from fear of punishments, nor do they perform good from hope of reward, but they do all things for the love of God alone, and seek nothing other than the honor of God.

This is the way proposed to those striving toward perfection; this is the true rule of holy justice: that we love God with a pure mind above all things, and do all our works for his honor. For the true lover of God neither fears punishment nor thinks of reward, but, walking in largeness of heart, commends his will to the divine ordering. For God, because he is supremely good, is to be loved not for the reward of the heavenly kingdom, nor for anything else, but for his own sake; and in every good work he must always be held principally in one’s intention.

Hasten, my dearest brothers, to ascend this degree of the spiritual ladder as quickly as possible, so that you may one day be able to reach the summit of perfection. For if you, who have been placed under the obedience of monastic perfection, have advanced to this fourth degree, you will then ascend the fifth without difficulty. For those who are placed in the fourth degree do the good works of justice by their own will, because they have not submitted themselves by vow or profession to monastic constitutions. And in this one respect they are inferior to those who follow: because a good work is so much the more acceptable to God, the more it is commended by the merit of obedience.

Therefore those ascend the fifth degree who guard themselves with all their strength from sins and, placed under obedience, always strong and steadfast, persevere in the purpose of holiness. They love God with a pure mind above all things.

217
gentes, propter eius amorem bona opera principaliter faciunt, et in sua intentione nec poenas metuunt, nec praemia requirunt. Praelatis suis propter amorem Dei humiliter obedient; et a puritate regularis observantiae in nullo penitus recedunt. Ex his sunt nonnulli, quos infirmitas carnis quandoque mente facit instabiles, et in suis opinionibus contra obedientiam aliquantulum pertinaces. Exercitia sua, et privatas observantiolas contra determinationem praelatorum interdum conantur defendere, et se prudentiores in examinatione spiritualium suis recto-ribus aestimare. Hoc fugite, o monachi, quia daemonium latet in in- sidiis; et quos aperta congresseione non potest vincere, occulta machi- natione nititur superare. Quanto enim monachus coram Deo sanctior, et perfectior fuerit, tanto praelato suo sine discussione promptius obedient. Quod si monachus perfectus abbati suo, licet imperfecto in licitis, et honestis obedere contempserit, iam certe perfectionis vocabulum amisit. Ita ergo unusquisque studio proficiendi curet insistere, ut obedientiam in nullo praesumat violare. Dicit enim scriptura: Melior est obedientia, quam victimae; et auscultare magis, quam immolare adipem arietum. Quicquid obtuleris, alienum est; verus autem obedientis offerit seipsum. Sextus ergo gradus illis maxime convenit, qui in omni puritate mentis, et corporis viventes Dominum super omnia diligunt; qui bonum omne, quod possunt, pro Dei solius honore faciunt; et, qui a mandatis prae- latorum non recedunt. Magna est virtus obedientiae; quae sanctum opus bonum duplicat, et meritum augens operanti, quasi arborum Deo cum fructu representat. Non vos permoveant verba hominum obedienti- tiam contemnentium, o fratres mei charissimi; qui libertatem volun- tatis subiectioni monachorum praefereunt, et opus bonum ex libertate factum, obedientiae meritis anteponunt. Nam, et si monachus ex ne- cessitate professionis sua obedient, bona tamen voluntas, qua se pro Dei amore obligavit ad obedientiam, hanc necessitatem multipliciter commendat. Est autem necessitas, qua homo ad faciendum aliquid com- pellitur, ubi voluntas non consensit, sed semper reluctatur. Haec ne- cessitas laudem virtutis minuit, quia bonum opus nunquam in voluntate fuit. Est et alia necessitas ex inclinatione mentis interiori proveniens, quae laudem boni operis auget, non minuit, propterea quod voluntatem in ipsum opus intensius accendit. Est necessitas tertia, quae finem res- picit, et voluntatem non compellit. Nam si volueris transire navigio Rhenum, necessitas conveniens postulat instrumentum. Necessitas autem, qua monachus obedienti suo pastori compellitur, non est coactionis pri- ma, neque inclinationis secundae, sed tertiae potius, quoniam ex pre- cedente voluntate ad finem ordinatur. Necessarium ergo est monacho propter finem, illud, quod abbas praecepit, facere, ut votum, quod emisit, pro Dei amore valeat implere. Cum ergo finis iste sit multum

For love of him they chiefly do good works, and in their intention they neither fear punishments nor seek rewards. They humbly obey their prelates for love of God, and in no respect at all do they depart from the purity of regular observance. Among these there are some whom the weakness of the flesh sometimes makes unstable in mind, and somewhat obstinate in their opinions against obedience. They sometimes try to defend their exercises and private little observances against the determination of their prelates, and think themselves more prudent than their rulers in the examination of spiritual matters. Flee this, O monks, because the devil lies hidden in ambush; and those whom he cannot conquer by open attack he strives to overcome by hidden contrivance. For the holier and more perfect a monk is before God, the more readily will he obey his prelate without debate. But if a perfect monk disdains to obey his abbot, even an imperfect one, in lawful and honorable matters, he has certainly already lost the name of perfection. Therefore let each one take care to devote himself to the pursuit of progress in such a way that he presumes in nothing to violate obedience. For Scripture says: Obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening more than offering the fat of rams. Whatever you offer is something external; but the truly obedient man offers himself.

The sixth degree, then, especially befits those who, living in all purity of mind and body, love the Lord above all things; who do every good they can for the honor of God alone; and who do not depart from the commands of their prelates. Great is the virtue of obedience, which doubles a holy good work, and, increasing merit for the worker, presents him to God like trees with fruit. Let not the words of men who despise obedience move you, my dearest brothers, men who prefer freedom of will to the subjection of monks, and set a good work done from freedom above the merits of obedience. For even if a monk obeys from the necessity of his profession, nevertheless the good will by which he bound himself to obedience for love of God commends this necessity in many ways.

There is, however, a necessity by which a man is compelled to do something where the will has not consented but always resists. This necessity lessens the praise of virtue, because the good work was never in the will. There is also another necessity, arising from the inward inclination of the mind, which increases, not lessens, the praise of the good work, because it kindles the will more intensely toward that very work. There is a third necessity, which has regard to the end and does not compel the will. For if you wish to cross the Rhine by boat, a fitting necessity requires the instrument. But the necessity by which a monk is compelled to obey his shepherd is not the first, of coercion, nor the second, of inclination, but rather the third, because it is ordered to the end from a preceding will. Therefore it is necessary for a monk, on account of the end, to do what the abbot has commanded, so that he may be able to fulfill, for love of God, the vow that he has made. Since, then, this end is very much

218
Sermo VII. 227 laudabilis, quo se creatori suo ex amore creatura subiicit, obediendi necessitas in monacho laudem boni operis non minuit, sed ampliorem facit. O foelix monachorum necessitas; quae de bonae voluntatis the- sauro sumpsit exordium, et ordinatur ad finem, qui Deus est, incommu- tabile bonum. Maioris est laudis, excellentioris est meriti, et abundan- tioris est praemii, ratione voti bonum opus ex obedientia facere, quam si fiat sine voto ex propriae voluntatis libertate. Monachus autem seipsum totum, et omnem voluntatem suam Deo semel obtulit, et sibi nihil penitus reservavit. Quicquid sub obedientia boni facit, ad finem assumptae religionis pro Christi amore servanda reducitur, cui nullum opus post martyrium comparatur. Qui sine voto continens est ab actu venereo, unam virtutem operatur, quae nominatur castitas: qui autem observat eam ratione voti, altius graditur; quoniam ad perfectionem totius religionis, quam professus est, singulae virtutes ordinate refe- runtur. Plus enim est religio monastica tota, quam una virtus privata. Nam, qui offerit Deo bonum opus, quod sine obedientia fecit, id praestat solum, relinquens sibi quod maius est, potentiam agendi, simul et pro- priam voluntatem. Monachus autem, qui ex obedientiae voto aliquid facit propter Deum, excellentioris est meriti; quoniam et actum offerit Deo, et potentiam agendi. Nemo enim Deo plus obtulit, quam mona- chus, qui semetipsum dedit. Huius autem sexti gradus nonnulli ascen- sores quendam in se defectum superbiae habent absconditum, quia dum ad seipsos incaute respicient, divinae voluntati, sicut oportuerat, non in omnibus se committunt. Is vero defectus ex quadam subtilissima vanitate sumit exordium, dum animus suae puritati confidens, revelari sibi a Domino petit aliquid secretum. Et in hoc uno sexti climatis ascensores distant a septimis, qui Deo mancipati signa refugiant vani- tatis. Signa enim non fidelibus, sed infidelibus data sunt: unde mo- nachus, qui signum a Domino postulat, quod se divinae voluntati ad- huc perfecte non submiserit, manifestat. Septimum ascendunt gradum, qui omnia praescripta studiosissime custodunt, et Deo in omnibus sub- iecti sine macula vanitatis vivunt. Peccatum omne tam veniale, quam mortale pro viribus fugiunt; opera virtutum pro solius amore Dei faciunt; suis in cunctis obedientiis pastoribus; nulla petunt miracula va- nitatis. Quicquid Omnipotens Deus ordinaverit super eos, gratauer suscipiant; de observantia monasticae puritatis in nullo penitus rece- dunt. In uno tamen sunt inferiores sequentibus, quia patiuntur fortassis aliquem defectum, quem nesciunt, cuius impulsu quandoque sensuali- tatis propriae aliquid committunt. Octavum gradum quicunque ascen- dere meruerit, sensualitati nihil amplius concedit. Hic requies animi dulcissima, hic mentis tranquillitas perfecta. Nihil in hoc gradu pulchri- tudinis vitosum relinquitur; nihil hic, quod contristare possit animum,

praiseworthy, by which the creature subjects itself to its Creator out of love, the necessity of obedience in a monk does not lessen the praise of a good work, but makes it greater. O happy necessity of monks, which took its beginning from the treasure of a good will and is ordered toward the end that is God, the unchangeable good. It is of greater praise, more excellent merit, and more abundant reward to do a good work out of obedience by reason of a vow than if it were done without a vow from the freedom of one’s own will.

The monk, moreover, once offered his whole self and all his will to God, and reserved absolutely nothing for himself. Whatever good he does under obedience is referred back to the end of the religious life he has undertaken, to be preserved for the love of Christ; and no work after martyrdom is comparable to this. One who is continent from sexual activity without a vow practices one virtue, which is called chastity; but one who observes it by reason of a vow walks on a higher path, since the individual virtues are ordered toward the perfection of the whole religious life that he has professed. For the whole monastic religious life is more than one private virtue.

For one who offers God a good work that he has done without obedience gives that alone, leaving to himself what is greater: the power of acting, and at the same time his own will. But the monk who does something for God from the vow of obedience has more excellent merit, since he offers God both the act and the power of acting. For no one has offered more to God than the monk who has given himself.

Some who climb this sixth step, however, have hidden within themselves a certain defect of pride, because, while they look incautiously to themselves, they do not entrust themselves in all things to the divine will as they ought. This defect takes its beginning from a certain very subtle vanity, when the soul, trusting in its own purity, asks that something secret be revealed to it by the Lord. And in this one respect the climbers of the sixth rung differ from those of the seventh: those who are bound to God flee the signs of vanity. For signs have been given not to believers, but to unbelievers; hence the monk who asks the Lord for a sign shows that he has not yet perfectly submitted himself to the divine will.

Those ascend the seventh step who most zealously keep all that has been prescribed, and live subject to God in all things without the stain of vanity. They flee every sin, both venial and mortal, as far as they can; they perform the works of virtue for the love of God alone; they obey their pastors in all things; they seek no miracles of vanity. Whatever almighty God has ordained concerning them, they receive gladly; they do not in any respect at all depart from the observance of monastic purity. Yet in one thing they are lower than those who follow, because perhaps they suffer some defect of which they are unaware, by the impulse of which they sometimes commit something of their own sensuality.

Whoever has deserved to ascend the eighth step grants nothing further to sensuality. Here is the sweetest rest of the soul; here is perfect tranquility of mind. Nothing flawed in beauty is left in this step; nothing is here that can sadden the soul.

219
228 De novem ascensionis gradibus. invenitur. Omnia sunt hic munda, omnia pura, omnia sancta, omnia charitatis fervore suavissime ardentia. O si hunc gradum contendamus ascendere? o si in hunc portum tranquillitatis aliquando mereamur pervenire? Quanto magis in hoc sancto climate consistens internae sua-vitatis dulcedinem gustare coeperit, tanto in anteriusa festinans amplius concupiscit. O sancti amoris praedicanda semper desideria; o venerandae perfectionis exercitia, ubi munda nitet sine peccatis Deum amantis conscientia, ubi cessarunt vitiorum improba certamina, et succ-cessit tranquillitas magna. Nonum gradum ascendunt in octavo iam consummati, qui omnia praescripta pure, et simpliciter propter amorem Dei custodiant; et nihil aliud, quam Deum laudare, benedicere, et glo-rificare concupiscunt. Quisquis hunc perfectionis gradum ascenderit, quasi oblitus sui Deo se totum resignans, humiliter submittit. Ad omnia Dei beneficia indignum se reputat; de seipso nihil penitus curat; quo-niam se totum Deo iam didicit committere, et eius ordinationi humi-liter in omnibus subiacere. Unde nec miracula petit, nec alias in hac vita consolationes postulat; sed cum sancto Christi Apostolo ver-raciter clamat, Mihi vivere Christus est, et mori lucrum. Mundus enim mihi crucifixus et ego mundo. Verus etenim Christi amator monachus, se totum Deo ex charitate obtulit, et mundum cum omnibus divitiis, honoribus, et vanitatibus contempsit. Unde mundus ei crucifixus di-citur, in quo nihil est, quod eius penetrare mentem posse videatur. foelices illi monachi, qui pura conscientia Domino Deo in vera char-ritate serviant; qui sub humilitatis, et obedientiae imperio sine off-en-sione currunt; qui gradum perfectionis hunc ultimum ascendunt. Hi sunt veri monachi, qui nihil aliud quaerunt, quam honorem Dei. Nempe, fratres mei quamvis monachi non teneantur de necessitate sa-lutis esse perfecti, alioquin paucissimi salvarentur, tenemur tamen omnes bona voluntate ad perfectionem tendere, et quantis possimus vi-ribus ad nonum hunc gradum anhelare. Monastico siquidem proposito valde contrarium est, nolle proficere; apostasiae genus, post votum perfectionis, in imperfectione velle permanere. Hostes enim sunt nostrae salutis vitia, quae nos impugnant, et donec aut vincant, aut vincantur, nos persequi non cessant. Imitemur veteris pugnae historiam, quando non uno die, sed successive hostes suos filii promissionis deleverunt. Difficile nanque est omnia vincere simul, nisi charitas Dei obumbraverit subito mentem. Adversum cuncta nos impugnantia quomodolibet vitia geramus bellum, vincamus hodie gulam; qua rite prostrata superemus accidiam; sicque agamus cum caeteris, ut victores tandem evadamus omnium. Aderit nobis pugnantibus Dominus, et dabit victoriam Deus amatoribus suis. Amen. FINIS. IOANNIS TRITEMII ABBATIS SPANHEIMENSIS ORDINIS SANCTI BENEDICTI DE OBSERVANTIA BURSZFELDENSIS LIBER LUGUBRIS DE STATU ET RUINA MONASTICI ORDINIS PARTIUM GERMANIAE, OMNIBUS RELIGIOSIS, AC DEVOTIS VIRIS, NON MINUS UTILIS, QUAM IUCUNDUS Venerabili, et amantissimo P. D. Blasio Abbati Hirszaugiensis Caenobii F. Iohannes vocatus Abbas Spanheimensis salutem, et charitatem.

228

On the nine degrees of ascent.

It is found there. Here all things are clean, all things pure, all things holy, all things most sweetly burning with the fervor of charity. Oh, if only we would strive to ascend to this degree! Oh, if only we might someday deserve to reach this harbor of tranquility! The more one, standing in this holy region, has begun to taste the sweetness of inward delight, the more, hastening toward what lies ahead, he desires still further.

Oh desires of holy love, always to be proclaimed; oh exercises of venerable perfection, where the clean conscience of one who loves God shines without sins, where the wicked contests of vices have ceased, and great tranquility has succeeded them.

Those already perfected in the eighth degree ascend to the ninth, who keep all the things prescribed purely and simply for the love of God, and desire nothing other than to praise, bless, and glorify God. Whoever has ascended this degree of perfection, as though forgetful of himself, resigns himself wholly to God and humbly submits. He regards himself as unworthy of all God’s benefits; he has no care at all for himself, because he has already learned to entrust himself wholly to God and humbly to be subject in all things to his ordering. Hence he neither asks for miracles nor seeks any other consolations in this life, but with the holy Apostle of Christ truly cries out: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” “For the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

For the true monk who loves Christ has offered himself wholly to God out of charity, and has despised the world with all its riches, honors, and vanities. Hence the world is said to be crucified to him, since there is nothing in it that seems able to penetrate his mind. Happy are those monks who with pure conscience serve the Lord God in true charity; who run without offense under the rule of humility and obedience; who ascend this last degree of perfection. These are true monks, who seek nothing other than the honor of God.

Indeed, my brothers, although monks are not bound by necessity of salvation to be perfect, for otherwise very few would be saved, yet we are all bound with good will to strive toward perfection, and with all the strength we can to yearn for this ninth degree. For it is very contrary to the monastic profession to be unwilling to make progress; it is a kind of apostasy, after a vow of perfection, to wish to remain in imperfection. For the vices that attack us are enemies of our salvation, and until they either conquer or are conquered, they do not cease to persecute us. Let us imitate the history of the ancient battle, when the children of promise destroyed their enemies not in one day, but successively. For it is difficult to conquer all things at once, unless the charity of God has suddenly overshadowed the mind. Against all the vices that in any way attack us, let us wage war. Let us conquer gluttony today; when it has been duly laid low, let us overcome sloth; and let us deal so with the rest, that at last we may come forth victors over them all. The Lord will be with us as we fight, and God will give victory to those who love him. Amen.

THE END.

JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF SPONHEIM, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT OF THE BURSZFELD OBSERVANCE

A MOURNFUL BOOK ON THE STATE AND RUIN OF THE MONASTIC ORDER IN THE PARTS OF GERMANY, NO LESS USEFUL THAN PLEASING TO ALL RELIGIOUS AND DEVOUT MEN

To the venerable and most beloved Father and Lord Blasius, Abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, Brother Johannes, called Abbot of Sponheim, sends greeting and charity.

220
T AMETSI vires ingenii mei procul excedat petilio tua, fratribusque tuorum (Dilectissime Pater) malni tamen arduum subire onus, quam tuae charitati proposse non satisfacere. Amor enim Dei, zelus ordinis, et fervor disciplinae dignum te faciunt; ut nihil tibi pro honore Dei postulanti debeam denegare: Rogasti me praesentem verbis, absentem crebrius epistolis, et quodammodo compulisti authoritate Praesidentiae quatenus de calamitate ordinis nostri aliquid tibi scriberem; quo patres aduandos capitulariter apud te ad compatiendum ei provocares: Sancta petitio, sed grandis obedientiendi difficultas. Lacerabor invidorum dentibus: Scio, qui me vel praesumptuosum indicabunt, vel nimum: sed obturatis auribus probra eorum securus transibo, modo sanctis, et eruditis viris placeat onus, quod porto. Nihil me scripsisse memini, quod aemuli inuste valeant lacerare, sed vera, sed manifesta, et quae oculis pateant omnium: quae, si scribi nolunt, doleant etiam facta: Solus in hac editione lepor non aderit dicendi: de quo reprehendi apud religiosos non timeo. Quid enim? Ergo ne veritas despicitur, quia facundiae ornatu non vestitur? Absit. Melior est enim sermo planus, et verus, quam ornatus, et falsus. Sed haec nihil ad propositum. Hoc ergo sintagma examini tuo subiicio, ut, si dignum indicaveris, legatur fratribus: sin autem indignum, oculos fugiat dominorum. Vale. An. Dom. MCCCCXCIII. kalen. Maii, 1493 LIBER PENTICHUS DOMINI IOANNIS SPANHEIMENSIS ABBATIS De ruina Ordinis Patris nostri sanctissimi Benedicti in parlibns Germaniae. Caput 1. CUM ordinis nostri pristinum decorem ad mentem revoco, eius, quam modo patimur, deformitati vehementer condoleo, ita ut lachrymas mihi emittere magis libeat, quam penthicum formare sermonem. Quis enim ruinam eius non defleat, si vetustam illius gloriam penset? O si ad memoriam aliquando revocemus, huius sacratissimi ordinis aurea quondam saecula, quando velut paradisi fluvius doctrina, et sanctitate totam per orbem irrigavit ecclesiam; quam nihil sit praesens eius status, facile perpenderemus. Observantia si qui- dem nostra (quam regulari vocamus) veterum institutis comparata, invenitur non solum minor, sed in multis quoque remissior; Quo- modo 'obscuratum est aurum, inmutatus est color optimus? Splendor sanctitatis eximiae, rutilans olim, terrenorum cupiditate obfuscatus est. Cessit honestatis norma illecebris voluptatum. Idcirco producant oculi mei lachrymas per diem, et noctem, et non taceant, quoniam contri- tione magna contrita est religio populi mei, plaga pessima vehementer. Si egressus fuero ad agros, ecce ociosi, et vani; si introiero coenobia, ecce attenuati voluptatibus; Multos enim professores regulae Benedicti Patris invenio: paucos ad eius traditionem ambulare cerno: Multipli- casti (ait prophetae Domino) gentem, non magnificasti laetitiam; quia dum sancta monachorum exercitia in multis deficunt, veram laetitiam, quae de virtute nascitur, prava corda non admittunt. Utinam evigi- lemus, vel sero tandem post tot perditionem animarum, quae, iugo regularis observantiae contempto, in abissum damnationis descenderunt: Utinam Benedicti legislatoris nostri metuamus sententiam, qui toties ad rationem Deo reddendam, Abbatis duri ferit insaniam. Ad vos nunc igitur, o Reverendissimi Patres, sermo meus dirigendus est, qui com- pellendi ad disciplinam rebellae, potestatem accipitis: qui ordinis nostri Zelum secundum scientiam habetis. Vos itaque alloquor; vobis, ut ordini prope labenti succurratis persuadere iuxta vires conabor; quod.

Although your request far exceeds the powers of my talent, and that of your brothers, most beloved Father, I have nevertheless preferred to undertake the arduous burden rather than fail to satisfy your charity as far as I can. For the love of God, zeal for the Order, and fervor for discipline make you worthy that I should deny you nothing when you ask for the honor of God. You asked me when I was present by word of mouth, and more often when I was absent by letters, and in a certain manner you compelled me by the authority of your presidency, to write you something concerning the calamity of our Order, so that you might stir up the fathers to be assembled with you in chapter to have compassion on it. The request is holy, but the difficulty of obeying is great.

I shall be torn by the teeth of the envious. I know that some will judge me either presumptuous or excessive; but with my ears stopped I shall pass securely by their reproaches, provided that the burden I bear is pleasing to holy and learned men. I do not remember having written anything that rivals can justly tear apart, but things true, manifest, and open to the eyes of all; and if they do not wish these things to be written, let them also grieve that they have been done. In this publication alone charm of speech will be lacking; on that point I do not fear being reproved among religious men. For what? Is truth therefore despised because it is not clothed with the ornament of eloquence? Far be it. For plain and true speech is better than adorned and false speech. But these things are nothing to the point.

I therefore submit this little treatise to your examination, so that, if you judge it worthy, it may be read to the brothers; but if unworthy, it may escape the eyes of the lords. Farewell. In the year of the Lord 1493, on the Kalends of May.

The Pentichus Book of Lord Johannes of Spanheim, Abbot

On the ruin of the Order of our most holy father Benedict in the regions of Germany.

Chapter 1

When I recall to mind the former beauty of our Order, I grieve deeply over the deformity that we now endure, so that I would rather shed tears than compose a lamenting discourse. For who would not weep over its ruin, if he weighed its ancient glory? O, if we were ever to call back to memory the golden ages once possessed by this most sacred Order, when like a river of paradise it watered the whole Church throughout the world with doctrine and holiness, we would easily perceive how little its present state is.

Indeed our observance, which we call regular, when compared with the institutions of the ancients, is found not only lesser, but also in many respects more lax. How has the gold been darkened, the finest color changed? The splendor of surpassing holiness, once shining bright, has been obscured by desire for earthly things. The rule of honor has yielded to the enticements of pleasures. Therefore let my eyes pour forth tears day and night, and let them not be silent, because the religion of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a very grievous wound. If I go out into the fields, behold the idle and vain; if I enter the monasteries, behold those thinned and weakened by pleasures. For I find many professing the rule of Father Benedict; I see few walking according to his tradition.

“You have multiplied the nation,” says the prophet to the Lord, “but you have not increased the joy”; because, while the holy exercises of monks fail in many, corrupt hearts do not admit the true joy that is born of virtue. Would that we might awake, even late at last, after the destruction of so many souls, which, having despised the yoke of regular observance, have descended into the abyss of damnation. Would that we might fear the sentence of Benedict our lawgiver, who so often strikes the madness of a harsh abbot by summoning him to render account to God.

To you now, therefore, most reverend Fathers, my speech must be directed, you who receive the power to compel rebellious men to discipline, you who have zeal for our Order according to knowledge. Thus I address you; to you I shall try, according to my strength, to persuade that you come to the aid of an Order close to falling.

Quamvis unius malo publica fama cor- rumpi non debat, tamen vulgus imperitus ex paucorum delicto omnes vituperat: Malos igitur, qui sua deformitate famam bonorum obnubilant, superiores, qui non puniunt, confortant: Ad vos itaque, Patres, pertinet Monachos deformatos pro posse corrigerre: Vestri officii est, ordinem in suo vigore conservare: Et quia stultus sermone non corri- pitur, quid hierofantes noster contra incorrigibles quasi monastice pos- sit, generaliter in istos referatur: Exurgite nunc, Patres, quia tempus est: armate vos zelo disciplinae regularis: haereditatem Divi Patris Be- neditici, oro, defendite: elatos pellite: rebellcs corripite, duros argue: pro conservatione nostri ordinis fortiter pugnate: Armate vos armatura Dei, et amore ordinis; non tam vestris laboribus, quam Christi auxilio pugnaturi. Illius gratia vobis praestabit auxilium, si in puritate cordis ad eum sedulas preces effuderitis: Cur ergo dissimulatis? Cur partem S. Benedicti non defenditis? Quamdiu, contra ordinem sanctum ini- quorum studia praevalebunt? Vere, Patres, vere necessitas magna or- dinis nostri citatum expostulat remedium. Conversations Abbatum, et monachorum irregularium intendite; et quam inique contra disciplinam ordinis calcitrent, ponderate. Praeter habitum, et hunc ipsum in multis dissolutum, nihil honestatis, vel religionis ostendunt: Sed haec suis deputata locis reservantes, ad intenta properemus. Facturus ne sim omnibus rem gratam, si priorem ordinis nostri statum paucis commendem, aliquantulum dubito; quippe qui ve- terum laudibus monachis nostri temporis, parum iudicer detulisse: sunt enim, qui se vel optimos arbitrentur monachos, vel optimis illis, qui nos praecesserunt, patribus audeant comparare. Utcunque autem se metiantur, non mihi succenseant, si veterum observantiae nostram non audeam adaequare. Nam, si recto lumine vitam eorum contem- plemur, optimum e nobis habitum, vix bono illius temporis monacho poterimus comparare. Sancta quippe illorum conversatio virtutibus cor- rusca, signis approbata, omniuque eruditione scripturarum illustris gratiam apud Deum promeruit, et homines. Audientes autem vocem dominicam, si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, et tollat 232 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

The Pentichus Book of Johannes Trithemius.

...which I earnestly exhort you to do: Attend, fathers, to the miserable state of our religion, and, so far as you are able, come to the aid of its calamity, if you desire it to endure to the end. You know well the wickedness of many who strive to sever themselves from it so that they may escape the discipline of the order. Their rashness must be firmly opposed, lest the unpunished malice of a few give many boldness to offend; for the wickedness of a few always grows when it is deferred.

Although public reputation ought not to be corrupted by one man’s evil, nevertheless the unskilled crowd blames all for the offense of a few. Therefore superiors who do not punish the bad, who by their deformity cloud the reputation of the good, strengthen them. It belongs to you, then, fathers, to correct deformed monks as far as you can. It is the duty of your office to preserve the order in its vigor. And because a fool is not corrected by speech, whatever our hierophant can do against the incorrigible, as it were in monastic fashion, should generally be brought to bear upon these men [unclear].

Rise now, fathers, for it is time. Arm yourselves with zeal for regular discipline. Defend, I beg you, the inheritance of holy Father Benedict. Drive out the proud; correct the rebellious; rebuke the hard; fight bravely for the preservation of our order. Arm yourselves with the armor of God and with love of the order, about to fight not so much by your own labors as by the help of Christ. His grace will provide you help, if in purity of heart you pour out diligent prayers to him.

Why, then, do you dissemble? Why do you not defend the portion of Saint Benedict? How long will the efforts of the wicked prevail against the holy order? Truly, fathers, truly, the great necessity of our order demands a swift remedy. Consider the conduct of irregular abbots and monks, and weigh how unjustly they kick against the discipline of the order. Apart from the habit, and that itself disordered in many, they show nothing of honesty or religion. But reserving these matters for their proper places, let us hasten to what we intended.

On the Most Holy Primitive State of Our Order. Chapter II.

Whether I shall be doing something pleasing to all if I commend in a few words the former state of our order, I somewhat doubt, since I may perhaps be judged, by praising the old monks, to have paid too little honor to those of our own time. For there are some who either think themselves the best of monks, or dare to compare themselves with those best fathers who went before us.

However they measure themselves, let them not be angry with me if I do not dare to equate our observance with that of the ancients. For if we contemplate their life with a right light, we shall scarcely be able to compare the best man among us with a good monk of that time. For their holy way of life, radiant with virtues, approved by signs, and illustrious with learning in all the Scriptures, won favor with God and men. Hearing the Lord’s voice, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up...”

crucem suam quotidie, et sequatur me. Contempto saeculo ad coe- nobia convolarunt, subdentesque colla ingo regulae, obedientiae nor- main humiliter susceperunt, Deum ex toto corde diligentcs, nihil in hac vita mundanum quaesierunt; sed caducis omnibus spretis, atque in camino paupertatis probati, ad caeleste regnum foeliciter pervenerunt. Erant viri, maturi; zelosi, atque doctissimi, fide firmi, spe robusti, gemina charitate fulgidi, mente puri, devotione praecipui, omniumque virtutum honestate decori. Nulla illis cura terrenorum; nulla inerat ille- cebra voluptatum; sed toxis viribus ad Deum conversi, mundum cum suis vanitatibus devicerunt; Unde Reges, et Principes huius saeculi Viri devoti; et Deo chari, propter conversationem monachorum san- ctissimam, ordinis amatores facti sunt, eunque donis et largitionibus magnifice exaltarunt. Gaudebant suis temporibus sancta monachorum studia dilatari, et in extremas mundi regiones cum gloria extendi: Sancti etenim monachi quanto plus Deum amabant, tanto et amplius ab hominibus amabantur; et quanto minus terrena ambiebant, tanto in necessariis corporis (Deo providente) amplius abundabant. Amantibus enim Deum, omnis mundus divitiarum est: O quam decora facies iu- ventutis tuae, sancta religio Benedicti: quam pulcher aspectus: quam ornata omnium virtutum splendore maiestas: Quis te digne pensiculare sufficeret? Tu viam trium dierum populo Dei de servitute Pharaonis in deserto liberato exhibes: Dum a Mundi tenebris ereptos, per tria substantialia religionis vota, homines ad desertum coenobiticae conver- sationis, pro Dei amore venire persuades: Beati professores tui, qui de huius saeculi Aegypto recedentes, per hanc viam trium dierum, ad aeternae promissionis terram totis desideriis anhelant: Hic est sanctae religionis triplex funiculus, qui facile non rumpitur; qui obedientiae, castimoniae, et paupertatis fulgore decoratur: qui suos amatores ad caelestem patriam revocat; qui cultores suos summo Imperatori Christo Iesu laetos repraesentat: Nam, et si ad regularem observantiam multa sint necessaria, ausim tamen dicere, quicunque haec tria illibata custo- dierit, ut funiculus triplex, securus in ordine consistit. Omnia enim statuta ordinis pro conservatione istorum substantialium facta sunt: Hoc monachi sancti antiquitus solerter intuentes, viam hanc trium sub- stantialium studiosissime observabant: Per contemptum omnium mun- danarum spiritu pauperes, per castitatem mentis, et corporis conti- nentes, per humilem subjectionem obedientes, et in omni virtute locu- ples, doctrina, et sanctitate charissimi effulserunt, et tam verbo, quam exemplo, multos ab iniquitate ad iustiam converterunt: Unde profi- cientibus meritis, ad ecclesiarum gubernacula multi eorum promoti sunt; qui quanto altius positi fuerunt, tanto virtutibus innotuerunt clari- ores. Quae autem ecclesia non expeteret sacerdotem de ordine Bene-

his cross daily, and follow me. Having despised the world, they flew to the monasteries, and, placing their necks beneath the yoke of the Rule, they humbly received the norm of obedience. Loving God with their whole heart, they sought nothing worldly in this life; but, scorning all passing things and being proved in the furnace of poverty, they happily reached the heavenly kingdom.

They were mature, zealous, and most learned men, firm in faith, strong in hope, radiant with twofold charity, pure in mind, outstanding in devotion, and adorned with the beauty of every virtue. They had no care for earthly things; no enticement of pleasures was in them; but, turned toward God with all their strength, they overcame the world with its vanities. Hence the kings and princes of this age, devout men and dear to God, because of the most holy way of life of the monks, became lovers of the order and magnificently exalted it with gifts and largess.

They rejoiced that in their times the holy pursuits of the monks were being spread abroad and extended with glory to the farthest regions of the world. For the more the holy monks loved God, the more they were loved by men; and the less they sought earthly things, the more they abounded in the necessities of the body, by God’s providence. For to those who love God, the whole world is riches.

O how fair was the face of your youth, holy religion of Benedict; how beautiful your appearance; how adorned with the splendor of all virtues your majesty. Who could suffice to weigh your worth duly? You show the way of three days to the people of God, freed from the servitude of Pharaoh in the desert, when you persuade men, snatched from the darkness of the world, to come for the love of God to the desert of cenobitic life through the three substantial vows of religion. Blessed are your professed members, who, departing from the Egypt of this age, long with all their desires for the land of eternal promise by this way of three days.

This is the threefold cord of holy religion, which is not easily broken, which is adorned with the brightness of obedience, chastity, and poverty; which calls back its lovers to the heavenly homeland; which presents its worshipers joyful to the supreme Emperor, Christ Jesus. For even if many things are necessary for regular observance, I would nevertheless dare to say that whoever has kept these three things inviolate stands secure in the order, like a threefold cord. For all the statutes of the order were made for the preservation of these substantial things.

The holy monks of old, carefully considering this, observed most zealously this way of the three substantial things. Poor in spirit through contempt for all worldly things, continent through chastity of mind and body, obedient through humble subjection, and rich in every virtue, they shone forth most beloved in learning and holiness, and both by word and by example converted many from wickedness to righteousness. Hence, as their merits increased, many of them were promoted to the government of churches; and the higher they were placed, the more illustrious they became known in virtues. But what church would not desire a priest from the order of Bene

Liber Pentichus Ioannis Trilemii. 233 dicti? Quae gens nomini Christiano devota, doctorem non cuperet ex collegio monachorum? Multis enim annis in ordine Sancti Patris Benedicti, viri in omni doctrina, et sanctitate praestantissimi claruerunt, sicut omnes pene testantur, qui veterum conscripserunt historias. Et re vera (ut absque invidia loquar) facile praecellit omnes ordines sancta religio Benedicti, si dignitatem, si latum in orbe dominium, si viros doctrina, et sanctitate insignes, si denique multitudinem eorum velis attendere. Protulit enim haec veneranda plantatio summos Pontifices decem et octo, Cardinales plus quam ducentos, Archipraesules mille sexcentos: Episcopos ter mille quingentos. Si quis autem hanc illustrium Praesulorum summam, velut nimiam vocat in dubium, chronicas, et gesta revolvat veterum, et paucos designatos comperiet, ex pluribus. Nemo autem ordinis pristinum decorum metiendum de praesenti existimet, cum nostri ad illum non sit aequa comparatio: quando nostris temporibus monachi, nec scientia scripturarum, nec morum sanctitate (ut olim) clarescunt. Invenies forsan etiam nunc devotos monachos, licet paucos, sed simplices, sed idiotas, sed omni disciplina bonarum artium expertes: sed ad regimen animarum, hoc tempore devotio non sufficit, si scripturarum scientia desit: Si autem monachi nostri, nec devoti fuerint, nec eruditi, ad regimen ecclesiarum merito censetur indigni: Multi denique subiecti bene ambulant, qui, si ad gubernationem aliorum fuerint sublimati, nunquam in tranquillitate prioris vitae subsisterent: et, ut breviter dicam, quod sentio, nec monachis Ecclesiae, nec Ecclesii monachi hoc tempore digni sunt. Causa autem prudenti non est abscondita, quae in lucem posthac suo tempore erit proferenda. Iam si libet praesentem ordinis nostri statum, qualis sit, paucis inquiramus. De ordinis nostri flebili statu praesenti. Capul III. DEFECERUNT praec lachrymis oculi mei: conturbata sunt viscera mea: effusum est in terra iecur meum, super contritione ordinis mei, cum deficeret in eo parvulus humilis, cum abiectus sine honore manibus pateat inimici. Lugentem me nemo despiciat, dolorem meum nemo incuset: honores non quaero terrenos, dignitates non ambio ecclesiasticas: sed doctrinam, et sanctitatem ab ordine meo defecisse ingemisco: Quid nobis cum vanis honoribus; qui vitam quaeritamus in caelis? Heu cecidit corona capitis nostri: devotio monastica tepuit: charitas refriguit: honestas regularis disciplinae, ut plurimum defecit: Ubi est nunc in ordine nostro sacratissimus illa, doctissimisque viris opulenta quondam devotio? Ubi in omni varietate scripturarum veneranda eruditio? Ubi Abbatum erga curam Dominici gregis sollicitudo? 234 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

of those mentioned? What people devoted to the Christian name would not desire a teacher from the company of monks? For through many years in the order of the holy Father Benedict there shone men most excellent in every learning and in holiness, as almost all who have written the histories of the ancients testify. And in truth, to speak without envy, the holy religion of Benedict easily surpasses all orders, if you choose to consider its dignity, its wide dominion in the world, its men distinguished in learning and holiness, and finally their multitude. For this venerable planting brought forth eighteen supreme pontiffs, more than two hundred cardinals, sixteen hundred archbishops, and three thousand five hundred bishops. But if anyone calls this total of illustrious prelates into doubt as excessive, let him turn over the chronicles and deeds of the ancients, and he will find that only a few have been designated out of many.

Yet let no one think that the order’s former splendor should be measured from its present state, since there is no fair comparison between our men and those men of old, for in our times monks do not shine, as once they did, either in knowledge of the Scriptures or in holiness of conduct. Perhaps even now you will find devout monks, though few, but simple men, unlearned, and without any training in the liberal arts. But for the government of souls in this age devotion is not enough, if knowledge of the Scriptures is lacking. But if our monks are neither devout nor learned, they are rightly judged unworthy of the government of churches. Many, indeed, walk well as subjects, who, if they were raised to the governance of others, would never continue in the tranquility of their former life. And, to say briefly what I think, neither are churches worthy of monks, nor monks of churches at this time. The cause, however, is not hidden from the prudent, and in due time hereafter it will be brought to light. Now, if it is pleasing, let us inquire briefly what the present state of our order is like.

On the Present Lamentable State of Our Order. Chapter III.

My eyes have failed from weeping; my inward parts are troubled; my liver is poured out upon the earth over the destruction of my order, because the humble little one has failed in it, because, cast down without honor, it lies open to the hands of the enemy. Let no one despise me as I mourn; let no one accuse my grief. I do not seek earthly honors; I do not covet ecclesiastical dignities. Rather, I groan that learning and holiness have failed from my order. What have we to do with empty honors, we who seek life in heaven? Alas, the crown of our head has fallen; monastic devotion has grown lukewarm; charity has grown cold; the honorable discipline of the Rule has for the most part failed. Where now in our order is that most holy devotion, once rich in most learned men? Where is the venerable learning in every variety of Scripture? Where is the abbots’ solicitude for the care of the Lord’s flock?

224
Multa coenobia secundum regulam Sancti Benedicti fundata conspicimus, in quibus praeter nomen, et habitum, nullum regularis disciplinae vestigium videmus. Super hoc, o Patres, lamentum assumite, ruinam sacratissimi ordinis nostri deplorate, si forte convertatur Deus ad veniam, et relinquat post se benedictionem: Et vos praevaricatores, qui causa istorum estis fletuum, redite vel sero tandem ad cor, redite: et Benedicti legislatoris vestri indignationem metuite. Attendite desolationem ordinis, quam malo vestro inducitis: timete omnipotentis iram, quam vestris sceleribus provocatis. Vae nobis: Urbs religionis nostrae ab inimicis in circuito nostro destruitur; disciplinae domus in nihilum rediguntur; et nemo invenitur, qui resistat; nemo, qui se murum pro domo Dei opponat: Omnes, quae nostra sunt, quaerimus; omnes communem necessitatem ordinis dissimulamus, donec et nos paulatim deficiamus: Haereditas nostra versa est ad alienos, domus nostrae ad extraneos: Coenobia, quae ad monachorum habitacula consecrata sunt, iam stabula fiunt clericorum, et militum fortilitia pugnantium. O quid dicam? Pudet me effari, quod homines sine conscientia in claustris monachorum non pudet perpetrae. Qui secretum religiosorum turbant, domos orationis inhabitacula negotiatorum commutant: Compator tuis calamitatibus, o Benedicti veneranda religio; te in direptionem omni transseunti expositam ingemisco. Non est, qui consoletur te ex omnibus caris tuis; quia, qui tibi possent succurrere, nolunt; qui volunt subvenire tibi, non possunt. O quam pulchra venustate quondam in ecclesia Dei floruit: quando viros omni sanctitate, et scientia insignes genuisti, et velut junior, fortis, et constans, omnem a te inhonestam conversationem solebas depellere. Nunc autem veluti senectute, et longa dierum oppressione fatigata defecisti, et virtus iuventutis tuae ablata est, eo quod non sit amplius in te fortitudo tua; Ubi est nunc zelus tuus? Ubi est decor vultus tui? Ubi honor? Ubi lata quondam in orbe universo potestas? Ubi est Deo, et angelis venerabile studium literarum, cuius fervor olim super omnes ordines te fecit sublimem? Ubi sunt filii tui in circuitu mensae tuae, viri eruditi, atque sanctissimi? Omnia defecerunt: et tu ad nihilum pene redacta es. Pulchritudinem iuventutis tuae amisisti, et fortitudo adolescentiae tuae dissipata est. Cui comparabo te, vel cui assimilabo te filia segregata: cui adaequabo te, et consolabor mater monachorum? Magna est, velut mare, contritio tua. Quis medebitur tui? O si hanc, quam modo experiris ruinam, cavisses, quam foelicem te dicerent omnes nationes: Sed dixisti in abundantia tua, non movebor in aeternum. Inopem te copia fecit; et temporalium abundantia rerum te omni ornatu tuo expoliavit: filios genuisti protervos, inobedientes, sanctis institutis rebellis; qui sub chlamide honestatis tuae latentes, te omni decore tuo nudaverunt: Heu

We see many monasteries founded under the Rule of Saint Benedict in which, apart from the name and the habit, we see no trace of regular discipline. Over this, O fathers, take up a lament; bewail the ruin of our most sacred order, if perhaps God may turn to pardon and leave a blessing behind him. And you transgressors, who are the cause of these tears, return, even late at last, to your heart; return, and fear the indignation of Benedict, your lawgiver. Consider the desolation of the order which you are bringing in to your own harm; fear the wrath of the Almighty, which you provoke by your crimes.

Woe to us: the city of our religion is being destroyed by enemies all around us; the houses of discipline are being reduced to nothing, and no one is found to resist; no one to set himself as a wall before the house of God. We all seek what is our own; we all ignore the common need of the order, until little by little we too fail. Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to outsiders. Monasteries consecrated as dwellings for monks are now becoming stables for clerics and fortresses for fighting soldiers.

O what shall I say? I am ashamed to utter what men without conscience are not ashamed to perpetrate in the cloisters of monks. They disturb the solitude of religious men; they change houses of prayer into dwellings of merchants. I suffer with your calamities, O venerable religion of Benedict; I groan that you are exposed to plunder by every passerby. There is none to console you among all your dear ones, because those who could help you will not, and those who wish to come to your aid cannot.

O with what beautiful grace you once flourished in the Church of God, when you bore men distinguished in every holiness and learning, and, like one young, strong, and steadfast, you used to drive away from yourself every dishonorable way of life. But now, as if worn out by old age and the long oppression of days, you have failed, and the strength of your youth has been taken away, because your might is no longer in you. Where now is your zeal? Where is the beauty of your face? Where is your honor? Where is the power once widely spread throughout the whole world? Where is that zeal for letters, venerable to God and the angels, whose fervor once made you exalted above all orders? Where are your sons around your table, learned and most holy men? All have failed, and you have been brought almost to nothing. You have lost the beauty of your youth, and the strength of your adolescence has been scattered.

To whom shall I compare you, or to whom shall I liken you, O separated daughter? To whom shall I make you equal, and how shall I comfort you, mother of monks? Great as the sea is your ruin. Who will heal you? O if you had guarded against this ruin which you now experience, how blessed all nations would call you. But you said in your abundance, “I shall never be moved.” Plenty has made you poor, and the abundance of temporal things has stripped you of all your adornment. You have borne insolent sons, disobedient, rebellious against holy institutions; hiding beneath the cloak of your honor, they have stripped you of all your beauty. Alas.

225
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 235 mater, et virgo, inveterasti in terra aliena, deputata es cum mortuis, non est species decoris tui. Exurge nunc Benedicte; monachorum sacratissime princeps, et vide ordinem tuum, quem instituisti, et haereditatem tuam, quam plantasti; aspice monachos tuae professionis oblitos, terrenis immersos, voluptati deditos, omni scaturigine vitiorum plenos. Tu olim eis optima vivendi praecerta dedisti; tu a saecularium negotiorum curis alienos esse praecepsisti; tu corda eorum ad solius Dei amorem extendi iussisti: Surge, inquam, o beatissime Pater, et vide desolationem ordinis tui; quoniam a suis filiis intus confunditur, et foris ab hostibus dissipatur. Contemnunt instituta pietatis tuae monachi: rapiunt coenobia ordinis tui homines alieni: Non est, qui honorem nominis tui defendat: Non est, qui ordinis tui sacratissimi decorum tueat. Suscitare et tu o Magne Papa Gregori. Qui loca monachorum Deo sacra in usus secularium transferri sub anathemate prohibuisti, et vide monachos de coenobiis expulsos, et clericos mundanos intrusos. Tu quondam omnium ecclesiarum princeps, maximam honestati monasticae curam adhibere solebas, ingenti sollicitudine cavens, ne quid in ordine sacro contra regulam Benedicti praesumeretur. Intuere nunc Monachorum conversationes, o Reverendissime Praesul, omni honestate nudas, omni turpitudine plenas. Vide quomodo coenobia ordinis tui Deo dicata, in manus traduntur clericorum; et, quae olim angelicis choris poterant comparari, modo prostibula fiunt meretricum: Suscitare Imperatorum gloriosissime, et Christianae fidei defensor invicte Germanorum decus, Carole, et vide monachorum calamitatem. Qui ordinem Benedicti Patris quondam gloriosum reddidisti, et per universum pene mundum tuo studio dilatasti: Vide nunc, quae olim fundasti coenobia, omnia in direptionem inimicorum exposita: Qui quondam ordinem monasticum, ut castra Dei veneratus es, iam velut contemptum ab omnibus, mundata bonis, o Princeps sancte compater. Tu Abbates, et Monachos olim tepescentes cum ingenti cura ad observantiam regularis disciplinae consuevisti reducere, et iam reformatos ingenti sollicitudine ab omni molestia tuorum, vel quorumlibet defensare. Exurge et tu Berno Cluniacensis antistes coenobii cum successoribus tuis, qui ordinem sanctum collabentem antiquitus magnifice restaurasti, et ad pristinum decorum in toto orbe reduxisti: Surge, inquam, nunc, et vide quemadmodum monachorum abundet iniquitas; furor dominetur, exuberet scelus, universos pene faciat insanire voluptas: Decor tuae reformationis ablatus est; disciplina corruit: honestas fugit, zelus sanctae conversationis perit; humilitas expiravit. Suscitare Hirsaugiensis coenobii Abbas Gulielme, Reverendissime Pater; qui Cluniacensem instaurationem post lapsum in Alemania, reformasti; qui monasticae conversationi copiosa instituta providisti; qui tuis precibus 236 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

mother and virgin, you have grown old in a foreign land; you have been numbered with the dead; there is no beauty in your comeliness. Rise now, Benedict, most holy prince of monks, and see your order, which you established, and your inheritance, which you planted. Look upon the monks who have forgotten your profession, sunk in earthly things, given over to pleasure, full of every spring of vices. You once gave them the best precepts for living; you commanded them to be strangers to the cares of worldly business; you ordered their hearts to be stretched out toward the love of God alone. Rise, I say, most blessed Father, and see the desolation of your order, because within it is confounded by its own sons, and without it is scattered by enemies. The monks despise the institutions of your piety; strangers seize the monasteries of your order. There is no one to defend the honor of your name; there is no one to protect the beauty of your most holy order.

Awake also, great Pope Gregory, you who under anathema forbade places sacred to God for monks to be transferred to the uses of secular men, and see monks driven from their monasteries and worldly clerics thrust in. You, once prince of all the churches, used to apply the greatest care to monastic honor, guarding with immense solicitude lest anything be presumed in the sacred order against the Rule of Benedict. Behold now, most reverend prelate, the conduct of monks, bare of every honor, full of every shame. See how the monasteries of your order, dedicated to God, are handed over into the hands of clerics, and those places which once could be compared to angelic choirs now become brothels of harlots.

Awake, most glorious of emperors and unconquered defender of the Christian faith, Charles, glory of the Germans, and see the calamity of the monks. You once made the order of Father Benedict glorious, and through your zeal spread it through almost the whole world. See now how the monasteries which you once founded are all exposed to the plundering of enemies. You once venerated the monastic order as the camp of God; now, holy prince, behold it as though despised by all, stripped of its goods, [unclear]. You once used with immense care to bring back abbots and monks grown lukewarm to the observance of regular discipline, and, once reformed, to defend them with great solicitude from every molestation by your own men or by any others.

Rise also, Berno, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, with your successors, you who in ancient times magnificently restored the holy order when it was collapsing and brought it back to its former beauty throughout the whole world. Rise, I say, now, and see how the iniquity of monks abounds, fury rules, crime overflows, and pleasure makes almost all men mad. The beauty of your reform has been taken away; discipline has collapsed; honor has fled; zeal for holy conduct has perished; humility has breathed its last.

Awake, William, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, most reverend Father, you who after its fall restored the Cluniac renewal in Germany; you who provided abundant institutions for monastic conduct; you who by your prayers

226
infirmorum artus solidasti: Qui nationem Germanicam doctrina, et sanctitate, velut sydus fulgentissimum, illuminasti. Surgite, et vos Prae- stantissimi Patres, diversarum reformationum authores, et videite la- bores vestros iam periisse, constitutiones neglectas, exhortationes spretas, protestationes sollicitudinis contemptas. Vos ordinem monasticum vita, et doctrina reddidistis gloriosum, Deo dilectum, Angelis venerandum, vobis sanctum, hominibus reverendum. Ubi nunc ista merita? Ubi nunc istae operationes iustorum? Heu Mater veneranda religio, ad quantam calamitatem devenisti: Qui te olim glorificabant, modo despiciunt: qui honorabant, modo contemnunt. Dereliquisti mandata legislatoris tui, studium scripturarum abiecisti, propterea contemptibilis facta es: filii, quos genuisti, fecerunt hoc malum tibi. Mox etenim, ut monachi coe- perunt terrena sapere, lectiones sacras negligere, interna postponere, color tuus optimus in foedum mutatus est: sed quid? Qui cadit, fre- quenter apponit resurgere; tu autem semel lapse, nunquam in toto surrexisti. Quid Cluniacensis? Quid Specuensis? Quid Italensis? Quid Castellensis? Quid Melicensis? Quid novissime Bursfeldensis? et si quae aliae praeter eas reformationes fuerint, quid ad totum ordinem facere potuerunt universo diffusum in orbe? Nam et si Cluniacensis in omnibus mundi provinciis lumen suae honestatis effuderit, tamen multa coenobia in diversis regnis in pristina deformitate dereliquit: Ex eo enim tem- pore, quo religio nostra primo cecidit, nulla unquam generalis refor- matio fuit. O quam facilis descensus Averni; quam prompta voluntas delinquendi; quam maxima post lapsum resurgendi ad rectitudinem difficultas? Omnes (ut ita dicam) ceciderunt; pauci a deformitate sua surrexerunt: multi in suis voluptatibus computrescunt. Doleo super te, o flos Monastici decoris: Doleo et vehementer quidem: et si tibi aliter succurrere non valeo, lachrymas et calidas, et amarissimas pro tua contritione fundo: Sed et vos, o Colendissimi Patres, qui honorem ordinis vestri diligitis, qui contritionem Ioseph nostri mistici doletis, qui ad aeternam haereditatem venire cupitis, attendite statum nostrae religionis, desolationem eius inspicite, de remedio cogitate. Ecce ra- piuntur in circuitu de manibus Sancti Benedicti opulenta coenobia; ecce claustra monachorum clericorum fiunt habitacula: et de malis studiis monachi ad pessima transferuntur: Erras o prudentia mundi; potestas saeculi deciperis; nunquam ex malo monacho bonum canonicum poteris instituere. Sed et vos praevericatores attendite: apostatae or- dinis auscultate: Quae vos dementia impellit, ut coenobia, quae non extruxistis sancto Benedicto, destruatis? An putatis vos a damnatione liberos, si abieciro monastico schemate, Clerici peccetis? Salvabit ne vos in districto examine peccandi praesumpta licentia? Forsitan in alieno habitu daemonibus eritis incogniti? Videbimus, si Deus trans-

you strengthened the limbs of the weak; you who illuminated the German nation, in learning and holiness, like a most brilliant star. Rise up, you also, most excellent Fathers, authors of various reforms, and see that your labors have now perished, your constitutions are neglected, your exhortations spurned, the protests of your solicitude despised. You made the monastic order glorious in life and learning, beloved by God, venerable to the angels, holy to yourselves, reverenced by men.

Where now are those merits? Where now are those works of the just? Alas, venerable mother Religion, to what great calamity have you come! Those who once glorified you now despise you; those who honored you now hold you in contempt. You have abandoned the commandments of your lawgiver; you have cast aside the study of the Scriptures; therefore you have become contemptible. The sons whom you bore have done this evil to you.

For soon, when monks began to savor earthly things, to neglect sacred reading, to set inward things after outward, your excellent color was changed into foulness. But what then? He who falls often sets himself to rise again; but you, once fallen, have never wholly risen. What did the Cluniac reform do? What the Specuensian? What the Italensian? What the Castellensian? What the Melicensian? What, most recently, the Bursfeldensian? And if there were any other reforms besides these, what could they do for the whole order, spread throughout the entire world? For even if the Cluniac reform poured out the light of its honorableness in all the provinces of the world, nevertheless it left many monasteries in various kingdoms in their former deformity. For from that time when our religion first fell, there has never been any general reform.

O how easy is the descent to Avernus; how ready the will to offend; how very great, after a fall, the difficulty of rising again to righteousness! All, so to speak, have fallen; few have risen from their deformity; many are rotting away in their pleasures.

I grieve over you, O flower of monastic beauty; I grieve, and indeed vehemently. And if I cannot aid you otherwise, I pour out hot and most bitter tears for your contrition. But you also, most honored Fathers, who love the honor of your order, who grieve over the contrition of our mystical Joseph, who desire to come to the eternal inheritance, attend to the state of our religion, inspect its desolation, think upon a remedy.

Behold, all around, wealthy monasteries are snatched from the hands of Saint Benedict; behold, the cloisters of monks become dwellings of clerics, and from evil pursuits monks are transferred to the worst. You err, O prudence of the world; you are deceived, power of the age: never will you be able to make a good canon out of a bad monk.

But you also, transgressors, take heed; apostates of the order, listen. What madness drives you to destroy monasteries for Saint Benedict which you did not build? Or do you think yourselves free from damnation if, having cast off the monastic habit, you sin as clerics? Will the presumptuous license of sinning save you in the strict examination? Perhaps in another habit you will be unknown to the demons? We shall see whether God trans

227
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 237 lationem vestram approbet, cum in illo tremendo iudicio transgressionis vestrae rationem reddere fueritis exacti. Timeo autem, ne, modo sine ordine viventes, inter eos locum recipiatis, ubi nullus ordo, sed sempiternus horror inhabitat: Nam, quam aliam mansionem sit recepturus de malo monacho Canonicus peior effectus, non satis intelligo: O insensati, ac vobis ipsis inimici, quis docebit vos fugere a ventura ira? Quis causam vestram iniquam contra sanctum Benedictum in illo tremendo examine defensare vel poterit, vel audebit? Quem temeritatis vestrae advocatum habebit? Sanctus Benedictus princeps monachorum stabit in testimonium contra vos, accusabit vos, et condemnabit. Quis excusabit vos? Non tibi blandiaris voti regularis contemptor inique, conscientiam tuam ne palpes, si Benedictum habueris adversarium, nullum sanctorum invenies amicum. Nam, qui unum coelestis patriae civium offendit, omnes offendit: Ubi enim summa, et foelix tranquillitas, ibi erit et animorum indivisibilis unitas: Quis ergo te liberare poterit de manu Domini, si steterint adversum te omnes sancti? Invoca eos, qui te modo decipiunt; qui ordinis a te habitum tollunt; qui te blandis sermonibus abducunt; qui apostasiae tuae cooperatores existunt, ut te ab instante tribulatione defendant: Quod si iustus vix salvabitur, Apostata, et ordinis sancti destructor ubi parebunt? Non liberabit impium in illa die iustitia sancti: neque sibi miser alteri feret auxilium. Quin potius eos, quos tantae collaboratores praesumptionis nunc muneribus, et donis tibi concilias, tunc infoelicitatis tuae testes habebis, et socios: Nullus defensor pravae actionis ibi erit; nullus iniquitatis advocatus: quoniam ibi nuda erunt omnia; ibi ad damnationem unicuique satis erit accusatrix conscientia; ibi stabit exercitus sanctorum adversus eos, qui monachorum habitacula inique profanarunt, qui ordinem Divorum Patrum impie destruxerunt: Sed authores harum rerum, quas mihi iniuste videor dixisse iniquas, factum suum ita excusare nituntur, dicentes: Monachorum improba conversatio ad extremam paupertatem coenobia impellens corrigi, et emendari non potest, nisi in alium statum transferatur propter multas, quas sibi fingunt, rationes: quas etiam in sequentibus, Deo largiente, monstrabimus inanes: Aiunt denique, malos monachos per translationem corrige, non solum peccato caret, sed et iustitiae, et pietatis pars magna est: Sed ubi possunt haec discerni? Quemadmodum, quae dicitis, vera docebitis? Malos monachos ad bonitatem convertere, laudabile, et sanctum est, sed canonicos facere non est emendare monachos, sed depravare: Nunquam erit bonus canonicus monachus malus: bonus autem non exuet ordinem suum, sed diligit, colet, amabit. Nolo iam contendere verbis: nolo nimius esse aut vehemens: translationis huius effectum nolo depingere, quem paulatim non dubito in lucem venire: Si monachos malos 238 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

approve your transfer, when in that dreadful judgment you are required to render an account of your transgression. I fear, however, that, living now without order, you will receive a place among those where no order, but everlasting horror, dwells. For what other dwelling a man is to receive who, from a bad monk, has become a worse canon, I do not sufficiently understand.

O senseless men, enemies to yourselves, who will teach you to flee from the wrath to come? Who will be able, or will dare, to defend your wicked cause against Saint Benedict in that dreadful examination? Whom will your rashness have as advocate? Saint Benedict, prince of monks, will stand as witness against you; he will accuse you and condemn you. Who will excuse you? Do not flatter yourself, wicked despiser of your regular vow; do not soothe your conscience. If you have Benedict as your adversary, you will find none of the saints your friend. For he who offends one citizen of the heavenly country offends them all. For where there is supreme and blessed tranquility, there too there will be an indivisible unity of minds. Who, then, will be able to deliver you from the hand of the Lord, if all the saints stand against you?

Call upon those who now deceive you, who take from you the habit of the order, who lead you away with flattering speeches, who exist as accomplices of your apostasy, so that they may defend you from the tribulation that is at hand.
