But if the just man will scarcely be saved, where will the apostate and the destroyer of a holy order appear? On that day the justice of a saint will not deliver the impious man; nor will one wretch bring help to another. Rather, those whom you now win over to yourself with gifts and presents as collaborators in so great a presumption, you will then have as witnesses and companions of your unhappiness. There will be no defender of a depraved action there, no advocate of iniquity; for there all things will be bare. There, each person’s accusing conscience will be enough for his damnation. There the army of saints will stand against those who have wickedly profaned the dwellings of monks, who have impiously destroyed the order of the divine fathers.

But the authors of these things, which I seem to myself to have called wicked unjustly, try to excuse their deed in this way, saying: The improper way of life of monks, driving monasteries into extreme poverty, cannot be corrected and amended unless it is transferred into another state, on account of many reasons which they invent for themselves; reasons which, God granting, we shall also show in what follows to be empty. Finally they say that to correct bad monks through transfer not only is free from sin, but is also a great part of justice and piety.

But where can these things be discerned? How will you teach that what you say is true? To convert bad monks to goodness is praiseworthy and holy; but to make them canons is not to reform monks, but to corrupt them. A bad monk will never be a good canon; but a good monk will not cast off his order, but will cherish, cultivate, and love it. I do not now wish to contend with words; I do not wish to be excessive or vehement. I do not wish to depict the effect of this transfer, which I do not doubt will gradually come to light. If bad monks

228
voluystis canonicos facere, quare bonos in locum eorum non reposuystis? Non est sine voto transgressione commutatio, quae in deterius praesumpta mutatur: Vae vobis, desertores, qui, ut vestris voluptatibus satisfiat, ordinem contemnitis, votum negatis, aequitatis normam confunditis. Omnes stabimus ad tribunal Christi, ait Apostolus: ut accipiat unusquisque, prout gessit in corpore suo: Quid ibi destructores Monasteriorum accepturi sunt? qui omnipotenti honorem non deferunt, qui violent pactum, qui sanctorum evacuant voluntates, qui decreta iuris despiciunt? Si bonum est fundare coenobia, malum est (nemo dubitet) ea destruere. Actio contraria, mercedem non nisi contrariam accipiet. Denique, si hominis demortui ultimam voluntatem, in legatis, quamvis homini factis, nemo audet infringere: cur amatores mundi Deo, et sanctis oblata sibi praesumunt usurpare? Si reus est criminis, qui testamentum hominis violat, qua poena dignus est, qui fundationes coenobiorum a sanctis Episcopis, et Principibus factas in usus alienos inique commutat? Enimvero Reges, Principes, et Praesules, caeterique fideles, qui ad Dei honorem coenobia fundaverunt: hoc summopere voluisse comprobantur, ut fundationes huius instituti effectum inviolabilem sortirent: Si canonicos habere voluissent in coenobis, monachos non posuissent. Sed caeca hominum ambitio tantum invaluit, ut nihil minus, quam futura cogitet: nihil plus, quam caduca amet: O misera humanae fragilitatis conditio, o damnabilis semper mandatorum Dei oblivio: Consensere iura peccatis, et coepit esse licitum, quod publicum est: Flagrant ubique delicta, et passim multiformi genere peccandi per improbas mentes nocens virus dolos operatur, et fraudes: Hic ordinem confundit; ille poenitus destruit. Hic voluntatem sanctorum subducit: ille falsas dimembrationis allegationes conscribit. Hic arcentur coenobiis monachi, illic bonis ordinis dominantur alieni: Inimicus iustos insimulat, calumniator impugnat, testis mendax infamat: Esse iam inter nocentes innoxium, crimen est: Quis illic honestatis amor, quae posset esse mentibus integritas, ubi propositum ordinis deiicitur? Ubi a Deo facta vocatio revocatur? Quis maneat illic rerum pudor, quae virtus posset subsistere? Ubi ius violatur divinum: ubi nullus de legibus metus est; de iudice pavor nullus? Quid potest inhumanius, quid cru- delius dici; quamvis sibi velle usurpare divinum, fas confundere, infringere votum, debitum Deo subtrahere cultum! O dies illa tremenda, cunctisque horrenda mortalibus, qua diu tolerans haec mala monachorum vindicabitur ira Dei, qua debitam sentient apostatae poenam: qua temeritatis suae sancti ordinis adversarii luent vindictam: Quid vobis tunc proderit voti Deo facti negatio? Quid ordinis extinctio sacra? Quid brevis turpiter empta in carne voluptas? Cum coeperit Dominus suos recensere cultores, praemiis monachos veros donare

If you wished to make them canons, why did you not put good men in their place? A change is not made without transgression of the vow when it is presumptuously changed for the worse. Woe to you, deserters, who, so that your pleasures may be satisfied, despise the order, deny the vow, and confound the rule of equity.

“We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ,” says the Apostle, “so that each may receive according to what he has done in his body.” What will the destroyers of monasteries receive there, who do not render honor to the Almighty, who violate the covenant, who nullify the wills of the saints, who despise the decrees of law? If it is good to found monasteries, it is evil, let no one doubt it, to destroy them. A contrary action will receive only a contrary reward.

Finally, if no one dares to break the last will of a dead man in matters of bequests, even though made to a human being, why do lovers of the world presume to usurp what has been offered to God and the saints? If he is guilty of a crime who violates a man’s testament, what punishment does he deserve who unjustly diverts to alien uses the foundations of monasteries made by holy bishops and princes?

Indeed, kings, princes, prelates, and the other faithful who founded monasteries for the honor of God are proved to have wished above all that the foundations of this institution should obtain an inviolable effect. If they had wished to have canons in monasteries, they would not have placed monks there. But the blind ambition of men has grown so strong that it thinks of nothing less than the future, and loves nothing more than what is perishable.

O wretched condition of human frailty, O always damnable forgetfulness of the commandments of God! The laws have consented to sins, and what is public has begun to be lawful. Crimes blaze everywhere, and everywhere, through wicked minds, in manifold kinds of sinning, a harmful poison works deceits and frauds. This man confounds the order; that man utterly destroys it. This man withdraws the will of the saints; that man writes false allegations of dismemberment. Here monks are driven from monasteries; there outsiders lord it over the goods of the order. An enemy accuses the just, a slanderer attacks, a false witness defames. Now, among the guilty, to be innocent is a crime.

What love of honor can be there, what integrity could exist in minds, where the purpose of the order is cast down, where the calling made by God is revoked? What shame concerning affairs can remain there, what virtue could stand, where divine right is violated, where there is no fear of the laws, no dread of the judge? What can be called more inhuman, what more cruel, than to wish to usurp for oneself what is divine, to confound right, to break a vow, to withhold from God the worship owed to him?

O that dreadful day, terrible to all mortals, when the wrath of God, which has long endured these evils against the monks, will be avenged; when apostates will feel their due punishment; when the adversaries of the holy order will pay the penalty for their rashness. What then will it profit you to have denied the vow made to God? What will the destruction of the sacred order profit you? What will that brief pleasure in the flesh, shamefully bought, profit you, when the Lord begins to review his worshipers and to give rewards to true monks?

229
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 239 promissis, bonos disiungere malis, veraces dividere falsis, quem vos locum accepturi eritis, quem habituri successum, qui sanctum religionis propositum abnegatis, qui votum frangitis, qui ordinem spernitis, qui fidem violatis? Utinam huius vitae brevitatem pensaretis: Utinam futurae retributionis examen timeretis, ut salutaribus compuncti doctrinis, Domini vocem per poenitentiam attenderetis, dicentis: Nolo mortem morientis, sed ut revertatur, et vivat: Et per Prophetam: Revertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum: quoniam misericors, et pius est, patiens et multae miserationis, qui sententiam revocet, si vos lachrymis culpam velitis abluer: Vos autem iudicium Dei non timetis, clementiam spernitis: patientiam longanimitatis illius contemnitis. Idcirco in quemlibet vestrum, dicit Apostolus; Ignoras, quod patientia Dei ad poenitentiam te adducit? Tu autem secundum duritiam tuam, et cor impoenitens thesaurizas tibi iram, in die irae, et revelationis iusti iudicii Dei; qui reddet unicuique iuxta opera sua. Iustum iudicium Dei dixit esse, quia serum est, quia diu multum differtur, ut vobis ad vitam longa Dei patientia consulatur. Vos autem quemadmodum poenitentiam agitis, qui culpam non agnoscitis? Dolebitis, sed sero, quando iam locus non erit poenitentiae, sed retributio vindictae. Tunc ergo referetur poena impio, et peccatori, quando iam non potest poenitentia prodesse peccatori; O quam rei maneunt, quam miser, quam infoelices, qui propter brevissimam huius temporis voluptatem, Dei, ordinisque sui desertores, et contra Deum rebellres, voluntatem fecerunt diaboli, ut eos necesse sit cum ipso inextinguibili igne torqueri: Utinam haec cordibus haereant eorum. Utinam ista cogitarent, qui ordinem suum deserunt, qui votum infringunt, qui et Deo, et sanctis eius tamem audacter mentiuntur: sed frustra nitimur: verba nostra nunquam accipiunt: qui Dei, et Ecclesiae, et S. Benedicti sermones contemnunt. Idcirco haec causa ordinis, non verbis, sed rebus gerenda est: Armemur itaque, Patres, viribus totis, et paremur ad agonem mente incorrupta, virtute devota, conscientia firma, contra eos, qui ordinem nostrum delere cupiunt, qui monachum exuunt, qui coenobia auferunt, qui regulam deferunt, qui suis visitatoribus rebellres existunt: Armemur, obsecro, Patres, zelo disciplinae regularis, honore ordinis, nullis laboribus, nullis parcentes expensis, ne perniciosa pestis nostro silentio fota totum successive ordinem inficiat: Nunquam ordini nostro tanta necessitas incubuit; nunquam tot malis involutus fuit: Ecce monachi habitum exuunt, in habitacula clericorum coenobia transferunt; et dum commodis vacamus privatis, dum labores fugimus, dum expensis parcimus; dum avaritiae nostrae consulimus, ordo perit, religio transit, Dei cultus evanescit. Multa iam coenobia malitia temporum (ne dicam ignavia nostra) ab ordine translata sunt; et nisi aliter evigilemus, maiora damna nobis 240 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

The Pentichus Book of Johannes Trithemius.

...with the things promised, to separate the good from the wicked, the truthful from the false: what place will you receive, what success will you have, you who deny the holy purpose of religion, who break your vow, who despise your order, who violate your faith?

Would that you weighed the brevity of this life. Would that you feared the examination of future recompense, so that, pierced by saving teachings, you would heed through repentance the voice of the Lord, who says: “I do not desire the death of the one who is dying, but that he return and live”; and through the prophet: “Return to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and gracious, patient and of great compassion,” one who revokes his sentence if you wish to wash away your guilt with tears. But you do not fear the judgment of God; you despise his clemency; you scorn the patience of his long-suffering.

Therefore the Apostle says to each one of you: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works.” He said that the judgment of God is just because it is late, because it is long and greatly deferred, so that God’s long patience may provide for your life. But how do you do penance, when you do not acknowledge your guilt? You will grieve, but too late, when there will no longer be a place for repentance, but the repayment of vengeance.

Then, therefore, punishment will be rendered to the impious man and the sinner, when repentance can no longer profit the sinner. O how guilty, how wretched, how unhappy they remain, who, for the very brief pleasure of this present time, deserters of God and of their own order and rebels against God, have done the will of the devil, so that they must be tormented with him in unquenchable fire. Would that these things clung to their hearts. Would that they thought on these things, who desert their order, who break their vow, who so boldly lie both to God and to his saints. But we strive in vain: they never receive our words, who despise the words of God, of the Church, and of Saint Benedict.

Therefore this cause of the order must be carried on not with words but with deeds. Let us therefore arm ourselves, Fathers, with all our strength, and let us prepare for the struggle with an incorrupt mind, devoted virtue, and firm conscience, against those who desire to destroy our order, who strip off the monk, who take away monasteries, who cast aside the Rule, who exist as rebels against their own visitors. Let us arm ourselves, I beseech you, Fathers, with zeal for regular discipline and for the honor of the order, sparing no labors, no expenses, lest this pernicious plague, fostered by our silence, gradually infect the whole order.

Never has such necessity weighed upon our order; never has it been entangled in so many evils. Behold, monks put off the habit; they transform monasteries into dwellings of clerics; and while we attend to private advantages, while we flee labors, while we spare expenses, while we consult our own greed, the order perishes, religion passes away, the worship of God vanishes. Many monasteries have already, through the malice of the times, not to say through our own sloth, been transferred from the order; and unless we wake up in another way, greater losses will come upon us.

230
Audacia stultorum non statim repressa similia praesumendi occasionem caeteris praebet. Abbatibus deformatis nihil infoelicis. Nihil minus, quam regulam curant; nihil studiosius sectantur, quam libidinem, avaritiam, voluptatem, superbiam, et mundi vanitatem. Sic, capite infecto, omnia membra corporis corrumpuntur: iam in coenobiis ubi regula despicitur, ubi disciplina non servatur, quid aliud, quam quaedam scaturigo omnium vitiorum conspicitur? Nulla obedientia, nulla paupertas, nulla castitas apud illos virtutis amore tenetur; inter quos vivere sine crimine, crimen est: Hi sunt homines corrupti, monachi perversi, doli artifices, fraudis authores, iniquitatis ministri, scleris amici: qui disciplinam fugiunt, observiam contemnunt, ordinem destruunt, unitatem confundunt. Et re vera, Patres, nisi his malis cito provideatis remedio, in brevi ordinem videbitis, et dolebitis imminutum. Sed forte dicitis: Nunquam defectus vigilantia: diligentia nostra nunquam cessavit; semper nos malorum temeritati opposuimus: dimembrationes monasteriorum semper impedire conati sumus, et nihil unquam profecimus: Quid nostri labores, quid studia, quid expensae graves proficunt, dum se principes, ecclesiarumque rectores tam potenter oppovent? Scio, Patres, vera, quae dicitis: scio facta: scio continuata. Sed obsecro, ne verba mea in malam partem velitis accipere, si objectionibus istis ausim respondere. Vigilantia vestra in causis ordinis mihi nota est, labores perspicui, expensarum magnitude probata, continuatio in his semper adhibita: Sed velim vos reminisci, o Patres, duorum Horatii versuum, quibus dicit: Est modus in rebus, sunt certi denique fines: Quos ultra citraque nequit consistere rectum. Adversarios multos habemus, et diversos; non est uno contra omnes pugnandum modo sed diverso, sed vario, sed discreto. Monachi sumus, professores humilitatis; pugna nobis orationibus, precibus, supplicationibus inchoanda est, non feritate irritandus. Iupiter altus; non praecipis in Deum producenda sententia: precibus numina placantur, non minis: sed de hoc satis: Credo enim, vos, Patres, quid velim, intelligere. Neque haec passim elucidanda sunt omnibus; sed iis tantum, qui zelum ordinis habent, et exequendi potestatem: Contra eos, qui se ab ordine transferunt, vel iam dudum translulerunt. Caput IV. Iustene satis movear adversum illos, qui ab ordine nostro dimembrare conantur, nec satis scio, nec si sciam, facile ausim dicere, quippe quos omnipotens patientia tam diu tolerat, tam tarde flagellat.

The boldness of fools, if not at once checked, gives the rest occasion to presume similar things.

Nothing is more unhappy than deformed abbots. They care for nothing less than the rule; they pursue nothing more eagerly than lust, greed, pleasure, pride, and the vanity of the world. Thus, when the head is infected, all the members of the body are corrupted. Now in monasteries where the rule is despised, where discipline is not observed, what else is seen but a kind of spring of all vices? No obedience, no poverty, no chastity is maintained among them for love of virtue; among such men, to live without blame is a crime. These are corrupt men, perverse monks, craftsmen of deceit, authors of fraud, ministers of iniquity, friends of wickedness: they flee discipline, despise observance, destroy order, confound unity.

And truly, Fathers, unless you quickly provide a remedy for these evils, in a short time you will see the order diminished, and you will grieve over it.

But perhaps you say: “Our vigilance has never failed; our diligence has never ceased. We have always set ourselves against the rashness of the wicked; we have always tried to prevent the dismemberments of monasteries, and we have never accomplished anything. What do our labors, our efforts, our heavy expenses profit, when princes and rulers of churches oppose us with such power?”

I know, Fathers, that what you say is true. I know what has been done; I know it has been continuous. But I beg you not to take my words amiss if I dare to answer those objections. Your vigilance in the causes of the order is known to me, your labors are clear, the greatness of your expenses is proven, and continuance has always been applied in these matters. But I should like you to remember, O Fathers, two verses of Horace, in which he says:

“There is measure in things; there are, finally, fixed limits, beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.”

We have many and varied adversaries; we must not fight against all in one way, but in different ways, in varied ways, in discerning ways. We are monks, professors of humility. Our struggle must be begun with prayers, entreaties, and supplications; it must not be provoked by fierceness. God is high; no rash sentence is to be brought forth against God [unclear]. The divine powers are appeased by prayers, not by threats. But enough of this; for I believe, Fathers, that you understand what I mean. Nor are these things to be explained everywhere to everyone, but only to those who have zeal for the order and the power to carry it out.

Against those who transfer themselves from the order, or who have already long since transferred themselves.

Chapter IV.

Whether I am moved with sufficient justice against those who try to dismember themselves from our order, I do not sufficiently know; nor, if I did know, would I easily dare to say, since almighty patience tolerates them so long and scourges them so late.

231
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 241 Sed cum finem illorum intueor, qui se iam dudum ab ordine dimembrarunt, considero hanc longanimitatem patientiae Dei districta satis animadversione vindicatam. Nam, sicut ex eorum relatione accepimus, qui plures illorum noverunt, pauci ex eis, qui monachum exuerunt, bona morte decesserunt: Quin potius sine poenitentiae signis, sine sacramentis ecclesiasticis ex hac vita subitanee vocati manifestum suae infoelicitatis dedere indicium. Quid ergo dicemus ad haec? letabimurne in perditione morientium? Absit: Dominus est; qui peccatores, ut convertantur; diu hic tollerat, ipse est, qui non conversos durius damnat: nos autem cum propheta sententiam eius metuimus, dicentes; Iustus autem quacunque morte praecupatus fuerit, in refrigerio erit: De impiis autem Propheta dicit: Mors peccatorum pessima: Nos autem pravorum interitum ad mentem idcirco reducimus, ut vel timore caeteros ab incepto malo revocemus. Sed, quemadmodum verba nostra suscipient, qui superos, inferosque derident? Nisi verbis adiicientur opera, nihil apud malivolas mentes proficiunt hortamenta. Adhuc populus durae cervicis in deserto murmurat; adhuc gens impia legistatorem suum blasphemat; adhuc improba natio in Aegyptum redire deliberat, Timent, ne moriantur in solitudine, qui hoc solum timere debuerant, ne extra solitudinem morerentur. O dura mens hominum, o libertas pernitosia monachorum, quousque saevit crudelitas tua; quae nec illis parcere novit, quos authores habet, et amicos. Qui sibi nequam est, cui bonus erit? O monachorum inauditum scelus, o crimen immense: Deum irridere, promissum illi negare, fidem frangere, debitam servitutem subtrahere: Quid hac impietate crudelius? quid hoc sacrilegio sceleratius? O monachae perverse, o Apostata inique, o Periure sceleratissime, quousque Dei beniguitatem opponis, quamdiu omnipotentis pietatem derides? Monachus es; Monachus quoque iudicaberis, etiam si pellem cum habitu deposueris. Cur ab ordine sancto discedis? Cur Deo mentiris? Crede mihi, non dabit omnipotens honorem suum alteri; non remittet tibi in aeternum, quod solemniter semel acceptum oblatum. Antequam Deo promitteres, liber eras, et tui arbitrii: postquam autem promisisti, Dei esse caepisti: iam tibi non licet dimittere, quod iuris Dei est. Vox tua ligavit te Deo; aut monachus salvaberis, aut aliter non salvaberis. Ecce ante oculos tuos est via vitae, et via mortis, eligi, quam volueris: si servas Deo fidem, si promissum imples, praemium habebis; si negas, poenam pro contemptu recipies. Hinc Paulus te admonens dicit: Fratres nolite errare, Deus non irridetur. Quaecunque enim seminaverit homo, haec et metet: Quid te accepturum praesumis, qui seminas in carne? Ait enim: Qui seminat in carne, de carne et metet: Fructus autem carnis partem non habet in haereditate sanctorum; Quid ergo te ipsum decipsis? Quid frustra 242 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

But when I consider the end of those who long ago severed themselves from the order, I judge that this longsuffering patience of God has been avenged by a sufficiently severe punishment. For, as we have learned from the report of those who knew many of them, few of those who cast off the monk died a good death. Rather, called suddenly from this life without signs of repentance, without ecclesiastical sacraments, they gave a clear sign of their unhappiness. What then shall we say to these things? Shall we rejoice in the perdition of the dying? Far from it. It is the Lord who long tolerates sinners here so that they may be converted; he is also the one who condemns more harshly those who are not converted. But we fear his sentence with the prophet, saying: “The righteous man, by whatever death he has been overtaken, will be in refreshment.” But of the wicked the Prophet says: “The death of sinners is most evil.” We recall the destruction of the depraved to mind for this reason, that by fear at least we may call the rest back from an evil undertaking.

But how will they receive our words, who deride the things above and the things below? Unless deeds are added to words, exhortations accomplish nothing among malicious minds. Still the stiff-necked people murmurs in the desert; still the impious nation blasphemes its lawgiver; still the wicked people deliberates about returning to Egypt. They fear dying in solitude, when this alone they ought to have feared: dying outside solitude. O hard mind of men, O destructive liberty of monks, how long does your cruelty rage, which does not even know how to spare those whom it has as authors and friends? He who is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good?

O unheard-of crime of monks, O immeasurable offense: to mock God, to deny him what was promised, to break faith, to withdraw the service owed. What is more cruel than this impiety? What is more wicked than this sacrilege? O perverse monk, O unjust apostate, O most wicked perjurer, how long do you set God’s kindness against him, how long do you deride the mercy of the Almighty? You are a monk; you will also be judged a monk, even if you have laid aside the skin along with the habit. Why do you depart from the holy order? Why do you lie to God? Believe me, the Almighty will not give his honor to another; he will not forgive you forever for what, once solemnly received, you offered. Before you promised God, you were free and of your own judgment; but after you promised, you began to belong to God. Now it is not lawful for you to let go what belongs by right to God. Your voice bound you to God; you will be saved as a monk, or otherwise you will not be saved.

Behold, before your eyes are the way of life and the way of death; choose whichever you wish. If you keep faith with God, if you fulfill what was promised, you will have a reward; if you deny it, you will receive punishment for contempt. Hence Paul, admonishing you, says: “Brothers, do not err; God is not mocked. For whatever a man has sown, this also will he reap.” What do you presume you will receive, you who sow in the flesh? For he says: “He who sows in the flesh, from the flesh will also reap.” But the fruit of the flesh has no share in the inheritance of the saints. Why then do you deceive yourself? Why in vain...

232
in vanitate confidis? Cur terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt Patres sancti transgrederis? Votum, quod Deo solemniter fecisti, negas: et portionem cum electis Dei, velut iustus expectas? Non est pars impio cum filiis Dei: ecce haereditatem Domini dissipas; extraneos de bonis Sancti Patris Benedicti ditas; promissum negas: et, ut licenter delinquas, falsa pro veris ingeminas: Si bonus es monachus, noli propositum tuum deserere, noli Monasterii secreta declinare: si autem malus es monachus, nunquam bonus canonicus eris. Qui autem bonus non est; malus est: qui autem malus est, non est, ut esse debet, et ideo iniustus est: Iniusti autem partem non habent in regno Dei: et parum refert, ubi sis, dum ubique malus, ubique iniustus, ubique infoelix torquaris. Nisi forte duplici velis damnationi esse obnoxius, ut dum es Monachus malus, et canonicus iniquus, utrobique reus, utrobique mendax, mercedem utriusque expositules. Nec mihi dispensationem Romani Pontificis obiicias, quam nisi Deus approbet, te minime excusabit: Non omnia Deo placent, quae per sumnum Pontificem in terra geruntur. Iam si exclamans mihi succenseas, quasi facta Vicarii Christi dijudicem, Respondeo: Summum pontificem, ut Vicarium Christi verum, amplector, colo, et veneror, cuius facta nequaquam reprehendo, sed hominem esse scio, qui, ut homo, et falli potest, et fallere. Nec mirum. In tanta quippe sollicitudine omnium ecclesiarum, in tanta occupatione negotiorum, dum pro veris falsa narrantur, mens in multis distracta facile decipitur: Tu autem Sancti ordinis Apostata, qui de bulla dispensationis securum te existimas, vide, ne post mortem (ut vulgo dicitur) illiterato daemoni occurras, qui literas nesciat, qui appellatio non deferat, qui allegationes immunitatis tuae contemnat. Crede mihi, non est astutia, quae possit fallere Deum. O miser, o infoelix, o insensate apostata. Quid Sancto Benedicto respondebis de professione, quam spernis? Quid omnipotenti Deo de voto, quod contemnis? Quem in illo tremendo iudicio causae tuae procuratorem poteris constituisse? Ubi nihil poterit laterre: omnia ibi nuda, omnia erunt aperta. Ubi locus penitentiae salutaris iam non relinquitur: Ubi excusandi spatium omnibus negatur. Quid proderit ibi, hic temere praesumpta dispensatio; quam nec probare licebit testimonio, nec iure defendere. Tunc videbis o Monache perverse, tunc intelliges quid roboris in se contineat fraudulenter impetrata licentia, cum vindictam aeterni Iudicis senseris in poena: Quid mihi dispensationem allegas, quid licentiam peccandi praedicas? Putasne summi pontificis auctoritate iram Dei te posse effugere? Audeo dicere: Nihil tibi proderit dispensatio Papae, si fraude, si dolo, si mendacio, si iniuste fuerit impetrata. Non est bonum non est iustum, quod malis arribus acquiritur. Ad dispensationem ut iusta sit, quatuor requiruntur, sine quibus dispensatio te minime salvabit: Quae sunt illa? Neces-

Do you trust in vanity? Why do you transgress the ancient boundaries which the holy Fathers set? You deny the vow you solemnly made to God, and yet you expect a portion with God’s elect as though you were righteous? The ungodly man has no share with the sons of God. Behold, you squander the Lord’s inheritance; you enrich strangers from the goods of holy Father Benedict; you deny your promise; and, so that you may sin freely, you heap up falsehoods in place of truths.

If you are a good monk, do not abandon your profession; do not forsake the enclosure of the monastery. But if you are a bad monk, you will never be a good canon. For he who is not good is bad; and he who is bad is not as he ought to be, and therefore he is unjust. The unjust have no share in the kingdom of God; and it matters little where you are, so long as everywhere you are bad, everywhere unjust, everywhere wretchedly tormented. Unless perhaps you wish to be liable to a double damnation, so that, while you are a bad monk and an unrighteous canon, guilty in both states, false in both, you may demand the reward of both.

Nor should you set against me the dispensation of the Roman Pontiff, which, unless God approves it, will in no way excuse you. Not everything that is done on earth through the Supreme Pontiff is pleasing to God. Now if you cry out and are angry with me, as though I were judging the deeds of Christ’s Vicar, I answer: I embrace, honor, and venerate the Supreme Pontiff as the true Vicar of Christ, and I in no way censure his deeds; but I know that he is a man, who, as a man, can both be deceived and deceive. Nor is this surprising. For amid such great care for all the churches, amid such great occupation with affairs, when false things are reported as true, a mind distracted among many matters is easily deceived.

But you, apostate from the holy order, who think yourself secure because of a bull of dispensation, beware lest after death, as is commonly said, you meet an illiterate demon who does not know letters, who does not defer to an appeal, who despises the allegations of your immunity. Believe me, there is no cunning that can deceive God.

O wretched man, O unhappy man, O senseless apostate. What will you answer Saint Benedict concerning the profession that you despise? What will you answer almighty God concerning the vow that you contemn? Whom will you be able to appoint as advocate for your cause in that dreadful judgment? There nothing will be able to lie hidden; all things there will be bare, all things open. There no place for saving repentance will any longer be left; there every opportunity for excuse will be denied to all. What good will that dispensation rashly presumed here do you there, when it will not be permitted either to prove it by testimony or to defend it by law?

Then you will see, O perverse monk; then you will understand what strength a license fraudulently obtained contains in itself, when you have felt the vengeance of the eternal Judge in punishment. Why do you allege dispensation to me? Why do you proclaim a license to sin? Do you think that by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff you can escape the wrath of God? I dare to say: the Pope’s dispensation will profit you nothing if it was obtained by fraud, deceit, lying, or injustice. What is acquired by evil arts is not good, is not just.

For a dispensation to be just, four things are required, without which the dispensation will in no way save you. What are they? Necessity [unclear].

233
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 243 sitas, videlicet, Congruitas, Utilitas, et Honestas: Sed tu, Monache periure, qui sola voluntate duceris: qui Deum, et ordinem contemnis, necessitatem fingis, congruentiam falsam ostendis, utilitatem mentiris, honestatem fraude componis: Sit Necessitas evidens, et manifesta; Con- gruentia vera, Utilitas non privata, sed publica, Honestas non ficta, sed propria, alioquin dispensatio erit iniusta. Nihil, quo summo Pon- tifici in hac dispensatione succenseam, profero, nihil in factis illius re- prehendo, quem falsis narrationibus monachorum circumventum non ignoro: Vos estis rei, vos dolosi, vos iniquitate notandi, o perversi Monachi, Apostatae scellerati, qui mendacio, dolo, et fraude petitis, quod iustis obtinere precibus desperatis. Quae vos necessitas urget, ordinem deserere, et in saecularis vitae statum transire? Quae con- gruentia suadet id infringere, quod semel Deo promissum, nulli licet revocare? Quae utilitas habitum monasticum deponere, ordinem dese- rere, propositum negare, coenobium transferre. Votum coram omnibus sancitis Deo factum, non frangere, sed et penitus abiicere? Aut qua honestas est, Monachum Deo dicatum ad saeculum redire, fidem fran- gere, periurium committere, sacrilegium perpetra? O praevericatorés, et impíi: quomodo tam nephandám praesumptionem unquam poteritis excusare? Nullum ex his quatuor translationi vestrae consonat; nullum ex eis dispensationem vestram confirmat. Quae enim necessitas ad hanc temeritatem vos potuit impellere? Quam coram Vicario Christi potuistis causam huius dimembrationis allegare? Paupertatem, et ruinam coenobiorum? Sed hanc potuissetis cito instaurare, si secundum Regulam S. Bénedicti viveretis. Vos enim iniquis moribus pauperes facti estis, conversatione sancta rursum ditareminis: Videte in circuitu ve- stro monastica ab observantiam regularem reducta, quomodo post ex- tremam paupertatem, Domino largiente, ad divitias pristinas denuo pro- ficiunt: et quidem satis iuste: Promisit enim nobis in Evangelio Do- minus primum, inquiens, quaerite regnum Dei, et iustitiam eius, et haec omnia adiicientur vobis: Vos autem Dei amorem postponitis, cultum eius negligitis, ludis, commessionibus, ebrietatibus, et ingluvie vacatis, et opus Domini non respicitis, nihil de observantia regulari curatis. Idcirco neglectis spiritualibus, iusto Dei iudicio, etiam tempo- ralia vobis defecerunt: falsa est ergo necessitas, quam fingitis, et insufficiens dispensatio, quam allegatis. Sed forte dicitis. Nos filii rusti- corum non sumus, sed nobilium, nobiles, delicati, et infirmi observan- tiam sutorum, agricultarum, opilionumque servare non possumus. Ieiunia, abstinentia, vigiliae, disciplinae, ac caetera, quae habent exercitia, nobis importabilia sunt, quae imitari non possumus, nec debemus: Quid ergo? Nunquid monachus non es, quia nobilis, quia delicatus, quia tener, quia debilis? Non est, quo te possit contra sanctum Benedictum de- Monachis sancte vi- ventibus ni- hil decriit. Math. 6. Regula D. Benedicti omnibus providit. 244 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis. fendere, qui omni statui, omni gradui, omni aetati, in regula copiose providet: qui delicatis, et infirmis maxima discretionis succurrere Vos ne soli estis ex nobilibus, teneris, et delicatis ordinem professi monasticum? Multi nobilissimi iuvenes Imperatorum, Regum, Ducum, ac Principum filii, in ordine nostro sanctitate, et doctrina, sub regulari observantia militant. S. Benedicti in reg. 58. Nobilissimi et tenerissimi juvenes mul- ti sub regulari D. Be- nedicti ob- servantia militant. S. Bened. in reg. 58. Confiden- tia illa vana est qua quis sperat se consecutu- rum vitam aeternam, neglecta via que ad illam perducit. Coelorum regnum qui- bus modis acquiratur. Act. 14. Sap. 1. Act. 5. Voti tran- sgressor a regno Dei excludetur.

The Pentichus of Johannes Trithemius

...namely, necessity, fittingness, usefulness, and honorable propriety. But you, perjured monk, who are led by will alone, who despise God and the order, feign necessity, display false fittingness, lie about usefulness, and fashion honorable propriety by fraud. Let necessity be evident and manifest; fittingness true; usefulness not private but public; honorable propriety not fictitious but genuine. Otherwise the dispensation will be unjust.

I bring forward nothing for which I should be angry with the Supreme Pontiff in this dispensation; I blame nothing in his actions, since I know well that he was deceived by the false accounts of monks. You are the guilty ones, you the deceitful ones, you who must be marked with iniquity, O perverse monks, wicked apostates, who by lying, deceit, and fraud seek what you despair of obtaining by just prayers.

What necessity presses you to abandon the order and pass into the state of secular life? What fittingness urges you to break what, once promised to God, no one may revoke? What usefulness is there in putting off the monastic habit, abandoning the order, denying your profession, transferring from the monastery, and not merely breaking but utterly casting away the vow made to God before all the saints? Or what honorable propriety is there in a monk dedicated to God returning to the world, breaking faith, committing perjury, perpetrating sacrilege? O transgressors and impious men, how will you ever be able to excuse so unspeakable a presumption?

None of these four accords with your transfer; none of them confirms your dispensation. For what necessity could have driven you to this rashness? What cause for this dismemberment could you have alleged before the Vicar of Christ? The poverty and ruin of the monasteries? But you could quickly have restored this if you lived according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. For you became poor through wicked conduct; by holy living you would again be enriched. Look around you at monasteries brought back to regular observance, how, after extreme poverty, by the Lord’s bounty, they again advance toward their former wealth; and indeed quite justly. For the Lord first promised us in the Gospel, saying, “Seek the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you.” But you put the love of God after other things, neglect his worship, devote yourselves to games, feasts, drunkenness, and gluttony, and do not regard the work of the Lord; you care nothing for regular observance. Therefore, because spiritual things were neglected, by the just judgment of God even temporal things failed you. Thus the necessity you pretend is false, and the dispensation you allege is insufficient.

But perhaps you say: We are not sons of peasants, but of nobles; we are noble, delicate, and weak, and cannot keep the observance of cobblers, farmers, and shepherds. Fasts, abstinence, vigils, disciplines, and the other exercises they have are unbearable to us; we cannot imitate them, nor should we.

What then? Are you not a monk because you are noble, because delicate, because tender, because weak? There is nothing by which you can be defended against Saint Benedict, who in his Rule provides abundantly for every condition, every rank, every age; who provides for the delicate and the weak with the greatest discretion. Are you alone among the noble, tender, and delicate who have professed the monastic order? Many very noble young men, sons of emperors, kings, dukes, and princes, serve in our order in holiness and learning, under regular observance.

234
Regulam habes, ad eius praecerta vitam tuam institue: Nemo a te plus exigit, nec plus requirit. Exercitia monachorum, quae in observatoribus regulae damnas, ipsa docet, ipsa iubet, ipsa praecipit: quae si nolueris imitari; propria te oris tui sen- tentia perimisti: Conversionem quippe morum secundum regulam sancti Benedicti suis professoribus indicit: Ieiunia, abstinentiam, vigiliae, di- sciplinas, obedientiam, patientiam, humilitatem, paupertatem, caete- raque exercitia monasticae disciplinae, quae dura, et gravia iudicas, tam propria sunt regulae, ut sine his nemo monachus dici mereatur; Dic mihi, oro, transgressor voti, et ordinis tui, dic mihi: Vis etiam beate vivere? Speras etiam ad vitam aeternam te posse venire? Respondebis: Stulta est ista, quam facis, interrogatio: Quis non velit beate vivere? Quis ad vitam aeternam non speret venire? Igitur et beate vivere cupio, et ad patriam coelestiem venire me posse confido: si ergo ita est, si beatam vitam te accepturum confidis, cur viam, quae ducit ad illam, deseris, spernis, contemnis? erras miser, Infelix deciperis: ad regnum non venitur, nisi per humilitatem, ad requiem, nisi per laborem, per absti- nentiam, per obedientiam, paupertatem. Ait enim scriptura. Quoniam per multas tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum Dei. Tu autem infelix apostata, qui ordinem reicis, humilitatem spernis, obedientiam renuis, paupertatem odis, patientiam contemnis, qua temeritate tam alta pra- sumis? si os, quod mentitur, occidit animam; nisi poenitentiam egeris, non est tibi pars in regno Christi, et Dei, qui non homini, sed Deo mentiris, qui violas pactum, qui fidem negas, qui vatum religionis Deo factum retractas. Non salvabit te (audeo dicere) dispensatio Romani Pontificis, quam fraudae postulas, mendacio narras, importunis supplica- tionibus extorques. Quatuor enim, quae dispensationem debitam facere diximus, in tuis fraudibus minime concurrisse videntur; Nam illa, quam ab ordine sancto facis, translatio, nec utilis est, nec necessaria, et idcirco incongrua, et inhonesta. In ea enim pro necessitate voluntas, pro utilitate voluptas, pro congruentia carnalitas, pro honestate sup-

You have the Rule; shape your life according to its precepts: no one demands more of you, nor requires more. The exercises of monks, which you condemn in those who observe the Rule, the Rule itself teaches, itself commands, itself enjoins. If you refuse to imitate them, you have destroyed yourself by the sentence of your own mouth. For it imposes upon its professed members the conversion of morals according to the Rule of Saint Benedict: fasting, abstinence, vigils, disciplines, obedience, patience, humility, poverty, and the other exercises of monastic discipline, which you judge hard and burdensome, are so proper to the Rule that without them no one deserves to be called a monk.

Tell me, I beg you, transgressor of your vow and of your order, tell me: do you still wish to live blessedly? Do you still hope that you can come to eternal life? You will answer: “That question you ask is foolish. Who does not wish to live blessedly? Who does not hope to come to eternal life?” Therefore I both desire to live blessedly and trust that I can come to the heavenly homeland. If then this is so, if you trust that you will receive the blessed life, why do you abandon, scorn, and despise the way that leads to it?

You are mistaken, wretched man; unhappy man, you are deceived. One does not come to the kingdom except through humility; to rest, except through labor, through abstinence, through obedience, through poverty. For Scripture says: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.” But you, unhappy apostate, who reject the order, scorn humility, refuse obedience, hate poverty, despise patience: by what rashness do you presume to such heights? If the mouth that lies kills the soul, unless you do penance, you have no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God, you who lie not to man but to God, who violate the covenant, who deny your faith, who take back the vow of religion made to God.

The dispensation of the Roman Pontiff will not save you, I dare say, which you seek by fraud, describe with falsehood, and extort by importunate petitions. For the four things which we said make a due dispensation do not seem in the least to have come together in your frauds. For that transfer which you make from the holy order is neither useful nor necessary, and for that reason is unfitting and dishonorable. In it, indeed, will stands in place of necessity, pleasure in place of usefulness, carnality in place of fitness, and in place of honor [unclear].

235
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 245 ponitur impietas. Haec cine est debita dispensationis tuae occasio? Habeto tibi fraude impetratas literunculas, habeto instrumenta abnegationis, et apostasie; bonum est mihi sub regula pientissimi Patris Benedicti quiescere, in quam, si quid ex fragilitate deliquero, me pium advocationem apud districtum iudicem habere confido, cuius ordinem diligo, veneror, et ea, qua possim sedulitate, custodio. Tu autem quem sis habiturus patronum, nescio; qui ordinem abiicis, omnes sanctos offendis, Deoque publice mentiris. Nam qui post professionem ordinis aliter vivit, quam promisit, hunc regula, ut irrisorem Dei omnipotentis, damnandum fore ostendit. Sic enim habet: Idcirco si aliter fecerit, sciat se damnandum ab eo, quem irridet. Audite haec filii Belial: ordinis desertores attendite, et si ullus sensus in vobis est, horrire: sciat se, inquit, Monachus perversus damnandum ab eo, quem irridet: Quae maior derisio, quod crimen sceleratis, quam promissam Deo fidem negare, votum postponere, illi mentiri, illi famulatum subtrahere, illi sua diripere? Miror, et vehementer quidem, si unquam vel ad horam tam scelerati apostatae, praec confusionem conscientiae, et remorsu synderesis, veram possint habere laetitiam: Sed, ut fatear simpliciter, quod sentio, nullis suasionibus induci possum, ut credam, eos aliquando sine gravissimo conscientiae sua tormento deinceps esse victuros. Probabili enim experimento cognoscimus, quod monachi, de quibus loquimur, post ordinis translationem efficiuntur quasi furiosi, in omne opus turpe proclives, desperati, sine charitate Dei, sine devotione, sine affectu, sine pietate, sine conscientia, sine honestate, saevi, turbati, vecordes, et obstinati, adeo ut de Deo, de regno eius, de purgatorio, de inferno, de morte, de poenitentia, de virtute, de conversatione nihil curent, nihil advertant, nihil audire velint, impleaturque in eis illud sapientis: Impius, cum venerit in profundum malorum, contemptit. Et illud: Semper praesumit saeva perturbata conscientia. Unde tales Apostatae quasi diurno carcere liberati audacter in omne vitium se praecipitant, et temporis brevitatem scelerum magnitudine compensant. Offenduntur, si quis de amore Dei, de studio scripturarum, de honestate vitae coram eis loqui voluerit; Nec mirum, si Dei sermones audire non possint, cui post tam nefandam apostasiam infideles existunt: Oderunt corripientem in porta: Salutis verba non admittunt; poenitentiae sermonem contemnunt: Idcirco dicit vir sapiens: Considera opera Dei, quod nemo possit corriger, quem ille despectit: si Deus aliquem hominem unquam contemnere potuit, illi vel primi sunt, qui post votum infideles ei existunt: Unde propterea despecti a Deo ad poenitentiam raro confugunt; Idcirco damnandos se noverint ab eo, quem irrident: duplici enim sacrilegio rei sunt, quia se Deo, et coenobia Sancto Benedicto inuste auferunt: Et quicumque his dimembrat 246 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis. Apostatae ab ordine raro ad poenitentiam redunt. De reg. iur. in 6. Usurpantes monasteriorum bona districte indicabuntur. tionibus occasionem, favorem, consilium, auxiliumque praestitit, damnum hoc irrecuperabile ordini, et sancto Benedicto fecit: Dicit enim regula Iuris: Qui occasionem damni dat, damnum dedisse videtur. Sancto igitur legislatori monachorum hii tales obnoxii, et ad restitutionem astricti viderint, quemadmodum in extremo Iudicio Deo, et sanctis eius respondeant, quorum bona temporalia sibi, vel aliis inuuste usurpant. Vae autem illis, qui aliena inuuste tollunt, quae nec in hac vita, nec in futura unquam reddere possunt. Vae autem vobis monachis apostatis, et abnegatis, qui ius confunditis, aequitatem despicitis, fidem, et pactum violatis. Contra Abbates, qui Apostasie monachorum suorum, et dimembrationibus monasteriorum non se opponunt. Caput V. Zach. II. Praelati subditorum vi- corrigere negligentes in magno sunt periculo. Luc. 16.

impiety is set. Is this the proper occasion for your dispensation? Keep for yourself the little letters obtained by fraud; keep the documents of denial and apostasy. It is good for me to rest under the rule of most pious Father Benedict; if in it I have done any wrong through frailty, I trust that I have him as a pious advocate before the strict judge, whose order I love, venerate, and keep with whatever diligence I can. But what patron you will have, I do not know, you who cast off the order, offend all the saints, and publicly lie to God.

For whoever, after profession of the order, lives otherwise than he promised, the Rule shows that he will be condemned as a mocker of almighty God. For it says: “Therefore, if he has acted otherwise, let him know that he will be condemned by him whom he mocks.” Hear this, sons of Belial; take heed, deserters of the order, and, if there is any feeling in you, shudder: “let him know,” it says, “that the perverse monk will be condemned by him whom he mocks.” What greater mockery, what crime is more wicked, than to deny the faith promised to God, to set aside the vow, to lie to him, to withdraw service from him, to tear away from him what is his?

I wonder, and indeed greatly, whether such wicked apostates can ever, even for an hour, have true joy, because of the confusion of conscience and the remorse of synderesis. But, to state plainly what I think, I cannot be induced by any arguments to believe that they will ever afterward live without the gravest torment of their own conscience. For by probable experience we know that the monks of whom we speak, after transfer from the order, become almost mad, prone to every shameful work, desperate, without the charity of God, without devotion, without affection, without piety, without conscience, without honor, fierce, disturbed, senseless, and obstinate, so that they care nothing, notice nothing, and wish to hear nothing about God, his kingdom, purgatory, hell, death, repentance, virtue, or their way of life; and that saying of the wise man is fulfilled in them: “When the impious man has come into the depth of evils, he despises.” And this also: “A savage, troubled conscience always presumes.”

Hence such apostates, as if freed from a daytime prison, boldly cast themselves headlong into every vice, and compensate for the shortness of time by the magnitude of their crimes. They are offended if anyone wishes to speak before them of the love of God, the study of the Scriptures, or the honorableness of life. Nor is it any wonder if they cannot hear the words of God, to whom after such unspeakable apostasy they have become faithless. They hate the one who reproves in the gate; they do not admit words of salvation; they despise the sermon of repentance. Therefore the wise man says: “Consider the works of God, that no one can correct him whom he has despised.” If God could ever despise any man, those are among the first who, after their vow, become faithless to him. Therefore, being despised by God, they rarely flee to repentance. Therefore let them know that they are to be condemned by him whom they mock. For they are guilty of a double sacrilege, because they unjustly take themselves from God and their monasteries from Saint Benedict.

And whoever has supplied occasion, favor, counsel, or help for these dismemberments has done this irreparable loss to the order and to Saint Benedict. For the rule of law says: “He who gives occasion for loss is deemed to have caused the loss.” Therefore let such men see how they are liable to the holy lawgiver of monks and bound to restitution, and how they will answer at the Last Judgment to God and his saints, whose temporal goods they unjustly usurp for themselves or for others. But woe to those who unjustly take what belongs to another, which they can never repay either in this life or in the life to come. And woe to you, apostate and denying monks, who confound right, despise equity, and violate faith and covenant.

Against Abbots Who Do Not Oppose the Apostasy of Their Monks and the Dismemberments of Monasteries. Chapter V.

Apostates from the order rarely return to repentance. From the Rule of Law in the Sixth. Those who usurp the goods of monasteries will be judged strictly.

Prelates who neglect to correct the lives of their subjects are in great danger.

236
A vos nunc, o Abbates, mens dirigitur sermo, qui monachorum vestrorum mala studia non corrigitis, qui eorum apostasie consentitis, qui et ipsi cum illis ab ordine apostatatis. O Abba pastor et Idolum, qui ex ovibus lupos, ex monachis seculares facis. Quid respondebis summo Pastori; cum rationem villicationis tuae reddere compulsus fueris? Quid Sancto Benedicto oves suas a te reposcenti dicturus es? Monachos a te requiret, non canonicos: Quid illi tunc respondebis? Monachi ne sunt canonici? Cum venerit dies illa cunctis timenda mortalibus, qua iustus iudex unicuique reddet secundum opera sua, legislator monachorum Benedictus, non dubites, te graviter accusabit, adversum te producit testes omnes monachos veros ordinis sui. Qui unanime clamabunt ad iudicem: Iuste iudex Iesu Christe, qui omnia nости; attende huius apostatae vesaniaem, scelus, sacrilegium, crudelitatem, qui ordinem sanctum destruxit, monachos ad saeculum revocavit: fidem fregit: Votum tibi factum, et nobis inaudita praesumptione violavit. O Miser quid facies tam graviter accusatus? Quem sanctorum invocabis, qui omnes tibi adversarios fecisti? Quo fugies a facie furoris Domini? ad quem confugies? Non erit locus fugiendi, sed ante tribunal Christi stabis, duram accepturus sententiam, nisi hic per poenitentiam, et la- chrimas, faciem Domini praevenire curaveris. Excusationi denegabitur locus, cum accusatus fueris in iudicio, cuncta scientis. Quicquid enim volueris, nihil erit, quia foris accusatus, intus conscientiae testimonio damnandus iudicaberis: Ea, quae divini Iuris sunt, rapis, qui custos eorum positus fueras. Idcirco Dominum audies dicentem, Redde, quod debes: Hoc est, Redde monachos, quos tuae fidei commissi, redde coenobium, quod gubernandum acceptisti, redde fidem, redde votum, redde sanctitatem, redde lucrum, redde meritum, redde honorem; Redde, quod debes. Ego te pastorem ovium mearum constitui, ut eas in sancta

My discourse is now directed to you, O abbots, who do not correct the evil pursuits of your monks, who consent to their apostasy, and who yourselves apostatize with them from the order. O abbot, shepherd and idol, you who make wolves out of sheep, secular men out of monks. What will you answer to the supreme Shepherd when you are compelled to render an account of your stewardship? What will you say to Saint Benedict when he demands his sheep back from you? He will require monks from you, not canons. What then will you answer him? Are monks canons?

When that day comes, to be feared by all mortals, on which the just Judge will repay each one according to his works, Benedict, the lawgiver of monks, do not doubt it, will accuse you gravely; against you he will bring forth as witnesses all the true monks of his order. With one voice they will cry out to the Judge: “Just Judge, Jesus Christ, you who know all things, behold the madness, crime, sacrilege, and cruelty of this apostate, who destroyed the holy order, recalled monks to the world, broke faith, and with unheard-of presumption violated the vow made to you and to us.”

O wretched man, what will you do when so gravely accused? Which of the saints will you invoke, when you have made them all your adversaries? Where will you flee from the face of the Lord’s wrath? To whom will you flee for refuge? There will be no place for flight; rather, you will stand before the tribunal of Christ, about to receive a harsh sentence, unless here, through repentance and tears, you take care to appease the face of the Lord. No room will be granted for excuse when you have been accused in the judgment of him who knows all things. For whatever you may wish, it will be nothing, because, accused outwardly, inwardly by the testimony of conscience you will be judged condemned.

You seize the things that belong to divine right, though you had been appointed their guardian. Therefore you will hear the Lord saying: “Pay back what you owe.” That is: “Give back the monks whom I entrusted to your faith; give back the monastery which you received to govern; give back faith; give back the vow; give back holiness; give back the gain; give back the merit; give back the honor. Pay back what you owe. I appointed you shepherd of my sheep, so that them in holy…”

237
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 247 religione conservares, doceres, instituieres, emendares, corrigeres delinquentes. Tu autem odisti disciplinam, et proiecisti sermones meos retrosum: si videbas furem, currebas cum eo, et cum adulteris portio- nem tuam ponebas: Voluptatibus carnis intentus oves meas non custodisti. Idcirco redde, quod debes: Monachi postquam de seculo ad religionem venerunt, mei iuris facti sunt; et non licet eis ad saeculum ulterioris reverti: Tu autem minister ovium mearum constitutus es, non dominus, nec licebat tibi aliquid mei iuris, quo vis modo alienare, usurpare, vel diripere: Custos mearum rerum eras, non patronus; quaesita servare, dispersa require fideliter debueras: Tu vero mei oblitus, haereditatem meam dissipasti, oves dispersisti, immo ex ovibus beluas, ex servis inimicos, ex federatis infideles fecisti. Nunc ergo redde, quod debes: Ego monachos tibi commisi, quos in sancto proposito debueras conservare; iacentes erigere, infirmos curare: deficientes instaurare, torpentes charitate accendere, negligentes excutere, peccantes arguere, inobedientes corripere, dissolutos restringere, perversos a malis studiis eorum coercere. Sed nihil eorum, quae tuo incumbebant officio, curasti, avaritiae, luxuriae, ingluviaeque deditus, monachos non solum ad saeculum redire permisisti, sed etiam curae pastoralis penitus oblitus, dux, et consors apostasie eorum factus es. Iam itaque redde, quod debes, restitue, quod fidei tuae (ne dicam) perfidia commisi: sed quia reddere non poteris, in carcerem tenebrosum, et opertum mortis caligine proicieris: inde non exiturus, donec reddas debitum, quod nunquam redditurus es: Ibi non solum pro tuis factis poenam recipies, sed etiam pro omnium peccatis, quos tuo regimini commissos corrige re neglexisti: Sic enim sanctus Benedictus dicit in regula. Noverit Abbas culpae pastoris incumbere, si quid minus utilitatis paterfamilias in ovibus suis potuerit invenire. Igitur, o Abba, quicunque es, si sapis, si intelligis, si denique futurum iudicium credis, si tormenta inferni evadere cupis, noli acquiescere monachorum pravis desideriis, dimem brationibus noli consentire sceleratis. Quid prodest tibi in hac vita bre viissima voluptas, pro qua poenas aeternas cogeres recipere? Noli, oro, te sancto Benedicto tantam irrogare iniuriam: noli coenobia illi auferre, quae nec tu, nec omnes parentes tui extruxistis. Sufficiat tibi, quod Abbas es, quia de patrimonio eius vivis, noli ordinem deserere, noli suggestionibus diabolicis consentire, noli monachos tuos saeculares fa- cere, noli monasterium tibi commissum in manus alienorum resignare. Cognosce te hominem morti obnoxium brevis vitae super terram, noli tam perniciosam rem facere; noli hoc scelus committere: noli tam inestimabile sacrilegium perpetratre. Permane in ordine sancto; et pro- positum tuum noli deserere, si ad vitam aeternam desideras pervenire; Ait nanque Dominus: Qui mittit manum suam ad aratrum, et respicit 248 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

The Fifth Book of Johannes Trithemius.

...that you should preserve them in religion, teach them, instruct them, amend them, and correct those who did wrong. But you hated discipline and cast my words behind your back: if you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion. Intent on the pleasures of the flesh, you did not guard my sheep.

Therefore render what you owe. After monks have come from the world to religious life, they have become subject to my right, and it is not lawful for them afterward to return to the world. But you were appointed servant of my sheep, not their lord, and it was not lawful for you in any way you wished to alienate, usurp, or tear away anything belonging to my right. You were guardian of my possessions, not their owner; you ought faithfully to have preserved what had been acquired and sought out what had been scattered. But you, forgetful of me, squandered my inheritance, scattered the sheep, indeed made beasts out of sheep, enemies out of servants, and faithless men out of allies.

Now therefore render what you owe. I entrusted monks to you, whom you ought to have preserved in their holy purpose: to raise up those who had fallen, heal the sick, restore the failing, kindle the sluggish with charity, shake the negligent awake, rebuke sinners, correct the disobedient, restrain the dissolute, and keep the perverse from their evil pursuits. But you cared for none of the things that belonged to your office. Given over to greed, lust, and gluttony, you not only permitted monks to return to the world, but, utterly forgetful of pastoral care, became the leader and partner in their apostasy.

And so now render what you owe; restore what I entrusted to your faith, or rather, not to say, to your faithlessness. But because you will not be able to render it, you will be cast into a dark prison, covered with the gloom of death, never to come out from there until you render the debt, which you will never render. There you will receive punishment not only for your own deeds, but also for the sins of all those whom, though committed to your rule, you neglected to correct. For thus Saint Benedict says in the Rule: “Let the abbot know that the fault of the shepherd falls upon him if the father of the household can find any lack of profit in his sheep.”

Therefore, O abbot, whoever you are, if you are wise, if you understand, if at last you believe in the judgment to come, if you desire to escape the torments of hell, do not yield to the wicked desires of monks; do not consent to criminal dismemberments. What does the briefest pleasure in this life profit you, for which you would be forced to receive eternal punishments? Do not, I beg you, inflict so great an injury on Saint Benedict; do not take away from him monasteries which neither you nor all your parents built. Let it suffice you that you are abbot, because you live from his patrimony. Do not desert the order; do not consent to diabolical suggestions; do not make your monks secular; do not resign the monastery entrusted to you into the hands of strangers.

Recognize that you are a man subject to death, of brief life upon the earth. Do not do so ruinous a thing; do not commit this crime; do not perpetrate so inestimable a sacrilege. Remain in the holy order, and do not desert your purpose if you desire to arrive at eternal life. For the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back...”

238
retro, non est aptus regno Dei: Ecce misisti manum tuam ad stivam, ecce cum Loth de Sodoma egressus es, si resplexeris retro, si propositum tuum corrupseris, si ad saeculum reversus fueris, non es aptus regno Dei, et illud nequaquam mereberis accipere: Si autem in vocazione tua perseveraveris: si voluntatem bonam custodieris; si charitatem Dei in corde habueris, Crede mihi, etiam si in aliquibus negligentiter vixeris, pium ad Deum intercessorem invenies sanctum Benedictum, ob cuius amorem ordinem, cum potuisses, noluitis deserere. Memento obsecro foederis Domini, quod ordinem ingressus, cum illo pepigisti; et noli esse infidelis tuo redemptori, noli votum infringere, noli tam scelerato periurio pactum violare: Considera pactum, conditionem attende, et cave, ne Deo mendax existas: Antequam illi promitteres, liber eras, postquam autem promisisti, non amplius liber, sed servus Dei factus es. Non licet tibi deinceps hanc servitutem spontanee assumptam deserere, non licet tibi, nec alicui, post professionem ad saeculum redire. Quod si propositum tuum corrupseris, si votum negaveris, si ad saeculum reversus fueris, non habebit te in illo gradu Deus, in quo prius habuisset; antequam intrares coenobium: Nam ante religionis ingressum, eras quasi de familia Domini, de subditis illius, et agricultoribus: eras, inquam, creatura Dei, eras famulus, eras servus, sed non eras amicus, misterialis, intimus, secretarius. At postquam monachus factus es, fidelitatem Domino promisisti, ut ei iugiter adhaereres, ut ubi Dominus est, illic sis et tu minister eius. Elegit te in amicum, et (ut ita dixerim) custodem corporis sui, ut in conspectu eius illi semper ministres, eiusque in omnibus perficias voluntatem: Hoc enim promisisti. Si ergo recesseris ab eo, cui te vovisti, si infidelis et voti contemptor inventus fueris, non te habebit de familia sua, ut prius antequam monachus fieres, sed certe fugitivum, infidelem, praevericatorem, periurum, et mendacem. Monachus enim, qui votum suum negat, Christum negat: Dicit enim beatus Hieronymus: Ego, qui videor esse monachus, si propositum meum corrupero, Christum negavi. Vos autem praevericatores, qui, ordine sacro contempto, de monachis facti estis canonici, vos, inquam, propositum vestrum non solum corrupstis, sed, quod sceleratus est, prorsus destruxistis: Nunc ergo aut vos Christum negastis, aut falsum est, quod dicit Hieronymus; sed quia falsum esse non potest, quod vir tantis edocuit, restat vos Christi negatores esse, periuros, et infideles. Utinam, vel sero tandem poenitentiae remedia subiretis, qui in tantis periculis constituti estis: Si Christum negavit, qui monasticum propositum violavit; Qui totum ordinem, omnes sanctos, Deumque fraudat, quid meretur? Si semper ardebit, qui possessiones hominum iniuste occupat, qua poena dignus est, qui bona Deo, et sanctis dicata sibi usurpat? Si iuxta traditionem

looking back is not fit for the kingdom of God. Behold, you have put your hand to the plough; behold, you have gone out with Lot from Sodom. If you look back, if you corrupt your purpose, if you return to the world, you are not fit for the kingdom of God, and you will by no means deserve to receive it. But if you persevere in your calling, if you preserve your good will, if you have the love of God in your heart, believe me: even if in some matters you have lived negligently, you will find Saint Benedict a gracious intercessor with God, for love of whom you were unwilling to abandon the order when you could have done so.

Remember, I beseech you, the covenant of the Lord which, when you entered the order, you made with him; and do not be unfaithful to your Redeemer, do not break your vow, do not violate the pact by so wicked a perjury. Consider the pact, attend to the condition, and beware lest you prove a liar to God. Before you promised him, you were free; but after you promised, you were no longer free, but were made a servant of God. It is not permitted to you henceforth to abandon this servitude voluntarily assumed; it is not permitted to you, nor to anyone, after profession to return to the world.

But if you corrupt your purpose, if you deny your vow, if you return to the world, God will not have you in that rank in which he would formerly have had you before you entered the monastery. For before your entrance into religion, you were as it were of the household of the Lord, among his subjects and laborers. You were, I say, a creature of God; you were a servant, you were a bondsman, but you were not a friend, an attendant of his mysteries, an intimate, a secretary. But after you became a monk, you promised fidelity to the Lord, that you would cling to him continually, so that where the Lord is, there you also, his minister, might be. He chose you as a friend and, so to speak, as guardian of his body, that in his sight you might always minister to him and carry out his will in all things. For this is what you promised.

Therefore, if you withdraw from him to whom you vowed yourself, if you are found unfaithful and a despiser of your vow, he will not have you as one of his household, as before you became a monk, but certainly as a fugitive, an unfaithful man, a transgressor, a perjurer, and a liar. For the monk who denies his vow denies Christ. Blessed Jerome says: “I, who seem to be a monk, if I corrupt my purpose, have denied Christ.”

But you transgressors, who, after despising the sacred order, from monks have become canons, you, I say, have not only corrupted your purpose, but, what is more wicked, have utterly destroyed it. Therefore now either you have denied Christ, or what Jerome says is false. But since what so great a man taught cannot be false, it remains that you are deniers of Christ, perjurers, and unfaithful men. Would that, even late at last, you might take up the remedies of repentance, you who are placed in such great dangers. If he has denied Christ who has violated the monastic purpose, what does he deserve who defrauds the whole order, all the saints, and God? If he who unjustly occupies the possessions of men will burn forever, what punishment is he worthy of who usurps for himself goods dedicated to God and the saints? If according to the tradition

239
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 249 ecclesiasticam, mortaliter peccat, qui domum, vel agrum alterius in- iuste ad usum suum vendicat, quanto crimine reus est, qui domum, et possessiones Dei, et sanctorum in mansiones saecularium commutat? Et si ad restitutionem indebito ablatorum homo homini constringitur, quanto magis Deo, et sancto Benedicto coenobia afferentes ad resti- tutionem tenentur? Si peccatum non remittitur, nisi ablatum restitutur, quando a reatu absolvi poterunt, qui habitationes servorum Dei in usus convertunt alienos? Caenobia enim semel ablata nunquam ad ordinem reducuntur: Vae illis, qui hoc sibi testamentum condere non timuerunt; quod nulla unquam satisfactione poterint revocare. O Monache, o Abba, qui votum vestrum Deo solemniter factum revocatis: Qui habitum sanctae religionis abicitis: qui coenobia sancto Benedicto consecrata in manus clericorum transfertis: Quid accusati coram omnipotenti Deo respondebitis? Forsitan dicetis: Votum in melius commutavimus? Cui hoc persuadebitis? Certe nec Deo, nec hominibus sanis, quippe qui voti differentiam non ignorant: Canonicum vivere, bonum, et sanctum est, si ad eum statum a Deo fuerit vocatus: sin autem ad monasticae professionis gradum vocatus fuerit nunquam ei licebit ad canonicatum descendere: Nemo enim dubitet monachis inferiores esse canonicos: Dic mihi, quisquis es, qui monachorum pravitati cooperator existis, qui eos ab ordine transfers, qui contra Deum, et sanctum Be- nedictum causas defendis; qui apostasie eorum fautor, et patronus ha- beris. Dic ergo: Quid tibi videtur? licet monachis canonicos saeculares fieri? si licitum est, cur dispensationem Romani Pontificis, tantis ex- pensis, laboribus, importunisque precibus impetras? Licta enim dispen- satione non indigent: Sin autem illicitum est: Quis licitum faciet? Di- ispensatio? Vehementer dubito; Vtrum Papa in hac re dispensare possit, vel non possit, non est meum discutere, quem constat plenitudinem potestatis habere. Absit ergo a me, ut autoritati summi Pontificis, vel in minimo derogem? Vicarius enim Christi est, nec licet homini aliquid de illo iudicare. Ergo ne tu securus es, si faciat ille, quod posse videtur? Crede mihi, non es securus, quia causam translationis tuae falsam narrasti: Vicarium Christi fraudulenter decipiisti: Quia et narratio mendax, et supplicatio (ne dicam extorsio) fuit importuna; Denique bulla translationis tuae diligentiter, et caute conscripta te non absolvit ab ordine, nec votum auertit, nec religionem tollit, nec mona- sticum schema deponere consentit. Putas, quod summus Pontifex tuis peccatis suam conscientiam velit inviolare? Legito bullam attente; considera verba; Intentionem dispensantis nota, et, quod etiam post dispen- sationem monachus sis coram Deo, et ecclesia, invenies. Ego enim huius translationis bullam et vidi, et legi, in qua Papa consentit, ut praebendas, et beneficia monachi habeant, et nihilominus praecipit, ut 250 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis. Sancto Benedicto, quod voverint, reddant: Habitum canonicius illis concedit, sed monasticum schema minime tollit; Ecce quam securus es, qui limites indulti transgrederis, qui pro veris falsa fingis, qui Vicario Christi mentiris: qui bullas non minus extorques, quam impetras. In his, quae sunt de iure positivo, dispensatio licitum facit, quod alioquin non licuit, si causa rationabilis exposcat: Votum autem Deo, factum, in lege divina reddere iuberis, a quo Papa sine necessitate te nunquam intendit absolvere: Sed oro, dic mihi; quae est causa translationis tuae. Respondebis forsitan, quod omnes translati sic responderent: Causae multae sunt, quae ad hanc rem me necessario impulserunt. Quae ergo sunt, Paupertas coenobii, incursum vastantium, exactio Principum, malum regimen Abbatum. Hae sunt causae translationis nostrae. Contra rationes falsas, et dispensationes subreptitias, quibus apostatae suam praetendunt tueri apostasiam. Cap. VI.

If the man who unjustly claims another’s house or field for his own use sins mortally, of how great a crime is he guilty who turns the house and possessions of God and the saints into dwellings for secular men? And if a man is bound to make restitution to another man for things unduly taken away, how much more are those who bring monasteries owed to God and Saint Benedict bound to restitution? If a sin is not remitted unless what was taken away is restored, when will those be able to be absolved from guilt who turn the dwellings of God’s servants to alien uses? For monasteries once taken away are never restored to the order. Woe to those who did not fear to establish for themselves this disposition, which they will never be able to revoke by any satisfaction.

O monk, O abbot, you who revoke the vow solemnly made to God; you who cast off the habit of holy religion; you who transfer monasteries consecrated to Saint Benedict into the hands of clerics: what will you answer when accused before almighty God? Perhaps you will say, “We changed our vow for a better one.” Whom will you persuade of this? Certainly neither God nor sound-minded men, since they are not ignorant of the difference between vows. To live as a canon is good and holy, if one has been called by God to that state; but if one has been called to the rank of monastic profession, it will never be lawful for him to descend to a canonry. For no one should doubt that canons are inferior to monks.

Tell me, whoever you are, who are an accomplice in the depravity of monks, who transfer them from their order, who defend causes against God and Saint Benedict, who are regarded as the supporter and patron of their apostasy. Tell me, then: how does it seem to you? Is it lawful for monks to become secular canons? If it is lawful, why do you obtain the dispensation of the Roman pontiff at such great expense, with such labors and importunate prayers? Lawful things have no need of dispensation. But if it is unlawful, who will make it lawful? Dispensation? I greatly doubt it. Whether the pope can dispense in this matter or cannot, it is not mine to discuss, since it is agreed that he has the fullness of power. Far be it from me, then, to detract even in the least from the authority of the supreme pontiff. For he is the vicar of Christ, and it is not lawful for a man to judge anything concerning him.

Are you therefore secure, if he does what he seems able to do? Believe me, you are not secure, because you gave a false account of the reason for your transfer; you fraudulently deceived the vicar of Christ, because both the narrative was false and the supplication, not to call it extortion, was importunate. Finally, the bull of your transfer, carefully and cautiously written, does not absolve you from the order, nor turn aside your vow, nor remove your religious life, nor consent that you lay aside the monastic form. Do you think that the supreme pontiff wishes to stain his conscience with your sins? Read the bull attentively; consider the words; note the intention of the one dispensing, and you will find that even after the dispensation you are a monk before God and the Church. For I have both seen and read the bull of this transfer, in which the pope consents that the monks may have prebends and benefices, and nevertheless commands that they render to Saint Benedict what they have vowed. He grants them the habit of canons, but by no means removes the monastic form.

See how secure you are, you who transgress the limits of the indult, who fabricate falsehoods as truths, who lie to the vicar of Christ, who no less extort bulls than obtain them. In matters that belong to positive law, dispensation makes lawful what otherwise was not lawful, if a reasonable cause requires it. But a vow made to God you are commanded by divine law to pay; from this the pope never intends to absolve you without necessity.

But I ask you, tell me: what is the cause of your transfer? Perhaps you will answer as all those transferred would answer: “There are many causes that necessarily drove me to this matter.” What, then, are they? The poverty of the monastery, the incursion of ravagers, the exaction of princes, the bad governance of abbots. These are the causes of our transfer.

Against the false arguments and surreptitious dispensations by which apostates claim to defend their apostasy. Chapter VI.

240
Facile rumpitur rethe aranearum, sanguine fictum, si quid gravitatis fuerit impositum: Vos autem apostatae pro veris falsa narratis et sub figmento paupertatis vicarium Christi, immo vosmetipsos decipitis. Utinam paupertas vera effet, quam allegatis: utinam de terrena substantia, ut mendaciter fingitis, minus haberetis. Quid paupertatem allegatis, qui divitias maximas possidetis? Quis nesciat statum coenobii S. Albani in temporalibus ante translationem fuisse abundantissimum? Quid dicam de Elvangensi insigni quondam coenobio, cuius divitiae Principi potuissent sufficere? Nunquid Monasterium Sancti Burchardi propter paupertatem transferri potuit, quod multis divitiis semper abundavit? Nunquid propter paupertatem coenobium Cambergense ab ordine dimembrari debuit, quod in hodiernum diem omnia monastica illius provinciae divitiis excedit? Quid dicam de Selszi. Quid de Clingenmonstersi coenobiis, quantum ad mediocritatem pertinet, abundantisimis? Nunquid in eorum translatione paupertas veraciter potuit allegari? O praevericatores ordinis vestri, et voti transgressores, creditis mendacia verba posse latere? Non sunt nobis fallaciae vestrae absconditae; nec divitias, quas negatis, ignoramus: si pauperes essetis, quemadmodum fingitis, non aliis duo, aliis tria, aliis quatuor millia florenorum, et nonnulli amplius pro translatione vestra possetis exponere: Cur ergo pauperateim allegatis, qui pauperes non estis? Cur dicitis vos nihil habere, unde possitis monachi vivere, qui tantas pecuniarum summas, ut canonici sitis, potestis exponere?
