Denique si paupertas coenobiorum vos opprimit, quare reformationem non assumitis? Cur privatas contra regulam possessiones ad communem usum non redigitis? Dum enim

A spider’s web, made as if of blood, is easily broken if any weight is placed on it; but you apostates tell falsehoods for truths, and under the fiction of poverty you deceive the vicar of Christ, indeed you deceive your very selves. Would that the poverty you allege were true; would that, as you mendaciously pretend, you had less earthly substance. Why do you allege poverty, you who possess very great riches? Who does not know that the condition of the monastery of S. Albani in temporal goods before its transfer was most abundant? What shall I say of the once distinguished monastery of Elwangen, whose riches could have sufficed for a prince? Could the monastery of S. Burchard have been transferred because of poverty, when it always abounded in many riches? Ought the monastery of Camberg to have been dismembered from the order because of poverty, when to this day it surpasses all the monastic houses of that province in riches? What shall I say of Selsz? What of the monasteries of Clingenmünster, most abundant as far as moderate measure is concerned? Could poverty truly have been alleged in their transfer?

O betrayers of your order and transgressors of your vow, do you believe that lying words can remain hidden? Your deceits are not hidden from us, nor are we ignorant of the riches that you deny. If you were poor, as you pretend, some of you could not lay out two, others three, others four thousand florins, and some still more, for your transfer. Why, then, do you allege poverty, when you are not poor? Why do you say that you have nothing from which you can live as monks, when you can lay out such great sums of money in order to become canons? Finally, if the poverty of your monasteries oppresses you, why do you not undertake reform? Why do you not bring private possessions, contrary to the Rule, back to common use? For while...

241
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 251 unusquisque marsupium suum diligit, status communitatis cadit. Si autem secundum regulam, quam professi estis, sine proprio viveretis, Domino providente; omnibus abundaretis divitiis: Sed vos, neglectis spiritualibus, voluptati carnis operam impenditis, propterea ad egestatem temporalium rerum devenistis. Haec dixerim in eos, qui propter contemptum spiritualium, et temporalium inopiam patiuntur. Illi vero, qui se ab ordine transtulerunt, si pauperes fuissent, in eo perseverassent: Multis enim expensis, sumptibus, et propinis opus est, quas pauperes nunquam potuissent exponere: Mentiuntur ergo, qui paupertatem in causam translationis assumunt: Quod vero guerras, bella, et vastationes inimicorum in patrocinium dimembrationis suae allegant, quam sit frivolum, et vanum, insufficiens, nemo prudens, qui nesciat. Omnia enim, quae narrant, non minus canonicis, quam monachis possunt esse infesta. Quod autem regimen Abbatum vocat in causam, eorum culpa non immerito ascribitur, quorum electione malus rexor coenobio praeficitur. Nec immerito: Quales Monachi, talis Abbas monachorum. Mali enim monachi, bono Abbatie indigni censentur: Denique si Abbas malus est, quomodo erit Praepositus bonus? Alia vobis fuerant ab expertis quaerenda remedia, quibus in ordine sine querela proficeretis: Sed occasionem quaerit, qui vult ab amico recedere: causas fingit innumerabas, qui se ab ordine cupit dimembrare, iam debitis narrat oneratum coenobium, iam hostilitatis mentitur incommodum. Iam grave fingit dominium, iam ignaviam inculpat praelatorum: Omnia quaerit, omnia fingit, omnia assumit; ut vel ordinem totum vituperet, vel locum pro regulari observantia inhababilem demonstret: si transferatur, inquit, Beattissime Pater, tale coenobium in ecclesiam secularem, maxime cultus inde augetur divinus, facit principes Romanae ecclesiae semper obnoxios, pacem in circuitu populis, et Christiani nominis maximum parabit honorem: O lingua dolosa, o labium mendax, o concinnator doli, o fraudis inventor, o Minister iniquitatis, quam falsa pro veris, quam mala pro bonis, quam sacrilega narras pro sanctis? Reges, et principes monasteria aedificare consueverunt, non etiam destruere, quos mendaciter patronos tuae perfidia non debueras allegare. Nam si laudem Dei quaerunt, nunquam coenobia transferri ab ordine Sancto consentiunt. Sin autem utilitates suas velint attendere, plus de coenobiis quam de collegiatis ecclesiis se norunt lucri accipere. Unde igitur tibi tam inaudita praesumptio, ut coram Vicario Christi rem gratam mentiaris principibus, quam constat illis esse contrariam? Sic agis, sic vicarium Christi decipis, magister mali, machinator doli, inventor mendacii, author sceleris, iniquitatis artifex, qui fraude vivis, qui te impietate munis, qui religionem oppugnas, qui lucris inhias, qui voluptate pasceris, cui de scelere totum, de amore Dei nihil constat? Absit a fidelibus principibus, 252 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

Each man loves his own purse, and the state of the community falls. But if, according to the rule which you have professed, you were to live without private property, with the Lord providing, you would abound in all riches. But you, neglecting spiritual things, devote your efforts to the pleasure of the flesh; for that reason you have come to poverty in temporal goods.

I have said these things against those who suffer want of temporal things because of their contempt for spiritual things. But those who have transferred themselves from the order, if they had been poor, would have remained in it. For many expenses, outlays, and gifts are needed, which the poor could never have furnished. Therefore they lie who take poverty as the reason for their transfer. But as for their alleging wars, battles, and the devastations of enemies in defense of their dismemberment, no prudent man fails to know how frivolous, vain, and insufficient this is. For everything they recount can be no less hostile to canons than to monks.

And as for their calling the rule of abbots the cause, the blame is not undeservedly ascribed to those by whose election a bad ruler is placed over the monastery. Nor undeservedly: as the monks are, so is the abbot of the monks. For bad monks are judged unworthy of a good abbot. Finally, if the abbot is bad, how will the provost be good? Other remedies should have been sought by you from experienced men, by which you might have made progress in the order without complaint. But he who wishes to withdraw from a friend seeks an occasion; he who desires to dismember himself from the order invents countless causes. Now he says the monastery is burdened with debts; now he falsely claims the inconvenience of hostility. Now he invents a harsh lordship; now he blames the sloth of the prelates. He seeks everything, invents everything, assumes everything, so that he may either disparage the whole order or show that the place is unfit for regular observance.

“If such a monastery,” he says, “Most Blessed Father, is transferred into a secular church, divine worship will be greatly increased thereby; it will make princes always devoted to the Roman Church; it will provide peace for the peoples round about and the greatest honor for the Christian name.”

O deceitful tongue, O lying lip, O contriver of fraud, O inventor of deceit, O minister of iniquity, how false are the things you tell as true, how evil the things you tell as good, how sacrilegious the things you tell as holy. Kings and princes have been accustomed to build monasteries, not to destroy them; you ought not deceitfully to have alleged them as patrons of your treachery. For if they seek the praise of God, they never consent that monasteries be transferred from the holy order. But if they wish to consider their own advantages, they know that they receive more profit from monasteries than from collegiate churches.

Whence, then, comes to you such unheard-of presumption, that before the Vicar of Christ you falsely claim as pleasing to princes a thing which is known to be contrary to them? Thus you act, thus you deceive the Vicar of Christ, master of evil, contriver of fraud, inventor of falsehood, author of crime, craftsman of iniquity, you who live by deceit, who fortify yourself with impiety, who attack religion, who gape after profits, who are fed by pleasure, for whom everything rests on crime and nothing on the love of God. Far be it from faithful princes,

242
ut Monasteria Sancto Benedicto auferant, quae devoti quondam eorum progenitores illi construxerunt. Vae tibi, Monache perverse, qui ordini tantam praesumis inferre contumeliam, ut coenobia destruas, quae nec tu, nec parentes tui extruxistis. Vae tibi etiam, qui malis rebus patroncinium contra Deum, et sanctos eius praestas, qui te peccatis alienis involvis, qui linguam vendis, qui pro vili pretio indignationem Dei, et omnium sanctorum incurris. Vae tibi, inquam, monachorum reproborum advocate, qui Deo facis injuriam, qui sanctos eius opere scelerato derides, qui ius aequitatis abnegas, qui monachos ad seculum redire verbis, et factis cohortaris. O quid respondebis omnipotenti Deo, quando omnium a te ratio tuorum operum exigetur, quando a S. Benedicto, velut ordinis sui destructor accusaberis? Quid tunc accusationi sanctorum obiciens? Quid respondebis? Quomodo te excusabis? Quis orationem ad iudicem districtum pro liberatione tui habiturus est? Quem advocationem tunc habere poteris, qui modo contra Deum pravorum advocate es? Utinam saperes, et intelligeres, utinam novissima provideres; alienis peccatis te minime involveres. Sed avaritiae facibus inflammatus, lucra huius vitae tantummodo cogitas, de futuris calamitatibus nihil omnino te sapere manifestas: Idcirco sic ut aves capiuntur laqueo, sic in peccatis tuis, et eorum, quos ab ordine apostatare fecisti, cum non aestimas, capieris. O quam duram sententiam excipient, quorum consilio monachi suum ordinem contempterunt. Magnam in supplicatione utilitatem mentitus es, qui hoc solum intendis, ut honestatem ordinis turpiter evacuare possis: Siccine Dei cultus augetur? Haecce est pax illa in circuitu promissa hominibus? Malos Monachos nunquam bonos canonicos facies: Qui autem malos facit, quid meretur, nisi mercedem malorum? Mali sunt Monachi, qui, ordine contempto, ad seculum revertuntur. Nisi enim mali, et peccatores essent, ordinem sanctum nequaquam desererent: Nemo enim odit bonum, nisi malus; nemo recedit a sancto proposito, quod vovit, nisi perversus: Qui autem perversis patronum se praebet in causis malis, se participem constituit peccatis alienis. Canonicum esse in ecclesia Dei, bonum, et sanctum est: sed monachus pro amore Dei esse maioris perfectionis. Canonicus ad monachos transire tanquam ad altiorem gradum permittitur: sed ad canonicos descendere monachus prohibetur: Nec dispensatio facit licitum, quae falsis narrationibus fuerit impetrata. Si adsit in supplicatione necessitas, in intentione supplicantis integritas, in usu dispensationis honestas, audacter dico, quod Papa cum monacho possit dispensare, ut fiat canonicus, sic tamen ut ab eo, quo Deo nescitur obligatus, sine necessitate non absolvatur: Certus sum etenim, quod summus Pontifex neminem sine evidenti utilitate communi, et necessitate manifesta ab aliqua approbata religione intendit absolvere. Advocati autem Aposta-

that they may take from Saint Benedict the monasteries which their devout ancestors once built for him. Woe to you, perverse monk, who presume to inflict so great an insult on the order that you destroy monasteries which neither you nor your parents built. Woe also to you, who provide patronage in evil matters against God and his saints, who entangle yourself in the sins of others, who sell your tongue, who for a paltry price incur the indignation of God and of all the saints. Woe to you, I say, advocate of reprobate monks, who do injury to God, who mock his saints by a wicked deed, who deny the right of equity, who encourage monks by words and deeds to return to the world.

O what will you answer to almighty God when an account of all your works is demanded from you, when you are accused by Saint Benedict as the destroyer of his order? What will you then set against the accusation of the saints? What will you answer? How will you excuse yourself? Who will make a plea before the strict judge for your deliverance? What advocacy will you then be able to have, you who now are an advocate of the wicked against God? Would that you were wise and understood; would that you foresaw the last things; you would by no means entangle yourself in the sins of others. But inflamed by the torches of greed, you think only of the profits of this life, and show plainly that you have no understanding at all of future calamities. Therefore, just as birds are caught in a snare, so you will be caught, when you do not expect it, in your own sins and in the sins of those whom you have made apostatize from the order.

O how harsh a sentence they will receive by whose counsel monks have despised their order. You have falsely claimed great usefulness in your petition, you who intend this alone: that you may shamefully empty the order of its honor. Is the worship of God increased in this way? Is this that peace promised to men round about? You will never make bad monks into good canons. But he who makes men bad, what does he deserve except the reward of the bad? Bad are the monks who, despising the order, return to the world. For unless they were bad and sinful, they would by no means abandon the holy order. For no one hates the good except a bad man; no one withdraws from the holy purpose which he vowed except a perverse man. And he who offers himself as a patron to the perverse in evil causes makes himself a sharer in the sins of others.

To be a canon in the Church of God is good and holy; but to be a monk for the love of God is of greater perfection. A canon is permitted to pass over to the monks as to a higher degree; but a monk is forbidden to descend to the canons. Nor does a dispensation make lawful what has been obtained by false representations. If there is necessity in the petition, integrity in the intention of the petitioner, and honorableness in the use of the dispensation, I say boldly that the pope can dispense with a monk so that he may become a canon, yet in such a way that he is not, without necessity, released from that by which he is known to be bound to God. For I am certain that the supreme pontiff intends to release no one from any approved religious order without evident common benefit and manifest necessity. But the advocates of aposta-

243
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 253 tarum causas falsas narrant pro veris, necessitatem fingunt; utilitatem mentiuntur, honestatem praetendunt, quam fugiunt. Radix; et causa totius mali huius in sola voluptate, et odio disciplinae fundata est; Quando autem causa narrationis falsa est; dispensatio non liberat, sed damnat impetrantem. Summus Pontifex, auditis narrationibus supplicantium, caute respondere consuevit: si ita est, inquiens, ut narratur, fiat, quod petitur, eo modo, et forma, qua sequitur. Respondet caute, indulget secrete, et sub certis limitibus dispensat: Sed Monachi effrenati, mox ut bullas acceperint, sub constitutis in ea non manent limitibus, sed modum dispensationis transgressuntur, non quid impetraverint, sed quid impetrare voluerint attendentes. O Miseri, O Insensati, O Infelices, quare vos metipsis decipitis? Cur animas vestras voluntarie perditis? Non absolvit vos dispensantis intentio ab eo, quod sancto Benedicto promisistis. Vos autem plus usurpatis vobis, quam Papa concessit, imo totum assumitis sine licentia, quod obtinere illice concupistis. Verum est, quod de quibusdam e vobis dixit quidam adhuc superestes, cum ex commissione Apostolica illis habitum monasticum exuisset. Etsi, inquit, deposuerim eis habitum, tamen iuxta tenorem bullae, adhuc coram Deo monachi sunt. Infelices apostatae, quis liberabit vos de manu Dei viventis? Quis ab incusatione Sancti Benedicti vos poterit defendere? Quid proderit vobis, quod hic sine impetitione facti estis ex monachis canonici, si in extremo iudicio Dei vos cum reprobis deputari contingat? Enimvero nisi translationem vestram omnipotens arbiter approbet, nisi Sanctus Benedictus princeps monachorum consentiat, nulla vos dispensatio excusat: Translatio vestra debitum finem non respicit; et idcirco inexcusabilis erit. Conscientias vestras interrogate, et qua intentione ab ordine recessistis, perpendite: Si amore Dei, si desiderio patriae coelestis, si propter salutem animarum, si ob profectum virtutum, et statum vitae sanctioris, habitum exuistis, approbat Deus factum, quod fecistis: Sed omnibus his intentio vestra fuit contraria, idcirco translation ab ordine merito censetur a voluntate Dei aliena: Nam, ut sine lege viveretis, abiecistis habitum: sine obedientia, sine humilitate, sine paupertate vivere, prima fuit intentio vestra. Non est timor Dei ante oculos vestros: de animarum salute nihil cogitatis; de vita aeterna nihil sapitis: in sola voluptate carnis ambulare concupiscitis: Omnes causae, et rationes, quas in supplicatione narrasti, confictae, et falsae sunt. Quomodo dispensatio legitima erit? Quomodo excusabit vos summi Pontificis authoritas, quam mendacio, fraude, dolo, et importunis precibus circumvenire non timuistis? Quid de vobis sentiendum sit, mores vestri inspecti declarabunt. Ait enim de lupis rapacibus in Evangelio Dominus; Ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos. Nunquam veraciter apud vos mens in Deo laeta conspicitur; nunquam 254 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

They relate false causes as true ones; they invent necessity; they lie about usefulness; they put forward the appearance of honor, which they in fact flee. The root and cause of this whole evil is founded in pleasure alone and in hatred of discipline. But when the cause stated in the petition is false, the dispensation does not free the one who obtained it, but condemns him. The Supreme Pontiff, after hearing the accounts of petitioners, is accustomed to reply cautiously: “If it is as it is related,” he says, “let what is requested be done, in the manner and form that follows.” He replies cautiously, grants indulgence discreetly, and dispenses within fixed limits. But unbridled monks, as soon as they have received the bulls, do not remain within the limits established in them, but transgress the manner of the dispensation, considering not what they have obtained, but what they wished to obtain.

O wretches, O senseless men, O unhappy men, why do you deceive your very selves? Why do you voluntarily destroy your souls? The intention of the one dispensing does not absolve you from what you promised to Saint Benedict. But you claim for yourselves more than the Pope granted; indeed, you take entirely without permission what you unlawfully desired to obtain. What a certain man, still living, said of some of you is true, when by apostolic commission he had stripped them of the monastic habit: “Although,” he said, “I have taken the habit from them, nevertheless, according to the tenor of the bull, they are still monks before God.”

Unhappy apostates, who will deliver you from the hand of the living God? Who will be able to defend you from the accusation of Saint Benedict? What will it profit you that here, without challenge, you have been made canons from monks, if at the final judgment of God you should be numbered with the reprobate? Indeed, unless the almighty judge approves your transfer, unless Saint Benedict, prince of monks, consents, no dispensation excuses you. Your transfer does not look to its proper end, and therefore it will be inexcusable.

Question your consciences, and weigh with what intention you withdrew from the order. If you took off the habit for love of God, from desire for the heavenly homeland, for the salvation of souls, for advancement in virtues and a holier state of life, then God approves the deed you have done. But your intention was contrary to all these things; therefore your transfer from the order is rightly judged alien to the will of God. For you cast off the habit in order to live without law; your first intention was to live without obedience, without humility, without poverty. There is no fear of God before your eyes; you think nothing of the salvation of souls; you understand nothing of eternal life; you desire to walk in the pleasure of the flesh alone. All the causes and reasons that you stated in your petition are fabricated and false. How, then, will the dispensation be legitimate? How will the authority of the Supreme Pontiff excuse you, when you did not fear to circumvent it by lying, fraud, deceit, and importunate prayers?

What is to be thought of you will be made clear when your conduct is examined. For in the Gospel the Lord says of ravening wolves: “By their fruits you shall know them.” Among you a mind truly joyful in God is never seen; never

244
secura conscientia esse potest: sed semper de reatu suo ansia, semper turbulenta, quippe qui ad desperationem incentorem habetis diabolum, cuius instinctu ab ordine recessitis. Hinc est, quod de amore Dei, animatorumque salute nihil estis solliciti: sed terrenis vanitatibus, et desideriis carnalibus intenti, nihil minus, quam vitam aeternam cogitatis: Quo spiritu facta sit in vobis ista translatio, conversatio vestra ostendit: Nam qui spiritu Dei aguntur, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitis, et concupiscentiis: Vos autem non sic: Mox enim ut habitum religionis abiecistis, quasi boves lascivientes a ingo subiectionis absoluti, in omnem turpitudinem, quasi licenter, vos mergitis, omnem honestatem abiicitis, cum vitis pactum, cum virtutibus geritis bellum: Non est charitas Dei in cordibus vestris: misericordiam, et pietatem contemnitis, dilitis vanitatem, et vani facti estis. Mali estis bonis omnibus; peiores mo- nachis pessimi vobis. Non est translatio facta in melius, quae aditum vitis reservat. Amor Dei, et odium fratris in eodem pectore non mo- rantur. Vos autem transgressores voti, ordinis desertores, honestatis inimici, adversarii pietatis, si Deum diligitis, si boni estis, si religionem amatis, cur monachos oditis? Odistis autem eos maxime, qui in ordine perseverant, unde excidistis: Quoniam quos in sua vocazione nunc fortiter stare conspicitis, eorum contra vos in iudicio testimonia for- midatis, Stabunt ergo in districto examine contra vos, laturi testimonium, monachi omnes in sancta conversatione perseverantes, qui universas narrationes, et causas apostasie vestrae, hic iam fraudulentis palliatus sermonibus, falsas, et inanes suis operibus demonstrabunt: Odio habetis ordinis vestri monachos, quia re vera quales vos esse cognoscitis, tales alios esse iudicatis, et bonum, quod in vobis non aspicitis, etiam aliis invidetis: Non miramur cordis vestri adversum monachos insaniam, cum eam iniuriam, et contumeliam cogitamus, quam Deo, et sancto legislatori vestro intulistis: Qui enim Deum non diligit, qui votum illi solemniiter factum infringit, qui habitum religionis abiicit, mirandum non est, si monachos servos eius odit. Omnis namque Apostata ordinis sui adversarius, et contemptor est: Sed oro, sed hortor, sed suadeo omnes, qui ordinem vestrum deseruistis, derelinquite furorem, mitigate rabiem, quiescite sevire in monachos, ne, quos odio nunc persequimini, in iudicio contra vos testes habeatis, et iudices: Agite poenitentiam super hac impietate vestra, dum tempus habetis, ne mors festina vos rapiat imparatos: Nolite, obsecro, cornua malignitatis contra sanctum Benedictum erigere: nolite vestris translationibus ordinem eius vene- randum velle destruere; nolite poenitentiae opportunitatem contemnere, si ad vitam aeternam cupitis pervenire. Vos nullum sancto Benedicto construxistis coenobium, oro, et exhortor, ne ab aliis illi condita in usus saecularium transferatis: Mementote, quam brevis sit vita praesens,

A secure conscience can exist; but it is always anxious over its guilt, always troubled, since you have the devil as instigator toward despair, by whose prompting you withdrew from the order. Hence it is that you are not at all concerned for the love of God and the salvation of souls; but, intent on earthly vanities and carnal desires, you think of nothing less than eternal life. Your way of life shows by what spirit this transfer of state has been made in you. For those who are led by the Spirit of God have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. But you are not so. For as soon as you cast off the habit of religion, like wanton oxen freed from the yoke of subjection, you plunge yourselves into every shameful thing as though it were permitted; you cast aside all honesty; you make a pact with vices and wage war against virtues.

The charity of God is not in your hearts. You despise mercy and piety; you love vanity and have become vain. You are evil to all the good; worse than the worst monks to yourselves. No transfer has been made for the better when it preserves access to vices. Love of God and hatred of one’s brother do not dwell in the same breast. But you, violators of your vow, deserters of the order, enemies of honesty, adversaries of piety, if you love God, if you are good, if you love religion, why do you hate monks? And you hate especially those who persevere in the order from which you have fallen away, because, when you now see them standing firmly in their vocation, you fear their testimony against you at the judgment.

Therefore all monks who persevere in holy conduct will stand against you in the strict examination to bear testimony, and by their works they will show that all the stories and reasons for your apostasy, already cloaked here in deceitful words, are false and empty. You hate the monks of your order because, in truth, judging others to be what you know yourselves to be, you envy in others also the good that you do not see in yourselves. We do not marvel at the madness of your heart against monks when we consider the injury and insult you have offered to God and to your holy lawgiver. For if someone does not love God, if he breaks the vow solemnly made to him, if he casts aside the habit of religion, it is no wonder if he hates monks, his servants. For every apostate is an adversary and despiser of his own order.

But I beg, I exhort, I urge all of you who have deserted your order: abandon your fury, soften your rage, cease to rage against monks, lest those whom you now persecute with hatred become witnesses and judges against you at the judgment. Do penance for this impiety of yours while you have time, lest swift death snatch you away unprepared. Do not, I beseech you, raise the horns of wickedness against Saint Benedict; do not wish, by your transfers, to destroy his venerable order; do not despise the opportunity for penance, if you desire to reach eternal life. You have built no monastery for Saint Benedict; I beg and exhort you not to transfer to secular uses those founded for him by others. Remember how brief this present life is.

245
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 255 quam certa mors, quam districtus Iudex: et nolite cervicibus vestris tam grave sacrilegii onus imponere, quod nulla unquam satisfactio digna poteritis restituere: Nolite sanctum Benedictum vobis concitare adversarium, si amicitiam aliorum sanctorum cupitis invenire: Uno enim offenso, caeterorum nullus amicus erit: Considerate finem illorum, qui se dudum ab ordine sancto transtulerunt, et de vestro similiter metuite: Ubi sunt Abbates, et Monachi, qui olim ab ordine recesserunt, et Monasteria sancti Patris Benedicti in manus saecularium tradiderunt? Omnes aut mortui sunt, aut brevi morientur; Vos etiam, qui adhuc vivitis, qui praecedentium exemplo ab ordine recessistis, cum non putabitis, ad illos ibitis, quorum imitatores estis; Utinam alterius periculo, vestrum timeretis: et dum tempus est, poenitentiam ex toto corde assumeretis. Audivi a multis, quanta mentis amaritudine in mortis articulo plerique ordinis transgressores constricti fuerint, qui de monachis canonici facti fuerunt, vel etiam, qui huiusmodi translationum authores extiterunt: De nullo enim peccato se adeo dolere dicebant, quam de illo, quod se in translationem ordinis consensus dedisse noverant, vel auxilium. Si bona est monasteriorum ab ordine translatio, quare factam morituri doluerunt? Sin autem mala est, quare vos eam facitis, et assummitis? Meminerint omnes, qui coenobia monachorum occupant, quam duro notentur anathemate a beato Papa Gregorio: qui res monasteriorum Deo consecratas in alienos usus convertere non verentur. Sit eis in exemplum Thiergandus Treverorum quondam Archiepiscopus, qui cum coenobium Sancti Andreae in mansionem ab Adriano Papa in urbe Roma suscipisset ab eodem Apostolo, et S. Gregorio in visu tertio monitus, ne habitacula monachorum diutius occuparet, cum inde recedere iussus dissimularet cum omnibus suis dura morte interiit: Si coenobia monachorum occupantes coram Deo securi sint, eorum conscientiae relinquimus. Homo, qui hominis alterius bona sine voluntate ipsius possidet, ad restitutionem tenetur. Qui bona sancti allicius contra eius voluntatem occupat, quid mereatur, ipse consideret. Longo iam satis sermone in transgressores ordinis nostri usi sumus; ad ea, quae restant, nunc veniamus. Quemadmodum his dismembrationibus Monachorum apostatantium obviandum sit. Cap. VII. Q UAMQUAM et animus, et ipsa necessitas contra destructores ordinis nostri copiam offerant invehendi, tamen, cum praesentes non sint, qui exhortationibus ad poenitentiam revocentur, satis in eos dictum existimo. Insensati sunt enim, quicunque ordinis sui honorem tam nefarie opprimunt, quibus non verbis tantum, sed operibus censeo resi- 256 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

how certain death is, how strict the Judge; and do not lay upon your necks so heavy a burden of sacrilege, which you will never be able to make good by any worthy satisfaction. Do not rouse Saint Benedict against yourselves as an adversary, if you desire to find the friendship of the other saints; for if one is offended, none of the others will be your friend. Consider the end of those who long ago transferred themselves from the holy order, and likewise fear for your own. Where are the abbots and monks who once withdrew from the order and handed over the monasteries of the holy Father Benedict into the hands of secular men? All are either dead or will die soon. You also, who are still alive, who have withdrawn from the order after the example of those before you, when you do not expect it, will go to those whose imitators you are. Would that, from another’s danger, you feared your own, and, while there is time, took up repentance with your whole heart.

I have heard from many with what great bitterness of mind, at the point of death, many transgressors of the order were constrained, who from monks had become canons, or who had even been the authors of such transfers. For they said that they grieved over no sin so much as over that one, because they knew they had given consent or help to the transfer of the order. If the transfer of monasteries from the order is good, why did those who were dying grieve that it had been done? But if it is evil, why do you do it and undertake it?

Let all who occupy the monasteries of monks remember with how severe an anathema they are marked by blessed Pope Gregory: those who do not fear to turn the possessions of monasteries consecrated to God to alien uses. Let Thiergandus, once archbishop of Trier, be an example to them. When he had taken the monastery of Saint Andrew as a dwelling from Pope Adrian in the city of Rome, and had been warned in a third vision by the same Apostle and by Saint Gregory not to occupy the dwellings of monks any longer, and, though ordered to depart from there, pretended not to notice, he perished with all his people by a harsh death. Whether those who occupy the monasteries of monks are secure before God, we leave to their own consciences. A man who possesses another man’s goods without his will is bound to restitution. Let him who occupies the goods of any saint against that saint’s will consider what he deserves. We have now used a long enough discourse against the transgressors of our order; let us now come to what remains.

How these dismemberments by apostate monks are to be opposed. Chapter VII.

Although both my spirit and necessity itself offer abundant matter for inveighing against the destroyers of our order, nevertheless, since those are not present who might be called back to repentance by exhortations, I think enough has been said against them. For all who so wickedly oppress the honor of their own order are senseless; and I judge that they must be resisted not only with words, but with deeds [unclear].

246
stendum: Nam, qui Deum non timent, nostris cohortationibus minime acquiscent: Eia nunc Reverendissimi Patres, qui ad decorum nostris capitulariter convenistis, qui pro instauratione eius laboratis, ad mentem reducite pristinum illius statum, et, in quantam sit devolutus calamitatem hoc tempore considerate: Ecce de manibus Sancti Benedicti coenobia rapiuntur: ordo noster ab inimicis Dei in circuitu de- structur; ad saeculum monachi revertuntur; religionem nostram lacerant impii; bonis nostris donantur alieni: Quid loquar de bellis intestinis? Quid referam de malis civilibus? Mirum non est (Patres attendite) si foris confudimur, qui a nostris intus laceramur. Abbates nostri contra disciplinam calcitrant, unitatem ordinis lacerant, statuta capitularum negligent. Visitationes spernunt, censuras vestras, o Patres, contemnunt. Hos, nisi quantocius ad observantiam regularem studetis reducere, non diu sub ordine poteritis retinere: Quid ergo dissimulatis? Quousque dormitis? Quando evigilabitis? Quando pro haereditate Sancti Benedicti pugnabitis? O Patres, Patres, armate vos zelo Dei, ordinis, et disciplinae, quia tempus est; pugnate pro legitimis vestris: Iura sanctitatis defendite; contra translationes ordinis viriliter state. Ecce iam ab ordine nostro in sola provincia Maguntina sex monasteria nostris temporibus translata sunt, et nisi aliter vigilemus, graviora damna in dies patiemur. Sic nobis dissimulantibus (ne dicam torpentibus) ordo paulatim mi- nuitur, quousque tandem ex toto dissipetur: Cur tantis periculis non obviamus? An pereuntibus caeteris, nos de securitate sapienter confi- dimus? Non ne veraciter dixit Poeta. Tua res agitur, paries- cum proximus ardet? Illis heri, nobis simile cras imminebit periculum. Unus- quisque vestrum (non dubito) Monasterium suum diligit; et nullatenus consentiret ab ordine illud transferri, adeo ut non solum praesentem, sed etiam futuram eius felicitatem in annos aeternos cupiat dilatari. Quare ergo non defenditis communiter, quod singulariter timetis amit- tere? Vereor, Patres, ne in hac dissimulatione pessima nostra tenacitas arguatur. Diligimus numquam, et amittimus coenobium, metuimus paucas expensas, et perdimus latas mansiones. Pecuniam modicam non vo- lumus exponere, et abundantissima coenobia patimur ab ordine ad externos transire. Vtilitati communi privata commoda praeponimus, et honorem ordinis conservare non curamus. Multa dicimus, multa pro utili defen- sione ordinis concludimus; sed exponere denarios omnes formidamus: O zelus debilis, quem tenacitas inutilem facit: Si pecuniam pro fra- tribus nostris non tribuimus, quando vitam exponemus? Si pro con- servatione ordinis expensas pauculas non conferimus, quando corpora tribuemus? Qui in modico tenax est: quando liberalis in magno erit? Ad vos nunc loquar, Patres, qui ordini subvenire in tantis periculis constituto dissimulatis: Beatus Benedictus ex pauperibus vos divites

For those who do not fear God will by no means acquiesce in our exhortations. Come now, most reverend Fathers, you who have assembled in chapter for the honor of our order, you who labor for its restoration: recall to mind its former state, and consider into how great a calamity it has fallen in this time. Behold, monasteries are being snatched from the hands of Saint Benedict; our order is being destroyed all around by the enemies of God; monks are returning to the world; the impious tear apart our religious life; strangers are endowed with our goods. What shall I say of internal wars? What shall I report of civil evils? It is no wonder, Fathers, take heed, if we are put to shame from without, since we are torn apart by our own people within.

Our abbots kick against discipline, tear apart the unity of the order, neglect the statutes of chapters. They spurn visitations; they despise your censures, O Fathers. Unless you strive very quickly to bring them back to regular observance, you will not be able to keep them long under the order. Why then do you dissemble? How long will you sleep? When will you awaken? When will you fight for the inheritance of Saint Benedict? O Fathers, Fathers, arm yourselves with zeal for God, for the order, and for discipline, because it is time. Fight for your lawful rights. Defend the rights of holiness; stand manfully against transfers of the order.

Behold, already in our own times, in the province of Mainz alone, six monasteries have been transferred from our order; and unless we watch more carefully, we shall suffer graver losses day by day. Thus, while we dissemble, not to say grow sluggish, the order is gradually diminished, until at last it is entirely scattered. Why do we not meet such great dangers? Or, while the others perish, do we wisely trust in our own security? Did not the poet truly say: “Your own affair is at stake when the neighboring wall is burning”? Yesterday the danger was theirs; tomorrow a like danger will hang over us.

Each one of you, I do not doubt, loves his own monastery, and would by no means consent that it be transferred from the order, so that he desires not only its present happiness but also its future happiness to be prolonged for eternal years. Why then do you not defend in common what each of you fears to lose individually? I fear, Fathers, that in this dissembling our very wicked tenacity is being exposed. We love, and yet we lose, a monastery; we fear a few expenses, and lose spacious dwellings. We are unwilling to lay out a small sum of money, and we allow most abundant monasteries to pass from the order to outsiders. We put private advantages before the common good, and we do not care to preserve the honor of the order. We say many things, we determine many things for the useful defense of the order; but all of us are afraid to spend coins. O feeble zeal, which stinginess renders useless. If we do not give money for our brothers, when shall we lay down our life? If we do not contribute a few expenses for the preservation of the order, when shall we give our bodies? He who is grasping in a small matter: when will he be generous in a great one?

Now I shall speak to you, Fathers, who dissemble while the order has been placed amid such great dangers and needs aid. Blessed Benedict made you rich from poverty.

247
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 257 fecit, iam a vobis eleemosynam petit et (proh pudor) non accipit: Ecce quam multi reperiuntur e nobis (quod venia dixerim) qui substantiam levibus partiuntur personis, avibus, canibusque convivia parant; parentes, et cognatos suis de bonis Monasterii ditant, reliqua in vaus, voluptuosique commessionibus dilapidant. Pauci sunt, qui desolationem ordinis nostri doleant; pauciores de remedio cogitant: paucissimi auxilia subministrant: Siccine sacer ordo Benedicti quondam inter omnes excellentissimus ab hostium incursione defenditur? Evigilate Patres, quando vigilantia prodest, ne sero vos dormitasse poeniteat: Intueamini ordinum aliorum professores, quam sollicite, quam zelose, quam constanter Iura, privilegia, coenobia religionis suae defendant, non parcentes expensis, neque laboribus, neque contributionibus, ut ordines suis in vigore conservent. Nunquid illis inferiores estis? Nunquid mendicantibus pauperioris? si numerum coenobiorum ordinis considerare libeat, plures sumus, si substantiam rerum temporalium, ditores, si vim et authoritatem, indubie praestantiores. Quid nobis deest, (praeter zelum, et constantiam) quod illis adsit? Cur ergo haesitamus? Cur inerti ocio languescimus? Quare pro defensione ordinis nostri non vigilamus? Nescitis, o Patres, quoniam vigilantibus iura subveniunt? Non est bona patientia, qua Dei honor negligitur, cultus illi debitus minuitur, integritas ordinis sancti violatur: Quid dicam? Doletis iam translata coenobia, et tamen non assumitis servare transferenda: Anteponitis privata communibus, idcirco zelus vester parum fructificat: Unusquisque nostrum (ut video) se tutum existimat, si ardentе domo proximi, suus non illico paries incalescat: Sed o fatuitas: sed o merito vituperanda stultitia: Qui tot involutus periculis de securitate sua modo erigitur, post paululum lapsus, se plangere cogetur: Nos ergo Patres, si domus nostras ab incendio illaesas servare cupimus, igni cum aqua, si longe distat, occuramus: Nam si flamma usque ad vicina transire permititur, de remedio nimis tarde cogitatur. Hinc Poeta dicit, Principiis obsta, sero medicina paratur, Dum mala per longas convaluer moras: Pericula dissimulata ex tempore roborantur; et quod in principio curam facile recipit, paulatim incurabile efficitur vulnus. Simul attendite, ne modo neglectus error in immensus successu temporis crescat: quando nullus invenietur, qui se pro ordine constanter opponat: Quod si dixeritis dimembrationis authoribus litem semper fuisse oppositam, cosque nihilominus praevaluisse, illud Virgilianum respondeo. Quoniam tarde venere bubulci. Post firmamentum literarum, lata non facile revocatur sententia. Nam si Pilatus, quod semel scripsit, immutare non voluit: quomodo summus Pontifex Vicarius Christi semel decreatum revocabit? Facilius impeditur sententia, quam revocatur. Ius autem suum, qui negligent, adversario concedit: Vigilandum est omnibus in causa, quae 258 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

has made, now asks alms from you and, shameful to say, does not receive them. Behold how many are found among us, if I may say so with your pardon, who distribute the substance of the monastery to frivolous persons, prepare banquets for birds and dogs, enrich parents and kinsmen from the monastery’s goods, and squander the rest in vain and voluptuous feasts.

Few there are who grieve over the desolation of our order; fewer think about a remedy; very few supply help. Is this how the holy order of Benedict, once most excellent among all, is defended from the enemy’s assault? Wake up, Fathers, while watchfulness is useful, lest too late you repent of having slept. Look at the professors of other orders, how carefully, how zealously, how steadfastly they defend the rights, privileges, and monasteries of their religion, sparing neither expenses nor labors nor contributions, so that they may preserve their orders in their strength.

Are you inferior to them? Are you poorer than the mendicants? If one chooses to consider the number of monasteries of the order, we are more numerous; if the substance of temporal goods, richer; if power and authority, undoubtedly superior. What do we lack, except zeal and constancy, that they possess? Why then do we hesitate? Why do we grow feeble in idle inactivity? Why do we not keep watch for the defense of our order?

Do you not know, O Fathers, that the laws aid those who are watchful? That is not good patience by which God’s honor is neglected, the worship due to him is diminished, and the integrity of the holy order is violated. What shall I say? You grieve over monasteries already transferred, and yet you do not undertake to preserve those that are to be transferred. You put private interests before common ones; therefore your zeal bears little fruit. Each of us, as I see, thinks himself safe if, when his neighbor’s house is burning, his own wall does not at once grow hot. But O folly, O stupidity deservedly to be blamed: he who, wrapped in so many dangers, now raises himself up in confidence of his own security will shortly, once fallen, be compelled to lament.

Therefore, Fathers, if we desire to preserve our houses unharmed from fire, let us meet the fire with water while it is still far away. For if the flame is allowed to pass as far as the neighboring houses, thought is taken for a remedy too late. Hence the poet says: “Resist beginnings; too late is medicine prepared when evils have grown strong through long delays.” Dangers that are ignored gain strength with time, and what at the beginning easily admits a cure gradually becomes an incurable wound.

At the same time take care that an error now neglected does not, in the course of time, grow without measure, when no one will be found who will steadfastly oppose himself for the order. But if you say that litigation was always brought against the authors of the dismemberment, and that they nevertheless prevailed, I answer with that Virgilian saying: “Because the herdsmen came too late.” After the confirmation of letters, a sentence once issued is not easily revoked. For if Pilate was unwilling to change what he had once written, how will the supreme Pontiff, the Vicar of Christ, revoke what has once been decreed? A sentence is more easily prevented than revoked. But he who neglects his own right concedes it to his adversary. All must keep watch in a cause which

248
omnes tangit, quia quod ab uno eripitur, omnibus ablatum iudicatur. Quotiescunque Monasterium ab ordine nostro rapitur, haereditas nostra communis in parte dissipatur: si quis domum, vel agrum tuum occupare tentaverit, coram Iudice mox illum accusas, inhibitionem mox postulas, et donec vincas adversarium, a lите non cessas; Cur ergo nos omnes non facimus in causis ordinis publicis, quod quilibet facit in privatis? Nunquid impossible erit multis, quod facit unus? Nisi for- sitan ubi multitudine, ibi sit et confusio, ut quod diversis committitur, negligentius conservetur. Libenter enim amplectimur, quod sibi proximus esse quilibet iubetur. Sed dum contracto undique corpore, quasi Ericius in nobis nostra revolventes, curam ordinis abiicimus, capti tandem venatorum insidiis: de remedio fugae sero cogitamus. Vos iam igitur Patres Reverendi ea, qua decet benevolentia monacho, qua possim attentione, requiro, ordini vestro prope labenti succurrite, et his di- membrationibus quantocius obviate. Nolite pecuniam necessitatibus tantis praepone: nolite denarios plusquam ordinem amare. Turpis est divi- tiarum custodia, qua non iuvatur in necessitate resp. Quid pro- derit vobis auri insatiabilis cupido, si ordinis vestri tam sancti, tam venerandi, tam gloriosi, praevaleat desolatio? Si antecessores nostri, non maiori cura, quam nos, vigilassent pro ordine; dudum in multis coenobiis nomen religionis nostrae decessisset: Imitemur ergo constantiam, quorum suscepimus haereditatem. Si Deum diligimus, si honorem ordinis amamus, si conservare illum cupimus, de remedio in tempore cogitemus. Conferamus ad conservationem ordinis paucā, ut mereamur multa recipere: expendamus partem, ut possimus totum con- servare: offeramus vilia, ut preciosa valeamus acquirere, demus terrena, ut coelestia valeamus possidere: impendamus pecuniam: impendamus et orationem, quoniam illa homo, hac Deus placatur. Quicquid habemus, ad ius Sancti Patris nostri Benedicti pertinet, cui pro conservatione ordinis dum aliquid impendimus, non nostra damus, sed sua illi red- dimus. Enimvero non solum pro animabus nobis commissis illi sumus obnoxii, sed etiam pro substantia Monasterii ad rationem obligati. Nunquam autem tutior de censu ratio redditur, quam si pecunia in causis Domini opportune exponatur. Si autem pecuniis in necessitate Domini parcitur, de infidelitate famuli suspicio generatur. In exordio huius capituli titulum de modo resistendi dimembrationibus pravorum praescripsimus, quae, ne intactum praeteriisse videamur, breviter expli- cemus. Et quamvis ad me non pertineat ista tractatio, tamen, cum sim eiusdem ordinis vestri alumnus, et amator capituli, non erit (ut reor) vobis onerosa admonitio discipuli: Vestrum est, o Patres, verum a falso discernere, mihi sufficiat, quod sentio, explanasse. Modus autem ob- viandi his monachorum praesumptionibus facile discitur, si ab exemplo

It touches all, because what is snatched from one is judged to have been taken from all. Whenever a monastery is seized from our order, our common inheritance is in part wasted. If anyone has attempted to occupy your house or field, you immediately accuse him before the judge, immediately ask for an injunction, and until you conquer your adversary you do not cease from the lawsuit. Why, then, do we all not do in public causes of the order what each person does in private ones? Will what one man does be impossible for many, unless perhaps where there is a multitude there is also confusion, so that what is entrusted to several is preserved more negligently? For we gladly embrace the command that each man be nearest to himself. But while, with our body drawn in on every side, like a hedgehog, we roll our own affairs about within ourselves and cast aside care for the order, at last, caught by the snares of hunters, we think too late about the remedy of flight.

Therefore now, reverend Fathers, with the goodwill that befits a monk and with all the attention I can, I beg you: come to the aid of your order, which is nearly falling, and oppose these dismemberments as quickly as possible. Do not put money before such necessities; do not love coins more than the order. Shameful is the keeping of riches by which the commonwealth is not helped in necessity. What will an insatiable desire for gold profit you, if the desolation of your order, so holy, so venerable, so glorious, should prevail? If our predecessors had watched over the order with no greater care than we do, long ago in many monasteries the name of our religion would have perished. Let us therefore imitate the constancy of those whose inheritance we have received. If we love God, if we love the honor of the order, if we desire to preserve it, let us think in time about a remedy. Let us contribute a little to the preservation of the order, that we may deserve to receive much; let us spend a part, that we may be able to preserve the whole; let us offer worthless things, that we may be able to acquire precious ones; let us give earthly things, that we may be able to possess heavenly ones. Let us spend money and also prayer, since by the former man is appeased, by the latter God.

Whatever we have belongs to the right of our holy father Benedict; when we spend anything for the preservation of the order, we do not give him what is ours, but restore to him what is his. Indeed, we are bound to him not only for the souls entrusted to us, but are also obliged to give an account for the substance of the monastery. Yet an account of revenue is never rendered more safely than when money is opportunely expended in the causes of the Lord. But if money is spared in the Lord’s necessity, suspicion is generated of the servant’s unfaithfulness.

At the beginning of this chapter we set down the title concerning the manner of resisting the dismemberments of the wicked; lest we seem to have passed over these matters untouched, let us briefly explain them. And although this treatment does not pertain to me, nevertheless, since I am a foster-son of your same order and a lover of the chapter, the admonition of a disciple will not, as I think, be burdensome to you. It is yours, O Fathers, to distinguish the true from the false; let it suffice for me to have explained what I think. The manner of opposing these presumptions of monks is easily learned, if from the example

249
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 259 in praxim convertatur: Videte ordines caeteros, et ex eorum diligentia, quid vobis faciendum sit, agnoscetis. De suis Procuratores in Urbe Romana constituant, qui malorum principiis viriliter obstinent, et nihil contra ordinem suum convalescere permitunt: Et vos, Patres, nisi simile feceritis, gravia damna in posterum sentietis. Si ergo fieri potest, si placet, eligatur aliquis ex ordine, vir zelosus, devotus, doctus, et expertus, qui non minus favore, quam zelo pugnet, qui publicis commodis sua non praferat, qui labores non fugiat, qui contra commisionem sibi faciendam, nihil sua temeritate attentet, qui procurator ordinis constitutus in urbe, pro eodem semper sollicite invigilet. Credo, si talis haberetur, multa pericula ordinis constitutus in urbe, pro eodem semper sollicite invigilet. Credo, si talis haberetur, multa pericula ordinis praeveniret. Maxima enim providentia est, si procurator in urbe, falsa et ficta denuntiare coram Papa potuerit, quae perversi monachi pro dismembratione sua, ut vera, mentiuntur: Et hoc non magnae difficultatis opus est: Omnes enim causae, quas allegant, formidine, et mendacio plenae sunt. Vicarius autem Christi, qui magis importunitate, quam favore translationes monachorum concedit, cum allegationes eorum diligentia, procuratoris nostri repulsas perspexerit, gaudebit se occasionem invenisse negandi, quod invitus concedesit: Nam et ipse iudicium Domini sui pertimescit: si ergo vigilaremus, defensorem ordinis nostri illum haberemus, et advocatum: sola negligentia nostra arguitur. Sola parcitas damnatur, Contra eos, qui bona Monasteriorum inutiliter consumunt, et ordini vel in modo subvenire contemnunt. Cap. VIII. SED libet iam impetum verborum in eos vertere, qui ordini sancto in tantis necessitatibus, nec in modo dignantur subvenire. Isti sunt Abbates mundani, inutiles, voluptatibus dediti, qui (ut verbis Mantuani utar) neglecto superum cultu, spretoque tonantis imperio, Baccho indulgent, Venerique ministrant: Sacra ferunt auro, numis altaria condunt, Auro vina libant, auro laquearia fulgent: Scorta tegunt gemmis, canibus convivia ponunt: Exuviis inopum culti, ditesque rapinis, Successu elati, superos, Acherontaque rident: Nulla eis de animarum salute cura est, amor Dei nullus; nulla reverentia sanctorum, exercitatio nulla virtutum: Hii sunt Abbates capitulo vestro rebellis, qui statuta negligunt, sanctiones spernunt, regulam contemnunt: Ex abjectis magnificati sunt, sed honorantem ordinem impie contemperunt: S. Benedictus te, o Abba ingrata, sublimavit, divitem te fecit, monachum susceptit, fratrum suorum pastorem constituit. Quare ergo non cognoscis munificentiam legislatoris tui? Quare vicem non rependis beneficiis eius? 260 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

Let it be put into practice: look at the other orders, and from their diligence you will recognize what you must do. They appoint procurators from among their own men in the city of Rome, who vigorously resist the beginnings of evils and allow nothing to gain strength against their order. And you, Fathers, unless you do the same, will suffer serious losses in the future. Therefore, if it can be done, if it is pleasing, let someone be chosen from the order: a zealous, devout, learned, and experienced man, who will fight no less by influence than by zeal, who will not prefer his own interests to the common good, who will not flee labors, who will attempt nothing rashly beyond the commission to be entrusted to him, and who, once appointed procurator of the order in the city, will always keep careful watch on its behalf. I believe that, if such a man were available, he would forestall many dangers to the order.

For it is the greatest foresight if the procurator in the city can denounce before the Pope the false and fictitious allegations which perverse monks falsely present as true for the sake of their own dismemberment. And this is not a work of great difficulty, for all the causes they allege are full of fear and falsehood. But the Vicar of Christ, who grants transfers of monks more because of importunity than out of favor, when he has seen their allegations refuted by the diligence of our procurator, will rejoice that he has found an occasion for denying what he was unwillingly granting. For he too fears the judgment of his Lord. Therefore, if we were watchful, we would have him as defender and advocate of our order. Our negligence alone is accused. Our stinginess alone is condemned.

Against those who uselessly consume the goods of monasteries and disdain to assist the order even in any measure. Chapter VIII.

But now I am pleased to turn the force of my words against those who, amid such great necessities, do not deign to assist the holy order even in any measure. These are worldly abbots, useless men, given over to pleasures, who, to use the words of Mantuan, neglecting the worship of those above and despising the command of the Thunderer, indulge Bacchus and serve Venus. They carry sacred things with gold, build altars with coins; with gold they pour libations of wine, with gold their paneled ceilings gleam. They cover whores with jewels, set banquets before dogs; adorned with the spoils of the poor and enriched by plunder, puffed up by success, they laugh at heaven and Acheron alike.

They have no care at all for the salvation of souls, no love of God, no reverence for the saints, no practice of the virtues. These are the abbots rebellious against your chapter, who neglect the statutes, spurn the sanctions, and despise the Rule. From the rejected they have been raised to greatness, but they impiously despise the order that honored them. Saint Benedict exalted you, ungrateful abbot; he made you rich, received you as a monk, and appointed you shepherd of his brothers. Why, then, do you not acknowledge the generosity of your lawgiver? Why do you not repay his benefits in return?

250
Quid habes, quod de regula eius non acceptisti? Quis tibi commissum dotavit coenobium? Nonne devotio Principum, et eleemosinae fidelium populum? Cur ergo beneficiis tantis ingratus es? Ecce nihil minus, quam observantiam regularem cogitas: disciplinam respuis; Deum spernis, eius praecerta contemnis, et de securitate praesumis. Ecce in avibus coeli contra regulam ludis: ecce in canibus immunditiae contra legem Clericorum venaris: ecce in voluptatibus carnis contra honestatem delectaris: ecce quod turpissimum est, contempto casitatis iuramento, cum meretricibus, et leonibus substantiam sancti Benedicti consumis. Triginta, vel quadraginta nummos auri in balneo non times expendere, et sancto Benedicto vel unum renuis offerre? Mentior, si non novi Abbates, qui plusquam quinquaginta florenos in thermis consumpserunt, equibus nonnulli primi sunt, qui subsidiis capituli resistunt: Alii etiam ex his, qui Observantiales dici volunt, secreti, et quietis impatiens, diu in coenobio non valentes consistere, omnem aestimant occasionem idoneam, qua possunt cum magnis expensis hinc inde transmigrare. Quid dicam de structuris, et curiosis, et superfluis, quae non minus reprehensioni, quam expensis obnoxiae sunt? Picturis ornantur parietes, auro pinnacula fulgent, monumentis fenestrae notantur; clamant ad ianuam pauperes, ordo sacer angustiatus petit auxilium, et nullus dignatur subvenire. O Abba, minister voluptatis, cultor vanitatis, pietatis inimice, qui substantiam Monasterii turpiter effundis, qui auro vina libas, qui ordini tuo subsidium negas, quemadmodum sancto Benedicto rationem villicationis tuae redditurus es? Si dives epulo in inferno sepultus est, quia Lazaro de suo propter Deum auxilium non contulit, ubi sepelietur Abbas, qui aliena suo domino negavit? Si semper ardebit, qui de suo non fecit eleemosynam: quid meretur Abbas, qui fecerit rapinam? Quid habes, o Abba, quod non acceptisti? Omnia enim quae possides, ad ius sancti Benedicti pertinent: Morale autem est omnibus, ut, qui vivet iustitiae subsidio, nulli quod iustum est, audeat denegare: Diffinitio iustitiae est, reddere unicuique quod sibi iure debetur. Nos autem in coenobiis constituti, nihil habemus proprium, sed sub bona fide possidemus alienum: Alienum autem restitutioni censetur obnoxium: Omnia enim, quae ad monachorum substantiationem principes, ac fideles populi coenobiis contulerunt, sancto Benedicto tradidisse memorantur. Si ergo substantiam eius dissipaveris, si quod suum est, illi reddere contempseris; duplici damnationi subiacebis, quippe qui de infidelitate sacrilegus, denegata fide iudicaberis criminosus. Redde igitur unicuique quod suum est: et tibi non usurpaveris, quod tuum non est. Da legislatori tuo, quod iure postulat: da ordini eius auxilium, quo subsistat. Quare non impendis religioni tuae debita subsidia? Quare non reddis illi partem, qui tibi conculit totum? Cur illi negas modicum, a quo multum recipisti? Nunquid

What do you have that you did not receive from his Rule? Who endowed the monastery entrusted to you? Was it not the devotion of princes and the alms of faithful peoples? Why, then, are you ungrateful for such great benefits? See, you think of nothing less than regular observance: you reject discipline; you spurn God, despise his precepts, and presume upon security. See, with the birds of the sky you sport against the Rule; see, with unclean dogs you hunt against the law of clerics; see, in the pleasures of the flesh you delight against decency; see, what is most shameful, despising your oath of chastity, you consume the property of Saint Benedict with prostitutes and pimps. You are not afraid to spend thirty or forty gold coins at the baths, and yet you refuse to offer even one to Saint Benedict? I lie if I have not known abbots who spent more than fifty florins at the hot springs, some of whom are foremost among those who resist the subsidies of the chapter. Others also among those who wish to be called Observant, unable to endure seclusion and quiet, and unable to remain long in the monastery, judge every occasion suitable by which they can migrate here and there at great expense.

What shall I say about buildings, both curious and superfluous, which are liable to blame no less than to expense? Walls are adorned with paintings, pinnacles gleam with gold, windows are marked with monuments; the poor cry out at the door, the sacred order, being in straits, asks for help, and no one deigns to assist. O abbot, servant of pleasure, cultivator of vanity, enemy of piety, you who shamefully pour out the substance of the monastery, you who drink wines from gold, you who deny aid to your order, how will you render an account of your stewardship to Saint Benedict? If the rich glutton was buried in hell because he did not give Lazarus help from his own goods for God’s sake, where will the abbot be buried who denied to his lord what belonged to another? If he who did not give alms from his own goods will burn forever, what does the abbot deserve who has committed robbery?

What do you have, O abbot, that you did not receive? For everything you possess belongs to the right of Saint Benedict. It is a moral principle for all that he who lives by the support of justice should dare to deny no one what is just. The definition of justice is to render to each what is owed to him by right. But we who are established in monasteries have nothing of our own, but possess another’s goods in good faith. What belongs to another is judged liable to restitution. For all things that princes and faithful peoples bestowed on monasteries for the sustenance of monks are remembered as having been handed over to Saint Benedict. If, then, you have squandered his substance, if you have despised rendering to him what is his, you will be subject to a twofold condemnation, since from your unfaithfulness you will be judged sacrilegious, and from your denial of trust, criminal.

Render therefore to each what is his, and do not usurp for yourself what is not yours. Give to your lawgiver what he rightly demands; give aid to his order, that it may subsist. Why do you not spend the subsidies owed to your religion? Why do you not render a part to him who bestowed the whole on you? Why do you deny a little to him from whom you have received much? Surely...

251
Liber Pentichus Ioannis Tritemii. 261 coenobii tui paupertatem allegare poteris, qui tam multa turpiter consumis? Pudet me dicere, quod facere Abbates multi non verentur; qui voluptatibus carnis non tam summersi, quam furiosi, nihil honestatis monasticae costodiunt; nihil turpitudinis mundanae omittunt: Omnia sibi licere existimabant, qui non, quid deceat, sed quid libeat, explorant: Ecce ille monasticam abhorrens quietem, vagis discursibus in mundo quaerit solatium; iste secreti regularis impatiens, pomposus procedit in publicum: alter disciplinam honestatis vituperans, tota die levibus personis conviva ebriosus assidet: hic mansuetudinem sanctorum contemnens, se litigantium causis immiscet: ad tabulam ludens alius resident: alius ad tympanum stolidus saltat: Quid non praesumunt Abbates ambitiosi? Quid voluptatibus transeunt intemptatum? Coenanti famulorum curvantur genua: transeunti ecclesiarum sternuntur tapetia: progrediventem in publicum servorum ingens sequitur copia. Invenies (non mentior) Abbatem inter eos, et qui reformationis nomine gloriantur, cuius tanta sit ambitio, ut Episcopo non velit dici inferior: qui ad mensam cum tanto apparatu resident, ut cuilibet Principi copia vasorum, cibi, potusque varietas, ac ministrantium multitudine possit sufficere: Denique, si procedenti per civitatem, huic dederes obviam, tanta famulorum multitudine vallatum cerneres, ut, non Abbatem, sed Archiepiscopum transire putares: Si pauperes se non fingerent, sed essent, in tanta solemnitate vanitas minime effluerent: Certus enim sum, quod praedam sequitur ista turba, non hominem: De pauperibus praedam invenire quis possit, aut optet? O Abba pastor fugitivus, dispensator bonorum Domini tui ingrate, et infidelis, qui substantiam monasterii tam inutiliter expendis; qui voluptuose, et turpiter vivis. Quis in extremo exame auxiliabitur tui? Quem rationis reddendae procuratorem constitues? Ecce bona sancti Benedicti in voluptate consumis: parentibus tuis inde subvenis: turpibus hominibus munera largiris: adulatoribus tuis dona dividis: ingluviei, et ebrietati die, nocteque inservis. Tu pinguissima terrae comedis, optimaque vina bibis; monachi pauperes in egestate vivunt, fratres humiles panem doloris edunt; oves tibi commissae vilibus pascuntur: O Pastor vane, qui gregem Dominicum negligis, qui necessitates fratrum tuorum contemnis, memento, cui rationem redditurus sis, reminiscere, quam horrendum sit incidere in manus Dei viventis: Qui personam hominis non respicit, qui unicusque iuxta opera sua mercedem rependit: Sed audi consilium meum, et age poenitentiam, et peccata tua eleemosynis redime, imino debiti redditionem absolve, quatenus apud internum iudicem misericordiam merearis invenire. Depone supercilias: fastum abiice, vanitatem dernelinque. Esto Abbas fratrum tuorum secundum regulam; Esto Pastor sollicitudine: Pater charitate. Pasce illos verbo, pasce exemplo, pasce 262 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

Will you be able to plead the poverty of your monastery, you who so shamefully squander so much? I am ashamed to say what many abbots are not ashamed to do: sunk, or rather maddened, in the pleasures of the flesh, they preserve nothing of monastic honor and omit nothing of worldly baseness. They think everything is permitted to them, since they consider not what is fitting, but what pleases them.

See: one, abhorring monastic quiet, seeks comfort in the world by wandering about; another, impatient of the seclusion required by the rule, goes out pompously in public; another, despising honorable discipline, sits all day as a drunken dinner-companion among frivolous people; this one, scorning the meekness of the saints, entangles himself in the lawsuits of litigants; another sits playing at the gaming-board; another foolishly dances to the drum.

What do ambitious abbots not presume to do? What do they leave untried in their pleasures? When they dine, the knees of servants are bent before them; when they pass through churches, carpets are spread beneath them; when they go forward in public, a huge crowd of servants follows. You will find, I am not lying, an abbot among them, even among those who boast in the name of reform, whose ambition is so great that he does not wish to be called inferior to a bishop; who sits at table with such display that the abundance of vessels, the variety of food and drink, and the multitude of attendants would suffice for any prince. In short, if you met him as he proceeded through a city, you would see him surrounded by such a crowd of servants that you would think not an abbot but an archbishop was passing by. If they did not pretend to be poor, but were poor, vanity would by no means pour itself out in such great solemnity. For I am certain that this crowd follows prey, not a man. Who could find prey among the poor, or would wish to?

O abbot, fugitive shepherd, ungrateful and faithless steward of the goods of your Lord, who spend the substance of the monastery so uselessly, who live voluptuously and shamefully: who will help you at the final examination? Whom will you appoint as advocate when you must render your account? Behold, you consume the goods of Saint Benedict in pleasure; from them you aid your relatives; you lavish gifts on base men; you distribute presents to your flatterers; day and night you serve gluttony and drunkenness. You eat the richest things of the earth and drink the best wines; poor monks live in want, humble brothers eat the bread of sorrow; the sheep entrusted to you are fed on worthless fare.

O vain shepherd, who neglect the Lord’s flock, who despise the necessities of your brothers, remember to whom you are going to render an account; call to mind how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God, who does not regard the person of any man, who repays each one according to his works. But hear my counsel: do penance, redeem your sins with alms, indeed discharge the repayment of what is owed, so that before the eternal judge you may deserve to find mercy. Lay aside your arrogance; cast off pride; abandon vanity. Be the abbot of your brothers according to the rule; be a shepherd in solicitude, a father in charity. Feed them by word, feed them by example, feed them...

252
alimento, quorum si unum omniseris, pastor inutilis eris. Nam sine spiritualibus ad aeternam salutem temporalia nihil faciunt: sine auxilio temporalium spiritualia in hac vita diu non subsistunt. Si ergo bonus vis esse pastor, utriusque pastionis curam, spiritualis videlicet, et corporalis tibi noveris esse impositam: Debiti dixeram redditione peccata tua solvenda: Cuius debiti? Illius videlicet, quo S. Benedicto censeris obligatus; Quod est illud; Id totum, quod habes. Ab eo enim habes, quod monachus es; ab eo quod locuplex. Nunc itaque is, a quo haec omnia habes, ad ianuam tuam pulsat; pro necessitate ordinis sui auxilium postulat; minima de maximis, quae tibi commisit, recipere desiderat. Cur bona sua illi denegas? Cur tibi credita; dum exigeris, non illico resignas? Scriptura divina praecipiens dicit: si videris nudum, operi eum; et carnem tuam ne desplexeris: Ecce nudus ordo tuus; ecce lacera clamat religio tua, eleemosinam petit, suum repetit, auxilium quaerit: si ulla in te sunt viscera pietatis, si ulla praecordia dulcedinis, si ulla tui ordinis dilectio, si amor Dei ullus, carnem tuam ne despicias, tantam necessitudinem publicam ne contemnas. Honora eum, qui te prius honoravit; da illi eleemosinam, qui te sublimavit; largire modicum illi, qui te in multis divitem fecit: Quantumcunque illi dederis, non minuitur tibi quicquam, si bonam tantum modo adhibeas voluntatem: modicum dabis, et multum recipies: terrena largiter tribues, et caelestia sperabis. Nec te lateat (quoniam ut vulgo dicitur) quicquid honori subtrahitur, turpitudini reservatur. Dicit enim sententiator Iuris, Hoc tollit fiscus, quod non accipit Christus. Non caret reatu criminis, qui avaritiam praeponit ordini pietatis. Sed quid frustra nitimur! Non habet locum in cordibus pravis sermo pietatis. Qui verba Dei despiciunt, quid mirum, si nostra contemnunt? Multa licet eloquar, multa dicam, egregia suadeam verbis ad contribuendum ordini, rebellis nunquam inclinavero. Enimvero, nisi authoritas vestra, Domini Praesidentes, interveniat, monentis sermo in vanum laborat: Ad officium igitur vestrum pertinet rebellis flectere; vobis committitur inobedientes humiliare, nostrum est vestris sanctionibus humiliter obtemperare. Si ergo cupitis ordinem nostrum a pravorum incursu defendere, curate in primis Abates rebellis ad obedientiam revocare, quia nisi ordinis instauretur unanimitas, facile praevalebit adversariorum impietas. Ait namque in Evangelio Dominus. Omne regnum in seipsum divisum desolabitur; et domus supra domum cadet: Sola divisio confundit ordinem. Liber Pentichus Ioannis Trilemii. 263 Quemadmodum sint cogendi, ad subveniendum ordini Abbates inobedientes et rebelles. Caput IX.

with nourishment; if you omit either of these, you will be a useless shepherd. For without spiritual things, temporal things do nothing toward eternal salvation; without the aid of temporal things, spiritual things do not long subsist in this life. Therefore, if you wish to be a good shepherd, know that the care of both kinds of feeding has been laid upon you, namely spiritual and bodily.

I had said that your sins must be discharged by repayment of a debt. Of what debt? Of that, namely, by which you are deemed bound to St. Benedict. What is that debt? Everything that you have. For from him you have it that you are a monk; from him, that you are wealthy. And now he from whom you have all these things knocks at your door; for the necessity of his order he asks help; he desires to receive back the least part of the very great things he has entrusted to you. Why do you deny him his own goods? Why, when they are demanded of you, do you not at once restore what was entrusted to you?

Divine Scripture commands and says: If you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Behold, your order stands naked; behold, your torn religion cries out, begs alms, asks back what is its own, seeks help. If there are in you any bowels of pity, any heart of sweetness, any love for your order, any love of God, do not despise your own flesh; do not scorn so great a public kinship. Honor him who first honored you; give alms to him who raised you up; bestow a little on him who made you rich in many things. However much you give him, nothing at all is diminished for you, if only you apply a good will: you will give a little and receive much; you will generously bestow earthly things and hope for heavenly things.

Nor should it escape you, since, as is commonly said, whatever is withdrawn from honor is reserved for shame. For the legal maxim says: The treasury takes what Christ does not receive. He is not free from the guilt of crime who sets greed before the order of piety.

But why do we strive in vain? The word of piety has no place in wicked hearts. If they despise the words of God, what wonder if they scorn ours? Though I may speak many things, say many things, urge excellent things with words for contributing to the order, I shall never bend the rebellious man. Indeed, unless your authority, lord presidents, intervenes, the speech of one who admonishes labors in vain. It therefore belongs to your office to bend the rebellious; to you is committed the humbling of the disobedient; ours is humbly to obey your decrees. Therefore, if you desire to defend our order from the assault of the wicked, take care first of all to recall rebellious abbots to obedience, because unless the unity of the order is restored, the impiety of its adversaries will easily prevail. For the Lord says in the Gospel: Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house. Division alone confounds the order.

The Pentichus of Johannes Trithemius.

How disobedient and rebellious abbots are to be compelled to come to the aid of the order. Chapter IX.

253
S1 desit Iudicibus auctoritas cohercendi rebellis, frustra legislatio fiet: Semper enim nitimur in vetitum; et nisi coacti praceptis relucta- mur: Nam ubi non est metus potestatis, conditio Iuris cito contemni- tur. Conservatio ergo legis, timor est potestatis. Ubi autem remissio potestatis dissimulat, vigor Iuris vacillat: Constitutio enim quantum- libet sancta, vel necessaria in oblivionem cito rapitur, si desit aucto- ritas, qua contemptus puniatur. Tolle potestatem, et aliud non erit Respublica, quam plena seditionis confusio. Rustica enim feritas ratione non ducitur, mansuetudine non sedatur. Inter nostrates quoque (Deus emendet) multi sunt Abbates, et monachi rusticis grossiores, bestiis immitiiores, qui ad observantiam mandatorum Dei, et regulae mansue- tudine non flectuntur, exortationibus quantumlibet sanctis nunciam persuadentur. His, si auctoritas praesidentium non obviaverit, nulla unquam obedientia capitis ducerentur: Ob eam causam summi Ponti- fices huius sacratissimi Provincialis capitis fundatores multa nobis opportuna statuerunt remedia; quibus ad subventionem ordinis subjectos capitulo Abbates possimus compellere. Habemus auctoritatem, de pote- state haesitamus? Et quid valet auctoritas sine potestate? Si vultis, or- natissimi Patres, ut apertius dicam, quid de potestate auctoritatis fi- gurare voluerim, dabitis veniam, si pusillanimitatem vestram (ne dicam negligentiam) notavero: Ecce centum viginti septem Abbatias sub no- stro capitulo provinciali constitutas agnovimus, sed non ab omnibus subsidia contributionis debitate accipimus: Quare hoc? Auctoritatem exigendi recipimus: sed potestatem non exercemus. Sponte abIata re- cipimus, inobedientes cogere formidamus. Certus sum etenim, quod multi Abbates nostrae provinciae ad subventionem ordinis nihil con- tribuunt, immo, si requirantur, quasi ex praescriptione contradicunt. Qnid est, quod facimus? Quare diu tam dissimulamus? Sponte cur- renti adhibemus calcaria: iacenti, immo recalcitranti, nec verba quidem apponimus. Hinc statutorum nostrorum contemptus nascitur; auctoritas capituli despicitur: haereditas ordinis undique vastatur. In vos haec re- ferenda sunt, o Patres, qui rebellis in principio domare negligitis. Considerate, quid paritura sit tandem ista dissimulatio; et si ordinem vestrum diligitis, de remedio quantocius cogitate. Debole corpus est, et dissolutioni proximum, quod solatio membrorum suorum destituitur: Ecce de centum viginti septem Abbatibus, quam paucos cernitis in pra- senti capitulo, qui omnes interesse debuerant et statuto. Ubi sunt re- liqui? Ubi omnium procuratores absentium? Pauci ad necessitatem or- Legis con- servatio ti- mor est po- testatis. Auctori- tas sine po- testare nihil valet. Burfelden- sis congre- gatio quot olim Abba- tias tempore auctoris ha- buerit. Rebelles in principio domandi. 264 De statu et ruina monastici ordinis.

If judges lack authority to restrain the rebellious, legislation is made in vain. For we always strive after what is forbidden, and unless compelled we resist commands. For where there is no fear of power, the condition of law is quickly despised. The preservation of law, therefore, is fear of power. But where the relaxation of power looks the other way, the vigor of law totters; for a constitution, however holy or necessary, is quickly snatched into oblivion if authority is lacking by which contempt may be punished.

Take away power, and the commonwealth will be nothing other than a confusion full of sedition. For rustic savagery is not led by reason, nor quieted by gentleness.
